name: MySQL

beginner.content:
What is MySQL?
MySQL is currently the most popular database management system (DBMS) software used for managing databases.
- It is open-source database software which is supported by Oracle Company.
- It is fast, scalable and easy to use database management system.
- Common operations are: insert records, update records, delete records, select records, create tables, drop tables, etc.

What is a Database?
- A database is an application that stores an organized collection of records.
- It can be accessed and managed by the user very easily.
- It allows us to organize data into tables, rows, columns, and indexes to find the relevant information very quickly.
- Each database contains distinct API for performing database operations such as creating, managing, accessing, and searching the data it stores.
- There are many databases available like MySQL, Sybase, Oracle, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, etc.

What is a Table?
A table is where data actually lives inside a database - organized into rows (records) and columns (fields).

expert.content:
RDBMS vs DBMS

MySQL is a Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) - it stores data in related tables (using keys) rather than a single flat file, and enforces relationships/constraints between them.

DBMSRDBMS
Stores data as files, no relationships enforced.Stores data in tables with rows/columns linked by keys.
No constraints like PRIMARY KEY / FOREIGN KEY.Supports PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE constraints.
Example: file systems, flat XML stores.Example: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.

ACID Properties

Every transaction in MySQL (with the InnoDB storage engine) is expected to follow ACID properties - this is a very common interview topic.

PropertyMeaning
AtomicityA transaction is all-or-nothing - either every statement in it commits, or none do.
ConsistencyA transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, never violating constraints.
IsolationConcurrent transactions don't interfere with each other's intermediate state.
DurabilityOnce committed, changes survive even a server crash (written to disk/redo log).

Storage Engines

MySQL lets each table choose a storage engine, which decides how data is stored/retrieved and which features (transactions, locking) are available.

EngineTransactionsRow LockingUse case
InnoDB (default)YesYesGeneral purpose, foreign keys, ACID compliance.
MyISAMNoTable-level onlyRead-heavy, legacy workloads.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What is the difference between DBMS and RDBMS?RDBMS stores data in related tables and enforces keys/constraints; plain DBMS does not.
What does ACID stand for?Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - the guarantees a transaction provides.
Which storage engine does MySQL use by default?InnoDB, since MySQL 5.5 - it supports transactions and row-level locking.
Is MySQL open-source?Yes, it is open-source and currently maintained/supported by Oracle Corporation.

beginner.content:
MySQL follows Client-Server Architecture.

- This model is designed for the end-users called clients to access the resources from a central computer known as a server using network services.
- Here, the clients make requests through a graphical user interface (GUI) or application code, and the server gives back the desired output once the instructions are matched.

Common MySQL Clients:
- MySQL Workbench (GUI tool)
- MySQL command-line client
- Application code using a JDBC/driver connection (e.g. a Java or Node.js app)
codeExamples:
mysql -u root -p
-- connects the command-line CLIENT to the MySQL SERVER

/*
RESULT:
Enter password: ****
Welcome to the MySQL monitor...
mysql>
*/

expert.content:
How a Query Travels: Client to Server

When a client sends a SQL statement, the MySQL server processes it through several internal stages before returning a result.

Client (App / CLI / Workbench)
      |
      |  1. TCP connection + authentication
      v
+----------------------+
|   Connection Layer    |  - Thread per connection, manages auth
+----------------------+
      |
      v
+----------------------+
|   SQL Parser          |  - Checks syntax, builds parse tree
+----------------------+
      |
      v
+----------------------+
|   Optimizer            |  - Chooses indexes, join order, access path
+----------------------+
      |
      v
+----------------------+
|   Executor              |  - Talks to Storage Engine (InnoDB)
+----------------------+
      |
      v
+----------------------+
|   Storage Engine        |  - Reads/writes data & index pages on disk
+----------------------+
      |
      v
   Result Set --------> back to Client

Connection Handling

Each client connection is handled by a dedicated thread on the server. Opening a connection is relatively expensive (TCP handshake + authentication), which is why applications use connection pooling instead of opening a new connection per query.

Without PoolingWith Pooling
New TCP + auth handshake for every query.Connections are reused from a pre-created pool.
High latency under load, connection exhaustion risk.Lower latency, predictable resource usage.

Query Cache / Buffer Pool (InnoDB)

InnoDB keeps frequently accessed data and index pages in memory in the Buffer Pool so repeated reads avoid disk I/O. This is the single biggest performance lever for read-heavy workloads.

Replication (Basics)

In production, MySQL is often set up with one primary (master) server that handles writes, and one or more replica servers that receive a copy of the data for read scaling and failover.

        writes
Client --------> [ Primary ]
                      |
                bin-log stream
                      v
              [ Replica 1 ]   [ Replica 2 ]
                  ^                 ^
                  |__ reads ________|
                    (Clients)

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What architecture does MySQL follow?Client-Server architecture - clients send SQL requests over the network, the server processes and returns results.
What happens inside the server when a query runs?Connection layer -> Parser -> Optimizer -> Executor -> Storage Engine -> Result set.
Why use connection pooling?Opening a raw connection is expensive (handshake + auth); pooling reuses connections to cut latency and resource use.
What is the InnoDB buffer pool?An in-memory cache of data/index pages that avoids repeated disk I/O for frequently accessed rows.

beginner.content:
What is a Data Type?
A Data Type specifies a particular type of data, like integer, floating points, Boolean, etc.
- It identifies the possible values for that type, the operations that can be performed on that type, and the way the values are stored.
- In MySQL, each table column has a specific data type (e.g. INT, VARCHAR, DATE).

1. WHERE clause

Used with SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE to filter which rows the operation applies to.

Syntax: SELECT * FROM student WHERE condition;

2. DISTINCT clause

Removes duplicate rows from the result and returns only unique values. Only used with SELECT.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM student;

/*
RESULT:
+--------+
| city   |
+--------+
| pune   |
| mumbai |
+--------+
*/

beginner.content:
3. FROM clause

Specifies which table (or tables, via JOIN) to select records from. It always follows the column list in a SELECT statement.
codeExamples: SELECT name FROM student;

beginner.content:
4. ORDER BY clause

Sorts the result set in ascending (ASC, default) or descending (DESC) order.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM student WHERE city = 'pune' ORDER BY salary DESC;

/*
RESULT:
+----+--------+------+--------+
| id | name   | city | salary |
+----+--------+------+--------+
|  3 | Rohan  | pune | 45000  |
|  1 | Aditi  | pune | 30000  |
+----+--------+------+--------+
*/

expert.content:
Choosing the Right Data Type: Storage & Precision Tradeoffs

Picking the smallest/most precise data type that fits your data saves storage and speeds up indexes.

TypeStorageNotes
TINYINT1 byteRange -128 to 127 (or 0-255 unsigned) - good for flags/status codes.
INT4 bytesStandard integer, ~ +/-2.1 billion range.
BIGINT8 bytesUse for very large IDs (e.g. distributed system IDs).
FLOAT / DOUBLE4 / 8 bytesApproximate - never use for money (rounding errors).
DECIMAL(p,s)VariableExact precision - correct choice for currency/financial data.
VARCHAR(n)n+1 or n+2 bytesVariable-length, stores only what's used.
CHAR(n)n bytes (fixed)Fixed-length, padded - faster for fixed-size codes (e.g. country code).

Logical Clause Execution Order

SQL is written in one order (SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ...) but the MySQL engine logically executes clauses in a different order. Understanding this explains why you can't reference a SELECT alias in WHERE, but you can in ORDER BY.

1. FROM        -- pick base table(s), resolve JOINs
2. WHERE       -- filter individual rows (no aggregates allowed)
3. GROUP BY    -- group filtered rows into buckets
4. HAVING      -- filter groups (aggregates allowed here)
5. SELECT      -- compute final columns/expressions/aliases
6. ORDER BY    -- sort the final result (aliases allowed)
7. LIMIT       -- cut down to requested row count
codeExamples:
SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM student
WHERE salary > 20000        -- step 2: row filter, before grouping
GROUP BY city                -- step 3: group rows
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1          -- step 4: filter groups
ORDER BY total DESC          -- step 6: can use alias "total" here
LIMIT 5;                     -- step 7

/*
RESULT:
+--------+-------+
| city   | total |
+--------+-------+
| pune   |     3 |
| mumbai |     2 |
+--------+-------+
*/

expert.content:
WHERE vs HAVING

WHEREHAVING
Filters individual rows before grouping.Filters groups after GROUP BY / aggregation.
Cannot use aggregate functions like COUNT(), SUM().Designed to use aggregate functions.
Executes earlier (logical step 2).Executes later (logical step 4).

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Why prefer DECIMAL over FLOAT for money?DECIMAL stores exact fixed-point values; FLOAT/DOUBLE are binary approximations that cause rounding errors.
What is the logical order of SQL clause execution?FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT.
Why can't you filter on an aggregate in WHERE?WHERE runs before grouping/aggregation happens, so aggregate values don't exist yet - use HAVING instead.
Difference between CHAR and VARCHAR?CHAR is fixed-length (padded with spaces), VARCHAR is variable-length and stores only the actual data used.

beginner.content:
1. Primary Key

- A primary key is used to identify each record in a table uniquely.
- It cannot be NULL or empty.
- A table can have only one primary key.
- It always contains a unique value in that column.

2. Foreign Key

- A foreign key is used to link two tables together. It is also known as the referencing key.
- A foreign key column in one table refers to the primary key column of another table.

3. Aggregate Functions - the basics

Aggregate functions calculate a single value from a set of rows.
- COUNT() returns the number of rows matching a condition.
- MIN() / MAX() return the smallest / largest value in a column.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(emp_name) FROM employees;
SELECT MIN(income) AS Minimum_Income FROM employees;

/*
RESULT:
+-------------------+
| COUNT(emp_name)   |
+-------------------+
|                 25 |
+-------------------+

+-----------------+
| Minimum_Income  |
+-----------------+
|          18000  |
+-----------------+
*/

expert.content:
Primary Key vs Foreign Key vs Unique Key

student table                      orders table
+----+-------+                     +----------+------------+
| id | name  |  <--- referenced --- | order_id | student_id |
+----+-------+     by foreign key   +----------+------------+
| PK |       |                     |    PK    |     FK      |
+----+-------+                     +----------+------------+
"id" is UNIQUE + NOT NULL           "student_id" must exist
in student (Primary Key)            in student.id (Foreign Key)
KeyPurposeNULL allowed?Count per table
Primary KeyUniquely identifies each row.NoOnly one (can be composite).
Foreign KeyLinks to another table's primary key, enforces referential integrity.YesMany allowed.
Unique KeyEnsures column values are distinct (not necessarily the row identifier).Yes (one NULL allowed)Many allowed.

Composite Keys

A composite key is a primary (or unique) key made up of two or more columns together - used when no single column is unique on its own.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE enrollment (
  student_id INT,
  course_id INT,
  enrolled_on DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)   -- composite key
);
-- Same student can enroll in many courses, and vice versa,
-- but the SAME (student_id, course_id) pair cannot repeat.

expert.content:
Aggregate Functions with GROUP BY - Edge Cases

Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) are usually paired with GROUP BY. A common pitfall: NULL values are ignored by aggregate functions except COUNT(*).

FunctionBehavior with NULL
COUNT(*)Counts all rows, including ones with NULL columns.
COUNT(column)Counts only rows where column IS NOT NULL.
SUM(column) / AVG(column)NULL values are skipped, not treated as 0.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS total_emp, AVG(income) AS avg_income
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;

/*
RESULT:
+---------+-----------+-------------+
| dept_id | total_emp | avg_income  |
+---------+-----------+-------------+
|       1 |         5 |    42000.00 |
|       3 |         4 |    38500.00 |
+---------+-----------+-------------+
*/

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Can a table have more than one primary key?No, only one primary key per table, though it can span multiple columns (composite key).
Difference between Primary Key and Unique Key?Primary key disallows NULL and there's only one per table; Unique key allows multiple NULLs (in MySQL, NULL is never equal to NULL) and a table can have several.
Does COUNT(column) count NULL values?No - COUNT(column) skips NULLs; only COUNT(*) counts every row regardless of NULLs.
What is a composite key?A primary/unique key formed from two or more columns combined, used when no single column is unique.

beginner.content:
SQL commands are grouped into 4 categories based on what they do:



1. DDL (Data Definition Language) - defines structure: CREATE, ALTER, DROP
2. DML (Data Manipulation Language) - works with data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
3. DCL (Data Control Language) - manages permissions: GRANT, REVOKE
4. TCL (Transaction Control Language) - manages transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK
DDL example - creating structure
DML example - working with data
DCL example - controlling access
codeExamples:
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON school.student TO 'app_user'@'localhost';
REVOKE INSERT ON school.student FROM 'app_user'@'localhost';

beginner.content: TCL example - controlling a transaction

expert.content:
1. DDL Statements
DDL is short name of Data Definition Language, which deals with database schemas and descriptions of how the data should reside in the database.

Command Description
CREATE Used to create a database or table.
ALTER Alters the structure of the existing database or table.
DROP Deletes objects from the database.
TRUNCATE Removes all records from a table and frees allocated space.
COMMENT Adds comments to the data dictionary.
RENAME Renames an existing database object.

2. DML Statements
DML is short name of Data Manipulation Language which deals with data manipulation and includes most common SQL statements such SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, etc., and it is used to store, modify, retrieve, delete and update data in a database.
Command Description
SELECT Retrieve data from a database.
INSERT Insert data into a table.
UPDATE Updates existing data within a table.
DELETE Deletes records from a database table.
MERGE Not available in MySQL (Oracle/standard SQL). MySQL uses INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE or REPLACE for upserts.
CALL Calls a stored procedure (in MySQL these are written in its own procedural SQL; PL/SQL is Oracle).
EXPLAIN (MySQL has no EXPLAIN PLAN - that is Oracle) Shows interpretation of the data access path.
LOCK TABLE Used for concurrency control.

3. DCL Statements
DCL is short name of Data Control Language which includes commands such as GRANT and mostly concerned with rights, permissions and other controls of the database system.
Command Description
GRANT Allows users access privileges to the database.
REVOKE Withdraws user access privileges previously granted using the GRANT command.

4. TCL Statements
TCL is short name of Transaction Control Language which deals with a transaction within a database.
Command Description
COMMIT Commits a transaction.
ROLLBACK Rolls back a transaction if an error occurs.
SAVEPOINT Creates rollback points within a transaction.
SET TRANSACTION Specifies characteristics of a transaction.

DDL vs DML vs DCL vs TCL - Quick Comparison

CategoryPurposeAuto-committed?Example
DDLDefines/alters schema structure.Yes - implicit commit.CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE
DMLManipulates row data.No - part of a transaction.INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT
DCLManages permissions/access.Yes - implicit commit.GRANT, REVOKE
TCLControls DML transactions.N/A - this IS the commit control.COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT

Key gotcha: DDL statements in MySQL cause an implicit COMMIT - so you cannot ROLLBACK a CREATE/ALTER/DROP once it has run, even inside a transaction.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
What are the 4 categories of SQL commands?DDL (structure), DML (data), DCL (permissions), TCL (transactions).
Is TRUNCATE DDL or DML?DDL - it resets the table and cannot be rolled back like DELETE can (in most engines).
Why can't you ROLLBACK after a CREATE TABLE in the same transaction?DDL statements cause an implicit COMMIT in MySQL, ending the current transaction early.
What's the difference between GRANT/REVOKE and COMMIT/ROLLBACK?GRANT/REVOKE (DCL) manage who can access data; COMMIT/ROLLBACK (TCL) manage whether pending data changes are saved or undone.

beginner.content:
1. CREATE TABLE

Creates a new table with the given columns and their data types.

Syntax: CREATE TABLE table_name (column_name column_type);
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE User (
  id INT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  FirstName VARCHAR(255),
  City VARCHAR(255),
  Salary VARCHAR(255),
  PRIMARY KEY(id)
);

/*
RESULT:
Query OK, 0 rows affected
*/

beginner.content:
2. INSERT INTO

Adds new row(s) of data into a table.

Syntax: INSERT INTO table_name (column1, column2, ...) VALUES (value1, value2, ...);

3. SELECT

Retrieves data from a table.

Syntax: SELECT field_name1, field_name2 FROM table_name [WHERE condition];

4. UPDATE

Modifies existing rows in a table.

Syntax: UPDATE table_name SET column1 = value1 [WHERE condition];

5. DELETE

Removes row(s) from a table. Always use a WHERE clause unless you intend to remove every row.

Syntax: DELETE FROM table_name WHERE condition;

expert.content:
ALTER TABLE - Add, Drop, Modify Columns

ALTER TABLE changes the structure of an existing table without dropping and recreating it.

Table Alter (Add, Drop, Modify)
Add Column
ALTER TABLE table_name ADD column_name datatype;

Drop Column
ALTER TABLE table_name DROP column_name;

Modify Column
ALTER TABLE table_name MODIFY column_name datatype;

Constraints on Columns

Constraints enforce rules on the data a column can hold.

ConstraintEffect
NOT NULLColumn cannot store NULL values.
UNIQUEAll values in the column must be distinct.
DEFAULTSets a fallback value when none is provided.
CHECKValidates values against a boolean condition.
AUTO_INCREMENTGenerates sequential numeric values automatically.

Indexes

An index speeds up SELECT/WHERE lookups on a column at the cost of slightly slower writes (the index must also be updated).
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_city ON User(City);

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM User WHERE City = 'pune';

/*
RESULT (EXPLAIN, simplified):
+----+-------+----------+------+---------------+
| id | table | type     | key  | possible_keys |
+----+-------+----------+------+---------------+
|  1 | User  | ref      | idx_city | idx_city  |
+----+-------+----------+------+---------------+
-- "ref" access via idx_city instead of a full table scan
*/

expert.content:
DELETE vs TRUNCATE

Sr. No. DELETE TRUNCATE
1 DELETE command is used to delete specified rows (one or more). TRUNCATE command deletes all rows from a table.
2 It is a DML (Data Manipulation Language) command. It is a DDL (Data Definition Language) command.
3 DELETE command can use a WHERE clause to filter records. TRUNCATE command cannot use a WHERE clause.
4 In DELETE, each row (tuple) is locked before removal. In TRUNCATE, the data page is locked before removing table data.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?DELETE is DML, can use WHERE, can be rolled back; TRUNCATE is DDL, removes all rows, resets AUTO_INCREMENT, cannot be rolled back.
How do you rename a column with ALTER TABLE?ALTER TABLE table_name CHANGE old_name new_name datatype;
Why add an index?To speed up SELECT/WHERE/JOIN lookups by avoiding a full table scan, at the cost of extra write overhead.
What does AUTO_INCREMENT do?Automatically generates the next sequential integer value for a column (typically the primary key) on each INSERT.

beginner.content:
Why Join?

- If we want to retrieve data from multiple tables, we use join queries.
- Using one SELECT statement, we can retrieve data from multiple tables.
- It fetches related records from two or more tables based on a common column.

Common Types of MySQL Joins:
1. INNER JOIN
2. LEFT (OUTER) JOIN
3. RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN
4. FULL (OUTER) JOIN

INNER JOIN - the basics

Returns only the rows that have a match in BOTH tables.

Syntax:
SELECT columns FROM table1
INNER JOIN table2
ON table1.column = table2.column;
codeExamples:
-- students table: id, name
-- marks table:    student_id, score

SELECT s.name, m.score
FROM students s
INNER JOIN marks m
ON s.id = m.student_id;

/*
RESULT (only students who HAVE a marks row):
+-------+-------+
| name  | score |
+-------+-------+
| Aditi |    90 |
| Rohan |    75 |
+-------+-------+
*/

beginner.content:
LEFT JOIN - the basics

Returns ALL rows from the left table, plus matching rows from the right table. Unmatched right-side columns come back as NULL.

Syntax:
SELECT columns FROM table1
LEFT JOIN table2
ON table1.column = table2.column;
codeExamples:
SELECT s.name, m.score
FROM students s
LEFT JOIN marks m
ON s.id = m.student_id;

/*
RESULT (every student, even without a marks row):
+-------+-------+
| name  | score |
+-------+-------+
| Aditi |    90 |
| Rohan |    75 |
| Kabir |  NULL |   -- no matching row in marks
+-------+-------+
*/

expert.content:
Setting up the example tables

Customers Table
create table customers(
  customerid int(10) primary key auto_increment not null,
  customername varchar(32),
  email varchar(32),
  phone varchar(255)
);

Modify Column Size
ALTER TABLE customers
MODIFY phone varchar(255);
Accounts Table
create table accounts(
  customerid int,
  accountsid int primary key auto_increment not null,
  accountstype varchar(10),
  balance int(50),
  foreign key(customerid) references customers(customerid)
);

INNER JOIN

Returns only matching rows from both tables.

   customers          accounts
  +---------+        +---------+
  |    A    |        |    B    |
  |   ___   |        |   ___   |
  |  /   \  |        |  /   \  |
  | (  X )--INNER JOIN--( X )  |     result = only the overlap (X)
  |  \___/  |        |  \___/  |
  +---------+        +---------+
describe accounts;

Select customers.customerid,
  customername,
  email,
  accountsid,
  balance
from customers
INNER JOIN accounts
on customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;
codeExamples:
SELECT c.customername, a.balance
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a
ON c.customerid = a.customerid;

/*
RESULT (only customers WITH an account):
+--------------+---------+
| customername | balance |
+--------------+---------+
| Jay Naik     |   25000 |
| Ashok Patil  |   45000 |
+--------------+---------+
*/

expert.content:
LEFT (OUTER) JOIN

Returns all rows from the left-hand table (customers) and only matching rows from accounts. If no match exists, NULL values are returned.

   customers (ALL)     accounts
  +----------------+   +---------+
  |  #########      |   |   ___   |
  |  ##  X  ##------LEFT JOIN--( X )   result = ALL of left + overlap
  |  #########      |   |  \___/  |
  +----------------+   +---------+
Syntax
SELECT columns
FROM table1
LEFT [OUTER] JOIN table2
ON table1.column = table2.column;

Example
select customername, email, accountsid, balance
from customers
left join accounts
on customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;
codeExamples:
SELECT customername, email, accountsid, balance
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN accounts
ON customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;

/*
RESULT (every customer, accounts columns NULL if none):
+---------------+-----------+------------+---------+
| customername  | email     | accountsid | balance |
+---------------+-----------+------------+---------+
| Jay Naik      | jay@x.com |          1 |   25000 |
| Rajaram Patil | ram@x.com |       NULL |    NULL |
+---------------+-----------+------------+---------+
*/

expert.content:
RIGHT (OUTER) JOIN

Returns all rows from the right-hand table (accounts) and only matching rows from customers. If no match exists, NULL values are returned.

Syntax
SELECT columns
FROM table1
RIGHT [OUTER] JOIN table2
ON table1.column = table2.column;

Example
select customername, email, accountsid, balance
from customers
right join accounts
on customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;
codeExamples:
SELECT customername, email, accountsid, balance
FROM customers
RIGHT JOIN accounts
ON customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;

/*
RESULT (every account row, customer columns NULL if orphaned):
+--------------+---------------+------------+---------+
| customername | email         | accountsid | balance |
+--------------+---------------+------------+---------+
| Jay Naik     | jay@x.com     |          1 |   25000 |
| NULL         | NULL          |          7 |    9000 |
+--------------+---------------+------------+---------+
*/

expert.content:
FULL (OUTER) JOIN

MySQL does not directly support FULL OUTER JOIN. It is emulated by combining LEFT JOIN and RIGHT JOIN with UNION (UNION also removes duplicate matching rows).

   customers            accounts
  +----------------+   +----------------+
  |  ############# |   | ############## |
  |  ####  X  ######FULL JOIN###  X  ### |   result = everything, both sides
  |  ############# |   | ############## |
  +----------------+   +----------------+
Syntax / Example
select * from customers left join accounts
on customers.customerid = accounts.customerid
union
select * from customers right join accounts
on customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;
codeExamples:
SELECT *
FROM customers
LEFT JOIN accounts
ON customers.customerid = accounts.customerid

UNION

SELECT *
FROM customers
RIGHT JOIN accounts
ON customers.customerid = accounts.customerid;

/*
RESULT: all customers (even without accounts) + all accounts
(even orphaned ones), each row appearing once.
*/

expert.content:
CROSS JOIN & SELF JOIN

CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product - every row of table1 paired with every row of table2 (no ON condition).
SELF JOIN joins a table to itself, using table aliases, typically to compare rows within the same table (e.g. employee-manager).
codeExamples:
-- CROSS JOIN: 2 sizes x 3 colors = 6 combinations
SELECT s.size, c.color
FROM sizes s
CROSS JOIN colors c;

/*
RESULT:
+------+--------+
| size | color  |
+------+--------+
| S    | Red    |
| S    | Blue   |
| S    | Green  |
| M    | Red    |
| M    | Blue   |
| M    | Green  |
+------+--------+
*/

-- SELF JOIN: find each employee's manager name
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employee e
JOIN employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

/*
RESULT:
+----------+---------+
| employee | manager |
+----------+---------+
| Rohan    | Aditi   |
| Kabir    | Aditi   |
+----------+---------+
*/

expert.content:
Join Performance & Index Tips

TipWhy
Index the join columns (usually the FK).Without an index, MySQL does a full scan of the joined table per outer row.
Join on matching, indexed data types.Implicit type conversion (e.g. INT vs VARCHAR) can silently disable index usage.
Filter early with WHERE on indexed columns.Reduces the row set the optimizer has to join.
Use EXPLAIN to check the join plan.Confirms whether MySQL is using "ref"/"eq_ref" (index) vs "ALL" (full scan).
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN
SELECT c.customername, a.balance
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN accounts a ON c.customerid = a.customerid;

/*
RESULT (simplified):
+----+-------+--------+---------------+
| id | table | type   | key           |
+----+-------+--------+---------------+
|  1 | c     | ALL    | PRIMARY       |
|  1 | a     | ref    | customerid_fk |   <- using index, good
+----+-------+--------+---------------+
*/

expert.content:
Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
Difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables; LEFT JOIN returns all left-table rows plus matches, with NULLs where no match exists.
Does MySQL support FULL OUTER JOIN directly?No - it must be emulated using LEFT JOIN UNION RIGHT JOIN.
What is a SELF JOIN used for?Comparing rows within the same table, e.g. finding an employee's manager from the same employee table.
What does CROSS JOIN produce?The Cartesian product - every row of one table paired with every row of the other, with no ON condition.
How do you speed up a slow JOIN?Index the join columns, avoid implicit type conversions, filter early, and check the plan with EXPLAIN.

beginner.content:
Setup
create table employee( id int(10) primary key auto_increment not null, name varchar(32), salary int);

Finding the Nth highest salary in a table is one of the most common SQL interview questions.

Highest (1st) salary

The simplest case - just sort descending and take the top row.
codeExamples:
SELECT MAX(salary) AS highest_salary FROM employee;

/*
RESULT:
+----------------+
| highest_salary |
+----------------+
|          90000 |
+----------------+
*/

beginner.content:
2nd highest salary - using LIMIT with OFFSET

Sort all salaries descending, skip the first row (OFFSET 1), then take 1 row.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employee
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

/*
RESULT:
+--------+
| salary |
+--------+
|  80000 |
+--------+
*/

expert.content:
Approach 1: Subquery with LIMIT

Sort salaries descending, LIMIT to N rows, then re-sort ascending and take the top - the last of the top-N when sorted descending.

Approach 2: LIMIT with OFFSET (no subquery)

The shorter, more idiomatic MySQL way - LIMIT offset,count skips "offset" rows then returns "count" rows.

Note: use DISTINCT salary, otherwise tied salaries (like Rohan and Kabir both at 80000) will shift the offset incorrectly.
codeExamples:
-- 2nd highest salary
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1,1;
-- first "1" = OFFSET (skip 1 row = the highest), second "1" = fetch only 1 row

/*
RESULT:
+--------+
| salary |
+--------+
|  80000 |
+--------+
*/

expert.content:
Approach 3: DENSE_RANK() window function (MySQL 8.0+)

The most robust and readable approach - correctly handles duplicate/tied salaries because DENSE_RANK() assigns the same rank to ties without skipping the next rank.
codeExamples:
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee
) ranked
WHERE rnk = 2;

/*
RESULT (Rohan and Kabir are tied at rank 1 for 80000 being rank 2
after 90000 - DENSE_RANK gives both 80000 rows rank 2):
+--------+
| salary |
+--------+
|  80000 |
|  80000 |
+--------+
*/

expert.content:
Approach 4: Correlated subquery (COUNT DISTINCT higher salaries)

Works on any MySQL version (pre-8.0 too, no window functions needed). For each salary, count how many DISTINCT salaries are strictly greater; the Nth highest is where that count equals N-1.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employee e1
WHERE (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary)
  FROM employee e2
  WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary
) = 1;   -- 1 = (N-1) for the 2nd highest

/*
RESULT:
+--------+
| salary |
+--------+
|  80000 |
+--------+
*/

expert.content:
Which approach should you use?

ApproachHandles ties correctlyMySQL versionReadability
Subquery + LIMITOnly with DISTINCTAnyMedium
LIMIT OFFSETOnly with DISTINCTAnyHigh (shortest)
DENSE_RANK() window functionYes, naturally8.0+High, most correct
Correlated subquery (COUNT DISTINCT)YesAny (pre-8.0 friendly)Medium, but scales poorly on large tables

Recommendation: use DENSE_RANK() on MySQL 8.0+; fall back to the correlated subquery or DISTINCT + LIMIT OFFSET on older versions.

Interview Questions

QuestionAnswer
How do you find the 2nd highest salary without LIMIT?A correlated subquery: WHERE (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM t WHERE salary > outer.salary) = 1.
Why use DISTINCT when finding Nth highest with LIMIT?Duplicate salary values would otherwise consume extra "slots" and shift the offset, giving a wrong answer.
What's the advantage of DENSE_RANK() over LIMIT/OFFSET?It correctly ranks tied values without gaps or skips, avoiding manual DISTINCT handling.
Difference between RANK() and DENSE_RANK()?RANK() leaves gaps after ties (1,2,2,4); DENSE_RANK() does not (1,2,2,3).

beginner.content:
Introduction

A database is an organised collection of data stored so that programs can store, find, change and protect it reliably. Unlike a loose file, a database adds structure, indexing, concurrency control and crash recovery.
codeExamples:
-- A database groups related tables; here we create one and put one fact in it
CREATE DATABASE school_demo;                 -- new empty database
USE school_demo;                             -- make it the current one
CREATE TABLE student (id INT, name VARCHAR(40));   -- structure for the facts
INSERT INTO student VALUES (1, 'Abaji');      -- store a fact
SELECT * FROM student;                       -- read it back

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | Abaji |
-- +------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Spreadsheets and text files break down when many users write at once, when data must stay consistent after a power cut, or when you must find one row among millions in milliseconds. A database solves sharing, integrity, speed and security together.
codeExamples:
-- Finding one row in a file means scanning it all; a database uses an index
CREATE TABLE big (id INT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO big VALUES (1,'a'),(2,'b'),(3,'c');
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM big WHERE id = 2;      -- shows the optimizer uses the PK, not a scan

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+-------+-------+---------+-------+------+
-- | id | table | type  | key     | ref   | rows |
-- +----+-------+-------+---------+-------+------+
-- |  1 | big   | const | PRIMARY | const |    1 |
-- +----+-------+-------+---------+-------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Every shop checkout, bank transfer, booking and login reads or writes a database. A web request typically opens a connection, runs a few SQL statements inside a transaction and returns.
codeExamples:
-- A typical order write: two facts must be saved together or not at all
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, total DECIMAL(8,2));
START TRANSACTION;                           -- begin an atomic unit
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (101, 499.00);     -- the sale
COMMIT;                                      -- make it permanent and visible
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_saved FROM orders;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | orders_saved |
-- +--------------+
-- |            1 |
-- +--------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Application ──SQL──►  Database Server  ──►  Disk
   (Java/Python)         ┌───────────────┐     ┌────────────┐
                         │ parser        │     │ data files │
                         │ optimizer     │     │ redo/undo  │
                         │ storage engine│     │ binlog     │
                         └───────────────┘     └────────────┘
   Many clients share one consistent copy of the data.

Fresher Notes

  • A database is an organised collection of data stored so that it can be searched, updated and kept consistent by many users at once.
  • Files (CSV, Excel) cannot safely handle concurrent writers, fast lookups or rules like "email must be unique". A database can.
  • Common kinds: relational (MySQL, PostgreSQL), document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis), graph (Neo4j). MySQL is relational.

Worked Example 1

A database holds many tables; the server holds many databases. Inspect that hierarchy.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_schema, COUNT(*) AS tables_count
FROM   information_schema.tables
WHERE  table_schema = 'school'
GROUP  BY table_schema;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_schema | tables_count
-- school       |            1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Data survives a reconnect because it is stored by the server, not the session.
codeExamples:
-- session 1
INSERT INTO school.students VALUES (3,'Moropant');
-- exit, reconnect (session 2)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM school.students;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create a database school, a table students(id, name), insert two rows and read them back.

Practice Exercise 2

List all databases on the server and show which one is currently selected.
codeExamples:
SHOW DATABASES;
SELECT DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Database
-- information_schema
-- mysql
-- performance_schema
-- school
-- sys
-- DATABASE()
-- school

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A database server is a long-running process that owns the data files. Clients never read those files directly: they send commands over a connection, the server parses them, plans them, executes them against pages cached in memory, and writes changes to a log before the data files are updated. This is why a database stays correct when ten users write at once or when the power fails mid-write.
codeExamples:
-- Everything you do goes through the server: ask the server about itself
SELECT @@version AS server_version, @@datadir AS data_directory, @@port AS port;
SHOW ENGINES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- server_version | data_directory                           | port
-- 8.0.36         | C:\ProgramData\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\Data | 3306
-- (SHOW ENGINES lists InnoDB as DEFAULT: it provides transactions and crash recovery)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

The same idea can be created with different levels of structure. A server holds many databases, a database holds tables, and a table holds typed columns. You create each level with its own statement, and you can inspect each level from the system catalog (information_schema).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: persistent storage, fast indexed lookup, many concurrent users, integrity rules, security (users and privileges), backup and recovery.
codeExamples:
-- Integrity rule enforced by the database itself, not by every app
CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 100.00);         -- accepted
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (2, -5.00);          -- rejected by the CHECK rule

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'acct_chk_1' is violated.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: needs administration (backups, tuning, upgrades), a server to run, schema design effort, and licence or hardware cost at scale. A simple config file is cheaper for tiny data.
codeExamples:
-- Cost of structure: you must design columns before you can store anything
INSERT INTO ghost_table VALUES (1);          -- table was never designed or created

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'school_demo.ghost_table' doesn't exist

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: one server has finite CPU, RAM and disk; very large write volumes need sharding or replication; relational schemas are awkward for deeply nested or constantly changing document shapes.
codeExamples:
-- A single row has a hard size ceiling (65,535 bytes across non-BLOB columns)
CREATE TABLE too_wide (a VARCHAR(40000) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4, b VARCHAR(40000) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1118 (42000): Row size too large. The maximum row size for the used table type,
-- not counting BLOBs, is 65535.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

A database is the system of record, so design for its failure modes first: backups and restore tests, replication, and an exit plan. Keep business invariants (keys, NOT NULL, CHECK) in the schema so every client benefits, and avoid using it as a queue or file store.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Think in terms of the workload: OLTP (many small reads/writes, MySQL) versus OLAP (few huge scans, a warehouse).
  • Durability comes from the write-ahead log and fsync settings, not from "saving a file"; know what innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit trades.
  • Data lives in a data directory, but applications must only touch it through the server, never by copying files while it runs.

Senior Notes

  • Pick the database from access patterns, consistency needs and scale, not fashion; polyglot persistence is normal (MySQL + Redis + search).
  • The database is usually the hardest tier to scale horizontally, so schema and query discipline early is cheaper than sharding later.
  • Treat the schema as a public contract: other services, reports and ETL jobs depend on it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

The classic beginner mistake is treating a database like a spreadsheet: storing lists in one cell, repeating the same fact in many rows, or relying on row order. The database cannot protect you from data it has no rules for. Fix it by giving every fact one home, a primary key and constraints.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Databases are fast because they avoid reading everything. An index is a sorted structure that finds a row in a handful of page reads, and the buffer pool keeps hot pages in RAM. You can see the difference by asking the optimizer for its plan before and after adding an index.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A realistic first design: a small library system. It shows the three ideas a beginner must master together: tables for entities, keys for identity, and relationships through foreign keys. Notice that the loan table records when something happened, not just that it did.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A DBMS is any software that manages data (files, hierarchical, key-value, document). An RDBMS is a DBMS that stores data in related tables, uses SQL and enforces relational rules (keys, constraints, ACID). MySQL, PostgreSQL and Oracle are RDBMSs.

Why Do We Need This?

Older file-based or hierarchical systems duplicated data and let programs break it. The relational model removes redundancy and lets the engine guarantee that references stay valid.
codeExamples:
-- Without relations, a typo creates an orphan; with an FK the engine refuses it
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (11,'Mina',99);       -- department 99 does not exist

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails
-- (school_demo.emp, CONSTRAINT emp_ibfk_1 FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept (id))

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Banks, ERP, e-commerce and HR systems use an RDBMS because they need accuracy and transactions. Non-relational DBMSs (Redis, MongoDB) are chosen for caches, documents and flexible schemas.
codeExamples:
-- RDBMS gives ACID: a failed step undoes the whole unit
CREATE TABLE bank (id INT PRIMARY KEY, bal INT);
INSERT INTO bank VALUES (1,500),(2,100);
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE bank SET bal = bal - 200 WHERE id = 1;   -- debit
-- crash or error happens here
ROLLBACK;                                       -- debit is undone
SELECT * FROM bank;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+
-- | id | bal  |
-- +----+------+
-- |  1 |  500 |
-- |  2 |  100 |
-- +----+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   DBMS (any data manager)
   ├── File / Hierarchical / Network
   ├── NoSQL: key-value | document | graph
   └── RDBMS ─ tables + keys + SQL + ACID
        ├── MySQL      ├── PostgreSQL
        └── Oracle     └── SQL Server

Fresher Notes

  • A DBMS is software that manages data; an RDBMS is a DBMS that stores data in related tables and uses SQL.
  • RDBMS adds rows and columns, keys, relationships and constraints. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server are RDBMS.
  • Classic interview line: all RDBMS are DBMS, not all DBMS are RDBMS (for example MongoDB or a file-based system).

Worked Example 1

Relational data lives in separate related tables joined by keys.

Worked Example 2

ACID transaction: either both inserts happen or neither.

Practice Exercise 1

Show that InnoDB enforces a foreign key (an RDBMS feature).

Practice Exercise 2

Check the storage engine of a table.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, engine FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | engine
-- dept       | InnoDB
-- emp        | InnoDB

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An RDBMS adds the relational model on top of storage: data lives in tables whose rows are identified by keys, and relationships are expressed by matching key values rather than by pointers. Because of that, the engine can verify relationships (foreign keys) and answer questions declaratively (SQL joins) without you writing navigation code.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Inside MySQL the difference shows up as a choice of storage engine. InnoDB behaves like a full RDBMS (transactions, foreign keys, crash recovery); MyISAM behaves more like a simple DBMS (table locks, no transactions). You can compare them directly by trying the same operations on both.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of RDBMS: standard SQL, joins across tables, integrity constraints, ACID transactions, mature tooling.
codeExamples:
-- One standard language across vendors: aggregate over a join
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS staff
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+
-- | name | staff |
-- +------+-------+
-- | IT   |     1 |
-- +------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: rigid schema, joins cost CPU at huge scale, and horizontal write scaling is hard.
codeExamples:
-- Changing the schema of a big table is a deliberate operation, not an ad-hoc write
ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN phone VARCHAR(15);   -- every existing row gains the column
DESCRIBE emp;

-- OUTPUT (trimmed):
-- | phone   | varchar(15) | YES  |     | NULL    |       |

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a plain DBMS (e.g. a key-value store) may offer no joins or constraints; a single-node RDBMS caps at one machine unless you add replication or sharding.
codeExamples:
-- Storage-engine choice matters: MyISAM is a DBMS-style engine without FK or transactions
SHOW ENGINES;                                   -- InnoDB is the transactional default

-- OUTPUT (trimmed):
-- | Engine | Support | Transactions | XA  | Savepoints |
-- | InnoDB | DEFAULT | YES          | YES | YES        |
-- | MyISAM | YES     | NO           | NO  | NO         |

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose RDBMS when correctness and ad-hoc querying matter, and add specialised stores (cache, search, document) around it rather than instead of it. The usual mistake is dropping integrity to gain a flexibility you never needed.

Mid-Level Notes

  • An RDBMS enforces integrity through primary keys, foreign keys and constraints; a plain DBMS often leaves this to the application.
  • RDBMS supports ACID transactions and a declarative query language, so you describe what you want, not how to fetch it.
  • Not every RDBMS feature is equal: MySQL engines differ (InnoDB has transactions and foreign keys, MyISAM does not).

Senior Notes

  • Relational does not mean slow or old: the optimizer, indexes and joins let one declarative query replace pages of procedural code.
  • The relational model gives data independence: you can change storage and indexes without changing queries.
  • Pick non-relational only when the relational constraint becomes the actual problem (schema agility, scale-out writes, graph traversal).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

A common mistake is assuming every MySQL table gives RDBMS guarantees. A table created on an old default or a MyISAM engine silently accepts foreign key syntax but ignores it. Always verify the engine, and treat missing constraints as a bug, not as flexibility.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

RDBMS rules cost a little on every write (checks, locks, logs), but they save far more time in debugging. You can measure what the integrity checks cost, and you can also see that a covering index keeps the check cheap because the parent lookup is a primary-key hit.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

In a real system the relational model pays off when requirements change. A report asking "which departments have more than 2 employees and what do they earn" is a single declarative query over related tables; with a non-relational file store you would write loops and joins by hand.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(*) AS staff, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_salary
FROM dept d JOIN emp_pay e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 2
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- department | staff | avg_salary
-- Engineering|     8 |      82000
-- Sales      |     5 |      54000

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL is an open-source relational database server (now owned by Oracle) that speaks SQL over TCP port 3306. It uses pluggable storage engines; InnoDB is the default and provides transactions, row locking and crash recovery.
codeExamples:
-- Ask the server who it is
SELECT VERSION() AS version, @@port AS port, @@default_storage_engine AS engine;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------+------+--------+
-- | version | port | engine |
-- +---------+------+--------+
-- | 8.0.36  | 3306 | InnoDB |
-- +---------+------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Teams need a free, fast, widely-supported relational database with good tooling and hosting everywhere (AWS RDS, Azure, GCP, shared hosting). MySQL is the "M" in the LAMP stack for exactly this reason.

Real-Time Use

WordPress, Facebook (early), Uber, Booking and countless Spring Boot / Django / Laravel apps run on MySQL. Apps connect through a driver (JDBC, mysqlclient, PDO).
codeExamples:
-- What an app sees: the user and database of the current connection
SELECT CURRENT_USER() AS who, DATABASE() AS db, CONNECTION_ID() AS conn;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------+--------+------+
-- | who            | db     | conn |
-- +----------------+--------+------+
-- | app_user@%     | shop   |   27 |
-- +----------------+--------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Client ──► Connection layer ──► Parser/Optimizer ──► Storage engine API
   (JDBC)     (threads, auth)      (plan)              ├─ InnoDB (default)
                                                       ├─ MyISAM
                                                       └─ MEMORY ...

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL is a free, open-source relational database server that stores data in tables and is queried with SQL.
  • It follows a client-server model: your app or the mysql CLI connects to the server over TCP (port 3306 by default).
  • It is owned by Oracle; MariaDB is a community fork. Both speak almost the same SQL.

Worked Example 1

Confirm a database can store emoji only with utf8mb4.

Worked Example 2

Peek at what the server is running right now.
codeExamples:
SHOW PROCESSLIST;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Id | User | Host            | db     | Command | Time | State    | Info
--  5 | root | localhost:51234 | school | Query   |    0 | executing| SHOW PROCESSLIST

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Print the server version and current user.
codeExamples:
SELECT VERSION(), CURRENT_USER();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- VERSION() | CURRENT_USER()
-- 8.0.36    | root@localhost

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Show the default storage engine and character set.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('default_storage_engine','character_set_server');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name        | Value
-- character_set_server | utf8mb4
-- default_storage_engine | InnoDB

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL has a layered architecture: a connection layer (threads, authentication), an SQL layer (parser, optimizer, executor) and a pluggable storage-engine layer (InnoDB by default). Your SQL text is parsed into a tree, optimized into a plan using table statistics, and executed by calling the storage engine for rows.
codeExamples:
-- Ask the server which layers/features are active
SELECT @@version, @@version_comment, @@default_storage_engine, @@character_set_server, @@sql_mode\G

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- @@version: 8.0.36
-- @@version_comment: MySQL Community Server - GPL
-- @@default_storage_engine: InnoDB
-- @@character_set_server: utf8mb4
-- @@sql_mode: ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY,STRICT_TRANS_TABLES,...

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

You can talk to MySQL in several ways: the mysql client, MySQL Shell, Workbench, or any driver. Variables can be read at three scopes: global (server), session (your connection), and per statement through hints. Knowing the scope tells you who is affected by a change.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@global.max_connections AS global_value, @@session.sql_mode AS session_mode;
SET SESSION sql_mode = 'STRICT_ALL_TABLES';        -- only my connection
SET GLOBAL max_connections = 300;                  -- everyone, until restart
SET PERSIST max_connections = 300;                 -- everyone, survives restart

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (x3)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: free community edition, easy install, fast reads, mature replication, huge community and managed cloud offerings.
codeExamples:
-- Replication and many engines are available out of the box
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin';                  -- binary log drives replication

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name | Value |
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | log_bin       | ON    |
-- +---------------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: fewer advanced SQL features than PostgreSQL historically (some, like window functions and CTEs, only arrived in 8.0), and Oracle controls the roadmap.
codeExamples:
-- Features differ by version: window functions need MySQL 8.0+
SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM (SELECT 1 AS id UNION SELECT 2) t;

-- OUTPUT on 8.0:                      OUTPUT on 5.7:
-- +----+                              -- ERROR 1064 (42000): You have an error in your
-- | rn |                              -- SQL syntax ... near '(ORDER BY id)'
-- +----+
-- |  1 |
-- |  2 |

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: single-primary writes by default, no native sharding (use Vitess or app-level), max_allowed_packet (64 MB default, 1 GB max) limits big BLOBs and rows, and some DDL still blocks.
codeExamples:
-- Statements larger than max_allowed_packet are rejected
SELECT @@max_allowed_packet / 1024 / 1024 AS mb;

-- OUTPUT (example, default 8.0 = 64 MB):
-- +--------+
-- | mb     |
-- +--------+
-- | 64.0000|
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Standardise on InnoDB, MySQL 8.0 LTS-style versions and utf8mb4. Plan scale-out early (read replicas, then partitioning or Vitess) because single-writer topology is the main ceiling. Prefer managed services unless you can staff DBA work.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Know the main pieces: server (mysqld), client tools, storage engines (InnoDB by default), data directory, config file (my.cnf / my.ini).
  • Check the version first: features like window functions, CTEs and EXPLAIN ANALYZE need 8.0+.
  • Use utf8mb4 and a sensible collation; plain utf8 in MySQL is only 3 bytes and breaks emoji.

Senior Notes

  • MySQL is strongest as a transactional OLTP store with read replicas; know its limits (single-writer primary, replication lag, schema-change cost on big tables).
  • Managed offerings (RDS, Cloud SQL, Aurora) change operations but not SQL semantics; verify version and parameter differences.
  • Plan upgrades (5.7 to 8.0) with query-plan and collation regression tests; defaults changed (auth plugin, charset).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Typical mistakes: using the old 3-byte utf8 charset, running with a loose sql_mode, and developing on one MySQL version while production runs another. The charset one is the most damaging because it silently loses emoji and some characters.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The two biggest levers for MySQL performance are memory for the buffer pool and proper indexes. Checking the buffer pool hit rate tells you in one query whether reads are coming from RAM or disk.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND((1 - Innodb_buffer_pool_reads.v / Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests.v) * 100, 2) AS hit_rate_pct
FROM (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE AS v FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_reads') Innodb_buffer_pool_reads,
     (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE AS v FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests') Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- hit_rate_pct
-- 99.87

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A first production habit: never develop as root. Create an application user, grant only the privileges it needs, and connect with it. This one practice limits the blast radius of bugs and leaks.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A database (schema) contains tables. A table is a grid: each column has a name and data type; each row (record/tuple) is one entity such as one student.
codeExamples:
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS uni;            -- container
USE uni;
CREATE TABLE student (
    id   INT,                                  -- column 1
    name VARCHAR(30),                          -- column 2
    age  INT                                   -- column 3
);
INSERT INTO student VALUES (1,'Abaji',20),(2,'Raoji',22);   -- two rows
SELECT * FROM student;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+-----+
-- | id | name  | age |
-- +----+-------+-----+
-- |  1 | Abaji |  20 |
-- |  2 | Raoji |  22 |
-- +------+------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Splitting data into tables of one subject each (students, courses) avoids repeating facts. Columns with types let the engine validate and store compactly; rows let you address one entity.
codeExamples:
-- Column types reject nonsense: age must be a number
INSERT INTO student VALUES (3,'Mina','twenty');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1366 (HY000): Incorrect integer value: 'twenty' for column 'age' at row 1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

A shop has tables like customers, products, orders. Reporting selects specific columns and filters rows.
codeExamples:
-- Projection = choose columns; selection = choose rows
SELECT name, age            -- columns
FROM student
WHERE age > 20;             -- rows

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-----+
-- | name  | age |
-- +-------+-----+
-- | Raoji |  22 |
-- +------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Database: uni
   └── Table: student
        ┌────┬───────┬─────┐
        │ id │ name  │ age │   <- columns (name + type)
        ├────┼───────┼─────┤
        │  1 │ Abaji │  20 │   <- row (one record)
        │  2 │ Raoji │  22 │
        └────┴───────┴─────┘

Fresher Notes

  • A server holds databases; a database holds tables; a table holds rows (records) and columns (fields).
  • Each column has a name and a data type; each row is one item, such as one student.
  • Use DESCRIBE table to see columns and SELECT * FROM table to see rows.

Worked Example 1

Read table structure from the catalog.
codeExamples:
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM   information_schema.columns
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'products'
ORDER  BY ordinal_position;

-- OUTPUT:
-- column_name | data_type | is_nullable
-- id          | int       | NO
-- name        | varchar   | YES
-- price       | decimal   | YES

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Row count versus column count.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM products;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS col_count FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='products' AND table_schema=DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- row_count
-- 3
-- col_count
-- 3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create products(id, name, price), insert 3 rows and count the columns using DESCRIBE.

Practice Exercise 2

Select only two columns and only the rows that cost more than 100.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 100;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | price
-- Book | 150.50
-- Bag  | 799.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Physically, an InnoDB table is a B-tree ordered by the primary key; each leaf page (16 KB) stores many rows, and each row stores its column values plus hidden fields (transaction id and roll pointer). A column is not stored separately: values of one row sit together, which is why reading a whole row is cheap and reading one column of a million rows still reads whole pages.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

A column definition is a name plus a type plus optional rules. You can add defaults, generated values, comments and visibility. Generated columns compute a value from other columns so it can never drift out of sync.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a uniform, easy-to-picture model; every row has the same shape so tools, indexes and reports are simple.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every row carries every column, so sparse attributes waste space (as NULLs), and rows have no inherent order.
codeExamples:
-- Rows have no guaranteed order unless you say so
SELECT name FROM student;                       -- order not promised
SELECT name FROM student ORDER BY name DESC;    -- order guaranteed

-- OUTPUT (second query):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Raoji |
-- | Abaji |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: max 4096 columns per table (InnoDB about 1017), 64 characters for identifiers, and 65,535 bytes of row width excluding BLOB/TEXT.
codeExamples:
-- Identifier names are limited to 64 characters
CREATE TABLE this_table_name_is_deliberately_made_far_too_long_to_be_accepted_by_mysql_ok (x INT);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1059 (42000): Identifier name 'this_table_name_is_...' is too long

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Model one entity per table, name things consistently (snake_case, singular or plural, but pick one) and give every table a primary key. Prefer narrow, well-typed columns; they shrink indexes and buffer-pool usage far more than they cost in design time.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Choose column types carefully: they decide storage, range, indexing speed and correctness (INT vs BIGINT, DECIMAL for money).
  • Row order is not guaranteed without ORDER BY; never rely on insertion order.
  • A table without a primary key is a smell: replication, ORMs and tools all behave better with one.

Senior Notes

  • Wide tables with many nullable columns hint at a missing entity; split or use a subtype table.
  • Row size affects how many rows fit per 16 KB InnoDB page, so narrow rows mean fewer page reads and better cache use.
  • Name things consistently (snake_case, singular or plural by convention); renames later are expensive across services.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on row order, using SELECT * in application code, and mixing up a row with a record in the application. Rows have no inherent order; only ORDER BY gives one. The fix is always to name columns and to order explicitly.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES ('Cap', 50);
SELECT * FROM products;                              -- order not guaranteed, columns may change later
SELECT id, name, price FROM products ORDER BY id;    -- explicit and stable

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name | price
--  1 | Pen  |  10.00
--  2 | Book | 150.00
--  3 | Bag  | 799.00
--  4 | Cap  |  50.00

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Row width affects performance: more rows per page means fewer page reads. Choosing types carefully and moving rarely-used large columns out of the main table keeps scans fast. You can measure rows per page with simple arithmetic from the catalog.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, table_rows, avg_row_length, ROUND(16384 / NULLIF(avg_row_length, 0)) AS approx_rows_per_page
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'products';

-- OUTPUT: (with realistic data)
-- table_name | table_rows | avg_row_length | approx_rows_per_page
-- products   |    1200000 |             62 |                  264

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A real onboarding task: read the structure of an unfamiliar database. Start from the catalog to list tables, columns and row counts, then sample a few rows. This is the first thing you do on a new project.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, table_rows FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY table_rows DESC;
SELECT column_name, column_type, is_nullable, column_key FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'shop' AND table_name = 'orders' ORDER BY ordinal_position;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name  | table_rows
-- order_items |    1840211
-- orders      |     612044
-- column_name | column_type  | is_nullable | column_key
-- id          | bigint       | NO          | PRI
-- customer_id | bigint       | NO          | MUL
-- total       | decimal(10,2)| NO          |

beginner.content:
Introduction

A schema is the blueprint of a database: tables, columns, types, keys and constraints. In MySQL the words SCHEMA and DATABASE are synonyms: CREATE SCHEMA equals CREATE DATABASE.
codeExamples:
CREATE SCHEMA library;                        -- same as CREATE DATABASE library
SHOW DATABASES LIKE 'library';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------------+
-- | Database (library)   |
-- +----------------------+
-- | library              |
-- +----------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A named blueprint lets teams agree on the shape of data, version it in source control and apply it to dev, test and production identically.

Real-Time Use

Real deployments keep one schema per application or tenant and refer across them with schema.table names.
codeExamples:
-- Cross-schema reference using qualified names
CREATE SCHEMA billing;
CREATE TABLE billing.invoice (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO billing.invoice VALUES (1);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM billing.invoice;      -- no USE needed

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 1 |
-- +---+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   MySQL server
   ├── schema = database : library
   │     ├── book
   │     └── member
   └── schema = database : billing
         └── invoice          (library.book , billing.invoice)

Fresher Notes

  • In MySQL a schema is the same as a database: a named collection of tables, views and routines.
  • "Schema" also describes the design of tables (columns, types, keys), as in "the schema of the orders table".
  • CREATE SCHEMA shop and CREATE DATABASE shop do exactly the same thing.

Worked Example 1

The schema as a catalog: list every schema with its table count.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_schema, COUNT(*) AS tables
FROM   information_schema.tables
WHERE  table_schema NOT IN ('mysql','sys','information_schema','performance_schema')
GROUP  BY table_schema;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_schema | tables
-- hr           |      0
-- school       |      1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Show the DDL that defines a table.
codeExamples:
SHOW CREATE TABLE school.students\G

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Table: students
-- Create Table: CREATE TABLE students (
--   id int NOT NULL,
--   name varchar(40) DEFAULT NULL,
--   PRIMARY KEY (id)
-- ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create a schema, switch to it and confirm it is empty.

Practice Exercise 2

Query a table using the fully qualified name without USE.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM school.students LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  1 | Abaji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In MySQL the words schema and database are synonyms: both map to a directory of tables inside the data directory. The catalog table information_schema.schemata lists them, and a fully qualified name schema.table lets one statement touch several.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Schema design means choosing tables, columns, types, keys and constraints. You can read the full definition of any table with SHOW CREATE TABLE, and you can export only the structure (no data) with mysqldump --no-data to review or version it.
codeExamples:
SHOW CREATE TABLE orders\G
-- shell: mysqldump -u root -p --no-data --routines shop > shop_schema.sql

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Create Table: CREATE TABLE orders (
--   id bigint NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, customer_id bigint NOT NULL, total decimal(10,2) NOT NULL,
--   PRIMARY KEY (id), KEY idx_customer (customer_id),
--   CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers (id)
-- ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: isolates applications, allows per-schema privileges, and the INFORMATION_SCHEMA exposes the blueprint as queryable data.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, table_rows
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'library';                 -- list tables of one schema

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | TABLE_ROWS |
-- +------------+------------+
-- | book       |          0 |
-- +------------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: schema changes (migrations) on large tables are slow or risky, and changing a design late is expensive.
codeExamples:
-- Dropping a column is irreversible without a backup
ALTER TABLE library.book ADD COLUMN isbn CHAR(13);
ALTER TABLE library.book DROP COLUMN isbn;      -- data in it is gone

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.05 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: unlike PostgreSQL, MySQL has no separate namespace layer inside a database, so a schema equals a database; cross-schema foreign keys work only within the same server and engine.
codeExamples:
-- There is no CREATE SCHEMA ... inside a database; nesting is not supported
CREATE SCHEMA library.sub1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): You have an error in your SQL syntax ... near '.sub1'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat schema as a versioned artifact: migrate with a tool (Flyway, Liquibase), review DDL like code and rehearse it on a production-sized copy. Use separate schemas for bounded contexts, but remember cross-schema joins couple deployments.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Unlike PostgreSQL or SQL Server, MySQL has no separate schema level inside a database; you use multiple databases instead.
  • Qualify names (shop.orders) in scripts that touch more than one database to avoid running against the wrong one.
  • Keep DDL in version control and apply it with a migration tool so every environment has the same schema.

Senior Notes

  • Cross-database joins work inside one server, but they couple services; microservices should own separate schemas and not share tables.
  • Schema changes on large tables are operations, not edits: plan online DDL, expand/contract and rollbacks.
  • Use information_schema and schema-diff checks in CI to catch drift between environments.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

A frequent mistake is letting schemas drift between environments: a column added by hand in production that no migration knows about. Comparing catalogs finds the difference quickly.
codeExamples:
-- run on both environments, then diff the outputs
SELECT table_name, column_name, column_type, is_nullable, column_default
FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY table_name, ordinal_position;

-- OUTPUT: (diff result)
-- < orders.note  varchar(100) YES NULL      (exists only in production: untracked change)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Schema choices decide performance for years. Wide VARCHAR(255) everywhere, missing foreign key indexes, and wrong types cost memory in every query. A catalog query can flag columns that look oversized or tables without a primary key.
codeExamples:
SELECT t.table_name FROM information_schema.tables t
LEFT JOIN information_schema.statistics s ON s.table_schema = t.table_schema AND s.table_name = t.table_name AND s.index_name = 'PRIMARY'
WHERE t.table_schema = 'shop' AND t.table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND s.index_name IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name
-- legacy_import     (table with no primary key: fix it)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A realistic team workflow: all schema changes are migration files in version control, applied by CI, and the production catalog is periodically compared to the expected one to catch drift.
codeExamples:
-- V7__add_orders_channel.sql   (reviewed in a pull request)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN channel VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'WEB', ALGORITHM=INSTANT;

SELECT version, description, success FROM flyway_schema_history ORDER BY installed_rank DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- version | description         | success
-- 7       | add orders channel  | 1
-- 6       | add customers index | 1

beginner.content:
Introduction

A primary key (PK) uniquely identifies each row (unique and NOT NULL, one per table). A foreign key (FK) is a column that holds another table's PK, creating a link and a rule that the referenced row must exist.

Why Do We Need This?

Without a PK you cannot reliably update or delete one specific row; without an FK, rows can point at things that do not exist.
codeExamples:
-- PK blocks duplicates
INSERT INTO author VALUES (1,'Someone Else');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1' for key 'author.PRIMARY'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Orders reference customers, order lines reference orders and products. Every join in reporting follows an FK path.
codeExamples:
-- FK stops orphan rows
INSERT INTO book VALUES (11,'Ghost Book',99);       -- author 99 absent

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails

beginner.content:
Diagram

   author (PK id)                book (PK id, FK author_id)
   ┌────┬────────┐               ┌────┬───────────┬───────────┐
   │  1 │ Tagore │ ◄─────────────│ 10 │ Gitanjali │     1     │
   └────┴────────┘   references  └────┴───────────┴───────────┘

Fresher Notes

  • A primary key (PK) uniquely identifies each row: no duplicates, no NULL. A foreign key (FK) points to a PK in another table.
  • A table has one primary key but can have many foreign keys.
  • FK values must exist in the parent table, so you cannot create an order for a customer that does not exist.

Worked Example 1

Valid parent then child; join them.

Worked Example 2

See the restrict rule in action when deleting the parent.

Practice Exercise 1

Create customers and orders with a PK and FK and try to insert an order for a missing customer.

Practice Exercise 2

Insert a duplicate primary key and read the error.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A primary key creates a unique index and, in InnoDB, becomes the clustered index: the table rows are stored in primary key order. A foreign key adds a second index on the child column (if none exists) and a check on every insert/update/delete that the referenced parent row exists. The check takes a shared lock on the parent row.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Keys can be declared inline, at the end of the table, or added later. Foreign keys accept actions: RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL on delete or update. Choose per relationship: cascade for owned children, restrict for independent data.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: guaranteed uniqueness and referential integrity; the PK is also the clustered index in InnoDB, so lookups by it are fastest.
codeExamples:
-- Lookup by PK is a single-row access
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM author WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | table  | type  | key     | rows |
-- | author | const | PRIMARY |    1 |

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: FKs add checks on every write and take locks on parent rows; a wide PK is copied into every secondary index.
codeExamples:
-- Parent cannot be removed while children exist (default RESTRICT)
DELETE FROM author WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB only (not MyISAM); parent and child column types must match; partitioned tables cannot have FKs; only one PK per table (but it may be composite).

Architect's Notes

Prefer short, immutable, meaningless PKs (BIGINT auto-increment or ordered UUID) for InnoDB. Declare FKs in OLTP schemas for integrity; in extreme-scale or sharded systems teams sometimes drop them and enforce integrity in code, accepting the risk.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Prefer a short, stable, meaningless PK (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT) over natural values like email that can change.
  • InnoDB stores the table in primary-key order (clustered), and every secondary index carries the PK, so a fat PK bloats all indexes.
  • Index the FK column in the child; MySQL does this automatically for FKs, but not for logical references without a constraint.

Senior Notes

  • UUID primary keys cause random inserts and page splits; use ordered IDs (UUIDv7, ULID, or auto-increment plus public id).
  • FKs add locking and write cost; some very high-scale systems drop them and enforce integrity in code, accepting the risk.
  • Choose ON DELETE behaviour deliberately (RESTRICT, CASCADE, SET NULL); accidental cascades delete data silently.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: foreign key type mismatch (INT vs BIGINT, signed vs unsigned, different charset), forgetting the index on the child column in logical (unconstrained) references, and cascading deletes on big trees. Error 1215/3780 means the two columns are not compatible.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE bad_child (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id));   -- parent is BIGINT

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3780 (HY000): Referencing column 'customer_id' and referenced column 'id' in foreign key constraint 'bad_child_ibfk_1' are incompatible.

-- Fix: use the same type
CREATE TABLE good_child (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id BIGINT, FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id));

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Primary key size multiplies through every secondary index. A BIGINT key is 8 bytes; a 36-character UUID string in utf8mb4 can be 144 bytes in every index entry. Compare index sizes to see the effect.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND(data_length/1048576,1) AS data_mb, ROUND(index_length/1048576,1) AS index_mb
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('orders_bigint_pk','orders_uuid_pk');

-- OUTPUT: (example, 5M rows each)
-- table_name       | data_mb | index_mb
-- orders_bigint_pk |   410.0 |    180.0
-- orders_uuid_pk   |   780.0 |    690.0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A real design decision: do you allow deleting a customer who has orders? Most businesses say no, so use RESTRICT and "deactivate" instead. The database then protects history even if the application has a bug.
