beginner.content:
Introduction

A candidate key is any minimal column set that could uniquely identify a row; one becomes the PK, the rest are alternates. A composite key uses two or more columns together. A unique key enforces uniqueness but, unlike a PK, may allow NULLs and a table can have many.

Why Do We Need This?

Real identity is often more than one column (a student in a course, an order line in an order). Composite keys model that exactly, and unique keys protect natural identifiers like email.

Real-Time Use

Login systems use unique email; junction tables use composite PKs; payroll uses a surrogate PK plus a unique employee code.
codeExamples:
-- Enforce "one email per account" at the database level
INSERT INTO person VALUES (2,'a@x.com','444455556666');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'a@x.com' for key 'person.email'

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Candidate keys:  {id}   {email}   {aadhar}   {first,last,dob}
                      │
                      ├─► PRIMARY KEY   (one, NOT NULL)
                      └─► UNIQUE keys   (alternates, NULL allowed)
   Composite: PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)

Fresher Notes

  • A candidate key is any column set that could uniquely identify a row; one is chosen as the primary key, the others are alternates.
  • A composite key uses two or more columns together, such as (student_id, course_id).
  • A unique key forbids duplicates but, unlike a primary key, allows NULLs and a table can have many.

Worked Example 1

The same student may enrol in different courses; same course by different students is also fine.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,11),(2,10);
SELECT * FROM enrollments ORDER BY student_id, course_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- student_id | course_id
--          1 |        10
--          1 |        11
--          2 |        10

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Inspect keys on a table.
codeExamples:
SHOW INDEX FROM members;

-- OUTPUT: (example, trimmed)
-- Key_name | Column_name | Non_unique
-- PRIMARY  | id          | 0
-- email    | email       | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create enrollments with a composite primary key (student_id, course_id) and insert the same pair twice.

Practice Exercise 2

Add a UNIQUE key on email and insert two NULL emails.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Every UNIQUE constraint is backed by a unique B-tree index; the engine checks it on each write by looking for an existing entry. A composite key sorts by the first column, then the second, so lookups on the left column alone still use the index but on the second column alone do not (leftmost prefix).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE enrolments (student_id INT, course_id INT, enrolled_on DATE, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrolments WHERE student_id = 7;      -- uses the primary key prefix
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrolments WHERE course_id = 3;       -- cannot seek (second column only)

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- query 1: type=ref  key=PRIMARY
-- query 2: type=index key=PRIMARY (scans the whole index)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

UNIQUE can be single or composite, named or unnamed, and MySQL 8 supports functional and prefix unique indexes. Name constraints so error messages and migrations are readable.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative integrity; unique keys double as indexes for fast lookup; composite keys avoid a meaningless extra column in junction tables.
codeExamples:
-- Unique indexes make the lookup fast
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM person WHERE email = 'a@x.com';

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key   | key_len | rows |
-- | const | email | 243     |    1 |

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: wide composite PKs enlarge every secondary index, and each unique key costs extra write work and space.
codeExamples:
-- Index size grows with key width; check it
SELECT index_name, stat_value * @@innodb_page_size / 1024 AS kb
FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats
WHERE table_name = 'person' AND stat_name = 'size';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+------+
-- | index_name | kb   |
-- +------------+------+
-- | PRIMARY    |   16 |
-- | email      |   16 |
-- | aadhar     |   16 |
-- +------------+------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a UNIQUE column may hold many NULLs (NULL is not equal to NULL); max 16 columns and 3072 bytes in an InnoDB index key.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE u (v INT UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO u VALUES (NULL),(NULL),(1);        -- both NULLs accepted
SELECT * FROM u;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | v    |
-- +------+
-- | NULL |
-- | NULL |
-- |    1 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick a short surrogate as the PK, keep natural identifiers (email, tax id) as UNIQUE, and use composite PKs for pure junction tables. Remember InnoDB clusters on the PK, so key width and insertion order directly affect page splits and index size.

Mid-Level Notes

  • In MySQL a UNIQUE index allows multiple NULLs, because NULL is not equal to NULL.
  • Composite keys are ideal for junction tables, and column order matters for index use (leftmost prefix).
  • Natural candidate keys (email, national id) are good UNIQUE constraints even when a surrogate PK is used.

Senior Notes

  • Composite primary keys are copied into every secondary index and every child FK; for deep hierarchies, a single surrogate key is lighter.
  • Unique constraints on soft-deleted rows need care: add a deleted-at or active flag into the unique key, or use generated columns.
  • Case-insensitive collations make "A@x.com" and "a@x.com" collide on UNIQUE, which is usually desired for email.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting UNIQUE to reject duplicate NULLs, forgetting case-insensitive collations treat "A@x.com" and "a@x.com" as equal, and choosing a composite key with the columns in the wrong order for the queries you run.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO members (tenant_id, email, national_id) VALUES (3,'n1@x.com',NULL),(3,'n2@x.com',NULL);   -- allowed: NULLs are distinct
INSERT INTO members (tenant_id, email) VALUES (3,'N1@X.COM');

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '3-N1@X.COM' for key 'members.uq_tenant_email'    (case-insensitive collation)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Composite key column order is a performance decision. Put the column you always filter by first. A key (tenant_id, email) serves "all rows of a tenant" and "one email in a tenant", while (email, tenant_id) serves neither as well.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Soft-deleted rows break plain UNIQUE (a deleted email blocks re-registration). A generated column that is NULL for deleted rows gives "unique among active rows" because NULLs never collide.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Constraints are rules attached to columns or tables that the database enforces on every write: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, DEFAULT and CHECK (enforced from MySQL 8.0.16).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE product (
    id    INT           PRIMARY KEY,                 -- unique + not null
    sku   VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL UNIQUE,             -- required and unique
    price DECIMAL(8,2)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.00,       -- fallback value
    qty   INT           NOT NULL CHECK (qty >= 0)    -- business rule
);
INSERT INTO product (id, sku, qty) VALUES (1,'P-1',5);
SELECT * FROM product;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+-------+-----+
-- | id | sku  | price | qty |
-- +----+------+-------+-----+
-- |  1 | P-1  |  0.00 |   5 |
-- +----+------+-------+-----+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Application code has bugs and many apps write to the same data. Constraints are the last line of defence that keeps bad data out, whoever the writer is.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO product (id, sku, qty) VALUES (2,'P-2',-3);   -- negative stock

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'product_chk_1' is violated.

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical use: email UNIQUE, status DEFAULT 'NEW', amount CHECK (amount > 0), orders.customer_id FK. Migrations add them with ALTER TABLE.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE product ADD CONSTRAINT chk_price CHECK (price >= 0);   -- add a rule later
SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type
FROM information_schema.table_constraints
WHERE table_name = 'product';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------+-----------------+
-- | CONSTRAINT_NAME | CONSTRAINT_TYPE |
-- +-----------------+-----------------+
-- | PRIMARY         | PRIMARY KEY     |
-- | sku             | UNIQUE          |
-- | product_chk_1   | CHECK           |
-- | chk_price       | CHECK           |
-- +-----------------+-----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   INSERT / UPDATE ──► constraint gate ──► table
                       ├─ NOT NULL  : value present?
                       ├─ UNIQUE/PK : no duplicate?
                       ├─ CHECK     : rule true?
                       ├─ FK        : parent exists?
                       └─ DEFAULT   : fill missing
                          fail = ERROR, statement rolled back

Fresher Notes

  • Constraints are rules the database enforces on data: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, DEFAULT and CHECK.
  • They protect data quality at the lowest level, no matter which application writes.
  • A violated constraint makes the statement fail with an error, so no bad row is stored.

Worked Example 1

List constraints on a table from the catalog.
codeExamples:
SELECT constraint_name, constraint_type
FROM   information_schema.table_constraints
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'accounts';

-- OUTPUT:
-- constraint_name | constraint_type
-- PRIMARY         | PRIMARY KEY
-- chk_balance     | CHECK

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

NOT NULL blocks a missing owner.

Practice Exercise 1

Create accounts with NOT NULL, DEFAULT and CHECK and attempt a bad insert.

Practice Exercise 2

Insert a row using the default balance.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Constraints are checked by the SQL layer (NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT) and by InnoDB indexes (PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY) at statement time. If any row violates a rule the whole statement is rolled back, not just that row, which is what keeps tables consistent under concurrency.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Constraints can be inspected and changed after creation: list them from the catalog, add new ones with ALTER, and in MySQL 8.0.16+ toggle CHECK constraints between ENFORCED and NOT ENFORCED to stage a rollout.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: central, declarative, always enforced, documented in the schema and used by the optimizer (unique keys).
codeExamples:
-- Defaults fill gaps automatically
INSERT INTO product (id, sku, qty) VALUES (3,'P-3',1);
SELECT price FROM product WHERE id = 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | price |
-- +-------+
-- |  0.00 |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each check costs write time; error messages are generic; adding a constraint to a large dirty table can fail or lock.
codeExamples:
-- Adding a rule to existing bad data fails
-- product row 1 already has qty = 5, which breaks the new rule
ALTER TABLE product ADD CONSTRAINT chk_big CHECK (qty < 3);        -- row 1 has qty 5

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_big' is violated.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: CHECK cannot reference other tables or non-deterministic functions; before 8.0.16 CHECK was parsed and ignored; FK needs InnoDB.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE product ADD CONSTRAINT chk_now CHECK (qty < RAND() * 100);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3814 (HY000): An expression of a check constraint 'chk_now' contains
-- disallowed function: rand.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Put invariants that must never be violated in constraints, and soft or changing business rules in the application. Name constraints explicitly (uq_, fk_, chk_) so migrations and error messages are readable, and add them before data grows.

Mid-Level Notes

  • CHECK constraints are enforced from MySQL 8.0.16; in older versions they were parsed and ignored.
  • Name constraints explicitly (CONSTRAINT chk_age CHECK (age >= 18)) so error messages and migrations are clear.
  • Enforce rules in both app and DB: the app gives friendly messages, the DB is the last line of defence.

Senior Notes

  • Constraints are cheap compared with the cost of cleaning corrupt data; add them at design time because adding later requires validating all rows.
  • Adding a constraint to a big table can block or rebuild it; backfill and validate in steps.
  • Business rules that span rows or tables (balance cannot go negative across accounts) still need transactions, locks or triggers.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying only on application validation, forgetting NOT NULL (so "required" fields hold NULLs), and writing CHECKs that depend on other rows (not allowed). NULL passes a CHECK, so combine CHECK with NOT NULL.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Adding a constraint to a big, live table validates every row. Do it safely: find violators first, fix them, then add the constraint, and watch for metadata lock waits.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Layered validation in a real application: the UI gives friendly messages, the service checks business rules, and the database enforces invariants as a final guard. When a bug slips through the upper layers, the database rejects the bad write instead of storing it.
codeExamples:
-- application passes a negative quantity through a bug; the database refuses
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, qty, unit_price) VALUES (1, 7, -3, 10.00);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'order_items_chk_1' is violated.

beginner.content:
Introduction

In a one-to-one relationship each row in table A matches at most one row in table B and vice versa, e.g. a user and the single profile row for that user. Implement it with a FK that is also UNIQUE (or the child's PK).

Why Do We Need This?

Splitting rarely used or sensitive columns into their own table keeps the hot table narrow and lets you apply different privileges or storage.
codeExamples:
-- Second profile for the same user is rejected
INSERT INTO user_profile VALUES (1,'Another bio');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1' for key 'user_profile.PRIMARY'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Examples: user and passport details, employee and payroll record, order and invoice header. Many apps keep large BLOB or audit data in a 1:1 side table.
codeExamples:
-- LEFT JOIN shows users who have no profile yet (optional side)
INSERT INTO app_user VALUES (2,'raoji');
SELECT u.login, p.bio
FROM app_user u LEFT JOIN user_profile p ON p.user_id = u.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | login | bio       |
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | abaji  | Loves SQL |
-- | raoji  | NULL      |
-- +-------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   app_user                    user_profile
   ┌────┬───────┐              ┌─────────┬───────────┐
   │ id │ login │ 1 ────── 0..1│ user_id │ bio       │
   │ PK │       │              │ PK + FK │           │
   └────┴───────┘              └─────────┴───────────┘

Fresher Notes

  • In a one-to-one relationship one row in table A relates to at most one row in table B (user and profile).
  • Implement it with a foreign key that is also UNIQUE (or the child primary key equals the parent id).
  • Often used to split rarely used or sensitive columns out of a main table.

Worked Example 1

Read both halves with a join.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, pp.number FROM persons p JOIN passports pp ON pp.person_id = p.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | number
-- Abaji | P123

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

UNIQUE foreign key alternative with its own id.

Practice Exercise 1

Create persons and passports as one-to-one and try to add two passports for one person.

Practice Exercise 2

List persons without a passport.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

One-to-one is a one-to-many with a rule: the foreign key column in the child is also unique (or is the child primary key). The unique index is what prevents a second child row for the same parent.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Two ways to model it: shared primary key (child PK = parent id) or a separate surrogate key plus a UNIQUE foreign key. Pick the shared key for pure extensions, the surrogate when the child could later have its own references.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: keeps the main table small and cache-friendly; isolates sensitive data; models true uniqueness.
codeExamples:
-- The narrow table scans fast because big text lives elsewhere
SELECT COUNT(*) AS users FROM app_user;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | users |
-- +-------+
-- |     2 |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: an extra join to read both halves, and two inserts must stay in step.

Limitations

Limitations: MySQL cannot enforce that the child row must exist (mandatory on both sides); that needs application logic or deferred constraints, which MySQL lacks.
codeExamples:
-- User 2 legally exists without any profile: "must have one" cannot be declared
SELECT COUNT(*) AS users_without_profile
FROM app_user u LEFT JOIN user_profile p ON p.user_id = u.id
WHERE p.user_id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------------+
-- | users_without_profile |
-- +-----------------------+
-- |                     1 |
-- +-----------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use 1:1 splits for vertical partitioning (hot vs cold columns), security boundaries or optional large payloads, not by habit. If both sides are always read together and always exist, merging into one table is simpler and faster.

Mid-Level Notes

  • The child can be optional (0..1) or required; the database cannot force that the child row exists, only that there is at most one.
  • Read both sides with a JOIN; use LEFT JOIN when the child may be missing.
  • If both tables are always loaded together, consider merging them to remove the join.

Senior Notes

  • One-to-one splits are a tool for hot/cold column separation, security separation and subtype tables (class-table inheritance).
  • Shared primary keys make joins and ORMs (JPA @MapsId) simple and cheap.
  • Do not use one-to-one to hide a design that really is one-to-many; confirm the business rule first.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting the UNIQUE (so it silently becomes one-to-many), creating the parent without the child and assuming it exists, and using INNER JOIN so parents without a child vanish from reports. Use LEFT JOIN when the child is optional.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('b@x.com');       -- no profile yet
SELECT u.email, p.bio FROM users u JOIN user_profiles p ON p.user_id = u.id;          -- hides b@x.com
SELECT u.email, p.bio FROM users u LEFT JOIN user_profiles p ON p.user_id = u.id;     -- shows both

-- OUTPUT:
-- first query : 1 row (a@x.com)
-- second query: 2 rows (b@x.com with NULL bio)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Splitting a table helps when some columns are large or rarely used. The hot table stays narrow so more rows fit per page. Measure the effect with the catalog.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, avg_row_length FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('employees_wide','employees_core');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name     | avg_row_length
-- employees_wide |           2240    (photo and resume inline)
-- employees_core |            120    (7 rows per page becomes 136)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A real pattern: credentials in a separate table with stricter privileges. Reporting users can read the profile table but have no grant on the credentials table, so a leaked reporting account cannot expose password hashes.

beginner.content:
Introduction

In a one-to-many relationship one parent row relates to many child rows, but each child belongs to one parent: one customer, many orders. The FK lives on the "many" side.

Why Do We Need This?

Storing the customer name inside every order duplicates it and invites inconsistency. A child table with a key reference stores each fact once.
codeExamples:
-- Rename once, every order reflects it through the join
UPDATE customer SET name = 'Abaji K' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customer c ON c.id = o.customer_id LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+
-- | id | name    |
-- +----+---------+
-- |  1 | Abaji K |
-- |  2 | Abaji K |
-- +----+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The most common relationship: department-employees, category-products, post-comments, order-order_items.
codeExamples:
-- Total per parent
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+--------+
-- | customer_id | total  |
-- +-------------+--------+
-- |           1 | 425.00 |
-- +-------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • One row in the parent relates to many rows in the child: one customer has many orders.
  • The "many" side holds the foreign key (orders.customer_id).
  • This is the most common relationship in databases.

Worked Example 1

Sum per parent.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.total) AS spent FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | spent
-- Abaji | 750.00

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

ON DELETE CASCADE removes children with the parent.

Practice Exercise 1

Create customers and orders, insert one customer with two orders and list orders per customer.

Practice Exercise 2

Find customers who have more than one order.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In a one-to-many relationship the child table stores the parent key. When you join, MySQL typically scans the parent rows (after filters) and, for each, does an index lookup into the child by that foreign key, which is why the child foreign key must be indexed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Query the relationship from either side: parent with child counts, children with parent details, parents with no children, and parents with more than N children.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no duplication, simple to model and query, FK index speeds child lookups.
codeExamples:
-- InnoDB auto-creates an index on the FK column
SHOW INDEX FROM orders;

-- OUTPUT (trimmed):
-- | Key_name    | Column_name |
-- | PRIMARY     | id          |
-- | customer_id | customer_id |

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: reading parent and children needs a join; deleting a parent must decide what happens to children.
codeExamples:
DELETE FROM customer WHERE id = 1;           -- children still exist

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a child cannot have two parents in the same relationship (that is many-to-many); a child row cannot be moved to a non-existent parent.
codeExamples:
UPDATE orders SET customer_id = 42 WHERE id = 1;   -- no such customer

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Always index the FK column (InnoDB does automatically) and pick ON DELETE behaviour deliberately: RESTRICT for business data, CASCADE only for true ownership like order lines. For very hot parents, watch FK lock contention on the parent row.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Always index the foreign key column in the child, so joins and parent lookups are fast.
  • Use GROUP BY parent_id with COUNT to see how many children each parent has, and LEFT JOIN to include parents with none.
  • Decide the delete rule: RESTRICT (safe), CASCADE (owned children), SET NULL (optional link).

Senior Notes

  • Very large children per parent (millions of events per device) call for composite indexes (parent_id, created_at) and possibly partitioning.
  • Pagination on the child list should be keyset on (parent_id, id), not OFFSET.
  • ORMs make one-to-many easy but also make N+1 easy; load children in batches.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: joining and then summing parent columns (fan-out inflates totals), forgetting to index the foreign key when the constraint is not declared, and deleting a parent with a cascade that wipes millions of children in one transaction.
codeExamples:
-- parent amount repeated for each child row: wrong total
SELECT SUM(c.credit_limit) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;      -- counts Abaji twice

-- correct: aggregate the child first or use EXISTS
SELECT SUM(c.credit_limit) FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- first query double counts; second returns the true total

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For large one-to-many lists use a composite index that matches the filter and sort, so MySQL reads the page of orders in order without a sort.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real life: an order history screen. Keyset pagination keeps page 500 as fast as page 1, and the composite index serves both the filter and the order.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, total, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 1 AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-04-30 10:00:00', 9120)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id   | total  | created_at
-- 9118 | 450.00 | 2026-04-30 09:58:11

beginner.content:
Introduction

In a many-to-many relationship rows on both sides relate to many on the other: students and courses. A relational DB cannot store it in two tables directly; you add a junction (bridge) table holding both FKs.

Why Do We Need This?

Putting a list of course ids in one column breaks atomic values, blocks indexing and makes counting painful. The junction table keeps each link as a normal row.
codeExamples:
-- Which students take SQL? A plain indexed query on the junction table
SELECT student_id FROM enrolment WHERE course_id = 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | student_id |
-- +------------+
-- |          1 |
-- |          2 |
-- +------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real examples: products and tags, actors and movies, users and roles, doctors and patients. The junction often carries its own attributes (enrolled_on, grade).
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE enrolment ADD COLUMN grade CHAR(1);       -- attribute of the relationship
UPDATE enrolment SET grade = 'A' WHERE student_id = 1 AND course_id = 10;
SELECT * FROM enrolment WHERE grade IS NOT NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----------+-------+
-- | student_id | course_id | grade |
-- +------------+-----------+-------+
-- |          1 |        10 | A     |
-- +------------+-----------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   student            enrolment (junction)          course
   ┌────┬───────┐     ┌────────────┬───────────┐   ┌────┬───────┐
   │  1 │ Abaji │◄────│ student_id │ course_id │──►│ 10 │ SQL   │
   │  2 │ Raoji │◄────│     1      │    10     │   │ 20 │ Java  │
   └────┴───────┘     │     1      │    20     │   └────┴───────┘
                      │     2      │    10     │
                      └────────────┴───────────┘

Fresher Notes

  • Many rows in A relate to many rows in B: students and courses.
  • Relational databases cannot store this directly; you add a third table (junction, bridge or link table) holding both ids.
  • The junction table normally has a composite primary key made of the two foreign keys.

Worked Example 1

Students not enrolled in anything.

Worked Example 2

Duplicate links are rejected by the composite key.

Practice Exercise 1

Model students and courses and list each student with their courses.

Practice Exercise 2

Count students per course.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.title, COUNT(*) AS students FROM courses c JOIN enrolments e ON e.course_id=c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

-- OUTPUT:
-- title | students
-- SQL   |        2
-- Java  |        1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A many-to-many relationship is stored as a junction table with two foreign keys. Its primary key (a_id, b_id) both prevents duplicate links and is the clustered index, so "all b for a given a" is a contiguous range scan.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical queries: courses of a student, students of a course, students in all of a set of courses, and students in none. The "all of" form uses GROUP BY with HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT).
codeExamples:
SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id IN (10, 11) GROUP BY s.id, s.name HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT e.course_id) = 2;   -- both courses
SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrolments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);                                                  -- none

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Moropant

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: normalised, supports attributes on the link, each side queryable in both directions.
codeExamples:
-- Count both directions
SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS students FROM enrolment GROUP BY course_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+----------+
-- | course_id | students |
-- +-----------+----------+
-- |        10 |        2 |
-- |        20 |        1 |
-- +-----------+----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: reads need two joins, and the junction can grow very large (rows = links).
codeExamples:
-- Reverse lookups need a secondary index on (course_id, student_id)
ALTER TABLE enrolment ADD INDEX idx_course_student (course_id, student_id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.03 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the composite PK serves only lookups that start with student_id; there is no native many-to-many column type.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM enrolment WHERE course_id = 20;   -- uses the extra index, not the PK

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type | key                | Extra       |
-- | ref  | idx_course_student | Using index |

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Make the junction PK composite (no surrogate unless the link has its own identity) and add the reverse-order index for the other direction. Store link attributes there; if the link becomes a business entity (enrolment with fees), promote it to a first-class table.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Extra data about the relationship (enrolled_on, grade) belongs in the junction table.
  • Index both directions: the composite PK covers (a_id, b_id); add an index on (b_id, a_id) for the reverse lookup.
  • Querying needs two joins: A to link to B.

Senior Notes

  • If the link table grows its own behaviour (an order line between order and product) model it as a real entity with its own id.
  • Large junction tables dominate storage; keep the key columns small and consider partitioning.
  • Avoid storing comma-separated ids in a column; it breaks joins, constraints and indexing.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: storing comma-separated ids, omitting the reverse index, and putting relationship data (grade, role) in one of the two main tables. Comma-separated lists defeat joins, constraints and indexes.
codeExamples:
-- BAD
CREATE TABLE courses_bad (id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(30), student_ids VARCHAR(200));
SELECT * FROM courses_bad WHERE FIND_IN_SET('7', student_ids);     -- full scan, no foreign keys

-- GOOD
SELECT c.title FROM courses c JOIN enrolments e ON e.course_id = c.id WHERE e.student_id = 7;

-- OUTPUT:
-- the bad version cannot use an index; the good version uses the primary key prefix

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Junction tables become the biggest tables in a system. Keep keys compact, and verify that both lookup directions use an index only (covering) scan.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

A real feature: "recommended courses": students who took the same courses as you also took X. It is a self join of the junction table.
codeExamples:
SELECT e2.course_id, COUNT(*) AS peers
FROM enrolments e1 JOIN enrolments e2 ON e2.student_id = e1.student_id AND e2.course_id <> e1.course_id
WHERE e1.course_id = 10 AND e2.course_id NOT IN (SELECT course_id FROM enrolments WHERE student_id = 7)
GROUP BY e2.course_id ORDER BY peers DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- course_id | peers
-- 14        | 120
-- 11        |  95

beginner.content:
Introduction

The relational model (E. F. Codd, 1970) stores data as relations (tables) of tuples (rows) with attributes (columns). Core ideas: keys, domains (types), integrity rules, and set-based operations (selection, projection, join).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',900),(2,'Raoji','HR',700),(3,'Mina','IT',800);
-- Selection (rows) + Projection (columns)
SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | salary |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Abaji |    900 |
-- | Mina  |    800 |
-- +------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Because queries state what you want, not how to find it, the optimizer can choose the best plan and the same SQL keeps working as data grows or indexes change.
codeExamples:
-- Declarative: no loops. The engine decides how.
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | dept | avg_sal |
-- +------+---------+
-- | IT   | 850.0000|
-- | HR   | 700.0000|
-- +------+---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Everyday work is relational algebra in SQL clothes: union of two result sets, join to combine, difference to find missing.
codeExamples:
-- Set operation: union of two relations
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'
UNION
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary < 800;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Mina  |
-- | Raoji |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Relation (table)          emp(id, name, dept, salary)   <- schema
   Tuple (row)               (1, Abaji, IT, 900)
   Attribute (column)        salary : INT                  <- domain
   Operators:  σ select   π project   ⋈ join   ∪ union   − difference

Fresher Notes

  • Data is stored in tables (relations) made of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes).
  • Tables are linked by keys, not by physical pointers, and you query with SQL.
  • Core ideas: primary key, foreign key, constraints, normalization and transactions.

Worked Example 1

A relational join combining two relations.
codeExamples:
SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id=s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id=e.course_id WHERE s.id = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | title
-- Raoji | SQL

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Set difference with NOT EXISTS (students not in any course).
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrolments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Show that NULL does not equal NULL.
codeExamples:
SELECT NULL = NULL AS eq, NULL IS NULL AS is_null;

-- OUTPUT:
-- eq   | is_null
-- NULL |       1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Project and select: only the name of students with id greater than 1.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM students WHERE id > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Raoji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SQL operations map to relational algebra: WHERE is selection, the SELECT list is projection, JOIN is a join, UNION/EXCEPT are set operations, GROUP BY is aggregation. The optimizer exploits the algebra (for example pushing filters below joins) because the results are provably the same.
codeExamples:
-- selection + projection + join in one declarative statement
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept       -- join
WHERE e.salary > 50000                                -- selection
;                                                     -- projection: only name, dept

EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT e.name FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept WHERE e.salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop inner join
--     -> Filter: (e.salary > 50000)   (the filter runs before the join: pushed down)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

The same question can often be written several ways: join, IN, EXISTS or set operations. They are equivalent in meaning but differ in clarity and sometimes in plan.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: data independence (storage can change without changing queries), integrity rules, a strong formal basis for optimization.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: impedance mismatch with object models (hence ORMs), and NULL brings three-valued logic that surprises beginners.
codeExamples:
-- NULL is "unknown": comparisons are neither true nor false
SELECT NULL = NULL AS eq, NULL IS NULL AS is_null;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | eq   | is_null |
-- +------+---------+
-- | NULL |       1 |
-- +------+---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a strict relation is a set (no duplicates, no order), but SQL tables are bags: duplicates and order need explicit constraints and ORDER BY.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE bag (x INT);                   -- no key: duplicates allowed
INSERT INTO bag VALUES (1),(1);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(DISTINCT x) AS distinct_n FROM bag;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+------------+
-- | n | distinct_n |
-- +---+------------+
-- | 2 |          1 |
-- +---+------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Think in sets, not loops: replace row-by-row application logic with joins and aggregates. Design with keys and functional dependencies first (normalisation), then denormalise only where measured read cost justifies it.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Relational algebra underlies SQL: selection (WHERE), projection (SELECT columns), join, union, difference.
  • Integrity types: entity (PK not null), referential (FK valid), domain (types/checks).
  • ACID transactions make multi-statement changes safe.

Senior Notes

  • The relational model separates logical design from physical storage; you can add indexes or change storage without rewriting queries.
  • NULL introduces three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN); many bugs come from forgetting it.
  • Normalize for integrity, denormalize deliberately for read performance, and measure.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes with NULL: it is not a value but "unknown", so comparisons give unknown. NOT IN with a NULL returns nothing, = NULL never matches, and aggregates skip NULLs. Use IS NULL, NOT EXISTS and COALESCE.
codeExamples:
SELECT NULL = NULL AS eq, NULL IS NULL AS is_null, 5 NOT IN (1, NULL) AS not_in, COALESCE(NULL, 0) AS fixed;

-- OUTPUT:
-- eq   | is_null | not_in | fixed
-- NULL |       1 | NULL   |     0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Because SQL is declarative, you can improve performance by changing physical design (indexes, statistics) without touching the query. Compare the plan before and after.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Relational thinking solves reporting problems cleanly. A department salary summary with the percentage of company payroll is a grouped aggregate plus a window function over the result.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, SUM(e.salary) AS payroll, ROUND(SUM(e.salary) / SUM(SUM(e.salary)) OVER () * 100, 1) AS pct_of_company
FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept GROUP BY d.id, d.name ORDER BY payroll DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | payroll | pct_of_company
-- IT   |  700000 | 57.4
-- HR   |  520000 | 42.6

beginner.content:
Introduction

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language (ANSI/ISO) for talking to relational databases. MySQL is one product that implements SQL, plus its own extensions. SQL is the language; MySQL is the engine.
codeExamples:
-- Standard SQL works on any RDBMS
SELECT 1 + 1 AS two;

-- MySQL-specific: administrative extras like SHOW
SHOW DATABASES;

-- OUTPUT (first query):
-- +-----+
-- | two |
-- +-----+
-- |   2 |
-- +-----+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Knowing the difference lets you write portable queries and recognise vendor-only features before they lock you in.
codeExamples:
-- Row limiting differs by vendor
-- MySQL / PostgreSQL : SELECT ... LIMIT 3
-- SQL Server         : SELECT TOP 3 ...
-- Oracle 12c+/ANSI   : SELECT ... FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY
SELECT n FROM (SELECT 1 n UNION SELECT 2 UNION SELECT 3 UNION SELECT 4) t ORDER BY n LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 1 |
-- | 2 |
-- | 3 |
-- +---+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

In real teams SQL skills transfer across MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, while administration (backup, replication, config) is product-specific.

Diagram

   SQL  (standard language: SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY ...)
     │ implemented by
     ├── MySQL       (+ ON DUPLICATE KEY, LIMIT, SHOW ...)
     ├── PostgreSQL  (+ RETURNING, arrays ...)
     ├── SQL Server  (T-SQL: TOP, ...)
     └── Oracle      (PL/SQL, FETCH FIRST ...)

Fresher Notes

  • SQL is the language used to talk to relational databases. MySQL is a database product that understands SQL.
  • Other products also use SQL with small differences: PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.
  • Analogy: SQL is like English; MySQL is one speaker of it.

Worked Example 1

Portable vs MySQL-specific null handling.
codeExamples:
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, 'x') AS standard_way, IFNULL(NULL, 'x') AS mysql_way;

-- OUTPUT:
-- standard_way | mysql_way
-- x            | x

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Strict mode rejects a too-long value.

Practice Exercise 1

Run one query in each style: DQL, DML and DDL.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE t (id INT);          -- DDL
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1);          -- DML
SELECT * FROM t;                   -- DQL

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
--  1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Show the current sql_mode.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SQL is a standard language; each database implements the standard plus extensions. MySQL parses your SQL text with its own grammar, so statements valid in PostgreSQL or Oracle may fail, and MySQL-only syntax (AUTO_INCREMENT, backticks, LIMIT) may not run elsewhere.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL-specific vs portable equivalents
SELECT IFNULL(NULL, 'x') AS mysql_only, COALESCE(NULL, 'x') AS portable;
SELECT id FROM emp ORDER BY id LIMIT 2;                          -- MySQL / PostgreSQL
-- SELECT id FROM emp ORDER BY id FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY;       -- standard SQL (supported by Oracle, PostgreSQL)

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysql_only | portable
-- x          | x

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

The statement families are DDL (structure), DML (data change), DQL (queries), DCL (permissions) and TCL (transactions). Learn them as a map: every statement you write belongs to one family and behaves accordingly (for example DDL auto-commits in MySQL).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE demo (id INT PRIMARY KEY);          -- DDL (auto-commits)
INSERT INTO demo VALUES (1);                      -- DML
SELECT * FROM demo;                               -- DQL
GRANT SELECT ON shop.demo TO 'report'@'%';        -- DCL
START TRANSACTION; DELETE FROM demo; ROLLBACK;    -- TCL

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of standard SQL: portable skills and mostly portable queries. Advantages of MySQL: practical extras such as upsert, simple admin and wide hosting.
codeExamples:
-- Standard ANSI quoting uses double quotes; MySQL defaults to backticks unless told
SET SESSION sql_mode = CONCAT(@@sql_mode, ',ANSI_QUOTES');
SELECT 5 AS "five";                              -- alias in ANSI style

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | five |
-- +------+
-- |    5 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: vendor extensions reduce portability; each product also treats edge cases (NULL ordering, case sensitivity, GROUP BY rules) differently.
codeExamples:
-- Case-sensitivity of table names depends on OS and lower_case_table_names
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'lower_case_table_names';

-- OUTPUT (example, Linux default):
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name          | Value |
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- | lower_case_table_names | 0     |
-- +------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL historically lacked some standard features (INTERSECT and EXCEPT only from 8.0.31, no FULL OUTER JOIN, no deferred constraints).
codeExamples:
-- FULL OUTER JOIN is not supported; emulate with UNION of LEFT and RIGHT joins
SELECT a.x FROM (SELECT 1 x) a FULL OUTER JOIN (SELECT 2 x) b ON a.x = b.x;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): You have an error in your SQL syntax ... near 'OUTER JOIN'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Write ANSI-leaning SQL for business queries and isolate vendor-specific code (upserts, pagination, JSON) behind a repository layer or documented list. Portability is rarely free, so decide consciously which MySQL extensions are worth the lock-in.

Mid-Level Notes

  • SQL is a standard (ANSI/ISO) with many dialect extensions; MySQL has its own functions and syntax such as LIMIT, AUTO_INCREMENT, backtick quoting.
  • Portable SQL sticks to the standard parts; use vendor features only when they pay off.
  • Language categories: DDL (CREATE), DML (INSERT), DQL (SELECT), DCL (GRANT), TCL (COMMIT).

Senior Notes

  • Dialect differences hit migrations: LIMIT vs FETCH FIRST, IFNULL vs COALESCE, identity vs auto-increment, date functions.
  • ORMs hide dialects but leak when you use native queries; test against the real engine, not an in-memory substitute.
  • Know sql_mode: strict mode changes whether bad data errors or silently truncates.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: writing code that only works in one dialect without knowing, ignoring sql_mode (so bad data is silently accepted), and using double quotes for strings (valid in MySQL by default, an identifier quote in standard SQL).
codeExamples:
SELECT 'text' AS single_quoted;                  -- portable string literal
SET SESSION sql_mode = CONCAT(@@sql_mode, ',ANSI_QUOTES');
SELECT "text" AS now_an_identifier;                -- fails: "text" is treated as a column name

-- OUTPUT:
-- single_quoted
-- text
-- ERROR 1054 (42S22): Unknown column 'text' in 'field list'

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Strict mode is a performance and correctness feature: it turns silent truncation into errors so bad data never enters. Check it and keep it on in every environment.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

In a real migration project you list dialect differences first. A small compatibility table drives the rewrite and the tests.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'LIMIT n' AS mysql, 'FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY' AS standard
UNION ALL SELECT 'IFNULL(a,b)', 'COALESCE(a,b)'
UNION ALL SELECT 'AUTO_INCREMENT', 'GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY'
UNION ALL SELECT 'NOW()', 'CURRENT_TIMESTAMP';

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysql          | standard
-- LIMIT n        | FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
-- IFNULL(a,b)    | COALESCE(a,b)
-- AUTO_INCREMENT | GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY
-- NOW()          | CURRENT_TIMESTAMP

beginner.content:
Introduction

Installing MySQL puts the server (mysqld), client tools and default data directory on your machine. Options: Windows MSI installer, Linux package manager (apt, yum), macOS dmg or Homebrew, or a Docker image.
codeExamples:
# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt update
sudo apt install mysql-server -y          # server + client from the distro repo
mysql --version                           # confirm what was installed

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- mysql  Ver 8.0.36-0ubuntu0.22.04.1 for Linux on x86_64 ((Ubuntu))

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You need a local server to practise SQL, run integration tests and develop apps without touching production. A repeatable install means every developer has the same version.
codeExamples:
# Docker: a throw-away, version-pinned MySQL in one command
docker run -d --name mysql8 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=Secret#123 -p 3306:3306 mysql:8.0
docker ps --filter name=mysql8            # confirm it is running

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- CONTAINER ID   IMAGE       STATUS         PORTS                    NAMES
-- 9c1d2e3f4a5b   mysql:8.0   Up 8 seconds   0.0.0.0:3306->3306/tcp   mysql8

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Dev laptops use the installer or Docker; production uses managed services (RDS, Cloud SQL) or configuration-managed packages with a pinned minor version.
codeExamples:
# RHEL / CentOS / Rocky: add Oracle's repo then install
sudo dnf install mysql-community-server -y
sudo systemctl enable --now mysqld        # start now and on every boot
sudo grep 'temporary password' /var/log/mysqld.log    # first-run root password

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- [Note] A temporary password is generated for root@localhost: Xk3;9aBc#t

beginner.content:
Diagram

   package / MSI / docker pull
          │
          ▼
   ┌────────────────┐   first start   ┌──────────────────┐
   │ binaries       │ ───────────────►│ initialise data  │
   │ mysqld, mysql  │                 │ dir, root account│
   └────────────────┘                 └──────────────────┘
          │ systemctl start mysql / Services / docker start
          ▼
   listening on 3306  ◄── clients connect

Fresher Notes

  • Download the MySQL Installer (Windows) or use the package manager (apt, brew, yum); choose "MySQL Server" plus Workbench.
  • During setup you set the root password and the port (default 3306). Remember both.
  • Verify with mysql --version and by logging in with mysql -u root -p.

Worked Example 1

Docker based dev server (shell commands).
codeExamples:
docker run --name mysql-dev -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=secret -p 3306:3306 -v mysqldata:/var/lib/mysql -d mysql:8.0
docker exec -it mysql-dev mysql -uroot -psecret -e "SELECT 1"

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1
-- 1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Create an application user right after install instead of using root.

Practice Exercise 1

Confirm your server version and uptime after installing.
codeExamples:
SELECT VERSION();
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Uptime';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- VERSION()
-- 8.0.36
-- Variable_name | Value
-- Uptime        | 120

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Find the data directory and port that your install uses.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('datadir','port');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name | Value
-- datadir       | C:\ProgramData\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\Data\
-- port          | 3306

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An installation creates three things: the program files (mysqld, client tools), a data directory initialised with system tables, and a service that starts the server. First start runs mysqld --initialize, which generates the root account and records a temporary password in the error log.
codeExamples:
# Linux package install and first start
sudo apt install mysql-server
sudo systemctl enable --now mysql
sudo mysql_secure_installation
mysql --version

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysql  Ver 8.0.36 for Linux on x86_64 (MySQL Community Server - GPL)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose the install method by purpose: OS package for servers, MSI installer for Windows desktops, Docker for development and CI, a managed service (RDS, Cloud SQL) for production. Docker gives a disposable, version-pinned instance with a named volume for data.
codeExamples:
docker run -d --name mysql-dev -p 3306:3306 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=secret -e MYSQL_DATABASE=shop -v mysqldata:/var/lib/mysql mysql:8.0
docker logs mysql-dev --tail 2
docker exec -it mysql-dev mysql -uroot -psecret -e "SELECT VERSION()"

-- OUTPUT:
-- [Server] /usr/sbin/mysqld: ready for connections. Version: '8.0.36'  port: 3306
-- VERSION()
-- 8.0.36

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: free, quick (minutes), cross-platform, and Docker gives disposable, reproducible environments.
codeExamples:
# Run two versions side by side on different ports
docker run -d --name my57 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=pw -p 3307:3306 mysql:5.7
docker run -d --name my80 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=pw -p 3308:3306 mysql:8.0

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- 5f0c...   (container id printed for each)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: distro repos often lag the newest release; Windows installers add services and registry entries that are tedious to clean; containers need a volume or data disappears.
codeExamples:
# Without a volume, removing the container deletes the data
docker rm -f mysql8
docker run -d --name mysql8 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=pw -p 3306:3306 mysql:8.0
# ...previous databases are gone. Use: -v mysqldata:/var/lib/mysql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (a fresh, empty server: SHOW DATABASES lists only system schemas)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the port may already be taken, the OS user needs admin rights, and some distros ship MariaDB under the name mysql.
codeExamples:
# Port 3306 busy: the new server will not start
sudo ss -ltnp | grep 3306                 # who owns the port?

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- LISTEN 0 151 *:3306 *:* users:(("mysqld",pid=1021,fd=24))
-- [ERROR] [MY-010119] [Server] Aborting   (seen in the second server's log)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pin an exact version (8.0.x or the current LTS) in Docker tags or package holds, use utf8mb4 from day one, and treat the install as code (Ansible, Terraform or managed service). Never run production data in a container without a persistent volume and backups.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Run MySQL in Docker for development: one command gives a disposable, version-pinned server.
  • Know the install layout: binaries, data directory, config file (my.ini on Windows, my.cnf on Linux), and the service name.
  • Run mysql_secure_installation (or equivalent) to remove test data and anonymous users.

Senior Notes

  • Pin exact minor versions in every environment; upgrades change defaults (auth plugin, charset, optimizer).
  • Prefer managed services or containers with persistent volumes for production; never keep data inside an ephemeral container layer.
  • Automate installs and config with IaC (Ansible, Terraform, Helm) so servers are reproducible.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: installing without a volume (data disappears with the container), exposing port 3306 to the internet, leaving the default empty or well-known root password, and mixing client and server major versions. Bind to localhost or a private network and set a strong password at once.
codeExamples:
# bad: public port, weak password, no volume
docker run -d -p 0.0.0.0:3306:3306 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root mysql:8.0
# good: loopback only, strong secret from env, persistent volume
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:3306:3306 -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD="$DB_ROOT_PW" -v mysqldata:/var/lib/mysql mysql:8.0

-- OUTPUT:
-- (the second container is reachable only from the same host and keeps its data across restarts)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance starts at install time: use a filesystem and storage suited to databases (SSD/NVMe, XFS or ext4), disable swap pressure, and set the buffer pool before loading data. A small my.cnf written at install avoids a restart later.
codeExamples:
# /etc/mysql/conf.d/tuning.cnf
[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size = 4G
innodb_flush_method = O_DIRECT
max_connections = 200
character-set-server = utf8mb4

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size / 1024 / 1024 / 1024;   =>  4.0000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a repeatable developer environment. A compose file pins the version, loads an init script and keeps data in a volume so every teammate gets the same database in one command.
codeExamples:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  db:
    image: mysql:8.0.36
    environment: { MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: secret, MYSQL_DATABASE: shop }
    ports: ["3306:3306"]
    volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/mysql, ./init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d]
volumes: { dbdata: {} }

-- OUTPUT:
-- docker compose up -d  =>  db  Started   (scripts in ./init run on first start)

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL is client/server. The server (mysqld) owns the data and listens on a port. A client (mysql CLI, Workbench, a JDBC driver) connects, sends SQL and prints results. They can run on different machines.
codeExamples:
# Server process
ps -ef | grep mysqld | head -1
# Client talks to it over TCP
mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 3306 -u root -p -e "SELECT 'hello from server' AS msg"

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- mysql  1021  1  0 09:01 ?  00:00:03 /usr/sbin/mysqld
-- +-------------------+
-- | msg               |
-- +-------------------+
-- | hello from server |
-- +-------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Separating them lets many applications share one managed data service, and lets you upgrade, secure and scale the server independently of client code.
codeExamples:
-- From any client: which server and which client connection am I?
SELECT @@hostname AS server_host, CONNECTION_ID() AS my_conn, USER() AS client_user;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+---------+----------------+
-- | server_host | my_conn | client_user    |
-- +-------------+---------+----------------+
-- | db01        |      42 | root@10.0.0.5  |
-- +-------------+---------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

App servers (clients) in one subnet connect to a database host; DBAs connect with the CLI; BI tools connect read-only to a replica.
codeExamples:
-- Everyone connected right now (clients as seen by the server)
SELECT id, user, host, db, command FROM information_schema.processlist;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+---------+----------------+------+---------+
-- | id | user    | host           | db   | command |
-- +----+---------+----------------+------+---------+
-- | 42 | root    | 10.0.0.5:51322 | NULL | Query   |
-- | 57 | app_usr | 10.0.1.7:40110 | shop | Sleep   |
-- +----+---------+----------------+------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   mysql CLI ─┐
   Workbench ─┼──► TCP 3306 / socket ──► mysqld ──► data directory
   JDBC app  ─┤        (protocol)         │  threads, caches, engines
   Python    ─┘                           └──► logs
   CLIENTS                                   SERVER

Fresher Notes

  • The server (mysqld) stores data and runs queries. A client (CLI, Workbench, your app) connects and sends SQL.
  • They talk over TCP (port 3306), a Unix socket or a named pipe.
  • You can have many clients connected to one server at the same time.

Worked Example 1

Session variables are per client.

Worked Example 2

Check whether the current connection uses TLS.
codeExamples:
SHOW SESSION STATUS LIKE 'Ssl_cipher';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name | Value
-- Ssl_cipher    | TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Count active connections.
codeExamples:
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name     | Value
-- Threads_connected | 3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Show the maximum allowed connections.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name   | Value
-- max_connections | 151

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The server listens for connections and creates one thread per client. During connection the handshake negotiates protocol, TLS and an authentication plugin; after success the client sends commands and the server replies with result sets or OK/ERROR packets. The client is just a program that speaks this protocol.
codeExamples:
-- see your own connection from the server's point of view
SELECT CONNECTION_ID() AS id, USER() AS client_user, CURRENT_USER() AS server_account, @@hostname AS server_host;
SHOW SESSION STATUS LIKE 'Ssl_version';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | client_user    | server_account | server_host
-- 12 | root@localhost | root@localhost | db1
-- Ssl_version | TLSv1.3

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Clients connect over TCP, a Unix socket or a Windows named pipe, with options for host, port, user, database and TLS. Option files (~/.my.cnf) keep credentials out of command lines.
codeExamples:
mysql -h 127.0.0.1 -P 3306 -u shop_app -p shop
mysql --protocol=SOCKET -u root -p
mysql --defaults-file=~/.my.cnf -e "SELECT 1"
mysql --ssl-mode=VERIFY_IDENTITY --ssl-ca=/etc/ssl/ca.pem -h db.internal -u shop_app -p

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysql>   (interactive prompt) or 1 for the -e form

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: central data, central security, many simultaneous clients, language-neutral wire protocol.
codeExamples:
# The same server answers a Python, Java or shell client identically
mysql -u root -p -e "SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected'"

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name     | Value |
-- +-------------------+-------+
-- | Threads_connected | 2     |
-- +-------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: network latency on every call, a single server is a single point of failure, and connection management becomes your job.
codeExamples:
# Server down: every client fails at once
mysql -h db01 -u app -p -e "SELECT 1"

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 2003 (HY000): Can't connect to MySQL server on 'db01:3306' (111)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: max_connections (default 151) caps concurrent clients; each connection uses memory and a thread.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name   | Value |
-- +-----------------+-------+
-- | max_connections | 151   |
-- +-----------------+-------+
-- (the 152nd client gets ERROR 1040: Too many connections)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep servers on private networks, require TLS and per-app accounts, and front them with connection pooling (HikariCP, ProxySQL) so thousands of app threads become tens of server connections.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Each client connection gets a session with its own variables, current database and transaction.
  • The command-line client is mysql; other client programs include mysqldump, mysqladmin and drivers (JDBC, mysqlclient, mysql2).
  • Use SHOW PROCESSLIST to see connected clients and what they run.

Senior Notes

  • The server is thread-per-connection by default, so unlimited connections are not free; use pooling and set max_connections sensibly.
  • Network exposure: bind to private interfaces, require TLS, and firewall port 3306.
  • Client and server version mismatches affect authentication plugins (caching_sha2_password vs mysql_native_password).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using localhost vs 127.0.0.1 interchangeably (localhost uses a socket, 127.0.0.1 uses TCP and matches different grants), and leaving idle connections open so the server runs out of connections.
codeExamples:
-- an account created for 'user'@'127.0.0.1' will not match a socket connection from 'localhost'
CREATE USER 'app'@'127.0.0.1' IDENTIFIED BY 'x';
-- mysql -u app -p            (connects via socket as app@localhost)

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'app'@'localhost' (using password: YES)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Every connection costs a thread and memory. Watch the ratio of connected to running threads, and use pooling so many app requests share a few connections.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Threads_connected','Threads_running','Max_used_connections');
SELECT @@max_connections AS max_connections;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Threads_connected    | 118
-- Threads_running      |   6
-- Max_used_connections | 143
-- max_connections | 300

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: find the sessions that are hogging the server and the clients they come from, then decide whether to fix the app or kill the session.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL Workbench is Oracle's free GUI for MySQL: a SQL editor, visual schema designer (EER diagrams), server administration (users, status) and data import/export.
codeExamples:
-- In Workbench's SQL editor: Ctrl+Enter runs the current statement.
-- The editor sends ordinary SQL; nothing here is Workbench-specific.
SELECT SCHEMA() AS current_db, CURRENT_USER() AS login_user;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+----------------+
-- | current_db | login_user     |
-- +------------+----------------+
-- | NULL       | root@localhost |
-- +------------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Beginners learn faster seeing tables, rows and diagrams; teams share and review schema visually; DBAs inspect performance without typing every command.

Real-Time Use

Used for ad-hoc queries, running EXPLAIN visually, exporting a table to CSV, comparing schemas and generating forward-engineer scripts from a model.

Diagram

   ┌──────────── MySQL Workbench ─────────────┐
   │ SQL Editor │ Schema Designer │ Admin     │
   └────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
                    │ standard MySQL protocol
                    ▼
                 mysqld

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL Workbench is the official graphical tool: write SQL, browse tables, design diagrams and manage users.
  • Create a connection (host, port, user), double-click it, and run queries in the SQL editor with the lightning button.
  • Use the schema panel to see tables and right-click for "Select Rows".

Worked Example 1

The Workbench "Select Rows" shortcut runs this query.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM school.students LIMIT 1000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  1 | Abaji
--  2 | Raoji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Export the same data from the CLI instead (repeatable).
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u root -p school students > students.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (file students.sql created with CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Check whether safe updates is on in your session.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@sql_safe_updates;

-- OUTPUT: (Workbench default)
-- @@sql_safe_updates
-- 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

See what safe updates blocks.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Workbench is a client that wraps the same protocol in a GUI: the SQL editor sends statements, the schema tree runs catalog queries, and the EER diagram tool reads or writes DDL. Everything it does can be reproduced in SQL, which is what you should commit to version control.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful features: forward/reverse engineering of EER diagrams, Visual Explain for plans, the Performance Dashboard, and data export wizards. Connection settings (SSL, SSH tunnel) live in the connection profile.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: low learning curve, schema modelling, performance dashboard, saved connections, free.
codeExamples:
-- Performance dashboard reads these same counters
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Questions';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+--------+
-- | Variable_name | Value  |
-- +---------------+--------+
-- | Questions     | 128734 |
-- +---------------+--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: GUI clicks are not repeatable or reviewable; it can freeze on very large result sets; auto-commit and safe-update defaults surprise users.
codeExamples:
-- Workbench enables "safe updates" by default; this fails without a key in WHERE
UPDATE wb_child SET p_id = NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Error Code: 1175. You are using safe update mode and you tried to update a table
-- without a WHERE that uses a KEY column.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: no native Linux ARM or very latest OS builds sometimes lag; not meant for scripted automation or production runbooks (use the CLI or Shell).
codeExamples:
# Automation needs a scriptable client, not a GUI
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM information_schema.tables" --batch --skip-column-names

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- 287

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use the GUI to explore and design, but commit the resulting DDL to version control and apply it via migrations. For production access prefer least-privilege accounts, read-only replicas and audited bastions over shared root in a desktop tool.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Reverse-engineer an EER diagram from a database, or forward-engineer a diagram into SQL.
  • Use the Performance Reports and query "Visual Explain" to inspect plans.
  • Turn off "safe updates" only knowingly; it protects against UPDATE/DELETE without a key in WHERE.

Senior Notes

  • GUI tools are for exploration; production changes go through versioned migrations, not clicks.
  • Do not connect Workbench directly to production with powerful accounts; use read-only users and bastion/VPN.
  • Alternative clients (DBeaver, DataGrip) may suit teams that use multiple databases.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: leaving safe-updates on and then bypassing it blindly, running a destructive statement against production because the connection tab looks like development, and editing schema in the GUI without saving a script.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Workbench helps tune queries: compare the plan before and after adding an index, and read the "Rows examined" and "Duration" in the output panel. Use it to learn, then automate checks in CI.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: use colour-coded connections (red for production), read-only accounts for investigation, and export the final change as a script for the migration tool rather than applying it from the GUI.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL Shell (mysqlsh) is an advanced client with three modes: SQL, JavaScript and Python. It supports the X DevAPI (port 33060), scripting, and administration of InnoDB Cluster and replica sets.
codeExamples:
# Connect with the URI form and switch modes
mysqlsh root@localhost:3306
 MySQL  localhost:3306 ssl  JS > \sql             # switch to SQL mode
 MySQL  localhost:3306 ssl  SQL > SELECT 1+1 AS two;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+
-- | two |
-- +-----+
-- |   2 |
-- +-----+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The classic mysql client is great for typing SQL but weak for scripting and cluster management. Shell adds real programming, JSON output and AdminAPI helpers.
codeExamples:
# Run a JavaScript one-liner against the server, no interactive session
mysqlsh --js -u root -p --uri root@localhost -e "print(session.runSql('SELECT VERSION()').fetchOne()[0])"

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- 8.0.36

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

DBAs use dba.createCluster() to build InnoDB Cluster, the dump and load utilities for fast logical backups, and the upgrade checker before a major upgrade.
codeExamples:
# Pre-upgrade compatibility report
mysqlsh root@localhost -- util checkForServerUpgrade

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- The MySQL server at localhost:3306, version 8.0.30, will now be checked for compatibility
-- issues for upgrade to MySQL 8.0.36 ...
-- No fatal errors were found that would prevent an upgrade.

beginner.content:
Diagram

   mysqlsh
   ├─ SQL mode ─────────► classic protocol 3306
   ├─ JavaScript mode ──► X DevAPI        33060
   └─ Python mode
        └─ dba.* / util.* : cluster, dump, load, upgrade checks

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL Shell (mysqlsh) is an advanced command-line client that supports SQL, JavaScript and Python modes.
  • Start it with mysqlsh root@localhost and switch modes with \sql, \js, \py.
  • It formats results nicely and can manage InnoDB Cluster.

Worked Example 1

Python mode example.
codeExamples:
\py
result = session.run_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM school.students")
print(result.fetch_one()[0])

-- OUTPUT:
-- 2

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Check the cluster status (AdminAPI).

Practice Exercise 1

Run a SQL statement from the shell in one line (shell command).
codeExamples:
mysqlsh --sql -u root -p -e "SELECT 1+1 AS two"

-- OUTPUT:
-- two
-- 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Dump a schema with the shell utility (JS mode).
codeExamples:
util.dumpSchemas(['school'], '/backup/school', {threads: 4})

-- OUTPUT: (summary)
-- Duration: 00:00:02s
-- Schemas dumped: 1
-- Tables dumped: 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL Shell connects through the classic protocol (3306) or the X protocol (33060) and offers three languages in one session: SQL, JavaScript and Python. Its admin API (dba) drives InnoDB Cluster, and its utilities (util) provide parallel dump and load.
codeExamples:
mysqlsh root@localhost:3306
\sql
SELECT @@version;
\js
shell.status()
\py
session.run_sql("SELECT 1+1").fetch_one()

-- OUTPUT:
-- 8.0.36
-- MySQL Shell version 8.0.36 ... Connection Id: 14, Current schema: ...
-- [2]

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Dump and load utilities are multi-threaded and chunk large tables, which makes them far faster than mysqldump for big data. Options include thread count, compression, filters and dry-run checks.
codeExamples:
util.dumpInstance('/backup/full', {threads: 8, compression: 'zstd', excludeSchemas: ['sandbox']})
util.dumpSchemas(['shop'], '/backup/shop', {threads: 4, dryRun: true})
util.loadDump('/backup/full', {threads: 8, ignoreVersion: false})

-- OUTPUT:
-- Duration: 00:01:12s  Schemas dumped: 4  Tables dumped: 61  Data size: 38.2 GB (compressed 6.1 GB)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: scripting in JS or Python, multi-threaded dump/load utilities, JSON output, cluster tooling, X DevAPI document store.
codeExamples:
# Fast parallel logical dump of one schema
mysqlsh root@localhost -- util dumpSchemas ["shop"] /backup/shop_dump --threads 4

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Dump duration: 00:00:02s
-- Rows written: 120034
-- Bytes written: 8.1 MB

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: another tool to install, learn and keep in step with the server version; output formats differ from the classic client.
codeExamples:
# Classic client batch output vs Shell: different default table formatting and flags
mysqlsh --sql -u root -p --table -e "SELECT 1 AS x"

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | x |
-- +---+
-- | 1 |
-- +---+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: X Protocol (33060) must be enabled and reachable; some AdminAPI features require MySQL 8.0 with GTID and a specific topology.
codeExamples:
# X Protocol port check
mysql -u root -p -e "SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'mysqlx_port'"

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name | Value |
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | mysqlx_port   | 33060 |
-- +---------------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use Shell for automation, parallel dump/load, cluster operations and upgrade checks; keep plain mysql for quick manual SQL. Script cluster changes in Shell so topology edits are reviewable code, not console history.

Mid-Level Notes

  • The shell has utilities for fast dump/load (util.dumpInstance, util.loadDump) that are parallel and much faster than mysqldump.
  • Use the X DevAPI for document-style access on port 33060.
  • Scriptable in JavaScript or Python for administration tasks.

Senior Notes

  • AdminAPI in MySQL Shell sets up and monitors InnoDB Cluster, ClusterSet and Replica sets.
  • Use dump/load utilities for migrations between servers and cloud; check compatibility with util.checkForServerUpgrade() before upgrades.
  • Automation: run shell scripts in CI for health checks and schema validation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: loading a dump into a server with a different sql_mode or charset, forgetting that loadDump needs local_infile, and running a dump on the primary during peak time. Use a replica or a quiet window and run the compatibility check first.
codeExamples:
util.checkForServerUpgrade('root@old-db:3306', {targetVersion: '8.4.0'})
-- on the target before loading:
SET GLOBAL local_infile = ON;

-- OUTPUT:
-- The MySQL server at old-db:3306 ... 0 errors, 2 warnings (deprecated syntax found in 2 views)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Because dumps run in parallel, tune threads to the number of cores and the storage speed; more threads than disks can slow things down. Compare timing between mysqldump and the shell utility on the same data.
codeExamples:
-- 100 GB database, same host
-- mysqldump | gzip   : 3 h 20 min dump,  9 h restore
-- util.dumpInstance  : 22 min dump,       41 min restore (8 threads, zstd)

SELECT ROUND(100 * 1024 / (41 * 60), 1) AS restore_mb_per_s;

-- OUTPUT:
-- restore_mb_per_s
-- 41.6

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a cluster in three commands, and a status check you can put in a monitoring script.
codeExamples:
dba.configureInstance('root@db1:3306')
var cluster = dba.createCluster('prod')
cluster.addInstance('root@db2:3306')
print(cluster.status({extended: 0}).defaultReplicaSet.status)

-- OUTPUT:
-- OK_NO_TOLERANCE      (becomes OK after adding a third instance)

topics.name: Connecting to MySQL & Basic CLI Commands

beginner.content:
Introduction

The mysql command-line client connects to a server with host, port, user and password, then accepts SQL ending in ; plus client commands such as status and exit.
codeExamples:
# Connect (-p prompts for the password; never put it on the command line in real life)
mysql -h localhost -P 3306 -u root -p
mysql> SELECT CURRENT_USER();

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | CURRENT_USER() |
-- +----------------+
-- | root@localhost |
-- +----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Every task, from a quick check to a restore, starts with a connection. Knowing the handful of CLI commands makes you productive on any server, even without a GUI.
codeExamples:
mysql> SHOW DATABASES;          -- list schemas
mysql> USE mysql;                -- choose one
mysql> SHOW TABLES LIKE 'user';  -- list tables matching a pattern

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------------+
-- | Tables_in_mysql (user) |
-- +------------------------+
-- | user                   |
-- +------------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Admins run one-off commands with -e, pipe SQL files with <, and connect over a UNIX socket locally or TLS remotely.
codeExamples:
# Run a statement and exit
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) AS dbs FROM information_schema.schemata"
# Run a script file
mysql -u root -p shop < create_schema.sql

-- OUTPUT (example, first command):
-- +-----+
-- | dbs |
-- +-----+
-- |   6 |
-- +-----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   mysql -h HOST -P PORT -u USER -p [DB]
        │
        ├─ local  : UNIX socket / named pipe (no network)
        └─ remote : TCP 3306 (+ TLS)
              ▼
   mysql> statement ;   ──► result table ──► exit / quit / Ctrl+D

Fresher Notes

  • Connect with mysql -u root -p and type the password. Use -h for host and -P for port.
  • Useful commands: SHOW DATABASES;, USE db;, SHOW TABLES;, DESCRIBE t;, EXIT.
  • Every SQL statement ends with a semicolon.

Worked Example 1

Run a script file.
codeExamples:
mysql> SOURCE C:/scripts/seed.sql;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 3 rows affected (0.01 sec)
-- Records: 3  Duplicates: 0  Warnings: 0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Show connection details.
codeExamples:
STATUS;

-- OUTPUT: (trimmed)
-- Connection id:   12
-- Current database: school
-- Connection:      localhost via TCP/IP
-- Server version:  8.0.36

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Connect and show who you are.
codeExamples:
mysql -u root -p
SELECT USER(), CURRENT_USER(), DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- USER()         | CURRENT_USER() | DATABASE()
-- root@localhost | root@localhost | NULL

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Run a statement without opening the shell and print vertically.
codeExamples:
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT id, name FROM school.students WHERE id=1\G"

-- OUTPUT:
-- *************************** 1. row ***************************
--   id: 1
-- name: Abaji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works
