The CLI reads your input, splits it at the delimiter (; by default), sends each statement, and prints results. Lines starting with a backslash are client commands, not SQL, so they are handled locally (\G, \s, \u).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common patterns: run one statement (-e), run a script file (< or SOURCE), print vertically (\G), page output, and write results to a file with tee.
codeExamples:
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders"
mysql -u root -p shop < seed.sql
mysql -u root -p -N -B -e "SELECT id, name FROM shop.customers" > customers.tsv
mysql> pager less -S;
mysql> tee session.log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 120450        (and customers.tsv contains tab-separated rows without headers)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fast, scriptable, available everywhere, tiny footprint, works over SSH.
codeExamples:
mysql> status                   -- client command: connection details
mysql> \G                         -- end a statement with \G for vertical output
mysql> SELECT VERSION()\G

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- *************************** 1. row ***************************
-- VERSION(): 8.0.36

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no visual aids; typos in multi-line statements are painful; a password on the command line leaks into history and process lists.
codeExamples:
# Warning shown when you pass the password inline
mysql -u root -pSecret123 -e "SELECT 1"

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysql: [Warning] Using a password on the command line interface can be insecure.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: accounts are host-specific ('root'@'localhost' is not 'root'@'%'), and a failed login is reported with the same generic message for security.
codeExamples:
mysql -h db01 -u root -p
# wrong password or wrong host entry in the grant tables:

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'root'@'10.0.0.5' (using password: YES)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use option files (login paths via mysql_config_editor) instead of inline passwords, require TLS for remote use, and give humans and applications separate accounts. Log in as root only for administration.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Run one statement without entering the shell: mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT 1"; run a script with mysql -u root -p db < file.sql.
  • Use \G instead of ; for vertical output of wide rows.
  • Do not put the password on the command line (-pPASSWORD); it appears in history and process lists. Use a login path or option file.

Senior Notes

  • Use mysql_config_editor to store credentials securely (login paths) for scripts.
  • Use dedicated, least-privilege accounts and TLS for remote connections.
  • For application connections use JDBC/driver URLs with timeouts and TLS options, never root.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: typing the password on the command line (visible in history), forgetting the semicolon (prompt changes to ->), and pasting a script that includes DELIMITER changes. Use mysql_config_editor to store credentials safely.
codeExamples:
mysql_config_editor set --login-path=shop --host=db.internal --user=shop_app --password
mysql --login-path=shop -e "SELECT 1"

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1          (no password appears on the command line or in shell history)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For large outputs avoid buffering everything: --quick streams rows, and -B batch mode plus -N removes formatting overhead.
codeExamples:
mysql --quick -B -N -e "SELECT * FROM shop.events" | gzip > events.tsv.gz

-- OUTPUT:
-- events.tsv.gz  (streamed, constant client memory)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a repeatable smoke test used after each deployment: connect with the application login, check version, row counts and replication state.
codeExamples:
mysql --login-path=shop -e "
SELECT @@version AS version, @@read_only AS read_only;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders FROM shop.orders;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G" | head -20

-- OUTPUT:
-- version | read_only
-- 8.0.36  | 0
-- orders
-- 612044

beginner.content:
Introduction

A MySQL account is 'user'@'host'. CREATE USER makes it; GRANT gives privileges. By default a new user can do almost nothing.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'app'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'Str0ng#Pass1';    -- account + password
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON shop.* TO 'app'@'localhost';       -- limited rights
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'app'@'localhost';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | Grants for app@localhost                                            |
-- +---------------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO app@localhost                                 |
-- | GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON shop.* TO app@localhost             |
-- +---------------------------------------------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Using root in an application means one bug or injection can drop everything. Separate accounts give auditing and blast-radius control.
codeExamples:
-- App user cannot drop tables
-- (connected as app)
DROP TABLE shop.orders;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): DROP command denied to user 'app'@'localhost' for table 'orders'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical set: an admin user, an application read-write user, a read-only reporting user, and a backup user, each restricted by host.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'report'@'10.0.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'R3port#Pwd';    -- any 10.0.x.x host
GRANT SELECT ON shop.* TO 'report'@'10.0.%';
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE user IN ('app','report');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-----------+
-- | user   | host      |
-- +--------+-----------+
-- | app    | localhost |
-- | report | 10.0.%    |
-- +--------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   CREATE USER 'app'@'host'  ──►  mysql.user (account)
   GRANT priv ON db.tbl      ──►  privilege tables
   login attempt: (user, host, password) ─► match account ─► check privileges per statement

Fresher Notes

  • Create a user with CREATE USER, then give permissions with GRANT.
  • A MySQL account is user plus host: app@localhost and app@% are different accounts.
  • Never use root for applications.

Worked Example 1

Role-based setup.

Worked Example 2

List users.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host, plugin FROM mysql.user WHERE user IN ('report','app');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- user   | host      | plugin
-- app    | localhost | caching_sha2_password
-- report | localhost | caching_sha2_password

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create a read-only reporting user and verify.

Practice Exercise 2

Try a forbidden write as that user.
codeExamples:
-- connected as report@localhost
INSERT INTO school.students VALUES (9,'X');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): INSERT command denied to user 'report'@'localhost' for table 'students'

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An account row lives in mysql.user as user + host, with an authentication plugin and credential. At login the server picks the most specific matching host entry, then checks the password; grants (global, schema, table, column, routine) are evaluated per statement.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: authentication plugins, password policy, resource limits, TLS requirements, default roles. Account locking disables login but keeps grants.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fine-grained privileges, per-host restriction, password policies, account locking and expiry.
codeExamples:
ALTER USER 'report'@'10.0.%' PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL 90 DAY;   -- force rotation
ALTER USER 'app'@'localhost' ACCOUNT LOCK;                        -- disable quickly

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: account per host combination multiplies entries; password handling needs care; revoking requires knowing what was granted.
codeExamples:
-- 'app'@'%' and 'app'@'localhost' are two different accounts
CREATE USER 'app'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'x';
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE user = 'app';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-----------+
-- | user | host      |
-- +------+-----------+
-- | app  | %         |
-- | app  | localhost |
-- +------+-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: creating an existing user errors; user names max 32 characters; the default plugin in 8.0 is caching_sha2_password, which older drivers may not support.

Architect's Notes

Apply least privilege: one account per application, minimal grants, host restrictions, strong plugin (caching_sha2_password), and rotate credentials from a secrets manager. Prefer roles for groups of privileges (MySQL 8.0).

Mid-Level Notes

  • Grant only what is needed: GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON shop.* TO ....
  • Remember FLUSH PRIVILEGES is not needed after CREATE USER/GRANT; only after editing grant tables directly.
  • Use ALTER USER ... PASSWORD EXPIRE and password policies for rotation.

Senior Notes

  • Authentication plugin matters: caching_sha2_password is the 8.0 default; older drivers may need mysql_native_password.
  • Use roles to manage groups of privileges and reduce drift.
  • Separate accounts for app, migrations (DDL), read-only reporting and admin.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: creating '%' hosts for everything, granting ALL, sharing one account across services, and forgetting that 'user'@'localhost' and 'user'@'%' are separate accounts with separate passwords.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE user = 'app';
-- connecting from 10.0.1.5 with a typo in the host pattern:
-- ERROR 1045 (28000): Access denied for user 'app'@'10.0.2.5' (using password: YES)

-- OUTPUT:
-- user | host
-- app  | 10.0.1.%        (no match for 10.0.2.5)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Too many unused accounts is also a performance and security cost (the grant tables are cached). List accounts and last-use through the Performance Schema and remove stale ones.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world account set for one application: runtime, migration and read-only reporting users, each tightly scoped.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The server reads settings from an option file (my.cnf on Linux, my.ini on Windows). The data directory (datadir) holds InnoDB files, system tables, logs and one folder per schema.
codeExamples:
# /etc/mysql/my.cnf  (or my.ini on Windows)
[mysqld]
port            = 3306
datadir         = /var/lib/mysql           # where data files live
character-set-server = utf8mb4
innodb_buffer_pool_size = 1G                # main memory cache

-- OUTPUT:
-- (no output; file is read at the next server start)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Defaults suit a laptop, not production. Tuning memory, logging, character sets and durability to your workload requires editing configuration.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'datadir';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_buffer_pool_size';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+-----------------+
-- | Variable_name | Value           |
-- +---------------+-----------------+
-- | datadir       | /var/lib/mysql/ |
-- +---------------+-----------------+
-- | innodb_buffer_pool_size | 134217728 |

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

DBAs set values in the file for permanence and use SET PERSIST (8.0) for runtime changes that survive restarts, written to mysqld-auto.cnf.
codeExamples:
SET PERSIST max_connections = 300;                 -- change now and keep after restart
SELECT variable_name, variable_value FROM performance_schema.persisted_variables;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+----------------+
-- | VARIABLE_NAME   | VARIABLE_VALUE |
-- +-----------------+----------------+
-- | max_connections | 300            |
-- +-----------------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   my.cnf  ──read at start──►  mysqld ──► datadir
   [client] [mysqld]                      ├─ ibdata1, undo_*, #innodb_redo
   precedence: /etc/my.cnf                ├─ mysql/ (system tables)
   ~/.my.cnf < command line               ├─ shop/ (per-schema files .ibd)
                                          └─ binlog.*, error log

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL reads settings from a config file (my.cnf / my.ini) when it starts.
  • The data directory holds databases as folders and files; find it with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE "datadir".
  • Do not edit or delete files in the data directory while the server runs.

Worked Example 1

A minimal config file.
codeExamples:
[mysqld]
character-set-server = utf8mb4
innodb_buffer_pool_size = 2G
slow_query_log = 1
long_query_time = 1

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'slow_query_log'; => ON

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

See where each variable came from.
codeExamples:
SELECT variable_name, variable_source FROM performance_schema.variables_info
WHERE variable_name IN ('max_connections','slow_query_log');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- max_connections | PERSISTED
-- slow_query_log  | CONFIG

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Show important server settings.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('innodb_buffer_pool_size','max_connections','datadir');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- innodb_buffer_pool_size | 134217728
-- max_connections         | 151
-- datadir                 | C:\ProgramData\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\Data

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Change a setting and persist it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

At startup mysqld merges option files in a fixed order (global, then user, then command line); later sources override earlier ones. The data directory holds one folder per schema, .ibd tablespace files, redo logs, undo tablespaces, the binary logs and the system tablespace.
codeExamples:
mysqld --verbose --help | grep -A1 "Default options"
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('datadir','innodb_data_home_dir','log_bin_basename','log_error');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Default options are read from the following files in the given order: /etc/my.cnf /etc/mysql/my.cnf ~/.my.cnf
-- datadir          | /var/lib/mysql/
-- log_bin_basename | /var/lib/mysql/binlog
-- log_error        | /var/log/mysql/error.log

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variables have scopes: GLOBAL, SESSION and PERSIST. Dynamic variables change at runtime; static ones need a restart. SET PERSIST writes mysqld-auto.cnf, which survives restarts without editing the main file.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: many knobs, dynamic variables change without restart, per-schema folders and files are easy to locate.
codeExamples:
# Look inside the data directory
ls /var/lib/mysql

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- auto.cnf  binlog.000001  ib_buffer_pool  ibdata1  ib_logfile0  mysql  mysql.ibd  shop  sys  ...

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: wrong values can slow or crash the server; settings are spread across files, command line and persisted config; copying files by hand corrupts data.
codeExamples:
-- Which file set which value? (8.0)
SELECT variable_name, variable_source, variable_path
FROM performance_schema.variables_info WHERE variable_name = 'max_connections';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------+-----------------+----------------------+
-- | VARIABLE_NAME   | VARIABLE_SOURCE | VARIABLE_PATH        |
-- +-----------------+-----------------+----------------------+
-- | max_connections | PERSISTED       | /var/lib/mysql/mysqld-auto.cnf |
-- +-----------------+-----------------+----------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: static variables (like innodb_log_file_size in old versions or datadir) need a restart, and a wrong option name stops the server from starting.

Architect's Notes

Keep configuration in version control and templated per instance size; set innodb_buffer_pool_size to about 60-75 percent of RAM on a dedicated host; place data, redo and binlogs on suitable disks. Never edit or copy datadir files while the server runs.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Settings can be changed at runtime with SET GLOBAL (lost on restart) or persisted with SET PERSIST (8.0).
  • Important settings: innodb_buffer_pool_size, max_connections, character_set_server, log_bin, slow_query_log.
  • Config sections: [mysqld] for the server, [client] for clients.

Senior Notes

  • Size the buffer pool to roughly 60-75% of RAM on a dedicated host; too large swaps, too small causes disk reads.
  • Keep config in version control; use performance_schema.variables_info to see where each value came from.
  • Put data, redo logs and binlogs on fast, separate, monitored storage with free-space alerts.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: editing the wrong file (an earlier file is overridden by a later one), changing a static variable and expecting immediate effect, and placing the data directory on the root disk that fills up. Find the effective source of any setting.
codeExamples:
SELECT variable_name, variable_source, variable_path FROM performance_schema.variables_info WHERE variable_name IN ('innodb_buffer_pool_size','max_connections');

-- OUTPUT:
-- variable_name           | variable_source | variable_path
-- innodb_buffer_pool_size | CONFIG          | /etc/mysql/conf.d/tuning.cnf
-- max_connections         | PERSISTED       | /var/lib/mysql/mysqld-auto.cnf

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Put data, redo/undo logs and binary logs on fast, separate, monitored volumes, and watch free space. A full disk stops writes immediately.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_schema, ROUND(SUM(data_length + index_length)/1073741824, 2) AS gb FROM information_schema.tables GROUP BY table_schema ORDER BY gb DESC LIMIT 3;
-- shell: df -h /var/lib/mysql

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_schema | gb
-- shop         | 184.30
-- analytics    |  96.12
-- /dev/nvme1n1  500G  312G  188G  63% /var/lib/mysql

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: keep config in version control and apply it with automation, with a health check that confirms the running values match the intended ones after each change.
codeExamples:
# conf.d/90-prod.cnf (managed by Ansible)
[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size = 24G
innodb_redo_log_capacity = 8G
slow_query_log = ON
long_query_time = 0.5
binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 604800

-- OUTPUT: (post-deploy check)
-- SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size/1073741824 AS bp_gb, @@slow_query_log, @@long_query_time;  =>  24 | 1 | 0.5

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL runs as a background service. On Linux use systemctl (mysql or mysqld), on Windows net start MySQL80 or the Services app. A clean stop flushes buffers and finishes transactions.
codeExamples:
sudo systemctl start mysql           # start now
sudo systemctl status mysql          # is it up?

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- * mysql.service - MySQL Community Server
--      Active: active (running) since Tue 2026-10-06 09:00:01 UTC; 5min ago

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You must restart after changing static options, patching or upgrading, and stop cleanly before maintenance so no data is lost and recovery is quick.
codeExamples:
sudo systemctl restart mysql         # stop then start
sudo systemctl enable mysql          # start automatically at boot
sudo systemctl is-enabled mysql

-- OUTPUT:
-- enabled

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Ops teams script restarts, check readiness before routing traffic, and use mysqladmin for a quick health ping.
codeExamples:
mysqladmin -u root -p ping          # is the server answering?
mysqladmin -u root -p shutdown       # graceful shutdown through the protocol

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysqld is alive

beginner.content:
Diagram

   systemctl start ─► mysqld ─► open data files ─► (crash recovery?) ─► accept clients
   systemctl stop  ─► stop new conns ─► flush dirty pages ─► checkpoint ─► exit
   kill -9 / power loss ──────────────────────────────────► recovery on next start

Fresher Notes

  • On Windows use Services (services.msc) or net start MySQL80 / net stop MySQL80.
  • On Linux use sudo systemctl start|stop|restart mysql (service name may be mysqld).
  • Check state with systemctl status mysql or by trying to connect.

Worked Example 1

Find the error log location.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_error';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name | Value
-- log_error     | C:\ProgramData\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\Data\HOST.err

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Confirm uptime after restart.

Practice Exercise 1

Stop and start the service (Windows PowerShell).
codeExamples:
net stop MySQL80
net start MySQL80

-- OUTPUT:
-- The MySQL80 service was stopped successfully.
-- The MySQL80 service was started successfully.

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Shut down from SQL.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

On start mysqld reads config, opens the data directory, runs InnoDB crash recovery if the last shutdown was unclean (replaying redo and rolling back uncommitted work), then accepts connections. On a clean shutdown it flushes dirty pages and writes a checkpoint, so the next start is quick.
codeExamples:
sudo systemctl stop mysql
sudo systemctl start mysql
sudo journalctl -u mysql --since "5 minutes ago" | tail -5

-- OUTPUT: (example log lines)
-- [InnoDB] Starting crash recovery from checkpoint LSN=118234567     (only after an unclean stop)
-- [InnoDB] Apply batch completed
-- [Server] /usr/sbin/mysqld: ready for connections.

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to control it: the service manager, SHUTDOWN from SQL, mysqladmin shutdown, and RESTART (8.0.4+). Windows uses net start/stop or the Services console.
codeExamples:
mysqladmin -u root -p shutdown
net stop MySQL80 & net start MySQL80
-- from SQL (needs the SHUTDOWN privilege):
RESTART;
SHUTDOWN;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected   (server restarts; client reconnects automatically on the next statement)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: systemd restarts crashed servers, logs to the journal, and start-on-boot is one command.
codeExamples:
sudo journalctl -u mysql -n 3 --no-pager     # recent service log lines

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Oct 06 09:00:01 db01 systemd[1]: Starting MySQL Community Server...
-- Oct 06 09:00:05 db01 systemd[1]: Started MySQL Community Server.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: killing the process (kill -9) or power loss forces crash recovery on the next start, which can take minutes with big redo logs.
codeExamples:
# After an unclean stop the error log shows InnoDB recovery
sudo tail -n 2 /var/log/mysql/error.log

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- [Note] [MY-012551] [InnoDB] Database was not shut down normally!
-- [Note] [MY-013575] [InnoDB] Starting crash recovery.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a stop waits for open transactions, and the unit name, paths and the root requirement differ across distros and Windows.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_fast_shutdown';   -- 1 = quick, 2 = crash-like, 0 = full purge

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name        | Value |
-- +----------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_fast_shutdown | 1     |
-- +----------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Always stop gracefully, drain connections at the load balancer first, and set a long enough systemd TimeoutStopSec for big buffer pools. In HA setups promote a replica instead of restarting the primary when you can.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Prefer a clean shutdown (SHUTDOWN or the service stop) so InnoDB flushes and no crash recovery is needed.
  • If the server will not start, read the error log first.
  • mysqld --initialize creates a new data directory; do not run it on an existing one.

Senior Notes

  • innodb_fast_shutdown=0 before major upgrades forces a full purge and change-buffer merge for a cleaner upgrade.
  • Rolling restarts of replicas, then switchover of the primary, minimise downtime.
  • Watch for long transactions before maintenance; shutdown waits for them to finish or roll back.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: killing mysqld with kill -9 (forces crash recovery and risks long startup), restarting during a long transaction rollback, and forgetting that a restart empties the buffer pool cache.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Warm up faster after restart by dumping and reloading the buffer pool content. Without it, queries are slow until the hot pages are read from disk again.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world rolling restart in a replicated setup: restart replicas first, switch over the primary, then restart the old primary, so the application sees only a short blip.
codeExamples:
-- 1. for each replica: STOP REPLICA; (restart server); START REPLICA; check lag = 0
-- 2. planned switchover with MySQL Shell
var c = dba.getCluster('prod'); c.setPrimaryInstance('db2:3306');
-- 3. restart the old primary db1, it rejoins as a secondary

-- OUTPUT:
-- Primary switched to db2:3306 in 4 seconds

topics.name: Database Operations: CREATE, SHOW, USE & DROP

beginner.content:
Introduction

CREATE DATABASE makes a schema, SHOW DATABASES lists them, USE selects the default one for the session and DROP DATABASE deletes it with everything inside.
codeExamples:
CREATE DATABASE shop CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;   -- new schema
SHOW DATABASES;                                                          -- list all
USE shop;                                                                -- make current
SELECT DATABASE() AS current_db;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | current_db |
-- +------------+
-- | shop       |
-- +------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Each application needs its own namespace, character set and privileges. Dropping and recreating test databases is a daily developer task.
codeExamples:
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS shop;      -- safe to re-run: no error if it exists
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS scratch;           -- safe cleanup

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected, 1 warning (0.00 sec)   -- warning: database exists
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected, 1 warning (0.00 sec)  -- warning: database doesn't exist

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

CI pipelines create a fresh schema per test run; production DBAs create schemas with an explicit charset and revoke DROP from applications.
codeExamples:
SHOW CREATE DATABASE shop;                -- exact definition incl. charset

-- OUTPUT:
-- CREATE DATABASE shop /*!40100 DEFAULT CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci */
-- /*!80016 DEFAULT ENCRYPTION='N' */

beginner.content:
Diagram

   CREATE DATABASE ─► SHOW DATABASES ─► USE db ─► work (tables...) ─► DROP DATABASE
                                          │
                       session default schema (DATABASE())

Fresher Notes

  • CREATE DATABASE name; makes a database; SHOW DATABASES; lists them; USE name; selects one; DROP DATABASE name; deletes it with everything inside.
  • Add IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS so scripts can be re-run.
  • DROP is permanent. There is no undo unless you have a backup.

Worked Example 1

Idempotent setup script.

Worked Example 2

Pattern search of databases.
codeExamples:
SHOW DATABASES LIKE 'd%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Database (d%)
-- demo

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create a database with utf8mb4, use it and show the definition.

Practice Exercise 2

Drop it safely.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A schema is a directory under the data directory plus a row in the data dictionary. CREATE DATABASE adds both and stores default charset and collation; DROP DATABASE deletes every table file inside it and cannot be rolled back.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: IF NOT EXISTS / IF EXISTS, charset/collation, encryption default, and ALTER DATABASE to change defaults (existing tables keep their own settings).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one-line isolation, per-schema privileges and backups, cheap to create.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: DROP DATABASE is instant and irreversible (DDL auto-commits), and a missing USE sends statements to the wrong schema.

Limitations

Limitations: names up to 64 characters, case sensitivity follows the OS, and a database cannot be renamed (RENAME DATABASE was removed); use dump/restore or move tables.

Architect's Notes

Create schemas via migrations with explicit charset and collation, not by hand. Deny DROP on production for application users and require a backup check before any DROP. Qualify names (db.table) in scripts rather than relying on USE.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Set charset and collation at creation: CREATE DATABASE app CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;.
  • Use SELECT DATABASE(); to confirm the current database before running DML.
  • Grant privileges per database to limit damage.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid giving applications DROP on production schemas.
  • In migrations, never rely on DROP DATABASE for resets outside test environments; guard with environment checks.
  • Case sensitivity of database names depends on OS and lower_case_table_names; set it at initialization and keep it consistent across environments.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting USE and creating tables in the wrong schema, DROP DATABASE on the wrong connection, and case-sensitivity differences between Linux (case sensitive) and Windows (insensitive) names.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATABASE();                        -- always check before DDL/DML
DROP DATABASE shop;                         -- no confirmation, no undo

-- safer habit: rename tables to _old first, drop later, and keep a verified backup
RENAME TABLE shop.orders TO shop.orders_old_20260501;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Dropping a database with many large tables can stall the server while files are removed. Drop big tables one at a time in a quiet window, then the empty schema.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: per-environment databases created by an idempotent script, with a guard that refuses to drop anything unless the environment flag allows it.

beginner.content:
Introduction

CREATE TABLE defines columns and constraints, SHOW TABLES lists tables, DESCRIBE (or SHOW COLUMNS) shows a table's structure.
codeExamples:
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS shop; USE shop;
CREATE TABLE customer (
    id         INT          NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,    -- surrogate key
    name       VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
    email      VARCHAR(80)  UNIQUE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP    DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,  -- auto-filled
    PRIMARY KEY (id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
SHOW TABLES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | Tables_in_shop |
-- +----------------+
-- | customer       |
-- +----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You must define a structure before storing rows. Clear types and constraints in the CREATE statement prevent bad data later.

Real-Time Use

Developers copy a table's shape with CREATE TABLE ... LIKE, and capture the exact DDL with SHOW CREATE TABLE for version control.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customer_archive LIKE customer;    -- same columns and indexes, no data
SHOW CREATE TABLE customer_archive\G

-- OUTPUT (trimmed):
-- Create Table: CREATE TABLE customer_archive (
--   id int NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
--   name varchar(50) NOT NULL,
--   ...
--   PRIMARY KEY (id), UNIQUE KEY email (email)
-- ) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4

beginner.content:
Diagram

   CREATE TABLE ─► definition stored in data dictionary
                ─► .ibd file created (file-per-table)
   SHOW TABLES    : names          DESCRIBE : columns
   SHOW CREATE TABLE : full DDL    INFORMATION_SCHEMA.COLUMNS : queryable

Fresher Notes

  • CREATE TABLE defines columns and types; SHOW TABLES lists tables; DESCRIBE t shows columns.
  • Always add a primary key. AUTO_INCREMENT generates ids.
  • SHOW CREATE TABLE t prints the exact DDL.

Worked Example 1

updated_at changes automatically.

Worked Example 2

See the next auto-increment value.
codeExamples:
SELECT AUTO_INCREMENT FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=DATABASE() AND table_name='employees';

-- OUTPUT:
-- AUTO_INCREMENT
-- 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create employees with audit columns and describe it.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
  salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
DESCRIBE employees;

-- OUTPUT: (trimmed)
-- Field | Type          | Null | Key | Default
-- id    | bigint        | NO   | PRI | NULL
-- name  | varchar(60)   | NO   |     | NULL
-- salary| decimal(10,2) | NO   |     | 0.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Clone the structure into a backup table.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

CREATE TABLE writes a definition into the data dictionary and creates an .ibd tablespace file (file-per-table). The primary key defines the clustered index; secondary indexes are separate B-trees that carry the primary key.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id BIGINT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
  dept_id INT NOT NULL,
  salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  KEY idx_dept (dept_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4;
DESCRIBE employees;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Field   | Type            | Null | Key | Default           | Extra
-- id      | bigint unsigned | NO   | PRI | NULL              | auto_increment
-- name    | varchar(60)     | NO   |     | NULL              |
-- dept_id | int             | NO   | MUL | NULL              |

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to create tables: from scratch, LIKE (copies structure and indexes), AS SELECT (copies data, not indexes), and TEMPORARY. SHOW commands inspect them.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative structure, rich options (engine, charset, comments), self-documenting via DESCRIBE.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customer_copy AS SELECT id, name FROM customer;   -- shape + data from a query
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_copied FROM customer_copy;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+
-- | rows_copied |
-- +-------------+
-- |           0 |
-- +-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT does not copy keys or indexes, and a poor first design is costly to change on big tables.
codeExamples:
DESCRIBE customer_copy;           -- note: no PRI key, no AUTO_INCREMENT

-- OUTPUT (trimmed):
-- | id   | int         | NO | | 0    |   |
-- | name | varchar(50) | NO | | NULL |   |

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: max 4096 columns (about 1017 for InnoDB), at most 16 columns per index, row size 65,535 bytes, and a table with an existing name raises an error unless IF NOT EXISTS is used.

Architect's Notes

Design the table on paper first: key choice, types, nullability, charset. Keep DDL in migration files, name constraints explicitly, and set ENGINE and COMMENT where it helps. Use IF NOT EXISTS only in idempotent bootstrap scripts, not to hide drift.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Specify ENGINE=InnoDB (default) and a charset explicitly in important scripts.
  • Create tables from queries with CREATE TABLE new AS SELECT ... (no keys copied) or CREATE TABLE new LIKE old (structure and indexes).
  • Use meaningful constraints at creation: NOT NULL, DEFAULT, UNIQUE, CHECK.

Senior Notes

  • Think about indexes at table creation; adding them on a big table later is slower and riskier.
  • Choose types for the long run: INT overflow at 2.1 billion has taken down real systems; use BIGINT where growth is plausible.
  • Add audit columns (created_at, updated_at) and consider soft delete, tenant id and optimistic-lock version where relevant.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no primary key, oversized types, no NOT NULL, using reserved words as names, and creating a table AS SELECT then forgetting it has no keys or indexes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Choose types for the long run: an INT id overflows at about 2.1 billion, and a wide VARCHAR(255) in every row costs cache. Check growth against the type limit.
codeExamples:
SELECT auto_increment, ROUND(auto_increment / 4294967295 * 100, 2) AS pct_of_unsigned_int
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' AND table_name = 'orders';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- auto_increment | pct_of_unsigned_int
--      912004113 | 21.23

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a table template with audit columns, soft delete and optimistic locking, applied to new tables so every table behaves the same.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE invoices (
  id BIGINT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  customer_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  total DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at DATETIME(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3),
  updated_at DATETIME(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3) ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3),
  deleted_at DATETIME(3) NULL,
  KEY idx_customer (customer_id, created_at)
);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

ALTER TABLE changes an existing table: add, modify or drop columns, indexes and constraints, rename things and change options. It is how schemas evolve.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20));
ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 AFTER name;   -- add column
ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL;                         -- change type
ALTER TABLE emp ADD INDEX idx_name (name);                                       -- add index
DESCRIBE emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+---------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
-- | Field  | Type          | Null | Key | Default | Extra |
-- +--------+---------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
-- | id     | int           | NO   | PRI | NULL    |       |
-- | name   | varchar(50)   | NO   | MUL | NULL    |       |
-- | salary | decimal(10,2) | NO   |     | 0.00    |       |
-- +--------+---------------+------+-----+---------+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Requirements change: a new field, a longer name, a new rule. Rebuilding the table by hand would be slow and error-prone.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE emp RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name;        -- 8.0 syntax
ALTER TABLE emp CHANGE COLUMN full_name emp_name VARCHAR(60);   -- rename + retype
ALTER TABLE emp DROP COLUMN salary;
SHOW COLUMNS FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
-- | Field    | Type        | Null | Key | Default | Extra |
-- +----------+-------------+------+-----+---------+-------+
-- | id       | int         | NO   | PRI | NULL    |       |
-- | emp_name | varchar(60) | YES  |     | NULL    |       |
-- +----------+-------------+------+-----+---------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Production migrations (Flyway, Liquibase, Rails/Django) are sequences of ALTER statements. Large tables use online DDL or tools like gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change.
codeExamples:
-- Ask for an online, non-blocking change; fail instead of silently locking
ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN dept_id INT, ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.02 sec)
-- Records: 0  Duplicates: 0  Warnings: 0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ALTER TABLE ... ADD / MODIFY / CHANGE / DROP / RENAME
        │
        ├─ INSTANT : change only metadata       (fast)
        ├─ INPLACE : rebuild inside engine      (online-ish)
        └─ COPY    : create new table, copy rows (slow, blocks)

Fresher Notes

  • ALTER TABLE changes an existing table: add, modify or drop columns, add indexes and constraints, rename.
  • Example: ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100);
  • Back up or test first; some changes rebuild the whole table.

Worked Example 1

Fail fast if the change is not online.

Worked Example 2

Rename a column and a table.

Practice Exercise 1

Add, modify and drop a column.

Practice Exercise 2

Add an index and a unique constraint.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

ALTER TABLE chooses an algorithm: INSTANT (metadata only), INPLACE (rebuilds in place, allows concurrent DML) or COPY (builds a new table and blocks writes). The operation and the version decide which is possible; adding a trailing column is usually INSTANT in 8.0.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common forms: add/drop/modify/rename columns, add/drop indexes and constraints, change engine, rename table, and add partitions. Several changes can be combined in one statement so the table is rebuilt only once.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE employees
  ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100) AFTER name,
  ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_email (email),
  RENAME COLUMN dept_id TO department_id,
  DROP COLUMN phone;
SHOW CREATE TABLE employees\G

-- OUTPUT:
-- (one table rebuild applies all four changes)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: keeps data while changing structure; INSTANT algorithm (8.0) adds a column in constant time; many ops run online.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(10), ALGORITHM=INSTANT;   -- metadata-only change

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: some alters rebuild the whole table (copy), blocking or slowing writes and needing extra disk; dropping a column loses data permanently.
codeExamples:
-- Changing a column type usually needs a full table copy
ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY emp_name TEXT, ALGORITHM=INPLACE;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1846 (0A000): ALGORITHM=INPLACE is not supported. Reason: Cannot change column type INPLACE. Try ALGORITHM=COPY.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL DDL is not transactional (it auto-commits and cannot be rolled back), a failed ALTER on a huge table is expensive, and replicas must also apply the change.

Architect's Notes

Explicitly state ALGORITHM and LOCK so a migration fails fast instead of locking production. For big tables use gh-ost or pt-osc, deploy in backward-compatible steps (add nullable, backfill, switch, drop later) and watch replica lag.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use ADD COLUMN ... AFTER col to place columns, MODIFY to change a type, CHANGE to rename and retype, DROP COLUMN to remove.
  • Specify ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE (or INSTANT) so MySQL fails instead of blocking if the change is not online.
  • Adding a NOT NULL column to a populated table needs a DEFAULT.

Senior Notes

  • Large-table changes: check online DDL support, run during low traffic, monitor replication lag, or use gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change.
  • ALGORITHM=INSTANT (8.0) adds columns without rebuilding, but only for supported operations.
  • Follow expand-contract: add new, dual-write, backfill, switch reads, then drop old in a later release.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: running a COPY alter on a huge production table at peak, adding NOT NULL without a default to a populated table, and dropping a column that old application versions still read. Ask the server to fail instead of blocking.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Monitor long alters and their replica impact. Online DDL runs concurrently with writes but replicas apply it serially, so lag can spike; use gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change with throttling on big tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, work_completed, work_estimated FROM performance_schema.events_stages_current WHERE event_name LIKE 'stage/innodb/alter%';
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name                          | work_completed | work_estimated
-- stage/innodb/alter table (read PK)  |        4120000 |       12000000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world expand/contract rename: never rename a column in place while old code runs. Add the new column, write both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name VARCHAR(120) NULL, ALGORITHM=INSTANT;
UPDATE users SET full_name = name WHERE full_name IS NULL AND id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000;   -- batched backfill
-- release N+1: application reads full_name
ALTER TABLE users DROP COLUMN name;                                                     -- release N+2

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 10000 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

DROP TABLE removes a table and its data. TRUNCATE TABLE empties it but keeps the structure. RENAME TABLE changes names atomically.

Why Do We Need This?

Cleaning test data, retiring old tables and swapping a rebuilt table into place are routine; each command has different speed, safety and side effects.
codeExamples:
-- DELETE vs TRUNCATE
INSERT INTO log_a (msg) VALUES ('p'),('q');
DELETE FROM log_a;                            -- row by row, can ROLLBACK, keeps counter
INSERT INTO log_a (msg) VALUES ('after');
SELECT id FROM log_a;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  4 |
-- +----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The classic zero-downtime swap: build a new table, then rename both in one atomic statement.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE log_new LIKE log_a;
RENAME TABLE log_a TO log_old, log_new TO log_a;    -- atomic swap
SHOW TABLES LIKE 'log%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------------------+
-- | Tables_in_shop (log%)      |
-- +----------------------------+
-- | log_a                      |
-- | log_old                    |
-- +----------------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

              rows   structure  rollback  triggers  speed   counter
   DELETE      yes     keep       yes      fire     slow    kept
   TRUNCATE    all     keep       NO       no       fast    reset
   DROP        all     removed    NO       no       fast    n/a
   RENAME      -       renamed    NO (atomic, instant)

Fresher Notes

  • DROP TABLE removes the table and its data. TRUNCATE TABLE removes all rows but keeps the table. RENAME TABLE changes the name.
  • TRUNCATE is faster than DELETE for emptying a table and resets AUTO_INCREMENT.
  • DROP and TRUNCATE cannot be rolled back (DDL auto-commits).

Worked Example 1

Atomic table swap.

Worked Example 2

DELETE can roll back but TRUNCATE cannot.

Practice Exercise 1

Compare DELETE and TRUNCATE on auto-increment.

Practice Exercise 2

Rename a table and verify.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DROP removes the table definition and its tablespace file. TRUNCATE is DDL: it drops and recreates the table (resetting AUTO_INCREMENT) instead of deleting rows one by one, so it is fast, takes a metadata lock and cannot be rolled back. DELETE writes undo and redo for every row.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE t (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, v INT);
INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES (1),(2),(3);
DELETE FROM t;  INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES (9);  SELECT id FROM t;     -- auto-increment continues
TRUNCATE TABLE t; INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES (9); SELECT id FROM t;    -- auto-increment resets

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 4
-- id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

RENAME TABLE renames atomically and can swap tables in one statement. Variants include moving a table to another schema and renaming multiple tables together.
codeExamples:
RENAME TABLE orders TO orders_old, orders_new TO orders;           -- atomic swap
RENAME TABLE shop.archive TO cold_storage.archive;                    -- move between schemas
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS tmp_import, tmp_stage;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: TRUNCATE is much faster than DELETE for all rows (drops and recreates), DROP frees disk, RENAME is atomic and instant.
codeExamples:
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS log_old;               -- no error if missing
SHOW TABLES LIKE 'log_old';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: TRUNCATE and DROP implicitly commit and cannot be rolled back; TRUNCATE does not fire DELETE triggers.

Limitations

Limitations: a table referenced by a foreign key cannot be dropped or truncated while the FK exists (unless FK checks are disabled, which is dangerous).

Architect's Notes

Make destructive commands unreachable for application accounts, take a backup or rename to *_old and drop later, and prefer RENAME swaps for rebuilds. Use DELETE with batches for partial purges on busy tables; use partition drops for time-based retention.

Mid-Level Notes

  • DELETE removes selected rows, can use WHERE and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE removes all rows, is DDL, and fires no delete triggers.
  • TRUNCATE is blocked on tables referenced by foreign keys (unless checks are disabled).
  • RENAME TABLE a TO b, c TO a swaps names atomically, useful for table swaps.

Senior Notes

  • The atomic rename swap pattern: build new, then RENAME TABLE live TO old, new TO live for near-instant cutover.
  • DROP on a very large table can stall the server (buffer pool and file removal); move or truncate data in chunks and drop during quiet periods.
  • Protect production with permissions, safe-delete workflows (rename to _deleted first, drop after a retention period).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: TRUNCATE on a table referenced by a foreign key (blocked), expecting TRUNCATE to roll back, and dropping a table that views or procedures depend on. Check dependencies and rename first.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Emptying a huge table: TRUNCATE is instant, while DELETE FROM runs for hours and bloats undo logs. When you need to keep some rows, copy the survivors, then swap names.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a safe drop procedure. Rename first, observe for a retention period (errors show up as "table not found"), then drop.

topics.name: Numeric Types: INT, BIGINT, SMALLINT & TINYINT

beginner.content:
Introduction

Integer types differ in storage and range: TINYINT 1 byte (-128..127), SMALLINT 2 (-32768..32767), MEDIUMINT 3, INT 4 (about +-2.1 billion), BIGINT 8 (about +-9.2e18). Add UNSIGNED to double the positive range.

Why Do We Need This?

Choosing the smallest type that fits saves disk, memory and index size; choosing too small causes overflow errors in production at the worst time.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO nums (t) VALUES (128);              -- one above TINYINT max

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1264 (22003): Out of range value for column 't' at row 1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Ages and flags use TINYINT UNSIGNED, counters use INT, user ids INT UNSIGNED, and event or order ids that may pass 4 billion use BIGINT.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE event_log (
    id     BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- will never run out
    status TINYINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,          -- 0..255 status code
    hits   INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
INSERT INTO event_log (status) VALUES (2),(1);
SELECT * FROM event_log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+------+
-- | id | status | hits |
-- +----+--------+------+
-- |  1 |      2 |    0 |
-- |  2 |      1 |    0 |
-- +----+--------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   type        bytes   signed range                    unsigned max
   TINYINT       1     -128 .. 127                     255
   SMALLINT      2     -32,768 .. 32,767               65,535
   MEDIUMINT     3     -8,388,608 .. 8,388,607         16,777,215
   INT           4     -2.147e9 .. 2.147e9             4.29e9
   BIGINT        8     -9.22e18 .. 9.22e18             1.84e19

Fresher Notes

  • Integer types differ in size: TINYINT 1 byte, SMALLINT 2, INT 4, BIGINT 8.
  • INT holds about -2.1 billion to 2.1 billion; UNSIGNED doubles the positive range to about 4.29 billion.
  • Use the smallest type that safely fits the data.

Worked Example 1

Integer division and modulo.
codeExamples:
SELECT 7 DIV 2 AS int_div, 7 / 2 AS real_div, 7 MOD 2 AS remainder;

-- OUTPUT:
-- int_div | real_div | remainder
--       3 |   3.5000 |         1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Check how close an id is to its limit.
codeExamples:
SELECT AUTO_INCREMENT, ROUND(AUTO_INCREMENT/2147483647*100,2) AS pct_used
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema=DATABASE() AND table_name='employees';

-- OUTPUT:
-- AUTO_INCREMENT | pct_used
--              2 |     0.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Show range behaviour of TINYINT.

Practice Exercise 2

Find the storage size of each integer type through arithmetic of the range.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Integer types are fixed width: TINYINT 1 byte, SMALLINT 2, MEDIUMINT 3, INT 4, BIGINT 8, stored in two's complement. UNSIGNED shifts the range to start at 0. The type decides how many keys fit in a 16 KB index page, so it directly affects cache efficiency.
codeExamples:
SELECT -128 AS tinyint_min, 127 AS tinyint_max, 255 AS tinyint_unsigned_max,
       -2147483648 AS int_min, 2147483647 AS int_max, 4294967295 AS int_unsigned_max,
       9223372036854775807 AS bigint_max;

-- OUTPUT:
-- tinyint_min | tinyint_max | tinyint_unsigned_max | int_min     | int_max    | int_unsigned_max | bigint_max
--        -128 |         127 |                  255 | -2147483648 | 2147483647 |       4294967295 | 9223372036854775807

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Declare ranges deliberately: TINYINT UNSIGNED for 0-255 codes, INT UNSIGNED for ids up to 4.29 billion, BIGINT UNSIGNED for very large counters. Display width (INT(11)) is deprecated and does not change storage.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: exact, fast arithmetic, tiny storage, great for keys and counters. UNSIGNED doubles the max for non-negative data.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE u8 (x TINYINT UNSIGNED);       -- 0..255 in the same 1 byte
INSERT INTO u8 VALUES (255);
SELECT x, x + 1 AS next_value FROM u8;        -- arithmetic is done in a wider type

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+------------+
-- | x   | next_value |
-- +-----+------------+
-- | 255 |        256 |
-- +-----+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: bigger types cost space in every index; the display width in INT(11) is meaningless (it affects nothing, deprecated in 8.0).

Limitations

Limitations: in strict mode (default) out-of-range inserts fail; with strict mode off MySQL silently clips to the max, hiding bugs. AUTO_INCREMENT stops at the type's max and then errors.

Architect's Notes

Use BIGINT UNSIGNED for ids of anything that grows unbounded; use the smallest type for lookup columns, since every secondary index copies the PK. Never rely on INT(N) display width, and keep sql_mode strict.

Mid-Level Notes

  • INT(11) does not mean 11 digits; the number is only a display width hint (deprecated in 8.0).
  • Out-of-range values error in strict mode and are clamped silently otherwise.
  • Use BIGINT for ids that may exceed 2 billion rows or for counters and money in minor units.

Senior Notes

  • Primary-key size is copied into every secondary index, so INT vs BIGINT affects index size and cache efficiency.
  • Plan id exhaustion: monitor AUTO_INCREMENT against the type maximum.
  • BOOLEAN is just TINYINT(1); do not store status codes there if more than two values are possible.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: INT primary keys on tables that will exceed 2.1 billion rows (ids stop with a duplicate-key error), UNSIGNED arithmetic that goes negative (error), and confusing INT(11) with a digit limit. Out of range values fail in strict mode and are clamped otherwise.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Smaller integers mean smaller indexes: every secondary index entry repeats the primary key. Switching an id from BIGINT to INT halves that overhead. Watch id growth against the limit and migrate before 70%.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, auto_increment, ROUND(auto_increment / 2147483647 * 100, 1) AS pct_of_int_max
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' AND auto_increment IS NOT NULL ORDER BY auto_increment DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | auto_increment | pct_of_int_max
-- events     |     1612004113 | 75.1      (plan the BIGINT migration now)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: widening a primary key online. Add the new column, backfill in batches, switch, then drop, or use ALTER with INPLACE where allowed. Foreign keys must be changed in lockstep.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE events MODIFY id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, ALGORITHM=COPY;   -- locks writes: only on small tables
-- large tables: gh-ost --alter="MODIFY id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT" --execute

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1612004113 rows affected  (or: gh-ost migration finished)

beginner.content:
Introduction

DECIMAL(p,s) is exact fixed-point (p total digits, s after the point) for money. FLOAT (4 bytes) and DOUBLE (8 bytes) are approximate binary floating point for scientific data.

Why Do We Need This?

Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums drift. Accounting must be exact to the paisa, so it uses DECIMAL.
codeExamples:
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3                    AS decimal_equal,        -- literals are DECIMAL
       CAST(0.1 AS DOUBLE) + CAST(0.2 AS DOUBLE) = CAST(0.3 AS DOUBLE) AS double_equal;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+--------------+
-- | decimal_equal | double_equal |
-- +---------------+--------------+
-- |             1 |            0 |
-- +---------------+--------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Prices, balances and tax use DECIMAL(12,2) or DECIMAL(19,4); measurements, coordinates and ML scores use DOUBLE or FLOAT.

Diagram

   DECIMAL(10,2)           FLOAT / DOUBLE
   digits stored exactly   binary fraction, approximate
   12345678.90             0.1 -> 0.100000000000000005551...
   money, tax, balances    sensors, GPS, statistics
   slower, bigger          fast, compact, IEEE-754

Fresher Notes

  • DECIMAL(10,2) is exact and ideal for money. FLOAT and DOUBLE are approximate binary numbers for science and measurements.
  • DECIMAL(p,s): p total digits, s digits after the decimal point.
  • Never store money in FLOAT or DOUBLE.

Worked Example 1

Sum 1000 times 0.1 with each type.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(0.1) AS exact FROM (SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns LIMIT 10) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- exact
-- 1.0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Overflow is an error.

Practice Exercise 1

Show the floating-point error.
codeExamples:
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 AS decimal_eq, CAST(0.1 AS DOUBLE) + CAST(0.2 AS DOUBLE) = CAST(0.3 AS DOUBLE) AS double_eq;

-- OUTPUT:
-- decimal_eq | double_eq
--          1 |         0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

DECIMAL rounds on insert.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

FLOAT (4 bytes) and DOUBLE (8 bytes) store IEEE-754 binary fractions, so many decimal values (0.1) are approximations. DECIMAL stores decimal digits exactly (in packed groups of 9 digits per 4 bytes) and does exact arithmetic, at some CPU and space cost.
codeExamples:
SELECT CAST(0.1 AS DOUBLE) + CAST(0.2 AS DOUBLE) AS dbl_sum, 0.1 + 0.2 AS decimal_sum, (CAST(0.1 AS DOUBLE) + CAST(0.2 AS DOUBLE)) = 0.3 AS dbl_equals, (0.1 + 0.2) = 0.3 AS dec_equals;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dbl_sum             | decimal_sum | dbl_equals | dec_equals
-- 0.30000000000000004 | 0.3         |          0 |          1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Declare precision and scale to match the business: DECIMAL(10,2) for currency, DECIMAL(9,6) for coordinates, DOUBLE for scientific measurements. Values are rounded to the scale on insert.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: DECIMAL gives exact results and predictable rounding; FLOAT and DOUBLE are compact and very fast with huge range.
codeExamples:
SELECT 1e308 * 10 AS big_double_attempt;      -- DOUBLE range is about 1.8e308

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1690 (22003): DOUBLE value is out of range in '(1e308 * 10)'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: DECIMAL uses more storage and is slower than native floats; FLOAT and DOUBLE accumulate rounding errors and cannot be compared with = safely.

Limitations

Limitations: DECIMAL max is 65 digits (30 after the point); excess fractional digits are rounded, and values beyond the declared precision are rejected.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO price (d) VALUES (123456789.99);   -- needs 9+2 = 11 digits, column holds 10
INSERT INTO price (d) VALUES (1.005);            -- rounds to 1.01 with a note

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1264 (22003): Out of range value for column 'd' at row 1
-- Query OK, 1 row affected, 1 warning   -- Note 1265: Data truncated for column 'd'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Money = DECIMAL, or integer minor units (paise) in BIGINT when you want the fastest and unambiguous arithmetic. Never use FLOAT for currency or equality filters; if you must compare doubles, use a tolerance or round first.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Floating-point cannot represent 0.1 exactly, so sums drift and equality tests fail.
  • DECIMAL arithmetic is exact but slower and uses more bytes (about 4 bytes per 9 digits).
  • Choose scale from the business: 2 for currency, 4 for FX rates, more for crypto.

Senior Notes

  • Round at defined points and store with extra precision when you must aggregate (fees on millions of rows).
  • Alternative: store integers in minor units (paise/cents) to avoid decimals entirely.
  • Be careful with division and averages: result scale follows div_precision_increment.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: storing money in FLOAT/DOUBLE, comparing floats with =, and summing floats in reports (errors accumulate). Compare with a tolerance or use DECIMAL.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Choose the smallest DECIMAL that fits: DECIMAL(10,2) uses 5 bytes, DECIMAL(20,2) uses 10. Indexing DECIMAL works fine but wide ones reduce keys per page. Store integer cents when you only add and compare.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: tax and rounding rules. Compute with full precision, round once at the defined step, and check that the parts sum to the whole.
codeExamples:
SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(qty * unit_price), 2) AS subtotal,
       ROUND(SUM(qty * unit_price) * 0.18, 2) AS gst,
       ROUND(SUM(qty * unit_price) * 1.18, 2) AS total
FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 1 GROUP BY order_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- order_id | subtotal | gst    | total
--        1 |   999.50 | 179.91 | 1179.41

beginner.content:
Introduction

CHAR(n) is fixed length, right-padded with spaces (padding stripped on read). VARCHAR(n) is variable length and stores a 1 or 2 byte length prefix plus the actual bytes. n counts characters, not bytes.

Why Do We Need This?

Choose by data shape: fixed-width codes (country codes, hashes) fit CHAR; names and emails vary, so VARCHAR saves space. The wrong choice wastes storage or breaks comparisons.

Real-Time Use

Typical sizes: email VARCHAR(254), URL VARCHAR(2048), name VARCHAR(100), UUID text CHAR(36), SHA-256 hex CHAR(64). Always use utf8mb4 so emoji and all scripts fit.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (
    id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    email VARCHAR(254) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 NOT NULL,
    hash  CHAR(64) CHARACTER SET ascii NOT NULL      -- ascii = 1 byte per char
);
SELECT CHAR_LENGTH('héllo') AS chars, LENGTH('héllo') AS bytes;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------+
-- | chars | bytes |
-- +-------+-------+
-- |     5 |     6 |
-- +-------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   CHAR(5)   'ab'  -> [a][b][ ][ ][ ]        fixed 5 chars
   VARCHAR(5)'ab'  -> [len=2][a][b]          1-2 byte prefix + data
   utf8mb4 : up to 4 bytes / char     ascii : 1 byte / char

Fresher Notes

  • CHAR(n) is fixed length (padded); VARCHAR(n) is variable length and stores only what is needed plus 1-2 bytes of length.
  • Use CHAR for fixed codes (country code, hash) and VARCHAR for names and emails.
  • n counts characters, not bytes.

Worked Example 1

Too long value is rejected in strict mode.

Worked Example 2

Case-insensitive comparison.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'Abaji' = 'abaji' AS ci_equal, 'Abaji' COLLATE utf8mb4_bin = 'abaji' AS bin_equal;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ci_equal | bin_equal
--        1 |         0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Compare trailing space handling.

Practice Exercise 2

Character count vs byte count.
codeExamples:
SELECT CHAR_LENGTH('हिन्दी') AS chars, LENGTH('हिन्दी') AS bytes;

-- OUTPUT:
-- chars | bytes
--     6 |    18

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

CHAR(n) reserves n characters (padded with spaces, trimmed on read). VARCHAR(n) stores the actual characters plus a 1 or 2 byte length prefix. The server sizes in-memory temporary tables and sort buffers from the declared maximum, so oversized VARCHARs waste memory even when values are short.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Charset and collation matter: utf8mb4 characters take 1-4 bytes. A VARCHAR(255) can use up to 1020 bytes, and index key limits are in bytes. Choose collations by comparison needs (case, accent sensitivity) and use BINARY or _bin for exact matches.
codeExamples:
SELECT CHAR_LENGTH('ab€😀') AS chars, LENGTH('ab€😀') AS bytes;
SELECT 'Apple' = 'apple' AS ci_equal, 'Apple' COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_as_cs = 'apple' AS cs_equal, 'cafe' = 'café' AS accent_insensitive;

-- OUTPUT:
-- chars | bytes
--     4 |     9
-- ci_equal | cs_equal | accent_insensitive
--        1 |        0 |                  1

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: VARCHAR saves space and is flexible; CHAR is slightly faster for fixed-width and avoids row-length changes on update.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'a' = 'a ' COLLATE utf8mb4_general_ci AS pad_space,   -- PAD SPACE: trailing blanks ignored
       'a' = 'a ' COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci  AS no_pad;      -- NO PAD (8.0 default): they count

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+--------+
-- | pad_space | no_pad |
-- +----------+--------+
-- |        1 |      0 |
-- +----------+--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: oversized VARCHAR still costs memory in temp tables and sorts (MySQL allocates the max); CHAR wastes space on short values; trailing-space rules differ by collation.
codeExamples:
-- Do not declare VARCHAR(10000) "just in case": sorts and temp tables size to the max
CREATE TABLE sloppy (note VARCHAR(10000) CHARACTER SET utf8mb4);   -- 4 bytes x 10000 = 40000 bytes max

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected  (works, but each sort buffer row is reserved at full size)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the row-size limit 65,535 bytes is shared by all columns (utf8mb4 uses up to 4 bytes per char, so VARCHAR(16383) is the max single column); CHAR max is 255; an index key is limited to 3072 bytes.

Architect's Notes

Default to VARCHAR sized to a real bound, CHAR only for fixed-width codes, and ASCII charset for hex hashes and UUID strings to halve index size. Store UUIDs as BINARY(16) when index size and insert locality matter.

Mid-Level Notes

  • With utf8mb4 a character can take up to 4 bytes, so VARCHAR(255) may need up to 1020 bytes in an index.
  • CHAR trims trailing spaces on read; VARCHAR keeps them.
  • Do not over-allocate; VARCHAR(255) vs VARCHAR(50) matters for temporary tables and memory (sized to the maximum).

Senior Notes

  • Index key length limit is 3072 bytes (InnoDB DYNAMIC); long strings need prefix indexes or hashed columns.
  • Collation decides comparison: ci collations treat "A" and "a" equal, which affects UNIQUE and lookups.
  • Row size limit is 65,535 bytes across columns; many large VARCHARs may force TEXT.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: VARCHAR(255) everywhere, CHAR for variable data, ignoring trailing spaces, and mixed collations in joins (error 1267 or lost index). Align collations of joined columns.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Index size depends on bytes: a VARCHAR(255) utf8mb4 index entry can take 1020 bytes. Use a smaller declared length, prefix indexes or hashes for long strings, and measure with the catalog.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE users MODIFY email VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL;           -- was VARCHAR(255)
SELECT index_name, ROUND(stat_value * @@innodb_page_size / 1048576, 1) AS mb FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE table_name = 'users' AND stat_name = 'size';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name | mb
-- PRIMARY    | 220.0
-- uq_email   |  96.0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: store normalized values for fast, correct comparisons: lowercase emails, trimmed names, fixed-length country codes as CHAR(2) with a CHECK.

beginner.content:
Introduction

TEXT types hold long character data: TINYTEXT 255 bytes, TEXT 64 KB, MEDIUMTEXT 16 MB, LONGTEXT 4 GB. They are stored off-page when large, unlike VARCHAR which is mostly stored inline.

Why Do We Need This?

Blog posts, comments, descriptions and JSON-as-text outgrow VARCHAR limits. TEXT stores them without hitting the row-size ceiling.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, CHAR_LENGTH(body) AS chars FROM article WHERE body LIKE '%MySQL%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | chars |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 |  6000 |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

CMS pages, product descriptions, logs and emails use TEXT or MEDIUMTEXT; short, searched fields stay VARCHAR. Large binary files belong in object storage, not LONGTEXT.

Diagram

   VARCHAR(255)   inline in the row page
   TEXT / LONGTEXT:   row ──► [20-byte pointer] ──► overflow pages
   TINYTEXT 255 B | TEXT 64 KB | MEDIUMTEXT 16 MB | LONGTEXT 4 GB

Fresher Notes

  • TEXT types store long strings: TEXT up to 64 KB, MEDIUMTEXT 16 MB, LONGTEXT 4 GB.
  • Use them for descriptions, articles and logs; use VARCHAR for short bounded values.
  • TEXT columns cannot have a DEFAULT value (before 8.0.13) and cannot be fully indexed.

Worked Example 1

Select only needed columns, not the body.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title
--  1 | Intro

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Fulltext search over TEXT.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a table with TEXT and a prefix index.

Practice Exercise 2

Show the limit of max_allowed_packet.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@max_allowed_packet / 1024 / 1024 AS mb;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- mb
-- 64.0000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

TEXT types hold long strings. In InnoDB large values are stored off the main row page (overflow pages) with a short pointer left in the row, so selecting them forces extra page reads. The row itself stays small, which keeps scans on other columns fast.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Sizes: TEXT 64 KB, MEDIUMTEXT 16 MB, LONGTEXT 4 GB. BLOB variants are the binary equivalents. Index a prefix or use FULLTEXT; a TEXT column cannot be a primary key and indexing needs a prefix length.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: huge capacity; only the pointer lives in the row, so row-size limits are not a problem; supports FULLTEXT indexes.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE article ADD FULLTEXT INDEX ft_body (title, body);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS hits FROM article WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('MySQL');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | hits |
-- +------+
-- |    1 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: TEXT cannot have a DEFAULT (before 8.0.13 expression defaults), fetching it needs extra page reads, and big sorts spill to disk temp tables. Avoid SELECT * on tables with TEXT.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE no_default (t TEXT DEFAULT 'abc');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1101 (42000): BLOB, TEXT, GEOMETRY or JSON column 't' can't have a default value
-- (allowed only as expression: DEFAULT ('abc') on 8.0.13+)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a normal index needs a prefix length; the packet limit max_allowed_packet caps what a single statement can carry.
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_body ON article (body);                 -- no prefix: not allowed
CREATE INDEX idx_body ON article (body(100));             -- prefix index works

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1170 (42000): BLOB/TEXT column 'body' used in key specification without a key length
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep hot rows narrow: move big text to a separate table or object storage and select it only when needed. Use FULLTEXT or an external search engine instead of LIKE '%word%' scans over TEXT.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Large values can be stored off-page, so reading them costs extra I/O; avoid SELECT * on tables with TEXT.
  • Index only a prefix: INDEX (body(100)), or use FULLTEXT for searching.
  • Sorting or grouping by TEXT uses on-disk temp tables.

Senior Notes

  • Consider storing large documents in object storage (S3) and keeping only a URL and metadata in MySQL.
  • Keep TEXT in a separate one-to-one table if it is rarely read, keeping the hot table compact.
  • Watch max_allowed_packet when inserting big values.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: SELECT * from tables with TEXT columns on list pages, sorting or grouping on TEXT (forces disk temp tables), and exceeding max_allowed_packet on insert. Select only the columns you need.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title FROM articles ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;         -- list page: no body
SELECT body FROM articles WHERE id = 1;                            -- fetch the body only for the detail page
SET GLOBAL max_allowed_packet = 128 * 1024 * 1024;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Move rarely read large text to a separate one-to-one table so the hot table stays compact and backups of the main table stay small. Measure the effect with row length.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: user generated content. Limit length in the application and with a CHECK, store large files in object storage, and keep a URL plus metadata in MySQL.

beginner.content:
Introduction

DATE stores a calendar day (3 bytes, 1000-01-01 to 9999-12-31), TIME a time or duration (-838:59:59 to 838:59:59), YEAR a 4-digit year (1901 to 2155, 1 byte).

Why Do We Need This?

Dates in VARCHAR cannot be sorted, compared or computed with correctly. Real date types give validation, compact storage and built-in date arithmetic.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO ev (d) VALUES ('2026-02-30');      -- no such day

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1292 (22007): Incorrect date value: '2026-02-30' for column 'd' at row 1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Birthdays and due dates use DATE, opening hours and durations TIME, and copyright or model year YEAR. Reports group by date parts.

Diagram

   DATE  'YYYY-MM-DD'          3 bytes   1000-01-01 .. 9999-12-31
   TIME  'HH:MM:SS[.ffffff]'   3 bytes   -838:59:59 .. 838:59:59
   YEAR  YYYY                  1 byte    1901 .. 2155
   no time zone information stored in any of them

Fresher Notes

  • DATE stores a calendar date (YYYY-MM-DD), TIME stores a time (HH:MM:SS) and YEAR stores a 4-digit year.
  • Use CURDATE() and CURTIME() for the current values.
  • Always store dates in date types, never as strings.

Worked Example 1

Day arithmetic.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE_ADD('2026-03-15', INTERVAL 30 DAY) AS plus30, DATEDIFF('2026-12-25','2026-03-15') AS days;

-- OUTPUT:
-- plus30     | days
-- 2026-04-14 |  285

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Invalid dates fail in strict mode.

Practice Exercise 1

Insert and format dates.

Practice Exercise 2

Rewrite a year filter to use an index.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ev WHERE d >= '2026-01-01' AND d < '2027-01-01';

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DATE (3 bytes) stores a calendar day, TIME (3 bytes plus fractions) a time or duration, YEAR (1 byte) a four-digit year. They are stored as integers, so comparison and range scans are cheap, and they have no time zone.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Date arithmetic and formatting: DATE_ADD, DATE_SUB, DATEDIFF, LAST_DAY, DATE_FORMAT, STR_TO_DATE. Input formats must match or be converted explicitly.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE_ADD('2026-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS next_month, LAST_DAY('2026-02-10') AS month_end,
       DATEDIFF('2026-12-25', '2026-05-01') AS days_left, DATE_FORMAT('2026-03-15', '%d %b %Y') AS pretty,
       STR_TO_DATE('15/03/2026', '%d/%m/%Y') AS parsed, MAKETIME(26, 5, 0) AS duration;

-- OUTPUT:
-- next_month | month_end  | days_left | pretty      | parsed     | duration
-- 2026-02-28 | 2026-02-28 |       238 | 15 Mar 2026 | 2026-03-15 | 26:05:00

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: small, validated, indexable, rich functions, comparisons work by value.
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_d ON ev (d);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM ev WHERE d BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-12-31';   -- range scan on index

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key   | rows |
-- | range | idx_d |    1 |

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no time zone in DATE or TIME; TIME mixes clock time and duration; zero dates and invalid dates behave differently under sql_mode.

Limitations

Limitations: DATE cannot go before year 1000 reliably or after 9999; YEAR is only 1901-2155 (and 0000); two-digit year input is ambiguous (70-99 means 19xx, 00-69 means 20xx).

Architect's Notes

Store dates as DATE (not strings or ints) and keep calendar logic in SQL functions. For anything that must be an instant, use DATETIME or TIMESTAMP in UTC instead, and avoid the legacy zero date by keeping NO_ZERO_DATE in sql_mode.

Mid-Level Notes

  • DATE uses 3 bytes, range 1000-01-01 to 9999-12-31.
  • Extract parts with YEAR(), MONTH(), DAY(); format with DATE_FORMAT().
  • TIME can be negative or exceed 24 hours, so it also works for durations.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid wrapping an indexed date column in a function in WHERE (WHERE YEAR(d)=2026); use a range (d >= ... AND d < ...).
  • Zero dates (0000-00-00) are rejected in strict mode; do not rely on them.
  • Birthdates and business dates are time-zone free, so use DATE, not a timestamp.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: storing dates as strings, wrapping the column in functions in WHERE (kills the index), and invalid dates like Feb 30 (error in strict mode). Use a half-open range instead of YEAR(date).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A calendar (date dimension) table makes reporting simple and fast: group by week, quarter or fiscal period without functions on big tables, and include days with zero activity.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: ages and tenure. Calculate with TIMESTAMPDIFF so leap years and month lengths are handled for you.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, birth_date, TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, birth_date, CURDATE()) AS age, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, join_date, CURDATE()) AS months_employed FROM staff;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- name  | birth_date | age | months_employed
-- Abaji | 1995-08-20 |  30 | 42

beginner.content:
Introduction

Both store date and time. DATETIME (5 bytes plus fraction, 1000 to 9999) stores the literal value with no time zone conversion. TIMESTAMP (4 bytes plus fraction, 1970-01-01 00:00:01 UTC to 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UTC) is stored as UTC and converted to and from the session time zone.

Why Do We Need This?

Systems with users in many time zones need a safe way to store instants. TIMESTAMP handles conversion automatically; DATETIME keeps what you gave it, which suits local wall-clock times such as a store opening time.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE audit (
    id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at TIMESTAMP     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,                              -- set on insert
    updated_at TIMESTAMP     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,  -- auto-refresh
    event_at   DATETIME(3)   NULL                                                             -- ms precision
);
INSERT INTO audit (event_at) VALUES ('2026-10-06 09:15:30.123');
SELECT event_at FROM audit;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------------------+
-- | event_at                |
-- +-------------------------+
-- | 2026-10-06 09:15:30.123 |
-- +-------------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

created_at and updated_at columns are almost universal. Bookings and schedules in a fixed local zone use DATETIME; global event logs use TIMESTAMP or DATETIME stored in UTC.
codeExamples:
UPDATE audit SET event_at = NOW(3) WHERE id = 1;     -- updated_at changes by itself
