SELECT created_at < updated_at OR created_at = updated_at AS auto_maintained FROM audit;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+
-- | auto_maintained |
-- +-----------------+
-- |               1 |
-- +-----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   client time zone ──► TIMESTAMP stored as UTC seconds ──► converted back on read
   client value     ──► DATETIME  stored as written     ──► returned unchanged
                         range: 1970..2038        range: 1000..9999

Fresher Notes

  • Both store date and time. TIMESTAMP is stored in UTC and converted to the session time zone; DATETIME is stored as typed.
  • TIMESTAMP range is 1970 to 2038 (4 bytes); DATETIME is 1000 to 9999 (5-8 bytes).
  • DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP works for both in modern versions.

Worked Example 1

Automatic created/updated columns.

Worked Example 2

Convert between zones.

Practice Exercise 1

See the TIMESTAMP shift with the time zone.

Practice Exercise 2

Out of range TIMESTAMP.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

TIMESTAMP stores seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC (4 bytes) and converts to the session time zone on read and write. DATETIME stores the literal date and time you gave (5 bytes plus fractions) with no conversion and a range from year 1000 to 9999.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Both accept fractional seconds (0-6) and automatic defaults/updates through DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP. Use precision 3 or 6 when ordering events within the same second.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: TIMESTAMP is smaller and time-zone aware with automatic defaults; DATETIME has a huge range and no conversion surprises.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@session.time_zone AS session_tz, @@global.time_zone AS global_tz;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | session_tz | global_tz |
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | +05:30     | SYSTEM    |
-- +------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: TIMESTAMP depends on the session time zone, so changing server time zone changes displayed values; DATETIME has no zone, so you must remember its convention.

Limitations

Limitations: TIMESTAMP stops at 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UTC (the Year 2038 problem), which matters for long-dated data such as 30-year bonds.

Architect's Notes

A common rule: store instants as UTC in DATETIME(6) or TIMESTAMP(6), convert to local time in the application, and keep the server and session time zone at UTC. Prefer DATETIME for future-dated business data to avoid the 2038 limit.

Mid-Level Notes

  • TIMESTAMP changes its displayed value when the session time zone changes; DATETIME does not.
  • Use DATETIME for fixed local business times (appointment at 10:00 local) and TIMESTAMP for event instants.
  • Fractional seconds are available with DATETIME(6) / TIMESTAMP(6).

Senior Notes

  • The 2038 limit is real for TIMESTAMP; long-lived data (contracts, leases) needs DATETIME or BIGINT.
  • Standardize: store UTC and convert in the application; set server time zone to UTC and avoid mixed time zones in sessions.
  • DST gaps/overlaps make local DATETIMEs ambiguous; store the zone name or UTC alongside.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: TIMESTAMP for dates beyond 2038, mixing server and session time zones, and DST ambiguity with local DATETIME values. Standardize on UTC storage and convert at the edge.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

TIMESTAMP is smaller (4 vs 5 bytes) and good for event instants; DATETIME is simpler for local business times. Index and range queries work the same way, so choose by semantics, not speed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a global app stores instants in UTC and the user's zone name separately, converting only when displaying. Appointment times in a local zone store the local DATETIME plus the zone id.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL has no real boolean: BOOLEAN is an alias for TINYINT(1) (0 false, nonzero true). JSON is a native validated document type. BINARY, VARBINARY, BLOB hold raw bytes.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE flags (
    id      INT PRIMARY KEY,
    active  BOOLEAN DEFAULT TRUE,          -- really TINYINT(1)
    prefs   JSON,                          -- validated JSON document
    token   BINARY(16)                     -- 16 raw bytes (for example a UUID)
);
INSERT INTO flags VALUES (1, TRUE, '{"theme":"dark","fonts":[12,14]}', UUID_TO_BIN(UUID()));
SELECT id, active, prefs, prefs->>'$.theme' AS theme FROM flags;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+----------------------------------+-------+
-- | id | active | prefs                            | theme |
-- +----+--------+----------------------------------+-------+
-- |  1 |      1 | {"fonts": [12, 14], "theme": "dark"} | dark |
-- +----+--------+----------------------------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Flags need a compact true/false, semi-structured settings need flexible storage, and binary data such as hashes and UUIDs need an exact byte comparison without character set rules.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO flags (id, prefs) VALUES (2, '{bad json}');     -- the server validates JSON

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3140 (22032): Invalid JSON text: "Invalid value." at position 1 in value for column 'flags.prefs'.

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Feature toggles use BOOLEAN, user preferences and API payloads JSON, password hashes BINARY or VARBINARY, UUID keys BINARY(16), and small icons BLOB.

Diagram

   BOOLEAN       -> TINYINT(1)       0 = false, nonzero = true
   JSON          -> binary-encoded document, validated on write
   BINARY(n)     fixed bytes   VARBINARY(n) variable   BLOB 64 KB .. LONGBLOB 4 GB

Fresher Notes

  • BOOLEAN is an alias for TINYINT(1): 0 is false, non-zero is true. JSON stores JSON documents. BINARY, VARBINARY and BLOB hold raw bytes.
  • TRUE and FALSE are just 1 and 0.
  • Use BLOB for files or hashes only when needed; usually store files elsewhere.

Worked Example 1

UUID as BINARY(16).

Worked Example 2

Invalid JSON is rejected.

Practice Exercise 1

BOOLEAN behaviour.

Practice Exercise 2

Store and read JSON.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

BOOLEAN is TINYINT(1): any non-zero value is true. JSON values are validated and stored in a binary format with a dictionary of keys, allowing fast path lookups without re-parsing. BINARY/VARBINARY/BLOB compare and sort by raw bytes with no collation.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common functions: JSON_OBJECT, JSON_ARRAY, JSON_SET, JSON_REMOVE, JSON_CONTAINS, MEMBER OF. For binary: UUID_TO_BIN, HEX, UNHEX and SHA2.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: JSON gives schema flexibility with validation, path queries and indexing via generated columns; BINARY(16) UUIDs are half the size of CHAR(36); TINYINT(1) is tiny.
codeExamples:
SELECT JSON_EXTRACT(prefs, '$.fonts[1]') AS second_font, JSON_LENGTH(prefs, '$.fonts') AS n FROM flags;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+---+
-- | second_font | n |
-- +-------------+---+
-- | 14          | 2 |
-- +-------------+---+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: BOOLEAN accepts any small integer, not only 0 and 1; JSON columns cannot be indexed directly, lack column-level types and constraints, and rewrite costs rise with document size.
codeExamples:
UPDATE flags SET active = 7 WHERE id = 1;       -- accepted: it is just a TINYINT
SELECT active, active = TRUE AS equals_true, active IS TRUE AS is_true FROM flags;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-------------+---------+
-- | active | equals_true | is_true |
-- +--------+-------------+---------+
-- |      7 |           0 |       1 |
-- +--------+-------------+---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: JSON documents are capped by max_allowed_packet; BLOB columns cannot have defaults and need prefix indexes; BINARY pads with 0x00 bytes, so lengths differ from VARBINARY.

Architect's Notes

Use JSON for genuinely variable attributes and keep queried or constrained fields as real columns (or generated, indexed columns). Store UUIDs as BINARY(16) with UUID_TO_BIN(uuid,1) to improve insert locality; keep large files in object storage.

Mid-Level Notes

  • JSON values are validated and stored in an efficient binary format; query with JSON_EXTRACT or -> / ->>.
  • Use BINARY(16) for UUIDs (UUID_TO_BIN()) to save space versus CHAR(36).
  • BLOB sorts and compares by bytes with no collation.

Senior Notes

  • JSON is for sparse, evolving attributes; stable, queried fields belong in real columns (use generated columns plus indexes if needed).
  • BINARY(16) UUIDs with swap_flag improve insert locality for time-based UUIDs.
  • Avoid BLOBs in hot tables: they bloat backups and replication; use object storage.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using JSON for fields you filter and join on (no constraints, weak indexing), storing UUIDs as CHAR(36), and expecting BOOLEAN to reject values like 5. Promote hot JSON fields to generated columns.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

BINARY(16) UUIDs halve key size versus CHAR(36), and swapping the time parts (flag 1) makes time-based UUIDs sort roughly in time order, which reduces page splits.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world hybrid: relational columns for what you query, JSON for flexible extras, and a generated column plus index for the one JSON field you filter on.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Every type has a storage size and a range; together they drive table size, buffer-pool use and speed. Smaller types mean more rows per 16 KB InnoDB page, so fewer disk reads.

Why Do We Need This?

At millions of rows, 4 spare bytes per row is gigabytes, and every secondary index repeats the primary key, so oversized keys multiply the waste.
codeExamples:
-- Measure real size per table
SELECT table_name,
       ROUND(data_length  / 1024 / 1024, 1) AS data_mb,
       ROUND(index_length / 1024 / 1024, 1) AS index_mb
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'sizes';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+---------+----------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | data_mb | index_mb |
-- +------------+---------+----------+
-- | sizes      |     0.0 |      0.0 |
-- +------------+---------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Architects review column types in design reviews: INT UNSIGNED ids, DECIMAL for money, ascii for hex, ENUM or lookup tables for small domains, fixed-width codes as CHAR.

Diagram

   16 KB InnoDB page
   ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ INT row 20 B  → ~ 700 rows per page        │
   │ wide row 200 B→ ~  70 rows per page        │
   └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   fewer rows/page = more I/O, bigger indexes, lower cache hit rate

Fresher Notes

  • Every type has a storage size and a range; smaller types use less disk and memory, so queries are faster.
  • Examples: TINYINT 1 byte, INT 4, BIGINT 8, DATE 3, DATETIME 5+, VARCHAR(n) length + 1-2 bytes.
  • Choose the type from real data limits, not "just in case".

Worked Example 1

Implicit conversion hides an index.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;   -- phone is VARCHAR

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | Extra
-- ALL  | NULL | Using where   (index on phone not used)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Fix by matching types.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key       | Extra
-- ref  | idx_phone | NULL

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Check table and index size.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND(data_length/1024/1024,2) AS data_mb, ROUND(index_length/1024/1024,2) AS idx_mb
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | data_mb | idx_mb
-- employees  |    0.02 |   0.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

IPv4 as integer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Every row is a record in a 16 KB page. Fixed fields cost their declared bytes, variable fields cost length plus data, NULL bits are kept in a header bitmap. Fewer bytes per row means more rows per page, so a scan or an index range reads fewer pages and the buffer pool holds more of your data.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, table_rows, avg_row_length, ROUND(16384 / avg_row_length) AS rows_per_page, ROUND(data_length/1048576) AS data_mb
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' AND table_rows > 0 ORDER BY data_length DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name  | table_rows | avg_row_length | rows_per_page | data_mb
-- order_items |    5400000 |             58 |           282 |     310
-- orders      |    1800000 |             96 |           171 |     165

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

A quick reference of storage: TINYINT 1, SMALLINT 2, INT 4, BIGINT 8, DECIMAL(10,2) 5, DATE 3, DATETIME 5, TIMESTAMP 4, CHAR(n) n x charset bytes, VARCHAR(n) length + 1-2, ENUM 1-2. Use PROCEDURE ANALYSE-style checks (MIN/MAX/LENGTH) on real data to size columns.
codeExamples:
SELECT MIN(price), MAX(price), MAX(CHAR_LENGTH(name)) AS longest_name, COUNT(DISTINCT status) AS statuses FROM products;

-- OUTPUT:
-- MIN(price) | MAX(price) | longest_name | statuses
--       9.00 |   99999.00 |           58 |        4        (so DECIMAL(7,2), VARCHAR(80), and ENUM/TINYINT for status)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of careful typing: smaller indexes, better cache hit ratio, faster scans and joins (integers compare faster than strings), and range validation for free.
codeExamples:
-- Integer joins and comparisons are cheaper than string ones
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sizes WHERE b = 1;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type | key  | rows | filtered |
-- | ALL  | NULL |    1 |   100.00 |     (add an INT index and this becomes ref)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: too-small types cause overflow incidents and painful migrations; tight typing needs forecasting growth.
codeExamples:
-- Changing INT to BIGINT on a billion-row PK rebuilds the table and every index
ALTER TABLE sizes MODIFY b BIGINT, ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1846 (0A000): ALGORITHM=INPLACE is not supported. Reason: Cannot change column type INPLACE.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: row size is limited to 65,535 bytes (excluding BLOB/TEXT payload); InnoDB page is 16 KB by default so rows over about 8 KB spill to overflow pages; an index key is at most 3072 bytes.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@innodb_page_size AS page_bytes, @@sql_mode LIKE '%STRICT_TRANS_TABLES%' AS strict_on;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | page_bytes | strict_on |
-- +------------+-----------+
-- |      16384 |         1 |
-- +------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Review types like you review APIs: right-size keys, avoid string keys for joins, keep nullable and large columns out of hot tables, and plan the INT-to-BIGINT jump early since it is a rebuild. Measure with information_schema and real EXPLAIN data, not guesses.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Smaller rows mean more rows per 16 KB page, fewer I/Os and better cache hit ratio; indexes shrink similarly.
  • Use ENUM or a lookup table for small fixed sets; use INT UNSIGNED for IPv4 (INET_ATON).
  • Avoid mixing types in join/where comparisons (INT vs VARCHAR), which can prevent index use.

Senior Notes

  • Estimate size: rows x row width x (1 + index overhead); capacity plan with real numbers.
  • NULL columns cost a bit in the row header bitmap; many nullable columns hint at design issues.
  • Measure with information_schema.tables (data_length, index_length) rather than guessing.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: oversizing types "just in case", VARCHAR(255) for 2-letter codes, storing IPs as strings, and comparing different types (index lost). Use INET6_ATON for IPs and a lookup table or ENUM for tiny sets.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Type mismatch in comparisons forces conversion on every row and disables the index. Always compare a column with a value of the same type.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;          -- phone is VARCHAR: converts each row
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210';        -- same type: index used

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- first : type=ALL  key=NULL
-- second: type=ref  key=idx_phone

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world capacity planning: estimate table and index size from row counts and widths before launch, then compare with a prototype loaded with realistic data.
codeExamples:
SELECT 50000000 AS expected_rows, 64 AS row_bytes, ROUND(50000000 * 64 / 1073741824, 1) AS data_gb,
       ROUND(50000000 * (8 + 4) / 1073741824 * 1.3, 1) AS one_secondary_index_gb;

-- OUTPUT:
-- expected_rows | row_bytes | data_gb | one_secondary_index_gb
--      50000000 |        64 |     3.0 |                    0.7

beginner.content:
Introduction

A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies every row. It implies UNIQUE plus NOT NULL, a table has at most one, and it may span several columns (composite). In InnoDB the primary key is also the clustered index: the table rows are physically stored in primary-key order.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE student (
    id    INT          NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,   -- surrogate key generated by the server
    email VARCHAR(60)  NOT NULL,
    name  VARCHAR(40),
    PRIMARY KEY (id)                              -- table-level declaration
);
INSERT INTO student (email, name) VALUES ('a@x.com', 'Abaji'), ('r@x.com', 'Raoji');
SELECT id, name FROM student;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | Abaji |
-- |  2 | Raoji |
-- +----+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without a key you cannot address one row safely: UPDATE ... WHERE name='Abaji' may hit several people. A primary key gives every row a stable identity that foreign keys, caches, URLs and replication row events can refer to.
codeExamples:
-- Duplicate identity and missing identity are both refused
INSERT INTO student (id, email) VALUES (1, 'dup@x.com');     -- id 1 already exists
INSERT INTO student (id, email) VALUES (NULL, 'n@x.com');    -- NULL means "generate" here
INSERT INTO student (id, email) VALUES (10, 'k@x.com');
SELECT id FROM student ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1' for key 'student.PRIMARY'
-- (the NULL insert succeeds because AUTO_INCREMENT replaces it with 3)
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  1 |
-- |  2 |
-- |  3 |
-- | 10 |
-- +----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical designs: a BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT surrogate for entities (orders, users), a composite key for pure junction tables, and a natural key (country code) for tiny lookup tables.

Diagram

   PRIMARY KEY (id)  =  UNIQUE + NOT NULL + clustered index

   Clustered B+tree (leaf = whole row)        Secondary index KEY(email)
   ┌──────────────┐                           ┌──────────────────────┐
   │ id 1 | row.. │                           │ email → id (PK copy) │
   │ id 2 | row.. │ ◄─── lookup by id ────────│ a@x.com → 1          │
   │ id 3 | row.. │      (second hop)         │ r@x.com → 2          │
   └──────────────┘                           └──────────────────────┘

Fresher Notes

  • A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each row; it cannot be NULL or duplicated. A table has only one.
  • Define inline (id INT PRIMARY KEY) or at the end (PRIMARY KEY (id)), composite as PRIMARY KEY (a,b).
  • Combine with AUTO_INCREMENT for automatic ids.

Worked Example 1

AUTO_INCREMENT gaps after rollback.

Worked Example 2

Gap-free counter with a lock.

Practice Exercise 1

Define a composite primary key and demonstrate uniqueness.

Practice Exercise 2

Primary key cannot be NULL.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

InnoDB stores a table as a B-tree ordered by the primary key (the clustered index). If you do not define one, it uses the first unique NOT NULL index, or creates a hidden 6-byte row id. Inserting in key order appends to the right-hand page; random keys split pages.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Ways to define a primary key: inline, table-level, composite, with AUTO_INCREMENT, with UUIDs, or added later. You can also rename nothing: the PK is always named PRIMARY.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: guaranteed uniqueness, the fastest lookup path (clustered index), automatic index creation, and a ready target for foreign keys. Sequential integer keys also append at the end of the B-tree, which keeps inserts cheap.
codeExamples:
-- A primary-key lookup reads exactly one row through the clustered index
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM student WHERE id = 2;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+---------+-------+---------+---------+-------+------+
-- | id | table   | type  | key     | key_len | ref   | rows |
-- +----+---------+-------+---------+---------+-------+------+
-- |  1 | student | const | PRIMARY | 4       | const |    1 |
-- +----+---------+-------+---------+---------+-------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every secondary index stores a copy of the primary key, so a wide key (long VARCHAR, random UUID in CHAR(36)) inflates all indexes. Changing a key value later rewrites rows and every referencing row. Random keys cause page splits.
codeExamples:
-- Compare secondary-index overhead: the PK value is appended to every index entry
CREATE TABLE t_int  (id INT         PRIMARY KEY, k INT, KEY (k));   -- 4 bytes per entry copy
CREATE TABLE t_uuid (id CHAR(36)    PRIMARY KEY, k INT, KEY (k));   -- 144 bytes (utf8mb4) copy
SELECT table_name, index_name
FROM information_schema.statistics
WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name IN ('t_int','t_uuid') AND index_name = 'k';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | INDEX_NAME |
-- +------------+------------+
-- | t_int      | k          |
-- | t_uuid     | k          |
-- +------------+------------+
-- (both work, but t_uuid's index k is several times larger on disk)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: only one primary key per table; key parts cannot be NULL; the index key is limited to 3072 bytes and 16 columns; and if you omit a primary key InnoDB silently builds a hidden 6-byte row id, which you cannot use and which is a shared counter that can contend under heavy insert load.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE bad (a INT PRIMARY KEY, b INT PRIMARY KEY);   -- two primary keys
CREATE TABLE bad2 (a INT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (a));            -- explicit NULL on a key column

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1068 (42000): Multiple primary key defined
-- (bad2 is accepted: MySQL silently turns a PRIMARY KEY column into NOT NULL)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose a short, immutable, meaningless key: BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT for single-node systems, or a time-ordered ID (UUIDv7, ULID stored as BINARY(16)) when IDs are generated by many writers. Avoid business values (email, phone) as the clustered key because they change and are wide. With auto-increment under replication and multi-source writes, plan offsets (auto_increment_increment) or use external ID generation.

Mid-Level Notes

  • In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index: rows are physically organised by it.
  • If you define none, InnoDB uses the first NOT NULL unique index or a hidden 6-byte row id.
  • Never update primary key values; it rewrites rows and every child reference.

Senior Notes

  • Random PKs (UUIDv4) fragment the clustered index; prefer monotonically increasing keys.
  • Hidden row id has a contention point under heavy inserts; explicit PKs are better and necessary for row-based replication efficiency.
  • Gaps in AUTO_INCREMENT are normal; do not use it for gap-free numbering such as invoice numbers.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no primary key (hidden row id, poor replication and ORM support), a mutable natural key, UUIDv4 strings, and expecting AUTO_INCREMENT to be gap free or reusable after rollback.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Auto-increment locking: with innodb_autoinc_lock_mode=2 (default in 8.0) concurrent inserts do not wait for each other, at the cost of gaps. For ordered, distributed ids use snowflake-style or UUIDv7 keys.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world gap-free numbering such as invoice numbers: do not use AUTO_INCREMENT. Use a counter row locked inside the same transaction as the invoice.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A FOREIGN KEY makes a column (or set of columns) in a child table refer to the primary or unique key of a parent table. The engine then guarantees every child value either matches an existing parent row or is NULL. This rule is called referential integrity. Only InnoDB enforces it.

Why Do We Need This?

Application code has bugs and people run ad-hoc scripts. Without an FK a deleted author leaves orphan books, and reports silently drop or miscount them. The database is the only place that sees every writer, so it should enforce the rule.
codeExamples:
-- Child row pointing at a parent that does not exist
INSERT INTO book VALUES (11, 'Ghost', 99);

-- Removing a parent that still has children
DELETE FROM author WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails (...)
-- ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails (...)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real schemas pair FKs with referential actions: ON DELETE CASCADE for owned data (order lines die with the order), SET NULL for optional links, and the default RESTRICT for everything else.

Diagram

   parent: author                         child: book
   ┌────┬────────┐   1 ◄──────── N       ┌────┬───────────┬───────────┐
   │ PK │ name   │                       │ PK │ title     │ FK author │
   │  1 │ Tagore │ ◄─────────────────────│ 10 │ Gitanjali │     1     │
   └────┴────────┘   ON DELETE rule      └────┴───────────┴───────────┘
   RESTRICT : block delete | CASCADE : delete children | SET NULL : orphan allowed

Fresher Notes

  • A FOREIGN KEY links a column in a child table to the primary (or unique) key of a parent table.
  • It blocks orphans: a child cannot reference a non-existent parent.
  • Syntax: FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id).

Worked Example 1

SET NULL option.

Worked Example 2

List the FKs on a table.
codeExamples:
SELECT constraint_name, referenced_table_name FROM information_schema.key_column_usage
WHERE table_schema=DATABASE() AND table_name='emp2' AND referenced_table_name IS NOT NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- constraint_name | referenced_table_name
-- emp2_ibfk_1     | dept

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create FK with cascade and test.

Practice Exercise 2

Type mismatch error.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When you insert or update a child row, InnoDB looks up the parent key (taking a shared lock on that parent row) to ensure it exists; when you delete or update a parent key, it looks into the child index to apply the action. That is why both sides need indexes, and why hot parent rows can become contention points.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Actions: RESTRICT/NO ACTION block the change, CASCADE propagates it, SET NULL clears the child column (it must be nullable). You can add or drop constraints later and disable checks temporarily for bulk loads.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: integrity enforced for every client, self-documenting relationships (visible in SHOW CREATE TABLE and ER tools), cascading cleanup, and the optimizer or MySQL requires an index on the FK column, which also speeds the joins.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL auto-creates an index on the FK column if you did not
SHOW INDEX FROM book;

-- OUTPUT (trimmed):
-- +-------+------------+----------------+-------------+
-- | Table | Non_unique | Key_name       | Column_name |
-- +-------+------------+----------------+-------------+
-- | book  |          0 | PRIMARY        | id          |
-- | book  |          1 | fk_book_author | author_id   |
-- +-------+------------+----------------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every insert or update on the child must check the parent (and takes a shared lock on the parent row), which adds latency and can create lock waits and deadlocks on hot parents. Cascades can delete huge row counts in one transaction. Bulk loads are slower.
codeExamples:
-- Bulk loading out of order: temporarily relax the checks (session only, use with care)
SET foreign_key_checks = 0;
INSERT INTO book VALUES (12, 'Loaded first', 2);     -- parent 2 not there yet
INSERT INTO author VALUES (2, 'Premchand');
SET foreign_key_checks = 1;                          -- NOT re-validated automatically!
SELECT b.title, a.name FROM book b JOIN author a ON a.id = b.author_id WHERE b.id = 12;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+-----------+
-- | title        | name      |
-- +--------------+-----------+
-- | Loaded first | Premchand |
-- +--------------+-----------+
-- (had parent 2 never been inserted, the bad row would remain after re-enabling)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB only; parent and child columns must have the same type, signedness and (for strings) charset and collation; partitioned tables cannot use FKs; cascaded actions do not fire triggers; generated columns have restrictions; and FKs cannot span servers or shards.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE p (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE c (pid BIGINT, FOREIGN KEY (pid) REFERENCES p (id));   -- BIGINT vs INT

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3780 (HY000): Referencing column 'pid' and referenced column 'id' in foreign key
-- constraint 'c_ibfk_1' are incompatible.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Declare FKs in OLTP systems and use RESTRICT unless the child truly cannot exist alone; avoid CASCADE on large fan-out relations because one DELETE becomes a long locking transaction. Index every FK column on the child. At extreme scale or when sharding, teams drop FKs and enforce integrity with application checks and periodic orphan-detection jobs, accepting the risk knowingly.

Mid-Level Notes

  • ON DELETE / ON UPDATE actions: RESTRICT/NO ACTION, CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT (not supported in InnoDB).
  • Both tables must be InnoDB and column types must match (including signedness and charset).
  • MySQL creates an index on the FK column if none exists.

Senior Notes

  • FKs add locking: inserting a child takes a shared lock on the parent row; heavy parents can contend.
  • Cascading deletes can be huge transactions; prefer soft deletes or batch deletion for large trees.
  • In sharded or highly distributed designs FKs are often dropped; compensate with checks, reconciliation and good ownership boundaries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mismatched column types, a missing index on a non-InnoDB or logical reference, long cascade deletes, and creating circular references that make loading order impossible. Detect orphans with an anti-join.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Foreign key checks add lock overhead on hot parents. Measure lock waits, and for very high write rates consider removing the constraint but keeping the index and running periodic orphan audits.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an order system uses CASCADE for order lines (owned by the order) and RESTRICT for customer references (history must survive), giving safe deletes where intended.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE order_lines (order_id BIGINT NOT NULL, line_no INT NOT NULL, product_id BIGINT NOT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no),
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT);
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 10;       -- removes its lines too
DELETE FROM products WHERE id = 7;      -- blocked while any line references it

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails

beginner.content:
Introduction

A UNIQUE constraint forbids two rows with the same value (or same combination of values) in the columns it covers. It is implemented as a unique B-tree index. Unlike the primary key, a table may have many unique keys and the columns may hold NULL.

Why Do We Need This?

Real-world identities (email, username, tax id, SKU) must not repeat, but they are not the primary key. A check in the application (SELECT then INSERT) races under concurrency; the unique index is the only race-free guard.
codeExamples:
-- Race-free "create if absent": let the constraint decide
INSERT IGNORE INTO app_user (email) VALUES ('a@x.com');          -- silently skips duplicates
INSERT INTO app_user (email, phone) VALUES ('a@x.com', '9111111111')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE phone = VALUES(phone);                   -- upsert instead
SELECT email, phone FROM app_user;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------------+
-- | email   | phone      |
-- +---------+------------+
-- | a@x.com | 9111111111 |
-- +---------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Composite uniqueness is common: one review per (user, product), one seat per (show, seat_no), one active subscription per user.

Diagram

   INSERT row
      │
      ▼
   probe unique B-tree ──► value found?  ── yes ──► ERROR 1062 (or IGNORE / ON DUPLICATE KEY)
      │ no
      ▼
   add entry to unique index + clustered row ──► COMMIT
   (NULL values bypass the probe, so many NULLs are allowed)

Fresher Notes

  • UNIQUE forbids duplicate values in a column (or combination). A table can have several UNIQUE keys.
  • Unlike PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE allows NULL (and multiple NULLs).
  • Typical: email, username, national id.

Worked Example 1

Composite unique per tenant.

Worked Example 2

Unique among active rows only.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN deleted_at DATETIME NULL,
  ADD COLUMN active_email VARCHAR(80) AS (IF(deleted_at IS NULL, email, NULL)) VIRTUAL,
  ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_active_email (active_email);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Duplicate email attempt.

Practice Exercise 2

Upsert pattern.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A UNIQUE constraint is a unique B-tree index. On INSERT or UPDATE InnoDB searches the index; if an entry with the same key exists (and is visible or locked), it raises a duplicate-key error. Concurrent inserts of the same value block on the first one's lock, so exactly one wins.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Handle duplicates intentionally: INSERT IGNORE skips them, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE upserts, REPLACE deletes and reinserts. Composite and functional unique indexes express richer rules.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative, race-free, doubles as an index (fast equality lookups and an index-only lookup of the key itself), and can be referenced by foreign keys.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each unique index slows writes (a uniqueness probe on every insert/update), uses disk and buffer-pool memory, and cannot use the change buffer, so random inserts become immediate I/O. Gap locks taken by duplicate checks can cause deadlocks in concurrent inserts.
codeExamples:
-- Comparison is governed by collation: case-insensitive by default
INSERT INTO app_user (email) VALUES ('A@X.COM');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'A@X.COM' for key 'app_user.uq_user_email'
-- (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci treats A@X.COM and a@x.com as equal; use a _bin collation to change that)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: multiple NULLs are allowed (NULL is not equal to NULL); a TEXT/BLOB column needs a prefix length; the key is limited to 3072 bytes; and MySQL has no partial or filtered unique index, so "unique among active rows" needs a generated column or a trick.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE coupon (code VARCHAR(10) UNIQUE, used_by INT);
INSERT INTO coupon VALUES (NULL, 1), (NULL, 2), ('SAVE5', 3);   -- both NULLs accepted
SELECT code, used_by FROM coupon;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+---------+
-- | code  | used_by |
-- +-------+---------+
-- | NULL  |       1 |
-- | NULL  |       2 |
-- | SAVE5 |       3 |
-- +-------+---------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Always back business-level uniqueness with a unique index and handle error 1062 in code instead of pre-checking. Remember collation decides what "same" means, and normalise input (lower-case, trim) or use a generated column for case rules. For soft-delete with re-use of values, include a deleted_at or active flag in a composite unique key, or use a functional generated column that is NULL for deleted rows.

Mid-Level Notes

  • MySQL creates a unique index behind the constraint; it speeds lookups by that column as well.
  • Case-insensitive collations make "A@x.com" equal "a@x.com" for uniqueness.
  • For INSERT of possibly existing rows use INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE or INSERT IGNORE.

Senior Notes

  • Concurrency: two sessions inserting the same value, one waits then fails with 1062; handle the error rather than check-then-insert.
  • Unique across soft-deleted rows needs a design (generated column or composite with deleted flag).
  • Long unique strings hit index length limits; use a hash column.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: check-then-insert (a race), assuming NULL duplicates are rejected, ignoring collation (case-insensitive equality), and adding UNIQUE to a table that already has duplicates. Let the constraint decide and handle error 1062.
codeExamples:
-- racy
-- SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE email = ?; if 0 then INSERT ...
-- safe
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('c@x.com');
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user LIMIT 0;   -- (placeholder to show nothing else needed)

-- finding duplicates before adding the constraint
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM legacy_users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- email   | COUNT(*)
-- a@x.com |        3

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Unique indexes speed lookups by that key but add write cost, and they cannot use the change buffer. Keep unique keys short and consider a hash column for very long values.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: idempotent API requests. Store the client's idempotency key with a UNIQUE constraint; a retried request hits the duplicate error and returns the first result instead of charging twice.

beginner.content:
Introduction

NOT NULL forbids the absence of a value in a column. DEFAULT supplies a value when an INSERT does not mention the column. Together they define what a valid row looks like when only some columns are provided. MySQL 8.0.13+ also allows expressions as defaults.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE ticket (
    id         INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    title      VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,                   -- must always be given
    status     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',    -- used when omitted
    priority   TINYINT     NOT NULL DEFAULT 3,
    created_at DATETIME    NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    note       VARCHAR(200) NULL                        -- optional: NULL is allowed
);
INSERT INTO ticket (title) VALUES ('Printer down');
SELECT id, title, status, priority FROM ticket;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------------+--------+----------+
-- | id | title        | status | priority |
-- +----+--------------+--------+----------+
-- |  1 | Printer down | open   |        3 |
-- +----+--------------+--------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

NULL means "unknown" and spreads through logic: NULL = NULL is not true, aggregates skip it, and every query must handle it. Making columns NOT NULL removes a whole class of bugs, and defaults keep inserts short and consistent (timestamps, statuses, flags).
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO ticket (title) VALUES (NULL);          -- explicit NULL into NOT NULL
INSERT INTO ticket (status) VALUES ('open');        -- title omitted, no default exists

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1048 (23000): Column 'title' cannot be null
-- ERROR 1364 (HY000): Field 'title' doesn't have a default value

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Audit columns (created_at, updated_at), state machines (status), counters (retries INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0) and flags are universal. ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP keeps a modified-time column current automatically.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE ticket
    ADD COLUMN updated_at DATETIME NOT NULL
        DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;
UPDATE ticket SET priority = 1 WHERE id = 1;       -- updated_at refreshed by the server
SELECT priority, updated_at >= created_at AS touched FROM ticket WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+---------+
-- | priority | touched |
-- +----------+---------+
-- |        1 |       1 |
-- +----------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   INSERT INTO ticket (title) VALUES ('x')
        │ column listed?  ── yes ──► use given value ──► NULL and NOT NULL? ─► ERROR 1048
        │ no
        ▼
   has DEFAULT?  ── yes ──► use default (literal or expression)
        │ no
        ▼
   nullable? ── yes ──► store NULL        no ──► ERROR 1364 (strict mode)

Fresher Notes

  • NOT NULL means a value is required. DEFAULT supplies a value when none is given.
  • Example: status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT "ACTIVE".
  • NULL means unknown or missing, which is different from 0 or an empty string.

Worked Example 1

NULL pitfalls: NOT IN with NULL.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) AS result;

-- OUTPUT:
-- result
-- NULL

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Count ignores NULL.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_n, COUNT(email) AS emails FROM (SELECT 'a' AS email UNION ALL SELECT NULL) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- rows_n | emails
--      2 |      1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Defaults at work.

Practice Exercise 2

Missing required column.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

NULL is stored as one bit in the row's NULL bitmap, so nullable columns cost almost nothing in space, but they cost in logic: comparisons with NULL are unknown, and aggregates skip them. NOT NULL plus DEFAULT guarantees a usable value on every row.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

DEFAULT can be a literal or, from 8.0.13, an expression in parentheses: DEFAULT (UUID()), DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE). Existing columns can be altered; instant default changes only touch metadata.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: tighter data quality, simpler queries (no IS NULL branches), slightly smaller rows and indexes, better optimizer estimates, and expression defaults (for example DEFAULT (UUID()) or DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE)) in 8.0.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: adding NOT NULL to a populated table needs a default or a backfill; wrong defaults hide bugs (a silent 0 or empty string is worse than an error); and in non-strict SQL modes MySQL quietly substitutes values instead of failing.
codeExamples:
-- Non-strict mode silently invents data: a classic trap
SET SESSION sql_mode = '';
INSERT INTO ticket (title, priority) VALUES ('Quiet bug', 'high');   -- not a number
SELECT title, priority FROM ticket WHERE title = 'Quiet bug';
SET SESSION sql_mode = DEFAULT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+----------+
-- | title     | priority |
-- +-----------+----------+
-- | Quiet bug |        0 |
-- +-----------+----------+
-- (strict mode, the 8.0 default, would raise ERROR 1366 instead)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: BLOB, TEXT, JSON and GEOMETRY columns can have a default only as a parenthesised expression (8.0.13+); DEFAULT cannot reference other columns or non-deterministic stored functions; and Oracle-style empty string equals NULL does not apply, as MySQL keeps '' and NULL different.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE doc (id INT PRIMARY KEY, body TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'empty');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1101 (42000): BLOB, TEXT, GEOMETRY or JSON column 'body' can't have a default value
-- (write DEFAULT ('empty') with parentheses on 8.0.13 or later)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Make columns NOT NULL by default and allow NULL only when absence has real meaning. Keep strict SQL mode on in every environment so bad values fail loudly. When adding a NOT NULL column to a huge table use ALGORITHM=INSTANT where supported with a constant default, or backfill in batches before tightening the constraint.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Prefer NOT NULL where the business requires a value: it enforces integrity and simplifies queries.
  • Expressions can be defaults in 8.0.13+: DEFAULT (UUID()), DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE).
  • In strict mode, omitting a NOT NULL column without default errors.

Senior Notes

  • Adding NOT NULL to a populated column needs a backfill; use a default or a staged migration.
  • Defaults on large tables: adding a column with a constant default is metadata-only with INSTANT in 8.0.
  • Nullable columns complicate unique indexes, joins and aggregates; model optionality explicitly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: leaving columns nullable by habit, using empty string or 0 as "missing", and adding NOT NULL to a populated table without a default or backfill. Model missing as NULL only when it is genuinely optional.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Adding a column with a constant default is metadata-only with ALGORITHM=INSTANT, but backfilling NOT NULL without a default rewrites the table. Check the algorithm supported before running on a big table.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: required business fields are NOT NULL with CHECKs, optional ones are NULL, and "unknown vs none" is modelled explicitly (for example a separate boolean).

beginner.content:
Introduction

A CHECK constraint is a boolean rule every row must satisfy. MySQL 8.0.16 and later enforce it; older versions parsed and ignored it, a common source of confusion. A row is rejected when the condition is FALSE; when it evaluates to NULL (UNKNOWN) the row is accepted.

Why Do We Need This?

Types alone cannot express business rules: an INT stock count can still be negative and a price can be zero. Putting the rule in the schema protects against every writer, including scripts and other services.
codeExamples:
UPDATE product SET stock = stock - 80 WHERE id = 1;     -- would oversell

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_stock' is violated.
-- (the UPDATE is rolled back as a whole statement; stock stays 50)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Common checks: ranges (age BETWEEN 0 AND 150), enumerations (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED')), cross-column rules (end_date >= start_date) and formats (REGEXP_LIKE for a PIN code).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE booking (
    id         INT PRIMARY KEY,
    start_date DATE NOT NULL,
    end_date   DATE NOT NULL,
    status     VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
    pin        CHAR(6) NOT NULL,
    CHECK (end_date >= start_date),                           -- cross-column rule
    CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','CANCELLED')),             -- allowed set
    CHECK (REGEXP_LIKE(pin, '^[0-9]{6}$'))                    -- format rule
);
INSERT INTO booking VALUES (1, '2026-03-10', '2026-03-05', 'NEW', '560001');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'booking_chk_1' is violated.

beginner.content:
Diagram

   INSERT / UPDATE row
        │
        ▼
   evaluate each CHECK (expr) on the NEW row values
        │
   ┌────┴─────────────┬──────────────────┐
   TRUE              NULL (unknown)      FALSE
   accept            accept              ERROR 3819, statement rolled back

Fresher Notes

  • CHECK validates a condition on each row, for example CHECK (age >= 18).
  • It is enforced in MySQL 8.0.16 and later.
  • A row that makes the condition false is rejected; NULL (unknown) passes.

Worked Example 1

Add a constraint as NOT ENFORCED then enable.

Worked Example 2

List check constraints.
codeExamples:
SELECT constraint_name, check_clause FROM information_schema.check_constraints WHERE constraint_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- constraint_name | check_clause
-- chk_dates       | (end_d >= start_d)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Row-level checks.

Practice Exercise 2

NULL passes the check.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A CHECK is a boolean expression evaluated per row on INSERT and UPDATE (when ENFORCED). A row is rejected only when the expression is FALSE; TRUE and UNKNOWN (NULL) pass. The expression may use columns of the row and deterministic functions, not subqueries or other rows.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Add, drop and toggle checks after creation. NOT ENFORCED keeps documentation of a rule without validating, useful while cleaning data.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative, enforced for all clients, can be added or dropped later, can be marked NOT ENFORCED for documentation or staged rollout, and are visible in information_schema.check_constraints.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE product ADD CONSTRAINT chk_name CHECK (CHAR_LENGTH(name) >= 2);
SELECT constraint_name, check_clause
FROM information_schema.check_constraints
WHERE constraint_schema = DATABASE() AND constraint_name LIKE 'chk_%'
ORDER BY constraint_name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+--------------------------+
-- | CONSTRAINT_NAME | CHECK_CLAUSE             |
-- +-----------------+--------------------------+
-- | chk_name        | (char_length(name) >= 2) |
-- | chk_price       | (price > 0)              |
-- | chk_stock       | (stock >= 0)             |
-- +-----------------+--------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each write evaluates the expression; adding a CHECK to a big table validates every existing row (a full scan, and it fails if one row is bad); and a hard rule is painful to change when the business changes.
codeExamples:
-- Existing bad data blocks the constraint
INSERT INTO product VALUES (3, 'Old', 5.00, 1);
UPDATE product SET price = -1 WHERE id = 3;           -- this is already refused...
-- ...but adding a rule over legacy data may fail on old rows:
ALTER TABLE product ADD CONSTRAINT chk_big CHECK (price > 100);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_price' is violated.
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_big' is violated.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the expression must be deterministic and may not use subqueries, stored functions, user variables, or nondeterministic functions such as NOW() or RAND(). It cannot look at other rows, so rules like "total of lines equals order total" or "no overlapping bookings" need triggers or application logic. CHECK on columns used by FK referential actions (CASCADE, SET NULL) is restricted.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE evt (id INT PRIMARY KEY, happens DATETIME, CHECK (happens > NOW()));

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3814 (HY000): An expression of a check constraint 'evt_chk_1' contains disallowed
-- function: now.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use CHECK for single-row invariants that rarely change (non-negative amounts, valid state sets) and name every constraint so migrations and error messages are traceable. Treat NULL carefully: pair CHECK with NOT NULL or the rule is bypassed. For lookup-style sets that evolve, a reference table with a foreign key is easier to change than an IN list. Verify your fleet runs 8.0.16 or later, and note replicas on 5.7 would not enforce it.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Name them (CONSTRAINT chk_age CHECK (...)) and keep conditions deterministic: no subqueries or non-deterministic functions.
  • Table-level checks can compare columns: CHECK (end_date >= start_date).
  • Add with ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK; existing rows are validated.

Senior Notes

  • Because NULL passes CHECK, combine with NOT NULL when a value is required.
  • Checks cannot reference other rows or tables; cross-row rules need transactions, locks or triggers.
  • Changing a check on huge tables validates every row; do it in a quiet window.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting NULL to fail a CHECK (it passes), trying cross-row rules (not supported), and old MySQL versions that ignored CHECK silently. Combine with NOT NULL, and use triggers or locks for multi-row invariants.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

CHECK has a small per-row CPU cost and no index effect. Adding it to a big table scans the table to validate existing rows, so test the count of violators first and schedule the change.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: state machines. A CHECK keeps status and timestamps consistent, for example a shipped order must have a ship date.

beginner.content:
Introduction

INSERT adds new rows to a table. You can list the target columns and supply one or many value tuples, copy rows from a query with INSERT ... SELECT, or set columns by name with INSERT ... SET. Columns you leave out get their DEFAULT, their AUTO_INCREMENT value, or NULL.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (
    id     INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    name   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    dept   VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'General',
    salary DECIMAL(9,2) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO emp (name, dept, salary) VALUES ('Abaji', 'IT', 60000);      -- one row, columns named
INSERT INTO emp (name, salary)       VALUES ('Raoji', 45000),            -- many rows, one statement
                                            ('Mina', 52000);
SELECT * FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+---------+----------+
-- | id | name  | dept    | salary   |
-- +----+-------+---------+----------+
-- |  1 | Abaji | IT      | 60000.00 |
-- |  2 | Raoji | General | 45000.00 |
-- |  3 | Mina  | General | 52000.00 |
-- +----+------+---------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Data enters a database through INSERT: sign-ups, orders, log events, imports. Listing columns explicitly keeps statements valid when someone later adds a column, and multi-row inserts cut network round trips.
codeExamples:
-- Always name the columns: positional VALUES breaks when the table changes
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (4, 'Kanhoji');                 -- wrong number of values

-- Retrieve the generated key right after inserting
INSERT INTO emp (name, salary) VALUES ('Dev', 70000);
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID() AS new_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1136 (21S01): Column count doesn't match value count at row 1
-- +--------+
-- | new_id |
-- +--------+
-- |      4 |
-- +--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real systems use upserts for idempotent writes, bulk INSERT ... SELECT to build summary or archive tables, and INSERT IGNORE for de-duplicating feeds.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp_archive LIKE emp;
INSERT INTO emp_archive (name, dept, salary)
SELECT name, dept, salary FROM emp WHERE salary < 50000;     -- copy rows from a query

CREATE TABLE stock (sku VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, qty INT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('PEN', 10);
INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('PEN', 5) AS new                   -- 8.0.19+ row alias
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE qty = stock.qty + new.qty;           -- add to existing row
SELECT * FROM stock;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-----+
-- | sku | qty |
-- +-----+-----+
-- | PEN |  15 |
-- +-----+-----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   INSERT INTO emp (cols) VALUES (...)
        │
        ▼
   parse ► check NOT NULL / DEFAULT / types ► check CHECK + FK + UNIQUE
        │
        ▼
   write clustered row (PK order) ► update each secondary index
        │
        ▼
   redo log + undo log ► COMMIT ► visible to others

Fresher Notes

  • INSERT INTO t (cols) VALUES (...) adds rows. Insert several at once with multiple value lists.
  • Always list column names so the statement does not break when the table changes.
  • Auto-increment ids are generated if omitted; read the last with LAST_INSERT_ID().

Worked Example 1

Upsert.

Worked Example 2

INSERT IGNORE counts.

Practice Exercise 1

Multi-row insert and LAST_INSERT_ID.

Practice Exercise 2

Insert from a select.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An INSERT parses and validates the row, checks constraints and foreign keys, writes a new record into the clustered index (and each secondary index, or the change buffer), and logs it to the redo and binary logs. A multi-row INSERT is a single statement with one parse and far less per-row overhead.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: VALUES, SET col=..., INSERT ... SELECT, INSERT IGNORE, ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, REPLACE and LOAD DATA. Always name the columns.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: simple, atomic per statement, supports batching (hundreds of rows per statement is far faster than one at a time), and combines with ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE for idempotency.
codeExamples:
-- Multi-row insert is all-or-nothing: one bad row cancels the statement
INSERT INTO emp (name, salary) VALUES ('Ok1', 1000), (NULL, 2000), ('Ok3', 3000);
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_now FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1048 (23000): Column 'name' cannot be null
-- +----------+
-- | rows_now |
-- +----------+
-- |        4 |
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every insert maintains all indexes and constraints, so heavy indexing slows writes. Auto-increment values are consumed even when the insert fails or rolls back, leaving gaps. INSERT IGNORE hides errors (truncation, bad values become warnings).
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO emp (name, salary) VALUES ('Gap', 100);        -- gets id 5
DELETE FROM emp WHERE name = 'Gap';
INSERT INTO emp (name, salary) VALUES ('Next', 200);       -- id 6, never reuses 5
SELECT id, name FROM emp WHERE name IN ('Next');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+
-- | id | name |
-- +----+------+
-- |  6 | Next |
-- +----+------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a statement is capped by max_allowed_packet (64 MB default), very large single inserts hold locks and bloat the undo log, and bulk loads of millions of rows belong in LOAD DATA or chunked batches. The auto-increment counter is per table and lives in memory plus redo (persisted since 8.0).
codeExamples:
-- Practical batch size: a few hundred to a few thousand rows per statement
SELECT @@max_allowed_packet / 1024 / 1024 AS packet_mb, @@autocommit AS autocommit;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------+------------+
-- | packet_mb | autocommit |
-- +-----------+------------+
-- |   64.0000 |          1 |
-- +-----------+------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Insert in batches inside one transaction (commit every 1,000 to 10,000 rows) for throughput without huge undo. Prefer idempotent upserts so retries are safe, never rely on contiguous auto-increment values, and monitor index count on write-heavy tables. For millions of rows use LOAD DATA INFILE, or disable secondary index work by loading into a staging table first.

Mid-Level Notes

  • INSERT ... SELECT copies rows from a query; INSERT IGNORE skips errors; ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE upserts; REPLACE deletes then inserts.
  • Batch inserts (hundreds of rows per statement) are much faster than one-by-one.
  • Wrap related inserts in a transaction.

Senior Notes

  • Bulk load with LOAD DATA INFILE or the shell loader; disable unnecessary indexes only in controlled offline loads.
  • REPLACE changes ids and triggers delete/insert side effects; prefer ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.
  • Watch max_allowed_packet and lock/undo growth for huge batches; chunk them.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: omitting the column list (breaks when the table changes), one INSERT per row in a loop (slow), REPLACE where an upsert is intended (it deletes and reinserts, firing cascades), and swallowing errors with IGNORE.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO items VALUES (NULL, 'x', 1, 99);           -- wrong column count
INSERT INTO items (name, qty) VALUES ('y');            -- value count mismatch

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1136 (21S01): Column count doesn't match value count at row 1
-- ERROR 1136 (21S01): Column count doesn't match value count at row 1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Bulk loading: batch hundreds of rows per statement, wrap batches in one transaction, and for very large loads use LOAD DATA or the shell loader. In Java set rewriteBatchedStatements=true.
codeExamples:
-- 100k rows: one by one ~ 90 s, 1000-row batches ~ 6 s, LOAD DATA ~ 2 s
LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE '/tmp/items.csv' INTO TABLE items FIELDS TERMINATED BY ',' LINES TERMINATED BY '\n' IGNORE 1 LINES (name, qty);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 100000 rows affected (1.9 sec)  Records: 100000  Deleted: 0  Skipped: 0  Warnings: 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: idempotent ingest from a queue. Use a natural unique key so redelivered messages do not create duplicates.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO events (event_id, user_id, kind, payload)
VALUES ('evt-81723', 7, 'login', JSON_OBJECT('ip', '10.0.0.5'))
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE event_id = event_id;      -- no-op on duplicate delivery

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (0 rows affected if the event was already stored)

beginner.content:
Introduction

SELECT reads data without changing it. The minimum form is SELECT columns FROM table. Pick columns (projection), rename them with AS, compute expressions, and use SELECT * only for quick exploration. The result is a set of rows with no guaranteed order.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), dept VARCHAR(20), salary DECIMAL(9,2));
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',60000),(2,'Raoji','HR',45000),(3,'Mina','IT',52000);

SELECT name,                          -- plain column
       salary * 12  AS annual_pay,    -- computed column with alias
       'INR'        AS currency       -- constant column
FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------------+----------+
-- | name  | annual_pay | currency |
-- +-------+------------+----------+
-- | Abaji | 720000.00  | INR      |
-- | Raoji | 540000.00  | INR      |
-- | Mina  |  624000.00 | INR      |
-- +------+------------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Every report, screen and API list starts with a query. Selecting only the columns you need reduces network traffic, memory and lets the engine answer from an index alone (covering index) instead of reading full rows.
codeExamples:
-- SELECT without FROM works for calculations and server facts
SELECT 2 + 3 AS five, UPPER('mysql') AS shout, CURRENT_DATE() AS today;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------+-------+------------+
-- | five | shout | today      |
-- +------+-------+------------+
-- |    5 | MYSQL | 2026-10-06 |
-- +------+-------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Dashboards, search pages and exports use SELECT with filters, sorting and limits. Table and column aliases keep long joins readable and are the only way to join a table to itself.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.dept
FROM emp AS e                 -- table alias
WHERE e.dept = 'IT';

SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp;     -- unique departments only

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+
-- | employee | dept |
-- +----------+------+
-- | Abaji    | IT   |
-- | Mina     | IT   |
-- +----------+------+
-- +------+
-- | dept |
-- +------+
-- | IT   |
-- | HR   |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SELECT name, salary*12 AS annual     table emp
   FROM emp                  ───────►   ┌────┬──────┬────────┐
                                        │ id │ name │ salary │
   projection = pick columns            └────┴──────┴────────┘
   selection  = pick rows (WHERE)       result: new temporary rowset
   (source table is never modified)

Fresher Notes

  • SELECT col1, col2 FROM table reads data. SELECT * returns all columns.
  • Use AS to give a column a readable alias.
  • SELECT does not change data.

Worked Example 1

Distinct columns only.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM items;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- pen
-- book
-- bag
-- cap

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Index-only scan with a narrow SELECT.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM items;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key  | Extra
-- index | name | Using index

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Select with expression and alias.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, qty, qty * 10 AS value FROM items;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | qty | value
-- pen  |  13 |   130
-- book |   5 |    50
-- bag  |   2 |    20

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

SELECT without a table.
codeExamples:
SELECT 2 * 3 AS product, NOW() IS NOT NULL AS has_time;

-- OUTPUT:
-- product | has_time
--       6 |        1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The server chooses an access path (primary key lookup, index range, full scan) from table statistics, reads rows through the storage engine, filters, projects the requested columns, and streams results to the client. The SELECT list determines whether an index alone can answer the query.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

You can select columns, expressions, aliases, constants, and use functions. Table and column aliases make joins readable. SELECT without FROM evaluates expressions.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative (you state what you want, the optimizer picks how), composable with joins, subqueries and functions, and read-only so it takes no row locks under the default isolation level (consistent snapshot reads).
codeExamples:
-- The optimizer chooses the access path; EXPLAIN reveals it
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp WHERE id = 2;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +-------+-------+---------+------+
-- | table | type  | key     | rows |
-- +-------+-------+---------+------+
-- | emp   | const | PRIMARY |    1 |
-- +-------+-------+---------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: SELECT * breaks when columns are added, reads unneeded data (including big TEXT/BLOB), and blocks index-only plans. Result order is undefined without ORDER BY, and a careless query on a huge table can scan everything.
codeExamples:
-- Column order of SELECT * depends on table definition; an added column changes the result
ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN city VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'Pune';
SELECT * FROM emp WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+------+----------+------+
-- | id | name  | dept | salary   | city |
-- +----+-------+------+----------+------+
-- |  1 | Abaji | IT   | 60000.00 | Pune |
-- +----+------+------+----------+------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a table alias is not visible in the same SELECT list's WHERE for column aliases (aliases cannot be used in WHERE), a result can have at most 4096 columns, and the whole result is held by the server or streamed to the client buffer, so very large results need LIMIT or streaming.
codeExamples:
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual FROM emp WHERE annual > 600000;     -- alias used in WHERE
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual FROM emp HAVING annual > 600000;      -- allowed in HAVING / ORDER BY

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1054 (42S22): Unknown column 'annual' in 'where clause'
-- +------------+
-- | annual     |
-- +------------+
-- |  720000.00 |
-- |  624000.00 |
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Name columns explicitly in application queries, keep result sets small, and let EXPLAIN verify that hot queries use indexes. Treat SELECT * as a development tool; in production code it hurts covering-index plans and causes silent contract changes. Add ORDER BY wherever the consumer depends on order.

Mid-Level Notes

  • List needed columns instead of *: less data, safer when the table changes, and allows covering indexes.
  • Expressions are allowed: SELECT price * qty AS total.
  • SELECT without FROM works for calculations: SELECT 1+1.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid SELECT * in application code and views; it couples code to table structure and prevents covering-index plans.
  • Result ordering is undefined without ORDER BY.
  • Check the plan with EXPLAIN when queries get slow; most issues are missing indexes or non-sargable predicates.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: SELECT * in application code, forgetting that column order can change, using ORDER BY positions, and relying on unspecified row order. List columns and order explicitly.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM emp;                                       -- breaks silently if a column is added or reordered
SELECT id, name, dept FROM emp ORDER BY id;                -- explicit, stable contract

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | dept
--  1 | Abaji | 10

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Select only needed columns and rows. Narrow projections enable covering indexes and cut network and memory. Compare the data volume returned.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a list endpoint selects exactly the fields the screen needs, with a stable order and a limit, backed by one index.

beginner.content:
Introduction

UPDATE changes column values in existing rows: UPDATE table SET col = expr WHERE condition. The right-hand side can use the current column values, and several columns can be set in one statement. Without WHERE every row is updated.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), dept VARCHAR(20), salary DECIMAL(9,2));
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',60000),(2,'Raoji','HR',45000),(3,'Mina','IT',52000);

UPDATE emp
SET salary = salary * 1.10,           -- 10 percent raise, computed from the old value
    dept   = 'Tech'
WHERE dept = 'IT';
SELECT id, dept, salary FROM emp ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected (0.01 sec)
-- Rows matched: 2  Changed: 2  Warnings: 0
-- +----+------+----------+
-- | id | dept | salary   |
-- +----+------+----------+
-- |  1 | Tech | 66000.00 |
-- |  2 | HR   | 45000.00 |
-- |  3 | Tech | 57200.00 |
-- +----+------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Data changes: a user edits a profile, an order moves from PAID to SHIPPED, stock decreases. Updating in place keeps one current row instead of piling up versions.
codeExamples:
-- Atomic arithmetic avoids the read-modify-write race
UPDATE emp SET salary = salary + 500 WHERE id = 2;     -- good: engine does it under a row lock

-- Bad pattern in application code:  x = SELECT salary; then UPDATE SET salary = x + 500
-- two concurrent requests would both read the same x and one raise would be lost

SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE id = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | salary   |
-- +----------+
-- | 45500.00 |
-- +----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Multi-table UPDATE with JOIN synchronises data (copy a looked-up value into a table), and ORDER BY ... LIMIT lets you update in batches to keep transactions short.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE dept_bonus (dept VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, bonus DECIMAL(9,2));
INSERT INTO dept_bonus VALUES ('Tech', 1000), ('HR', 250);

UPDATE emp e
JOIN dept_bonus b ON b.dept = e.dept       -- MySQL multi-table update syntax
SET e.salary = e.salary + b.bonus;
SELECT id, salary FROM emp ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----------+
-- | id | salary   |
-- +----+----------+
-- |  1 | 67000.00 |
-- |  2 | 45750.00 |
-- |  3 | 58200.00 |
-- +----+----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   UPDATE emp SET salary = salary*1.1 WHERE dept='IT'
        │
        ▼
   find rows (index on dept?) ──► lock each matching row (X lock)
        │
        ▼
   write old version to UNDO ──► change row + indexes ──► REDO log
        │
        ▼
   COMMIT releases locks ──► other sessions see the new value

Fresher Notes

  • UPDATE t SET col = value WHERE condition changes existing rows.
  • Always include WHERE; without it every row is updated.
  • Check the number of affected rows after running.

Worked Example 1

Optimistic locking.

Worked Example 2

Batched update loop (pseudo).
codeExamples:
UPDATE logs SET archived = 1 WHERE archived = 0 AND id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000;
-- repeat for next ranges, commit each time

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1000 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Update and verify affected rows.

Practice Exercise 2

Join update.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

UPDATE locates rows (ideally through an index), takes exclusive row locks, writes the old version to the undo log, changes the clustered record in place (or delete-marks and inserts if the key changes), updates affected secondary indexes, and logs to redo and binlog. The number of rows scanned, not just changed, decides the lock footprint.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: several columns, expressions, ORDER BY ... LIMIT (batching), multi-table UPDATE with JOIN, and CASE for conditional values. Note that MySQL evaluates SET assignments left to right.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: row-level locking in InnoDB, atomic multi-column changes, expressions and joins in one statement, and a clear affected-row count to detect whether anything happened (optimistic locking uses it).
codeExamples:
-- Optimistic locking: update only if the version is unchanged
ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN version INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
UPDATE emp SET salary = 70000, version = version + 1
WHERE id = 1 AND version = 0;
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS rows_changed;      -- 1 = we won, 0 = someone else changed it first

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | rows_changed |
-- +--------------+
-- |            1 |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a forgotten WHERE rewrites the whole table; updating an indexed column rewrites index entries; large updates create big undo logs and long row locks, and replicas apply them as one big transaction (replication lag). Old values are lost unless you audit.
codeExamples:
-- Safety net for interactive sessions: the server refuses WHERE-less updates
SET sql_safe_updates = 1;
UPDATE emp SET salary = 0;                 -- no WHERE, no key column

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1175 (HY000): You are using safe update mode and you tried to update a table without
-- a WHERE that uses a KEY column. To disable safe mode, toggle the option in Preferences.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: you cannot update a table using a subquery on that same table directly (ERROR 1093; wrap it in a derived table), the target column list in one statement is evaluated left to right in MySQL (unlike standard SQL), and a no-op update that sets the same value reports 0 rows changed.
codeExamples:
UPDATE emp SET salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp) WHERE id = 2;       -- same table in subquery
UPDATE emp SET salary = (SELECT m FROM (SELECT MAX(salary) AS m FROM emp) x)
WHERE id = 2;                                                              -- workaround

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1093 (HY000): You can't specify target table 'emp' for update in FROM clause
-- Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Always write the WHERE first, run it as a SELECT, and wrap risky changes in a transaction so you can ROLLBACK. Batch large updates (for example 5,000 rows by primary-key range) to bound lock time, undo size and replication lag. Make sure the WHERE column is indexed; an unindexed UPDATE locks far more rows than it changes under REPEATABLE READ.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Test with a SELECT using the same WHERE first, or run inside a transaction and verify before COMMIT.
  • Update several columns: SET a=1, b=2. Use expressions: SET qty = qty - 1.
  • Join updates: UPDATE a JOIN b ON ... SET a.x = b.y.

Senior Notes

  • Large updates should be batched (LIMIT 1000 in a loop) to keep locks and undo small and replicas in sync.
  • Optimistic locking: UPDATE ... SET ..., version = version+1 WHERE id=? AND version=? and check affected rows.
  • Row-based replication logs full rows; huge updates can create enormous binlogs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no WHERE, an unindexed WHERE that locks many rows, and read-modify-write in application code (lost updates). Use safe-updates in development, atomic expressions and conditional updates.
codeExamples:
UPDATE stock SET qty = 0;                                   -- every row!
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'B2' AND qty > 0;  -- atomic and safe
SELECT ROW_COUNT();                                           -- 0 means "sold out"

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected   (the first statement: all rows changed)
-- ROW_COUNT()
-- 1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Update in batches by primary key range for big tables, commit each batch, and pause when replicas lag. Check the plan of the UPDATE's WHERE with EXPLAIN.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world optimistic locking: users edit a record for minutes, so check a version in the UPDATE and tell the user if someone else saved first.

beginner.content:
Introduction

DELETE removes rows that match a condition: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition. It is DML, fully transactional, logged row by row, fires triggers and respects foreign keys. Without WHERE it deletes every row (slowly); use TRUNCATE to empty a table fast.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE session_log (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, user_id INT, seen DATE);
INSERT INTO session_log (user_id, seen) VALUES (1,'2026-01-01'),(2,'2026-06-01'),(3,'2026-09-30');

DELETE FROM session_log WHERE seen < '2026-03-01';       -- remove old rows only
SELECT id, user_id FROM session_log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected (0.00 sec)
-- +----+---------+
-- | id | user_id |
-- +----+---------+
-- |  2 |       2 |
-- |  3 |       3 |
-- +----+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Data must be removed: expired sessions, cancelled drafts, GDPR erasure requests, test data. Deleting with a precise filter keeps tables small, which keeps indexes and scans fast.
codeExamples:
-- Preview first: the same WHERE as a SELECT
SELECT COUNT(*) AS will_delete FROM session_log WHERE user_id = 3;
START TRANSACTION;
DELETE FROM session_log WHERE user_id = 3;
ROLLBACK;                                      -- changed my mind: nothing is lost
SELECT COUNT(*) AS still_there FROM session_log WHERE user_id = 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+
-- | will_delete |
-- +-------------+
-- |           1 |
-- +-------------+
-- +-------------+
-- | still_there |
-- +-------------+
-- |           1 |
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Production purge jobs delete in small batches with LIMIT to avoid long locks, and many systems prefer soft delete (a deleted_at column) so data is recoverable and auditable.
codeExamples:
-- Batch purge: repeat until ROW_COUNT() = 0
DELETE FROM session_log
WHERE seen < '2026-07-01'
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 1000;                                    -- bounded work per transaction
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS deleted_this_round;

-- Soft delete alternative: keep the row, hide it
ALTER TABLE session_log ADD COLUMN deleted_at DATETIME NULL;
UPDATE session_log SET deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------+
-- | deleted_this_round |
-- +--------------------+
-- |                  1 |
-- +--------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
   ┌──────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┬────────────┐
   │ command  │ WHERE?      │ logged        │ rollback     │ keeps table│
   ├──────────┼─────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┼────────────┤
   │ DELETE   │ yes         │ row by row    │ yes          │ yes        │
   │ TRUNCATE │ no          │ minimal (DDL) │ no (implicit │ yes, resets│
   │          │             │               │ commit)      │ AUTO_INC   │
   │ DROP     │ n/a         │ DDL           │ no           │ no         │
   └──────────┴─────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┴────────────┘

Fresher Notes

  • DELETE FROM t WHERE condition removes rows. Without WHERE it deletes all rows.
  • DELETE can be rolled back inside a transaction (unlike TRUNCATE).
  • Check how many rows were deleted with ROW_COUNT().

Worked Example 1

Batched purge.
codeExamples:
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 90 DAY LIMIT 1000;
-- loop until ROW_COUNT() = 0

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1000 rows affected

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Soft delete.

Practice Exercise 1

Delete with a condition and verify.

Practice Exercise 2

Rollback a delete.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DELETE finds rows, takes exclusive locks, writes each old row to the undo log, marks the clustered record delete-marked and does the same in secondary indexes; a purge thread removes them physically later once no snapshot can see them.
