That is why a big delete is slow and space is not returned immediately.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: with WHERE, with ORDER BY and LIMIT (batching), multi-table DELETE with JOIN, and soft delete via UPDATE. TRUNCATE empties a table quickly but is DDL.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: precise, transactional and reversible before COMMIT, honours FK rules (cascade or restrict), and supports multi-table delete with joins. Space is reused by later inserts.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: on huge tables it is slow (every row and index entry is logged), holds locks, bloats undo, and does not shrink the file: freed space stays inside the tablespace until OPTIMIZE TABLE or a rebuild. Deleted auto-increment values are not reused.
codeExamples:
-- File size does not drop after DELETE; pages are only marked free
DELETE FROM session_log;
SELECT table_rows, data_free > 0 AS has_free_space
FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'session_log';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+----------------+
-- | TABLE_ROWS | has_free_space |
-- +------------+----------------+
-- |          0 |              0 |
-- +------------+----------------+
-- (on a large table DATA_FREE would be big until OPTIMIZE TABLE session_log)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a parent row cannot be deleted while child rows reference it under RESTRICT; you cannot delete from a table using a subquery on the same table without a derived-table workaround; DELETE ... ORDER BY / LIMIT only works for single-table form; and a WHERE-less DELETE cannot be undone after COMMIT.

Architect's Notes

Delete in bounded batches during low traffic, always on an indexed predicate, and watch replication lag. For time-based retention, partition by date and DROP PARTITION instead of deleting rows: it is instant and leaves no fragmentation. Prefer soft delete only where recovery or audit is required, and then remember every query must filter it (a view helps).

Mid-Level Notes

  • Foreign keys can block deletes (RESTRICT) or cascade them.
  • Preview with SELECT ... WHERE first; use transactions for safety.
  • DELETE does not shrink the table file; space is reused, and OPTIMIZE TABLE reclaims it.

Senior Notes

  • Mass deletes: batch (DELETE ... LIMIT 1000 in a loop) to avoid long locks, big undo logs and replica lag.
  • Prefer soft delete (deleted_at) for recoverability and audit, with periodic purge jobs.
  • Partitioned tables allow instant data removal by dropping a partition.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: DELETE without WHERE, deleting through an unindexed column (locks and scans everything), one giant delete that bloats undo and lags replicas, and expecting disk space to drop. Preview with SELECT, delete in batches, and rebuild only if needed.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01' LIMIT 5000;     -- loop until ROW_COUNT() = 0
OPTIMIZE TABLE events;                                             -- reclaim space only when really needed

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 48200000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Partition by time to remove old data instantly: dropping a partition removes the files without per-row work. It is the right tool for retention on log and event tables.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world retention job: purge in small batches with a pause, so production traffic and replicas stay healthy, and log how many rows were removed.

beginner.content:
Introduction

WHERE filters rows before they are grouped or returned. Each row is tested against a boolean condition; only rows for which the condition is TRUE survive (FALSE and NULL are dropped). It works with SELECT, UPDATE and DELETE alike.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), dept VARCHAR(20), salary DECIMAL(9,2), city VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO emp VALUES
 (1,'Abaji','IT',60000,'Pune'), (2,'Raoji','HR',45000,'Delhi'),
 (3,'Mina','IT',52000,'Pune'), (4,'Kanhoji','Sales',38000,NULL);

SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' AND salary > 55000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+----------+
-- | name  | salary   |
-- +-------+----------+
-- | Abaji | 60000.00 |
-- +------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Returning every row is wasteful and rarely what the user asked for. Filtering in the database moves less data over the network, lets indexes narrow the search, and is the same predicate that makes UPDATE and DELETE safe.
codeExamples:
-- NULL is neither equal nor unequal to anything, so these rows vanish from both tests
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE city = 'Pune';
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE city <> 'Pune';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+        +-------+
-- | name  |        | name  |
-- +-------+        +-------+
-- | Abaji |        | Raoji |
-- | Mina  |        +-------+       <- Kanhoji (city NULL) appears in neither result
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real queries combine conditions, ranges and lists. Predicates that compare a bare indexed column to a value (sargable) can use the index; wrapping the column in a function usually cannot.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE emp ADD KEY idx_salary (salary);
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary >= 50000;         -- sargable: index range scan
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary + 0 >= 50000;     -- column inside expression: no range scan

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key        | rows |
-- | range | idx_salary |    3 |
-- | index | idx_salary |    4 |      <- scans the whole index instead of a range

beginner.content:
Diagram

   FROM emp ──► WHERE (row filter) ──► GROUP BY ──► HAVING ──► SELECT ──► ORDER BY ──► LIMIT
                  │
                  ├─ TRUE    : row kept
                  ├─ FALSE   : row dropped
                  └─ NULL    : row dropped (unknown)

Fresher Notes

  • WHERE filters rows before they are returned: SELECT * FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000.
  • Combine conditions with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses.
  • WHERE runs before GROUP BY, so it cannot use aggregate results.

Worked Example 1

Precedence trap: AND binds tighter than OR.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 20 OR dept = 10 AND salary > 100000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Moropant          (read as dept=20 OR (dept=10 AND salary>100000))

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Plan for a sargable filter.

Practice Exercise 1

Find employees earning above 50000 in department 10.

Practice Exercise 2

Use OR with parentheses correctly.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE (dept = 10 OR dept = 20) AND salary >= 60000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The optimizer splits a WHERE clause into conjuncts (parts joined by AND) and tries to push each one into an index range, an index lookup, or a row filter. Conditions that compare a bare indexed column to a constant become index access; everything else is evaluated on rows after they are read ("Using where").

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Predicates: comparison, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, IS NULL, EXISTS, and combinations with AND/OR/NOT. Row constructors and subqueries are allowed. Parentheses make precedence explicit because AND binds tighter than OR.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative and composable (AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, subqueries), index-friendly, and evaluated inside the server so only matching rows leave it.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE dept IN ('IT', 'HR')
  AND salary BETWEEN 45000 AND 55000
  AND city IS NOT NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Raoji |
-- | Mina  |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a non-sargable or low-selectivity predicate forces a full scan; implicit type conversion (comparing a string column with a number) can disable the index and silently match unexpected rows; NULL logic surprises beginners.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE phone_book (id INT PRIMARY KEY, phone VARCHAR(15), KEY (phone));
INSERT INTO phone_book VALUES (1,'9000000001'),(2,'9000000002');
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM phone_book WHERE phone = 9000000001;     -- number vs string column

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key   | rows | Extra                |
-- | index | phone |    2 | Using where; Using index |
-- (every phone value is cast to a number, so the index cannot do a lookup; quote the literal)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: column aliases from the SELECT list cannot be used in WHERE (it runs before SELECT); aggregates are not allowed in WHERE (use HAVING); and the optimizer may ignore an index when the predicate matches a large part of the table.

Architect's Notes

Write sargable predicates (column on one side, constant or parameter on the other), keep types identical, and index the columns used in highly selective filters. Check plans with EXPLAIN rather than guessing, and avoid functions on indexed columns, using a range (date >= x AND date < y) or a functional index instead.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Write sargable conditions: compare the bare column to a value so an index can be used (d >= ..., not YEAR(d) = ...).
  • A leading wildcard (LIKE "%x") or function on the column disables the index.
  • Compare like types; comparing a VARCHAR column to a number forces conversion on every row.

Senior Notes

  • Use EXPLAIN to confirm the filter becomes an index range or ref access, not a scan.
  • Combine selective predicates into a composite index ordered by equality first, then range.
  • OR across different columns often needs index_merge or UNION rewrite for speed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: functions on indexed columns, implicit type conversion, OR chains that defeat indexes, and forgetting precedence. The fix is to keep the column bare, compare matching types and use parentheses or UNION.
codeExamples:
-- bad: function on the column
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE YEAR(hired) = 2024;
-- good
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE hired >= '2024-01-01' AND hired < '2025-01-01';
-- precedence trap
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 20 OR dept = 10 AND salary > 100000;     -- means dept=20 OR (dept=10 AND salary>100000)

-- OUTPUT: (explain)
-- bad : type=ALL;  good: type=range key=idx_hired

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Selective predicates first in a composite index: equality columns, then one range column. Check rows and filtered in EXPLAIN, and use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for actual row counts.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id FROM emp WHERE dept = 10 AND salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 60000;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Filter: ((emp.dept = 10) and (emp.salary between 50000 and 60000))  (actual time=0.04..0.9 rows=240 loops=1)
--     -> Index range scan on emp using idx_dept_salary over (dept = 10 AND 50000 <= salary <= 60000)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a search form with optional filters. Build the WHERE from fixed fragments and bind every value, so unused filters cost nothing and nothing is concatenated.
codeExamples:
-- application builds: WHERE 1=1 [AND dept = ?] [AND salary >= ?] [AND name LIKE ?]
SELECT id, name, dept, salary FROM emp WHERE 1=1 AND dept = 10 AND salary >= 50000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | dept | salary
--  1 | Abaji |   10 | 60000

beginner.content:
Introduction

ORDER BY sorts the result by one or more expressions, ascending (default) or DESC. It is the only way to get a guaranteed order; without it MySQL may return rows in any order, which can change after an index or plan change.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), dept VARCHAR(20), salary DECIMAL(9,2));
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',60000),(2,'Raoji','HR',45000),(3,'Mina','IT',52000),(4,'Kanhoji','HR',45000);

SELECT name, dept, salary
FROM emp
ORDER BY dept ASC, salary DESC;          -- by department, then highest paid first

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------+----------+
-- | name    | dept | salary   |
-- +---------+------+----------+
-- | Raoji   | HR   | 45000.00 |
-- | Kanhoji | HR   | 45000.00 |
-- | Abaji   | IT   | 60000.00 |
-- | Mina    | IT   | 52000.00 |
-- +---------+------+----------+
-- (Raoji/Kanhoji tie on both keys: their relative order is not guaranteed; add id as a tie-breaker)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

People read lists sorted: newest first, alphabetical, top earners. Pagination, reports and deterministic tests all need a stable total order, which means adding a unique tie-breaker such as the primary key.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC, id ASC;      -- id makes ties deterministic

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+----------+
-- | name    | salary   |
-- +---------+----------+
-- | Abaji   | 60000.00 |
-- | Mina    | 52000.00 |
-- | Raoji   | 45000.00 |
-- | Kanhoji | 45000.00 |
-- +-------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Sorting can use column aliases, positions and expressions, and NULLs sort first in ASC and last in DESC in MySQL. Custom order uses FIELD() or CASE.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, dept FROM emp
ORDER BY FIELD(dept, 'IT', 'HR'),        -- custom rank: IT first
         name;                           -- then alphabetical

SELECT name, salary * 12 AS annual FROM emp ORDER BY annual DESC LIMIT 1;   -- alias allowed here

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------+
-- | name    | dept |
-- +---------+------+
-- | Abaji   | IT   |
-- | Mina    | IT   |
-- | Kanhoji | HR   |
-- | Raoji   | HR   |
-- +---------+------+
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | name  | annual    |
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | Abaji | 720000.00 |
-- +------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   rows from FROM/WHERE ──► ORDER BY
                              │
          index with same order? ── yes ──► read in index order (no sort)
                              │ no
                              ▼
          filesort: sort buffer ──► (too big) ──► temp files merge ──► sorted rows

Fresher Notes

  • ORDER BY sorts results: ORDER BY salary DESC. ASC is the default.
  • Sort by several columns: ORDER BY dept, salary DESC.
  • Without ORDER BY the row order is not guaranteed.

Worked Example 1

Detect filesort.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp ORDER BY name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | Extra
-- ALL  | NULL | Using filesort

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Index removes the sort.

Practice Exercise 1

Multi-column sort.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, dept, salary FROM emp ORDER BY dept ASC, salary DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | dept | salary
-- Abaji    |   10 | 60000
-- Raoji    |   10 | 45000
-- Moropant |   20 | 70000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Sort by expression and alias.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary * 12 AS yearly FROM emp ORDER BY yearly DESC LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | yearly
-- Moropant | 840000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL can return rows in order for free only when it reads an index in that order. Otherwise it collects rows into a sort buffer ("filesort"), sorting in memory or spilling to temporary files. With LIMIT it uses a priority queue holding only the top N rows.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Sort by several columns with mixed directions (8.0 supports descending indexes), by expressions, aliases and with NULLs-first/last tricks. Add a unique tiebreaker for deterministic results.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: deterministic output, multi-key sorting, and a matching index (same columns and direction; descending indexes are real in 8.0) lets MySQL read rows already sorted and skip the sort entirely.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: without a usable index the server does a filesort: it collects rows and sorts them in the sort buffer, spilling to disk for big sets. Sorting all rows to show ten is expensive, and mixed ASC/DESC directions defeat older index designs.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp ORDER BY name;          -- no index on name

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type | key  | rows | Extra          |
-- | ALL  | NULL |    4 | Using filesort |

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: ORDER BY inside a subquery or view without LIMIT may be ignored by the optimizer; collation affects string order (case, accents); sort memory is bounded by sort_buffer_size; and sorting very long values only compares the first max_sort_length bytes (default 1024).
codeExamples:
SELECT 'a' < 'B' AS ci_collation, 'a' COLLATE utf8mb4_bin < 'B' COLLATE utf8mb4_bin AS binary_order;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+--------------+
-- | ci_collation | binary_order |
-- +--------------+--------------+
-- |            1 |            0 |
-- +--------------+--------------+
-- (case-insensitive: a before B; binary: uppercase B (66) before a (97))

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Design composite indexes as equality columns first, then the ORDER BY column, so filter and sort share one index. Always include a unique tie-breaker for pagination. Avoid sorting wide rows: select the key, sort and limit, then join back for the remaining columns (deferred join).

Mid-Level Notes

  • You can sort by alias, expression or column position, but position numbers hurt readability.
  • NULLs sort first in ASC and last in DESC in MySQL.
  • Sorting large results needs memory or disk (filesort); an index in the same order avoids it.

Senior Notes

  • An index on (dept, salary) satisfies ORDER BY dept, salary without a sort; mixed ASC/DESC works in 8.0 with descending indexes.
  • ORDER BY ... LIMIT uses a priority queue and is cheap; ORDER BY without LIMIT on millions of rows is expensive.
  • Add a unique tiebreaker (id) to make pagination deterministic.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on implicit order, ordering without LIMIT on huge sets, ordering by a different column than the index, and unstable pagination from ties. Always add the primary key as the last sort key.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, created_at FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;          -- ties may repeat or skip rows between pages
SELECT id, created_at FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10;   -- deterministic

-- OUTPUT:
-- (the second form gives the same rows on every execution)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tune sorts: index the sort order, restrict rows before sorting, select fewer columns (smaller sort rows), and size sort_buffer_size only per session for heavy reports. Check the counters for merge passes.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: "latest N per user" feed screens use a composite index matching WHERE and ORDER BY so MySQL walks the index backwards and stops after N rows.

beginner.content:
Introduction

LIMIT n returns at most n rows; LIMIT n OFFSET m (or LIMIT m, n) skips m rows first. Together with ORDER BY it implements paging, "top N" and sampling.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE article (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, title VARCHAR(30), published DATE);
INSERT INTO article (title, published) VALUES
 ('A1','2026-01-01'),('A2','2026-01-02'),('A3','2026-01-03'),('A4','2026-01-04'),('A5','2026-01-05');

SELECT id, title FROM article ORDER BY published DESC LIMIT 2;              -- latest two
SELECT id, title FROM article ORDER BY published DESC LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2;     -- page 2

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+        +----+-------+
-- | id | title |        | id | title |
-- +----+-------+        +----+-------+
-- |  5 | A5    |        |  3 | A3    |
-- |  4 | A4    |        |  2 | A2    |
-- +----+-------+        +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Showing a million rows in a browser is impossible, so UIs and APIs return a page at a time. LIMIT bounds memory and latency on both server and client.
codeExamples:
-- Page p of size s:  OFFSET = (p - 1) * s
-- Always pair LIMIT with ORDER BY on a unique key, or pages can overlap or skip rows
SELECT id, title FROM article ORDER BY id LIMIT 2 OFFSET 4;       -- page 3, size 2

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | title |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  5 | A5    |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Deep OFFSET pages get slower because the server still reads and discards every skipped row. Production feeds use keyset (seek) pagination: remember the last key and ask for rows after it.
codeExamples:
-- Keyset pagination: the client sends back the last id it saw
SELECT id, title FROM article
WHERE id > 2                  -- last id of the previous page
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 2;                      -- cost stays flat however deep you go

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | title |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  3 | A3    |
-- |  4 | A4    |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   OFFSET paging                          Keyset (seek) paging
   page 1000: read 99,900 rows, drop       WHERE id > :last_id
   them, return 100                         ORDER BY id LIMIT 100
   ┌──────────────────────┐                ┌───────────────┬──────────┐
   │ skipped (wasted work)│ keep 100       │ jump via index │ keep 100 │
   └──────────────────────┘                └───────────────┴──────────┘
   cost grows with page number             cost constant

Fresher Notes

  • LIMIT n returns at most n rows; LIMIT n OFFSET m skips m first. Used for pages and "top N".
  • Always combine with ORDER BY, or the rows you get are arbitrary.
  • Page 3 of size 10 is LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20.

Worked Example 1

Keyset next page after id 1.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name FROM emp WHERE id > 1 ORDER BY id LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  2 | Raoji
--  3 | Moropant

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Deferred join.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.* FROM emp e JOIN (SELECT id FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1) t ON t.id = e.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | dept | salary
--  1 | Abaji |   10 | 60000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Top 2 highest paid.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary
-- Moropant | 70000
-- Abaji    | 60000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Second page of size 1.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Raoji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

LIMIT n OFFSET m asks the executor to produce rows in order, discard the first m and stop after n. Discarding still reads those rows, so the cost of a page grows with its offset. A keyset (seek) query instead starts the index scan at a known key, so every page costs the same.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: LIMIT n, LIMIT m, n, LIMIT n OFFSET m, keyset with row constructors, and "limit plus one" to know if a next page exists without counting.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: trivial to use, caps result size, lets the optimizer stop early (with an index matching ORDER BY, it reads only n rows), and keyset paging gives stable, fast deep pages.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM article ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key     | rows | Extra       |
-- | index | PRIMARY |    3 | Using index |      <- stops after 3 index entries

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: OFFSET cost grows linearly (OFFSET 1000000 reads a million rows to throw away); pages shift if rows are inserted or deleted between requests; and a total count needs a separate, possibly expensive, COUNT(*).
codeExamples:
-- Simulate a deep page: the engine must walk past 4 rows to return 1
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id FROM article ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 OFFSET 4;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- -> Limit/Offset: 1/4 row(s)  (actual rows=1 loops=1)
--     -> Index scan on article using PRIMARY  (actual rows=5 loops=1)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: LIMIT and OFFSET accept only non-negative integer literals or placeholders (no expressions or column values); LIMIT is not allowed inside IN/ANY/ALL/SOME subqueries; and using LIMIT without ORDER BY gives arbitrary rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM article WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM article ORDER BY id LIMIT 2);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1235 (42000): This version of MySQL doesn't yet support 'LIMIT & IN/ALL/ANY/SOME subquery'
-- (wrap it in a derived table: ... IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id FROM article ORDER BY id LIMIT 2) t))

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use OFFSET only for shallow, user-driven pages (admin grids). For infinite scroll and APIs use keyset pagination with a unique, indexed sort key (compound: created_at, id) and return an opaque cursor. Avoid exact total counts on large tables; show "next" or an estimate instead.

Mid-Level Notes

  • OFFSET becomes slow on large values because MySQL still reads and discards skipped rows.
  • Use keyset pagination (WHERE id < last_id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20) for deep or infinite lists.
  • Show "next/previous" instead of exact page counts when COUNT(*) is expensive.

Senior Notes

  • Cap page size server-side to avoid abusive requests.
  • Deferred join: select ids with OFFSET on a narrow index, then join to fetch full rows.
  • Pagination under concurrent inserts needs stable ordering and often an opaque cursor.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: LIMIT without ORDER BY, deep OFFSET in public APIs, exact COUNT(*) for every page on huge tables, and unbounded page sizes. Cap size and depth server side.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE kind = 'click';                  -- full scan on big tables
-- better: cached/approximate count or "10000+" display
SELECT table_rows FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = 'events';

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_rows
-- 48211034       (estimate, instant)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Deferred join makes OFFSET tolerable: page on a narrow covering index to find ids, then join to fetch only those rows.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world API: an opaque cursor token carries the last key. The server decodes it into the keyset predicate, so clients cannot jump to arbitrary pages but every page is fast and stable under inserts.
codeExamples:
-- cursor = base64({"c":"2026-05-01 10:00:00","i":120})
SELECT id, title, created_at FROM posts WHERE (created_at < ?) OR (created_at = ? AND id < ?) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 21;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id  | title | created_at
-- 119 | ...   | 2026-05-01 09:58:00

beginner.content:
Introduction

DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the result. Two rows are duplicates when every selected column is equal (NULLs count as equal for this purpose). COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts the unique non-NULL values.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sale (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region VARCHAR(10), product VARCHAR(10), qty INT);
INSERT INTO sale VALUES (1,'North','Pen',5),(2,'North','Pen',7),(3,'South','Pen',2),(4,'South','Ink',9),(5,NULL,'Ink',1),(6,NULL,'Pen',3);

SELECT DISTINCT region FROM sale;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | region |
-- +--------+
-- | North  |
-- | South  |
-- | NULL   |
-- +--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Joins and denormalised data repeat values. Business questions like "which regions did we sell in" or "how many distinct customers" need uniqueness, not raw rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT region, product FROM sale ORDER BY region, product;     -- applies to the whole column list
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_all, COUNT(DISTINCT region) AS regions, COUNT(DISTINCT product) AS products FROM sale;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+---------+
-- | region | product |
-- +--------+---------+
-- | NULL   | Ink     |
-- | NULL   | Pen     |
-- | North  | Pen     |
-- | South  | Ink     |
-- | South  | Pen     |
-- +--------+---------+
-- +----------+---------+----------+
-- | rows_all | regions | products |
-- +----------+---------+----------+
-- |        6 |       2 |        2 |      <- COUNT(DISTINCT) ignores NULL
-- +----------+---------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

DISTINCT often patches duplicates produced by an accidental one-to-many join. A better fix is EXISTS or a proper grouping, since DISTINCT hides the real problem and costs a sort or hash.

Diagram

   rows ──► project selected columns ──► de-duplicate ──► result
                                           │
                       index on columns?  ─┴─ yes ─► loose index scan / ordered skip
                                              no  ─► temporary table / hash (extra cost)
   (a,x) (a,x) (b,y)   ►   (a,x) (b,y)

Fresher Notes

  • SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp removes duplicate rows from the result.
  • DISTINCT applies to the whole row of selected columns, not just the first column.
  • Use it to list unique values such as cities or categories.

Worked Example 1

Distinct on combinations.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT dept, salary > 50000 AS high FROM emp ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | high
--   10 |    0
--   10 |    1
--   20 |    1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Use EXISTS instead of DISTINCT over a join.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name FROM departments d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e WHERE e.dept = d.id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- HR
-- IT

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Unique departments.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept
-- 10
-- 20

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Count distinct vs count.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(dept) AS all_rows, COUNT(DISTINCT dept) AS unique_depts FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- all_rows | unique_depts
--        3 |            2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows. The server does this with a temporary table that has a unique key over all selected columns, or by scanning an index that is already ordered (loose index scan). Cost grows with the number of rows and the width of the selected columns.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row, so SELECT DISTINCT a, b removes duplicates of the pair. COUNT(DISTINCT x) counts unique values; GROUP BY is an equivalent for simple uniqueness.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a one-word way to deduplicate; works across multiple columns; COUNT(DISTINCT) answers cardinality questions; an index on the column lets MySQL do a loose index scan instead of reading every row.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: needs a temporary table or sort to find duplicates (slow on millions of rows), masks join bugs, and DISTINCT with ORDER BY on a column not in the select list is rejected.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT region FROM sale ORDER BY qty;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3065 (HY000): Expression #1 of ORDER BY clause is not in SELECT list, references
-- column 'sale.qty' which is not in SELECT list; this is incompatible with DISTINCT

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: DISTINCT applies to the entire select list, not one column (there is no DISTINCT ON as in PostgreSQL); it cannot be used with window functions to dedupe by one column; and COUNT(DISTINCT a, b) ignores any row where either column is NULL.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT region, product) AS pairs FROM sale;     -- rows with NULL region are skipped

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | pairs |
-- +-------+
-- |     3 |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat an urgent need for DISTINCT as a smell: first check whether the join multiplies rows. For top-per-group (what DISTINCT ON does elsewhere) use ROW_NUMBER() with a filter. For approximate counts of huge sets consider HyperLogLog in the application or a pre-aggregated rollup table.

Mid-Level Notes

  • COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts unique values.
  • DISTINCT usually needs a temporary table or index scan; it can be expensive on large sets.
  • Do not use DISTINCT to hide a bad join that duplicates rows; fix the join.

Senior Notes

  • Often GROUP BY or EXISTS is a better tool than DISTINCT over a joined result.
  • An index on the distinct column lets MySQL do a loose index scan.
  • Duplicate rows after a join signal a one-to-many relationship that should be aggregated or filtered by EXISTS.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistake: using DISTINCT to hide duplicates created by a one-to-many join. The query then does extra work and may still be wrong. Use EXISTS for existence checks or aggregate the many side first.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: an index on the distinct columns lets MySQL skip duplicates without a temp table. COUNT(DISTINCT) on a huge table can use lots of memory; consider approximate counting or pre-aggregation.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: filling a filter dropdown with the available cities. DISTINCT with an index on the column is instant, and ordering gives a stable list.

beginner.content:
Introduction

GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same values in the listed columns into one row per group, so aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) are computed per group. HAVING filters those groups after aggregation, the way WHERE filters rows before it.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sale (id INT PRIMARY KEY, region VARCHAR(10), product VARCHAR(10), amount DECIMAL(8,2));
INSERT INTO sale VALUES (1,'North','Pen',100),(2,'North','Ink',250),(3,'South','Pen',80),
                        (4,'South','Pen',120),(5,'East','Ink',50);

SELECT region, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sale
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+--------+---------+
-- | region | orders | revenue |
-- +--------+--------+---------+
-- | North  |      2 |  350.00 |
-- | South  |      2 |  200.00 |
-- | East   |      1 |   50.00 |
-- +--------+--------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Reports ask about groups, not rows: sales per region, signups per day, errors per service. Aggregation in the database sends only the summary, not millions of rows, to the application.
codeExamples:
-- HAVING keeps only groups that pass an aggregate test
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sale
GROUP BY region
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 200;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+---------+
-- | region | revenue |
-- +--------+---------+
-- | North  |  350.00 |
-- | South  |  200.00 |
-- +--------+---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real dashboards group by several columns, expressions (month of a date) and combine WHERE (cheap row filter first) with HAVING (group filter). WITH ROLLUP adds subtotal rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sale
WHERE amount > 60                       -- filter rows first: less work to group
GROUP BY region, product WITH ROLLUP;   -- subtotals and grand total

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+---------+---------+
-- | region | product | revenue |
-- +--------+---------+---------+
-- | North  | Ink     |  250.00 |
-- | North  | Pen     |  100.00 |
-- | North  | NULL    |  350.00 |
-- | South  | Pen     |  200.00 |
-- | South  | NULL    |  200.00 |
-- | NULL   | NULL    |  550.00 |
-- +--------+---------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   sale rows                 GROUP BY region           HAVING SUM >= 200
   North 100                 ┌─ North: 100,250 ─► 350 ─────► keep
   North 250   ──hash/sort──►├─ South:  80,120 ─► 200 ─────► keep
   South  80                 └─ East :  50     ─►  50 ─────► drop
   South 120
   East   50

Fresher Notes

  • GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG) are computed per group.
  • HAVING filters groups after aggregation; WHERE filters rows before it.
  • Example: departments with average salary above 50000.

Worked Example 1

Subtotals with ROLLUP.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS total FROM emp GROUP BY dept WITH ROLLUP;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | total
--   10 | 105000
--   20 |  70000
-- NULL | 175000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Strict group-by error.

Practice Exercise 1

Average salary per department over 50000.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | avg_sal
--   10 | 52500.0000
--   20 | 70000.0000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Count rows per dept after filtering.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n FROM emp WHERE salary >= 50000 GROUP BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | n
--   10 | 1
--   20 | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

GROUP BY collects rows into groups either by scanning an index in group order (streaming aggregate, cheap) or by building a temporary table keyed by the group (hash aggregate). Aggregate functions are then computed per group, and HAVING filters the finished groups.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Group by columns or expressions, several columns at once, add subtotals with WITH ROLLUP, and filter groups with HAVING (which may use aggregates and aliases). Strict ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY requires every non-aggregated column to be grouped.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, YEAR(hired) AS yr, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(salary) AS payroll FROM emp GROUP BY dept, YEAR(hired) WITH ROLLUP;
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING avg_sal > 50000 AND COUNT(*) >= 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | yr   | n | payroll
--   10 | 2024 | 1 |   60000
--   10 | NULL | 2 |  105000
-- NULL | NULL | 3 |  175000

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: concise summarisation, server-side reduction of data, ROLLUP for totals, and an index on the grouping column can make aggregation stream without a temp table.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: grouping a large unindexed set builds a temporary table (hash or sort) that can spill to disk; high-cardinality groups are costly; and non-aggregated columns in the select list are errors under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (the 8.0 default) because their value would be ambiguous.
codeExamples:
SELECT region, product, SUM(amount) FROM sale GROUP BY region;      -- product is not grouped

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1055 (42000): Expression #2 of SELECT list is not in GROUP BY clause and contains
-- nonaggregated column 'sale.product' which is not functionally dependent on columns in
-- GROUP BY clause; this is incompatible with sql_mode=only_full_group_by

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: aggregates are not allowed in WHERE; HAVING without GROUP BY treats the whole table as one group; since 8.0.13 GROUP BY no longer sorts implicitly, so add ORDER BY when order matters; and WITH ROLLUP cannot be combined with ORDER BY directly in older versions.
codeExamples:
SELECT region FROM sale GROUP BY region;               -- order NOT guaranteed in 8.0
SELECT region FROM sale GROUP BY region ORDER BY region;  -- guaranteed

-- OUTPUT (second query):
-- +--------+
-- | region |
-- +--------+
-- | East   |
-- | North  |
-- | South  |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Filter with WHERE before grouping whenever possible, index the grouping columns in the order of GROUP BY, and keep ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY enabled to avoid nondeterministic results. For heavy, repeated dashboards precompute rollup tables or use summary tables refreshed by jobs instead of grouping the raw fact table on every request.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Every selected non-aggregated column must be in GROUP BY (ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode, default in 8.0).
  • You can group by expressions: GROUP BY YEAR(d).
  • Use WHERE to cut rows early so less data is grouped.

Senior Notes

  • An index on the GROUP BY columns allows streaming aggregation without a temporary table.
  • WITH ROLLUP adds subtotal rows.
  • Wide GROUP BY on huge tables is a good candidate for pre-aggregated summary tables.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: selecting a non-grouped column (error or arbitrary value), filtering rows in HAVING instead of WHERE, and grouping on expressions that block index use. Move row filters to WHERE so fewer rows are grouped.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept;                          -- ambiguous name
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING dept = 10;                 -- works but groups everything first
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE dept = 10 GROUP BY dept;                  -- filters first

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1055 (42000): Expression #2 of SELECT list is not in GROUP BY clause and contains nonaggregated column 'emp.name'

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For repeated dashboards, pre-aggregate: a summary table updated incrementally turns an expensive scan into a tiny lookup. Check temp-table spills with the status counters.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: top customers by spend with a minimum threshold, ranked and limited, the typical "VIP list" query.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING spent >= 10000 ORDER BY spent DESC LIMIT 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | orders | spent
-- 7           |     31 | 48200.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

SQL is written in one order but executed in another. Logical order: FROM / JOIN then WHERE then GROUP BY then HAVING then window functions, SELECT (with DISTINCT), then ORDER BY, then LIMIT. Knowing this explains which names are visible where.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',60),(2,'Raoji','HR',45),(3,'Mina','IT',52),(4,'Kanhoji','HR',40),(5,'Dev','IT',30);

SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal         -- 5. compute columns and aliases
FROM emp                                    -- 1. read table
WHERE salary >= 40                          -- 2. drop rows (Dev removed)
GROUP BY dept                               -- 3. build groups
HAVING AVG(salary) > 45                     -- 4. drop groups
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC                       -- 6. sort (alias is visible now)
LIMIT 1;                                    -- 7. cut

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | dept | avg_sal |
-- +------+---------+
-- | IT   | 56.0000 |
-- +------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without the mental model, errors look random: why can ORDER BY use an alias but WHERE cannot, why WHERE rejects SUM(), why a filter on a window function needs a subquery. The execution order answers all of them.
codeExamples:
SELECT salary * 2 AS double_sal FROM emp WHERE double_sal > 100;     -- WHERE runs before SELECT
SELECT salary * 2 AS double_sal FROM emp ORDER BY double_sal DESC LIMIT 1;   -- ORDER BY runs after

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1054 (42S22): Unknown column 'double_sal' in 'where clause'
-- +------------+
-- | double_sal |
-- +------------+
-- |        120 |
-- +------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Performance reasoning uses the same order: filter early (WHERE) to shrink what is grouped, then use HAVING only for conditions that need aggregates. Window functions run after HAVING, so filtering their result requires a derived table or CTE.
codeExamples:
-- Filter on a window function result: needs a wrapper because WHERE runs earlier
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT name, dept, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
    FROM emp
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;                              -- top earner per department

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+--------+-----+
-- | name  | dept | salary | rnk |
-- +-------+------+--------+-----+
-- | Abaji | IT   |     60 |   1 |
-- | Raoji | HR   |     45 |   1 |
-- +------+------+--------+-----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Written:  SELECT ─ FROM ─ WHERE ─ GROUP BY ─ HAVING ─ ORDER BY ─ LIMIT
   Runs as:
     1 FROM / JOIN      (build the row source)
     2 WHERE            (row filter, no aliases, no aggregates)
     3 GROUP BY         (form groups)
     4 HAVING           (group filter, aggregates allowed)
     5 Window functions (OVER ...)
     6 SELECT + DISTINCT(aliases are born here)
     7 ORDER BY         (aliases visible)
     8 LIMIT / OFFSET

Fresher Notes

  • SQL is written SELECT first but runs in a different order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
  • This explains why you cannot use a SELECT alias in WHERE.
  • WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

Worked Example 1

Alias allowed in ORDER BY and HAVING.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS total FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING total > 100000 ORDER BY total DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | total
--   10 | 105000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Window result needs an outer query.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn FROM emp) t WHERE rn = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | rn
-- Moropant | 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Alias in WHERE fails.

Practice Exercise 2

Fix with derived table.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, salary * 12 AS yearly FROM emp) t WHERE yearly > 600000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | yearly
-- Moropant | 840000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SQL has a logical processing order that differs from the written order: FROM and JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions, SELECT list, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. Each phase can only use what earlier phases produced, which explains alias and window-function restrictions.
codeExamples:
-- written order: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... HAVING ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT
-- logical order:  FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> DISTINCT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n              -- 5
FROM emp                                -- 1
WHERE salary > 40000                    -- 2
GROUP BY dept                           -- 3
HAVING n >= 1                           -- 4 (MySQL allows the alias)
ORDER BY n DESC                         -- 6
LIMIT 5;                                -- 7

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | n
--   10 | 2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

MySQL is lenient with aliases in GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY, but not in WHERE. Wrap the query in a derived table or CTE when a later step needs an alias or window result in a filter.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a simple, consistent rule that predicts name visibility and lets you restructure a slow query by moving filters to the earliest legal stage.
codeExamples:
-- HAVING vs WHERE: same result, very different work
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING dept = 'IT';   -- groups everything then filters
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' GROUP BY dept;    -- filters then groups (better)

-- OUTPUT (both):
-- +------+----------+
-- | dept | COUNT(*) |
-- +------+----------+
-- | IT   |        3 |
-- +------+----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the logical order is not the physical one: the optimizer reorders joins, pushes predicates down and may sort earlier, so never depend on side effects or evaluation order. MySQL also accepts a few non-standard conveniences (aliases in GROUP BY and HAVING) that make the model look looser than it is.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL allows an alias in GROUP BY and HAVING (extension, not portable SQL)
SELECT UPPER(dept) AS d, COUNT(*) AS n FROM emp GROUP BY d HAVING n > 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---+
-- | d    | n |
-- +------+---+
-- | IT   | 3 |
-- +------+---+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the model describes logical semantics only; EXPLAIN shows the actual plan. Short-circuit evaluation of AND/OR and the order of function calls are not guaranteed, so do not rely on one predicate protecting another from errors such as division by zero.

Architect's Notes

Use the logical order as a debugging checklist, then confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE because the physical plan differs. Push every filter as early as the semantics allow, and avoid writing queries whose correctness depends on short-circuit order; make guards explicit with CASE or NULLIF.

Mid-Level Notes

  • MySQL is lenient: it allows aliases in GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY, but not in WHERE.
  • Window functions run after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING and before ORDER BY/LIMIT.
  • Knowing the order lets you place filters where they cut data earliest.

Senior Notes

  • The optimizer may reorder physical steps (push predicates down, reorder joins) but must preserve this logical result.
  • DISTINCT is applied after SELECT expressions; LIMIT applies last, which is why LIMIT cannot reduce the cost of a full sort without an index.
  • Derived tables and CTEs create new scopes where earlier aliases become usable.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using a SELECT alias in WHERE, a window function in WHERE, or expecting ORDER BY to run before GROUP BY. These fail because the earlier phase does not know about the later one.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The optimizer may physically reorder work (push filters below joins, choose join order, use indexes) as long as results match the logical order. EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE shows what actually happens.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept WHERE e.salary > 50000 GROUP BY d.id;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Group aggregate: count(0)
--     -> Nested loop inner join
--         -> Filter: (e.salary > 50000)       (filter applied before the join: pushed down)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world debugging method: when a query returns surprising numbers, evaluate it in phases. Run the FROM/WHERE part alone, then add grouping, then HAVING, comparing counts at each step.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'PAID';          -- rows after FROM+WHERE
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT o.id) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.status = 'PAID';  -- distinct orders

-- OUTPUT:
-- 5400   then   1800           (each order has about 3 items: sums of order totals would be tripled)

beginner.content:
Introduction

Comparison operators compare two values and yield 1 (true), 0 (false) or NULL (unknown): = <> (or !=) < <= > >= plus the NULL-safe equality <=>. MySQL has no separate boolean type for these results; they are integers 1, 0 or NULL.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 = 5      AS eq,
       5 <> 6      AS ne,
       5 >= 7      AS ge,
       'a' = 'A'   AS ci_equal,        -- default collation ignores case
       NULL = NULL AS null_eq,         -- unknown, not true
       NULL <=> NULL AS null_safe;     -- NULL-safe equality

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----+----+----------+---------+-----------+
-- | eq | ne | ge | ci_equal | null_eq | null_safe |
-- +----+----+----+----------+---------+-----------+
-- |  1 |  1 |  0 |        1 |    NULL |         1 |
-- +----+----+----+----------+---------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Filtering, joining and validating all rest on comparisons. Understanding three-valued logic (true, false, unknown) and type conversion prevents wrong results, which are worse than errors because nothing fails.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE item (id INT PRIMARY KEY, code VARCHAR(10), price DECIMAL(6,2), disc DECIMAL(6,2));
INSERT INTO item VALUES (1,'10',99.50,NULL),(2,'2',50.00,5.00),(3,'abc',10.00,NULL);

SELECT id FROM item WHERE disc = NULL;       -- never matches
SELECT id FROM item WHERE disc <=> NULL;     -- matches rows where disc IS NULL

-- OUTPUT:
-- (first query: empty set)
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  1 |
-- |  3 |
-- +----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Application filters (price above a limit, date at or after a start) compare columns with parameters. Comparing different types triggers implicit conversion: a string compared with a number is converted to a number, which can match more than you expect.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, code FROM item WHERE code = 0;          -- 'abc' converts to 0
SELECT '10' < '9' AS as_text, 10 < 9 AS as_number, '10' + 0 < 9 AS cast_first;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+
-- | id | code |
-- +----+------+
-- |  3 | abc  |        <- surprise match, plus a warning about truncated value
-- +----+------+
-- +---------+-----------+------------+
-- | as_text | as_number | cast_first |
-- +---------+-----------+------------+
-- |       1 |         0 |          0 |
-- +---------+-----------+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   a  op  b            result
   ────────────        ──────────────────────────────
   5  =   5      ──►   1  (TRUE)
   5  =   6      ──►   0  (FALSE)
   5  =   NULL   ──►   NULL (UNKNOWN)  ──► WHERE drops the row
   5 <=>  NULL   ──►   0   (NULL-safe: NULL <=> NULL is 1)

Fresher Notes

  • Comparison operators: =, != or <>, >, <, >=, <=.
  • A single = is comparison in SQL (assignment in SET uses = or :=).
  • Comparing with NULL gives NULL; use IS NULL instead.

Worked Example 1

Row comparison.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE (dept, id) > (10, 1) ORDER BY dept, id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2
-- 3

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Unexpected string-number conversion.
codeExamples:
SELECT '12abc' = 12 AS match_flag;

-- OUTPUT:
-- match_flag
-- 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Basic comparisons.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 > 3 AS gt, 5 <> 5 AS neq, 'a' = 'A' AS ci, NULL = NULL AS null_eq, NULL <=> NULL AS safe_eq;

-- OUTPUT:
-- gt | neq | ci | null_eq | safe_eq
--  1 |   0 |  1 |    NULL |       1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Filter by inequality.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept <> 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Comparison operators return 1 (true), 0 (false) or NULL (unknown). When the two sides have different types MySQL converts them: strings to numbers for numeric comparison, and string collation rules decide string equality. The conversion happens for every row, so a mismatched column cannot use its index.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 > 3 AS gt, 5 <> 5 AS ne, 'a' = 'A' AS ci_equal, '10' = 10 AS coerced, '10abc' = 10 AS partial, NULL = NULL AS null_eq, NULL <=> NULL AS null_safe;

-- OUTPUT:
-- gt | ne | ci_equal | coerced | partial | null_eq | null_safe
--  1 |  0 |        1 |       1 |       1 |    NULL |         1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Operators: = <> != > < >= <=, the NULL-safe <=>, BETWEEN, IN, LIKE, REGEXP, and row comparisons for composite keys.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a small, familiar set that works on numbers, strings, dates and tuples, and combines with the optimizer: = and range operators on an indexed column can use the index. Row constructors compare several columns at once.
codeExamples:
-- Row (tuple) comparison: handy for keyset pagination
SELECT id FROM item WHERE (price, id) > (50.00, 2) ORDER BY price, id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  1 |
-- +----+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: string comparison depends on collation (case, accents, trailing spaces for PAD SPACE collations), floating-point values may not compare equal after arithmetic, and implicit casts can disable indexes.
codeExamples:
SELECT 0.1e0 + 0.2e0 = 0.3e0   AS double_eq,    -- DOUBLE literals: binary rounding error
       0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3           AS decimal_eq,   -- plain literals are exact DECIMAL
       'abc' = 'abc   '          AS pad_space;    -- 8.0 default collation is NO PAD

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+------------+-----------+
-- | double_eq | decimal_eq | pad_space |
-- +-----------+------------+-----------+
-- |         0 |          1 |         0 |
-- +-----------+------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: comparisons with NULL never return true; comparing JSON, BLOB or geometry values follows special rules; and = on very long strings compares the whole value, so prefix indexes cannot fully prove equality.

Architect's Notes

Keep compared types identical (bind numbers as numbers, dates as dates) so the index is used and no hidden conversion occurs. Use DECIMAL for money, choose collations deliberately (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci vs _bin) and use <=> only where NULL equality is genuinely meant.

Mid-Level Notes

  • <=> is the NULL-safe equal: NULL <=> NULL is 1.
  • String comparisons depend on collation (case and accent sensitivity).
  • Row comparison works: (a, b) < (1, 2), handy for keyset pagination.

Senior Notes

  • Type coercion can change results and kill indexes: comparing string columns to numbers converts every row.
  • Floating-point equality is unreliable; compare DECIMAL or use a tolerance.
  • Use consistent collations across joined columns to avoid "illegal mix of collations" errors and index loss.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: comparing a VARCHAR column to a number (index lost, odd matches), forgetting case rules, floating-point equality and writing = NULL. Match types and use IS NULL or the safe-equal operator.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;     -- phone VARCHAR: converts each row, type=ALL
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE phone = '9876543210';   -- type=ref
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE bonus = NULL;                -- always 0

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Collation sets comparison behaviour and performance: binary collations are fastest and exact; case/accent-insensitive ones are convenient. Mixing collations in a join makes MySQL convert and can block the index.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world keyset pagination uses a row comparison, which MySQL can turn into a single index range even though it spans two columns.

beginner.content:
Introduction

AND, OR, NOT (also written &&, || and !) combine conditions. XOR is true when exactly one side is true. They follow three-valued logic with NULL, and AND binds tighter than OR.

Why Do We Need This?

Real filters have several rules ("IT staff earning over 50k, or any manager"). Without parentheses the precedence (NOT, then AND, then OR) can silently change meaning.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT, is_mgr TINYINT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',60,0),(2,'Raoji','HR',70,1),(3,'Mina','IT',40,0),(4,'Kanhoji','HR',30,0);

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' AND salary > 50 OR is_mgr = 1;      -- (IT AND >50) OR mgr
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' AND (salary > 50 OR is_mgr = 1);    -- IT AND (>50 OR mgr)

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+        +-------+
-- | name  |        | name  |
-- +-------+        +-------+
-- | Abaji |        | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |        +-------+
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Search screens build WHERE clauses dynamically from optional filters. The robust pattern wraps each group in parentheses; NOT is used for exclusions, often as NOT EXISTS or NOT IN.
codeExamples:
-- Optional filters: a NULL parameter means "ignore this filter"
SET @dept = NULL, @min_sal = 50;
SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE (@dept IS NULL OR dept = @dept)
  AND (@min_sal IS NULL OR salary >= @min_sal);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   precedence (high ──► low)
        NOT   ──►   AND   ──►   XOR   ──►   OR

   a OR b AND c      =   a OR (b AND c)       <- surprise for beginners
   (a OR b) AND c    =   explicit grouping     <- always write this
   truth with NULL:  T AND U = U    F AND U = F    T OR U = T    F OR U = U

Fresher Notes

  • AND needs both conditions true; OR needs at least one; NOT reverses a condition.
  • Use parentheses to make intent clear.
  • AND is evaluated before OR.

Worked Example 1

NOT IN trap with NULL.

Worked Example 2

NOT EXISTS version.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM (SELECT 10 AS d) x WHERE x.d = e.dept);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Precedence demo.
codeExamples:
SELECT (TRUE OR FALSE AND FALSE) AS no_parens, ((TRUE OR FALSE) AND FALSE) AS with_parens;

-- OUTPUT:
-- no_parens | with_parens
--         1 |           0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Three-valued logic.
codeExamples:
SELECT TRUE AND NULL AS a, FALSE AND NULL AS b, TRUE OR NULL AS c, NOT NULL AS d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- a    | b | c | d
-- NULL | 0 | 1 | NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Logical operators use three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE and UNKNOWN (NULL). A WHERE clause keeps a row only when it evaluates to TRUE, so UNKNOWN rows are dropped. AND is evaluated before OR, and NOT inverts TRUE and FALSE but leaves UNKNOWN as UNKNOWN.
codeExamples:
SELECT TRUE AND NULL AS t_and_n, FALSE AND NULL AS f_and_n, TRUE OR NULL AS t_or_n, FALSE OR NULL AS f_or_n, NOT NULL AS not_n;

-- OUTPUT:
-- t_and_n | f_and_n | t_or_n | f_or_n | not_n
-- NULL    |       0 |      1 | NULL   | NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Combine conditions with parentheses. XOR exists, and short forms like IN and BETWEEN replace chains of OR/AND. De Morgan's laws help rewrite NOT conditions: NOT (A AND B) = NOT A OR NOT B.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE NOT (dept = 10 AND salary < 50000);
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept <> 10 OR salary >= 50000;          -- equivalent (when columns are NOT NULL)
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept IN (10, 20) AND NOT name LIKE 'R%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Moropant

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: readable, standard, and the optimizer can convert them: AND conditions on different indexes can be merged (index_merge intersection); OR on the same column becomes IN or a range union.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: OR across different columns often defeats a single index and falls back to a scan or an index merge; NOT and <> are rarely index-friendly; dynamic "(param IS NULL OR col = param)" patterns produce one plan that fits no case well.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM emp WHERE NOT (dept = 'IT');

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type | key      | rows | Extra       |
-- | ALL  | idx_dept |    4 | Using where |     <- for a tiny table; at scale it is a wide range or scan

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: evaluation order and short-circuiting are not guaranteed; the symbol || means OR (not string concat) unless the PIPES_AS_CONCAT mode is set; and XOR has no short-circuit at all.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'a' || 'b' AS pipes;                    -- logical OR on two strings: 0 || 0 = 0, with warnings
SELECT CONCAT('a', 'b') AS concat_result;       -- the portable way

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | pipes |
-- +-------+
-- |     0 |
-- +-------+
-- +---------------+
-- | concat_result |
-- +---------------+
-- | ab            |
-- +---------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Always parenthesise mixed AND/OR, name each group, and test with NULL inputs. For performance, rewrite OR over two columns as UNION ALL of two index-friendly queries when the optimizer will not merge them, and replace "param IS NULL OR col = param" with dynamically built SQL so each shape gets its own plan.

Mid-Level Notes

  • NULL logic: TRUE AND NULL is NULL; FALSE AND NULL is FALSE; TRUE OR NULL is TRUE.
  • NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows; prefer NOT EXISTS.
  • XOR exists but is rarely used.

Senior Notes

  • Complex OR conditions block index use; rewrite to UNION or use IN lists.
  • The optimizer reorders conditions by cost, so do not rely on short-circuit side effects.
  • Test boundary data (NULLs, empty strings) for every business filter.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: precedence surprises, NOT with NULL data (the rewrite is not equivalent when NULLs exist), and OR across different columns which blocks single-index access. Use UNION ALL with a guard for performance.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 10 OR dept = 20 AND salary > 60000;     -- AND first
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE (dept = 10 OR dept = 20) AND salary > 60000;   -- intended

-- OUTPUT:
-- first : Abaji, Raoji, Moropant       second: Moropant

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rewrite a slow OR over two indexed columns as two index lookups combined with UNION ALL, removing the overlap in the second branch.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world access rule: a user sees documents they own or that are shared with a group they belong to. Writing it with EXISTS keeps the logic clear and NULL-safe.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.id, d.title FROM documents d WHERE d.owner_id = 7 OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM shares s JOIN memberships m ON m.group_id = s.group_id WHERE s.document_id = d.id AND m.user_id = 7);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title
--  4 | Roadmap

beginner.content:
Introduction

x BETWEEN a AND b is shorthand for x >= a AND x <= b (both ends inclusive). x IN (v1, v2, ...) tests membership in a list or subquery; NOT IN is its negation. Both work on numbers, strings and dates.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT, joined DATE);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',60,'2025-01-15'),(2,'Raoji','HR',45,'2025-06-01'),
                       (3,'Mina','IT',52,'2025-12-31'),(4,'Kanhoji','Ops',40,'2026-01-01');

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary BETWEEN 45 AND 60;           -- 45 and 60 included
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept IN ('IT', 'HR');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+        +------+
-- | name |        | name |
-- +------+        +------+
-- | Abaji |        | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |        | Raoji |
-- | Mina |        | Mina |
-- +------+        +------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Ranges and sets appear everywhere: price bands, date windows, allowed statuses, a list of selected ids. These operators say it in one readable predicate instead of chains of OR.
codeExamples:
-- Date windows: prefer half-open ranges, since BETWEEN includes the end value itself
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE joined BETWEEN '2025-01-01' AND '2025-12-31';
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE joined >= '2025-01-01' AND joined < '2026-01-01';   -- same, and safe for DATETIME

-- OUTPUT (both):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- | Mina  |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

IN with a subquery filters by another table. The big trap is NOT IN when the list contains NULL: the whole predicate becomes unknown and returns no rows.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE blocked (dept VARCHAR(10));
INSERT INTO blocked VALUES ('HR'), (NULL);

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept NOT IN (SELECT dept FROM blocked);       -- returns nothing!
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept NOT IN (SELECT dept FROM blocked WHERE dept IS NOT NULL);
SELECT name FROM emp e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM blocked b WHERE b.dept = e.dept);

-- OUTPUT:
-- (first query: empty set)
-- +---------+       +---------+
-- | name    |       | name    |
-- +---------+       +---------+
-- | Abaji   |       | Abaji   |
-- | Mina    |       | Mina    |
-- | Kanhoji |       | Kanhoji |
-- +---------+       +---------+          (second and third queries agree)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   x BETWEEN 10 AND 20      10 ──────────── 20      (both ends included)
                            ├──────[ x ]─────┤
   x IN (3, 7, 9)           3     7     9           (discrete points)
   x NOT IN (3, NULL)       x <> 3 AND x <> NULL  ──►  never TRUE

Fresher Notes

  • BETWEEN a AND b is inclusive on both ends. IN (1,2,3) matches any value in the list.
  • NOT IN excludes the listed values.
  • Both are shorter than long OR/AND chains.

Worked Example 1

Half-open datetime range.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-31' AND created_at < '2026-02-01';

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 12

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Join with a temp list instead of a huge IN.

Practice Exercise 1

Salary band and dept list.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary BETWEEN 45000 AND 60000 AND dept IN (10, 30);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

NOT IN list.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE id NOT IN (1,2);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

BETWEEN a AND b is shorthand for >= a AND <= b (inclusive). IN (list) matches any listed value; for constants MySQL sorts the list and probes the index once per value, so a short IN list is an efficient multi-range lookup.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

IN accepts literals, subqueries and row tuples. BETWEEN works on numbers, dates and strings. Use half-open ranges for datetimes so the upper boundary and fractional seconds are handled precisely.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: concise, index-friendly (ranges and IN lists become range or multi-point lookups), and IN (subquery) is optimised as a semi-join in 8.0.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: BETWEEN is inclusive on both sides (easy to double-count boundaries, wrong for DATETIME end dates), the arguments must be in the order low AND high, and NOT IN with NULL is a notorious bug source.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 BETWEEN 10 AND 1 AS reversed,         -- low and high swapped: always false
       5 BETWEEN 1 AND 10 AS normal;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+--------+
-- | reversed | normal |
-- +----------+--------+
-- |        0 |      1 |
-- +----------+--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: very long IN lists use memory and planning time (controlled by range_optimizer_max_mem_size; beyond the limit MySQL falls back to index dives or scans), max_allowed_packet bounds the statement, and mixing types in the list triggers conversions.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@range_optimizer_max_mem_size AS range_mem_bytes, @@eq_range_index_dive_limit AS dive_limit;

-- OUTPUT (example, 8.0 defaults):
-- +------------------+------------+
-- | range_mem_bytes  | dive_limit |
-- +------------------+------------+
-- |          8388608 |        200 |
-- +------------------+------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use half-open ranges (>= start AND < end) for dates and timestamps, and prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN when the inner column can be NULL. Keep IN lists to hundreds, not tens of thousands: for large sets load the ids into a temporary table and join. Make sure the compared column and constants have the same type so the index is used.

Mid-Level Notes

  • BETWEEN works for numbers, dates and strings; with datetime be careful with end-of-day (use < next_day).
  • IN can take a subquery: WHERE dept IN (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE ...).
  • NOT IN with NULLs returns no rows; prefer NOT EXISTS.

Senior Notes

  • Huge IN lists (thousands) hurt parsing and planning; load ids into a temp table and join.
  • For date ranges use half-open intervals to avoid double-counting boundaries.
  • IN on an indexed column becomes range lookups; ensure types match.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: NOT IN with a NULL in the list (returns nothing), huge IN lists (slow to parse and plan), and BETWEEN on datetimes that excludes the last day. Use NOT EXISTS and half-open ranges.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);                       -- orders.customer_id has NULLs => empty
SELECT id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);   -- correct

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set      then      id: 2, 5

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For thousands of ids load them into a temporary table and join. It avoids a giant statement, can be indexed and plans predictably.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: filters from a UI (checkbox lists) map to IN with bound parameters, one placeholder per value, generated safely by code.
codeExamples:
-- selected statuses: ['PAID','SHIPPED'] -> sql = "WHERE status IN (?,?)"
SELECT id, status FROM orders WHERE status IN ('PAID','SHIPPED') AND created_at >= '2026-05-01' ORDER BY id LIMIT 50;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | status
--  9 | PAID

beginner.content:
Introduction

LIKE matches text against a pattern with two wildcards: % (any number of characters, including none) and _ (exactly one character). NOT LIKE negates it, and ESCAPE lets you match a literal % or _. For full regular expressions use REGEXP or REGEXP_LIKE().
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE person (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO person VALUES (1,'Abaji Rao','abaji@x.com'),(2,'Raoji Kumar','raoji@y.org'),
                          (3,'Mina Rao','mina@x.com'),(4,'Raj','raj@x.com');

SELECT name FROM person WHERE name LIKE 'Ra%';        -- starts with Ra
SELECT name FROM person WHERE name LIKE '%Rao';       -- ends with Rao
SELECT name FROM person WHERE name LIKE 'R_j';        -- R, any one char, j

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+  +----------+  +------+
-- | name       |  | name     |  | name |
-- +------------+  +----------+  +------+
-- | Raoji Kumar |  | Abaji Rao | | Raj |
-- | Raj        |  | Mina Rao |  +------+
-- +------------+  +----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Users do not type exact values. Autocomplete, name search and domain filters need partial matching, and LIKE is the simplest tool for it.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS gmail_like FROM person WHERE email LIKE '%@x.com';

-- Match a literal percent sign using ESCAPE
CREATE TABLE promo (id INT PRIMARY KEY, label VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO promo VALUES (1,'50% off'),(2,'50 items');
SELECT label FROM promo WHERE label LIKE '50!% off' ESCAPE '!';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | gmail_like |
-- +------------+
-- |          3 |
-- +------------+
-- +---------+
-- | label   |
-- +---------+
-- | 50% off |
-- +---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Whether LIKE can use an index depends on the pattern: a fixed prefix ("Ra%") is a range scan on a B-tree index; a leading wildcard ("%Rao") forces a scan. For real search, use FULLTEXT, a reversed-column index for suffix search, or a search engine.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE person ADD KEY idx_name (name);
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM person WHERE name LIKE 'Ra%';       -- prefix: index range
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM person WHERE name LIKE '%Rao';      -- leading wildcard: no range

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key      | Extra                 |
-- | range | idx_name | Using where; Using index |
-- | index | idx_name | Using where; Using index |      <- scans the whole index

beginner.content:
Diagram

   pattern       meaning                 index usable?
   'Ra%'         prefix                  yes  (B-tree range)
   '%Rao'        suffix                  no   (scan)
   '%av%'        contains                no   (scan) ──► use FULLTEXT / search engine
   'R_j'         one wildcard char       partly (fixed prefix R)
   %  any length   _  exactly one   ESCAPE '!'  makes !% a literal %

Fresher Notes

  • LIKE searches text patterns: % matches any number of characters, _ matches exactly one.
  • name LIKE "A%" starts with A; "%son" ends with son; "%an%" contains an.
  • Comparisons are case-insensitive with the default collation.

Worked Example 1

Escape a literal underscore.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'a_b' LIKE 'a\_b' AS literal_match, 'axb' LIKE 'a\_b' AS no_match;

-- OUTPUT:
-- literal_match | no_match
--             1 |        0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Plan: prefix uses index, contains does not.

Practice Exercise 1

Wildcards in action.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE name LIKE 'A%' OR name LIKE '_avi';

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Case-insensitive and exact length.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'MySQL' LIKE 'my___' AS five_chars, 'MySQL' LIKE 'my__' AS four_chars;

-- OUTPUT:
-- five_chars | four_chars
--          1 |          0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

LIKE compares strings with wildcards: % for any run of characters and _ for exactly one. A B-tree index is sorted, so a pattern with a fixed prefix ('abc%') becomes an index range, while a leading wildcard ('%abc') cannot and needs a scan.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: ESCAPE to match literal % or _, NOT LIKE, REGEXP/REGEXP_LIKE for complex patterns, collation for case sensitivity, and FULLTEXT for word search.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: simple and standard, readable for beginners, case-insensitive by default with the common collations, and prefix patterns are fast with an index.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM person WHERE name LIKE 'ABAJI%';                        -- matches 'Abaji Rao'
SELECT name FROM person WHERE name LIKE BINARY 'ABAJI%';                 -- case-sensitive version

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+
-- | name      |
-- +-----------+
-- | Abaji Rao |
-- +-----------+
-- (second query returns an empty set)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: leading-wildcard searches scan every row; there is no relevance ranking, stemming or typo tolerance; wildcards inside user input let users change the pattern (escape % and _ from input); and collation affects what counts as a match.
codeExamples:
-- User input must be escaped, or searching for "_" matches everything
SELECT COUNT(*) AS unsafe  FROM person WHERE name LIKE '%_%';          -- _ is a wildcard
SELECT COUNT(*) AS escaped FROM person WHERE name LIKE '%!_%' ESCAPE '!';   -- literal underscore

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+---------+
-- | unsafe | escaped |
-- +--------+---------+
-- |      4 |       0 |
-- +--------+---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: only two wildcards (no character classes, no alternation) so complex patterns need REGEXP_LIKE (ICU engine in 8.0, not indexable); there is no built-in fuzzy or phonetic match beyond SOUNDS LIKE; and a LIKE on a TEXT column without a prefix index scans the table.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM person WHERE REGEXP_LIKE(name, '^(Abaji|Mina) ');   -- alternation LIKE cannot do
SELECT 'Smith' SOUNDS LIKE 'Smyth' AS phonetic;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+      +----------+
-- | name     |      | phonetic |
-- +----------+      +----------+
-- | Abaji Rao |     |        1 |
-- | Mina Rao |      +----------+
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Design the query for the prefix case, escape user-supplied wildcards, and move contains-style, ranked or multilingual search to FULLTEXT or Elasticsearch/OpenSearch before the table is large. For suffix search store a reversed copy in a generated column and index it; for case rules choose the collation explicitly instead of sprinkling LOWER() on indexed columns.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Only prefix patterns ("abc%") can use a B-tree index.
  • Escape wildcards with \ or use ESCAPE when the text contains % or _.
  • REGEXP gives powerful patterns but cannot use indexes.

Senior Notes

  • For contains-search over large tables use FULLTEXT or an external search engine instead of LIKE "%x%".
  • User input in LIKE must be escaped to avoid wildcard injection and performance abuse.
  • Reverse-string generated columns can index suffix searches.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: wrapping user input in %...% without escaping wildcards (users can search with % or _ and cause scans), using LIKE for whole-word search, and expecting case-sensitive matches under a case-insensitive collation.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For "contains" search at scale use FULLTEXT or a reversed/generated column for suffix lookups. A reversed string column turns suffix search into prefix search.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: type-ahead search. Prefix LIKE with a limit and an index returns the first suggestions in milliseconds.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'abaji%' ORDER BY name LIMIT 8;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  1 | Abaji
-- 14 | Ashank

beginner.content:
Introduction

NULL means "unknown or missing", not zero and not an empty string. Because any comparison with NULL is unknown, you test for it with IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. MySQL also offers ISNULL(x) and the NULL-safe operator <=>.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT NULL, bonus DECIMAL(8,2) NULL);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji',NULL,500),(2,'Raoji',1,NULL),(3,'Mina',1,0),(4,'Kanhoji',2,NULL);

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL;        -- the top of the tree
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE bonus IS NOT NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
