-- +------+      +------+
-- | name |      | name |
-- +------+      +------+
-- | Abaji |      | Abaji |
-- +------+      | Mina |
--               +------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Optional data is real: no manager, no end date, no bonus yet. Writing = NULL is the most common beginner bug: it compiles and returns nothing, so the mistake stays hidden.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE bonus = NULL;           -- always empty
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE bonus <> 0;               -- Raoji and Kanhoji (NULL) are excluded too!
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE bonus <> 0 OR bonus IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- (first: empty set)
-- +------+     +-------+
-- | name |     | name  |
-- +------+     +-------+
-- | Abaji |     | Abaji |
-- +------+     | Raoji |
--              | Kanhoji |
--              +-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical uses: finding top-level nodes in hierarchies, open-ended date ranges (end_date IS NULL means current), unmatched rows after a LEFT JOIN, and data-quality audits. Aggregates ignore NULL, and COALESCE substitutes defaults.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(bonus) AS with_bonus,         -- COUNT(col) skips NULL
       AVG(bonus) AS avg_bonus,                                   -- average of 500 and 0 only
       AVG(COALESCE(bonus, 0)) AS avg_if_missing_is_zero
FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+-----------+------------------------+
-- | all_rows | with_bonus | avg_bonus | avg_if_missing_is_zero |
-- +----------+------------+-----------+------------------------+
-- |        4 |          2 |  250.0000 |               125.0000 |
-- +----------+------------+-----------+------------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   value    IS NULL   = NULL   <=> NULL   IS NOT NULL
   ─────    ───────   ──────   ────────   ───────────
   5          0        NULL      0           1
   NULL       1        NULL      1           0
   (only IS NULL / <=> can ever say TRUE about a missing value)

Fresher Notes

  • NULL means missing or unknown. Test it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL, never with = NULL.
  • NULL is not zero and not an empty string.
  • Aggregates such as SUM and AVG ignore NULLs; COUNT(col) ignores them too, COUNT(*) does not.

Worked Example 1

Customers without orders.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

IS NULL uses an index.

Practice Exercise 1

Find and replace NULL.

Practice Exercise 2

NULL vs empty string.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_n, COUNT(phone) AS non_null, SUM(phone = '') AS empty_n FROM contacts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- rows_n | non_null | empty_n
--      3 |        2 |       1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

NULL means "no value / unknown". InnoDB tracks nullability in a per-row bitmap and indexes NULL entries, so IS NULL can use an index. Because NULL is not equal to anything (even NULL), only IS NULL, IS NOT NULL and the NULL-safe operator can test it.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: IS [NOT] NULL, COALESCE, IFNULL, NULLIF, <=>, and ISNULL(). Aggregates ignore NULLs, and ORDER BY puts NULLs first in ascending order.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: NULL models missing information honestly (better than magic values such as -1 or 1900-01-01), and InnoDB indexes include NULLs, so IS NULL can use an index.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: three-valued logic complicates every query; NULL spreads (any arithmetic with NULL is NULL); NOT IN and subquery comparisons break; and nullable columns need extra bookkeeping (a NULL bitmap in the row) and care in unique keys.
codeExamples:
SELECT 10 + NULL AS arith, CONCAT('a', NULL) AS concat, NULL = NULL AS eq, IFNULL(NULL, 'default') AS rescued;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+------+---------+
-- | arith | concat | eq   | rescued |
-- +-------+--------+------+---------+
-- | NULL  | NULL   | NULL | default |
-- +-------+--------+------+---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: sorting puts NULL first in ASC and last in DESC (no NULLS FIRST/LAST clause, emulate with ORDER BY col IS NULL); GROUP BY and DISTINCT treat all NULLs as one group while UNIQUE allows many; and Oracle-style treating '' as NULL does not exist here.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, bonus FROM emp ORDER BY bonus IS NULL, bonus DESC;     -- push NULLs last, highest first

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+--------+
-- | name    | bonus  |
-- +---------+--------+
-- | Abaji   | 500.00 |
-- | Mina    |   0.00 |
-- | Raoji   |   NULL |
-- | Kanhoji | NULL   |
-- +---------+--------+
-- (relative order of the two NULL rows is not guaranteed)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Declare columns NOT NULL unless absence has a business meaning, and document what NULL means for each nullable column (unknown, not applicable, not yet). Test every query with NULL data, prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN, use COALESCE at the edges (reports, APIs), and remember a left-join anti-pattern (LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL) relies on a non-nullable column on the right.

Mid-Level Notes

  • COALESCE(col, default) replaces NULL with a value.
  • Joins on NULL never match; use LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL to find missing relations.
  • UNIQUE indexes allow multiple NULLs in MySQL.

Senior Notes

  • Nullable columns complicate semantics; use NOT NULL with explicit defaults when the business requires a value.
  • IS NULL can use an index; in InnoDB NULLs are indexed.
  • Beware ORM mapping of NULL vs empty values, which often causes inconsistent data.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: = NULL, NOT IN with NULLs, treating empty string as NULL, and counting with COUNT(col) when you meant COUNT(*). Decide per column whether missing is NULL or a real default.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM contacts WHERE phone = NULL;                  -- never true
SELECT id FROM contacts WHERE phone IS NULL OR phone = '';      -- both kinds of "missing"
SELECT id FROM contacts WHERE id NOT IN (1, NULL);              -- empty: NULL poisons NOT IN

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set
-- id: 2, 3
-- Empty set

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Anti-joins find rows without a partner. LEFT JOIN with IS NULL on the right key, or NOT EXISTS, are optimized into an efficient antijoin plan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop antijoin
--     -> Table scan on c
--     -> Single-row covering index lookup on o using idx_customer (customer_id=c.id)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world data quality report: how many rows are missing each optional field, to decide what to backfill or enforce.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers, SUM(phone IS NULL) AS no_phone, SUM(email IS NULL) AS no_email, ROUND(100 * SUM(phone IS NULL) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_no_phone FROM customers;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customers | no_phone | no_email | pct_no_phone
--     12044 |     2108 |       12 | 17.5

beginner.content:
Introduction

String functions take text and return text, numbers or positions: CONCAT, UPPER, LOWER, TRIM, SUBSTRING, REPLACE, CHAR_LENGTH. They run inside the server, row by row, so the client receives data already shaped.
codeExamples:
-- Basic string functions on literals (no table needed)
SELECT CONCAT('My', 'SQL')   AS joined,   -- glue strings together
       UPPER('mysql')        AS up,        -- all capitals
       LOWER('MySQL')        AS lo,        -- all lower case
       CHAR_LENGTH('hello')  AS len;       -- number of characters

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-------+-------+-----+
-- | joined | up    | lo    | len |
-- +--------+-------+-------+-----+
-- | MySQL  | MYSQL | mysql |   5 |
-- +--------+-------+-------+-----+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Real data is messy: stray spaces, mixed case, composite values like name@domain. Cleaning and reshaping text in SQL avoids pulling millions of rows into application code just to trim them.
codeExamples:
-- Normalise a dirty e-mail and split out its domain
SELECT LOWER(TRIM('  Ann@Example.COM  '))                    AS email,   -- strip spaces, lower-case
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(LOWER(TRIM('  Ann@Example.COM  ')), '@', -1) AS domain;  -- text after the last '@'

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+-------------+
-- | email           | domain      |
-- +-----------------+-------------+
-- | ann@example.com | example.com |
-- +-----------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical uses: building display names, masking phone numbers, zero-padding invoice codes, searching with LOCATE, and cleaning imports before loading them into final tables.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customers (          -- tiny self-contained table
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name VARCHAR(30),
  last_name  VARCHAR(30),
  phone      VARCHAR(15)
);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Abaji','Rao','9876543210'), (2,'Raoji',NULL,'9123456789');

SELECT CONCAT_WS(' ', first_name, last_name)                   AS full_name,  -- skips NULL parts
       CONCAT(LEFT(phone, 2), '******', RIGHT(phone, 2))      AS masked,     -- keep first and last 2 digits
       LPAD(id, 5, '0')                                       AS cust_code   -- zero padded to width 5
FROM customers;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+------------+-----------+
-- | full_name | masked     | cust_code |
-- +-----------+------------+-----------+
-- | Abaji Rao | 98******10 | 00001     |
-- | Raoji     | 91******89 | 00002     |
-- +-----------+------------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   'Abaji ' + 'Rao'         row-by-row inside the server
       |
       v
   +-----------------+    +---------+    +----------+
   | input string(s) | -> | function| -> | new value |
   +-----------------+    +---------+    +----------+
     TRIM  LOWER  SUBSTRING  CONCAT  REPLACE  LPAD

   WHERE col = 'x'          -> index lookup  (fast)
   WHERE LOWER(col) = 'x'   -> scan every row (slow)

Fresher Notes

  • Common string functions: CONCAT, LENGTH, UPPER, LOWER, SUBSTRING, TRIM, REPLACE.
  • CONCAT joins strings; if any part is NULL, the result is NULL (use CONCAT_WS to skip NULLs).
  • Strings are 1-indexed in SQL.

Worked Example 1

Functional index on lowercase email.

Worked Example 2

Pad and format.
codeExamples:
SELECT LPAD(7, 3, '0') AS padded, FORMAT(1234567.891, 2) AS formatted;

-- OUTPUT:
-- padded | formatted
-- 007    | 1,234,567.89

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Common functions together.
codeExamples:
SELECT CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT('abaji',1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING('ABAJI',2))) AS proper,
       TRIM('  hi  ') AS trimmed, REPLACE('a-b-c','-','/') AS replaced, CHAR_LENGTH('MySQL') AS n;

-- OUTPUT:
-- proper | trimmed | replaced | n
-- Abaji  | hi      | a/b/c    | 5

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

CONCAT with NULL.
codeExamples:
SELECT CONCAT('a', NULL, 'b') AS c1, CONCAT_WS('-', 'a', NULL, 'b') AS c2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- c1   | c2
-- NULL | a-b

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

String functions run per row inside the executor. They operate on characters or bytes depending on the function (CHAR_LENGTH vs LENGTH), obey the connection charset and collation, and return NULL if any argument is NULL (except CONCAT_WS and a few others).
codeExamples:
SELECT CHAR_LENGTH('हिंदी') AS chars, LENGTH('हिंदी') AS bytes, UPPER('mysql') AS up, REVERSE('abc') AS rev, CONCAT('a', NULL, 'b') AS c1, CONCAT_WS('-', 'a', NULL, 'b') AS c2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- chars | bytes | up    | rev | c1   | c2
--     4 |    12 | MYSQL | cba | NULL | a-b

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Everyday set: CONCAT, SUBSTRING, LEFT/RIGHT, TRIM, REPLACE, LOCATE/INSTR, LPAD/RPAD, FORMAT, SUBSTRING_INDEX, REGEXP_REPLACE, GROUP_CONCAT (aggregate).
codeExamples:
SELECT SUBSTRING('2026-05-01', 1, 4) AS yr, SUBSTRING_INDEX('a@x.com', '@', -1) AS domain, LPAD(7, 3, '0') AS padded, TRIM(BOTH '-' FROM '--x--') AS trimmed,
       REPLACE('a-b-c', '-', '/') AS replaced, REGEXP_REPLACE('a1b22', '[0-9]+', '#') AS regexed, FORMAT(1234567.891, 2) AS fmt;

-- OUTPUT:
-- yr   | domain | padded | trimmed | replaced | regexed | fmt
-- 2026 | x.com  | 007    | x       | a/b/c    | a#b#    | 1,234,567.89

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: set-based (one statement transforms every row), no extra network trips, work in SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and UPDATE, and are deterministic so they can be used in generated columns.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE people (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO people VALUES (1,'  anaji  '), (2,'BAJI');

-- One UPDATE cleans every row; no application loop needed
UPDATE people
SET name = CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT(TRIM(name),1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING(TRIM(name),2)));  -- Capitalise first letter

SELECT * FROM people;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | Anaji |
-- |  2 | Baji  |
-- +----+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: wrapping an indexed column in a function usually prevents the index from being used (not sargable), and heavy text processing burns database CPU that is harder to scale than app servers.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(100), KEY idx_email (email));

EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@x.com';  -- function on the column
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE email        = 'a@x.com';  -- plain comparison

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+-------+------+-------+-------------+
-- | id | table | type | key   | Extra       |
-- +----+-------+------+-------+-------------+
-- |  1 | users | index| idx_email | Using where; Using index |   <- scans the whole index
-- |  1 | users | ref  | idx_email | Using index              |   <- direct lookup
-- +----+-------+------+-------+-------------+
-- Tip: default collations are case-insensitive, so LOWER() is usually unnecessary.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: LENGTH counts bytes, not characters; any function receiving NULL mostly returns NULL; positions are 1-based; results depend on the column's character set and collation.
codeExamples:
SELECT LENGTH('héllo')               AS bytes,       -- utf8mb4: é takes 2 bytes
       CHAR_LENGTH('héllo')          AS chars,       -- 5 characters
       CONCAT('a', NULL, 'b')        AS concat_null, -- any NULL makes the result NULL
       CONCAT_WS('-', 'a', NULL, 'b') AS ws_null,    -- CONCAT_WS skips NULLs
       SUBSTRING('abcdef', 0, 2)     AS pos_zero;    -- position 0 returns an empty string

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------+-------------+---------+----------+
-- | bytes | chars | concat_null | ws_null | pos_zero |
-- +-------+-------+-------------+---------+----------+
-- |     6 |     5 | NULL        | a-b     |          |
-- +-------+-------+-------------+---------+----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep transformation out of predicates: normalise data on write (or use a generated column plus index) instead of calling functions on indexed columns at read time. Treat the database as a store, not a text-processing engine; move heavy parsing to the application or ETL, and fix collation and charset once at schema level.

Mid-Level Notes

  • LENGTH counts bytes, CHAR_LENGTH counts characters.
  • Useful extras: LEFT, RIGHT, LPAD, INSTR, FORMAT, REVERSE.
  • Putting a function on an indexed column in WHERE stops index use.

Senior Notes

  • Do formatting in the application where possible; keep the database for filtering and joining.
  • Normalize data on write (lowercase emails) instead of calling LOWER() in every query.
  • Functional indexes (8.0.13+) or generated columns can index expressions when needed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: functions on indexed columns in WHERE, assuming byte length equals character count, and formatting in SQL what the application should format. Normalize on write and keep functions out of predicates.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@x.com';            -- no plain index use
ALTER TABLE users ADD INDEX idx_lower_email ((LOWER(email)));       -- functional index (8.0.13+)
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@x.com';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key
-- ref  | idx_lower_email

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

String functions in SELECT lists cost CPU for each returned row; in WHERE or GROUP BY for each scanned row. Pre-compute with generated columns when the same expression is used repeatedly.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world data cleaning: standardize phone numbers and names in an UPDATE, checking the result with a SELECT first.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Numeric functions do arithmetic beyond the basic operators: ROUND, CEIL, FLOOR, TRUNCATE, ABS, MOD, POWER, SQRT, RAND.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(3.14159, 2) AS r2,     -- round to 2 decimals
       CEIL(4.1)         AS up,     -- smallest integer >= value
       FLOOR(4.9)        AS down,   -- largest integer <= value
       ABS(-7)           AS absval, -- absolute value
       POWER(2, 10)      AS p;      -- 2 to the power 10

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+----+------+--------+------+
-- | r2   | up | down | absval | p    |
-- +------+----+------+--------+------+
-- | 3.14 |  5 |    4 |      7 | 1024 |
-- +------+----+------+--------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Money, percentages, paging maths, bucketing and statistics all need controlled rounding and integer division. Doing it in SQL keeps reports consistent with the stored numbers.
codeExamples:
-- Price with 18% tax, rounded to paise; and bucket a value into tens
SELECT ROUND(499.99 * 1.18, 2) AS price_with_tax,  -- rounding to 2 decimals
       FLOOR(47 / 10) * 10     AS bucket,          -- 47 -> bucket 40
       47 DIV 10               AS int_div,         -- integer division operator
       MOD(47, 10)             AS remainder;       -- modulo

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+--------+---------+-----------+
-- | price_with_tax | bucket | int_div | remainder |
-- +----------------+--------+---------+-----------+
-- |         589.99 |     40 |       4 |         7 |
-- +----------------+--------+---------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used in invoice totals, discount tiers, pagination (CEIL(total/page_size)), even/odd row splits (MOD(id,2)), and sampling.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE items (id INT PRIMARY KEY, price DECIMAL(8,2));
INSERT INTO items VALUES (1, 19.99), (2, 5.50), (3, 100.00);

SELECT COUNT(*)                    AS total_rows,
       CEIL(COUNT(*) / 2)          AS pages_of_2,     -- pages needed with 2 rows per page
       ROUND(AVG(price), 1)        AS avg_price,      -- 41.83 -> 41.8
       TRUNCATE(AVG(price), 1)     AS avg_cut         -- cut, not round
FROM items;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+------------+-----------+---------+
-- | total_rows | pages_of_2 | avg_price | avg_cut |
-- +------------+------------+-----------+---------+
-- |          3 |          2 |      41.8 |    41.8 |
-- +------------+------------+-----------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   input --> [ ROUND | CEIL | FLOOR | TRUNCATE | MOD | DIV ] --> result

   ROUND(2.567,2)=2.57   TRUNCATE(2.567,2)=2.56
   CEIL(2.1)=3           FLOOR(2.9)=2

   value:  -2   -1.2   0   1.2   2
   FLOOR :  -2   -2    0    1    2
   CEIL  :  -2   -1    0    2    2

Fresher Notes

  • Common numeric functions: ROUND, CEIL, FLOOR, ABS, MOD.
  • ROUND(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimals; CEIL rounds up; FLOOR rounds down.
  • Use % or MOD for remainders.

Worked Example 1

Divide by zero.
codeExamples:
SELECT 10 / 0 AS result;

-- OUTPUT:
-- result
-- NULL

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Percent calculation.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, ROUND(salary / (SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp) * 100, 1) AS pct FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | pct
-- Abaji    | 34.3
-- Raoji    | 25.7
-- Moropant | 40.0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Rounding functions.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(3.567,2) AS r, CEIL(3.1) AS c, FLOOR(3.9) AS f, ABS(-7) AS a, MOD(10,3) AS m, TRUNCATE(3.789,1) AS t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- r    | c | f | a | m | t
-- 3.57 | 4 | 3 | 7 | 1 | 3.7

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Integer division.
codeExamples:
SELECT 17 DIV 5 AS quotient, 17 MOD 5 AS remainder, 17 / 5 AS decimal_result;

-- OUTPUT:
-- quotient | remainder | decimal_result
--        3 |         2 |         3.4000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Numeric functions operate on exact (DECIMAL, integer) or approximate (FLOAT, DOUBLE) values. ROUND on DECIMAL rounds half away from zero; on DOUBLE it follows the C library. Integer division DIV truncates, while / produces a decimal.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(2.5) AS r_dec, ROUND(2.5E0) AS r_dbl, ROUND(-2.5) AS r_neg, CEIL(2.1) AS c, FLOOR(-2.1) AS f, TRUNCATE(2.789, 2) AS t, 7 DIV 2 AS int_div, 7 / 2 AS real_div, MOD(-7, 3) AS m;

-- OUTPUT:
-- r_dec | r_dbl | r_neg | c | f  | t    | int_div | real_div | m
--     3 |     2 |    -3 | 3 | -3 | 2.78 |       3 |   3.5000 | -1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful set: ROUND(x, d), CEIL, FLOOR, TRUNCATE, ABS, SIGN, MOD/%, POWER, SQRT, LOG, GREATEST/LEAST, RAND, CONV and bit operators.
codeExamples:
SELECT GREATEST(3, 9, 5) AS g, LEAST(3, 9, 5) AS l, POWER(2, 10) AS p, SQRT(144) AS s, ABS(-7) AS a, SIGN(-5) AS sg, 6 & 3 AS bit_and, 1 << 4 AS shifted;

-- OUTPUT:
-- g | l | p    | s  | a | sg | bit_and | shifted
-- 9 | 3 | 1024 | 12 | 7 | -1 |       2 |      16

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: exact DECIMAL arithmetic for money, many rounding modes, integer DIV and MOD, and consistent results in every client.
codeExamples:
-- Rounding rules at a glance (exact values round half away from zero)
SELECT ROUND(2.5)   AS half_up,      -- 3
       ROUND(-2.5)  AS neg_half,     -- -3
       CEIL(-1.2)   AS ceil_neg,     -- -1
       FLOOR(-1.2)  AS floor_neg,    -- -2
       ROUND(1234.567, -2) AS to_hundreds;  -- negative digits round left of the point

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+----------+----------+-----------+-------------+
-- | half_up | neg_half | ceil_neg | floor_neg | to_hundreds |
-- +---------+----------+----------+-----------+-------------+
-- |       3 |       -3 |       -1 |        -2 |        1200 |
-- +---------+----------+----------+-----------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: FLOAT/DOUBLE are approximate, rounding of approximate values differs from exact values, and ORDER BY RAND() sorts the whole table.
codeExamples:
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2         AS exact_dec,     -- DECIMAL literals are exact
       0.1e0 + 0.2e0     AS approx_dbl,    -- DOUBLE literals are binary fractions
       ROUND(2.5e0)      AS dbl_round;     -- approximate values round half to even (C rint)

-- ORDER BY RAND() assigns a random number to every row, then sorts all of them:
-- SELECT * FROM big_table ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1;   -- O(n log n) on millions of rows

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+---------------------+-----------+
-- | exact_dec | approx_dbl          | dbl_round |
-- +-----------+---------------------+-----------+
-- |       0.3 | 0.30000000000000004 |         2 |
-- +-----------+---------------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: division by zero yields NULL (with a warning, or an error in strict mode for INSERT/UPDATE), overflow raises "value out of range", and DIV truncates toward zero.
codeExamples:
SELECT 1 / 0        AS div_zero,   -- NULL plus warning 1365
       10 / 4       AS normal_div, -- '/' always returns a decimal
       10 DIV 4     AS int_div,    -- 2
       -7 DIV 2     AS neg_div,    -- -3 (truncates toward zero)
       MOD(-7, 3)   AS neg_mod;    -- -1 (sign follows the dividend)

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+---------+---------+---------+
-- | div_zero | normal_div | int_div | neg_div | neg_mod |
-- +----------+------------+---------+---------+---------+
-- | NULL     |     2.5000 |       2 |      -3 |      -1 |
-- +----------+------------+---------+---------+---------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Store money as DECIMAL (or integer minor units) and round once, at the boundary defined by the business, not inside every intermediate step. Avoid randomness functions on large tables (use an indexed random key or sampling by id range) and decide a single rounding policy for the whole system.

Mid-Level Notes

  • ROUND on DECIMAL rounds half away from zero; on FLOAT/DOUBLE it uses the C library (banker-like behaviour in some cases).
  • Other useful ones: POWER, SQRT, TRUNCATE, RAND, SIGN.
  • Integer division with DIV avoids decimals.

Senior Notes

  • Rounding rules matter for money: define when and how to round, and keep scale in DECIMAL.
  • ORDER BY RAND() sorts the whole table and is slow; pick random ids another way.
  • Division by zero returns NULL (or errors in strict ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO with DML).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: dividing by zero (NULL, or error in DML under strict mode), using floats for money, and ORDER BY RAND() on big tables (sorts everything). Guard divisors with NULLIF and sample differently.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rounding rules matter at scale: round once at a defined step, sum unrounded values and round the total, and check that parts add up to the whole. DECIMAL avoids drift.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(ROUND(price * 0.18, 2)) AS sum_of_rounded, ROUND(SUM(price * 0.18), 2) AS rounded_sum FROM (SELECT 10.03 AS price UNION ALL SELECT 10.03 UNION ALL SELECT 10.03) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- sum_of_rounded | rounded_sum
-- 5.43           | 5.42

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world pricing: discounts, tax and percentages computed in DECIMAL with explicit rounding, plus a check that the invoice total equals the sum of its parts.
codeExamples:
SELECT order_id, ROUND(SUM(qty * unit_price), 2) AS subtotal, ROUND(SUM(qty * unit_price) * 0.10, 2) AS discount,
       ROUND(SUM(qty * unit_price) * 0.90 * 1.18, 2) AS total FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 1 GROUP BY order_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- order_id | subtotal | discount | total
--        1 |   999.50 |    99.95 | 1061.47

beginner.content:
Introduction

Date functions read, build, shift and format DATE, DATETIME and TIMESTAMP values: NOW, CURDATE, DATE_ADD, DATEDIFF, DATE_FORMAT, EXTRACT, LAST_DAY.

Why Do We Need This?

Almost every business question is time-based: "orders this week", "age of a customer", "invoice due in 30 days". Date arithmetic by hand (leap years, month lengths) is error-prone, so the database does it.

Real-Time Use

Used for rolling-window reports, subscription expiry, monthly billing, audit timestamps (DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP), and cohort analysis.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, placed_on DATE, amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'2024-03-01',100), (2,'2024-03-05',250), (3,'2024-02-20',80);

-- Monthly totals: group by a formatted month key
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(placed_on, '%Y-%m') AS month,   -- 2024-03
       SUM(amount)                     AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY DATE_FORMAT(placed_on, '%Y-%m')
ORDER BY month;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------+
-- | month   | revenue |
-- +---------+---------+
-- | 2024-02 |      80 |
-- | 2024-03 |     350 |
-- +---------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   timeline --------------------------------------------------->
        2024-01-31 --INTERVAL 1 MONTH--> 2024-02-29 (clamped)
        |<------ DATEDIFF = days ------>|

   function            returns
   NOW()/CURDATE()     current datetime / date
   DATE_ADD / INTERVAL shifted date
   DATEDIFF            integer days
   TIMESTAMPDIFF       integer in chosen unit
   DATE_FORMAT         text

Fresher Notes

  • Key functions: NOW(), CURDATE(), CURTIME(), DATE(), YEAR(), MONTH(), DAY(), DATEDIFF(), DATE_ADD(), DATE_SUB().
  • Add time with DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 7 DAY).
  • DATE_FORMAT(d, "%d-%m-%Y") formats dates for display.

Worked Example 1

Month start and end.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT('2026-07-15','%Y-%m-01') AS month_start, LAST_DAY('2026-07-15') AS month_end;

-- OUTPUT:
-- month_start | month_end
-- 2026-07-01  | 2026-07-31

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Monthly report with zero months.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE m AS (SELECT '2026-01-01' AS d UNION ALL SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 MONTH FROM m WHERE d < '2026-03-01')
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(m.d,'%Y-%m') AS month, COALESCE(SUM(o.total),0) AS revenue
FROM m LEFT JOIN orders o ON DATE_FORMAT(o.created_at,'%Y-%m') = DATE_FORMAT(m.d,'%Y-%m') GROUP BY m.d;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- month   | revenue
-- 2026-01 | 1200
-- 2026-02 |    0
-- 2026-03 |  800

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Date arithmetic and parts.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE_ADD('2026-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS plus_month, DATEDIFF('2026-03-01','2026-02-01') AS days,
       YEAR('2026-07-15') AS y, MONTHNAME('2026-07-15') AS m, DAYNAME('2026-07-15') AS dn;

-- OUTPUT:
-- plus_month | days | y    | m    | dn
-- 2026-02-28 |   28 | 2026 | July | Wednesday

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Age in years.
codeExamples:
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, '1995-08-20', '2026-08-19') AS age;

-- OUTPUT:
-- age
-- 30

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Date and time functions work on internal integer representations. NOW() returns the statement start time (constant within the statement), SYSDATE() the time of each call, UTC_TIMESTAMP() the UTC time. TIMESTAMP values convert through the session time zone; DATE and DATETIME do not.
codeExamples:
SELECT NOW() = NOW() AS now_stable, SYSDATE() = SYSDATE() AS sysdate_changes, @@session.time_zone AS tz, UTC_TIMESTAMP() AS utc_now;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- now_stable | sysdate_changes | tz     | utc_now
--          1 |               0 | +05:30 | 2026-05-01 10:00:00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Everyday set: DATE_ADD/SUB with INTERVAL, DATEDIFF, TIMESTAMPDIFF, DATE_FORMAT, STR_TO_DATE, EXTRACT, LAST_DAY, WEEK/YEARWEEK, DAYNAME, UNIX_TIMESTAMP and FROM_UNIXTIME, CONVERT_TZ.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE_ADD('2026-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS eom_plus, TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, '2026-05-01 08:00', '2026-05-02 10:30') AS hours,
       EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM '2026-08-15') AS q, YEARWEEK('2026-05-01', 3) AS iso_week, FROM_UNIXTIME(1777000000) AS from_epoch, UNIX_TIMESTAMP('2026-05-01 00:00:00') AS epoch;

-- OUTPUT:
-- eom_plus   | hours | q | iso_week | from_epoch          | epoch
-- 2026-02-28 |    26 | 3 |   202618 | 2026-04-24 07:46:40 | 1777593600

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: calendar-correct arithmetic, rich formatting codes, time-zone conversion with CONVERT_TZ, and automatic timestamps through column defaults.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE audit (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  note VARCHAR(20),
  created_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,                              -- set on insert
  updated_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP   -- refreshed on update
);
INSERT INTO audit(note) VALUES ('first');
SELECT note, created_at = updated_at AS same_time FROM audit;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | note  | same_time |
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | first |         1 |
-- +-------+-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: using YEAR(col) or DATE(col) in WHERE blocks index range scans; write half-open ranges instead.
codeExamples:
-- Slow: function on the column (cannot use an index on placed_on)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE YEAR(placed_on) = 2024;

-- Fast: a range the B-tree can seek into
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders
WHERE placed_on >= '2024-01-01' AND placed_on < '2025-01-01';   -- half-open range

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |        3 |      <- same answer, but the second form is index friendly
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: invalid dates become NULL or errors, TIMESTAMP stops at 2038-01-19, NOW() depends on the session time zone, and month arithmetic clamps days.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE('2024-02-30')                     AS bad_date,   -- NULL (with a warning)
       DATE_ADD('2024-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH)   AS clamped,    -- 29 Feb, not 31 Feb
       DATEDIFF('2024-03-01 23:59', '2024-03-01') AS ignores_time; -- time part ignored

-- NOW() changes with the time zone setting:
-- SET time_zone = '+00:00'; SELECT NOW();   SET time_zone = '+05:30'; SELECT NOW();

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+--------------+
-- | bad_date | clamped    | ignores_time |
-- +----------+------------+--------------+
-- | NULL     | 2024-02-29 |            0 |
-- +----------+------------+--------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Store instants in UTC (TIMESTAMP, or DATETIME holding UTC) and convert at the edge; use DATETIME(6) when you need microseconds. Always query with half-open ranges on the raw column, and for frequent calendar groupings add a generated column or a date dimension table so the work is indexed and consistent.

Mid-Level Notes

  • DATEDIFF(a, b) returns days between dates; TIMESTAMPDIFF(unit, a, b) returns any unit.
  • LAST_DAY(), DAYNAME(), WEEK() and EXTRACT() are common in reports.
  • NOW() is fixed for the statement; SYSDATE() changes per call.

Senior Notes

  • Avoid wrapping indexed date columns in functions in WHERE; use ranges.
  • Group by month with a computed column or a calendar table for fast, correct reporting (including missing months).
  • Keep session and server time zones explicit and preferably UTC.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: functions around indexed date columns, day-boundary bugs with BETWEEN on datetimes, mixing time zones, and local-time DATETIMEs across daylight saving changes. Use ranges and UTC.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-05-01';                      -- scans
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-05-02';  -- range scan

-- OUTPUT: (explain)
-- first : type=ALL     second: type=range key=idx_created

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Group by month efficiently: compute a month key from a range-friendly column, or add a generated month column with an index when many reports use it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: subscription renewals and trials, using date arithmetic to find who expires in the next 7 days and who was active last month.
codeExamples:
SELECT user_id, expires_on, DATEDIFF(expires_on, CURDATE()) AS days_left FROM subscriptions WHERE expires_on BETWEEN CURDATE() AND CURDATE() + INTERVAL 7 DAY ORDER BY expires_on;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id | expires_on | days_left
-- 41      | 2026-05-03 |         2

beginner.content:
Introduction

NULL means "unknown or missing". COALESCE(a,b,...) returns the first non-NULL argument, IFNULL(a,b) is its two-argument form, and NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when both are equal, otherwise a.
codeExamples:
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'third') AS first_non_null, -- scans left to right
       IFNULL(NULL, 'default')        AS fallback,       -- 2-argument version
       NULLIF(5, 5)                   AS equal_gives_null,
       NULLIF(5, 6)                   AS different_keeps;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+----------+------------------+-----------------+
-- | first_non_null | fallback | equal_gives_null | different_keeps |
-- +----------------+----------+------------------+-----------------+
-- | third          | default  | NULL             |               5 |
-- +----------------+----------+------------------+-----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

NULL poisons expressions: 5 + NULL is NULL and NULL = NULL is not true. Reports need readable defaults, and divisions need protection from zero.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 + NULL          AS arithmetic,  -- NULL
       NULL = NULL        AS equality,    -- NULL, not 1
       NULL IS NULL       AS is_null_test,-- the correct test
       10 / NULLIF(0, 0)  AS safe_divide; -- NULLIF turns 0 into NULL -> result NULL, no error

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+----------+--------------+-------------+
-- | arithmetic | equality | is_null_test | safe_divide |
-- +------------+----------+--------------+-------------+
-- | NULL       | NULL     |            1 | NULL        |
-- +------------+----------+--------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used to show "N/A" for missing values, pick the first available phone number, compute margins without division errors, and treat empty strings as missing.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE contacts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, mobile VARCHAR(15), home VARCHAR(15), email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO contacts VALUES (1, NULL, '0221234', NULL), (2, '98765', NULL, 'b@x.com'), (3, '', NULL, NULL);

SELECT id,
       COALESCE(NULLIF(mobile, ''), home, email, 'no contact') AS best_contact  -- '' counts as missing
FROM contacts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------------+
-- | id | best_contact |
-- +----+--------------+
-- |  1 | 0221234      |
-- |  2 | 98765        |
-- |  3 | no contact   |
-- +----+--------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   COALESCE(a, b, c, 'x')

   a --NULL?--> b --NULL?--> c --NULL?--> 'x'
   |            |            |
   v            v            v
  return a    return b    return c      (first non-NULL wins)

   NULLIF(a, b):  a = b ? NULL : a

Fresher Notes

  • COALESCE(a, b, c) returns the first non-NULL value. IFNULL(a, b) is the two-argument version.
  • NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a equals b, otherwise a.
  • Use them to show defaults or avoid division by zero.

Worked Example 1

Report with defaults.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, COALESCE(phone, 'no phone') AS phone FROM contacts ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | phone
--  1 | 9999
--  2 | no phone
--  3 |

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Normalize empty strings to NULL.

Practice Exercise 1

Defaults for missing values.
codeExamples:
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'third') AS first_non_null, IFNULL(NULL, 'fallback') AS fb, NULLIF(5,5) AS n1, NULLIF(5,6) AS n2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- first_non_null | fb       | n1   | n2
-- third          | fallback | NULL |  5

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Safe division.
codeExamples:
SELECT 100 / NULLIF(0, 0) AS safe;

-- OUTPUT:
-- safe
-- NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

COALESCE returns the first non-NULL of its arguments and evaluates left to right; IFNULL is the two-argument MySQL form; NULLIF returns NULL when two values are equal. The result type is derived from all arguments, which can change precision or string length.
codeExamples:
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 'c') AS first_non_null, IFNULL(NULL, 0) AS fallback, NULLIF(5, 5) AS nul, NULLIF(5, 6) AS keep, COALESCE(1, 'text') AS mixed_type;

-- OUTPUT:
-- first_non_null | fallback | nul  | keep | mixed_type
-- c              |        0 | NULL |    5 | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: default values, safe division, replacing sentinel values with NULL, picking the first available contact, and conditional expressions with CASE/IF as the general tool.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: COALESCE is standard SQL (portable), takes any number of arguments, evaluates lazily from left, and keeps default logic in one place.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, qty INT, discount DECIMAL(5,2));
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1, 2, NULL), (2, 3, 10.00);

SELECT id, qty * (100 - COALESCE(discount, 0)) / 100 AS net_qty   -- NULL discount treated as 0
FROM sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+
-- | id | net_qty |
-- +----+---------+
-- |  1 |  2.0000 |
-- |  2 |  2.7000 |
-- +----+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: hiding NULLs can mask data-quality bugs, and COALESCE(col, x) = y in WHERE stops index use on col.
codeExamples:
-- Index-friendly: express the NULL case as a separate OR condition
-- SELECT * FROM sales WHERE discount = 0 OR discount IS NULL;

-- Index-hostile: function wraps the column
-- SELECT * FROM sales WHERE COALESCE(discount, 0) = 0;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_without_discount
FROM sales WHERE discount IS NULL;       -- the honest question

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------------+
-- | rows_without_discount |
-- +-----------------------+
-- |                     1 |
-- +-----------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the result type is the common type of all arguments, aggregates silently skip NULLs, and COALESCE of all NULLs is still NULL.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE t (v INT);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (10), (NULL), (20);

SELECT COUNT(*)  AS count_all,       -- counts rows
       COUNT(v)  AS count_v,         -- skips NULL
       AVG(v)    AS avg_skips_null,  -- (10+20)/2, not /3
       AVG(COALESCE(v, 0)) AS avg_zero_filled,
       COALESCE(NULL, NULL) AS still_null;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+---------+----------------+-----------------+------------+
-- | count_all | count_v | avg_skips_null | avg_zero_filled | still_null |
-- +-----------+---------+----------------+-----------------+------------+
-- |         3 |       2 |        15.0000 |         10.0000 | NULL       |
-- +-----------+---------+----------------+-----------------+------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Decide per column whether NULL is meaningful (unknown) or should be prevented with NOT NULL and DEFAULT; do not paper over design problems with COALESCE in every query. Put defaults in views or generated columns if many queries need them, and remember that NULL semantics change results of NOT IN, joins and aggregates.

Mid-Level Notes

  • COALESCE is standard SQL and accepts many arguments; IFNULL is MySQL-specific.
  • x / NULLIF(y, 0) prevents divide-by-zero errors.
  • Return types are the compatible type of all arguments, which can change formatting.

Senior Notes

  • Wrapping an indexed column in COALESCE in WHERE disables the index; model the default in the column instead.
  • Use NULLIF to turn sentinel values like empty strings into real NULLs.
  • Be explicit about NULL semantics in API contracts (missing vs empty).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: COALESCE on an indexed column inside WHERE (index lost), turning NULL into 0 in aggregates and distorting averages, and relying on IFNULL when portability matters. Keep NULL as unknown where that is the truth.
codeExamples:
SELECT AVG(score) AS avg_ignoring_null, AVG(COALESCE(score, 0)) AS avg_treating_missing_as_zero FROM results;
SELECT id FROM results WHERE COALESCE(score, 0) = 0;                       -- no index use
SELECT id FROM results WHERE score = 0 OR score IS NULL;                   -- index friendly

-- OUTPUT:
-- avg_ignoring_null | avg_treating_missing_as_zero
-- 72.5000           | 48.3333

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

These functions are cheap per row, but in predicates they block index use. When a default is semantic, store it with NOT NULL DEFAULT so queries stay simple and indexable.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY discount DECIMAL(5,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE discount > 0;          -- plain range on idx_discount

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world reporting: show "unknown" for missing categories without changing the data, and compute conversion rates without divide-by-zero errors.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Aggregate functions collapse many rows into one value: COUNT (how many), SUM (total), AVG (mean), MIN and MAX (extremes). Without GROUP BY the whole table becomes one group.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',50000), (2,'Raoji','IT',70000),
                       (3,'Moropant','HR',40000), (4,'Jiva','HR',NULL), (5,'Zoya','OPS',60000);

SELECT COUNT(*)    AS rows_,     -- all rows
       SUM(salary) AS total,     -- NULL ignored
       AVG(salary) AS average,
       MIN(salary) AS lowest,
       MAX(salary) AS highest
FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+--------+------------+--------+---------+
-- | rows_| total  | average    | lowest | highest |
-- +------+--------+------------+--------+---------+
-- |    5 | 220000 | 55000.0000 |  40000 |   70000 |
-- +------+--------+------------+--------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Reports ask summary questions: total sales, number of customers, average rating. Computing them in the server sends one row to the client instead of millions.
codeExamples:
-- Without aggregates you would fetch every salary and add them up in application code.
-- With aggregates the server does it and returns a single row.
SELECT COUNT(salary)          AS paid_staff,     -- counts non-NULL salaries only
       COUNT(DISTINCT dept)   AS departments,    -- unique departments
       SUM(salary) / COUNT(*) AS naive_avg       -- divides by 5, not 4
FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-------------+------------+
-- | paid_staff | departments | naive_avg  |
-- +------------+-------------+------------+
-- |          4|           3 | 44000.0000 |
-- +------------+-------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Dashboards (daily revenue), monitoring (max latency), inventory (min stock), finance (average order value) and data-quality checks (count of NULLs).
codeExamples:
-- Data quality check: how many rows miss a salary?
SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(salary) AS missing_salary,       -- COUNT(col) skips NULLs
       SUM(salary IS NULL)      AS missing_via_sum,      -- boolean is 0/1, so SUM counts true
       MAX(salary) - MIN(salary) AS spread
FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+-----------------+--------+
-- | missing_salary | missing_via_sum | spread |
-- +----------------+-----------------+--------+
-- |              1 |               1 |  30000 |
-- +----------------+-----------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • Aggregate functions summarise many rows into one value: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
  • COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values.
  • Aggregates ignore NULLs (except COUNT(*)).

Worked Example 1

Conditional aggregate.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(salary > 50000) AS high_earners, SUM(CASE WHEN dept = 10 THEN salary ELSE 0 END) AS dept10_total FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- high_earners | dept10_total
--            2 |       105000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Fast MIN with index.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT MIN(salary) FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT: (example, with an index on salary)
-- Extra
-- Select tables optimized away

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

All aggregates at once.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(salary) AS total, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal, MIN(salary) AS lo, MAX(salary) AS hi FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- n | total  | avg_sal    | lo    | hi
-- 3 | 175000 | 58333.3333 | 45000 | 70000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

NULL handling.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_n, COUNT(phone) AS phones, SUM(NULL) AS s FROM contacts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- rows_n | phones | s
--      3 |      2 | NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Aggregates reduce many rows to one value. COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values, SUM/AVG ignore NULLs, MIN/MAX use the index ends when possible. InnoDB has no stored row count (MVCC), so COUNT(*) scans the smallest index.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_n, COUNT(bonus) AS with_bonus, SUM(salary) AS total, AVG(salary) AS mean, MIN(salary) AS lo, MAX(salary) AS hi, SUM(bonus) AS bonus_sum FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- rows_n | with_bonus | total  | mean       | lo    | hi    | bonus_sum
--      3 |          1 | 175000 | 58333.3333 | 45000 | 70000 | 5000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: COUNT(DISTINCT), conditional aggregation with CASE or boolean expressions, GROUP_CONCAT, STDDEV/VARIANCE, bit aggregates, and aggregation with FILTER-style SUM(condition).
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT dept) AS depts, SUM(salary > 50000) AS high_earners, SUM(CASE WHEN dept = 10 THEN salary ELSE 0 END) AS dept10_payroll,
       GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY name SEPARATOR ', ') AS names, ROUND(STDDEV_POP(salary), 0) AS spread FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- depts | high_earners | dept10_payroll | names                  | spread
--     2 |            2 |         105000 | Abaji, Moropant, Raoji | 10274

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative, optimised (COUNT(*) and MIN/MAX on an indexed column can be answered from the index), work on any expression, and combine freely in one SELECT.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN dept = 'IT' THEN salary END) AS it_payroll,   -- conditional aggregate
       SUM(CASE WHEN dept = 'HR' THEN salary END) AS hr_payroll,
       MAX(name)                                  AS last_name_alpha  -- MIN/MAX work on text too
FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+------------+-----------------+
-- | it_payroll | hr_payroll | last_name_alpha |
-- +------------+------------+-----------------+
-- |     120000 |      40000 | Zoya            |
-- +------------+------------+-----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: they must read every qualifying row; COUNT(*) on a big InnoDB table is a scan (no stored row count), and DISTINCT aggregates need extra memory.
codeExamples:
-- InnoDB keeps no exact row counter because of MVCC (each transaction sees different rows),
-- so this walks the smallest index:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp;

-- Approximate alternative for huge tables (statistics, not exact):
-- SELECT TABLE_ROWS FROM information_schema.TABLES
--  WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = DATABASE() AND TABLE_NAME = 'emp';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |        5 |
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: aggregates ignore NULL (except COUNT(*)); on an empty set COUNT gives 0 but SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX give NULL; aggregates cannot be used in WHERE.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*)    AS cnt,        -- 0 on empty set
       SUM(salary)  AS total,      -- NULL on empty set
       COALESCE(SUM(salary), 0) AS safe_total
FROM emp WHERE dept = 'NONE';

-- This is an error: aggregate not allowed in WHERE
-- SELECT * FROM emp WHERE salary > AVG(salary);   -- ERROR 1111 Invalid use of group function

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-------+------------+
-- | cnt | total | safe_total |
-- +-----+-------+------------+
-- |   0 | NULL  |          0 |
-- +-----+-------+------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Aggregates are cheap on indexed columns and expensive on wide scans. For dashboards over big tables precompute summary tables (maintained by jobs or triggers) rather than scanning facts each time, and be explicit about NULL semantics so averages are not silently biased.

Mid-Level Notes

  • AVG ignores NULLs, so it may not equal SUM / COUNT(*).
  • Combine with GROUP BY for per-group results.
  • SUM of an empty set is NULL, COUNT of an empty set is 0.

Senior Notes

  • COUNT(*) on InnoDB must scan an index (no stored row count); big counts are expensive, so cache or approximate.
  • Use covering indexes for MIN/MAX: MySQL can answer from index ends instantly.
  • Use DECIMAL for sums of money; floating sums drift.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: SUM on an empty set is NULL (use COALESCE), AVG ignoring NULLs unexpectedly, COUNT(col) when COUNT(*) was meant, and summing after a one-to-many join (double counting).
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(qty) AS total, COALESCE(SUM(qty), 0) AS total_or_zero FROM order_items WHERE order_id = 999;
SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id;                 -- order total repeated per item
SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders;                                                             -- correct

-- OUTPUT:
-- total | total_or_zero
-- NULL  |             0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

MIN/MAX on an indexed column are instant (read one end of the index); COUNT(*) on a big table scans an index. Cache counts or keep a counter table for hot dashboards, and use covering indexes for filtered counts.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world KPI query in one pass over the data with conditional aggregates, instead of several queries.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(status = 'PAID') AS paid, SUM(status = 'CANCELLED') AS cancelled,
       ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'PAID' THEN total END), 2) AS revenue, ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN status = 'PAID' THEN total END), 2) AS avg_order
FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-06-01';

-- OUTPUT:
-- orders | paid | cancelled | revenue   | avg_order
--   8201 | 7010 |       412 | 981204.50 | 139.97

beginner.content:
Introduction

GROUP BY splits rows into groups that share the same value(s), then applies aggregates to each group separately, returning one row per group.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',50000), (2,'Raoji','IT',70000),
                       (3,'Moropant','HR',40000), (4,'Jiva','HR',45000), (5,'Zoya','OPS',60000);

SELECT dept,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount,   -- rows in each group
       SUM(salary) AS payroll
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept                      -- one output row per distinct dept
ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-----------+---------+
-- | dept | headcount | payroll |
-- +------+-----------+---------+
-- | HR   |         2 |   85000 |
-- | IT   |         2 |  120000 |
-- | OPS  |         1 |   60000 |
-- +------+-----------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A single total is rarely enough; managers want totals per department, per month, per product. GROUP BY gives the breakdown in one pass.
codeExamples:
-- Group by two columns: each distinct (dept, salary band) pair is a group
SELECT dept,
       salary >= 50000 AS high_pay,    -- expression used as a grouping key (0 or 1)
       COUNT(*)        AS n
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept, salary >= 50000
ORDER BY dept, high_pay;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+----------+---+
-- | dept | high_pay | n |
-- +------+----------+---+
-- | HR   |        0 | 2 |
-- | IT   |        1 | 2 |
-- | OPS  |        1 | 1 |
-- +------+----------+---+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Sales by region, signups per day, error count per service, top customers by spend, with WITH ROLLUP for subtotals.
codeExamples:
-- Subtotals and a grand total in one query
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS payroll
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept WITH ROLLUP;       -- adds a final row where dept is NULL = grand total

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | dept | payroll |
-- +------+---------+
-- | HR   |   85000 |
-- | IT   |  120000 |
-- | OPS  |   60000 |
-- | NULL |  265000 |
-- +------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   emp                      GROUP BY dept               aggregate per group
   IT  50000  --+                +-> [IT : 50000,70000]  -> SUM=120000
   IT  70000  --+--- bucket ---> +-> [HR : 40000,45000]  -> SUM= 85000
   HR  40000  --+                +-> [OPS: 60000]        -> SUM= 60000
   HR  45000  --+
   OPS 60000  --+

Fresher Notes

  • GROUP BY plus aggregates answers "per" questions: salary per department, orders per customer.
  • Every column in SELECT must be grouped or aggregated.
  • Group by several columns for finer detail.

Worked Example 1

Join fan-out inflates sums.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id;   -- wrong when items repeat the order

-- OUTPUT:
-- 3000   (each order counted once per item)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Correct: aggregate before joining.

Practice Exercise 1

Sales per dept with list of names.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(salary) AS total, GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY name SEPARATOR ', ') AS names FROM emp GROUP BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | n | total  | names
--   10 | 2 | 105000 | Abaji, Raoji
--   20 | 1 |  70000 | Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Pivot with CASE.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN dept=10 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS d10, SUM(CASE WHEN dept=20 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS d20 FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- d10 | d20
--   2 |   1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Combining GROUP BY with aggregates computes one value per group. MySQL either streams the groups from an index that is already in group order or builds a temporary hash/sort structure. The grouping key set decides the number of output rows and the memory needed.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(salary) AS payroll, AVG(salary) AS mean, MAX(salary) AS top FROM emp GROUP BY dept ORDER BY payroll DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | n | payroll | mean       | top
--   10 | 2 |  105000 | 52500.0000 | 60000
--   20 | 1 |   70000 | 70000.0000 | 70000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Group by multiple columns, add totals with ROLLUP, pivot with conditional sums, list members with GROUP_CONCAT, and compute shares with window functions over the grouped result.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one scan produces all groups; can group by expressions; MySQL 8 no longer sorts groups implicitly (use ORDER BY) so the optimiser is free to hash or use an index.
codeExamples:
-- Which department has the highest average salary?
SELECT dept, ROUND(AVG(salary)) AS avg_sal
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept
ORDER BY avg_sal DESC     -- sort the groups by their aggregate
LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | dept | avg_sal |
-- +------+---------+
-- | OPS  |   60000 |
-- +------+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: grouping may need a temporary table or filesort on large inputs, and with many distinct groups the result (and memory) approaches the table size.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept;

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+-------+------+------+-----------------+
-- | id | table | type | key  | Extra           |
-- +----+-------+------+------+-----------------+
-- |  1 | emp   | ALL  | NULL | Using temporary |   <- no index on dept: a temp table holds the groups
-- +----+-------+------+------+-----------------+
-- Fix: CREATE INDEX idx_dept ON emp(dept);  -- lets MySQL stream groups in order

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY (default) every selected column must be grouped, aggregated, or functionally dependent on the group key; NULLs form one group.
codeExamples:
-- Rejected under ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY: 'name' is neither grouped nor aggregated
-- SELECT dept, name, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept;
--   ERROR 1055: Expression #2 of SELECT list is not in GROUP BY clause

-- Fix 1: aggregate it            Fix 2: ANY_VALUE() if any row will do
SELECT dept, ANY_VALUE(name) AS some_name, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM emp GROUP BY dept ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT (example, ANY_VALUE picks an arbitrary row):
-- +------+-----------+---+
-- | dept | some_name | n |
-- +------+-----------+---+
-- | HR   | Moropant  | 2 |
-- | IT   | Abaji     | 2 |
-- | OPS  | Zoya      | 1 |
-- +------+-----------+---+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Index the grouping columns (or a composite covering index) so MySQL can do a loose or ordered scan instead of a temp table. Beware high-cardinality grouping on OLTP databases; push heavy analytics to replicas or a warehouse and keep ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY enabled to avoid nondeterministic results.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use HAVING to filter on aggregate results and WHERE to filter input rows.
  • Conditional aggregation with CASE builds pivot-style reports.
  • GROUP_CONCAT lists values per group (watch group_concat_max_len).

Senior Notes

  • Pre-aggregate heavy reports into summary tables refreshed by jobs or events.
  • An index on grouping columns allows streaming aggregation without temp tables.
  • Check for fan-out: joining before aggregating can multiply rows and inflate sums.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: aggregating after a fan-out join, grouping by too many columns, and filtering with HAVING when WHERE would do. Pre-aggregate each many-side separately, then join.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id, SUM(i.qty * i.price) AS items_total, SUM(p.amount) AS paid_total          -- both inflated by the cross of items x payments
FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id GROUP BY o.id;

SELECT o.id, i.items_total, p.paid_total FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * price) AS items_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_total FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) p ON p.order_id = o.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | items_total | paid_total
--  1 |      900.00 |     900.00

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Speed grouped reports with an index that matches the grouping and the aggregated columns, which gives streaming aggregation without temp tables. Check Created_tmp_disk_tables for spills.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: daily revenue by channel for a dashboard, stored in a summary table and refreshed incrementally rather than recomputed from raw rows on each page view.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO daily_channel_revenue (day, channel, orders, revenue)
SELECT DATE(created_at), channel, COUNT(*), SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= CURDATE() GROUP BY DATE(created_at), channel
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE orders = VALUES(orders), revenue = VALUES(revenue);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 6 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation and may use aggregate functions.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',50000), (2,'Raoji','IT',70000),
                       (3,'Moropant','HR',40000), (4,'Jiva','HR',45000), (5,'Zoya','OPS',60000);

SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS payroll
FROM emp
WHERE salary >= 45000          -- row filter: Moropant (40000) is dropped before grouping
GROUP BY dept
HAVING SUM(salary) > 60000;    -- group filter: keep big payrolls only

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | dept | payroll |
-- +------+---------+
-- | IT   |  120000 |
-- +------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You need both: remove irrelevant rows cheaply first, then keep only groups that satisfy an aggregate condition ("departments with more than 1 employee").
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1          -- cannot be written in WHERE: the count does not exist yet
ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---+
-- | dept | n |
-- +------+---+
-- | HR   | 2 |
-- | IT   | 2 |
-- +------+---+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Find customers with more than 5 orders, products sold fewer than 10 times, duplicate e-mails (HAVING COUNT(*) > 1), or days with revenue above target.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(30));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com'), (2,'b@x.com'), (3,'a@x.com');

-- Classic duplicate finder
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+--------+
-- | email   | copies |
-- +---------+--------+
-- | a@x.com |      2 |
-- +---------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   FROM emp
     |
     v   WHERE salary >= 45000        (rows)    <- indexes help here
   GROUP BY dept
     |
     v   HAVING SUM(salary) > 60000   (groups)  <- aggregates allowed
   SELECT / ORDER BY / LIMIT

Fresher Notes

  • WHERE filters individual rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
  • You cannot use aggregates like SUM() in WHERE.
  • Put as many conditions as possible in WHERE to reduce work.

Worked Example 1

Different meaning of WHERE vs HAVING.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000 GROUP BY dept;     -- average of high earners
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000; -- groups with high average

-- OUTPUT: (first)  10 | 60000.0000   20 | 70000.0000
-- OUTPUT: (second) 10 | 52500.0000   20 | 70000.0000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Proportion with HAVING.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary > 50000) > 0.4;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept
-- 10
-- 20

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

WHERE then HAVING.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n FROM emp WHERE salary >= 45000 GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | n
--   10 | 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Aggregate in WHERE is an error.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

WHERE filters input rows before grouping, so it reduces the data that is aggregated and can use indexes. HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can use aggregate results but cannot reduce the work already done. They answer different questions and can give different results.
codeExamples:
-- average of only well-paid people, per department
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_of_high FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000 GROUP BY dept;
-- departments whose overall average is high
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_all FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | avg_of_high        dept | avg_all
--   10 | 60000.0000           10 | 52500.0000
--   20 | 70000.0000           20 | 70000.0000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use both together: WHERE for row filters, HAVING for aggregate conditions. MySQL allows aliases in HAVING. Conditions on grouped columns can go in either place, but WHERE is cheaper.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary) AS mean FROM emp WHERE hired >= '2024-01-01' GROUP BY dept HAVING n >= 2 AND mean > 40000;
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING dept = 10;         -- legal, but WHERE dept = 10 is better

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | n | mean
--   10 | 2 | 52500.0000

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: putting row conditions in WHERE shrinks the data before grouping, so less work and index use; HAVING expresses what WHERE cannot.
codeExamples:
-- Same result, but the first form filters rows before grouping (preferred)
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' GROUP BY dept;
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING dept = 'IT';   -- groups everything, then discards

-- OUTPUT (both):
-- +------+----------+
-- | dept | COUNT(*) |
-- +------+----------+
-- | IT   |        2 |
-- +------+----------+
-- The optimiser often moves simple HAVING conditions down, but do not rely on it.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: HAVING conditions on aggregates cannot use indexes directly, and mixing the two clauses confuses beginners about evaluation order.
codeExamples:
-- Aggregate in WHERE is illegal because groups do not exist yet:
-- SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 GROUP BY dept;
--   ERROR 1111 (HY000): Invalid use of group function

-- Logical order:  FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT -> ORDER BY -> LIMIT
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING n > 1 ORDER BY dept;  -- MySQL lets HAVING use a select alias

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---+
-- | dept | n |
-- +------+---+
-- | HR   | 2 |
-- | IT   | 2 |
-- +------+---+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: WHERE cannot see select aliases or aggregates; HAVING without GROUP BY treats the whole table as one group; alias use in HAVING is a MySQL extension, not portable.
codeExamples:
-- HAVING without GROUP BY: the whole table is a single group
SELECT SUM(salary) AS total
FROM emp
HAVING SUM(salary) > 100000;     -- returns the row only if the condition holds

SELECT SUM(salary) AS total
FROM emp
HAVING SUM(salary) > 999999;     -- returns no rows at all

-- OUTPUT (first query, then second):
-- +--------+
-- | total  |
-- +--------+
-- | 265000 |
-- +--------+
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Rule of thumb: anything that can be decided per row goes in WHERE, only aggregate conditions go in HAVING. Use EXPLAIN to confirm filtering happens before grouping and index the WHERE and GROUP BY columns together as a composite index.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use WHERE for conditions on raw columns and HAVING only for conditions on aggregates.
  • Moving a non-aggregate condition from HAVING to WHERE often allows an index and reduces rows grouped.
  • MySQL allows aliases in HAVING.

Senior Notes

  • The optimizer may push some HAVING predicates down, but do not rely on it; write them as WHERE.
  • Filtering before aggregation changes results versus after (for example excluding rows from the average); be explicit about intent.
  • For top-N groups, HAVING with ORDER BY and LIMIT is fine but window functions are clearer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: aggregate functions in WHERE (error), non-aggregate row filters in HAVING (extra work), and mixing up which one changes the aggregate values. Ask: should the row take part in the calculation (WHERE) or should the finished group be kept (HAVING)?

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Compare costs: with a filter in WHERE the engine reads and groups far fewer rows. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the row counts entering each step.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: customers with at least 3 paid orders in the last 90 days: WHERE narrows the rows, HAVING keeps the qualifying customers.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS paid_orders, SUM(total) AS spent FROM orders
WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 90 DAY
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY spent DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | paid_orders | spent
-- 7           |           5 | 1842.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

An INNER JOIN combines rows from two tables where the ON condition is true. Rows without a match on either side are dropped. Plain JOIN means INNER JOIN.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE dept (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE emp  (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), dept_id INT);
INSERT INTO dept VALUES (1,'IT'), (2,'HR'), (3,'Legal');
INSERT INTO emp  VALUES (1,'Abaji',1), (2,'Raoji',1), (3,'Moropant',2), (4,'Jiva',NULL);

SELECT e.name AS employee, d.name AS department
FROM emp e
INNER JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;    -- match emp.dept_id to dept.id

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+
-- | employee | department |
-- +----------+------------+
-- | Abaji    | IT         |
-- | Raoji    | IT         |
-- | Moropant | HR         |
-- +----------+------------+
-- Jiva (no dept) and Legal (no staff) are both missing.

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Normalised data is split across tables (employees in one, departments in another). Joins put it back together at query time without storing the same department name many times.
codeExamples:
-- Without a join you would need two queries and manual matching in code:
--   SELECT * FROM emp;   SELECT * FROM dept;
-- With a join the server pairs them and can filter on both tables at once:
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id      -- JOIN = INNER JOIN
WHERE d.name = 'IT';                            -- filter by a column of the other table

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+
-- | name  | dept |
-- +-------+------+
-- | Abaji | IT   |
-- | Raoji | IT   |
-- +------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Orders with customer names, invoices with line items, students with courses: any report that needs attributes from two related entities.

Diagram

   emp                          dept
   +----+----------+---------+  +----+-------+
   | 1  | Abaji    | 1  -----+--> | 1  | IT    |
   | 2  | Raoji    | 1  -----+    | 2  | HR    |
   | 3  | Moropant | 2 --------> | 3  | Legal | (no match: dropped)
   | 4  | Jiva     | NULL (dropped)+----+-------+
   +----+----------+---------+

   INNER JOIN = the overlap of the two circles only

Fresher Notes

  • INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables.
  • Syntax: FROM a INNER JOIN b ON a.id = b.a_id. JOIN alone means INNER JOIN.
  • Rows without a partner are dropped from the result.

Worked Example 1

Three-way join.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept, l.city FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept JOIN locations l ON l.id = d.location_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | dept | city
-- Abaji    | HR   | Pune
-- Moropant | IT   | Delhi

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Check the join plan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT e.name, d.name FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table | type   | key     | rows
-- e     | ALL    | NULL    |    3
-- d     | eq_ref | PRIMARY |    1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Employees with department names.

Practice Exercise 2

Count employees per department with a join and group.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | n
-- HR   | 2
-- IT   | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL executes joins with nested loops: it picks a driving table, reads each qualifying row, then looks up matching rows in the next table through an index. The optimizer chooses the join order from statistics. Without a usable index on the inner side it falls back to a hash join (8.0.18+) or a join buffer.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax variants: JOIN ... ON, USING(col) when names match, NATURAL JOIN (avoid), several joins chained, and the older comma syntax with WHERE (works but easy to break).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: returns only complete, related data; the optimiser can reorder INNER joins freely and use indexes on either side; it is the most common and best-optimised join.
codeExamples:
-- Equivalent old-style syntax (comma join + WHERE). Same plan, but easy to forget the condition.
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM emp e, dept d
WHERE d.id = e.dept_id;

-- Preferred explicit syntax keeps join logic apart from row filters:
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;

-- OUTPUT (both):
-- +----------+------+
-- | name     | dept |
-- +----------+------+
-- | Abaji    | IT   |
-- | Raoji    | IT   |
-- | Moropant | HR   |
-- +-------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: silently loses unmatched rows (employees with a NULL department disappear from reports), and a one-to-many join multiplies parent rows.
codeExamples:
-- Parent columns repeat once per child, so SUM on the parent side over-counts:
CREATE TABLE budget (dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY, amount INT);
INSERT INTO budget VALUES (1, 1000), (2, 500);

SELECT SUM(b.amount) AS wrong_total     -- IT budget counted twice (two IT employees)
FROM budget b JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = b.dept_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+
-- | wrong_total |
-- +-------------+
-- |        2500 |   <- expected 1500
-- +-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: NULL never equals NULL, so NULL keys never match; joining on mismatched types or collations can disable index use; a missing ON in MySQL acts like a cross join.
codeExamples:
-- NULL = NULL is not true, so Jiva (dept_id NULL) matches nothing
SELECT COUNT(*) AS matched
FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON e.dept_id = d.id;

-- Null-safe equality operator <=> would match NULL with NULL (rarely wanted for keys)
SELECT NULL = NULL AS plain_eq, NULL <=> NULL AS null_safe_eq;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+
-- | matched |
-- +---------+
-- |       3 |
-- +---------+
-- +----------+--------------+
-- | plain_eq | null_safe_eq |
-- +----------+--------------+
-- | NULL     |            1 |
-- +----------+--------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Index the join column on the child (foreign key) side and make types and collations identical on both sides. Prefer explicit JOIN ... ON over comma joins, and when aggregating parent values across a one-to-many join, aggregate in a derived table first to avoid fan-out errors.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use table aliases (e, d) and qualify columns to avoid ambiguity.
  • Always index the join column on the child side (foreign key).
  • Put row filters in WHERE; for INNER JOIN, conditions in ON or WHERE give the same result.

Senior Notes

  • The optimizer chooses the join order from statistics; stale statistics produce bad plans, so run ANALYZE TABLE after bulk loads.
  • A missing join condition creates a Cartesian product; guard with code review and EXPLAIN row estimates.
  • Joining on mismatched types or collations disables indexes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: missing join condition (Cartesian product), joining on a mismatched type or collation (index unused), selecting ambiguous column names, and joining before filtering in the ON clause by mistake. Always check row counts.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp e JOIN departments d;             -- no ON: 3 x 4 = 12 rows (in MySQL a JOIN without ON is a cross join)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 12
-- COUNT(*)
-- 3

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Join performance depends on the driving table size after filters and on indexes for the inner lookups. Index the foreign keys, filter early, and read EXPLAIN ANALYZE for actual rows per step.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.country = 'IN' AND o.created_at >= '2026-05-01';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop inner join (actual rows=8200 loops=1)
--     -> Index range scan on o using idx_created (actual rows=51000)
--     -> Filter: (c.country = 'IN') -> Single-row index lookup on c using PRIMARY (actual rows=0.16 loops=51000)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: order detail screen joining orders, customers, items and products, selecting only needed columns and using primary-key lookups on the inner tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id, c.name AS customer, p.name AS product, i.qty, i.unit_price, i.qty * i.unit_price AS line_total
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id WHERE o.id = 1001;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id   | customer | product | qty | unit_price | line_total
-- 1001 | Abaji    | Pen     |   2 |      10.00 | 20.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN) keeps every row of the left table; when no right row matches, the right-side columns are filled with NULL.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE dept (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE emp  (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), dept_id INT);
INSERT INTO dept VALUES (1,'IT'), (2,'HR'), (3,'Legal');
INSERT INTO emp  VALUES (1,'Abaji',1), (2,'Raoji',1), (3,'Moropant',2), (4,'Jiva',NULL);

SELECT e.name AS employee, d.name AS department
FROM emp e
LEFT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;     -- all employees, even without a department

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+
-- | employee | department |
-- +----------+------------+
-- | Abaji    | IT         |
-- | Raoji    | IT         |
-- | Moropant | HR         |
-- | Jiva     | NULL       |
-- +----------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Reports often must show everything on the main side, including items with no related rows: customers who never ordered, products never sold, employees not yet assigned.
codeExamples:
-- Anti-join: find rows with NO match (left join then keep the NULLs)
SELECT d.name AS empty_department
FROM dept d
LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL;                    -- no employee row was found

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+
-- | empty_department |
-- +------------------+
-- | Legal            |
-- +------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

"Customers with their order count including zero", "all days with and without sales" (calendar table left joined to facts), and optional profile data.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customer (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, total INT);
