INSERT INTO customer VALUES (1,'Abaji'), (2,'Raoji'), (3,'Zoya');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,500), (11,1,300), (12,2,200);

SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(o.id)             AS orders_placed,   -- COUNT(column) ignores NULL, so Zoya gets 0
       COALESCE(SUM(o.total),0) AS spent
FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+---------------+-------+
-- | name  | orders_placed | spent |
-- +-------+---------------+-------+
-- | Abaji |             2 |   800 |
-- | Raoji |             1 |   200 |
-- | Zoya  |             0 |     0 |
-- +------+---------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   customer (LEFT, kept)         orders (RIGHT)
   +----+-------+               +-----+-------------+
   | 1  | Abaji | ------------> | 10  | cust 1      |
   | 2  | Raoji | ------------> | 12  | cust 2      |
   | 3  | Zoya  | -- no match -> NULL NULL NULL
   +----+-------+               +-----+-------------+

   LEFT JOIN = the whole left circle (overlap + left-only)

Fresher Notes

  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills the right columns with NULL when there is no match.
  • Use it to keep rows such as customers without orders.
  • To find rows with no match, add WHERE right.id IS NULL.

Worked Example 1

Filter in ON to keep unmatched rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, e.name AS employee FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id AND e.salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | employee
-- HR    | Abaji
-- IT    | Moropant
-- Sales | NULL

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Same filter in WHERE drops Sales.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id WHERE e.salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | name
-- HR   | Abaji
-- IT   | Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Departments including those without employees.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name AS dept, COUNT(e.id) AS staff FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept  | staff
-- HR    | 2
-- IT    | 1
-- Sales | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Departments with no employees.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id WHERE e.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Sales

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table; for rows with no match the right-side columns are NULL. The optimizer executes it as a nested loop in a fixed direction (left drives right), which limits join reordering compared with an inner join.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name AS dept, e.name AS employee FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id ORDER BY d.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept  | employee
-- HR    | Abaji
-- HR    | Raoji
-- IT    | Moropant
-- Sales | NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where a condition goes decides the result. Conditions on the right table belong in ON to keep unmatched left rows; in WHERE they turn the join into an inner join. Use IS NULL on a right key for an anti-join.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id AND e.salary > 50000;      -- keeps Sales
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id WHERE e.salary > 50000;      -- drops Sales
SELECT d.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id WHERE e.id IS NULL;                  -- departments without staff

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Sales

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no data loss on the preserved side, makes missing relationships visible, and is the basis of the "find orphans" anti-join pattern.
codeExamples:
-- Filter on the right table in ON (keeps left rows) rather than WHERE (drops them)
SELECT d.name, e.name AS employee
FROM dept d
LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.id AND e.name LIKE 'A%'   -- condition inside ON
ORDER BY d.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+----------+
-- | name  | employee |
-- +-------+----------+
-- | IT    | Abaji    |
-- | HR    | NULL     |
-- | Legal | NULL     |
-- +-------+----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a condition on the right table in WHERE silently turns the query back into an INNER JOIN, and the optimiser has less freedom to reorder tables.
codeExamples:
-- BUG: WHERE on the right table removes the NULL rows, so the LEFT JOIN is pointless
SELECT d.name, e.name AS employee
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.name LIKE 'A%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+----------+
-- | name | employee |
-- +------+----------+
-- | IT   | Abaji     |      <- HR and Legal vanished
-- +------+----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: NULLs in the result are ambiguous (no match, or a real NULL value), so test the right table's primary key; MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN and emulates it with LEFT UNION RIGHT.
codeExamples:
-- Emulate FULL OUTER JOIN: left join UNION right join (UNION removes the duplicates)
SELECT e.name AS employee, d.name AS department
FROM emp e LEFT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
UNION
SELECT e.name, d.name
FROM emp e RIGHT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+
-- | employee | department |
-- +----------+------------+
-- | Abaji    | IT         |
-- | Raoji    | IT         |
-- | Moropant | HR         |
-- | Jiva     | NULL       |
-- | NULL     | Legal      |
-- +----------+------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose the side that must be preserved as the left table and put right-table predicates in ON. For anti-joins, LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and NOT EXISTS usually perform alike in MySQL 8 (it converts both to an anti join), but avoid NOT IN with nullable columns.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Filtering the right table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN; put such filters in the ON clause.
  • COUNT(right.col) counts only matches, COUNT(*) counts the left rows too.
  • LEFT JOIN order matters: A LEFT JOIN B is not the same as B LEFT JOIN A.

Senior Notes

  • The optimizer can convert LEFT JOIN to INNER JOIN when a null-rejecting WHERE exists; confirm intent.
  • Chains of LEFT JOINs against one-to-many tables multiply rows; aggregate subqueries first.
  • Anti-join forms: LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL, NOT EXISTS; NOT EXISTS is usually clearest and null-safe.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: filtering the right table in WHERE, counting with COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(right.id), and chaining LEFT JOINs to several one-to-many tables (row explosion). Aggregate each many-side first.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) AS wrong, COUNT(e.id) AS right_count FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | wrong | right_count
-- HR    |     2 |           2
-- Sales |     1 |           0          (COUNT(*) counts the NULL-extended row)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Anti-join form: MySQL 8 recognises LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL and NOT EXISTS as an antijoin and avoids building the full join. Verify in the plan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT c.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop antijoin
--     -> Table scan on c
--     -> Single-row covering index lookup on o using idx_customer (customer_id=c.id)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a customer list with order counts and last order date, including customers who never ordered, built from a pre-aggregated derived table.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COALESCE(x.orders, 0) AS orders, x.last_order
FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, MAX(created_at) AS last_order FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) x ON x.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY x.last_order DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | orders | last_order
--  1 | Abaji |      9 | 2026-04-30 18:20:11
--  2 | Raoji |      0 | NULL

beginner.content:
Introduction

A RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image of LEFT JOIN: all rows of the right table are kept and unmatched left columns become NULL.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE dept (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE emp  (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), dept_id INT);
INSERT INTO dept VALUES (1,'IT'), (2,'HR'), (3,'Legal');
INSERT INTO emp  VALUES (1,'Abaji',1), (2,'Raoji',1), (3,'Moropant',2), (4,'Jiva',NULL);

SELECT e.name AS employee, d.name AS department
FROM emp e
RIGHT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;     -- every department is kept

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+
-- | employee | department |
-- +----------+------------+
-- | Abaji    | IT         |
-- | Raoji    | IT         |
-- | Moropant | HR         |
-- | NULL     | Legal      |
-- +----------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Sometimes the table you must preserve is the one you wrote second. RIGHT JOIN lets you keep that order, though it can always be rewritten as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the tables.
codeExamples:
-- These two queries are identical in meaning
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM emp e RIGHT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM dept d LEFT  JOIN emp  e ON d.id = e.dept_id;

-- OUTPUT (both, row order may differ):
-- +-------+----------+
-- | name  | name     |
-- +-------+----------+
-- | IT    | Abaji    |
-- | IT    | Raoji    |
-- | HR    | Moropant |
-- | Legal | NULL     |
-- +-------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rare in hand-written code; it appears mostly in generated SQL (ORMs, BI tools) and when extending an existing query by adding a table whose rows must be preserved.
codeExamples:
-- Count employees per department, showing departments with zero staff
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS staff
FROM emp e
RIGHT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY d.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------+
-- | name  | staff |
-- +-------+-------+
-- | IT    |     2 |
-- | HR    |     1 |
-- | Legal |     0 |
-- +-------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   emp (left)                   dept (RIGHT, kept)
   +----------+---------+       +----+-------+
   | Abaji    | 1  ------------>| 1  | IT    |
   | Moropant | 2  ------------>| 2  | HR    |
   | NULL     | NULL  <-no match| 3  | Legal |
   +----------+---------+       +----+-------+

   RIGHT JOIN = whole right circle (overlap + right-only)

Fresher Notes

  • RIGHT JOIN keeps every row from the right table, with NULLs for unmatched left columns.
  • It is the mirror of LEFT JOIN: A RIGHT JOIN B equals B LEFT JOIN A.
  • Most developers write LEFT JOIN only, by swapping table order.

Worked Example 1

Employees with no valid department (orphans).

Worked Example 2

Rewrite as LEFT JOIN.

Practice Exercise 1

Departments with employee counts (right side preserved).
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS staff FROM emp e RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | staff
-- HR    | 2
-- IT    | 1
-- Sales | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Equivalent LEFT JOIN.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS staff FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | staff
-- HR    | 2
-- IT    | 1
-- Sales | 0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL rewrites every RIGHT JOIN into the equivalent LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped before optimizing. There is no extra capability; it is a different way to write the same preserved-side rule.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use RIGHT JOIN when you read legacy SQL, otherwise write LEFT JOIN with the preserved table first. The same ON versus WHERE rules apply.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS staff FROM emp e RIGHT JOIN departments d ON e.dept = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name;
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS staff FROM departments d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept = d.id GROUP BY d.id, d.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | staff
-- HR    | 2
-- IT    | 1
-- Sales | 0

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: lets you keep a natural left-to-right table order when the preserved side is last; useful when patching existing queries.
codeExamples:
-- Adding a RIGHT JOIN to an existing chain keeps the earlier joins untouched
SELECT e.name, d.name AS dept
FROM emp e
JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id          -- existing inner join
RIGHT JOIN dept all_d ON all_d.id = d.id -- keep every department row (illustrative)
WHERE all_d.name = 'Legal';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+
-- | name | dept |
-- +------+------+
-- | NULL | NULL |
-- +------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: reading order and logic order disagree, which hurts readability; teams commonly ban it in style guides in favour of LEFT JOIN.
codeExamples:
-- A reader must remember: the table AFTER the keyword is the preserved one.
-- A three-table chain mixing LEFT and RIGHT is hard to reason about:
-- FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON ... RIGHT JOIN c ON ...   -- which side survives?
-- Rewrite with only LEFT JOINs, starting from the table you want to keep:
-- FROM c LEFT JOIN b ON ... LEFT JOIN a ON ...

SELECT 'prefer LEFT JOIN' AS style_guide;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+
-- | style_guide      |
-- +------------------+
-- | prefer LEFT JOIN |
-- +------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: still no FULL OUTER JOIN; every RIGHT JOIN is internally rewritten to a LEFT JOIN, so it gives no performance benefit.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT e.name, d.name FROM emp e RIGHT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+-------+--------+
-- | id | table | type   |
-- +----+-------+--------+
-- |  1 | d     | ALL    |     <- the preserved table is read first (outer table)
-- |  1 | e     | ALL    |
-- +----+-------+--------+
-- The plan shows dept as the driving table, exactly as if you wrote dept LEFT JOIN emp.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Standardise on LEFT JOIN across a codebase so every query reads the same way, and let linters flag RIGHT JOIN. Behaviourally they are equivalent, so the choice is purely about maintainability.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use RIGHT JOIN rarely; consistent LEFT JOIN style is easier to read and review.
  • Behaviour with WHERE on the left table mirrors LEFT JOIN rules.
  • MySQL internally rewrites RIGHT JOIN to LEFT JOIN.

Senior Notes

  • Mixed LEFT/RIGHT joins in one query are hard to reason about; standardize on LEFT in team style guides.
  • Apply the same ON versus WHERE care as for LEFT JOIN.
  • ORMs usually only generate LEFT joins, so RIGHT join knowledge is mostly for reading legacy SQL.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mixing LEFT and RIGHT joins in one query (hard to reason about) and putting a filter on the preserved side's partner in WHERE. A consistent style prevents review mistakes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance is the same as the equivalent LEFT JOIN, so tune indexes on the non-preserved side's join column and filter the preserved side early.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: converting legacy reports. Many older BI tools generate RIGHT JOINs; rewriting to LEFT JOIN makes them reviewable and aligns with ORM-generated SQL.
codeExamples:
-- legacy
SELECT p.name, s.qty FROM sales s RIGHT JOIN products p ON p.id = s.product_id;
-- rewrite
SELECT p.name, COALESCE(s.qty, 0) AS qty FROM products p LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.product_id = p.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | qty
-- Pen  |  12
-- Cap  |   0

beginner.content:
Introduction

A CROSS JOIN returns the Cartesian product: every row of the first table paired with every row of the second (n x m rows), with no join condition.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE size  (s VARCHAR(2));
CREATE TABLE color (c VARCHAR(6));
INSERT INTO size  VALUES ('S'), ('M'), ('L');
INSERT INTO color VALUES ('red'), ('blue');

SELECT s, c FROM size CROSS JOIN color ORDER BY s, c;    -- 3 x 2 = 6 rows

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+
-- | s  | c    |
-- +----+------+
-- | L  | blue |
-- | L  | red  |
-- | M  | blue |
-- | M  | red  |
-- | S  | blue |
-- | S  | red  |
-- +----+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some tasks truly need every combination: product variants, test-data generation, calendars (dates x stores), matrix-style reports.
codeExamples:
-- Generate every (store, day) pair so missing sales can later show as zero
CREATE TABLE store (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE day_list (d DATE PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO store VALUES (1), (2);
INSERT INTO day_list VALUES ('2024-05-01'), ('2024-05-02');

SELECT s.id AS store_id, dl.d AS day
FROM store s CROSS JOIN day_list dl
ORDER BY s.id, dl.d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+
-- | store_id | day        |
-- +----------+------------+
-- |        1 | 2024-05-01 |
-- |        1 | 2024-05-02 |
-- |        2 | 2024-05-01 |
-- |        2 | 2024-05-02 |
-- +----------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used to build SKU grids, scheduling slots, number tables, and "all employees x all months" skeletons that are then LEFT JOINed with facts.
codeExamples:
-- Skeleton + LEFT JOIN fact pattern: show zero where nothing happened
CREATE TABLE sales (store_id INT, d DATE, amt INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'2024-05-01',100), (2,'2024-05-02',70);

SELECT s.id AS store_id, dl.d AS day, COALESCE(x.amt, 0) AS amount
FROM store s
CROSS JOIN day_list dl
LEFT JOIN sales x ON x.store_id = s.id AND x.d = dl.d
ORDER BY s.id, dl.d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+--------+
-- | store_id | day        | amount |
-- +----------+------------+--------+
-- |        1 | 2024-05-01 |    100 |
-- |        1 | 2024-05-02 |      0 |
-- |        2 | 2024-05-01 |      0 |
-- |        2 | 2024-05-02 |     70 |
-- +----------+------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   size x color
   S --+-- red        rows = |size| * |color|
       +-- blue         3   *    2   = 6
   M --+-- red
       +-- blue
   L --+-- red
       +-- blue

Fresher Notes

  • CROSS JOIN pairs every row of one table with every row of another (Cartesian product).
  • If A has 3 rows and B has 4, the result has 12 rows.
  • It has no ON condition.

Worked Example 1

Zero-filled report.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.d, p.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.qty),0) AS qty
FROM calendar d CROSS JOIN products p LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.day = d.d AND s.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY d.d, p.id, p.name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- d          | name | qty
-- 2026-01-01 | Pen  |   5
-- 2026-01-01 | Book |   0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Guard against runaway joins.

Practice Exercise 1

Sizes and colours.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sizes (s VARCHAR(2)); INSERT INTO sizes VALUES ('S'),('M'),('L');
CREATE TABLE colours (c VARCHAR(10)); INSERT INTO colours VALUES ('Red'),('Blue');
SELECT s, c FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colours ORDER BY s, c;

-- OUTPUT:
-- s | c
-- L | Blue
-- L | Red
-- M | Blue
-- M | Red
-- S | Blue
-- S | Red

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Row count check.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colours;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 6

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A cross join pairs every row of the left table with every row of the right table. The result size is the product of the row counts, and the executor simply loops over both inputs. In MySQL, JOIN without ON behaves like CROSS JOIN.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Legitimate forms: generating combinations, building a calendar-by-product grid for zero-filled reports, and joining a one-row configuration or aggregate result to every row. Add WHERE to turn it into an inner join.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: simple, produces complete combination sets, and the planner treats it like any other join when a WHERE condition links the tables.
codeExamples:
-- In MySQL, CROSS JOIN ... WHERE is the same as an INNER JOIN ... ON
SELECT COUNT(*) AS pairs
FROM size a CROSS JOIN size b       -- all ordered pairs of sizes
WHERE a.s < b.s;                    -- keep each unordered pair once

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | pairs |
-- +-------+
-- |     3 |      (S,M) (S,L) (M,L)
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: row count explodes multiplicatively; an accidental cross join (forgotten ON / WHERE) on two large tables can run for hours.
codeExamples:
-- 10,000 x 10,000 rows = 100,000,000 rows produced
-- SELECT COUNT(*) FROM big_a, big_b;      -- a missing join condition looks exactly like this

SELECT 3 * 2                 AS small_case,
       10000 * 10000         AS big_case;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | small_case | big_case  |
-- +------------+-----------+
-- |          6 | 100000000 |
-- +------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: output size is bound only by n x m (memory, temp tables, network); the old comma syntax hides the intent. Use sql_select_limit or max_join_size guards in shared environments.

Architect's Notes

Use CROSS JOIN deliberately and write the keyword so intent is visible; always bound both inputs (small dimension tables, number tables with LIMIT). For gap-filling reports, build the skeleton once (a calendar or dimension table) and LEFT JOIN facts to it.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Useful for generating combinations: sizes x colours, dates x products, test data.
  • A forgotten join condition accidentally produces a cross join; row counts explode.
  • CROSS JOIN with a WHERE equality is the same as an INNER JOIN.

Senior Notes

  • Use cross joins on small, controlled sets (calendar, dimensions) to build reports that show zero values.
  • Guard against huge Cartesian products with LIMIT, row-estimate checks and code review.
  • Row explosion is multiplicative: 100k x 100k is 10 billion rows.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: an accidental cross join from a missing condition (rows multiply and the query never finishes), and using it with large tables. Protect production with max_join_size and code review of every JOIN without ON.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cross joins of small dimension tables are cheap and feed LEFT JOINs to facts, producing complete matrices. Filter the dimensions first.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.d, p.name, COALESCE(SUM(s.qty), 0) AS qty
FROM calendar c CROSS JOIN products p LEFT JOIN sales s ON s.day = c.d AND s.product_id = p.id
WHERE c.d >= '2026-05-01' AND c.d < '2026-05-08' GROUP BY c.d, p.id, p.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- d          | name | qty
-- 2026-05-01 | Pen  |  12
-- 2026-05-02 | Pen  |   0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a pricing grid of every product-size-colour variant, generated once and then filled with prices by an UPDATE.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A SELF JOIN joins a table to itself using two different aliases, so one row can be compared with or linked to another row of the same table. It is not a special keyword, just a normal join with the same table twice.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), mgr_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji',NULL), (2,'Raoji',1), (3,'Moropant',1), (4,'Jiva',2);

SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM emp e                              -- alias e = the employee role
LEFT JOIN emp m ON m.id = e.mgr_id      -- alias m = the manager role (same table)
ORDER BY e.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+---------+
-- | employee | manager |
-- +----------+---------+
-- | Abaji    | NULL    |
-- | Raoji    | Abaji   |
-- | Moropant | Abaji   |
-- | Jiva     | Raoji   |
-- +----------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Hierarchies (manager/employee, category/parent) and row-to-row comparisons (pairs, duplicates, consecutive rows) live inside one table. Aliases let SQL treat the table as two roles.
codeExamples:
-- Pairs of employees reporting to the same manager
SELECT a.name AS emp1, b.name AS emp2
FROM emp a
JOIN emp b ON a.mgr_id = b.mgr_id   -- same manager
        AND a.id < b.id;            -- id order avoids (x,x) and mirrored duplicates

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+----------+
-- | emp1  | emp2     |
-- +-------+----------+
-- | Raoji | Moropant |
-- +-------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Org charts, comment threads, bill-of-materials, finding duplicate rows, and "earns more than their manager" reports.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE pay (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), mgr_id INT, salary INT);
INSERT INTO pay VALUES (1,'Abaji',NULL,90000), (2,'Raoji',1,95000), (3,'Moropant',1,60000);

SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS mgr_salary
FROM pay e JOIN pay m ON m.id = e.mgr_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;          -- compare a row with its parent row

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+---------+------------+
-- | name  | salary | manager | mgr_salary |
-- +-------+--------+---------+------------+
-- | Raoji |  95000 | Abaji   |      90000 |
-- +------+--------+---------+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   emp as "e" (employee)              emp as "m" (manager)
   +----+-------+--------+          +----+-------+
   | 4  | Jiva  | 2 -----+--------->| 2  | Raoji |
   | 2  | Raoji | 1 -----+--------->| 1  | Abaji |
   +----+-------+--------+          +----+-------+
          same physical table, two aliases

Fresher Notes

  • A self join joins a table to itself using two aliases, for example employees and their managers.
  • Alias is mandatory: FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.id.
  • It models hierarchies and comparisons within one table.

Worked Example 1

Duplicate emails as pairs.
codeExamples:
SELECT a.id, b.id FROM users a JOIN users b ON a.email = b.email AND a.id < b.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | id
--  4 |  9

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Whole tree with recursive CTE.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS lvl FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, t.lvl + 1 FROM staff s JOIN tree t ON s.manager_id = t.id)
SELECT CONCAT(REPEAT('  ', lvl), name) AS org FROM tree ORDER BY lvl, id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- org
-- Annaji
--   Raoji
--   Moropant
--     Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Employee and manager.

Practice Exercise 2

Find managers who have reports and their counts.
codeExamples:
SELECT m.name, COUNT(*) AS reports FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id GROUP BY m.id, m.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name   | reports
-- Annaji | 2
-- Raoji  | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A self join uses the same table twice under different aliases, so each row can be matched with other rows of the same table. The optimizer treats the two aliases as independent tables, so an index on the join column (for example manager_id) is used for the inner lookups.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical patterns: employee and manager, pairs within a table (duplicates, adjacent rows), and comparisons between rows (earns more than manager). Use LEFT JOIN to keep top-level rows and a.id < b.id to avoid mirrored pairs.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name AS employee, COALESCE(m.name, '(top)') AS manager FROM staff e LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id;
SELECT a.id, b.id AS duplicate_of FROM users a JOIN users b ON a.email = b.email AND a.id > b.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- employee | manager
-- Annaji   | (top)
-- Raoji    | Annaji
-- Moropant | Annaji
-- Kanhoji  | Raoji

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no extra tables, expresses one level of hierarchy simply, and works with indexes on the parent key.
codeExamples:
-- Count direct reports per manager (a self join plus GROUP BY)
SELECT m.name AS manager, COUNT(e.id) AS direct_reports
FROM emp m
LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.mgr_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY m.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+----------------+
-- | manager  | direct_reports |
-- +----------+----------------+
-- | Abaji    |              2 |
-- | Raoji    |              1 |
-- | Moropant |              0 |
-- | Jiva     |              0 |
-- +---------+----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each self join walks exactly one level; deeper hierarchies need one join per level or a recursive query, and unindexed self joins are quadratic.
codeExamples:
-- Three-level chain needs two self joins (grandmanager)
SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager, g.name AS grand_manager
FROM emp e
LEFT JOIN emp m ON m.id = e.mgr_id
LEFT JOIN emp g ON g.id = m.mgr_id
WHERE e.name = 'Jiva';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+---------------+
-- | name | manager | grand_manager |
-- +------+---------+---------------+
-- | Jiva | Raoji   | Abaji         |
-- +------+---------+---------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: unknown depth cannot be handled by plain joins; use a recursive CTE (MySQL 8) with a depth guard.
codeExamples:
-- Whole chain of command for Jiva, any depth
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, mgr_id, 0 AS lvl FROM emp WHERE name = 'Jiva'   -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.mgr_id, c.lvl + 1
  FROM emp e JOIN chain c ON e.id = c.mgr_id                      -- climb one level per round
)
SELECT lvl, name FROM chain ORDER BY lvl;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-------+
-- | lvl | name  |
-- +-----+-------+
-- |   0 | Jiva  |
-- |   1 | Raoji |
-- |   2 | Abaji |
-- +------+------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Adjacency lists (parent_id) are simple and write-friendly, with recursive CTEs for reads. If subtree queries dominate, consider closure tables or nested sets. Always index the parent column and cap recursion with cte_max_recursion_depth to protect against cycles.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use LEFT JOIN to keep top-level rows with no manager.
  • Self joins also find pairs (duplicate emails, adjacent rows) with conditions such as a.id < b.id.
  • Index the parent column (manager_id).

Senior Notes

  • Multi-level hierarchies need recursive CTEs, not repeated self joins.
  • Alternative hierarchy models: adjacency list (parent id), materialized path, nested sets, closure table; pick by read/write pattern.
  • Large self joins can square the row count; filter early.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting aliases (ambiguous columns), using INNER JOIN and losing root rows, producing both (a,b) and (b,a) pairs, and attempting arbitrary-depth hierarchies with a fixed number of self joins. Use a recursive CTE for depth.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A self join on a non-indexed column is a nested loop over n x n rows. Index the join key, and for pairwise comparisons restrict candidates (same group, narrow date window) so the join does not square the table.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: find employees earning more than their manager, a classic audit query.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- OUTPUT:
-- employee | salary | manager | manager_salary
-- Kanhoji  |  90000 | Raoji   | 80000

beginner.content:
Introduction

Queries can chain many joins: each JOIN adds a table to the result so far. A many-to-many relationship needs a junction table, so reading it takes two joins (A to junction to B).

Why Do We Need This?

A student has many courses and a course has many students, which one table cannot store without repeating or packing data. Splitting it into three tables and joining on demand keeps data atomic.
codeExamples:
-- Which students take SQL? Filter on the far table
SELECT s.name
FROM course c
JOIN enrollment e ON e.course_id = c.id
JOIN student s    ON s.id = e.student_id
WHERE c.title = 'SQL'
ORDER BY s.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Orders-items-products-customers, users-roles-permissions, tags on articles: real reports routinely join four to eight tables.
codeExamples:
-- Count students per course, including courses with nobody (LEFT JOINs keep them)
SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS students
FROM course c
LEFT JOIN enrollment e ON e.course_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.title
ORDER BY c.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+----------+
-- | title  | students |
-- +--------+----------+
-- | SQL    |        2 |
-- | Java   |        1 |
-- | Python |        0 |
-- +--------+----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   student             enrollment (junction)          course
   +----+-------+      +------------+-----------+     +----+--------+
   | 1  | Abaji | <--- | student_id | course_id | --> | 1  | SQL    |
   | 2  | Raoji | <--- |     1      |     1     | --> | 2  | Java   |
   +----+-------+      |     1      |     2     |     | 3  | Python |
                       |     2      |     1     |     +----+--------+
                       +------------+-----------+
   one-to-many  +  many-to-one  =  many-to-many

Fresher Notes

  • You can chain joins: A JOIN B ON ... JOIN C ON ....
  • A many-to-many query goes through the junction table: students JOIN enrolments JOIN courses.
  • Use clear aliases and join one relationship at a time.

Worked Example 1

Fix fan-out with pre-aggregation.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id, i.item_total, p.paid_total
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(price*qty) AS item_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i ON i.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid_total FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) p ON p.order_id = o.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | item_total | paid_total
--  1 |       900  |       900

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Students without any course.
codeExamples:
SELECT s.name FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.course_id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Students with courses.
codeExamples:
SELECT s.name, c.title, e.enrolled_on
FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id
ORDER BY s.name, c.title;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | title | enrolled_on
-- Abaji | Java  | 2026-01-06
-- Abaji | SQL   | 2026-01-05
-- Raoji | SQL   | 2026-01-07

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Course popularity with students listed.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.title, COUNT(*) AS n, GROUP_CONCAT(s.name ORDER BY s.name) AS students
FROM courses c JOIN enrolments e ON e.course_id = c.id JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;

-- OUTPUT:
-- title | n | students
-- SQL   | 2 | Abaji,Raoji
-- Java  | 1 | Abaji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

With several joins, the optimizer evaluates many possible join orders (up to optimizer_search_depth) and picks the cheapest from table statistics. The SQL text order is only logical; the executor may start from the most selective table.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.title = 'SQL';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop inner join
--     -> Nested loop inner join
--         -> Filter: (c.title = 'SQL') -> Table scan on c
--         -> Index lookup on e using idx_course (course_id=c.id)
--     -> Single-row index lookup on s using PRIMARY (id=e.student_id)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Many-to-many queries join through the junction table. Variants: students per course, courses per student, students with all of several courses, students with none.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: flexible reporting from normalised data; the optimiser picks the join order using statistics and indexes, so you write what you want, not how to get it.
codeExamples:
-- Aggregate across the junction and list the courses as one text value
SELECT s.name, GROUP_CONCAT(c.title ORDER BY c.title SEPARATOR ', ') AS courses
FROM student s
JOIN enrollment e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN course c ON c.id = e.course_id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | name  | courses   |
-- +-------+-----------+
-- | Abaji | Java, SQL |
-- | Raoji | SQL       |
-- +------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every extra join multiplies the plan search space and the chance of row fan-out; a single missing key index can make the whole query crawl.
codeExamples:
-- Fan-out: joining two independent one-to-many children inflates counts
CREATE TABLE phone (student_id INT, num VARCHAR(5));
INSERT INTO phone VALUES (1,'p1'), (1,'p2');

SELECT s.name, COUNT(*) AS rows_returned          -- 2 courses x 2 phones = 4 rows for Abaji
FROM student s
JOIN enrollment e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN phone p      ON p.student_id = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------------+
-- | name | rows_returned |
-- +------+---------------+
-- | Abaji |             4 |    <- not 2 courses or 2 phones; use COUNT(DISTINCT) or pre-aggregate
-- +------+---------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a single join is limited to 61 tables; very wide joins may fall back to a greedy search (optimizer_search_depth) and pick a poor order.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@optimizer_search_depth AS search_depth;   -- how exhaustively join orders are explored

-- Force a specific order only as a last resort (hint, MySQL 8):
-- SELECT /*+ JOIN_ORDER(s, e, c) */ s.name, c.title
-- FROM student s JOIN enrollment e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN course c ON c.id = e.course_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | search_depth |
-- +--------------+
-- |           62 |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Give the junction table a composite primary key (both foreign keys) plus a reverse-order index so both directions are fast. When combining several one-to-many branches, aggregate each branch in a derived table before joining to prevent fan-out.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Mix INNER and LEFT joins carefully: a later INNER JOIN on a LEFT-joined table filters out unmatched rows.
  • Join order in SQL text is logical; the optimizer chooses the physical order (use STRAIGHT_JOIN only as a last resort).
  • Index every join column, especially both sides of the junction table.

Senior Notes

  • Aggregates across several one-to-many joins double count (fan-out); aggregate subqueries separately.
  • Wide joins increase memory for hash joins and temp tables; select only needed columns.
  • Consider denormalized read models for heavy multi-join screens.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: fan-out when joining two one-to-many branches (totals multiply), mixing INNER and LEFT joins so an inner join discards the preserved rows, and selecting wide columns through many joins. Aggregate branches separately.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id, SUM(i.qty * i.unit_price) AS items_total, SUM(p.amount) AS paid FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id JOIN payments p ON p.order_id = o.id GROUP BY o.id;
-- both sums are inflated (every item row repeats for every payment row)

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | items_total | paid
--  1 |        1800 | 1800        (true values are 900 and 900)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Tune many-join queries from the plan: find the step with the largest actual rows, add the missing index, filter earlier, and reduce selected columns. Only if the optimizer keeps a bad order consider STRAIGHT_JOIN or hints.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... ;                                  -- find the biggest actual rows step
SELECT /*+ JOIN_ORDER(c, e, s) */ s.name FROM students s JOIN enrolments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.title = 'SQL';

-- OUTPUT:
-- (the hint forces courses first because the title filter is the most selective)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a report of orders with customer, products and payment status. Pre-aggregate items and payments in derived tables, then join them to orders one-to-one.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id, c.name, i.items_total, COALESCE(p.paid, 0) AS paid
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS items_total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) i ON i.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id) p ON p.order_id = o.id WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-05-01';

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | items_total | paid
--  1 | Abaji |      900.00 | 900.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A join combines tables side by side; a subquery nests one query in another. Many questions can be written either way, and the MySQL 8 optimiser often rewrites subqueries into joins (semi-join) so performance is frequently equal.

Why Do We Need This?

You must choose the clearest and fastest form. Joins let you return columns from both tables; subqueries express "exists / not exists / compare to an aggregate" without duplication.
codeExamples:
-- Need columns from both tables -> join
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id FROM customer c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id ORDER BY o.id;

-- Need only a yes/no test on the other table -> EXISTS subquery
SELECT c.name FROM customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- OUTPUT (first, then second):
-- +-------+----------+
-- | name  | order_id |
-- +-------+----------+
-- | Abaji |       10 |
-- | Abaji |       11 |
-- | Raoji |       12 |
-- +-------+----------+
-- +------+
-- | name |
-- +------+
-- | Zoya |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Performance tuning in practice: read the plan with EXPLAIN, index the join keys, shrink inputs early, and test both formulations on real data volumes.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT c.name FROM customer c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+-------------+-------+--------+--------------------------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type   | Extra                    |
-- +----+-------------+-------+--------+--------------------------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | o     | index  | Using index; LooseScan   |   <- IN became a semi-join
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | c     | eq_ref | NULL                     |
-- +----+-------------+-------+--------+--------------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Query                         Optimizer view
   JOIN  : A --- B ----------->  nested loop / hash join
   IN (subquery) ------------->  semi-join  (LooseScan, FirstMatch, Materialize)
   NOT EXISTS ---------------->  anti-join
   correlated scalar --------->  per-row lookup (needs index!)

   Always: EXPLAIN -> index join keys -> filter early

Fresher Notes

  • Many problems can be written with a JOIN or a subquery. Both can be correct; choose the clearer one and check the plan.
  • JOIN returns columns from both tables; a subquery in WHERE only filters.
  • EXISTS/IN subqueries often read more naturally for "has at least one".

Worked Example 1

Slow correlated subquery in SELECT.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS n FROM customers c;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | n
--  1 | 2
--  2 | 0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Faster join to a pre-aggregate.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id, COALESCE(x.n,0) AS n FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) x ON x.customer_id = c.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | n
--  1 | 2
--  2 | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Same result, two styles.

Practice Exercise 2

Find the strategy used.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop semijoin
--     -> Table scan on c
--     -> Single-row index lookup on o using idx_customer

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Since MySQL 8, many subqueries are transformed into joins internally: IN and EXISTS become semijoins, NOT EXISTS becomes an antijoin, and simple derived tables are merged. So the choice between join and subquery is mostly about clarity, not speed; the plan decides performance.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE total > 1000);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop semijoin
--     -> Filter: (orders.total > 1000) -> Table scan on orders
--     -> Single-row index lookup on customers using PRIMARY (id=orders.customer_id)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Equivalent forms: JOIN with DISTINCT, IN, EXISTS, and a derived table. They differ in duplicates: a join repeats parents per child, while IN/EXISTS return each parent once.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of joins: flexible ordering and algorithms (nested loop, hash join in 8.0.18+), all columns available. Of subqueries: readable, no row duplication, natural for aggregates and existence tests.
codeExamples:
-- Compare against an aggregate: subquery reads naturally
SELECT name, total FROM (
  SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS total FROM customer c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.name
) t
WHERE total > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) x);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------+
-- | name  | total |
-- +-------+-------+
-- | Abaji |     2 |
-- +------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: joins may duplicate rows and need DISTINCT; correlated subqueries can execute once per outer row; derived tables may be materialised into temporary tables.
codeExamples:
-- Correlated scalar subquery: logically runs once per customer row
SELECT c.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS n   -- needs index on customer_id
FROM customer c;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+---+
-- | name  | n |
-- +-------+---+
-- | Abaji | 2 |
-- | Raoji | 1 |
-- | Zoya  | 0 |
-- +-------+---+
-- Without an index on orders.customer_id this is a full scan per customer (O(n x m)).

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: performance depends on data size, indexes, statistics and version; blanket rules such as "joins are always faster" are wrong. Join performance is bound by the join algorithm chosen.
codeExamples:
-- Without a usable index, MySQL 8.0.18+ uses a hash join instead of block nested loop
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT c.name FROM customer c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id + 0 = c.id;   -- expression blocks the index

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- -> Inner hash join (o.customer_id + 0 = c.id)
--     -> Table scan on o
--     -> Hash
--         -> Table scan on c

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Write the clearest query first, then verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-sized data. Ensure join columns share type and collation and are indexed; prefer EXISTS or joins for existence tests, avoid NOT IN on nullable columns, and avoid scalar subqueries in SELECT lists over large outer sets.

Mid-Level Notes

  • MySQL 8 rewrites many IN/EXISTS subqueries into semijoins and anti-joins, so performance is often equal.
  • JOIN can duplicate rows for one-to-many relations; semi-join (EXISTS) never does.
  • Correlated subqueries in the SELECT list run per row and can be slow; replace with a join to a pre-aggregated derived table.

Senior Notes

  • Always compare with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on production-like data; differences come from statistics and indexes, not syntax.
  • Hash joins (8.0.18+) help joins without usable indexes; do not rely on them for OLTP latency.
  • Join performance is dominated by the access path of the driving table, the selectivity of filters, and index availability on inner tables.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: correlated subqueries in the SELECT list that run once per row, derived tables that cannot be merged and are materialized, and assuming one form is always faster. Test with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS orders FROM customers c;                  -- one subquery per customer
SELECT c.id, COALESCE(x.n, 0) AS orders FROM customers c LEFT JOIN (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) x ON x.customer_id = c.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | orders
--  1 | 9

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hash joins (8.0.18+) help when no index exists on the inner join column; indexes still win for selective lookups. Check which algorithm was chosen and adjust buffers only for heavy reports.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world decision rule: use EXISTS for "has at least one", a join when you need columns from both sides, a derived table to aggregate one side first, and always confirm with the plan on production-sized data.
codeExamples:
-- need orders columns too: join
SELECT c.name, o.id, o.total FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.total > 1000;
-- only need the customers: EXISTS
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 1000);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | id | total
-- Abaji | 77 | 1500.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A scalar subquery returns exactly one value (one row, one column) and can be used wherever a single value is allowed: in WHERE, SELECT or HAVING. A single-row subquery returns one row and is compared with operators like =, >.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), dept VARCHAR(5), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',50000), (2,'Raoji','IT',70000),
                       (3,'Moropant','HR',40000), (4,'Jiva','HR',45000), (5,'Zoya','OPS',60000);

SELECT name, salary
FROM emp
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);   -- inner query yields one number: 53000

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | salary |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Raoji | 70000  |
-- | Zoya  |  60000 |
-- +------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You cannot write WHERE salary > AVG(salary) because aggregates are not allowed in WHERE. A scalar subquery computes the aggregate first and hands the result to the outer query.
codeExamples:
-- Highest paid employee(s): compare with MAX computed by a subquery
SELECT name, salary
FROM emp
WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);   -- ties would all be returned

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | salary |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Raoji | 70000  |
-- +------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Show each row next to a global figure (difference from average), find the latest order, or the second highest salary.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary,
       salary - (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp) AS diff_from_avg   -- scalar subquery in SELECT list
FROM emp
ORDER BY salary DESC;

-- Second highest salary
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM emp
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);

-- OUTPUT (first query, then second):
-- +----------+--------+---------------+
-- | name     | salary | diff_from_avg |
-- +----------+--------+---------------+
-- | Raoji    |  70000 |    17000.0000 |
-- | Zoya     |  60000 |     7000.0000 |
-- | Abaji    |  50000 |    -3000.0000 |
-- | Jiva     |  45000 |    -8000.0000 |
-- | Moropant | 40000  | -13000.0000   |
-- +----------+--------+---------------+
-- +----------------+
-- | second_highest |
-- +----------------+
-- |          60000 |
-- +----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   outer query                       inner (scalar) query
   SELECT ... WHERE salary > ( SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp )
                                      |
                                      v   runs once
                                    53000
   outer becomes: WHERE salary > 53000

Fresher Notes

  • A scalar subquery returns exactly one value, so it can be used wherever a value fits: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp).
  • It must return one column and at most one row.
  • Wrap it in parentheses.

Worked Example 1

Too many rows error.

Worked Example 2

Latest order per customer via scalar subquery.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.name, (SELECT MAX(o.created_at) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS last_order FROM customers c;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | last_order
-- Abaji | 2026-03-05 10:00:00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Above-average earners.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary
-- Moropant | 70000
-- Abaji    | 60000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Compare to department maximum with a scalar subquery.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp) - salary AS gap_to_top FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary | gap_to_top
-- Abaji    |  60000 | 10000
-- Raoji    |  45000 | 25000
-- Moropant |  70000 | 0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A scalar subquery returns one column and at most one row and can be used as a value. If it does not depend on the outer query it is evaluated once and the result is cached; if it returns more than one row you get error 1242, and no rows becomes NULL.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Where it can appear: WHERE, HAVING, SELECT list, ORDER BY, SET of an UPDATE and VALUES of an INSERT. Use LIMIT 1 or aggregates to guarantee a single row, and COALESCE for the empty case.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: uncorrelated scalar subqueries run once and are cached, are easy to read, and avoid a join when you need one global number.
codeExamples:
-- Percentage of total payroll for each employee
SELECT name,
       ROUND(100 * salary / (SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp), 1) AS pct_of_payroll
FROM emp
ORDER BY pct_of_payroll DESC
LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+----------------+
-- | name  | pct_of_payroll |
-- +-------+----------------+
-- | Raoji |           26.4 |
-- | Zoya  |           22.6 |
-- +------+----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: if the subquery returns more than one row the query fails; if it returns no rows the value is NULL and the comparison is not true.
codeExamples:
-- Returns several rows where one is expected:
-- SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary = (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT');
--   ERROR 1242 (21000): Subquery returns more than 1 row

-- Empty result becomes NULL, so nothing matches:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary = (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'NONE');

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: must return exactly one column; scalar subqueries in the SELECT list that are correlated run per row; LIMIT inside IN subqueries is not supported but is fine in scalar ones.
codeExamples:
-- Force a single row safely with ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1
SELECT name,
       (SELECT d.salary FROM emp d WHERE d.dept = e.dept ORDER BY d.salary DESC LIMIT 1) AS top_in_dept
FROM emp e
WHERE e.id IN (1, 3);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------------+
-- | name     | top_in_dept |
-- +----------+-------------+
-- | Abaji    |       70000 |
-- | Moropant |       45000 |
-- +-------+-------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use scalar subqueries for global constants and lookups; for per-row values prefer a join to a pre-aggregated derived table or a window function (OVER) which scans once. Guard against multi-row errors with MAX/MIN or LIMIT 1 only when the business rule really means "the one".

Mid-Level Notes

  • If it returns more than one row you get error 1242; use IN or ANY, or add LIMIT/aggregation.
  • Empty result becomes NULL.
  • It can appear in SELECT, WHERE, HAVING and even ORDER BY.

Senior Notes

  • Uncorrelated scalar subqueries run once and are cached; correlated ones run per outer row.
  • Use a CTE or join when the same subquery repeats many times.
  • NULL results silently make comparisons unknown; check data and use COALESCE.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: a subquery returning several rows, relying on the first row without ORDER BY, and correlated scalar subqueries in the SELECT list on big tables. Make the single-row guarantee explicit.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

An uncorrelated scalar subquery costs one evaluation; a correlated one costs one per outer row. Replace correlated scalars with a join to an aggregated derived table or a window function.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name, e.salary, ROUND(e.salary - AVG(e.salary) OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept), 0) AS diff_from_dept_avg FROM emp e;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | salary | diff_from_dept_avg
-- Abaji |  60000 | 7500
-- Raoji |  45000 | -7500

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: compare each row to a global baseline, such as orders above the average order value this month.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01') ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | total
-- 77 | 1500.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A multi-row subquery returns a list of values (one column, many rows). IN tests whether a value appears in that list; NOT IN tests that it does not.

Why Do We Need This?

Filters often depend on a set computed from another table ("employees in departments located in Pune") that cannot be written as one simple comparison.
codeExamples:
-- Same question as a join, to show the equivalence
SELECT e.name
FROM emp e JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE d.city = 'Pune';

-- NOT IN: employees outside Pune departments
SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE dept_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM dept WHERE city = 'Pune');

-- OUTPUT (first, then second):
-- +----------+
-- | name     |
-- +----------+
-- | Abaji    |
-- | Moropant |
-- +----------+
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Raoji |
-- +-------+
-- Jiva is excluded from NOT IN: NULL dept_id gives unknown, not true.

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Customers who bought a product on offer, users in blocked-country lists, orders whose items are low on stock, and data-cleanup deletes.
codeExamples:
-- Delete users who have no valid order (typical clean-up with IN)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, emp_id INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1), (11,1), (12,3);

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE id IN (SELECT emp_id FROM orders);   -- who has orders

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | name     |
-- +----------+
-- | Abaji    |
-- | Moropant |
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   dept (inner)                 emp (outer)
   WHERE city='Pune'            WHERE dept_id IN ( ... )
   +----+------+
   | 1  | IT   |  --- list {1,3} ---> Abaji(1) yes, Raoji(2) no,
   | 3  | OPS  |                      Moropant(3) yes, Jiva(NULL) no
   +----+------+

Fresher Notes

  • A multi-row subquery returns several values; use IN to test membership: WHERE dept IN (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE city = "Pune").
  • It must return one column.
  • NOT IN excludes members of the set.

Worked Example 1

NOT IN with a NULL.

Worked Example 2

Tuple IN.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE (dept, salary) IN (SELECT dept, MAX(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Employees in HR or IT.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept IN (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE name IN ('HR','IT'));

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Departments with no employees (NOT IN).
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM departments WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE dept IS NOT NULL);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Sales

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An IN subquery returns a set of values. The optimizer converts it to a semijoin and can execute it with FirstMatch, LooseScan, Materialization or DuplicateWeedout strategies, or as a plain index lookup into the subquery results, whichever is cheapest.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept IN (SELECT id FROM departments WHERE active = 1);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop semijoin
--     -> Filter: (departments.active = 1) -> Table scan on departments
--     -> Index lookup on emp using idx_dept (dept=departments.id)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: single column IN, tuple IN, NOT IN, = ANY (same as IN), and IN with a literal list. Tuples compare several columns at once.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: reads like English, duplicates in the subquery do not duplicate outer rows, and MySQL 8 transforms IN into an efficient semi-join.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp WHERE id IN (SELECT emp_id FROM orders);

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+-------------+-------+--------+-----------------------------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type   | Extra                       |
-- +----+-------------+-------+--------+-----------------------------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | orders| ALL    | Start temporary             |
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | emp   | eq_ref | End temporary               |
-- +----+-------------+-------+--------+-----------------------------+
-- "SIMPLE" with temporary markers shows the semi-join (duplicate weedout) strategy.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: NOT IN misbehaves with NULLs; very large IN lists or subqueries may be materialised into temporary tables.
codeExamples:
-- If the subquery contains a NULL, NOT IN never returns true:
SELECT 'row appears' AS result FROM DUAL
WHERE 5 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL);        -- 5<>1 AND 5<>2 AND 5<>NULL(unknown) = unknown

SELECT 'row appears' AS result FROM DUAL
WHERE 5 NOT IN (1, 2, 3);

-- OUTPUT (first query, then second):
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)
-- +-------------+
-- | result      |
-- +-------------+
-- | row appears |
-- +-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the subquery must return one column; LIMIT is not allowed in an IN subquery (ERROR 1235) unless wrapped in a derived table; multi-column IN uses row constructors.
codeExamples:
-- Row constructor: compare two columns at once
SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE (id, dept_id) IN (SELECT emp_id, 1 FROM orders);   -- pairs (1,1), (1,1), (3,1)

-- LIMIT workaround: wrap in a derived table
SELECT name FROM emp
WHERE id IN (SELECT emp_id FROM (SELECT emp_id FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 2) t);

-- OUTPUT (first, then second):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- +-------+
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer EXISTS (or a join) when the subquery column can be NULL and you need negation. Make sure the column used inside IN is indexed on the inner table, and check EXPLAIN to confirm a semi-join rather than a dependent subquery on old versions.

Mid-Level Notes

  • NOT IN returns no rows if the subquery produces a NULL; use NOT EXISTS.
  • MySQL 8 optimizes IN subqueries as semijoins; older versions were slow.
  • You can use tuple IN: (a,b) IN (SELECT a,b FROM ...).

Senior Notes

  • Check EXPLAIN for "FirstMatch" or "LooseScan" semijoin strategies.
  • For very large lists consider joining a temp table instead.
  • Keep subquery selective; unfiltered IN over big tables materializes huge sets.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

The classic bug: NOT IN with a NULL in the subquery returns no rows because x NOT IN (1, NULL) is unknown. Filter NULLs or use NOT EXISTS.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM departments WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT dept FROM emp);                                       -- emp.dept has a NULL: empty
SELECT id FROM departments d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e WHERE e.dept = d.id);                   -- correct

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set
-- id
-- 30

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A large IN subquery result is materialized into a temporary table with a unique index and probed. When the subquery side is huge, flip it: drive from the smaller set or join explicitly.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: orders for customers in a segment, a typical filter from a marketing tool. Keep the subquery selective and indexed.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query, so it is logically re-evaluated for each outer row. It cannot run on its own because it depends on the outer alias.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), dept VARCHAR(5), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',50000), (2,'Raoji','IT',70000),
                       (3,'Moropant','HR',40000), (4,'Jiva','HR',45000), (5,'Zoya','OPS',60000);

-- Employees earning more than the average of THEIR OWN department
SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary
FROM emp e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept);   -- e.dept is the correlation

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+--------+
-- | name  | dept | salary |
-- +-------+------+--------+
-- | Raoji | IT   |  70000 |
-- | Jiva  | HR   |  45000 |
-- +------+------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some questions are relative to each row's own context (own department, own customer, previous value). A single global subquery cannot express "compare to my group".
codeExamples:
-- Top earner per department (row has no higher-paid colleague in its dept)
SELECT e.dept, e.name, e.salary
FROM emp e
WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(x.salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept)
ORDER BY e.dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+--------+
-- | dept | name  | salary |
-- +------+-------+--------+
-- | HR   | Jiva  |  45000 |
-- | IT   | Raoji |  70000 |
-- | OPS  | Zoya  |  60000 |
-- +------+-------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Latest record per user, running comparisons, "customers whose last order was over 90 days ago", and per-row lookups in reports.
codeExamples:
-- Number of colleagues in the same department (per-row count)
SELECT e.name,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept AND x.id <> e.id) AS colleagues
FROM emp e
ORDER BY e.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+
-- | name     | colleagues |
-- +----------+------------+
-- | Abaji    |          1 |
-- | Raoji    |          1 |
-- | Moropant |          1 |
-- | Jiva     |          1 |
-- | Zoya     |          0 |
-- +-------+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   for each outer row e:             emp e          inner query
     +--------------------+         +---------+    +----------------------+
     | Abaji    IT 50000  ---+--- e.dept='IT' ---->   | AVG(salary) WHERE    |
     | Raoji    IT 70000  ---+--- e.dept='IT' ---->   |   x.dept = e.dept    |
     | Moropant HR 40000  ---+--- e.dept='HR' ---->   +----------------------+
     +--------------------+
   inner query is re-run (logically) per outer row

Fresher Notes

  • A correlated subquery refers to a column of the outer query, so it is evaluated for each outer row.
  • Example: employees earning more than the average of their own department.
  • It reads like a loop: for each employee, compute the department average.

Worked Example 1

Rewrite with derived table join.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name FROM emp e JOIN (SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS a FROM emp GROUP BY dept) d ON d.dept = e.dept WHERE e.salary > d.a;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rewrite with window function.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM (SELECT name, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS a FROM emp) t WHERE salary > a;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Above own department average.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name, e.dept, e.salary FROM emp e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | dept | salary
-- Abaji |   10 | 60000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Latest order per customer.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.* FROM orders o WHERE o.created_at = (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | customer_id | created_at
-- 11 |           1 | 2026-03-05 10:00:00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so it must be re-evaluated for each outer row (dependent subquery). MySQL may decorrelate simple cases into joins, but in general cost equals outer rows times the cost of one inner execution.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT e.name FROM emp e WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | select_type        | table | type | key      | Extra
--  1 | PRIMARY            | e     | ALL  | NULL     |
--  2 | DEPENDENT SUBQUERY | x     | ref  | idx_dept | Using index condition

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical forms: above own group average, latest row per key, existence checks with EXISTS, and top per group. Correlated EXISTS short-circuits at the first match.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: expresses per-row logic directly; with an index on the correlated column each probe is a cheap lookup.
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_dept ON emp(dept, salary);   -- makes each inner probe an index lookup

EXPLAIN SELECT e.name FROM emp e
WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(x.salary) FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = e.dept);

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+--------------------+-------+------+-----------+
-- | id | select_type        | table | type | key       |
-- +----+--------------------+-------+------+-----------+
-- |  1 | PRIMARY            | e     | ALL  | NULL      |
-- |  2 | DEPENDENT SUBQUERY | x     | ref  | idx_dept  |   <- runs once per outer row
-- +----+--------------------+-------+------+-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: can degrade to O(n x m) when the inner side is unindexed; harder to read than a join or window function.
codeExamples:
-- Same result with a window function: one pass, no per-row subquery
SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM (SELECT dept, name, salary,
             RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
      FROM emp) t
WHERE rnk = 1
ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+--------+
-- | dept | name  | salary |
-- +------+-------+--------+
-- | HR   | Jiva  |  45000 |
-- | IT   | Raoji | 70000  |
-- | OPS  | Zoya  |  60000 |
-- +------+------+--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL 8 can decorrelate only some patterns; correlation is allowed only to the immediately enclosing queries' columns, and derived tables in FROM cannot reference sibling tables unless LATERAL (8.0.14+) is used.
codeExamples:
-- LATERAL derived table: top-1 salary per department row, correlated in FROM
SELECT d.dept, t.name, t.salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp) d,
LATERAL (SELECT name, salary FROM emp x WHERE x.dept = d.dept ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1) t
ORDER BY d.dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+--------+
-- | dept | name  | salary |
-- +------+-------+--------+
-- | HR   | Jiva  |  45000 |
-- | IT   | Raoji | 70000  |
-- | OPS  | Zoya  |  60000 |
-- +------+------+--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Index the correlation column on the inner table, or rewrite as a join to a grouped derived table or a window function when the outer set is large. Use EXPLAIN to spot DEPENDENT SUBQUERY and measure; for top-N-per-group, window functions or LATERAL are usually best.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Often can be rewritten as a JOIN to an aggregated derived table, which can be much faster.
  • MySQL may decorrelate some forms automatically.
  • Index the correlated columns inside the subquery.

Senior Notes

  • Per-row execution scales as outer rows x inner cost; verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE loops counts.
  • Window functions replace many correlated aggregates (rank, running total, top N).
  • Correlated EXISTS is efficient because it stops at the first match.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: correlated subqueries on unindexed columns (quadratic work), ties in "latest row" queries returning several rows, and assuming results are cached. Index the inner correlation column and add a tiebreaker.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.* FROM orders o WHERE o.created_at = (SELECT MAX(created_at) FROM orders WHERE customer_id = o.customer_id);   -- ties return 2 rows
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_customer_created (customer_id, created_at, id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rewrite with a window function or a join to a grouped derived table; both scan the data once.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: top 3 recent orders per customer using a correlated count, then the faster window version for large data.

beginner.content:
Introduction

EXISTS returns true if the subquery returns at least one row, otherwise false. What the subquery selects does not matter (convention: SELECT 1); only existence counts.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customer (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10));
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, KEY (customer_id));
INSERT INTO customer VALUES (1,'Abaji'), (2,'Raoji'), (3,'Zoya');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1), (11,1), (12,2);

SELECT c.name
FROM customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);   -- at least one order

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Existence checks are the cleanest way to express "has related rows" or "has no related rows" without duplicates and without NULL traps, and it can stop at the first match.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.name
FROM customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);   -- never ordered

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | name |
-- +------+
-- | Zoya |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Find orphan rows, customers with unpaid invoices, users with a given role, products never sold, and conditional business rules in UPDATE or DELETE.
codeExamples:
-- Mark customers who ordered (EXISTS inside UPDATE)
ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN active TINYINT DEFAULT 0;
UPDATE customer c SET active = 1
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
SELECT name, active FROM customer;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | active |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Abaji |      1 |
-- | Raoji |      1 |
-- | Zoya  |      0 |
-- +------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   customer c                       orders o
   +----+-------+      probe        +----+-------------+
   | 1  | Abaji | ---- c.id=1 ----> | 10 | customer 1  |  found -> TRUE (stop)
   | 3  | Zoya  | ---- c.id=3 ----> |    nothing      |  -> FALSE
   +----+-------+                   +----+-------------+
   EXISTS = TRUE/FALSE per outer row; NOT EXISTS = the opposite

Fresher Notes

  • EXISTS (subquery) is true if the subquery returns at least one row.
  • Typical: customers that have at least one order.
  • The SELECT list inside EXISTS does not matter; SELECT 1 is common.

Worked Example 1

Relational division: customers who bought every product.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM order_lines l JOIN orders o ON o.id = l.order_id WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND l.product_id = p.id));

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Plan shows semijoin.

Practice Exercise 1

Customers with orders and without.

Practice Exercise 2

Departments that have a high earner.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name FROM departments d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e WHERE e.dept = d.id AND e.salary > 65000);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- IT

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

EXISTS tests whether the subquery returns at least one row and stops at the first match. MySQL turns EXISTS into a semijoin and NOT EXISTS into an antijoin, so the inner side is typically a single index probe per outer row.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop semijoin
--     -> Table scan on c
--     -> Single-row covering index lookup on o using idx_customer (customer_id=c.id)  (LooseScan/FirstMatch)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: EXISTS, NOT EXISTS, nested EXISTS for "for all" logic (relational division), and EXISTS combined with extra conditions. The select list is irrelevant; SELECT 1 is a convention.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM products p WHERE p.featured = 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items i JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND i.product_id = p.id));

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji         (customers who bought every featured product)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: short-circuits on the first match, NULL-safe (unlike NOT IN), no duplicate outer rows, and converted to a semi-join or anti-join by MySQL 8.
codeExamples:
-- NULL-safe negation: EXISTS is not fooled by NULL customer_id values
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (13, NULL);

SELECT c.name FROM customer c
WHERE c.id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);                     -- returns nothing!

SELECT c.name FROM customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);   -- still correct

-- OUTPUT (first query, then second):
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)
-- +------+
-- | name |
-- +------+
-- | Zoya |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: without an index on the inner correlated column each probe scans the inner table, and the correlated syntax is more verbose than IN.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT c.name FROM customer c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- OUTPUT (example, abbreviated):
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+---------------+------------------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type | key           | Extra            |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+---------------+------------------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | c     | ALL  | NULL          | NULL             |
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | o     | ref  | customer_id   | Using index; FirstMatch(c) |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+---------------+------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: EXISTS only tests presence, it cannot return the matched values; the SELECT list inside is ignored so errors in it are not raised; it cannot compare counts without extra logic.
codeExamples:
-- "At least 2 orders" needs aggregation, EXISTS alone cannot count
SELECT c.name FROM customer c
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) >= 2;

-- EXISTS ignores the select list entirely, so even this does not raise an error:
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1/0) AS still_true;   -- 1/0 is never evaluated as a row filter

-- OUTPUT (first query, then second):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- +-------+
-- +------------+
-- | still_true |
-- +------------+
-- |          1 |
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to EXISTS / NOT EXISTS for presence tests, especially negations, and index the inner correlation column (typically a foreign key). Use IN when the subquery is a small independent list and readability matters.

Mid-Level Notes

  • NOT EXISTS finds rows with no match and is NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN.
  • EXISTS usually correlates with the outer table.
  • It never duplicates outer rows, unlike JOIN.

Senior Notes

  • MySQL executes EXISTS as semijoin/antijoin where possible; plans should show index lookups on the inner table.
  • Index the correlated column in the inner table (orders.customer_id).
  • For "all" conditions use double negation NOT EXISTS (... NOT EXISTS ...) (relational division).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting the correlation (the subquery is then true for everyone or no one), using COUNT(*) > 0 instead of EXISTS, and NOT IN where NOT EXISTS is needed. Always reference the outer row.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders);                        -- true for all customers if any order exists
SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) > 0;   -- counts everything
SELECT name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);        -- stops at first row

-- OUTPUT:
