-- (first query ignores the relationship)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

EXISTS needs an index on the inner correlated column to be cheap. Check that the plan shows an index lookup, not a table scan, on the inner table.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: access control. Show documents the user owns or that were shared with them, using EXISTS so each document appears once.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.id, d.title FROM documents d WHERE d.owner_id = 7 OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM document_shares s WHERE s.document_id = d.id AND s.user_id = 7);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title
--  4 | Roadmap

beginner.content:
Introduction

ANY (or SOME) is true if the comparison holds for at least one value of the subquery; ALL is true only if it holds for every value.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(10), dept VARCHAR(5), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',50000), (2,'Raoji','IT',70000),
                       (3,'Moropant','HR',40000), (4,'Jiva','HR',45000), (5,'Zoya','OPS',60000);

-- Earns more than SOME HR employee  (i.e. more than the minimum HR salary, 40000)
SELECT name, salary FROM emp
WHERE salary > ANY (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'HR')
ORDER BY salary;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | salary |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Jiva  |  45000 |
-- | Abaji | 50000  |
-- | Zoya  |  60000 |
-- | Raoji | 70000  |
-- +------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Comparing with a whole set ("higher than everyone in HR") needs quantifiers. They express MAX/MIN-style logic directly over a list.
codeExamples:
-- Earns more than ALL HR employees (more than the maximum HR salary, 45000)
SELECT name, salary FROM emp
WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'HR')
ORDER BY salary;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | salary |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Abaji | 50000  |
-- | Zoya  |  60000 |
-- | Raoji | 70000  |
-- +------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used for threshold rules: "bids above every reserve price", "products cheaper than some competitor offer", and eligibility checks across a set.
codeExamples:
-- Equivalences worth memorising
--   = ANY  is the same as IN
--   <> ALL is the same as NOT IN
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = ANY (SELECT 'IT')         -- same as IN ('IT')
ORDER BY name;

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept <> ALL (SELECT 'IT')        -- same as NOT IN ('IT')
ORDER BY name;

-- OUTPUT (first, then second):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- +-------+
-- +----------+
-- | name     |
-- +----------+
-- | Jiva     |
-- | Moropant |
-- | Zoya     |
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   salary > ANY (40000, 45000)        salary > ALL (40000, 45000)
   ==  salary > MIN  (40000)          ==  salary > MAX  (45000)

   value:     39000  42000  47000
   > ANY :      no     yes    yes
   > ALL :      no      no    yes

Fresher Notes

  • > ANY (subquery) is true if the value is greater than at least one returned value; > ALL if greater than every value.
  • = ANY is the same as IN; <> ALL is the same as NOT IN.
  • Example: salary above all salaries in department 10.

Worked Example 1

Equivalent MAX/MIN rewrites.

Worked Example 2

ALL on empty set is true.
codeExamples:
SELECT 1 > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE 1 = 0) AS vacuous;

-- OUTPUT:
-- vacuous
-- 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Earn more than everyone in dept 20.

Practice Exercise 2

Earn more than at least one HR person.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > ANY (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 10);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

x > ANY (set) is true if x is greater than at least one value, which equals x > MIN(set); x > ALL (set) is true if greater than every value, which equals x > MAX(set). On an empty set ALL is true and ANY is false.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 > ANY (SELECT 3 UNION SELECT 9) AS any_gt, 5 > ALL (SELECT 3 UNION SELECT 9) AS all_gt, 5 > ALL (SELECT 1 WHERE 1 = 0) AS all_empty, 5 = ANY (SELECT 5 UNION SELECT 7) AS eq_any;

-- OUTPUT:
-- any_gt | all_gt | all_empty | eq_any
--      1 |      0 |         1 |      1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

= ANY is IN, <> ALL is NOT IN. The optimizer often rewrites ANY/ALL with MIN/MAX. Writing MIN/MAX explicitly is clearer and handles NULL intent.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative set comparison, no need to compute MIN/MAX manually, and it reads close to the business rule.
codeExamples:
-- Equivalent rewrite with MIN/MAX (often clearer and faster)
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = 'HR') ORDER BY name;   -- same as > ALL
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = 'HR') ORDER BY name;   -- same as > ANY

-- OUTPUT (first, then second):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- | Zoya  |
-- +-------+
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Jiva  |
-- | Raoji |
-- | Zoya  |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: rarely used, so many developers misread them; NULL values in the subquery make results unintuitive; MIN/MAX rewrites are usually more explicit.
codeExamples:
-- ALL over an EMPTY set is TRUE (vacuous truth); ANY over an empty set is FALSE
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_empty
FROM emp WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'NONE');   -- every row qualifies

SELECT COUNT(*) AS any_empty
FROM emp WHERE salary > ANY (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'NONE');   -- no row qualifies

-- OUTPUT (first, then second):
-- +-----------+
-- | all_empty |
-- +-----------+
-- |         5 |
-- +-----------+
-- +-----------+
-- | any_empty |
-- +-----------+
-- |         0 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the subquery must return a single column; a NULL in the subquery makes ALL yield unknown (no rows) unless a definite false occurs; they are not supported with a list literal, only a subquery.
codeExamples:
-- A NULL in the set breaks "> ALL" for rows that are greater than every non-NULL value
CREATE TABLE bonus (amt INT);
INSERT INTO bonus VALUES (10), (NULL);

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_matching
FROM emp WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT amt FROM bonus);    -- 50000 > 10 true, 50000 > NULL unknown

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+
-- | rows_matching |
-- +---------------+
-- |             0 |
-- +---------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer explicit MIN/MAX (with NULL handling) or EXISTS in production code, since ANY/ALL semantics with NULLs and empty sets surprise people. Keep them for places where they make a business rule read naturally, and always test the empty-set case.

Mid-Level Notes

  • > ANY is equivalent to greater than the minimum; > ALL to greater than the maximum.
  • On empty sets ALL is true and ANY is false.
  • Rewrite with MIN/MAX for readability and speed.

Senior Notes

  • ANY/ALL with NULLs follow three-valued logic; one NULL in the set can turn ALL into unknown.
  • MAX/MIN rewrites let the optimizer use indexes more simply.
  • Rarely used in application code; recognise them in legacy SQL and exams.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: NULLs inside the set (ALL becomes unknown), empty sets giving surprising true results, and using ALL where NOT EXISTS is intended. Filter NULLs explicitly.
codeExamples:
SELECT 5 > ALL (SELECT 3 UNION SELECT NULL) AS result;
SELECT 5 > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 99) AS empty_is_true;

-- OUTPUT:
-- result
-- NULL
-- empty_is_true
-- 1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

MIN/MAX form lets the optimizer use index ends and avoid materializing a subquery set. Prefer it for performance and clarity.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = 20);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- select_type | table | type  | Extra
-- SUBQUERY    | emp   | ref   | Select tables optimized away? (MAX uses idx_dept_salary)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: find products priced above every competitor price, or employees paid more than anyone in a given team, written with MAX for readability.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name FROM products p WHERE p.price > (SELECT MAX(price) FROM competitor_prices c WHERE c.product_id = p.id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Premium Pen

beginner.content:
Introduction

UNION stacks the rows of two or more SELECTs into one result and removes duplicate rows. UNION ALL stacks them and keeps every row, duplicates included. Both need the same number of columns, matched by position.
codeExamples:
-- Two customer lists that overlap on one person (Raoji)
CREATE TABLE web_cust  (name VARCHAR(20), city VARCHAR(20));
CREATE TABLE shop_cust (name VARCHAR(20), city VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO web_cust  VALUES ('Abaji','Pune'),('Raoji','Delhi'),('Mina','Pune');
INSERT INTO shop_cust VALUES ('Raoji','Delhi'),('Karan','Goa');

SELECT name, city FROM web_cust
UNION                                         -- duplicates removed
SELECT name, city FROM shop_cust
ORDER BY name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------+
-- | name  | city  |
-- +-------+-------+
-- | Abaji | Pune  |
-- | Karan | Goa   |
-- | Mina  | Pune  |
-- | Raoji | Delhi |
-- +-------+-------+
-- (UNION ALL on the same query would return 5 rows: Raoji appears twice.)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Data often lives in several places: per-year tables, per-region tables, live plus archive. Reports need them as one list. UNION ALL is the cheap way to concatenate; UNION is for when the same entity may appear in more than one source and you want it once.
codeExamples:
-- Keep the source visible: the extra literal column makes rows distinct,
-- so UNION ALL is the right (and cheaper) choice here
SELECT name, 'web'  AS src FROM web_cust
UNION ALL
SELECT name, 'shop' AS src FROM shop_cust
ORDER BY name, src;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+
-- | name  | src  |
-- +-------+------+
-- | Abaji | web  |
-- | Karan | shop |
-- | Mina  | web  |
-- | Raoji | shop |
-- | Raoji | web  |
-- +-------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

A classic production pattern is "hot and archive" or one table per year. A view or query unions them with UNION ALL, then aggregates the combined set.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sales_2025 (amt INT);
CREATE TABLE sales_2026 (amt INT);
INSERT INTO sales_2025 VALUES (100),(200);
INSERT INTO sales_2026 VALUES (500);

SELECT yr, SUM(amt) AS revenue
FROM (SELECT 2025 AS yr, amt FROM sales_2025
      UNION ALL
      SELECT 2026,       amt FROM sales_2026) AS t
GROUP BY yr
ORDER BY yr;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | yr   | revenue |
-- +------+---------+
-- | 2025 |     300 |
-- | 2026 |     500 |
-- +------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   web_cust            shop_cust
   ┌───────┬───────┐   ┌───────┬───────┐
   │ Abaji │ Pune  │   │ Raoji │ Delhi │
   │ Raoji │ Delhi │   │ Karan │ Goa   │
   │ Mina  │ Pune  │   └───────┴───────┘
   └───────┴───────┘
        │                    │
        └──────┬─────────────┘
               ▼
   UNION ALL : 5 rows (keeps both Raoji rows)
   UNION     : 4 rows (dedupe via temp table + unique index)

Fresher Notes

  • UNION combines results of two queries and removes duplicates; UNION ALL keeps duplicates.
  • Both queries need the same number of columns with compatible types.
  • UNION ALL is faster because it skips duplicate removal.

Worked Example 1

Sorting and limiting the union.
codeExamples:
(SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 10) UNION ALL (SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 20)
ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary
-- Moropant | 70000
-- Abaji    | 60000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rewrite an OR into UNION ALL with a guard.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE dept = 10
UNION ALL
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000 AND dept <> 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1
-- 2
-- 3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Combine two lists.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 10
UNION
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

UNION ALL keeps duplicates.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 10
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji
-- Moropant
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

UNION ALL simply concatenates the result sets of its branches. UNION must also remove duplicates, so the server writes rows into a temporary table with a unique key (or sorts), which costs memory, CPU and sometimes disk. Branch column names come from the first SELECT.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 10
UNION ALL
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000;
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp WHERE dept = 10 UNION SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji
-- Moropant
-- Abaji          (UNION ALL keeps the duplicate)
-- EXPLAIN: UNION RESULT <union1,2> uses a temporary table

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Combine more than two branches, give individual branches ORDER BY/LIMIT with parentheses, sort the final result once, and add a literal column to label the source of each row.
codeExamples:
(SELECT id, 'emp' AS src, name FROM emp ORDER BY id LIMIT 2)
UNION ALL
(SELECT id, 'cust' AS src, name FROM customers ORDER BY id LIMIT 2)
ORDER BY src, id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | src  | name
--  1 | cust | Abaji
--  2 | cust | Raoji
--  1 | emp  | Abaji
--  2 | emp  | Raoji

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: UNION ALL streams rows with no extra work. UNION needs a temporary table with a unique index to detect duplicates, so it costs memory, CPU and possibly disk. Knowing which one you need is a free speed-up.
codeExamples:
-- Compare plans: plain UNION adds a "UNION RESULT" step with a temporary table
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM web_cust UNION     SELECT name FROM shop_cust;
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM web_cust UNION ALL SELECT name FROM shop_cust;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- UNION:
-- | id   | select_type  | table      | Extra           |
-- |    1 | PRIMARY      | web_cust   | NULL            |
-- |    2 | UNION        | shop_cust  | NULL            |
-- | NULL | UNION RESULT | <union1,2> | Using temporary |
-- UNION ALL:
-- |    1 | PRIMARY      | web_cust   | NULL            |
-- |    2 | UNION        | shop_cust  | NULL            |   (no temporary table step)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: UNION silently removes legitimate duplicates, such as two identical sales of the same amount, which corrupts totals without any error. Choosing UNION out of habit is a common data bug.
codeExamples:
-- Two real sales of 50 each: UNION collapses them, UNION ALL keeps them
SELECT SUM(amt) AS total_union
FROM (SELECT 50 AS amt UNION SELECT 50 UNION SELECT 70) AS a;

SELECT SUM(amt) AS total_union_all
FROM (SELECT 50 AS amt UNION ALL SELECT 50 UNION ALL SELECT 70) AS b;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+      +-----------------+
-- | total_union |      | total_union_all |
-- +-------------+      +-----------------+
-- |         120 |      |             170 |
-- +-------------+      +-----------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: column names come from the first SELECT only, and a trailing ORDER BY can refer only to those result names or positions, not to columns of later SELECTs. To sort or limit one branch, wrap that branch in parentheses.
codeExamples:
-- ORDER BY sees the result column name (who), not the original column name
SELECT name AS who FROM web_cust
UNION
SELECT name        FROM shop_cust
ORDER BY name;                                -- wrong name

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1054 (42S22): Unknown column 'name' in 'order clause'

-- Fix: ORDER BY who   (or ORDER BY 1)
-- Per-branch limit needs parentheses:
(SELECT name FROM web_cust  ORDER BY name LIMIT 1)
UNION ALL
(SELECT name FROM shop_cust ORDER BY name LIMIT 1);

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to UNION ALL and reach for UNION only when duplicates across sources are truly possible and unwanted; if you can make the branches disjoint with a literal source column or a WHERE range, do so. For very large unions prefer partitioning or a single table over a view that unions many tables, because the optimizer plans each branch separately and cannot prune them like partitions.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Column names come from the first query; ORDER BY applies to the whole union result at the end.
  • Use UNION ALL by default when duplicates are impossible or acceptable.
  • Wrap each part in parentheses to give individual ORDER BY/LIMIT.

Senior Notes

  • UNION needs a temporary table with a unique index to deduplicate, costing memory and time.
  • Partition-style reporting: UNION ALL monthly tables, or better a single partitioned table.
  • A UNION of two selective index queries is a classic rewrite for OR conditions.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: UNION when duplicates cannot occur (wasted work), mismatched column counts or types, ORDER BY on a branch without parentheses, and expecting UNION to keep the order of branches. Default to UNION ALL.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name FROM emp UNION SELECT id FROM customers;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1222 (21000): The used SELECT statements have a different number of columns

SELECT id FROM emp UNION SELECT name FROM customers;       -- types converted to a common (string) type

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A selective OR across two indexed columns can be faster as two index lookups with UNION ALL, adding a guard in the second branch to avoid duplicates.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7
UNION ALL
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE sales_rep_id = 9 AND (customer_id <> 7 OR customer_id IS NULL);

-- OUTPUT: (explain, example)
-- two ref lookups (idx_customer, idx_rep) instead of a full scan

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a combined activity feed from several tables, each branch limited and indexed, merged and sorted by time.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM (
  (SELECT created_at, 'order' AS kind, id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20)
  UNION ALL (SELECT created_at, 'ticket', id FROM tickets WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20)
  UNION ALL (SELECT created_at, 'review', id FROM reviews WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20)) f
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- created_at          | kind   | id
-- 2026-05-01 09:58:00 | order  | 77

beginner.content:
Introduction

INTERSECT returns only the rows present in both queries; EXCEPT returns rows of the first query that are not in the second. Both were added in MySQL 8.0.31, remove duplicates by default, and accept ALL to keep multiplicities.
codeExamples:
-- (tables web_cust and shop_cust from the UNION topic)
-- Customers who bought both online and in the shop
SELECT name, city FROM web_cust
INTERSECT
SELECT name, city FROM shop_cust;

-- Customers who bought online but never in the shop
SELECT name, city FROM web_cust
EXCEPT
SELECT name, city FROM shop_cust
ORDER BY name;

-- OUTPUT (INTERSECT):          OUTPUT (EXCEPT):
-- +------+-------+             +------+------+
-- | name | city  |             | name | city |
-- +------+-------+             +------+------+
-- | Raoji | Delhi |             | Abaji | Pune |
-- +------+-------+             | Mina | Pune |
--                              +------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

"Who is in A and B?" and "who is in A but not B?" are everyday questions: loyal customers, churned users, records missing from a sync. Before 8.0.31 you had to emulate them with joins or subqueries, which is longer and easy to get wrong with NULLs.
codeExamples:
-- Emulation for older servers (5.7 / early 8.0)
-- INTERSECT: EXISTS with a NULL-safe comparison (<=>)
SELECT DISTINCT w.name, w.city
FROM web_cust w
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM shop_cust s
              WHERE s.name <=> w.name AND s.city <=> w.city);

-- EXCEPT: NOT EXISTS (never NOT IN when NULLs may occur)
SELECT DISTINCT w.name, w.city
FROM web_cust w
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM shop_cust s
                  WHERE s.name <=> w.name AND s.city <=> w.city)
ORDER BY w.name;

-- OUTPUT (first query):        OUTPUT (second query):
-- | Raoji | Delhi |             | Abaji | Pune |
--                              | Mina | Pune |

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Reconciliation jobs use EXCEPT in both directions to find rows missing or extra between a source and a copy; marketing uses INTERSECT to find users who match two segments.
codeExamples:
-- Data-sync check: what is in the web list but missing from the shop list, and vice versa
SELECT 'only_web'  AS side, name FROM (SELECT name FROM web_cust  EXCEPT SELECT name FROM shop_cust) AS a
UNION ALL
SELECT 'only_shop' AS side, name FROM (SELECT name FROM shop_cust EXCEPT SELECT name FROM web_cust)  AS b
ORDER BY side, name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+-------+
-- | side      | name  |
-- +-----------+-------+
-- | only_shop | Karan |
-- | only_web  | Abaji |
-- | only_web  | Mina  |
-- +-----------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   A = web_cust       B = shop_cust
        ┌───────────┬───────────┐
        │  Abaji    │   Karan   │
        │  Mina     │           │
        │       ┌───┴───┐       │
        │       │ Raoji │       │
        └───────┴───────┴───────┘
   A INTERSECT B = {Raoji}
   A EXCEPT    B = {Abaji, Mina}
   B EXCEPT    A = {Karan}
   A UNION     B = {Abaji, Mina, Raoji, Karan}

Fresher Notes

  • INTERSECT returns rows present in both queries; EXCEPT returns rows in the first but not in the second.
  • MySQL supports them from 8.0.31.
  • Both remove duplicates unless you add ALL.

Worked Example 1

Emulate for older MySQL.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.id FROM emp e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp x WHERE x.id = e.id AND x.salary > 50000);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Reconcile two tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, amount FROM src_payments
EXCEPT
SELECT id, amount FROM dst_payments;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | amount
--  9 | 120.00     (present in source, missing or different in target)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Departments in both lists.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000
INTERSECT
SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept
-- 10

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Rows only in the first set.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM emp
EXCEPT
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

INTERSECT returns distinct rows present in both inputs; EXCEPT returns distinct rows from the first input that are absent from the second. They compare entire rows and treat NULLs as equal. MySQL supports them from 8.0.31; the server implements them with temporary tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000
INTERSECT
SELECT dept FROM emp WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

SELECT id FROM emp
EXCEPT
SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept
-- 10
-- id
-- 2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Add ALL to keep duplicates (multiset semantics). Precedence: INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT; use parentheses to be explicit.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative and readable, NULLs are treated as equal (unlike the = operator), and the ALL variants give true multiset arithmetic.
codeExamples:
-- NULL = NULL is unknown in WHERE, but set operators treat NULLs as the same value
SELECT NULL AS v INTERSECT SELECT NULL;

-- ALL keeps counts: left has two 1s, right removes one of them
(SELECT 1 AS v UNION ALL SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 2)
EXCEPT ALL
(SELECT 1 AS v)
ORDER BY v;

-- OUTPUT (first):    OUTPUT (second):
-- +------+           +---+
-- | v    |           | v |
-- +------+           +---+
-- | NULL |           | 1 |
-- +------+           | 2 |
--                    +---+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: precedence surprises people: INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT, so mixed chains do not read left to right unless you add parentheses.

Limitations

Limitations: not available before MySQL 8.0.31 (syntax error on 5.7 and older 8.0); EXCEPT is not symmetric; every branch must have the same column count; and set operators compare whole rows, so you cannot intersect on just one column while selecting more.
codeExamples:
-- Order matters for EXCEPT
SELECT name FROM shop_cust EXCEPT SELECT name FROM web_cust;

-- On a server older than 8.0.31:
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): You have an error in your SQL syntax; ... near 'EXCEPT SELECT ...'

-- OUTPUT (8.0.31+):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Karan |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer INTERSECT/EXCEPT for clarity in reporting and reconciliation code, but check the minimum server version across every environment, including replicas and managed services. In hot paths, an indexed EXISTS or NOT EXISTS is usually planned as a semi or anti join and can beat the temporary-table approach of set operators; benchmark both.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Before 8.0.31 emulate INTERSECT with INNER JOIN or IN, and EXCEPT with NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL.
  • Column count and types must match, as in UNION.
  • INTERSECT has higher precedence than UNION and EXCEPT.

Senior Notes

  • NULLs are treated as equal in set operations (unlike comparisons), which is useful for diffing datasets.
  • EXCEPT is handy for reconciliation: rows in source but missing in target.
  • Verify support on managed services and replicas of mixed versions.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using them on MySQL older than 8.0.31, comparing too many columns (extra columns make rows distinct), and expecting column-by-name matching. Match columns by position and select only the keys you compare.
codeExamples:
-- emulate for older versions
SELECT DISTINCT e.id FROM emp e WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp x WHERE x.id = e.id AND x.salary > 50000);          -- INTERSECT
SELECT e.id FROM emp e WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp x WHERE x.id = e.id AND x.salary > 50000);             -- EXCEPT

-- OUTPUT:
-- same rows as the native operators

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For reconciliation of large tables compare keys and a hash of the remaining columns instead of all columns, keeping the set operation narrow and fast.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', amount, status, updated_at)) AS h FROM src_payments
EXCEPT
SELECT id, MD5(CONCAT_WS('|', amount, status, updated_at)) FROM dst_payments;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | h
--  9 | 2a9f...        (missing or different in the destination)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world data audit: customers who exist in the CRM but not in billing, and customers present in both systems.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Every SELECT in a set operation must return the same number of columns, and columns are paired by position, never by name. The result takes its names from the first SELECT, and its column types are merged to a common type.
codeExamples:
SELECT 1 AS a, 'x' AS b
UNION ALL
SELECT 2,        'y';                         -- names a, b come from the first SELECT

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+---+
-- | a | b |
-- +---+---+
-- | 1 | x |
-- | 2 | y |
-- +---+---+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Because matching is positional, swapping two columns still runs without error and silently mixes unrelated data. Understanding the rules protects you from this class of bug.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE person (name VARCHAR(20), city VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO person VALUES ('Abaji','Pune');

SELECT name, city FROM person
UNION ALL
SELECT city, name FROM person;                -- columns swapped by mistake

-- OUTPUT (no error, wrong data):
-- +-------+-------+
-- | name  | city  |
-- +-------+-------+
-- | Abaji | Pune  |
-- | Pune  | Abaji |
-- +------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

When sources have different shapes (users, leads), pad the missing columns with NULL of the right type and add a source label. This builds one unified feed.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, email, NULL  AS phone, 'user' AS kind FROM (SELECT 1 AS id, 'a@x.com' AS email) AS u
UNION ALL
SELECT id, NULL,  phone,     'lead'         FROM (SELECT 9 AS id, '98450' AS phone) AS l;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+-------+------+
-- | id | email   | phone | kind |
-- +----+---------+-------+------+
-- |  1 | a@x.com | NULL  | user |
-- |  9 | NULL    | 98450 | lead |
-- +----+---------+-------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SELECT  c1   c2   c3          position 1 ── position 1
   ───────────────────          position 2 ── position 2
   UNION ALL                    position 3 ── position 3
   SELECT  d1   d2   d3         names   : from the FIRST select
                                 types   : merged to a common type
                                 dedupe  : by collation, NULL = NULL

Fresher Notes

  • Set operations need the same number of columns and compatible types in the same order.
  • UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT remove duplicates; UNION ALL does not.
  • Column names come from the first query.

Worked Example 1

Dedupe with ROW_NUMBER.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name FROM (
  SELECT id, name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM (SELECT * FROM staff_a UNION ALL SELECT * FROM staff_b) u) t WHERE rn = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  1 | Abaji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Align collations.
codeExamples:
SELECT name COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci FROM a UNION SELECT name COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci FROM b;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Pad columns and label sources.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name, 'emp' AS src, NULL AS phone FROM emp
UNION ALL
SELECT id, name, 'cust', phone FROM customers;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | name  | src  | phone
--  1 | Abaji | emp  | NULL
--  1 | Abaji | cust | 9999

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Mismatch error.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Set operations match columns by position, require the same count and convert types to a common type (numbers with strings become strings). The result column names come from the first branch. UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT remove duplicates across all columns; the ALL variants keep them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Align branches explicitly: pad missing columns with NULL or a literal of the right type, cast to a common type, align collations, and add a source label so you can tell rows apart.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name, CAST(NULL AS CHAR(20)) AS phone, 'emp' AS src FROM emp
UNION ALL
SELECT id, name, phone, 'cust' FROM customers;
SELECT code COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci FROM t1 UNION SELECT code COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci FROM t2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | phone | src
--  1 | Abaji |  NULL | emp
--  1 | Abaji |  9999 | cust

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: MySQL converts mixed types to one common type, so a number and a string can still be combined, and the rules (first SELECT names, positional match) are simple and predictable.
codeExamples:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE mixed AS
SELECT 1 AS v UNION ALL SELECT 'abc';          -- INT meets VARCHAR
SHOW COLUMNS FROM mixed;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +-------+------------+------+
-- | Field | Type       | Null |
-- +-------+------------+------+
-- | v     | varchar(3) | NO   |
-- +-------+------------+------+
-- The INT 1 became the string '1'.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: duplicate detection uses the column collation, so with a case-insensitive collation (the default) 'Abaji' and 'abaji' count as the same row, and NULLs are treated as equal. Which spelling you get back is not guaranteed.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'Abaji' AS name
UNION
SELECT 'abaji';                                -- default collation is case-insensitive

SELECT 'Abaji' AS name
UNION
SELECT 'abaji' COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_as_cs;     -- case-sensitive collation on one side

-- OUTPUT (first):    OUTPUT (second):
-- | name |           | name |
-- | Abaji |           | Abaji |
--                     | abaji |

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a different column count is an error, incompatible collations can raise "illegal mix" errors, and implicit conversion can change data (long string to short type, number to string sort order).
codeExamples:
SELECT 1, 2
UNION
SELECT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1222 (21000): The used SELECT statements have a different number of columns

-- Sorting hazard after type merging: the column becomes text, so 10 sorts before 9
SELECT 9 AS v UNION ALL SELECT '10' ORDER BY v;

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat each branch of a union as an interface: list columns explicitly (never SELECT *), cast to the intended types, and add a source column. Put these unions behind a view with a test that checks column count and types so a later schema change in one source table fails loudly instead of silently shifting data.

Mid-Level Notes

  • MySQL converts types to a common type (INT with VARCHAR becomes string), which may surprise sorting and comparisons; cast explicitly.
  • Use NULL or literals to pad missing columns: SELECT id, name, NULL AS phone.
  • Collation conflicts can raise "illegal mix of collations"; use COLLATE to align.

Senior Notes

  • Add a source label column ("A" AS src) to know where each row came from.
  • Duplicate removal compares all columns, so extra columns make rows distinct.
  • For deduplicating by key use window functions (ROW_NUMBER) after UNION ALL.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on implicit casts that change sort order, forgetting that different extra columns make duplicate rows distinct, and comparing branches whose column order differs. Normalise before the union.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, 'x' AS tag FROM a UNION SELECT name, 'y' FROM b;      -- same names appear twice: tag differs

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | tag
-- Abaji | x
-- Abaji | y

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

To deduplicate by a business key (not the whole row) after UNION ALL, rank rows and keep one per key, with an index-friendly ordering rule.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, name FROM (
  SELECT id, name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM (SELECT id, name, updated_at FROM staff_a UNION ALL SELECT id, name, updated_at FROM staff_b) u) t WHERE rn = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  1 | Abaji          (newest version of each id)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: merging data from two systems during a migration, labelling the origin and resolving duplicates by priority so the target table receives one clean row per key.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO customers_merged (email, name, source)
SELECT email, name, source FROM (
  SELECT email, name, 'crm' AS source, 1 AS prio FROM crm_customers
  UNION ALL SELECT email, name, 'billing', 2 FROM billing_customers) u
WHERE (email, prio) IN (SELECT email, MIN(prio) FROM (SELECT email, 1 AS prio FROM crm_customers UNION ALL SELECT email, 2 FROM billing_customers) z GROUP BY email);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 12044 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

A one-to-one relationship means each row in table A matches at most one row in table B, and the reverse. In MySQL you build it by making the child's foreign key also UNIQUE (or by making the foreign key the child's primary key).

Why Do We Need This?

Why split one entity into two tables? To keep rarely used or large columns out of the hot table, to separate sensitive data for tighter permissions, or to model an optional extension that only some rows have.
codeExamples:
-- Hot table stays narrow and cache friendly; the heavy BLOB lives elsewhere
CREATE TABLE employee_photos (
  employee_id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  photo       MEDIUMBLOB NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (employee_id) REFERENCES employees(id)
);
SELECT e.name FROM employees e WHERE e.id = 7;    -- never reads the photo pages

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Raoji        (photo bytes were not touched)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical uses: user and profile, order and invoice, account and credentials, and subtype tables (a vehicles table plus trucks holding only truck columns). Optional sides are read with a LEFT JOIN.
codeExamples:
SELECT u.id, u.email, p.bio
FROM   users u
LEFT   JOIN user_profiles p ON p.user_id = u.id    -- profile may not exist yet
ORDER  BY u.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | email            | bio
--  1 | abaji@example.com | Backend developer
--  2 | raoji@example.com | NULL

beginner.content:
Diagram

   users                     user_profiles
  ┌────────────┐  1 ─── 0..1 ┌────────────────┐
  │ id  (PK)   │◄────────────│ user_id (PK,FK)│   FK is also the PK  => one row max
  │ email      │             │ bio            │
  └────────────┘             └────────────────┘
   Alternative: user_id BIGINT UNIQUE NOT NULL + its own surrogate id

Fresher Notes

  • One-to-one means a row in A matches at most one row in B. Make the child foreign key UNIQUE, or use it as the primary key.
  • Use it for optional extra data (profile), large rarely used columns or sensitive data.
  • Read both sides with a JOIN (LEFT JOIN when the child is optional).

Worked Example 1

Optional child with LEFT JOIN.
codeExamples:
SELECT a.owner, COALESCE(s.theme,'default') AS theme FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN account_settings s ON s.account_id = a.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- owner | theme
-- Abaji | dark

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Atomic creation.

Practice Exercise 1

Create one-to-one with shared PK.

Practice Exercise 2

Second settings row is rejected.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In a one-to-one design the child row is located by the parent key. With a shared primary key (child PK = parent id) the child clustered index is ordered the same way as the parent, so a join is a pair of primary-key lookups. A UNIQUE foreign key on a separate surrogate key gives the same guarantee through a unique secondary index.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choices: shared PK vs surrogate + UNIQUE FK; optional vs mandatory child; ON DELETE CASCADE for owned data. Create both rows in one transaction, and read optional children with LEFT JOIN.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the database itself guarantees the "only one" rule, wide or sensitive columns are isolated, and each table can have its own indexes, privileges and lifecycle.
codeExamples:
-- Least privilege: reporting can read users but never the credentials table
GRANT SELECT ON shop.users TO 'report_user'@'%';
-- credentials (password_hash) sit in a one-to-one table with no grant for report_user
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'report_user'@'%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Grants for report_user@%
-- GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO report_user@%
-- GRANT SELECT ON shop.users TO report_user@%

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every read of both halves needs a JOIN, inserts must create two rows (ideally in one transaction), and over-splitting a table that is always read whole only adds cost.

Limitations

Limitations: MySQL cannot enforce that the child row must exist; a foreign key only stops a child without a parent. "Exactly one" on both sides needs application logic, a trigger, or merging the tables.
codeExamples:
-- The UNIQUE / PK on the child blocks a second profile for the same user
INSERT INTO user_profiles (user_id, bio) VALUES (1, 'Second profile');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1' for key 'user_profiles.PRIMARY'

-- But a user with NO profile is perfectly legal; the schema cannot forbid it.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use a shared primary key (child PK = parent id) for true extensions; use a separate surrogate key plus UNIQUE FK when the child may be re-pointed or has its own references. If both sides are always created and read together, merge them into one table. Split only for a measurable reason: size, security, or optionality.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Shared primary key: child PK = parent id. It is compact and guarantees one row per parent.
  • Separate surrogate key plus UNIQUE FK is flexible if the relation may later become one-to-many.
  • Create both rows in one transaction.

Senior Notes

  • Split for a measurable reason: hot/cold columns, security boundary or subtype data; otherwise merge into one table.
  • MySQL cannot force that the child must exist; enforce with transactions or application rules.
  • ORMs: JPA @OneToOne @MapsId maps the shared primary key.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting the UNIQUE or PK on the child (becomes one-to-many), splitting tables that are always read together, and assuming the database can force the child to exist. Add the key and merge tables that gain nothing from the split.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Split for performance only when it pays off: move large or rarely used columns to the child so the hot table has more rows per page. Compare row sizes before and after.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, avg_row_length, ROUND(16384 / avg_row_length) AS rows_per_page FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('employees_wide','employees_hot');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name     | avg_row_length | rows_per_page
-- employees_wide |           2400 |             7
-- employees_hot  |            140 |           117

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: credentials, PII and payment data live in separate one-to-one tables with stricter grants, encryption and auditing than the main profile table.

beginner.content:
Introduction

In a one-to-many design the foreign key lives on the many side: each employee row stores one dept_id. A many-to-many relationship cannot be stored in either table, so it gets a third table holding one row per pair.

Why Do We Need This?

Beginners often store a many-to-many list in one column, such as "10,20". It looks easy but breaks indexing, integrity and querying. The design rule exists to avoid exactly this.
codeExamples:
-- Anti-pattern: comma list in a column
CREATE TABLE bad_student (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), course_ids VARCHAR(50));
INSERT INTO bad_student VALUES (1,'Abaji','10,20'),(2,'Raoji','20');
SELECT name FROM bad_student WHERE FIND_IN_SET(10, course_ids) > 0;   -- full scan, no FK, no index

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- +-------+
-- Nothing stops course_ids = '10,999' (course 999 may not exist).

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Shops model orders (one customer, many orders), order items (one order, many items) and products (many orders contain many products) with the same two patterns.

Diagram

   One-to-many                       Many-to-many
   dept (1) ───────< emp (N)         student (N) >──── enrol ────< course (M)
   ┌────┐            ┌────┬─────┐       ┌────┐   ┌──────────┬─────────┐   ┌────┐
   │ id │◄───────────│dept│ ... │       │ id │◄──│student_id│course_id│──►│ id │
   └────┘   FK on    └────┴─────┘       └────┘   └──────────┴─────────┘   └────┘
            many side                        two 1:N links + composite PK

Fresher Notes

  • One-to-many: the child table has a foreign key to the parent. Many-to-many: add a junction table with two foreign keys.
  • Index every foreign key column.
  • Name keys clearly (customer_id, order_id).

Worked Example 1

Cascade delete of owned children.

Worked Example 2

Reverse lookup uses the second index.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT order_id FROM order_items WHERE product_id = 7;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key      | Extra
-- ref  | idx_prod | Using index

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Orders and items design.

Practice Exercise 2

Order total from snapshot prices.
codeExamples:
SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS total FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- order_id | total
--        1 | 900.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

One-to-many stores the parent key in the child. Many-to-many needs a junction table whose composite primary key makes (a, b) unique and clusters rows by a; a secondary index (b, a) serves the opposite direction. Together they cover every join path with index lookups.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design checklist: name keys consistently, choose ON DELETE by ownership, store relationship attributes in the link table, snapshot values that must not change (price at order time), and index both directions.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id BIGINT NOT NULL, line_no INT NOT NULL, product_id BIGINT NOT NULL, qty INT NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,            -- snapshot of the price when ordered
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no), KEY idx_product (product_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id));

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: each fact is stored once, the engine enforces the links, and InnoDB automatically indexes the foreign key column so joins from parent to children are fast.
codeExamples:
SHOW INDEX FROM emp;                          -- FK column dept_id got an index for free

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +-------+------------+----------+-------------+
-- | Table | Non_unique | Key_name | Column_name |
-- +-------+------------+----------+-------------+
-- | emp   |          0 | PRIMARY  | id          |
-- | emp   |          1 | dept_id  | dept_id     |
-- +-------+------------+----------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: reads need joins, and joining a parent to its children repeats the parent columns on every row. Aggregating parent values after such a join (fan-out) double counts.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE dept ADD COLUMN budget INT DEFAULT 1000;   -- IT budget 1000, HR 1000
SELECT SUM(d.budget) AS wrong_total               -- budget repeated once per employee
FROM dept d JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.id;
SELECT SUM(budget) AS right_total FROM dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+      +-------------+
-- | wrong_total |      | right_total |
-- +-------------+      +-------------+
-- |        3000 |      |        2000 |
-- +-------------+      +-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the FK and referenced column must have identical types (and signedness, charset), and both tables must be InnoDB. A mismatch is rejected at DDL time.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp2 (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    dept_id BIGINT,                             -- parent id is INT
    CONSTRAINT fk_e2 FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(id)
);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3780 (HY000): Referencing column 'dept_id' and referenced column 'id' in
-- foreign key constraint 'fk_e2' are incompatible.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Model first in terms of cardinality questions: can one X have many Y, and can one Y have many X? Always put the FK on the child, make it NOT NULL when the relationship is mandatory, and promote any M:N to a table the moment it needs its own attributes (date, status, quantity). Resist storing lists in a column; JSON is acceptable for opaque, never-joined data only.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Choose ON DELETE rules by ownership: CASCADE for owned children (order lines), RESTRICT for independent entities.
  • Junction tables use a composite primary key (a_id, b_id), plus a reverse index (b_id, a_id).
  • Put relationship attributes (quantity, role, date) in the junction table.

Senior Notes

  • When a junction table has its own lifecycle (order_items with price at purchase), give it a surrogate key and treat it as an entity.
  • Snapshot values that must not change later (price at purchase, address at shipping) instead of joining to current data.
  • Plan growth: the junction table is usually the largest table; keep its columns narrow.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: comma-separated id lists, storing relationship data on the wrong entity, missing reverse index, and referencing the current product price instead of a snapshot (history changes when prices change).
codeExamples:
-- BAD: list in a column
SELECT * FROM products WHERE FIND_IN_SET('hot', tag_list);
-- GOOD: junction table with an index
SELECT p.id, p.name FROM tags t JOIN product_tags pt ON pt.tag_id = t.id JOIN products p ON p.id = pt.product_id WHERE t.label = 'hot';

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  7 | Pen

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The junction table is usually the largest table. Keep its keys small, avoid wide extra columns, and use covering indexes so lookups never touch the table rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, table_rows, ROUND((data_length + index_length) / 1073741824, 2) AS gb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('product_tags','order_items');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name  | table_rows | gb
-- order_items |   54000000 | 6.80
-- product_tags|   12000000 | 0.90

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: tags and search. "Products having all of these tags" uses GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT) over the junction index.
codeExamples:
SELECT pt.product_id FROM product_tags pt JOIN tags t ON t.id = pt.tag_id WHERE t.label IN ('organic','vegan','gluten-free')
GROUP BY pt.product_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT t.id) = 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- product_id
-- 118
-- 342

beginner.content:
Introduction

A junction table (bridge, link or associative table) resolves a many-to-many relationship. It holds one row per pair, with a foreign key to each side, usually a composite primary key made of both, and optionally extra columns that describe the pair itself.

Why Do We Need This?

Real relationships have properties: when did the student enrol, what grade did they get, what is the line quantity? Those facts belong to the pair, so they need a place in the bridge table, not in either parent.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE enrolment
    ADD COLUMN enrolled_on DATE DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE),   -- facts about the pair
    ADD COLUMN grade       CHAR(1) NULL;
UPDATE enrolment SET grade = 'A' WHERE student_id = 1 AND course_id = 100;
SELECT student_id, course_id, grade FROM enrolment ORDER BY student_id, course_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----------+-------+
-- | student_id | course_id | grade |
-- +------------+-----------+-------+
-- |          1 |       100 | A     |
-- |          1 |       101 | NULL  |
-- |          2 |       100 | NULL  |
-- +------------+-----------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Tags on posts, roles for users, products in carts, actors in films and permissions on roles are all junction tables. A report typically collapses the bridge rows back into a list.
codeExamples:
SELECT s.name, GROUP_CONCAT(c.title ORDER BY c.title) AS courses
FROM student s
JOIN enrolment e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN course c    ON c.id = e.course_id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name
ORDER BY s.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+----------+
-- | name  | courses  |
-- +-------+----------+
-- | Abaji | Java,SQL |
-- | Raoji | SQL      |
-- +------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   student                enrolment                   course
   ┌────┬───────┐    ┌────────────┬───────────┬───────┐     ┌─────┬───────┐
   │  1 │ Abaji │◄───│     1      │    100    │ grade │────►│ 100 │ SQL   │
   │  2 │ Raoji │◄┐  │     1      │    101    │ ...   │──┐  │ 101 │ Java  │
   └────┘         │  │     2      │    100    │       │  │  └─────┴───────┘
                  └──│            PK(student_id, course_id)  │
                     └────────────┴───────────┴───────┘     (two FKs, one per side)

Fresher Notes

  • A junction (bridge, link) table resolves a many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships.
  • It contains the primary keys of both tables as foreign keys.
  • Example: student_courses(student_id, course_id).

Worked Example 1

Temporal link table.

Worked Example 2

Duplicate link rejected.

Practice Exercise 1

Users and roles.

Practice Exercise 2

Users having both roles.
codeExamples:
SELECT user_id FROM user_roles WHERE role_id IN (1,2) GROUP BY user_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT role_id) = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A junction table has one row per link. Its composite primary key clusters rows by the first column, so all links of one parent are physically adjacent and read together; the second index serves the reverse lookup. InnoDB also keeps the primary key columns in the secondary index automatically.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE user_roles (user_id BIGINT NOT NULL, role_id INT NOT NULL, granted_on DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE), granted_by BIGINT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role_id), KEY idx_role_user (role_id, user_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, FOREIGN KEY (role_id) REFERENCES roles(id));
SHOW INDEX FROM user_roles;

-- OUTPUT: (trimmed)
-- Key_name      | Seq_in_index | Column_name
-- PRIMARY       | 1            | user_id
-- PRIMARY       | 2            | role_id
-- idx_role_user | 1            | role_id

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: pure link table, link with attributes, link with its own surrogate id (when other tables reference the link), and temporal links with valid-from/valid-to to keep history.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the composite PK makes duplicate pairs impossible, and FKs guarantee both sides exist. Either side can be queried and either can change independently.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO enrolment (student_id, course_id) VALUES (1,100);   -- same pair twice

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1-100' for key 'enrolment.PRIMARY'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more tables, more joins, and more indexes. The PK (student_id, course_id) only serves lookups that start with student_id, so InnoDB adds a second index for course_id, which every insert must also maintain.

Limitations

Limitations: a bridge row can exist only when both parents exist, so you cannot record a pair first and the entity later; and MySQL has no native many-to-many type, so every query pays the join.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO enrolment (student_id, course_id) VALUES (1, 999);   -- course 999 does not exist

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails
-- (school.enrolment, CONSTRAINT fk_enr_course FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES course (id))

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Decide the bridge PK deliberately: a composite PK is compact and prevents duplicates, but if other tables must reference a single enrolment row, add a surrogate id and keep a UNIQUE (student_id, course_id). Index both directions, and order the composite so the more frequent lookup side comes first. If the bridge grows to billions of rows, partitioning or sharding by one side becomes a design topic.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Composite PK prevents duplicate links; add extra columns for link data (enrolled_on, role, status).
  • Index both directions.
  • Query through it with two joins.

Senior Notes

  • If the link is referenced by other tables or has many attributes, promote it to an entity with its own id.
  • Large junction tables dominate size; use compact key types and consider partitioning by time.
  • Soft-deleting links needs a unique rule such as unique on (a_id, b_id, active_flag).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: duplicate links because there is no composite key, missing reverse index, and deleting parents without cleaning links (use ON DELETE CASCADE or application logic). Detect duplicates and orphans with simple queries.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large junction tables benefit from covering index scans for counts and existence checks. Measure with EXPLAIN that both directions show "Using index".

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: permission checks. "Does user 7 have permission P?" is an indexed lookup through two junction tables and must stay fast, so verify the plan.
codeExamples:
SELECT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM user_roles ur JOIN role_permissions rp ON rp.role_id = ur.role_id JOIN permissions p ON p.id = rp.permission_id WHERE ur.user_id = 7 AND p.code = 'orders.refund') AS allowed;

-- OUTPUT:
-- allowed
-- 1

beginner.content:
Introduction

Referential integrity means every foreign key value either is NULL or points to an existing row in the parent table. InnoDB enforces it for you on every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE that touches a foreign key.

Why Do We Need This?

Without enforcement, bugs, manual fixes and race conditions create orphan rows (orders for deleted customers) that make reports wrong and joins silently drop data.
codeExamples:
-- Same tables but WITHOUT an FK: the orphan is accepted
CREATE TABLE orders_nofk (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT);
INSERT INTO orders_nofk VALUES (100,1),(101,42);

-- Orphan hunt: children with no parent
SELECT o.id, o.customer_id
FROM orders_nofk o LEFT JOIN customer c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-------------+
-- | id  | customer_id |
-- +-----+-------------+
-- | 101 |          42 |
-- +-----+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Operations teams inspect the declared rules from the catalog, and DBAs audit them before migrations. The delete and update rule shows what happens to children.
codeExamples:
SELECT constraint_name, table_name, referenced_table_name, update_rule, delete_rule
FROM information_schema.referential_constraints
WHERE constraint_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------+------------+-----------------------+-------------+-------------+
-- | CONSTRAINT_NAME | TABLE_NAME | REFERENCED_TABLE_NAME | UPDATE_RULE | DELETE_RULE |
-- +--------------+------------+-----------------------+-------------+-------------+
-- | fk_ord_cust  | orders     | customer              | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION   |
-- +--------------+------------+-----------------------+-------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   parent: customer                 child: orders
   ┌────┬───────┐                   ┌─────┬─────────────┐
   │  1 │ Abaji │◄──────────────────│ 100 │      1      │  valid
   └────┴───────┘                   │ 102 │    NULL     │  valid (optional)
                       X───────────│ 101 │     42      │  REJECTED 1452
   DELETE parent 1 while 100 exists ──► REJECTED 1451 (RESTRICT/NO ACTION)

Fresher Notes

  • Referential integrity means every foreign key value must match an existing primary key in the parent (or be NULL).
  • It prevents orphan rows: orders without customers.
  • InnoDB enforces it through foreign key constraints.

Worked Example 1

Disable and re-enable checks.

Worked Example 2

Inspect the constraint rules.
codeExamples:
SELECT constraint_name, update_rule, delete_rule FROM information_schema.referential_constraints WHERE constraint_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- constraint_name | update_rule | delete_rule
-- c_ibfk_1        | NO ACTION   | NO ACTION

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Block orphan insert and parent delete.

Practice Exercise 2

Find orphans in an unconstrained table.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 42

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Referential integrity is enforced by InnoDB at statement time: inserting or updating a child checks that the parent key exists (a shared lock on the parent record), and deleting or updating a parent applies the declared action by looking up matching child rows through the child's index.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Control checks with foreign_key_checks for bulk loads and restores, and inspect rules through the catalog. Re-enable and verify afterwards, because disabled checks let bad rows in.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the guarantee lives in one place for every client, and a nullable FK models an optional relationship: NULL means "no parent", and is always allowed.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (102, NULL);          -- guest order, no customer: allowed
SELECT id, customer_id FROM orders ORDER BY id;

-- And the parent is protected too:
DELETE FROM customer WHERE id = 1;                -- order 100 still points at it

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-------------+
-- | id  | customer_id |
-- +-----+-------------+
-- | 100 |           1 |
-- | 102 |        NULL |
-- +-----+-------------+
-- ERROR 1451 (23000): Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key constraint fails

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every write checks the other table, and locks the parent row it references. Bulk loads are therefore often done with checks turned off, which can quietly let orphans in.
codeExamples:
SET foreign_key_checks = 0;                      -- session-level switch, used by dump/restore
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (103, 777);             -- no error, 777 does not exist
SET foreign_key_checks = 1;                       -- constraint is NOT re-verified
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphans FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN customer c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL AND c.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+
-- | orphans |
-- +---------+
-- |       1 |
-- +---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB checks each row immediately (no DEFERRABLE constraints like PostgreSQL), so a single statement that inserts a child before its parent fails even if the parent is in the same statement. FKs are also not supported on partitioned tables.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE person (
    id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), boss_id INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (boss_id) REFERENCES person(id)
);
INSERT INTO person VALUES (2,'Kid',1),(1,'Boss',NULL);   -- child row is checked first

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails
-- Fix: insert (1,'Boss',NULL) first, or insert in two statements.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep FKs in transactional schemas; they are cheap compared with the cost of one corrupted ledger. If you must drop them (huge sharded systems, online migration tools), replace them with automated orphan-detection jobs and make that a monitored invariant. After any foreign_key_checks=0 load, run the orphan query before re-opening the system.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Actions on parent change: RESTRICT/NO ACTION (block), CASCADE (propagate), SET NULL.
  • FK checks can be disabled for loads with SET foreign_key_checks = 0; re-enable and validate afterwards.
  • The child column and parent key must have matching types and be indexed.

Senior Notes

  • Without FKs, integrity depends on every code path; add reconciliation jobs that find orphans.
  • Orphan detection query: LEFT JOIN parent WHERE parent.id IS NULL.
  • In sharded or cross-service data, referential integrity becomes eventual: use ids, outbox events and periodic audits.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: disabling checks and forgetting to re-validate, orphans created by deletes outside the database's knowledge (no FK), and foreign keys to non-unique columns. Audit orphans with an anti-join on a schedule.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 42       (a row that bypassed integrity while checks were off)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Foreign key checks take locks and run index lookups on every write. On very hot parents consider moving to application-level integrity with reconciliation, only after measuring contention.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world across services: you cannot have a foreign key between databases, so store the other service's id, validate through its API or events, and run reconciliation jobs that flag dangling references.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.id, p.customer_ref FROM payments p LEFT JOIN customer_snapshot s ON s.id = p.customer_ref WHERE s.id IS NULL AND p.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 1 DAY;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | customer_ref
-- 90 | c-4412           (alert: payment references a customer unknown to this service)

beginner.content:
Introduction

A foreign key can declare what happens to child rows when the parent is deleted or its key changes: ON DELETE / ON UPDATE with CASCADE (apply the same change to children), SET NULL, RESTRICT or NO ACTION (block the change, the default).

Why Do We Need This?

Different relationships need different behaviour. Order lines should vanish with their order (CASCADE); a ticket should survive its assignee leaving (SET NULL); an invoice must block deleting its customer (RESTRICT).

Real-Time Use

ON UPDATE CASCADE is used when a referenced key legitimately changes, for example a code like a department code or a username that is the join key. The change ripples to every child in the same statement.

Diagram

   DELETE author 1
        │
        ▼
   author ──► book (FK ON DELETE ...)
                 ├─ CASCADE   : child rows deleted too
                 ├─ SET NULL  : child FK becomes NULL
                 └─ RESTRICT / NO ACTION : delete refused (default)

   ON UPDATE CASCADE : change parent key  ──► children follow

Fresher Notes

  • Cascading means a change in the parent is applied to children automatically: ON DELETE CASCADE, ON UPDATE CASCADE.
  • Other actions: SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION.
  • CASCADE deletes dependent rows without extra code.

Worked Example 1

Batched purge instead of one huge cascade.

Worked Example 2

Soft-delete pattern.

Practice Exercise 1

Cascade demo.

Practice Exercise 2

SET NULL demo.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

With ON DELETE CASCADE InnoDB deletes matching child rows inside the same statement and transaction, recursively through further foreign keys (up to a depth limit). Each cascaded deletion takes row locks and writes undo and redo like a normal delete, but does not fire triggers on the child table.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Actions: CASCADE, SET NULL (column must be nullable), RESTRICT/NO ACTION. ON UPDATE CASCADE propagates key changes (rarely needed with surrogate keys).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one statement keeps a whole object graph consistent, with no application code, no multi-step cleanup and no chance of forgetting a child table.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: cascades are powerful and silent: one wrong DELETE on a parent can wipe thousands of child rows across several tables with no warning, and the cascade can hold locks for a long time on large trees. Cascaded changes also do not fire triggers in InnoDB, so audit triggers miss them.

Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB rejects ON DELETE/UPDATE SET DEFAULT (it is parsed but not supported), cascades stop at a depth of 15 levels, and SET NULL needs a nullable child column.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE p (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE c (id INT PRIMARY KEY, p_id INT DEFAULT 0,
    FOREIGN KEY (p_id) REFERENCES p(id) ON DELETE SET DEFAULT);

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 1215 (HY000): Cannot add foreign key constraint

CREATE TABLE c2 (id INT PRIMARY KEY, p_id INT NOT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (p_id) REFERENCES p(id) ON DELETE SET NULL);   -- SET NULL on NOT NULL column

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 1830 (HY000): Column 'p_id' cannot be NOT NULL: needed in a foreign key constraint
-- 'c2_ibfk_1' SET NULL

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use CASCADE only for true ownership (composition): order lines, post comments, session rows. Use RESTRICT for reference data and financial records, and prefer soft deletes (a deleted_at column) for anything that is legally or historically important. Because cascades skip triggers and can lock large ranges, delete big trees in batches from the application instead.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use CASCADE only for true ownership (order → order_items). For independent data prefer RESTRICT.
  • Cascades do not fire triggers on child rows in InnoDB for the cascaded action.
  • Updating primary keys with ON UPDATE CASCADE is rare; avoid changing keys.

Senior Notes

  • A cascade can delete millions of rows in one transaction, growing undo, locking and lagging replicas; use batched deletes or soft delete for big trees.
  • Cascade chains across many tables are hard to reason about and audit.
  • Binlog contains only the parent delete in statement format; row format logs affected rows, which is also why large cascades inflate it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: cascading deletes over millions of rows (huge transaction, long locks, replica lag), cascades that silently destroy audit data, and triggers expected on cascaded rows (they do not fire). Prefer soft deletes and batch purges for big trees.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM comments WHERE post_id = 1;          -- how big would the cascade be?
UPDATE posts SET deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = 1;           -- soft delete, children untouched
DELETE FROM comments WHERE post_id = 1 LIMIT 5000;          -- batched purge later

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 2400000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A giant cascade holds locks for its whole duration and generates a big binlog event. Measure the affected rows first and purge children in batches before deleting the parent.
codeExamples:
DELETE FROM comments WHERE post_id = 1 LIMIT 5000;     -- repeat until ROW_COUNT() = 0
DELETE FROM posts WHERE id = 1;                          -- now a trivial cascade

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 5000 rows affected   (x480), then Query OK, 1 row affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: owned data (order lines, session rows, draft attachments) uses CASCADE; shared or historical data (customers, products referenced by orders) uses RESTRICT so deletes must be deliberate.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE order_lines (order_id BIGINT NOT NULL, line_no INT NOT NULL, product_id BIGINT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no),
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

Redundancy is the same fact stored in more than one place. A functional dependency (FD) A -> B means: if two rows have the same A they must have the same B (product_id determines product_name). Normalization is the discipline of removing redundancy that FDs reveal.
codeExamples:
-- One flat table that mixes orders, products and customers
CREATE TABLE order_flat (
    order_id INT, product_id INT, product_name VARCHAR(30), unit_price DECIMAL(8,2),
    cust_name VARCHAR(30), cust_city VARCHAR(30), qty INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
INSERT INTO order_flat VALUES
 (1,7,'Pen', 10.00,'Abaji','Pune', 3),
 (1,8,'Book',50.00,'Abaji','Pune', 1),
 (2,7,'Pen', 10.00,'Raoji','Delhi',5);
SELECT * FROM order_flat;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+--------------+------------+-----------+-----------+-----+
-- | order_id | product_id | product_name | unit_price | cust_name | cust_city | qty |
-- +----------+------------+--------------+------------+-----------+-----------+-----+
-- |        1 |          7 | Pen          |      10.00 | Abaji     | Pune      |   3 |
-- |        1 |          8 | Book         |      50.00 | Abaji     | Pune      |   1 |
-- |        2 |          7 | Pen          |      10.00 | Raoji     | Delhi     |   5 |
-- +----------+------------+--------------+------------+-----------+-----------+-----+
-- "Pen/10.00" and "Abaji/Pune" are repeated: product_id -> name,price  and  order_id -> customer.

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Redundant copies drift apart. A single price change must touch every row that repeats it, and missing one produces a database that contradicts itself, which no query can fix afterwards.
codeExamples:
-- Update anomaly: the price is changed on only one of the Pen rows
UPDATE order_flat SET unit_price = 12.00 WHERE order_id = 1 AND product_id = 7;

SELECT product_id, COUNT(DISTINCT unit_price) AS prices
FROM order_flat GROUP BY product_id ORDER BY product_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+--------+
-- | product_id | prices |
-- +------------+--------+
-- |          7 |      2 |        <- Pen now has two prices
-- |          8 |      1 |
-- +------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Data engineers check a suspected FD with a GROUP BY: if any left-hand value maps to more than one right-hand value, the dependency does not hold. An empty result means the data is consistent with it.
codeExamples:
-- Test the FD  product_id -> product_name  (reset the price first so only names matter)
SELECT product_id
FROM order_flat
GROUP BY product_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_name) > 1;         -- violators of the dependency

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

-- Test order_id -> cust_city  (expected to hold too)
SELECT order_id FROM order_flat GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cust_city) > 1;
-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   order_flat  (order_id, product_id | product_name, unit_price, cust_name, cust_city, qty)
                  │          │               ▲   ▲                ▲   ▲        ▲
                  │          └─ product_id ──┘───┘   (FD)         │   │        │
                  └──────── order_id ────────────────────────────┘───┘        │
                  └────────────── (order_id, product_id) ─────────────────────┘
   Each arrow is a functional dependency; each one points at a table waiting to be split out.

Fresher Notes

  • Data redundancy means the same fact is stored in several places, such as a customer’s address repeated on every order.
  • It causes anomalies: update (change in some places only), insert and delete anomalies.
  • A functional dependency A → B means A determines B (employee_id → name).

Worked Example 1

Detect a violated dependency.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer FROM orders_flat GROUP BY customer HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT customer_city) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Deliberate snapshot is fine.
codeExamples:
SELECT oi.product_id, oi.unit_price AS price_when_ordered, p.price AS price_now FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- product_id | price_when_ordered | price_now
--          1 |             100.00 |    120.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Redundant design.

Practice Exercise 2

Fix with a separate table.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A functional dependency A → B means every value of A determines exactly one value of B (employee id determines name). Redundancy appears when a non-key attribute depends on something that is not the whole key, so the same fact is stored in many rows and can become inconsistent.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Find dependencies with GROUP BY + HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT). Decompose by moving the dependent columns to a table keyed by the determinant, and replace them with a foreign key.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of studying FDs: they tell you exactly which attributes belong together, which sets are keys, and where to cut a table into smaller, anomaly-free tables.
codeExamples:
-- Candidate-key check using the FDs: does (order_id, product_id) determine everything?
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_total,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id, product_id) AS distinct_keys
FROM order_flat;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+---------------+
-- | rows_total | distinct_keys |
-- +------------+---------------+
-- |          3 |             3 |
-- +------------+---------------+
-- Equal counts: the pair is a key, and every other column is a function of it.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: FDs cannot be proven from data. A query can only show that the current rows do not violate a dependency; the real rule comes from the business. Small samples satisfy many accidental FDs.
codeExamples:
-- On this tiny sample, qty looks like it "determines" cust_name... by accident
SELECT qty FROM order_flat GROUP BY qty HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT cust_name) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)
-- Yet nothing in the business says quantity decides the customer; do not model it.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a flat table also suffers insertion and deletion anomalies: you cannot record a product that has not been ordered yet, and deleting the last order for a product erases the product itself.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO order_flat (product_id, product_name, unit_price) VALUES (9,'Pencil',5.00);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1364 (HY000): Field 'order_id' doesn't have a default value

-- Deletion anomaly: the Book row is the only record of the Book product
DELETE FROM order_flat WHERE product_id = 8;     -- product 8 is now unknown to the database

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

List the FDs from business rules before drawing tables, then confirm them with GROUP BY checks on real data as a sanity test, never as proof. Redundancy is a defect in the write path (anomalies) but sometimes a deliberate feature of the read path, so the goal is controlled redundancy, not zero redundancy.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Find dependencies to find bad design: if city depends on zip and zip is not the key, then city should live in a zip table.
  • Keys are attributes that functionally determine all others.
  • Normalization removes redundancy by decomposing tables along dependencies.

Senior Notes

  • Not all redundancy is bad: deliberate duplication for performance or history (price at order time) is fine when documented and controlled.
  • Redundancy shows up as inconsistent reports; build reconciliation queries to detect it.
  • Functional dependencies are business rules; confirm them with domain experts, not only data samples.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: normalizing without confirming the real business rule (data samples can mislead), and "fixing" inconsistent rows by guessing. Ask which value is correct before merging.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer_id, customer_city, COUNT(*) AS n, MAX(order_id) AS latest_order FROM orders_flat GROUP BY customer_id, customer_city;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | customer_city | n | latest_order
-- 7           | Pune          | 2 |            2
-- 7           | Delhi         | 1 |            3      (which one is current? ask the business)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Redundancy costs storage, cache and write amplification: updating one fact touches many rows. Compare the cost of renaming a city in both designs.
codeExamples:
UPDATE orders_flat SET customer_city = 'Mumbai' WHERE customer_id = 7;       -- touches every order row
UPDATE customers SET city = 'Mumbai' WHERE id = 7;                             -- touches one row

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 3 rows affected
-- Query OK, 1 row affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: some redundancy is intentional. An invoice stores the customer's address as it was on the day of sale, because later address changes must not rewrite history. That is a snapshot, not a normalization error.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A table is in First Normal Form when every column holds a single atomic value (no lists in a cell), there are no repeating column groups (phone1, phone2, phone3), and every row is uniquely identifiable by a key.

Why Do We Need This?

Lists in a cell cannot be searched with an index, validated per item, or joined. Each query becomes string surgery and every rule has to be re-implemented in application code.
codeExamples:
-- Finding the owner of phone 98451: pattern matching, full scan, false positives possible
SELECT name FROM person_bad WHERE phones LIKE '%98451%';

-- 1NF version: exact match on an indexed column
SELECT p.name FROM person p
JOIN person_phone pp ON pp.person_id = p.id
WHERE pp.phone = '98451';

-- OUTPUT (both):
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
