-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Spreadsheet imports often arrive with repeating columns (phone1, phone2, phone3). Converting them to rows is a routine ETL step, here written with UNION ALL.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE import_wide (id INT, phone1 VARCHAR(15), phone2 VARCHAR(15), phone3 VARCHAR(15));
INSERT INTO import_wide VALUES (1,'98450','98451',NULL),(2,'99000',NULL,NULL);

SELECT id, phone FROM (
    SELECT id, phone1 AS phone FROM import_wide
    UNION ALL SELECT id, phone2 FROM import_wide
    UNION ALL SELECT id, phone3 FROM import_wide
) AS x
WHERE phone IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY id, phone;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+
-- | id   | phone |
-- +------+-------+
-- |    1 | 98450 |
-- |    1 | 98451 |
-- |    2 | 99000 |
-- +------+-------+

beginner.content:
Fresher Notes

  • First Normal Form: every column holds a single atomic value, there are no repeating groups, and each row is unique.
  • Bad: phones = "999,888" in one cell. Good: one row per phone in a child table.
  • A primary key identifies each row.

Worked Example 1

Explode the CSV into rows with JSON_TABLE.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id, jt.phone FROM contacts_bad c,
JSON_TABLE(CONCAT('["', REPLACE(c.phones, ',', '","'), '"]'), '$[*]' COLUMNS (phone VARCHAR(15) PATH '$')) jt;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | phone
--  1 | 999
--  1 | 888
--  2 | 777

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Count phones per contact.
codeExamples:
SELECT contact_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM contact_phones GROUP BY contact_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- contact_id | n
--          1 | 2
--          2 | 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Violating 1NF and the query pain.

Practice Exercise 2

1NF design.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

First normal form requires atomic values: each cell holds one value of one type, rows are unique, and there are no repeating groups. Atomicity is what lets the engine index, compare and join the values; a comma-separated list is opaque to all of them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Migrate a list column into rows with JSON_TABLE or a numbers table, then drop the old column. Repeating columns (phone1, phone2, phone3) are converted the same way with UNION ALL.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO contact_phones SELECT c.id, jt.phone FROM contacts_bad c,
  JSON_TABLE(CONCAT('["', REPLACE(c.phones, ',', '","'), '"]'), '$[*]' COLUMNS (phone VARCHAR(20) PATH '$')) jt;
SELECT id, phone1 AS phone FROM wide_contacts WHERE phone1 IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL SELECT id, phone2 FROM wide_contacts WHERE phone2 IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL SELECT id, phone3 FROM wide_contacts WHERE phone3 IS NOT NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | phone
--  1 | 999
--  1 | 888

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: each value can be constrained, indexed, counted and joined on its own, and there is no limit of "three phones".
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, COUNT(pp.phone) AS phone_count
FROM person p LEFT JOIN person_phone pp ON pp.person_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.id;

INSERT INTO person_phone VALUES (1,'98450');       -- duplicate phone for the same person

-- OUTPUT (first query):          OUTPUT (insert):
-- +------+-------------+         ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1-98450' for key
-- | name | phone_count |         'person_phone.PRIMARY'
-- +-------+---+
-- | Abaji | 2 |
-- | Raoji | 1 |
-- +------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more rows and more joins, and displaying the data as one line needs aggregation to put the list back together.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, GROUP_CONCAT(pp.phone ORDER BY pp.phone) AS phones
FROM person p JOIN person_phone pp ON pp.person_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY p.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------------+
-- | name  | phones      |
-- +-------+-------------+
-- | Abaji | 98450,98451 |
-- | Raoji | 99000       |
-- +------+-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: "atomic" depends on how the data is used. A DATE has year, month and day parts yet is treated as atomic because queries use it as a unit, and MySQL allows JSON columns, which hold structured values by design.

Architect's Notes

1NF is non-negotiable for data you filter, join or constrain. For opaque payloads that you only store and return (webhook bodies, user preferences), a JSON column is a pragmatic exception, but index any field you search through a generated column and keep a relational column for anything with an integrity rule.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Comma-separated lists, repeating columns (phone1, phone2, phone3) and arrays violate 1NF.
  • They break searching, indexing, constraints and joins.
  • JSON columns are acceptable for truly opaque payloads, not for data you filter and join on.

Senior Notes

  • 1NF violations show up as FIND_IN_SET, LIKE "%,5,%" and sprawling columns; refactor to child tables.
  • Migrate safely: create the child table, backfill by splitting values, switch the app, drop the old column.
  • Atomicity is contextual: a full address may be atomic for shipping labels but not for city-level analytics.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: JSON arrays for data you query by element, delimiters inside values, and a "fixed number of columns" for a variable count. Use JSON only for opaque payloads, otherwise a child table.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM contacts_bad WHERE phones LIKE '%88%';       -- also matches 888, 188, 880...
ALTER TABLE contacts_bad DROP COLUMN phones;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1                    (wrong matches are easy with substring tests on lists)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Child-table lookups use indexes and constraints; list columns use scans. Verify with EXPLAIN, and measure the speed difference at scale.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: user interests, skills and tags always belong in child tables so you can ask "who has skill X" or count users per tag with ordinary joins and indexes.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A table is in Second Normal Form when it is in 1NF and no non-key column depends on part of a composite key. In order_flat the key is (order_id, product_id), but product_name depends only on product_id, a partial dependency. Fix it by moving that data to its own table.

Why Do We Need This?

Partial dependencies cause update, insert and delete anomalies: the same product facts repeat in every order that includes it. After the split, each product fact exists exactly once.
codeExamples:
UPDATE product SET unit_price = 12.00 WHERE product_id = 7;   -- one row, every order sees it
SELECT product_id, unit_price FROM product ORDER BY product_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- +------------+------------+
-- | product_id | unit_price |
-- +------------+------------+
-- |          7 |      12.00 |
-- |          8 |      50.00 |
-- +------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Careful: an order must usually keep the price at the time of sale. That column depends on the whole key (this product in this order), so storing price in order_item is correct and is not a 2NF violation. Normal forms follow the real business rule.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE order_item ADD COLUMN sold_price DECIMAL(8,2);    -- snapshot of the price at sale time
UPDATE order_item i JOIN product p ON p.product_id = i.product_id
SET i.sold_price = 10.00 WHERE p.product_id = 7;                 -- sales made at the old price
SELECT order_id, product_id, sold_price FROM order_item WHERE product_id = 7 ORDER BY order_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------------+------------+
-- | order_id | product_id | sold_price |
-- +----------+------------+------------+
-- |        1 |          7 |      10.00 |
-- |        2 |          7 |      10.00 |
-- +----------+------------+------------+
-- Product list price is now 12.00, history stays 10.00.

beginner.content:
Diagram

   BEFORE (key = order_id + product_id)       AFTER 2NF
   ┌───────┬───────┬──────────────┬─────┐     product                 order_item
   │ order │ prod  │ product_name │ qty │     ┌──────┬──────┐         ┌───────┬──────┬─────┐
   └───────┴───┬───┴──────▲───────┴─────┘     │ prod │ name │◄────────│ order │ prod │ qty │
               └──────────┘                    └──────┴──────┘   FK    └───────┴──────┴─────┘
        name depends on prod only (partial)    every column now depends on its whole key

Fresher Notes

  • Second Normal Form: the table is in 1NF and no non-key column depends on only part of a composite key.
  • It matters only for composite keys.
  • Example: in order_items(order_id, product_id, product_name), product_name depends only on product_id.

Worked Example 1

Rename once instead of in millions of rows.

Worked Example 2

Detect a partial dependency.

Practice Exercise 1

Partial dependency table.

Practice Exercise 2

2NF solution.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Second normal form applies when the key is composite: every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not part of it. A column that depends on only one key part is repeated for every row sharing that part, so it is stored redundantly and can drift.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Fix by moving the partially dependent column into a table keyed by that part, and keep the composite-key table for facts about the pair (quantity, price at time of order).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the decomposition is lossless: joining the pieces gives back exactly the original data, with smaller rows and no repeated facts.
codeExamples:
-- Reconstruct and compare row count with the original 3 rows
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rebuilt_rows
FROM order_item i JOIN product p ON p.product_id = i.product_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | rebuilt_rows |
-- +--------------+
-- |            3 |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: reading an order now requires a join, and more tables mean more keys, more indexes and more places to forget a foreign key.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT i.order_id, p.product_name
FROM order_item i JOIN product p ON p.product_id = i.product_id WHERE i.order_id = 1;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | table | type   | key     | ref                         | rows |
-- | i     | ref    | PRIMARY | const                       |    2 |
-- | p     | eq_ref | PRIMARY | shop.i.product_id           |    1 |
-- Two lookups instead of one row; cheap with indexes, but not free.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: 2NF only matters for composite keys. A table with a single-column primary key is automatically in 2NF, yet it can still hold transitive dependencies (see 3NF).

Architect's Notes

Apply 2NF whenever you see a composite key and a column that mentions only half of it. Keep columns that genuinely belong to the whole key, such as the price at the time of sale, even when they look duplicated. In transactional systems prefer a surrogate key on the fact table and a UNIQUE on the business pair.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Fix by moving partial dependencies to their own table: products(product_id, product_name).
  • Tables with a single-column primary key are automatically in 2NF if in 1NF.
  • Look for columns that repeat for each value of part of the key.

Senior Notes

  • Partial dependencies cause update anomalies in large link tables where one product name is repeated millions of times.
  • Keep a deliberate snapshot (unit_price at order time) distinct from a partial dependency (product name that should follow the product).
  • Review composite-key tables during design review for stray descriptive columns.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: confusing a partial dependency with a deliberate snapshot. A unit price copied at order time depends on the whole (order, product) fact, so it belongs in the link table; the product's current name does not.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE order_items ADD COLUMN unit_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0;       -- price when ordered: correct here
UPDATE order_items oi JOIN products_price pp ON pp.product_id = oi.product_id SET oi.unit_price = pp.price;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 3 rows affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Redundant partial-dependency columns inflate the biggest table in the system. Compare the size before and after the split.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, avg_row_length, table_rows FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('order_items_bad','order_items');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name      | avg_row_length | table_rows
-- order_items_bad |             92 |   54000000
-- order_items     |             48 |   54000000      (about 2.4 GB saved)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: renaming a product used to need an update on millions of order lines; after normalization it is one row, and old orders can still show the historical name if a snapshot column was kept intentionally.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A table is in Third Normal Form when it is in 2NF and no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency). Memory aid: every attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

Why Do We Need This?

With the transitive dependency left in, Abaji moving cities means updating every one of her orders. Miss one and the database disagrees with itself about where she lives.
codeExamples:
-- Un-normalized: one UPDATE touches several rows and can be partial
UPDATE orders_bad SET cust_city = 'Mumbai' WHERE order_id = 1;   -- forgot orders 2

SELECT cust_id, COUNT(DISTINCT cust_city) AS cities FROM orders_bad GROUP BY cust_id;

-- 3NF: a single row changes
UPDATE customer SET cust_city = 'Mumbai' WHERE cust_id = 5;

-- OUTPUT (first query):
-- +---------+--------+
-- | cust_id | cities |
-- +---------+--------+
-- |       5 |      2 |      <- customer 5 lives in two cities?
-- |       6 |      1 |
-- +---------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical 3NF splits: address data out of orders, department name out of employee, category name out of product, city and pincode out of address. Reporting joins them back with views.
codeExamples:
CREATE VIEW order_report AS
SELECT o.order_id, c.cust_name, c.cust_city
FROM orders o JOIN customer c ON c.cust_id = o.cust_id;

SELECT * FROM order_report WHERE cust_city = 'Mumbai';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-----------+-----------+
-- | order_id | cust_name | cust_city |
-- +----------+-----------+-----------+
-- |        1 | Abaji     | Mumbai    |
-- |        2 | Abaji     | Mumbai    |
-- +----------+-----------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   orders_bad                              3NF
   order_id ──► cust_id ──► cust_name       orders(order_id, cust_id) ──FK──► customer(cust_id, name, city)
                      └───► cust_city
   key ──► non-key ──► non-key  (transitive)   every non-key column depends on its own table's key only

Fresher Notes

  • Third Normal Form: 2NF plus no non-key column depends on another non-key column (no transitive dependency).
  • Example: employee(id, dept_id, dept_name): dept_name depends on dept_id, not on id.
  • Fix: put departments in their own table.

Worked Example 1

Rename a department once.

Worked Example 2

Anomaly in the unnormalized version: rename misses rows.

Practice Exercise 1

Transitive dependency.

Practice Exercise 2

3NF solution.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Third normal form removes transitive dependencies: a non-key column must not depend on another non-key column. If department name depends on department id and department id depends on the employee id, the name belongs with the department, not in every employee row.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Decompose: create a table for the determinant (dept_id) holding its dependent columns, reference it with a foreign key, and drop the copied columns.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: each fact has one home, so there are no update, insert or delete anomalies, storage is smaller and constraints (UNIQUE name, CHECK city) can be applied once.
codeExamples:
-- A customer can now exist before any order is placed (no insertion anomaly)
INSERT INTO customer VALUES (7,'Mina','Goa');
SELECT COUNT(*) AS customers_without_orders
FROM customer c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.cust_id = c.cust_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------+
-- | customers_without_orders |
-- +--------------------------+
-- |                        1 |
-- +--------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more joins per read. At large scale those joins, and the extra indexes they need, are measurable costs on hot read paths.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT order_id, cust_name FROM order_report;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | table | type   | key     | rows |
-- | o     | index  | cust_id |    3 |
-- | c     | eq_ref | PRIMARY |    1 |      <- one extra lookup per order row

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: 3NF still allows a dependency whose right side is part of a candidate key (X -> prime attribute). Tables with overlapping candidate keys can be in 3NF and still show anomalies, which BCNF resolves.
codeExamples:
-- Each teacher teaches ONE subject (teacher -> subject), a student has one teacher per subject
CREATE TABLE enrol3 (student VARCHAR(10), subject VARCHAR(10), teacher VARCHAR(10),
    PRIMARY KEY (student, subject));
INSERT INTO enrol3 VALUES ('Abaji','Math','Rao'),('Raoji','Math','Rao'),('Abaji','Physics','Iyer');
SELECT * FROM enrol3 ORDER BY student, subject;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------+---------+
-- | student | subject | teacher |
-- +---------+---------+---------+
-- | Abaji   | Math    | Rao     |
-- | Abaji   | Physics | Iyer    |
-- | Raoji   | Math    | Rao     |
-- +---------+---------+---------+
-- In 3NF (subject is a prime attribute) yet "Rao teaches Math" is stored twice: see BCNF.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Design to 3NF by default for OLTP, then measure. Expose the joined shape through views so application code stays simple, and denormalize only specific, measured hot paths. For snapshot data (prices, addresses on a shipped order), copy deliberately and document why.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Slogan: every non-key attribute depends on "the key, the whole key and nothing but the key".
  • Typical transitive cases: zip → city, product → category name, country → currency.
  • 3NF removes most update anomalies and is the usual target for OLTP.

Senior Notes

  • 3NF can cost extra joins on hot read paths; denormalize deliberately with measurements.
  • Beware synthetic "dependencies" that are really business choices (price at time of sale).
  • Document every deliberate violation with its reason and its maintenance mechanism.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: keeping derived data such as totals as stored columns without maintenance, and copying lookup values into every row. If you need a copy for speed it is denormalization: document it and keep it in sync.
codeExamples:
UPDATE emp_bad SET dept_city = 'Mumbai' WHERE id = 1;           -- only one of two HR rows changed
SELECT DISTINCT dept_city FROM emp_bad WHERE dept_id = 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept_city
-- Mumbai
-- Pune           (update anomaly: department 10 now has two cities)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

3NF costs a join to read an employee with their department, but the join is a primary-key lookup. Check the plan to confirm it is cheap before denormalizing.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT e.name, d.name, d.city FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept_id WHERE e.id = 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table | type  | key
-- e     | const | PRIMARY
-- d     | const | PRIMARY        (two single-row lookups)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: the "address" of a customer, the country of a city, the category of a product are classic transitive dependencies; keeping them in their own tables makes a change one update and keeps reports consistent.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name AS product, c.name AS category, pc.name AS parent_category FROM products p JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id LEFT JOIN categories pc ON pc.id = c.parent_id WHERE p.id = 7;

-- OUTPUT:
-- product | category | parent_category
-- Pen     | Stationery | Office

beginner.content:
Introduction

Boyce-Codd Normal Form is a stricter 3NF: for every functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey (a key or a superset of one). In enrol3, teacher -> subject holds but teacher alone is not a key, so the table violates BCNF.

Why Do We Need This?

In the 3NF design nothing stops contradictory data: the rule "a teacher teaches one subject" is not backed by any key, so a bad row is accepted silently.
codeExamples:
-- enrol3 table from the 3NF topic: Rao now "teaches" Physics too, contradicting Math
INSERT INTO enrol3 VALUES ('Mina','Physics','Rao');       -- accepted by the PK (Mina, Physics)

SELECT teacher, COUNT(DISTINCT subject) AS subjects FROM enrol3 GROUP BY teacher ORDER BY teacher;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+----------+
-- | teacher | subjects |
-- +---------+----------+
-- | Iyer    |        1 |
-- | Rao     |        2 |      <- violates teacher -> subject, undetected by the database
-- +---------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Anywhere two independent keys overlap (room and time slots, instructor and subject, warehouse and region) BCNF appears. The decomposition turns the rule into a primary key so the engine enforces it.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO teacher_subject VALUES ('Rao','Physics');   -- try the same contradiction after decomposition

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'Rao' for key 'teacher_subject.PRIMARY'

beginner.content:
Diagram

   enrol3 (3NF, not BCNF)                      BCNF split
   key: (student, subject)                     teacher_subject             student_teacher
   teacher ──► subject  (teacher not a key)    ┌─────────┬─────────┐       ┌─────────┬─────────┐
                                               │ teacher*│ subject │◄──────│ student │ teacher │
   determinant must be a (super)key ─────────► └─────────┴─────────┘  FK   └─────────┴─────────┘
                                                 * PRIMARY KEY            PK(student, teacher)

Fresher Notes

  • Boyce-Codd Normal Form is a stricter 3NF: for every functional dependency X → Y, X must be a candidate key (a superkey).
  • It matters when a table has several overlapping candidate keys.
  • Most 3NF tables are already BCNF.

Worked Example 1

Enforcement of the dependency via PK.

Worked Example 2

Rebuild the original view.

Practice Exercise 1

BCNF violation.

Practice Exercise 2

BCNF decomposition.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Boyce-Codd normal form is stricter than 3NF: for every functional dependency X → Y, X must be a superkey. A violation shows up when two candidate keys overlap and a non-superkey attribute determines part of a key, producing redundancy even in a 3NF table.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Decompose so that every determinant is a key: one table for teacher → subject, one for student → teacher. Enforce teacher → subject with a primary key on teacher.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: every dependency is guaranteed by a key, so the redundancy and anomalies caused by dependencies are eliminated completely, and rules are enforced declaratively.
codeExamples:
-- Change what Rao teaches: one row instead of every enrolment row
UPDATE teacher_subject SET subject = 'Statistics' WHERE teacher = 'Rao';
SELECT * FROM teacher_subject ORDER BY teacher;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------------+
-- | teacher | subject    |
-- +---------+------------+
-- | Iyer    | Physics    |
-- | Rao     | Statistics |
-- +---------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: BCNF decomposition can lose dependency preservation. The original rule "a student has one teacher per subject" cannot be a key in the new tables, so the database can no longer enforce it declaratively.
codeExamples:
-- Abaji now has two Math teachers: allowed by PRIMARY KEY (student, teacher)
INSERT INTO teacher_subject VALUES ('Das','Statistics');
INSERT INTO student_teacher VALUES ('Abaji','Das');         -- Rao and Das both teach Abaji statistics

SELECT st.student, ts.subject, COUNT(*) AS teachers
FROM student_teacher st JOIN teacher_subject ts ON ts.teacher = st.teacher
GROUP BY st.student, ts.subject HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------------+----------+
-- | student | subject    | teachers |
-- +---------+------------+----------+
-- | Abaji   | Statistics |        2 |
-- +---------+------------+----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a lossless, dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition does not always exist. When it does not, you choose between BCNF (and a trigger or application check) or 3NF (and a stored redundancy).

Architect's Notes

Go to BCNF when the violating dependency is a real, frequently-edited business rule; stay at 3NF when decomposition would lose an important rule you cannot enforce cheaply. Document the decision, and back any non-key rule with a trigger, a check job, or a redundant column plus UNIQUE as shown.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Classic case: a table where a non-key attribute determines part of a key (teacher → subject in (student, subject, teacher)).
  • Decomposing to BCNF can lose the ability to enforce some dependencies with simple constraints.
  • In practice teams target 3NF and fix BCNF only where anomalies appear.

Senior Notes

  • BCNF decomposition is lossless but may not be dependency-preserving; sometimes 3NF is the practical optimum.
  • Use unique constraints on the determinants to enforce dependencies the decomposition keeps.
  • Validate with real business rules; sample data can mislead.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: over-normalizing without reason, and losing the ability to enforce a rule. In the decomposed design "a student cannot take the same subject twice" is no longer a simple key; enforce it with a view and a trigger, or accept 3NF.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

BCNF decomposition may need extra joins; confirm the join paths are indexed and that the read pattern justifies the change. Rebuild the original shape with a view when applications need it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: most teams aim for 3NF and apply BCNF only where an overlapping-key anomaly is actually observed, for example room and time slot scheduling tables.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Denormalization is the deliberate addition of redundancy to a normalized design to make reads faster or simpler. Typical forms: stored totals, counters, copied columns, and pre-aggregated summary tables.

Why Do We Need This?

Listing screens, dashboards and APIs read totals constantly but change them rarely. Computing SUM over joins on every read costs CPU and I/O; a stored value answers in a single indexed row.
codeExamples:
-- Normalized read: aggregate every time
SELECT o.id, SUM(i.price * i.qty) AS total
FROM d_orders o JOIN d_item i ON i.order_id = o.id GROUP BY o.id;

-- Denormalized read: just a column
SELECT id, total FROM d_orders;

-- OUTPUT (both):
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | total |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | 80.00 |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Analytics systems maintain summary tables incrementally. Here each sale updates a daily total with an upsert, so reports read one row per day instead of scanning millions of sales.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day DATE PRIMARY KEY, orders INT NOT NULL, revenue DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO daily_sales VALUES ('2026-10-06', 1, 80.00)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE orders = orders + 1, revenue = revenue + 80.00;   -- first sale: inserts
INSERT INTO daily_sales VALUES ('2026-10-06', 1, 25.00)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE orders = orders + 1, revenue = revenue + 25.00;   -- second sale: updates
SELECT * FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+--------+---------+
-- | day        | orders | revenue |
-- +------------+--------+---------+
-- | 2026-10-06 |      2 |  105.00 |
-- +------------+--------+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Normalized                         Denormalized
   orders ──< items                   orders (id, ..., item_count, total)   <- copy
      read = JOIN + SUM                    read = one indexed row
      write = 1 table                      write = items + keep the copy in sync
   Correct by construction            Fast reads, needs a sync strategy:
                                       generated column | trigger | app transaction | batch job

Fresher Notes

  • Denormalization deliberately adds redundancy to speed up reads, such as storing a total or a name copy.
  • It trades write complexity and storage for fewer joins.
  • Normalize first, denormalize only when measurements justify it.

Worked Example 1

Generated column keeps in-row values consistent.

Worked Example 2

Summary table for dashboards.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO daily_sales (day, revenue) SELECT DATE(placed_at), SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY DATE(placed_at)
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE revenue = VALUES(revenue);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Order total column maintained with a transaction.

Practice Exercise 2

Reconciliation query.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Denormalization stores redundant data deliberately to remove joins or aggregations from hot read paths. It trades extra storage and write cost for read speed, so it is only justified by measurement. The redundant data must have a single source of truth and a defined way to stay in sync.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques: stored summary columns, copied lookup values, generated columns (always consistent inside a row), summary tables, and counter tables. Pick the one whose synchronisation is simplest.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: faster reads, fewer joins, simpler queries. A STORED generated column gives a safe kind of redundancy: the engine recomputes it, so it can never drift.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the copy can drift from the truth. Any code path that changes an item without updating the order total (a manual fix, a forgotten API, a failed job) leaves wrong numbers that look right.
codeExamples:
UPDATE d_item SET qty = 5 WHERE order_id = 1 AND line_no = 1;     -- total column not updated

-- Drift detector: stored total versus recomputed total
SELECT o.id, o.total AS stored, SUM(i.price * i.qty) AS actual
FROM d_orders o JOIN d_item i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY o.id, o.total HAVING o.total <> SUM(i.price * i.qty);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+--------+
-- | id | stored | actual |
-- +----+--------+--------+
-- |  1 |  80.00 | 100.00 |
-- +----+--------+--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: generated columns are row-local: they may use only deterministic expressions over the same row, not other tables, subqueries or functions like NOW(). Cross-table copies therefore need triggers, application code or batch jobs.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE bad_gen (id INT, created DATETIME AS (NOW()) STORED);

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 3102 (HY000): Expression of generated column 'created' contains a disallowed function: now.

-- Keep cross-table aggregates correct with a repair statement run by a job:
UPDATE d_orders o
JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(price*qty) AS s, COUNT(*) AS c FROM d_item GROUP BY order_id) x
  ON x.order_id = o.id
SET o.total = x.s, o.item_count = x.c;

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Normalize first, denormalize with evidence: an EXPLAIN or slow-log entry that shows the join or aggregate is the bottleneck. Choose the safest mechanism available (generated column, then same-transaction update, then trigger, then async job), add a drift-detection query to monitoring, and record each denormalized column and its source of truth in the schema documentation.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Common forms: summary/counter columns, copied columns, pre-joined tables, summary tables, caches.
  • You must keep copies in sync: in the same transaction, via triggers, events or jobs.
  • Document each denormalized column and its source of truth.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer read models (materialized aggregates, search indexes, cache) over polluting the core schema.
  • Use generated columns for derived values inside the same row; use counter tables for hot counters to avoid row contention.
  • Add reconciliation jobs that recompute and compare to catch drift.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: denormalizing without reconciliation, updating the copy in a different transaction than the source, and counters on one hot row. Update in the same transaction or recompute, and always add a drift check query.
codeExamples:
SELECT o.id FROM orders o JOIN (SELECT order_id, SUM(qty * unit_price) AS s FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id) x ON x.order_id = o.id WHERE o.total <> x.s;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 812         (drifted: total does not equal the sum of the lines)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hot counters contend for one row lock. Spread writes over several slots and sum them on read, or aggregate asynchronously in batches.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a product listing shows rating and review count on every card. Store them on the product, update them transactionally when a review is added, and run a nightly reconciliation.

beginner.content:
Introduction

An alternate key is a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. It still identifies a row uniquely, so in MySQL you declare it as UNIQUE (and normally NOT NULL).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE app_user (
    id       BIGINT       AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- chosen candidate key
    email    VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,              -- alternate key 1
    username VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL UNIQUE               -- alternate key 2
);
INSERT INTO app_user (email, username) VALUES ('abaji@x.com','abaji'),('raoji@x.com','raoji');
SHOW INDEX FROM app_user;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----------+------------+----------+-------------+
-- | Table    | Non_unique | Key_name | Column_name |
-- +----------+------------+----------+-------------+
-- | app_user |          0 | PRIMARY  | id          |
-- | app_user |          0 | email    | email       |
-- | app_user |          0 | username | username    |
-- +----------+------------+----------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

People and systems look rows up by what they know (an email at login, an ISBN at a till), not by an internal id. Alternate keys make those lookups both unique and fast, and prevent two accounts for one email.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM app_user WHERE email = 'abaji@x.com';

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +------+-------+-------+------+
-- | type | key   | ref   | rows |
-- +------+-------+-------+------+
-- | const| email | const |    1 |
-- +------+-------+-------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

A foreign key may reference any unique key in InnoDB, not only the primary key. Referencing a stable alternate key like a country code makes child tables readable without a join.

Diagram

   Candidate keys of app_user:   {id}    {email}    {username}
                                   │         │           │
                                   ▼         └─────┬─────┘
                              PRIMARY KEY     ALTERNATE KEYS
                              (clustered)     UNIQUE, NOT NULL  (secondary indexes)
                                   ▲               ▲
                                   └── FKs may reference either ──┘

Fresher Notes

  • An alternate key is a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key.
  • Example: user id is the primary key; email and username are alternate keys.
  • In MySQL, define alternate keys with UNIQUE NOT NULL.

Worked Example 1

Reference an alternate key.

Worked Example 2

List unique keys.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, column_name FROM information_schema.statistics WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'app_users' AND non_unique = 0;

-- OUTPUT:
-- index_name  | column_name
-- PRIMARY     | id
-- uq_email    | email
-- uq_username | username

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Primary and alternate keys.

Practice Exercise 2

Look up by an alternate key.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM app_users WHERE email = 'a@x.com';

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An alternate key is any candidate key not chosen as the primary key. In MySQL it is a UNIQUE NOT NULL index. It is a normal secondary index that stores the primary key value, so lookups by it need a second step into the clustered index unless the query is covered.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Foreign keys may reference an alternate key, and you can mark which key is the "business key" by naming. Composite alternate keys and functional unique keys express rules such as case-insensitive uniqueness.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the database guarantees uniqueness of every real-world identifier you care about, not just the surrogate id.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each alternate key is another B-tree: extra disk, extra memory and extra work on every insert and update. And a nullable alternate key allows many NULLs, so declare NOT NULL when the value is mandatory.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE weak (id INT PRIMARY KEY, passport VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE);   -- NULL allowed
INSERT INTO weak VALUES (1,NULL),(2,NULL),(3,'P123');
SELECT * FROM weak ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----------+
-- | id | passport |
-- +----+----------+
-- |  1 | NULL     |
-- |  2 | NULL     |
-- |  3 | P123     |
-- +----+----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: uniqueness follows the column collation. The default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci ignores case and accents, so 'Abaji@x.com' collides with 'abaji@x.com'. That is often desirable for email, but not for case-sensitive identifiers. Index keys are also limited to 3072 bytes.

Architect's Notes

Declare every identifier the business treats as unique as an alternate key, even if you always join on the surrogate. Normalise values before they reach the index (lower-case email, trim spaces), and mind index width: a long VARCHAR alternate key is stored in the index and increases buffer-pool pressure.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Alternate keys give business-level uniqueness and fast lookups by that column.
  • Foreign keys can reference an alternate key (UNIQUE), though referencing the PK is conventional.
  • Name unique constraints (uq_users_email).

Senior Notes

  • Keep alternate keys short and stable; they are also indexes that consume memory.
  • Changing an alternate key (email change) is easy because it is not used as the clustered key; this is a reason to use surrogate PKs.
  • Case/collation rules define what counts as duplicate; decide them deliberately.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: nullable alternate keys (many NULLs are allowed, so uniqueness is not guaranteed), forgetting collation effects, and using a long string as an alternate key that bloats every index. Make them NOT NULL and keep them short.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Each alternate key is another B-tree to maintain on every write and another structure in the buffer pool. Keep only those used for lookups or required for integrity, and drop unused ones.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: expose a stable public identifier (UUID) as an alternate key while the internal BIGINT stays the primary key, so URLs do not leak counts and shards can generate ids independently.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A natural key is made of real-world data that already identifies the row (email, ISBN, country code). A surrogate key is a meaningless value created by the database (AUTO_INCREMENT, UUID) whose only job is to identify the row.

Why Do We Need This?

Real-world identifiers change: people change email, companies reissue codes, standards rename things. A natural PK that changes must be rewritten in every child table. A surrogate never has to change.

Real-Time Use

Most OLTP systems use BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT. Distributed systems that generate ids on many nodes use UUIDs; MySQL 8 offers UUID_TO_BIN with a swap flag so time-ordered UUIDs insert sequentially and stay index-friendly.

Diagram

   Natural key                          Surrogate key
   PK = email VARCHAR(60)               PK = id BIGINT (8 bytes)    + UNIQUE(email)
   ┌──────────────────┐                 ┌────┬──────────────────┐
   │ abaji@x.com       │                 │  1 │ abaji@x.com       │
   └──────────────────┘                 └────┴──────────────────┘
   meaningful, wide, can change         meaningless, narrow, never changes
   copied into every child + 2nd index  copied into every child + 2nd index (small)

Fresher Notes

  • A natural key is real-world data that identifies a row (email, passport number). A surrogate key is a system-generated meaningless id (AUTO_INCREMENT, UUID).
  • Surrogate keys are stable and compact; natural keys can change.
  • Most designs use a surrogate PK plus UNIQUE on natural keys.

Worked Example 1

Public id alongside internal id.

Worked Example 2

Natural key problem: changed value needs cascades.
codeExamples:
UPDATE customer_nat SET email = 'new@x.com' WHERE email = 'a@x.com';   -- email was the PK

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (plus ON UPDATE CASCADE work in every child table)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Natural vs surrogate design.

Practice Exercise 2

Email change with a surrogate key touches one row.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index and is copied into every secondary index entry. A short, monotonic surrogate key (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT) keeps the tree compact and inserts sequential; a long or random natural key makes every index larger and splits pages.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: auto-increment ids, UUIDv7/ULID (time-ordered, globally unique), snowflake ids, and natural keys for tiny stable reference data such as ISO country codes (CHAR(2)). Keep natural uniqueness as a UNIQUE constraint.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of surrogate keys: short, fixed width and immutable. In InnoDB every secondary index entry stores the primary key, so a narrow PK shrinks all indexes. Inserts in increasing order also avoid page splits.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO book_sur (isbn, title) VALUES ('9780201633610','Design Patterns');
SELECT LAST_INSERT_ID() AS new_id;               -- id handed back to the application

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | new_id |
-- +--------+
-- |      2 |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages of surrogate keys: they carry no meaning and prevent no real-world duplicates. If you forget a UNIQUE on the natural identifier, the same book can be entered twice under different ids.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE book_oops (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, isbn CHAR(13), title VARCHAR(50));  -- no UNIQUE
INSERT INTO book_oops (isbn, title) VALUES ('9780131103627','C Book'),('9780131103627','C Book');
SELECT id, isbn FROM book_oops;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------------+
-- | id | isbn          |
-- +----+---------------+
-- |  1 | 9780131103627 |
-- |  2 | 9780131103627 |      <- same book twice
-- +----+---------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: an AUTO_INCREMENT column has a ceiling (INT is about 2.1 billion; use BIGINT UNSIGNED for large tables), can have gaps after rollbacks and failed inserts, and sequential public ids can be guessed by outsiders. Natural keys have their own limits: width, change, privacy.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE tiny (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO tiny VALUES (2147483647);            -- INT maximum
INSERT INTO tiny VALUES (NULL);                  -- next value would overflow

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '2147483647' for key 'tiny.PRIMARY'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use a surrogate PK with a UNIQUE constraint on each natural identifier: you get a small immutable key for joins and indexes plus real-world integrity. Choose BIGINT auto-increment for single-writer OLTP, ordered UUID or snowflake ids when many writers or shards create ids, and keep a natural PK only for small, stable code tables such as country or currency.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Natural keys are good as UNIQUE constraints and for lookup; weak as primary keys because values change, can be long and sometimes get reused.
  • Composite natural keys make foreign keys wide.
  • Surrogate keys leak meaning if exposed (guessable counts); expose a separate public id if needed.

Senior Notes

  • Time-ordered ids (UUIDv7, ULID, Snowflake) give global uniqueness with good index locality.
  • Auto-increment is simple but limits multi-writer or sharded systems.
  • Natural keys still win for reference tables with truly stable codes (ISO country code).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using an email or phone as the primary key (changes ripple through every child table), random UUIDv4 strings (page splits), and exposing sequential ids publicly (enumeration). Keep the surrogate internal and add a separate public id.
codeExamples:
UPDATE cust_nat SET email = 'new@x.com' WHERE email = 'a@x.com';      -- with ON UPDATE CASCADE this rewrites every child row and index entry
UPDATE cust_sur SET email = 'new@x.com' WHERE id = 1;                  -- one row

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (plus cascaded updates in all child tables for the natural key)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Insert speed differs: monotonic keys append at the right edge, random keys land anywhere. Compare time and fragmentation for sequential and random keys of the same size.
codeExamples:
-- 1M inserts
-- AUTO_INCREMENT BIGINT : ~ 6 s,  table 44 MB,  fill factor ~ 94 %
-- UUID v4 CHAR(36)       : ~ 24 s, table 96 MB,  fill factor ~ 69 %
-- UUID v7 BINARY(16)     : ~ 8 s,  table 52 MB,  fill factor ~ 90 %

SELECT 24 / 6 AS random_key_slowdown;

-- OUTPUT:
-- random_key_slowdown
-- 4.0000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: distributed systems need ids generated without a central counter. A time-ordered UUID in BINARY(16) gives uniqueness and good locality.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Both enforce uniqueness, but they differ in role. A table has one primary key, which can never contain NULL and is the row's identity (and the InnoDB clustered index). A table can have many unique keys, which may allow NULLs and are alternate access paths.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (
    id    INT         PRIMARY KEY,                 -- 1 per table, NOT NULL, clustered
    email VARCHAR(60) UNIQUE,                      -- many allowed, NULLs allowed
    pan   CHAR(10)    UNIQUE
);
SHOW INDEX FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +-------+------------+----------+-------------+
-- | Table | Non_unique | Key_name | Column_name |
-- +-------+------------+----------+-------------+
-- | emp   |          0 | PRIMARY  | id          |
-- | emp   |          0 | email    | email       |
-- | emp   |          0 | pan      | pan         |
-- +-------+------------+----------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You need both: the primary key says "this is row number N" for joins, foreign keys and updates; unique keys say "no two rows may share this business value". One mechanism cannot do both jobs.
codeExamples:
-- PK identifies the row to change; UNIQUE protects the business rule
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'abaji@x.com','ABCDE1234F');
UPDATE emp SET email = 'abaji@corp.com' WHERE id = 1;       -- identify by PK
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (2,'abaji@corp.com','ZZZZZ9999Z');   -- breaks the unique rule

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'abaji@corp.com' for key 'emp.email'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Optional identifiers (a tax number that some customers lack) belong in a UNIQUE column that allows NULL. A PK cannot be NULL, so it suits only mandatory identity.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (3,NULL,NULL),(4,NULL,NULL);     -- many NULLs in UNIQUE columns
SELECT id, email FROM emp WHERE email IS NULL ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | email |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  3 | NULL  |
-- |  4 | NULL  |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

                      PRIMARY KEY                     UNIQUE KEY
   per table          exactly 1                       0..many
   NULL allowed       never                           yes (many NULLs)
   InnoDB structure   clustered index (the table)     secondary index -> stores PK value
   default name       PRIMARY                         column or chosen name
   FK target          yes (usual)                     yes (allowed)
   purpose            row identity                    business uniqueness / alternate lookup

Fresher Notes

  • Both enforce uniqueness. A table has one primary key (NOT NULL) and can have many unique keys (NULLs allowed).
  • The primary key is the main row identifier; unique keys are alternate identifiers.
  • In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index.

Worked Example 1

Show keys of the table.
codeExamples:
SHOW INDEX FROM k;

-- OUTPUT: (trimmed)
-- Key_name | Column_name | Non_unique
-- PRIMARY  | id          | 0
-- code     | code        | 0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Tables without PK cause slow row-based replication (check).
codeExamples:
SELECT t.table_name FROM information_schema.tables t LEFT JOIN information_schema.statistics s
  ON s.table_schema=t.table_schema AND s.table_name=t.table_name AND s.index_name='PRIMARY'
WHERE t.table_schema = DATABASE() AND t.table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND s.index_name IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set  (all tables have a primary key)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Compare behaviour.

Practice Exercise 2

Primary key rejects NULL.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Both are backed by unique B-tree indexes, but the primary key is the clustered index: the leaf level stores the full row. A unique key is a secondary index whose leaf stores the key columns plus the primary key. That is why PK lookups return rows directly and unique-key lookups need an extra step for non-covered columns.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Differences in syntax and behaviour: one PRIMARY KEY per table (no NULLs), many UNIQUE keys (NULLs allowed, multiple NULLs allowed), the PK is named PRIMARY, only the PK defines the clustering, and replication tools prefer the PK.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO members (email, nick) VALUES ('a@x.com', NULL), ('b@x.com', NULL);       -- two NULL nicks: fine for UNIQUE
INSERT INTO members (id, email) VALUES (NULL, 'c@x.com');                         -- id gets AUTO_INCREMENT
SHOW KEYS FROM members WHERE Non_unique = 0;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Key_name | Column_name | Non_unique
-- PRIMARY  | id          | 0
-- uq_email | email       | 0
-- uq_nick  | nick        | 0

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of unique keys: they can be composite, so they express rules like "one seat per show", and there can be several per table.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a table without a primary key is allowed by default, and InnoDB then silently picks the first UNIQUE NOT NULL index or creates a hidden 6-byte row id. That hurts replication, row-based binlog performance and online tools. Teams enforce a PK with a server setting.
codeExamples:
SET SESSION sql_require_primary_key = 1;         -- 8.0.13+
CREATE TABLE no_pk (a INT UNIQUE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3750 (HY000): Unable to create or change a table without a primary key, when the
-- system variable 'sql_require_primary_key' is set. Add a primary key to the table or unset
-- this variable to avoid this message. Note that tables without a primary key can cause
-- performance problems in row-based replication, so please consult your DBA before changing this setting.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: primary key columns must be NOT NULL (MySQL rejects an explicit NULL), the key is always named PRIMARY, and changing it rebuilds the whole table and every secondary index because the clustered index is rewritten.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE bad_pk (a INT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (a));

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1171 (42000): All parts of a PRIMARY KEY must be NOT NULL; if you need NULL in a key,
-- use UNIQUE instead

-- Changing a PK is a table rebuild; plan it as a migration:
-- ALTER TABLE emp DROP PRIMARY KEY, ADD PRIMARY KEY (id, email);   -- copies the table

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Give every table a short, immutable primary key, and add UNIQUE constraints for each business identifier. Turn on sql_require_primary_key in production, because key-less tables cause replication lag and block tools such as online schema change. Remember that every unique index adds write cost and that the clustered PK is stored inside every secondary index entry.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Unique keys allow multiple NULLs in MySQL; primary keys never allow NULL.
  • Foreign keys normally reference the primary key.
  • Both create an index automatically.

Senior Notes

  • Primary key choice shapes physical storage and every secondary index; unique key choice shapes lookup and constraint behaviour.
  • A table without an explicit PK relies on the hidden row id, which hurts replication tools and ORMs.
  • Unique keys on nullable columns rarely mean what people expect; add NOT NULL when uniqueness must always hold.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no primary key (InnoDB invents a hidden one and row-based replication becomes slow), promoting a nullable unique column to a primary key (impossible), and expecting UNIQUE to reject duplicate NULLs. Define an explicit PK on every table.
codeExamples:
SELECT t.table_name FROM information_schema.tables t LEFT JOIN information_schema.statistics s ON s.table_schema = t.table_schema AND s.table_name = t.table_name AND s.index_name = 'PRIMARY'
WHERE t.table_schema = DATABASE() AND t.table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND s.index_name IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name
-- legacy_import        (needs a primary key)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Choose the primary key for physical effects (size, order) and unique keys for business rules. Changing the PK later rebuilds the table and every secondary index, so decide early.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: multi-tenant tables put tenant_id first in the primary key so each tenant's rows are contiguous, with a unique key on (tenant_id, email) for the business rule.

beginner.content:
Introduction

An index is a separate, sorted data structure (in InnoDB a B+Tree) that maps column values to the rows holding them, so MySQL can jump to matching rows instead of reading the whole table. Think of the index at the back of a book.
codeExamples:
-- Build a table, then ask the optimizer how it finds a row.
CREATE TABLE emp (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,          -- PRIMARY KEY is automatically indexed (clustered)
  email VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,     -- no index yet
  dept  INT
);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'a@x.com',10),(2,'b@x.com',20),(3,'c@x.com',10);

SHOW INDEX FROM emp;              -- list indexes on the table

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------------+----------+--------------+-------------+
-- | Table | Non_unique | Key_name | Seq_in_index | Column_name |
-- +-------+------------+----------+--------------+-------------+
-- | emp   |          0 | PRIMARY  |            1 | id          |
-- +-------+------------+----------+--------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without an index, WHERE email = ... must read every row (a full scan). Cost grows linearly with table size; an index makes it grow with the tree height (about 3-4 page reads even for hundreds of millions of rows).
codeExamples:
-- Same query, before and after an index on email.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM emp WHERE email = 'b@x.com';   -- type = ALL  (full scan)

CREATE INDEX idx_emp_email ON emp(email);            -- build a secondary index

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM emp WHERE email = 'b@x.com';   -- type = ref  (index lookup)

-- OUTPUT (key columns only):
-- +------+---------------+---------------+------+
-- | type | possible_keys | key           | rows |
-- +------+---------------+---------------+------+
-- | ALL  | NULL          | NULL          |    3 |   <- before
-- | ref  | idx_emp_email | idx_emp_email |    1 |   <- after
-- +------+---------------+---------------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical uses: login by email, order lookup by customer_id, foreign keys, sorting for pagination, enforcing uniqueness. Rule of thumb: index columns used in WHERE, JOIN ON, ORDER BY and GROUP BY of frequent queries.
codeExamples:
-- A realistic orders table with indexes that match its main queries.
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INT NOT NULL,
  status      VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
  created_at  DATETIME NOT NULL,
  KEY idx_cust_created (customer_id, created_at)   -- serves: "latest orders of a customer"
);
INSERT INTO orders(customer_id,status,created_at)
VALUES (7,'PAID','2024-01-02 10:00:00'),(7,'NEW','2024-02-01 09:00:00'),(8,'PAID','2024-01-05 08:00:00');

SELECT id, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;   -- no sort needed, index is ordered

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------------------+
-- | id | created_at          |
-- +----+---------------------+
-- |  2 | 2024-02-01 09:00:00 |
-- +----+---------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SELECT ... WHERE email='b@x.com'

   no index                      with index
   +-----+                       +---------+
   | row1| <- check              |  root   |
   | row2| <- check              +----+----+
   | row3| <- check (ALL)             |
   +-----+                       +----v----+
   O(n) page reads               |  leaf   | -> pointer to row
                                 +---------+
                                 O(log n) page reads

Fresher Notes

  • An index is a separate sorted structure that lets MySQL find rows without scanning the whole table, like a book index.
  • Create one with CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email);.
  • Indexes speed up reads (WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY) but slow writes and use disk.

Worked Example 1

Find redundant indexes.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name FROM sys.schema_redundant_indexes WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | redundant_index_name | dominant_index_name
-- people     | idx_a                | idx_a_b

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Index maintenance cost shows on bulk insert.
codeExamples:
-- 1M rows: no secondary indexes ~ 8 s, 5 secondary indexes ~ 30 s
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.statistics WHERE table_name = 'people';

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Index speeds up a lookup.

Practice Exercise 2

List indexes.
codeExamples:
SHOW INDEX FROM people;

-- OUTPUT: (trimmed)
-- Key_name  | Column_name
-- PRIMARY   | id
-- idx_email | email

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An index is a separate B-tree keyed by the indexed columns, whose entries point to rows. Without it the engine reads every row (a table scan). With it the engine descends 3-4 pages to the first match and then reads neighbouring entries in sorted order, which is why indexes serve equality, ranges, ordering and grouping.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Create indexes with CREATE INDEX, ALTER TABLE ADD INDEX, or inline. Variants: UNIQUE, composite, prefix, descending, functional, FULLTEXT, SPATIAL, and INVISIBLE indexes (8.0) that the optimizer ignores so you can test dropping safely.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: orders-of-magnitude faster lookups, range scans and ORDER BY; enforces uniqueness; speeds up joins and foreign-key checks; can answer a query without touching the table (covering).
codeExamples:
-- Index gives sorted output for free: no "Using filesort".
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at;

-- OUTPUT (Extra column):
-- +------+-----------------+--------------------------+
-- | type | key             | Extra                    |
-- +------+-----------------+--------------------------+
-- | ref  | idx_cust_created| Using where; Using index |   -- (example) ordered + covering
-- +------+-----------------+--------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must also maintain each index (slower writes), indexes consume disk and buffer-pool memory, and too many indexes confuse the optimizer and bloat backups.

Limitations

Limitations: an index helps only if the predicate can use it: functions on the column, leading wildcards, implicit type conversions and low-selectivity columns defeat it. InnoDB allows max 64 secondary indexes per table and 16 columns per composite index; key length is limited to 3072 bytes.
codeExamples:
-- A function on the indexed column disables the index.
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024;          -- scans: index unusable
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2025-01-01';       -- range scan on i2

-- OUTPUT (type column):
-- +-------+
-- | type  |
-- +-------+
-- | index |   <- full index scan (function hides the order)
-- | range |   <- sargable rewrite
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat indexes as a write-cost-for-read-speed trade. Derive them from the real query workload (slow log, performance_schema), keep them few and composite, drop redundant ones, and re-verify with EXPLAIN after data growth. Remember that every index competes for the buffer pool.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY, starting with the most selective and frequently filtered.
  • Each INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must maintain every index on the table, so do not index everything.
  • Use EXPLAIN to confirm an index is actually used.

Senior Notes

  • Indexes cost memory in the buffer pool; a few well-designed composite indexes beat many single-column ones.
  • Remove unused and duplicate indexes (sys.schema_unused_indexes, sys.schema_redundant_indexes).
  • Design indexes from the query workload, not from table columns.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: indexing every column, indexing low-selectivity flags alone, duplicate and redundant indexes, and functions on the indexed column in queries. Each index slows writes and uses memory; find waste with the sys schema.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name FROM sys.schema_redundant_indexes WHERE table_schema = 'shop';
SELECT object_name, index_name FROM sys.schema_unused_indexes WHERE object_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | redundant_index_name | dominant_index_name
-- orders     | idx_customer         | idx_customer_created
-- object_name | index_name
-- people      | idx_old_city

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Indexes cost write time: every INSERT, DELETE and indexed UPDATE maintains each index. Measure bulk insert speed with and without secondary indexes, and add indexes after large loads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world method: collect the top queries by total time, design one composite index per access pattern, test it as INVISIBLE or on a copy, compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE, then roll out with online DDL.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL InnoDB indexes are B+Trees: a balanced, sorted tree where internal nodes hold keys and leaf nodes hold all entries, chained left-to-right in a doubly linked list. Each node is a 16 KB page, so the tree is very wide and very shallow.
codeExamples:
-- Which index type does a table use?  InnoDB: BTREE (hash is only for MEMORY/ADAPTIVE).
CREATE TABLE t_bt (k INT, v VARCHAR(10), INDEX idx_k (k) USING BTREE);

SELECT index_name, index_type FROM information_schema.statistics
WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 't_bt';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+------------+
-- | INDEX_NAME | INDEX_TYPE |
-- +------------+------------+
-- | idx_k      | BTREE      |
-- +------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A B+Tree supports equality, range, prefix and ORDER BY efficiently because keys stay sorted, and it stays balanced as rows are inserted (pages split) or deleted (pages merge), so every lookup costs the same number of page reads.
codeExamples:
-- Sorted leaves => range scans are cheap and ordered.
CREATE TABLE nums (n INT PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO nums VALUES (10),(20),(30),(40),(50);

EXPLAIN SELECT n FROM nums WHERE n BETWEEN 20 AND 40;   -- type=range, one descent + leaf walk
SELECT n FROM nums WHERE n BETWEEN 20 AND 40;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+
-- | n  |
-- +----+
-- | 20 |
-- | 30 |
-- | 40 |
-- +----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real-world sizing: with a 4-byte INT key a page holds about 1000 entries, so 3 levels address ~1 billion rows. That is why a primary-key lookup on a huge table still takes only ~3 page reads (the root is nearly always cached).
codeExamples:
-- Estimate the tree for your table: pages used by the clustered index.
SELECT table_name, table_rows, ROUND(data_length/1024/1024,1) AS data_mb,
       ROUND(index_length/1024/1024,1) AS index_mb
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'orders';

-- Height rule of thumb:  levels ~ ceil( log_fanout(rows) ),  fanout ~ 16384 / (key_bytes + 6~12)

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+------------+---------+----------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | TABLE_ROWS | data_mb | index_mb |
-- +------------+------------+---------+----------+
-- | orders     |          3 |     0.0 |      0.0 |
-- +------------+------------+---------+----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

                    [ root page: 40 | 80 ]
                   /          |                  [10 20 30]       [40 50 60 70]     [80 90 99]     <- internal / leaf pages
         | | |  <---->     | | | |   <---->  | | |         leaves chained
         rows               rows              rows

   lookup 50: root -> middle child -> leaf (3 page reads)
   range 20..60: seek 20, then walk the leaf chain

Fresher Notes

  • The default MySQL index type is a B-tree (B+tree in InnoDB): a balanced, sorted tree of pages.
  • It supports equality (=), ranges (>, <, BETWEEN), prefix LIKE and ORDER BY.
  • Lookups take a few page reads even for millions of rows.

Worked Example 1

Estimate tree height from rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT CEIL(LOG(1000000) / LOG(500)) AS approx_levels;

-- OUTPUT:
-- approx_levels
-- 3

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rebuild a fragmented table.

Practice Exercise 1

Range query uses the B-tree order.

Practice Exercise 2

Index size on disk.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, ROUND(stat_value * @@innodb_page_size / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS mb
FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE database_name = DATABASE() AND table_name = 'people' AND stat_name = 'size';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name | mb
-- PRIMARY    | 12.00
-- idx_city   |  5.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An InnoDB index is a B+tree of 16 KB pages: internal pages hold keys and child pointers, leaf pages hold entries and are chained left to right. A page with 8-byte keys holds hundreds of entries, so a 100-million-row table needs only about 4 levels. Range scans walk the leaf chain without going back up.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, stat_name, stat_value, stat_description FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE database_name = 'shop' AND table_name = 'orders' AND stat_name IN ('n_leaf_pages','size');
SELECT CEIL(LOG(100000000) / LOG(400)) AS approx_levels_for_100m_rows;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name | stat_name    | stat_value
-- PRIMARY    | n_leaf_pages |      22000
-- approx_levels_for_100m_rows
-- 4

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

A B-tree supports equality, ranges, prefix LIKE, ORDER BY, MIN/MAX, and the leftmost prefix of composite keys. It does not help with suffix or contains LIKE, with functions on the column, or with conditions that skip the leading column.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-07';          -- range: yes
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM customers WHERE name LIKE 'As%';                                           -- prefix: yes
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM customers WHERE name LIKE '%sha';                                          -- suffix: no seek
EXPLAIN SELECT MIN(created_at) FROM orders;                                                       -- index end: instant

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- range / range / index (full index scan) / Select tables optimized away

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: handles =, <, >, BETWEEN, LIKE 'abc%', ORDER BY and MIN/MAX; predictable O(log n); stays balanced automatically; sequential leaf chain gives fast range scans.
codeExamples:
-- MIN/MAX are answered by walking to the end of the tree: "Select tables optimized away".
EXPLAIN SELECT MAX(n), MIN(n) FROM nums;

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +------------------------------+
-- | Extra                        |
-- +------------------------------+
-- | Select tables optimized away |
-- +------------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: random-key inserts (e.g. UUID v4) cause page splits and fragmentation; every write may touch several pages; deep trees from wide keys cost more I/O; a LIKE '%abc' search cannot use the tree order.
codeExamples:
-- Leading wildcard: the sorted order is useless.
CREATE TABLE people (name VARCHAR(30), INDEX (name));
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM people WHERE name LIKE 'Ann%';    -- range: uses the tree
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM people WHERE name LIKE '%ann';    -- full index/table scan

-- OUTPUT (type):
-- +-------+
-- | range |   <- 'Ann%'
-- | index |   <- '%ann'  (scans whole index, cannot seek)
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: pages are 16 KB by default (innodb_page_size, fixed at initialisation), index key max 3072 bytes, and B-Trees do not support hashed O(1) lookup or text relevance search (use hash/Adaptive Hash Index or FULLTEXT). Descending indexes are real only since MySQL 8.0.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL 8: descending index keys are honoured.
CREATE TABLE ev (id INT PRIMARY KEY, ts DATETIME, KEY idx_ts_desc (ts DESC));
SHOW INDEX FROM ev WHERE Key_name = 'idx_ts_desc';

-- OUTPUT (Collation: D = descending):
-- +----------+-------------+-----------+
-- | Key_name | Column_name | Collation |
-- +----------+-------------+-----------+
-- | idx_ts_desc | ts       | D         |
-- +----------+-------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer monotonically increasing primary keys (AUTO_INCREMENT, UUIDv7/ULID, or UUID_TO_BIN(uuid,1)) to avoid page-split churn. Keep keys narrow because every secondary index entry stores the primary key too. Rebuild (OPTIMIZE / ALTER ... ENGINE=InnoDB) only when fragmentation is measured, not by habit.

Mid-Level Notes

  • InnoDB pages are 16 KB; each node holds many keys, so the tree is shallow (usually 3-4 levels).
  • Leaf pages are linked, making range scans fast.
  • Random inserts cause page splits; ordered inserts append efficiently.

Senior Notes

  • Tree height grows slowly, so lookup cost is nearly constant; the real cost is cache misses when the index does not fit in the buffer pool.
  • Wide keys reduce fan-out, increasing height and I/O; keep keys small.
  • Fill factor and fragmentation: heavy random deletes/updates leave pages half empty; rebuild with ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=InnoDB when needed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: random keys (UUIDv4) causing page splits and fragmentation, very wide keys lowering fan-out, and never rebuilding indexes after heavy churn. Watch page fill and rebuild when needed.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND(data_free / 1048576) AS free_mb, ROUND(data_length / 1048576) AS data_mb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY data_free DESC LIMIT 2;
ALTER TABLE events ENGINE = InnoDB;          -- rebuild table and indexes online

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | free_mb | data_mb
-- events     |    4200 |   11000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The buffer pool caches index pages. A hot index that fits in memory makes lookups cost zero disk reads. Compare the index size to the pool and check hit rates.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(stat_value) * @@innodb_page_size / 1073741824, 2) AS index_gb FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE database_name = 'shop' AND stat_name = 'size';
SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size / 1073741824 AS pool_gb;

-- OUTPUT:
-- index_gb
-- 18.40
-- pool_gb
-- 24.0000          (all indexes fit: lookups are served from memory)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: monotonic keys such as auto-increment ids and time-ordered UUIDs append at the right edge, keep pages full and make bulk insert fast; plan the key type to match the access pattern.

beginner.content:
Introduction

In InnoDB the table is its clustered index: a B+Tree on the primary key whose leaf pages contain the full rows. A secondary index is another B+Tree whose leaves hold the indexed columns plus the primary-key value, not a row address.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE cust (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,         -- clustered: leaves store the entire row
  email VARCHAR(50),
  city  VARCHAR(20),
  KEY idx_city (city)            -- secondary: leaves store (city, id)
);
INSERT INTO cust VALUES (1,'a@x','Pune'),(2,'b@x','Delhi'),(3,'c@x','Pune');

SHOW INDEX FROM cust;

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +----------+-------------+
-- | Key_name | Column_name |
-- +----------+-------------+
-- | PRIMARY  | id          |
-- | idx_city | city        |
-- +----------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The design matters for performance: primary-key lookups are one tree walk, but a secondary lookup is two (secondary tree, then clustered tree via the PK, called a "bookmark lookup"). It also means the PK size is copied into every secondary index.
codeExamples:
-- Secondary lookup returning non-indexed columns costs the second descent.
EXPLAIN SELECT email FROM cust WHERE city = 'Pune';     -- ref on idx_city, then fetch row by id
EXPLAIN SELECT id    FROM cust WHERE city = 'Pune';     -- id is already inside idx_city leaves

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +-------------+
-- | Extra       |
-- +-------------+
-- | NULL        |   <- needs the clustered index lookup for email
-- | Using index |   <- covering: PK is stored in the secondary leaf
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real design rules: always declare a short, stable, increasing PK. If you do not, InnoDB picks the first NOT NULL UNIQUE index, otherwise a hidden 6-byte row id. Wide PKs (long VARCHAR, UUID text) inflate every secondary index.
codeExamples:
-- Compare secondary index size with narrow vs wide PK (conceptual measure).
CREATE TABLE a_int  (id INT PRIMARY KEY, c INT, KEY(c));                -- entry ~ 4 + 4 bytes
CREATE TABLE a_uuid (id CHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY, c INT, KEY(c));           -- entry ~ 4 + 36 bytes

SELECT table_name, index_length FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name IN ('a_int','a_uuid');

-- OUTPUT (example, after loading 1M rows each):
-- +------------+--------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | INDEX_LENGTH |
-- +------------+--------------+
-- | a_int      |     21495808 |
-- | a_uuid     |     86114304 |   <- ~4x bigger secondary index
-- +------------+--------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Clustered (PRIMARY KEY id)            Secondary (city)
   +----------------------+              +--------------------+
   | leaf: id=1 | full row|              | leaf: (Delhi , 2)  |
   | leaf: id=2 | full row| <------------| leaf: (Pune  , 1)  |
   | leaf: id=3 | full row|   PK value   | leaf: (Pune  , 3)  |
   +----------------------+   = pointer  +--------------------+

   SELECT email WHERE city='Pune':  secondary tree -> id -> clustered tree -> row

Fresher Notes

  • In InnoDB the table itself is the clustered index: rows are stored in primary-key order inside the PK B-tree.
  • Every other index is a secondary index: it stores its columns plus the primary key value.
  • A secondary lookup finds the PK, then does a second lookup in the clustered index (bookmark lookup).

Worked Example 1

Make it covering.

Worked Example 2

Random PK causes splits; compare sizes.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND(data_length/1024/1024) AS data_mb, ROUND(index_length/1024/1024) AS idx_mb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('ord_uuid','ord_seq');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | data_mb | idx_mb
-- ord_uuid   |     780 |    410
-- ord_seq    |     520 |    230

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Secondary index covers PK.

Practice Exercise 2

Needs a row lookup for total.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT total FROM ord WHERE customer_id = 5;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key      | Extra
-- ref  | idx_cust | NULL            (back to clustered index for total)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In InnoDB the table is the clustered index: its leaf pages hold full rows ordered by the primary key. A secondary index leaf holds its key columns plus the primary key. A query that needs other columns first finds the primary key in the secondary index, then performs a lookup in the clustered index (a "bookmark lookup").

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Control the cost of lookups: choose a small primary key, add covering secondary indexes for hot queries, and use deferred joins when a query selects wide rows after sorting by a narrow index.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: clustered: row access by PK is the fastest possible and range scans on PK read contiguous pages. Secondary: unlimited extra access paths, and moving a row does not require pointer updates (they store the PK, not a physical address).
codeExamples:
-- PK range scan reads physically adjacent pages.
CREATE TABLE log_t (id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, msg VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO log_t(msg) VALUES ('a'),('b'),('c'),('d');
SELECT id, msg FROM log_t WHERE id BETWEEN 2 AND 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+
-- | id | msg  |
-- +----+------+
-- |  2 | b    |
-- |  3 | c    |
-- +----+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: secondary lookups pay a double traversal; updating the PK moves the row and rewrites all secondary entries; random PKs fragment the table; only one clustered index exists per table.
codeExamples:
-- Changing a PK value is expensive: the row relocates and every secondary entry changes.
UPDATE cust SET id = 100 WHERE id = 1;     -- avoid; treat PKs as immutable
SELECT id, city FROM cust ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-------+
-- | id  | city  |
-- +-----+-------+
-- |   2 | Delhi |
-- |   3 | Pune  |
-- | 100 | Pune  |
-- +-----+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: you cannot choose a different clustering key without redefining the PK; MyISAM uses non-clustered (heap) tables with row pointers instead, so these rules are InnoDB-specific. Tables without a PK also break row-based replication efficiency and Group Replication.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL 8.0.13+: enforce that every new table has a PK (important for replication).
SET SESSION sql_require_primary_key = ON;
CREATE TABLE no_pk (x INT);                 -- rejected

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3750 (HY000): Unable to create or change a table without a primary key,
--   when the system variable 'sql_require_primary_key' is set.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick the PK for locality and brevity: BIGINT auto-increment for write-heavy OLTP, or time-ordered IDs when ids must be generated client side.
