Because secondary indexes embed the PK, a 16-byte BINARY(16) UUID beats CHAR(36) by a wide margin. Consider covering indexes to dodge the second traversal on hot queries.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Primary-key lookups are the fastest because the row is right at the leaf.
  • Secondary indexes silently include the PK columns, so you can use them for covering queries on (indexed cols + PK).
  • Large PKs enlarge every secondary index.

Senior Notes

  • Choose a short, monotonic PK: it keeps the clustered tree compact and inserts sequential.
  • Use covering indexes to avoid the second lookup on hot queries.
  • Without an explicit PK InnoDB uses the first unique NOT NULL index or a hidden 6-byte row id.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: wide or random primary keys (copied into every secondary index), updating primary key values, and expecting a secondary index scan to be cheap when it returns a large fraction of rows (many random lookups). The optimizer then prefers a table scan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM ord WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 1 AND 90000;     -- most of the table: scan chosen
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM ord FORCE INDEX (idx_customer) WHERE customer_id BETWEEN 1 AND 90000;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- first : type=ALL                (cheaper than 800k bookmark lookups)
-- second: type=range              (much slower in practice)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Check how many bytes each secondary index entry carries and whether a covering index is worth it: if the extra columns are small, covering removes the random reads.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, ROUND(SUM(stat_value) * @@innodb_page_size / 1048576) AS mb FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE database_name = 'shop' AND table_name = 'ord' AND stat_name = 'size' GROUP BY index_name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name         | mb
-- PRIMARY            | 520
-- idx_customer       | 120
-- idx_customer_total | 150

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a feed query returns many columns but sorts by a narrow key. Fetch ids from the narrow covering index, then fetch rows by primary key, reducing random I/O.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.id, p.title, p.body FROM posts p JOIN (SELECT id FROM posts WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20) x ON x.id = p.id ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title | body
-- 88 | ...   | ...

beginner.content:
Introduction

A composite (multi-column) index sorts entries by the first column, then the second within equal firsts, and so on, like a phone book sorted by last name then first name. The leftmost-prefix rule: it can serve predicates on (a), (a,b), (a,b,c), but not (b) or (c) alone.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp2 (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept INT, grade INT, name VARCHAR(20),
  KEY idx_dept_grade (dept, grade)         -- sorted by dept, then grade
);
INSERT INTO emp2 VALUES (1,10,3,'A'),(2,10,5,'B'),(3,20,3,'C'),(4,20,4,'D');

EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp2 WHERE dept = 10 AND grade = 5;   -- uses both columns (key_len 10)

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +------+----------------+---------+
-- | type | key            | key_len |
-- +------+----------------+---------+
-- | ref  | idx_dept_grade | 10      |   <- 5 + 5 bytes (INT NULL = 5)
-- +------+----------------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

One composite index replaces several single-column ones and supports multi-column filters plus sorting. Two single-column indexes cannot be combined as efficiently (index merge is a fallback, not a plan to rely on).
codeExamples:
-- Filter on dept, sort on grade: composite index gives both with no filesort.
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp2 WHERE dept = 20 ORDER BY grade;

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +-------+
-- | Extra |
-- +-------+
-- | NULL  |    <- no "Using filesort": rows come out ordered by grade within dept=20
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real-world: "orders of a customer by date", "events by tenant + type + time". Column order rule: equality columns first, then range column, and a sort column last; the first range predicate stops further columns from filtering.
codeExamples:
-- Equality on dept, range on grade: both used. Reverse: only the leading range column is used.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM emp2 WHERE dept = 10 AND grade > 3;    -- key_len 10 (both columns)
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM emp2 WHERE dept > 10 AND grade = 3;    -- key_len 5  (grade checked after)

-- OUTPUT (key_len):
-- +---------+
-- | 10      |
-- | 5       |
-- +---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   idx (dept, grade)  sorted entries:
   (10,3)(10,5) | (20,3)(20,4)
     ^ group by dept; inside a group, sorted by grade

   WHERE dept=10               -> seek group 10           OK  (prefix)
   WHERE dept=10 AND grade=5   -> seek (10,5)             OK
   WHERE grade=5               -> grades scattered        NO  (no leftmost)
   WHERE dept>10 AND grade=3   -> range on dept, filter   PARTIAL

Fresher Notes

  • A composite index covers several columns: INDEX (last_name, first_name, city).
  • MySQL can use it from the left: (a), (a,b), (a,b,c) work; (b) or (c) alone does not use it efficiently.
  • Column order matters most.

Worked Example 1

Index that serves filter plus sort.

Worked Example 2

Redundant single column index.
codeExamples:
SELECT redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name FROM sys.schema_redundant_indexes WHERE table_name = 'ord';

-- OUTPUT:
-- redundant_index_name | dominant_index_name
-- idx_cust             | idx_cust_date

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Leftmost prefix demo.

Practice Exercise 2

Range stops later columns.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM emp2 WHERE last_name = 'Rao' AND first_name > 'A' AND city = 'Pune';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key           | key_len
-- range | idx_name_city | 164   (city used only as a filter, not a seek)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A composite index sorts entries by the first column, then by the second within equal first values, and so on. A lookup can seek only through a prefix of those columns: equality on leading columns, then at most one range. Columns after a range column are used for filtering inside the scanned range, not for seeking.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Rules of thumb for ordering columns: equality predicates first, then the range column, then ORDER BY columns; put the most selective equality first only when queries differ. MySQL 8.0.13+ may use skip scan when the leading column has few values.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fewer indexes to maintain, covers many query shapes, supports ORDER BY after equality columns, and enables covering reads when all needed columns are included.
codeExamples:
-- The leading column alone is served too (prefix rule).
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp2 WHERE dept = 10;     -- uses idx_dept_grade (key_len 5)

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +------+----------------+---------+
-- | ref  | idx_dept_grade | 5       |
-- +------+----------------+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: wrong column order makes it useless for important queries; wide composites cost more space and write time; it is easy to create near-duplicates like (a) and (a,b).
codeExamples:
-- Skipping the leading column: the index cannot seek.
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM emp2 WHERE grade = 3;

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +-------+----------------+
-- | type  | key            |
-- +-------+----------------+
-- | ALL   | NULL           |    <- (example) tiny table: optimizer may also pick "index" full scan
-- +-------+----------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: max 16 columns; MySQL 8.0.13+ may use skip scan when the leading column has few distinct values, but this is a narrow optimisation, not a replacement for correct ordering. After a range predicate, later columns cannot narrow the seek.
codeExamples:
-- Skip scan (8.0.13+): few distinct leading values -> optimizer probes each one.
EXPLAIN SELECT dept, grade FROM emp2 WHERE grade = 3;

-- OUTPUT (Extra, example, only on larger data sets):
-- +------------------------------------------+
-- | Extra                                    |
-- +------------------------------------------+
-- | Using where; Using index for skip scan   |
-- +------------------------------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Design composites from the query list: equality columns, then range or sort column, with the most selective equality first only when it does not break ordering needs. Audit with sys.schema_redundant_indexes. Prefer one carefully ordered composite over three single-column indexes, and verify with EXPLAIN key_len which columns are really used.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Rule of thumb: equality columns first, then the range column, then ORDER BY columns.
  • A range condition stops index use for columns after it.
  • A composite (a,b) makes a separate index on (a) redundant.

Senior Notes

  • Order by selectivity and query shape, not blindly highest cardinality first; test with EXPLAIN on real data.
  • Index skip scan in 8.0.13 can use a composite when the leading column has few values, but do not rely on it.
  • Include columns of GROUP BY / ORDER BY to avoid filesort and temporary tables.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: wrong column order, many overlapping indexes, and a range column placed before equality columns. Remove indexes that are prefixes of others: (a) is redundant when (a,b) exists.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name FROM sys.schema_redundant_indexes WHERE table_schema = 'shop';
ALTER TABLE orders DROP INDEX idx_customer;          -- covered by idx_cust_status_created

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name | redundant_index_name | dominant_index_name
-- orders     | idx_customer         | idx_cust_status_created

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Sorting through the index removes filesort. The index must match the equality columns, then the ORDER BY columns in the same direction (or all reversed).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: design the index from the query, not from the table. For the order history screen "my orders by status, newest first" the index (customer_id, status, created_at, id) serves list, count and keyset pagination.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, total, created_at FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'PAID' AND (created_at, id) < ('2026-05-01', 9120) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id   | total  | created_at
-- 9118 | 450.00 | 2026-04-30 09:58:11

beginner.content:
Introduction

A UNIQUE index is a B-Tree that also rejects duplicate keys (NULLs are allowed and may repeat). A prefix index indexes only the first N characters/bytes of a string column, e.g. url(20), to save space.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  bio   TEXT,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_email (email),        -- no two users share an email
  KEY idx_bio (bio(30))               -- prefix index: only first 30 chars (required for TEXT)
);
INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('a@x.com');
INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('a@x.com');    -- duplicate

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'a@x.com' for key 'users.uq_email'

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Uniqueness is best enforced by the database, not application code (which races under concurrency). Prefix indexes exist because TEXT/BLOB columns cannot be indexed in full and long VARCHARs make fat trees.
codeExamples:
-- Pick a prefix length that keeps selectivity close to the full column.
CREATE TABLE urls (u VARCHAR(200));
INSERT INTO urls VALUES ('https://a.com/x'),('https://a.com/y'),('https://b.org/z'),('https://c.net/q');

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT u)                AS full_sel,
       COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(u,13))       AS p13,
       COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(u,16))       AS p16
FROM urls;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-----+-----+
-- | full_sel | p13 | p16 |
-- +----------+-----+-----+
-- |        4 |   3 |   4 |      <- 16 chars is enough here, 13 loses uniqueness
-- +----------+-----+-----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: UNIQUE on email, username, SKU, (tenant_id, external_id); prefix on long URLs, file paths and tokens where the first 10-20 characters discriminate well.
codeExamples:
-- Composite unique: unique per tenant, not globally. NULL values do not conflict.
CREATE TABLE sku (tenant INT, code VARCHAR(20), UNIQUE KEY uq_t_code (tenant, code));
INSERT INTO sku VALUES (1,'A'),(2,'A'),(1,NULL),(1,NULL);   -- all accepted
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sku;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 4 |
-- +---+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   full index on url(200)            prefix index url(16)
   +---------------------------+     +------------------+
   | https://a.com/xyz...(200) |     | https://a.com/x  |  -> candidates
   +---------------------------+     +------------------+
   big entries, fewer per page       small entries, more per page
                                     then re-check full value in the row

   UNIQUE: insert -> probe index -> found? -> ERROR 1062

Fresher Notes

  • A unique index forbids duplicate values and also speeds lookups. A prefix index indexes only the first N characters of a string column.
  • Create prefix: CREATE INDEX idx_title ON posts (title(20));
  • Prefix indexes are needed for long strings and TEXT columns.

Worked Example 1

Hash column for long values.

Worked Example 2

Unique prefix pitfall.

Practice Exercise 1

Pick a prefix length.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT title) AS full_cnt, COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(title,10)) AS p10, COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(title,20)) AS p20 FROM posts;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- full_cnt | p10   | p20
--    98000 | 81000 | 97500

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Create and use it.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A unique index is a B-tree that also rejects duplicate keys. A prefix index stores only the first N characters (or bytes) of a string column, making the index much smaller; entries with the same prefix are then compared on the full value in the row, so selectivity depends on how distinct the prefixes are.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Uses: UNIQUE for business rules; prefix indexes for long VARCHAR/TEXT; hash columns for very long strings; functional unique indexes for case-insensitive rules. Prefix indexes cannot cover queries or serve ORDER BY on the whole value.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: UNIQUE gives correctness plus fast lookups and lets INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE work; prefix indexes shrink index size and speed up writes.
codeExamples:
-- UNIQUE enables atomic upsert, race-free.
INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('b@x.com')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE bio = 'seen again';       -- first time: insert
INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('b@x.com')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE bio = 'seen again';       -- second time: update
SELECT email, bio FROM users WHERE email = 'b@x.com';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------------+
-- | email   | bio        |
-- +---------+------------+
-- | b@x.com | seen again |
-- +---------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: unique checks add locking on insert (and can deadlock); prefix indexes cannot be used as covering indexes, cannot satisfy ORDER BY fully, and a poor prefix length gives many false candidates.
codeExamples:
-- A prefix index is never covering: the full value must be read from the row.
EXPLAIN SELECT bio FROM users WHERE bio LIKE 'hello%';

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +-------------+
-- | Extra       |
-- +-------------+
-- | Using where |    <- no "Using index": table row must be fetched to verify the whole value
-- +-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB prefix length max 767 bytes (REDUNDANT/COMPACT) or 3072 bytes (DYNAMIC, default); with utf8mb4 that is 768 characters. Case/accent rules follow the collation, so 'A' and 'a' collide under utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci. A unique index cannot span a hash expression without a generated column.

Architect's Notes

Use UNIQUE for every natural business key; it is the only safe race-proof guard. For long strings consider a generated column holding a hash (e.g. SHA2 or CRC32) with an index instead of a prefix when equality search is the only need. Choose prefix length by measuring selectivity, not by guessing.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Choose the prefix length by selectivity: compare COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(col,N)) with COUNT(DISTINCT col).
  • Prefix indexes cannot be covering indexes and cannot be used for ORDER BY of the full value.
  • Unique prefix indexes enforce uniqueness only on the prefix, which can wrongly reject different values.

Senior Notes

  • Alternatives to long indexed strings: a hash column (CRC32/SHA2) with an index plus equality check, or a generated column.
  • Index key length limit is 3072 bytes in InnoDB (utf8mb4 is 4 bytes per char).
  • Do not use UNIQUE on prefixes unless the semantic rule is truly "prefix is unique".

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: UNIQUE on a prefix (different values rejected as duplicates), index key length over the limit (3072 bytes in InnoDB DYNAMIC rows), and a prefix too short to be selective.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Smaller keys mean more entries per page, a shallower tree and a smaller buffer pool footprint. Measure index size before and after shortening.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, ROUND(SUM(stat_value) * @@innodb_page_size / 1048576) AS mb FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE table_name = 'posts' AND stat_name = 'size' GROUP BY index_name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name  | mb
-- idx_title   | 410          (full VARCHAR(255) utf8mb4)
-- idx_title16 |  62

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: deduplicating imported URLs or documents uses a hash unique key, so equality lookups are tiny and exact, and collisions are checked by comparing the full value.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A FULLTEXT index (InnoDB: inverted index of word to document) powers natural-language search with MATCH ... AGAINST. A SPATIAL index is an R-Tree over geometry columns (POINT, POLYGON) used for location queries.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE article (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  title VARCHAR(100),
  body  TEXT,
  FULLTEXT KEY ft_title_body (title, body)       -- inverted index
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO article VALUES
 (1,'MySQL indexing','B-tree and fulltext indexes explained'),
 (2,'Cooking pasta','boil water add salt'),
 (3,'Index tuning','choose good indexes for MySQL queries');

SELECT id, title FROM article WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----------------+
-- | id | title          |
-- +----+----------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL indexing |
-- |  3 | Index tuning   |
-- +----+----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

LIKE '%word%' cannot use a B-Tree and scans everything; it also has no ranking. FULLTEXT tokenises words, ignores stop-words, and returns a relevance score. Spatial indexes make "within 5 km" a tree probe, not a calculation on every row.
codeExamples:
-- Relevance score and boolean mode operators (+ must, - must not, * prefix).
SELECT id, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql indexes') AS score
FROM article
WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('+mysql -tuning' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+---------------------+
-- | id | score               |
-- +----+---------------------+
-- |  1 |  0.2272727340459824 |
-- +----+---------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: site search, help-desk ticket search, log keyword search (small scale); store locator and geofencing with POINT + SPATIAL index and ST_Distance_Sphere or ST_Contains.
codeExamples:
-- Spatial index requires NOT NULL geometry and an SRID (use 4326 for lat/long on Earth).
CREATE TABLE store (
  id  INT PRIMARY KEY,
  loc POINT NOT NULL SRID 4326,
  SPATIAL INDEX sp_loc (loc)
);
INSERT INTO store VALUES (1, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(18.52 73.85)', 4326)),   -- Pune-ish (lat long order for SRID 4326)
                         (2, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(28.61 77.20)', 4326));   -- Delhi-ish

-- Distance in km from a reference point to each store.
SELECT id, ROUND(ST_Distance(loc, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(18.52 73.85)', 4326)) / 1000) AS km
FROM store ORDER BY km;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+------+
-- | id | km   |
-- +----+------+
-- |  1 |    0 |
-- |  2 | 1170 |
-- +----+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   documents                 inverted index (FULLTEXT)
   1: "mysql indexing"       mysql    -> [1, 3]
   2: "cooking pasta"        indexing -> [1]
   3: "index tuning mysql"   pasta    -> [2]
                             query 'mysql' -> docs 1,3 (ranked)

   SPATIAL (R-Tree): nested bounding rectangles
   +----------------------+
   | R1 +-----+  +----+   |   query box overlaps R1 only
   |    | s1  |  | s2 |   |   -> examine s1, skip R2 subtree
   +----------------------+

Fresher Notes

  • A FULLTEXT index supports searching words inside text with MATCH ... AGAINST. A SPATIAL index supports geographic queries on geometry columns.
  • Create: FULLTEXT (title, body) and SPATIAL INDEX (location).
  • Normal B-tree indexes cannot search inside text or by area.

Worked Example 1

Relevance score.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql indexes') AS score FROM docs ORDER BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | score
--  1 | 1.2
--  2 | 0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Minimum word size setting.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_ft_min_token_size';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name            | Value
-- innodb_ft_min_token_size | 3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

FULLTEXT search.

Practice Exercise 2

Spatial index and distance.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A FULLTEXT index stores an inverted index: for each word (token) a list of document ids and positions, with relevance statistics. MATCH AGAINST looks tokens up directly instead of scanning text. A SPATIAL index is an R-tree over minimum bounding rectangles, so geometric queries visit only nearby boxes.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

FULLTEXT modes: natural language, boolean (+must -not "phrase" prefix*), and query expansion; token size and stop words are configurable; the ngram parser handles CJK. Spatial: POINT/POLYGON columns with SRID and functions like ST_Distance_Sphere and ST_Contains.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fast word search with ranking, boolean operators, query expansion, ngram parser for CJK; R-Tree makes bounding-box and containment queries sub-linear.
codeExamples:
-- Boolean prefix search.
SELECT title FROM article WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('index*' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | title          |
-- +----------------+
-- | MySQL indexing |
-- | Index tuning   |
-- +----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: FULLTEXT is not a search engine: no fuzzy matching or stemming, results of newly inserted rows appear only after commit, large DML is slower, and relevance tuning is limited. Spatial index only helps MBR-based functions.
codeExamples:
-- Words shorter than innodb_ft_min_token_size (default 3) and stop-words are not indexed.
SELECT id FROM article WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('and');   -- 'and' is in the default stop-word list

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)      <- 'and' is a stop-word, nothing matches

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MATCH columns must equal exactly the columns of one FULLTEXT index; the 50 percent threshold rule applies in natural mode only for MyISAM, not InnoDB; spatial indexes require NOT NULL columns, and SRID-aware functions must use matching SRIDs.
codeExamples:
-- Columns in MATCH must correspond to an existing FULLTEXT index.
SELECT id FROM article WHERE MATCH(title) AGAINST('mysql');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1191 (HY000): Can't find FULLTEXT index matching the column list

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use FULLTEXT for modest, in-database search where operational simplicity wins; move to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch when you need typo tolerance, facets, analyzers or scale. For geo, keep SRID consistent across tables and use ST_Distance_Sphere with a bounding-box pre-filter so the spatial index is actually used.

Mid-Level Notes

  • FULLTEXT works with InnoDB and MyISAM; it ignores stop words and short words by default (innodb_ft_min_token_size).
  • Spatial indexes use R-trees and need NOT NULL geometry columns with an SRID.
  • Spatial functions: ST_Distance_Sphere, ST_Contains.

Senior Notes

  • For advanced relevance, typo tolerance and facets use a search engine; MySQL FULLTEXT is fine for basic site search.
  • Spatial: store points with SRID 4326 and use ST_Distance_Sphere with a bounding-box pre-filter.
  • Large FULLTEXT updates are async in the FTS cache; plan for slight indexing delay.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting FULLTEXT to find short or stop words, using LIKE '%x%' for word search, putting geometry into non-indexed columns, and ignoring SRID (distance results differ). Check innodb_ft_min_token_size.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_ft_min_token_size';
SELECT id FROM docs WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('db');     -- 2-letter word: not indexed with token size 3

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name            | Value
-- innodb_ft_min_token_size | 3
-- Empty set

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Bulk-load first and create the FULLTEXT index afterwards, since building it row by row is slow. For nearby searches prefilter with a bounding box so the R-tree is used before the exact distance function.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM shops WHERE MBRContains(ST_Buffer(ST_SRID(POINT(18.52, 73.85), 4326), 0.02), loc)
  AND ST_Distance_Sphere(loc, ST_SRID(POINT(18.52, 73.85), 4326)) < 2000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a help-centre search with FULLTEXT ranking, restricted to published articles, and a "stores near me" query using the spatial index.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('refund policy') AS score FROM articles WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED' AND MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('refund policy') ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title            | score
-- 12 | Refund policy    | 3.4

beginner.content:
Introduction

A covering index contains every column a query needs, so MySQL answers it from the index alone without reading the table rows. EXPLAIN shows Using index in Extra.

Why Do We Need This?

Row fetches are the expensive part of an index lookup: each one may be a random disk read into the clustered index. Eliminating them can turn a slow query into a memory-only one, especially for large result sets.
codeExamples:
-- Selecting a column that is not in the index forces row lookups.
EXPLAIN SELECT cust, note FROM sales WHERE cust = 7;       -- note not in index
EXPLAIN SELECT cust, amount, id FROM sales WHERE cust = 7; -- id (PK) is implicitly in every secondary index

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +-------------+
-- | NULL        |    <- must read table row for note
-- | Using index |    <- covered by (cust, amount, id)
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: hot list/dashboard queries (counts, sums by key), existence checks, pagination of ids, and "deferred join" tricks where a covering index finds the ids first and the table is read only for the page.
codeExamples:
-- Deferred join pagination: scan the narrow covering index, then fetch only 2 rows.
SELECT s.*
FROM (SELECT id FROM sales WHERE cust = 7 ORDER BY amount DESC LIMIT 2) AS p
JOIN sales s ON s.id = p.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------+--------+------+
-- | id | cust | amount | note |
-- +----+------+--------+------+
-- |  2 |    7 |  25.50 | y    |
-- |  1 |    7 |  10.00 | x    |
-- +----+------+--------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Normal secondary lookup            Covering lookup
   idx(cust) ---> PK id               idx(cust,amount) --> value found in leaf
        |                                   |
        v                                   v
   clustered tree --> row --> amount   return (Extra: Using index)
   (2 trees touched)                   (1 tree touched)

Fresher Notes

  • A covering index contains every column the query needs, so MySQL answers from the index without reading the table rows.
  • EXPLAIN shows Using index.
  • It avoids the extra lookup in the clustered index.

Worked Example 1

Covering with ORDER BY and LIMIT.

Worked Example 2

Compare rows read.

Practice Exercise 1

Make a list query index-only.

Practice Exercise 2

Selecting an uncovered column breaks it.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT status, note FROM orders2 WHERE customer_id = 7;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key     | Extra
-- ref  | idx_cov | NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When every column a query needs is in one secondary index, InnoDB answers it from the index leaf pages alone, with no clustered index lookup. Secondary indexes already include the primary key, so selecting the primary key is free. EXPLAIN shows "Using index".

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Order columns: equality filters first, then range/order columns, then payload columns at the end. MySQL has no INCLUDE columns, so payload columns become part of the key. Keep it narrow and only for hot queries.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: avoids the clustered-index lookup, reduces random I/O, keeps hot data compact in the buffer pool, and often removes the sort too.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL 8: INCLUDE-style trick - add trailing columns purely to cover.
ALTER TABLE sales ADD KEY idx_cover (cust, amount, note(20));   -- prefix: not truly covering for note
SHOW INDEX FROM sales WHERE Key_name = 'idx_cover';

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +----------+--------------+-------------+-----------+
-- | Key_name | Seq_in_index | Column_name | Sub_part  |
-- +----------+--------------+-------------+-----------+
-- | idx_cover|            1 | cust        | NULL      |
-- | idx_cover|            2 | amount      | NULL      |
-- | idx_cover|            3 | note        | 20        |
-- +----------+--------------+-------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a wide covering index uses more memory and slows writes; it is tuned to a specific query, so changing the SELECT list silently breaks covering; SELECT * almost never covers.
codeExamples:
-- SELECT * destroys covering.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sales WHERE cust = 7;

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +-------+
-- | NULL  |     <- (example) row lookups needed for every match
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: there is no INCLUDE clause in MySQL (unlike SQL Server/PostgreSQL), so covering columns also join the sort key; prefix-indexed, TEXT/BLOB and spatial columns cannot cover; max key length applies.
codeExamples:
-- No INCLUDE syntax in MySQL.
CREATE INDEX idx_inc ON sales (cust) INCLUDE (amount);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): You have an error in your SQL syntax ... near 'INCLUDE (amount)'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Add covering columns only for the few queries that dominate load and are stable. Weigh the extra index bytes against saved I/O; use the sys schema and Handler_read_* counters to prove the gain. Avoid SELECT * in application code so covering remains possible.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Include filter columns first, then ORDER BY columns, then selected columns at the end.
  • Because secondary indexes already contain the primary key, you can select the PK for free.
  • 8.0 supports INCLUDE-like behaviour only by adding columns to the index key.

Senior Notes

  • Covering indexes are the biggest single win for read-heavy list queries, but each extra column grows the index and slows writes.
  • Keep covering indexes narrow: only for hot, stable queries.
  • Watch for TEXT/BLOB columns, which cannot be fully included.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: covering indexes with TEXT/BLOB columns (cannot), many wide covering indexes that slow writes and fill memory, and selecting extra columns that silently break the coverage. Select exactly what you cover.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders2 WHERE customer_id = 7;                 -- not covered
EXPLAIN SELECT id, status, total FROM orders2 WHERE customer_id = 7;  -- covered

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- first : Extra=NULL (bookmark lookups)       second: Extra=Using index

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Covering indexes shine for list pages, existence checks and counts. Compare rows read and time with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an autocomplete or lookup endpoint that returns two columns for thousands of requests per second. A narrow covering index keeps it entirely in memory.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Cardinality is the estimated number of distinct values in an index. Selectivity = distinct values / total rows (0 to 1). High selectivity (near 1, like email) means an index narrows to few rows; low selectivity (like gender) does not.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE person (id INT PRIMARY KEY, gender CHAR(1), email VARCHAR(40), KEY(gender), KEY(email));
INSERT INTO person VALUES (1,'M','a@x'),(2,'F','b@x'),(3,'M','c@x'),(4,'F','d@x');

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT gender)/COUNT(*) AS sel_gender,
       COUNT(DISTINCT email)/COUNT(*)  AS sel_email
FROM person;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | sel_gender | sel_email |
-- +------------+-----------+
-- |     0.5000 |    1.0000 |
-- +------------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The optimizer decides whether an index is worth using from cardinality statistics. If a predicate matches more than roughly 20-30 percent of rows, scanning the table sequentially is cheaper than thousands of random index lookups, so the index is ignored.
codeExamples:
-- SHOW INDEX exposes the optimizer's cardinality estimate.
SHOW INDEX FROM person;

-- OUTPUT (partial, example):
-- +----------+-------------+-------------+
-- | Key_name | Column_name | Cardinality |
-- +----------+-------------+-------------+
-- | PRIMARY  | id          |           4 |
-- | gender   | gender      |           2 |
-- | email    | email       |           4 |
-- +----------+-------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: decide index order in composites (selective column early, unless ordering needs dictate otherwise), spot useless indexes, and refresh stale statistics after bulk loads so plans stay good.
codeExamples:
-- Statistics are sampled; refresh after big data changes.
ANALYZE TABLE person;

-- MySQL 8: histograms help when the column is NOT indexed or data is skewed.
ANALYZE TABLE person UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON gender WITH 4 BUCKETS;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+---------+----------+----------+
-- | Table            | Op      | Msg_type | Msg_text |
-- +------------------+---------+----------+----------+
-- | db.person        | analyze | status   | OK       |
-- | db.person        | histogram | status | Histogram statistics created for column 'gender'. |
-- +------------------+---------+----------+----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   selectivity = distinct / rows

   email   1.00  |############################| great index
   city    0.05  |##                          | ok with other columns
   gender  0.00  |                            | poor (2 values)

   WHERE gender='F' -> 50% of rows -> optimizer: full scan cheaper

Fresher Notes

  • Cardinality is the number of distinct values in a column; selectivity is distinct values divided by total rows (closer to 1 is better).
  • A unique column has the best selectivity; a boolean flag has very poor selectivity.
  • The optimizer uses these statistics to decide whether to use an index.

Worked Example 1

Skewed value check.
codeExamples:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n, ROUND(COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER () * 100, 2) AS pct FROM orders2 GROUP BY status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- status | n     | pct
-- NEW    |   120 |  0.12
-- DONE   | 91000 | 91.00

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Create a histogram.
codeExamples:
ANALYZE TABLE orders2 UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON status WITH 8 BUCKETS;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table          | Op        | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.orders2   | histogram | status   | Histogram statistics created for column 'status'.

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Compute selectivity.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT status) / COUNT(*) AS sel_status, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) / COUNT(*) AS sel_customer FROM orders2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- sel_status | sel_customer
--     0.0001 |       0.2300

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

See cardinality estimates.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Cardinality is the estimated number of distinct values in an index; selectivity is cardinality divided by rows. InnoDB estimates cardinality by sampling pages (persistent statistics), and the optimizer uses it to estimate how many rows a lookup returns and whether using the index is cheaper than scanning.
codeExamples:
ANALYZE TABLE orders;
SELECT index_name, column_name, cardinality FROM information_schema.statistics WHERE table_name = 'orders' ORDER BY index_name, seq_in_index;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name   | column_name | cardinality
-- PRIMARY      | id          |     1800000
-- idx_customer | customer_id |      410000
-- idx_status   | status      |           5

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: ANALYZE TABLE (refresh statistics), sample page settings, and histograms (8.0) for columns without indexes or with skewed values. Histograms tell the optimizer how values are distributed.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: measuring selectivity turns indexing from guesswork into evidence; stats guide join order and index choice automatically; histograms fix skew misestimates.
codeExamples:
-- Inspect the histogram MySQL built.
SELECT JSON_EXTRACT(histogram, '$."histogram-type"') AS htype,
       JSON_EXTRACT(histogram, '$."number-of-buckets-specified"') AS buckets
FROM information_schema.column_statistics
WHERE table_name = 'person' AND column_name = 'gender';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+---------+
-- | htype         | buckets |
-- +---------------+---------+
-- | "singleton"   | 4       |
-- +---------------+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: InnoDB statistics are sampled (default 20 pages), so cardinality can be badly off on skewed or huge tables, causing wrong plans; low-selectivity indexes still cost write time.
codeExamples:
-- Increase sampling for better estimates on a specific table.
ALTER TABLE person STATS_SAMPLE_PAGES = 100;
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_stats_persistent_sample_pages';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name                        | Value |
-- +--------------------------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_stats_persistent_sample_pages | 20    |
-- +--------------------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: low-selectivity columns are still useful when the value is rare (skew): "status='FAILED'" at 0.01 percent benefits even though status has 3 distinct values. Cardinality of a composite index only counts its leading prefixes, and histograms are ignored for indexed-equality lookups that use index dives.
codeExamples:
-- Skew example: a rare value is selective even if the column is not.
CREATE TABLE job (id INT PRIMARY KEY, st VARCHAR(8), KEY(st));
-- (imagine 1,000,000 rows: 999,990 'DONE' and 10 'FAILED')
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM job WHERE st = 'FAILED';   -- index used
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM job WHERE st = 'DONE';     -- optimizer prefers scanning

-- OUTPUT (type, example on such data):
-- +-------+
-- | ref   |
-- | index |    <- or ALL: most rows match, index no help
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Do not index by rule of thumb; index by workload plus data distribution. For skewed columns use histograms (8.0+) and watch for plan flips after statistics refresh; pin critical plans with index hints or optimizer hints only as a last resort. Schedule ANALYZE TABLE after bulk loads.

Mid-Level Notes

  • SHOW INDEX reports estimated cardinality; refresh with ANALYZE TABLE.
  • A low-selectivity index (status with 3 values) is rarely useful alone, but can help inside a composite or with skewed values.
  • Histograms (8.0) help the optimizer with skewed non-indexed columns.

Senior Notes

  • Data skew matters: status = "NEW" may be 0.1% of rows (great for an index) while "DONE" is 90% (scan is better).
  • Persistent statistics sample pages; for very large or skewed tables raise innodb_stats_persistent_sample_pages.
  • Create histograms on filtered but unindexed columns: ANALYZE TABLE t UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON col.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: judging an index by cardinality alone (skew matters), stale statistics after a bulk load, and indexing booleans. A value matching 90% of rows is better scanned; a value matching 0.1% is a great index lookup even on a low-cardinality column.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Wrong estimates cause wrong join orders. Compare estimated and actual rows in EXPLAIN ANALYZE; a big gap means refresh statistics, add a histogram or an index.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE channel = 'APP' AND status = 'NEW';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Filter: ((orders.channel = 'APP') and (orders.status = 'NEW'))  (cost=185000 rows=9000) (actual time=0.1..380 rows=210 loops=1)
-- estimate 9000 vs actual 210: correlated columns, consider a composite index or histogram

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: after a large import the optimizer chose a bad plan until statistics were refreshed. Make ANALYZE TABLE part of the load procedure.

beginner.content:
Introduction

EXPLAIN shows the execution plan the optimizer chose for a statement without running it: which tables are read, in which order, with which access type and index, and how many rows it expects to examine.

Why Do We Need This?

Guessing why a query is slow wastes time. EXPLAIN tells you whether an index is used, how rows are joined, and where sorting or temporary tables appear, so you fix the actual bottleneck.
codeExamples:
-- Compare plans before and after adding an index.
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM cust WHERE name = 'C';          -- no index on name
ALTER TABLE cust ADD KEY idx_name (name);
EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM cust WHERE name = 'C';

-- OUTPUT (type / key / rows):
-- +------+----------+------+
-- | ALL  | NULL     |    3 |   <- full scan
-- | ref  | idx_name |    1 |   <- index lookup (also "Using index": covering)
-- +------+----------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: code review of any new query, investigating slow-log entries, and checking plans after upgrades or data growth. FORMAT=TREE and FORMAT=JSON give more detail; EXPLAIN works for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REPLACE.

Diagram

   SQL text -> Parser -> Optimizer (cost model + statistics)
                               |
                               v
                       EXPLAIN prints the chosen plan

   type quality:  system > const > eq_ref > ref > range > index > ALL
                  (best)                                        (worst)

Fresher Notes

  • EXPLAIN shows how MySQL plans to run a query: which indexes, join order and access types.
  • Use it as EXPLAIN SELECT ... and read the columns type, key, rows and Extra.
  • Good access types: const, eq_ref, ref, range. Bad: ALL (full table scan).

Worked Example 1

Spot a full scan caused by a function.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders2 WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | rows   | Extra
-- ALL  | NULL | 100000 | Using where

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rewrite as a range.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders2 WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key        | rows
-- range | idx_created | 8200

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Basic EXPLAIN.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders2 WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'NEW';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | select_type | table   | type | key     | key_len | rows | filtered | Extra
--  1 | SIMPLE      | orders2 | ref  | idx_cov | 48      |   12 |   100.00 | Using index

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Tree format.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer would use without running the query: the table order, access type, candidate and chosen keys, key length used, estimated rows and filter percentage, and Extra notes. Read it from the first row (driving table) downward.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT o.id, c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND c.country = 'IN';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | select_type | table | type   | possible_keys | key         | key_len | rows  | filtered | Extra
--  1 | SIMPLE      | o     | range  | idx_created   | idx_created | 5       | 51000 |   100.00 | Using index condition
--  1 | SIMPLE      | c     | eq_ref | PRIMARY       | PRIMARY     | 8       |     1 |    10.00 | Using where

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Formats: tabular, FORMAT=TREE (iterator tree), FORMAT=JSON (costs and used columns), and EXPLAIN ANALYZE (actual execution). Access types from best to worst: system, const, eq_ref, ref, range, index, ALL.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7;
EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7\G
EXPLAIN FOR CONNECTION 31;          -- plan of a running statement

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Index lookup on orders using idx_customer (customer_id=7)  (cost=1.4 rows=12)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: free, safe (does not execute SELECT), shows access type (const, eq_ref, ref, range, index, ALL), chosen key, key_len, estimated rows, and Extra hints like Using filesort / Using temporary / Using index.
codeExamples:
-- key_len reveals how much of a composite index is used.
CREATE TABLE ord (a INT, b INT, c INT, KEY k (a,b,c));
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM ord WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2;     -- key_len 10: a and b (5 bytes each, nullable INT)

-- OUTPUT (key_len):
-- +---------+
-- | 10      |
-- +---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it shows estimates, not reality: rows and filtered can be far off with stale statistics; it does not tell actual time or loops (use EXPLAIN ANALYZE).
codeExamples:
-- Estimated rows vs actual rows can diverge; EXPLAIN alone cannot show it.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM cust WHERE city = 'Pune';
-- rows = 2 is a guess from index statistics

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------+------+----------+
-- | type | rows | filtered |
-- +------+------+----------+
-- | ref  |    2 |   100.00 |
-- +------+------+----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: output for DML is a plan of the statement, not its side effects; it cannot show lock waits or I/O; plans can change between executions (different parameters, statistics), and prepared statements may plan differently.
codeExamples:
-- Different literal, different plan (skew): plan for a rare value vs a common value.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM cust WHERE city = 'Pune';      -- may be ref
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM cust WHERE city > '';          -- may be ALL, most rows match

-- OUTPUT (type, example):
-- +------+
-- | ref  |
-- | ALL  |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Make EXPLAIN part of code review and CI for critical queries. Read type, key, key_len, rows, filtered and Extra in that order. Use FORMAT=JSON for cost details, and always pair plans with real timings, since estimate quality depends on fresh statistics.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Key columns: type (access method), key (index used), rows (estimated rows), Extra (Using index, Using filesort, Using temporary).
  • EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE and FORMAT=JSON give more detail.
  • EXPLAIN only estimates; it does not run the query.

Senior Notes

  • Estimates can be wrong with stale statistics or skew; verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  • Look for large rows x filtered, filesort on large sets, temporary tables, and non-sargable predicates.
  • Treat plans as part of code review for critical queries; capture baseline plans to detect regressions after upgrades.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: trusting estimated rows blindly, ignoring key_len (shows how many index columns are really used), missing "Using filesort/temporary", and testing on tiny data where a scan looks fine. Test with production-sized data.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'NEW' AND created_at > '2026-05-01';
-- key_len 8   => only customer_id used
-- key_len 8+32 => customer_id and status used

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- key=idx_cust_status_created  key_len=47  (the three columns are used)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Use EXPLAIN to find the fix pattern: full scan means missing or unusable index; filesort means order not served; temporary means grouping not served; big rows x filtered means a poor predicate order. Re-run after each change.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: add an EXPLAIN check in code review for every new query on a big table, and keep the plan in the pull request. Plans change as data grows, so recheck periodically from the digest.
codeExamples:
SELECT digest_text, count_star, avg_timer_wait/1e9 AS avg_ms FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 1;
EXPLAIN SELECT ... ;      -- paste the digest query with real parameters

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- digest_text                          | count_star | avg_ms
-- SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE ...     |     912000 | 3.2

beginner.content:
Introduction

EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+) actually executes the query and reports, per plan step, the estimated cost/rows next to the measured time, rows and loops. Output format is a TREE.

Why Do We Need This?

Estimates can be wrong. Only measured numbers show the real hot spot, e.g. a nested-loop step executed a million times whose estimate said "10 loops".
codeExamples:
-- Compare estimated rows with actual rows at each node: a big gap = bad statistics.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT b1.id FROM big b1 JOIN big b2 ON b2.grp = b1.grp WHERE b1.v > 10;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- -> Nested loop inner join  (cost=2.1 rows=4) (actual time=0.05..0.09 rows=5 loops=1)
--     -> Filter: (b1.v > 10)  (cost=0.65 rows=2) (actual time=0.02..0.03 rows=3 loops=1)
--     -> Index lookup on b2 using idx_grp (grp=b1.grp)  (cost=0.30 rows=2) (actual time=0.01..0.01 rows=2 loops=3)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: investigating slow queries in staging or a replica, validating that an index change really reduced rows read, and spotting plan steps with large loops counts.
codeExamples:
-- Reading a node:  actual time=first_row..all_rows  rows=N  loops=L
-- Total time of the node  ~ (all_rows time) x loops
-- Rows touched overall    ~ rows x loops
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM big WHERE v > 25;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- -> Filter: (big.v > 25)  (cost=0.65 rows=1.3) (actual time=0.03..0.04 rows=2 loops=1)
--     -> Table scan on big  (cost=0.65 rows=4) (actual time=0.02..0.03 rows=4 loops=1)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   EXPLAIN          -> estimates only            (does NOT run query)
   EXPLAIN ANALYZE  -> estimates + actuals       (RUNS query)

   node: cost=0.7 rows=2  |  actual time=0.02..0.03 rows=2 loops=3
         ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^    ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
         optimizer guess     measured  (look for big mismatch)

Fresher Notes

  • EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows estimated versus actual rows and time for each step (MySQL 8.0.18+).
  • Syntax: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ....
  • Use it to find which step of a plan is slow.

Worked Example 1

A slow plan shows its culprit.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders2 WHERE note LIKE '%refund%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Filter: (note like '%refund%')  (cost=10000 rows=11000) (actual time=0.2..420 rows=35 loops=1)
--    -> Table scan on orders2  (actual time=0.1..380 rows=100000 loops=1)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

After adding a FULLTEXT index.

Practice Exercise 1

Compare estimates and actuals.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) FROM customers c JOIN orders2 o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'NEW' GROUP BY c.id;

-- OUTPUT: (example, trimmed)
-- -> Group aggregate  (actual time=3.1..3.2 rows=95 loops=1)
--    -> Nested loop inner join  (cost=1.2 rows=120) (actual time=0.1..2.9 rows=120 loops=1)
--       -> Index lookup on o using idx_status (status='NEW')  (rows=120) (actual rows=120 loops=1)
--       -> Single-row index lookup on c using PRIMARY  (actual rows=1 loops=120)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Safe use with DML.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports, for each iterator node, the estimated cost and rows next to the actual first-row time, last-row time, rows returned and number of loops. Actual rows multiplied by loops is the real work done by that node.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.status = 'NEW' GROUP BY c.id;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Group aggregate: count(0)  (actual time=3.4..3.6 rows=95 loops=1)
--    -> Nested loop inner join  (cost=1.2 rows=120) (actual time=0.1..3.2 rows=120 loops=1)
--       -> Index lookup on o using idx_status (status='NEW')  (rows=120) (actual time=0.05..0.9 rows=120 loops=1)
--       -> Single-row index lookup on c using PRIMARY (id=o.customer_id)  (actual time=0.01..0.01 rows=1 loops=120)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Because it runs the statement, wrap DML in a transaction and roll back. Read nodes bottom-up for data flow; compare cost estimates with actual rows to see where the optimizer was wrong.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: real timings, real row counts and loops per step, no guessing; works on joins, subqueries, derived tables; shows iterator-based execution of the 8.0 executor.
codeExamples:
-- Shows hash join usage and build/probe costs (8.0.18+).
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM big a JOIN big b ON a.v = b.v + 0;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- -> Inner hash join (no condition)... (a.v = (b.v + 0))  (actual time=0.1..0.1 rows=4 loops=1)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it runs the statement; on a heavy query or an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE it does the work (wrap DML in a transaction and roll back); timing adds small overhead; output is TREE only.
codeExamples:
-- DML under EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes. Protect production data:
START TRANSACTION;
EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE big SET v = v + 1 WHERE grp = 2;   -- 8.0.19+ supports DML analysis
ROLLBACK;                                                   -- undo the change

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- -> Update big (actual time=0.1..0.1 rows=0 loops=1)
--     -> Index lookup on big using idx_grp (grp=2) (actual time=0.02..0.03 rows=2 loops=1)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: available only in MySQL 8.0.18+ (SELECT; DML and multi-table later); not supported with FORMAT=JSON/other formats; results include cache effects (a cold vs warm buffer pool changes times) and it cannot be used on a statement that is already running.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE FORMAT=JSON SELECT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1235 (42000): This version of MySQL doesn't yet support 'EXPLAIN ANALYZE with JSON format'
--   (MySQL 8.0.x; newer 8.4 releases add FORMAT=JSON support for some cases)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a replica or staging copy with production-sized data. Hunt for mismatches between estimated and actual rows, which point at stale stats or missing histograms, and for inner nodes with large loops. Never run it on heavy DML in production without a rollback plan.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Read each node: actual time=first_row..last_row rows=N loops=L.
  • Compare estimated rows to actual rows; big gaps mean bad statistics or skew.
  • Be careful with DML: it executes the statement (use in a transaction and roll back, or on a SELECT).

Senior Notes

  • Total time of a node is roughly time x loops; the real cost of nested loops is in the inner side loops count.
  • Combine with the slow log and digest to pick targets, then verify the fix by repeating EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  • In production prefer replicas and off-peak runs for heavy statements.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: running it on a production primary during peak, testing DML without rollback, comparing cold-cache and warm-cache runs, and reading only the top line. Run twice, discard the first, compare actual rows.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Look for the node where actual time jumps, estimated and actual rows differ greatly, or loops are large. Fixes: add an index, rewrite the predicate, update statistics or add a histogram.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE note LIKE '%refund%' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Limit: 20 row(s)  (actual time=0.3..412 rows=20 loops=1)
--    -> Filter: (orders.note like '%refund%')  (cost=190000 rows=21000) (actual time=0.3..412 rows=20 loops=1)
--       -> Index scan on orders using PRIMARY (reverse)  (actual time=0.1..380 rows=1100000 loops=1)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a regression after a release. Capture the plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a replica using the exact parameters from the slow log, compare with the previous plan and fix the index or the query.

topics.name: Full Table Scan vs Index Scan

beginner.content:
Introduction

A full table scan (EXPLAIN type ALL) reads every row of the clustered index. An index scan reads index entries: ref/range seeks to matching entries, while type index reads the whole index (smaller than the table).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE logs (id INT PRIMARY KEY, lvl VARCHAR(5), msg VARCHAR(50), KEY idx_lvl (lvl));
INSERT INTO logs VALUES (1,'INFO','a'),(2,'ERROR','b'),(3,'INFO','c'),(4,'INFO','d');

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE msg = 'b';       -- no index on msg
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE lvl = 'ERROR';   -- idx_lvl

-- OUTPUT (type / key):
-- +------+----------+
-- | ALL  | NULL     |   <- full table scan
-- | ref  | idx_lvl  |   <- index seek
-- +------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Seeking costs a tree descent per lookup; scanning is sequential and cheap per row. Neither is always better: choosing correctly is the optimizer's job, and your job is to give it good indexes and fresh statistics.
codeExamples:
-- Index scan over all entries (type=index) beats a table scan when the index is narrower.
EXPLAIN SELECT lvl FROM logs;          -- covering: scans idx_lvl, not the wide table

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+---------+-------------+
-- | type  | key     | Extra       |
-- +-------+---------+-------------+
-- | index | idx_lvl | Using index |
-- +-------+---------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real systems: nightly reports legitimately scan whole tables; OLTP lookups must seek. When a query matches a large fraction of rows (about 20-30 percent or more) the optimizer rightly chooses a table scan.
codeExamples:
-- Matching most rows: scan wins even though an index exists.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE lvl = 'INFO';

-- OUTPUT (example, on large skewed data where INFO is 90 percent):
-- +------+------+
-- | type | key  |
-- +------+------+
-- | ALL  | NULL |
-- +------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Full table scan (ALL)        Index seek (ref/range)        Index scan (index)
   [r1][r2][r3]...[rN]          root -> leaf -> few rows      [e1][e2]...[eN]  (narrow)
   reads N rows                 reads ~log N pages + k rows   reads N entries, not rows
   cheap per row                cheap if k small              cheaper than ALL if covering

Fresher Notes

  • A full table scan reads every row (type=ALL). An index scan or lookup reads only the needed index entries or rows.
  • Scans are fine for small tables; for large tables they are slow.
  • Add an index on the filtered column to avoid them.

Worked Example 1

Optimizer picks scan when value is common.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders2 WHERE status = 'DONE';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | rows  | filtered
-- ALL  | NULL | 98000 | 91.00

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rare value uses the index.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders2 WHERE status = 'NEW';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key        | rows
-- ref  | idx_status |  120

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Scan vs lookup.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders2 WHERE note = 'x';               -- no index
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders2 WHERE id = 5;                    -- primary key

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key     | rows
-- ALL  | NULL    | 100000
-- const| PRIMARY | 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Index scan still O(n).
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key     | Extra
-- index | idx_cov | Using index

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A full table scan (type ALL) reads every leaf page of the clustered index in order, which is fast sequential I/O. An index lookup (ref, range) jumps to specific entries and then, if needed, does random lookups into the clustered index. When a query touches a large share of the table, the sequential scan wins.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'DONE';           -- 91% of rows
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'DISPUTED';        -- 0.03% of rows

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- first : type=ALL                 (scan is cheaper than 1.6M random lookups)
-- second: type=ref key=idx_status

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Access types: const/eq_ref (single row), ref (equality), range, index (full index scan: reads a whole index, narrower than the table) and ALL. Index hints and optimizer switches can steer the choice when estimates are wrong.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: table scan: no index needed, sequential read-ahead is fast, best for big aggregations. Index seek: touches few pages and scales with tree height, ideal for selective lookups.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: table scan: cost grows linearly, pollutes the buffer pool, holds many row locks under REPEATABLE READ for UPDATE/DELETE. Index seek: random I/O per matching row and extra index maintenance.
codeExamples:
-- An UPDATE with no usable index locks (scans) every row it walks past.
UPDATE logs SET msg = 'x' WHERE msg = 'b';     -- no index on msg: full scan, locks all rows examined

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (but 4 rows were examined and locked in REPEATABLE READ)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the optimizer's choice depends on statistics; implicit conversions, functions on columns, OR across different columns and LIKE with a leading wildcard force scans; hints (FORCE INDEX) can override but may regress later.
codeExamples:
-- Type mismatch: comparing a string column to a number blocks the index.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE lvl = 0;          -- converts every lvl to number: scan
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE lvl = 'ERROR';    -- seeks

-- OUTPUT (type):
-- +-------+
-- | index |    <- or ALL
-- | ref   |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Do not chase "no full scans" blindly. Scans are right for analytics and unselective predicates; they are wrong when an OLTP query on a growing table lacks an index. Alert on Select_scan and Handler_read_rnd_next growth, then verify with EXPLAIN which queries cause them.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Index access types: ref/eq_ref (lookups), range (range scan), index (full index scan), ALL (full table scan).
  • Even with an index, the optimizer may choose a scan when most rows match.
  • "Using index" means a covering index scan, not a table scan.

Senior Notes

  • A full index scan (type=index) is still O(n); it is better than ALL only because indexes are narrower.
  • Scans are good for analytics (read sequentially, prefetch); lookups are good for OLTP.
  • Plan flips (index to scan) occur when statistics change; pin with hints only as a last resort.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forcing an index that is not selective, assuming "index used" means fast (a full index scan is still O(n)), and ignoring predicates that make the column unusable (function, mismatched type, leading wildcard).
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-05-01';       -- type=ALL
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-05-02';   -- type=range
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '7';                       -- string to int: still fine
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM users WHERE phone = 9876543210;                       -- VARCHAR vs INT: ALL

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- ALL / range / ref / ALL

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Scans are right for analytics (large fractions, sequential read-ahead) and wrong for OLTP point queries. Use summary tables, partition pruning and replicas for analytics so scans do not evict hot OLTP pages.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01';          -- big range scan: run on a replica
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_read_ahead | 912330

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an "admin search" page does a leading-wildcard LIKE on a 50M-row table and times out. Replace it with a FULLTEXT index or a prefix search and add a mandatory filter.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL joins tables with Nested Loop Join (for each outer row, look up matches in the inner table, ideally via an index), Block Nested Loop (legacy, buffered), and Hash Join (8.0.18+, builds an in-memory hash table on the smaller input then probes it).

Why Do We Need This?

The algorithm decides if a join takes milliseconds or hours. With an index on the join column nested loop is excellent; without it, older MySQL did quadratic block-nested-loop work, which hash join now fixes.

Real-Time Use

Real use: OLTP joins (orders to customers) rely on indexed nested loops; reporting joins of big unindexed sets use hash joins; the optimizer picks the join order (smallest driving table with the most selective filter first).
codeExamples:
-- Index on the inner table's join column is the key OLTP tuning step.
EXPLAIN SELECT d.name, e.n FROM d JOIN e ON e.d_id = d.id WHERE d.name = 'IT';

-- OUTPUT (selected):
-- +----+-------+------+---------+------+
-- | id | table | type | key     | rows |
-- +----+-------+------+---------+------+
-- |  1 | d     | ALL  | NULL    |    2 |   <- driving table (filtered)
-- |  1 | e     | ref  | idx_d   |    2 |   <- one index probe per driving row
-- +----+-------+------+---------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Nested Loop (indexed)            Hash Join
   for each row r in OUTER          1. BUILD: hash(small side) in memory
       probe INNER index (r.key)    2. PROBE: scan big side, look up hash
       emit matches                 no index needed, equality only

   OUTER --r--> [idx on INNER]      small --> [ hash table ] <-- big (probe)

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL joins tables with algorithms: Nested Loop Join (default), Block Nested Loop (older) and Hash Join (8.0.18+).
  • Nested loop: for each row in the outer table, look up matching rows in the inner table (best with an index).
  • Hash join: build a hash table of one input and probe it with the other (best without indexes).

Worked Example 1

Session-level buffer for a heavy report.

Worked Example 2

Force join order only as a last resort.
codeExamples:
SELECT STRAIGHT_JOIN a.id FROM small s JOIN big_a a ON a.s_id = s.id WHERE s.flag = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 5

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

See hash join.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT a.id FROM big_a a JOIN big_b b ON b.val = a.val;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Inner hash join (b.val = a.val)
--     -> Table scan on b
--     -> Hash
--         -> Table scan on a

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Add an index and see nested loop.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL implements joins as nested loops: for each row of the driving table it looks up matching rows in the next table. With an index on the inner column this is an index nested loop (cheap per row). Without one, MySQL 8.0.18+ uses a hash join: build a hash table of the smaller input in memory, then probe it with the other.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choosing: indexes make nested loops efficient for selective OLTP joins; hash joins suit large equi-joins without indexes (reports). Memory comes from join_buffer_size; when exceeded the hash join spills chunks to disk.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: nested loop: low memory, streams first rows fast, perfect with indexes. Hash join: linear time for equi-joins without indexes. The optimizer reorders inner joins freely.
codeExamples:
-- Straight join forces the written order (useful to test a plan, risky in production).
EXPLAIN SELECT STRAIGHT_JOIN d.name, e.n FROM e JOIN d ON d.id = e.d_id;

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +-------+--------+---------+
-- | table | type   | key     |
-- +-------+--------+---------+
-- | e     | ALL    | NULL    |
-- | d     | eq_ref | PRIMARY |
-- +-------+--------+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: nested loop without an index is O(n x m); hash join needs memory (spills to disk if join_buffer_size is exceeded) and only works for equality conditions; bad join order from poor stats can be catastrophic.
codeExamples:
-- Hash join memory is governed by join_buffer_size (default 256 KB).
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'join_buffer_size';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+--------+
-- | Variable_name    | Value  |
-- +------------------+--------+
-- | join_buffer_size | 262144 |
-- +------------------+--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL has no merge join and no parallel query for joins (InnoDB parallel read is for scans/COUNT only); hash joins need equality (or cross) conditions; since 8.0.20 the old block nested loop is replaced by hash join; FULL OUTER JOIN is not supported (emulate with UNION).
codeExamples:
-- FULL OUTER JOIN is unsupported in MySQL; emulate it.
SELECT x.a, y.a FROM x LEFT JOIN y ON x.a = y.a
UNION
SELECT x.a, y.a FROM x RIGHT JOIN y ON x.a = y.a;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+
-- | a    | a    |
-- +------+------+
-- |    1 | NULL |
-- |    2 |    2 |
-- |    3 |    3 |
-- | NULL |    4 |
-- +------+------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Index every join column on the inner side of OLTP joins and keep join keys the same type and collation so the index is usable. Use hash join as a safety net, not a design goal; if it shows up in hot paths, add an index. Raise join_buffer_size per session only for specific reports.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Nested loop with an index on the inner join column is fast for selective OLTP queries.
  • Hash join helps large unindexed equi-joins; it uses join_buffer_size memory and may spill to disk.
  • EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE shows "Inner hash join" or "Nested loop inner join".

Senior Notes

  • The driving (outer) table should be the one with fewer rows after filters; the optimizer picks it from statistics.
  • Hash join does not replace indexes: for OLTP point lookups keep indexes on join columns.
  • Tune join_buffer_size per session for specific big reports instead of globally.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on hash join for latency-sensitive queries, joining on mismatched types or collations (index not usable, even hash join cannot compare efficiently), and leaving huge join buffers globally. Fix types and add the index.
codeExamples:
SELECT a.id FROM a JOIN b ON a.code = b.code;      -- a.code utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, b.code utf8mb4_unicode_ci: conversion on each row
ALTER TABLE b MODIFY code VARCHAR(20) COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1200000 rows affected (after the change the join uses the index)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The join order matters more than the algorithm: start from the most selective table. Statistics decide; fix them with ANALYZE, histograms or, rarely, join-order hints.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id WHERE c.country = 'IN' AND o.status = 'NEW';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop inner join  (actual rows=4100 loops=1)
--     -> Index lookup on o using idx_status (status='NEW') (actual rows=9000)
--     -> Filter: (c.country = 'IN')  -> Single-row index lookup on c using PRIMARY (loops=9000)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nightly report joining two 100M-row tables without a join index ran 40 minutes with block nested loop on MySQL 5.7 and 6 minutes with hash join after upgrading to 8.0.

beginner.content:
Introduction

In EXPLAIN's Extra column, Using temporary means MySQL builds an internal temporary table (for GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION, derived tables). Using filesort means it sorts rows itself instead of reading them in index order; despite the name it may be done fully in memory.

Why Do We Need This?

Both are extra work: a temp table holds an intermediate result and sorting costs O(n log n) CPU plus memory or disk. Spotting them tells you where an index could provide pre-grouped or pre-sorted rows.
codeExamples:
-- An index on the GROUP BY column removes the temporary table and the sort.
ALTER TABLE sales2 ADD KEY idx_region (region);
EXPLAIN SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM sales2 GROUP BY region;

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +-------------+
-- | Extra       |
-- +-------------+
-- | Using index |
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: slow reports with GROUP BY on unindexed columns, ORDER BY RAND(), pagination on non-indexed sort keys, big derived tables. Check how often they spill to disk via status counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Created_tmp%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name           | Value |
-- +-------------------------+-------+
-- | Created_tmp_disk_tables |     0 |   <- should stay tiny relative to the next one
-- | Created_tmp_files       |     5 |
-- | Created_tmp_tables      |   231 |
-- +-------------------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   no suitable index                        suitable index
   rows -> [temp table] -> [sort] -> out    rows already in order -> out
          Using temporary   Using filesort         (nothing extra in Extra)

   fix: index (group_col) or (filter_col, sort_col); select fewer columns

Fresher Notes

  • Using temporary means MySQL builds an internal temp table (often for GROUP BY, DISTINCT or UNION). Using filesort means it sorts rows itself.
  • Both are extra work and can spill to disk on large sets.
  • They are not always bad for small results.

Worked Example 1

Disk temp table counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Created_tmp%tables';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name           | Value
-- Created_tmp_disk_tables |   120
-- Created_tmp_tables      | 52000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Top queries creating temp tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT digest_text, sum_created_tmp_disk_tables FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_created_tmp_disk_tables DESC LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- digest_text                               | sum_created_tmp_disk_tables
-- SELECT ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY ...      |                         90

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Spot them in a plan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders2 GROUP BY status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | Extra
-- ALL  | NULL | Using temporary

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Index removes both.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

"Using temporary" means MySQL builds an internal table to hold intermediate rows (for GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION, derived tables or some ORDER BY). "Using filesort" means rows are sorted by the server instead of read in index order. Small ones stay in memory (TempTable engine / sort buffer); big ones spill to disk files.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: tmp_table_size, max_heap_table_size, temptable_max_ram, sort_buffer_size, max_length_for_sort_data. Counters: Created_tmp_tables, Created_tmp_disk_tables, Sort_merge_passes.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: these mechanisms let MySQL answer any GROUP BY or ORDER BY even without a suitable index; 8.0 uses the in-memory TempTable engine and small sorts stay in memory (sort_buffer_size).
codeExamples:
-- Filesort in memory is fine for small results; check sort statistics.
SHOW SESSION STATUS LIKE 'Sort%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name     | Value |
-- +-------------------+-------+
-- | Sort_merge_passes |     0 |   <- >0 means the sort spilled to disk files
-- | Sort_range        |     0 |
-- | Sort_rows         |     4 |
-- | Sort_scan         |     1 |
-- +-------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: large temporary tables spill to disk (slow), filesort over wide rows copies lots of data, both consume memory per connection, and ORDER BY ... LIMIT on unindexed data sorts the whole set first.
codeExamples:
-- ORDER BY RAND() always needs a temp table + filesort over all rows.
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM sales2 ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT (Extra):
-- +---------------------------------+
-- | Using temporary; Using filesort |
-- +---------------------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: temp tables with TEXT/BLOB columns go to disk (internal on-disk engine is InnoDB in 8.0.16+); in-memory limit is tmp_table_size / max_heap_table_size (TempTable engine uses temptable_max_ram); mixed ASC/DESC sorts needed a descending index before 8.0.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('tmp_table_size','sort_buffer_size','internal_tmp_mem_storage_engine');

-- OUTPUT (defaults):
-- +---------------------------------+-----------+
-- | Variable_name                   | Value     |
-- +---------------------------------+-----------+
-- | internal_tmp_mem_storage_engine | TempTable |
-- | sort_buffer_size                | 262144    |
-- | tmp_table_size                  | 16777216  |
-- +---------------------------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Do not panic at every filesort: small in-memory ones are cheap. Worry when Sort_merge_passes or Created_tmp_disk_tables climb, or when it sorts huge sets for a LIMIT. Design composite indexes (equality columns then sort column) and avoid ORDER BY RAND(); prefer keyset pagination over big OFFSET sorts.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Avoid filesort by creating an index in ORDER BY order matching the filter columns.
  • Avoid temporary tables by grouping on indexed columns, or by lowering the number of rows before grouping.
  • Memory limits: tmp_table_size, max_heap_table_size, sort_buffer_size.

Senior Notes

  • MySQL 8 uses the TempTable engine and spills to disk files when memory limits are exceeded; check Created_tmp_disk_tables.
  • A large sort with LIMIT uses a priority queue and is cheaper than a full sort.
  • Window functions and ORDER BY on expressions often need sorts; precompute and index generated columns.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes
