Mistakes: sorting or grouping on TEXT columns (forces disk), ORDER BY on an expression, large OFFSET sorts, and raising memory limits globally instead of fixing the query. Add the right index or reduce the rows first.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Find which statements create disk temporary tables and fix the worst. The digest table counts them.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 70) AS q, sum_created_tmp_disk_tables AS disk_tmp, sum_sort_merge_passes AS merge_passes FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_created_tmp_disk_tables DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- q                                          | disk_tmp | merge_passes
-- SELECT ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY note      |    18200 |          0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a dashboard query grouped by a TEXT column created a disk temp table on every refresh. Group by a short generated column or a lookup id instead.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE tickets ADD COLUMN category_id INT NULL;
SELECT category_id, COUNT(*) FROM tickets GROUP BY category_id;        -- was GROUP BY category_text

-- OUTPUT:
-- category_id | COUNT(*)
-- 3           |     410

beginner.content:
Introduction

The optimizer is cost-based: it estimates the cost of alternative plans using statistics (cardinality, row counts) and constants for I/O and CPU, then picks the cheapest. The slow query log records statements slower than long_query_time.
codeExamples:
-- Turn on the slow log at runtime.
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log      = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL long_query_time     = 0.5;                 -- seconds
SET GLOBAL log_queries_not_using_indexes = 'ON';      -- also log scans (noisy)
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'slow_query_log_file';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------------+-----------------------------+
-- | Variable_name       | Value                       |
-- +---------------------+-----------------------------+
-- | slow_query_log_file | /var/lib/mysql/host-slow.log|
-- +---------------------+-----------------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You cannot optimise what you do not measure. Slow logs and the performance schema find the queries that cost the most in total, which is rarely the single slowest one but the moderately slow ones run millions of times.
codeExamples:
-- Top statements by total time from performance_schema (8.0).
SELECT DIGEST_TEXT, COUNT_STAR AS execs,
       ROUND(SUM_TIMER_WAIT/1e12,2) AS total_s,
       ROUND(AVG_TIMER_WAIT/1e12,4) AS avg_s
FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
ORDER BY SUM_TIMER_WAIT DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------------------------------+--------+---------+--------+
-- | DIGEST_TEXT                           | execs  | total_s | avg_s  |
-- +---------------------------------------+--------+---------+--------+
-- | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE cust = ?   | 120000 |  310.40 | 0.0026 |
-- | UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - ? ...    |  80000 |  190.12 | 0.0024 |
-- +---------------------------------------+--------+---------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real workflow: enable slow log, aggregate with pt-query-digest or mysqldumpslow, EXPLAIN the top offenders, add/adjust indexes, retest, repeat. Cost constants live in mysql.server_cost and mysql.engine_cost.
codeExamples:
SELECT cost_name, cost_value FROM mysql.server_cost;

-- shell:  mysqldumpslow -s t -t 5 /var/lib/mysql/host-slow.log     (top 5 by total time)

-- OUTPUT (defaults are NULL = built-in constants):
-- +----------------------------+------------+
-- | cost_name                  | cost_value |
-- +----------------------------+------------+
-- | disk_temptable_create_cost | NULL       |
-- | row_evaluate_cost          | NULL       |
-- | key_compare_cost           | NULL       |
-- +----------------------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   query -> optimizer: for each candidate plan  cost = IO + CPU(rows x row_cost)
                         |
          statistics (cardinality, histograms) feed the estimates
                         v
                    cheapest plan -> executor -> slow log if time > long_query_time
                                                      |
                                    digest tools -> top offenders -> fix -> retest

Fresher Notes

  • The optimizer assigns a cost to each possible plan and picks the cheapest, using row estimates (cardinality).
  • Slow queries are those that take longer than long_query_time and are logged in the slow query log.
  • Fixing slow queries usually means adding or fixing an index, or rewriting the query.

Worked Example 1

Rows examined ratio.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 50) AS q, sum_rows_examined / NULLIF(sum_rows_sent, 0) AS examined_per_sent
FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest WHERE sum_rows_sent > 0 ORDER BY examined_per_sent DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- q                                  | examined_per_sent
-- SELECT * FROM posts WHERE title LIK | 1450.2

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Look at cost constants.
codeExamples:
SELECT cost_name, cost_value FROM mysql.server_cost;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- cost_name                 | cost_value
-- disk_temptable_create_cost | NULL   (default used)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Enable the slow log.

Practice Exercise 2

Top queries by total time.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 60) AS q, count_star AS calls, ROUND(sum_timer_wait/1e12, 2) AS total_s
FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- q                                      | calls  | total_s
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id | 900000 | 410.55

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The optimizer assigns each plan a cost from constants for reading pages, evaluating conditions and creating temporary tables (mysql.server_cost, mysql.engine_cost), multiplied by estimated row counts. It picks the lowest cost, so wrong cardinality estimates produce slow plans even with correct indexes.
codeExamples:
SELECT cost_name, cost_value, default_value FROM mysql.server_cost;
EXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7\G

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- cost_name                  | cost_value | default_value
-- row_evaluate_cost          | NULL       | 0.1
-- disk_temptable_create_cost | NULL       | 20
-- "query_cost": "1.40"

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Find slow queries with the slow query log (long_query_time, log_slow_extra), the Performance Schema digest table, and sys.statement_analysis. Rank by total time (calls x average) and by rows examined per row sent.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: cost-based planning adapts to data size and distribution, picks join order and indexes automatically, and histograms plus optimizer trace let you see why a plan was chosen.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: decisions are only as good as the statistics; sampled cardinality, correlated columns and data skew cause misestimates; a plan can flip after ANALYZE or an upgrade, causing sudden regressions.
codeExamples:
-- Correlated columns (city and state) are assumed independent -> row count underestimated.
-- Remedies: histograms, composite indexes, optimizer hints.
EXPLAIN SELECT /*+ INDEX(cust idx_city) */ * FROM cust WHERE city = 'Pune';

-- OUTPUT (partial):
-- +------+----------+
-- | type | key      |
-- +------+----------+
-- | ref  | idx_city |
-- +------+----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL has no persistent plan cache or plan guides like some databases, so plan stability is controlled with hints and statistics; the slow log reflects wall time (including lock waits), and long_query_time only logs after completion.
codeExamples:
-- Slow log entry shows rows examined vs sent: a high ratio = missing index.
-- # Query_time: 2.31  Lock_time: 0.00  Rows_sent: 10  Rows_examined: 1850000
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE note LIKE '%late%';

SELECT 1850000/10 AS examined_per_row_sent;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------------+
-- | examined_per_row_sent |
-- +-----------------------+
-- |          185000.0000  |
-- +-----------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Manage performance as a loop: measure (slow log, performance_schema), explain, change one thing, re-measure. Keep statistics fresh, add histograms for skew, and use optimizer hints sparingly to pin plans that matter. Track query digests over releases to catch regressions before users do.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Enable the slow log: slow_query_log=1, long_query_time=1, log_queries_not_using_indexes if useful.
  • Summarise slow logs with mysqldumpslow or Percona pt-query-digest.
  • Check Rows_examined vs Rows_sent: a big gap means wasted work.

Senior Notes

  • Use performance_schema digests to rank queries by total time, not just single slow executions: a 5 ms query run 10M times matters more.
  • Cost model constants live in mysql.server_cost and mysql.engine_cost; rarely tuned.
  • Build a regular review loop: top 10 queries weekly, regress after deployments.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: tuning single slow queries while a frequent medium-speed query consumes the most time, ignoring Rows_examined, and measuring on a cold cache. Prioritise by total resource use.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 60) AS q, count_star, ROUND(sum_timer_wait/1e12, 1) AS total_s, ROUND(sum_rows_examined / NULLIF(sum_rows_sent, 0)) AS examined_per_sent
FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- q                                         | count_star | total_s | examined_per_sent
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id    |     912000 |   410.5 |            12
-- SELECT * FROM events WHERE note LIKE ...  |       5200 |   380.2 |         94000      (a rare but very wasteful query)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Close the loop: change, re-measure, keep a baseline. Capture plans before and after, and keep the improvement in a changelog so regressions are visible.
codeExamples:
-- baseline
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... ;   -- actual time=0.2..95 rows=20
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_cust_status_created (customer_id, status, created_at);
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT ... ;   -- actual time=0.04..0.1 rows=20

-- OUTPUT:
-- 950x faster; record before/after in the pull request

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: after each release compare digests with the previous release and alert on queries whose average latency or rows examined grew by more than a set threshold.
codeExamples:
SELECT digest, ROUND(avg_timer_wait/1e9, 2) AS avg_ms, ROUND(sum_rows_examined / count_star) AS rows_examined_avg FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest WHERE schema_name = 'shop' ORDER BY avg_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- digest           | avg_ms | rows_examined_avg
-- 8b1f...          | 412.30 |            250000

beginner.content:
Introduction

ACID is the contract of a transaction: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold before and after), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not see each other's half-done work), Durability (committed data survives a crash). InnoDB implements them with undo logs, redo log, locks/MVCC and the doublewrite buffer.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, bal DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (bal >= 0)) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1,100.00),(2,50.00);

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE id = 1;   -- debit
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 30 WHERE id = 2;   -- credit
COMMIT;                                        -- both changes become permanent together

SELECT * FROM acct;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+
-- | id | bal    |
-- +----+--------+
-- |  1 |  70.00 |
-- |  2 |  80.00 |
-- +----+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Money transfers, order placement and inventory updates involve several statements that must succeed or fail as a unit. Without ACID a crash or error mid-way leaves data corrupted (money debited but never credited).
codeExamples:
-- Atomicity + Consistency: the CHECK constraint fails, so the whole transaction is undone.
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 500 WHERE id = 2;     -- ok so far
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 1;     -- violates bal >= 0
ROLLBACK;                                         -- we undo the first update too
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'acct_chk_1' is violated.
-- +--------+
-- | bal    |
-- +--------+
-- |  80.00 |      <- the +500 credit was rolled back
-- +--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: banking, e-commerce checkout, booking systems, ledger entries. Durability is tuned by innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit (1 = flush redo to disk at every commit, the safe default) and sync_binlog.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit','sync_binlog','innodb_doublewrite');

-- OUTPUT (defaults):
-- +--------------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name                  | Value |
-- +--------------------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_doublewrite             | ON    |
-- | innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit | 1     |   <- fully durable
-- | sync_binlog                    | 1     |
-- +--------------------------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   BEGIN --> statements --> COMMIT
                 |            |
          undo log (rollback) redo log flushed (durable)

   A tomicity   -> undo log
   C onsistency -> constraints, FK, CHECK
   I solation   -> locks + MVCC snapshots
   D urability  -> redo log + doublewrite buffer

Fresher Notes

  • ACID describes reliable transactions: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules stay valid), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
  • InnoDB supports ACID; MyISAM does not.
  • Classic example: a bank transfer debits one account and credits another as one unit.

Worked Example 1

Consistency: constraint rejects an invalid state.

Worked Example 2

Isolation: reader does not see uncommitted data.
codeExamples:
-- session A
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = 0 WHERE id = 1;
-- session B
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT: (session B)
-- bal
-- 1000.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Atomicity demo.

Practice Exercise 2

Check durability settings.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit','sync_binlog');

-- OUTPUT:
-- innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit | 1
-- sync_binlog                    | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

InnoDB implements ACID with four mechanisms. Atomicity: the undo log lets it roll back a transaction. Consistency: constraints are checked on every statement. Isolation: MVCC read views plus row locks. Durability: the redo log is written (and by default fsynced) at commit, before data pages reach disk.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Durability is configurable: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit (1 = fsync each commit, 2 = write each commit and fsync each second, 0 = once per second) and sync_binlog. Isolation is set per session or globally; atomicity and consistency are always on for InnoDB.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: data integrity under failure and concurrency, simple mental model (all-or-nothing), crash recovery via redo log replay and undo rollback of uncommitted work.
codeExamples:
-- Autocommit means every single statement is its own atomic transaction.
SELECT @@autocommit;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 1 WHERE id = 1;   -- implicitly committed

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | @@autocommit |
-- +--------------+
-- |            1 |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: overhead (logging, locks, undo versions), long transactions bloat undo history and block purge, and strict isolation lowers concurrency.
codeExamples:
-- Spot long-running transactions that hold undo and locks.
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, trx_started, NOW()) AS age_s
FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+---------------------+-------+
-- | trx_id | trx_started         | age_s |
-- +--------+---------------------+-------+
-- | 421847 | 2024-05-01 10:00:03 |  1840 |   <- 30 minutes old: investigate
-- +--------+---------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: only transactional engines (InnoDB) provide ACID; MyISAM and MEMORY ignore ROLLBACK. DDL statements cause an implicit commit (MySQL 8 DDL is atomic per statement but cannot be rolled back).
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (3, 10.00);
CREATE TABLE tmp_x (a INT);       -- DDL: implicit COMMIT happens here
ROLLBACK;                         -- too late, nothing to roll back
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM acct WHERE id = 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 1 |    <- the insert survived because DDL committed it
-- +---+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep transactions short and scoped to one business invariant. Decide durability versus latency explicitly (flush settings, group commit, replication semi-sync) and never rely on application-side retries without idempotency. For cross-service work, ACID ends at the database boundary: use sagas/outbox.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Atomicity uses the undo log; durability uses the redo log flushed at commit.
  • Isolation is configurable through isolation levels and implemented with MVCC and locks.
  • Consistency means constraints (PK, FK, CHECK, UNIQUE) hold after each transaction, but business rules still need correct code.

Senior Notes

  • Durability depends on settings: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 and sync_binlog=1 for full safety; relaxing them trades safety for speed.
  • ACID is per node; across services you need sagas, outbox or two-phase commit, which change guarantees.
  • Know what your isolation level really promises before relying on it for invariants.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: assuming atomicity across statements without a transaction (autocommit makes each statement its own), using MyISAM tables inside transactions (no rollback), and relaxing durability settings on money data. Verify the engine and the settings.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, engine FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() AND engine <> 'InnoDB';
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 400 WHERE id = 1;       -- autocommit: committed immediately
-- application crashes here: the matching credit never runs

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name | engine
-- audit_log  | MyISAM       (convert it)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Durability costs an fsync per commit. Group commit batches commits from concurrent sessions into one fsync, so throughput rises with concurrency. Relaxing to 2 is a conscious trade of up to a second of commits on an OS crash.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a funds transfer. All four properties matter: both updates or neither, balances never negative, concurrent transfers do not interfere, and a committed transfer survives a crash.

beginner.content:
Introduction

START TRANSACTION (or BEGIN) opens an explicit transaction and suspends autocommit until it ends. COMMIT makes all its changes permanent and visible; ROLLBACK discards them.

Why Do We Need This?

Multi-step business operations need a grouping tool. ROLLBACK lets you cancel when a later step fails, so you never leave half-finished data.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'B';
SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'B';          -- we see our own change: 4
ROLLBACK;                                       -- cancel
SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'B';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- |    4 |
-- +------+
-- +------+
-- |    5 |     <- restored
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: checkout flows (decrement stock + create order + payment record), batch imports in chunks, and tests that roll back. Options: START TRANSACTION READ ONLY, WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT, and SET autocommit=0.

Diagram

   autocommit=1 (default)          explicit
   stmt -> auto COMMIT             START TRANSACTION
                                      stmt1
                                      stmt2 --error--> ROLLBACK (all undone)
                                      stmt3
                                   COMMIT (all persisted)

Fresher Notes

  • START TRANSACTION (or BEGIN) opens a transaction, COMMIT saves the changes, ROLLBACK cancels them.
  • By default MySQL runs in autocommit mode: each statement commits itself.
  • Inside a transaction, other sessions do not see your changes until COMMIT.

Worked Example 1

Find long transactions.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, trx_started, NOW()) AS secs, trx_rows_locked
FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- trx_id | trx_started         | secs | trx_rows_locked
-- 12345  | 2026-05-01 10:00:00 |  900 | 120

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

DDL commits implicitly.

Practice Exercise 1

Commit and rollback.

Practice Exercise 2

Rollback restores values.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

START TRANSACTION turns autocommit off for the session until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Changes are made to pages in the buffer pool, undo records are written for rollback, and redo records for durability. COMMIT writes the commit record and releases locks; ROLLBACK applies the undo records in reverse.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: BEGIN, START TRANSACTION READ ONLY, WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT, SET autocommit = 0, and COMMIT AND CHAIN. DDL and some statements cause an implicit commit.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: explicit control over atomic units; READ ONLY transactions skip some overhead; COMMIT AND CHAIN starts the next transaction immediately in the same settings.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: forgetting COMMIT leaves locks held and connections stuck "idle in transaction"; large transactions are slow to roll back (undo must be applied); errors do not auto-rollback the whole transaction in most cases.
codeExamples:
-- A statement error does NOT roll back earlier statements in the transaction.
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE stock SET qty = 99 WHERE sku = 'A';        -- ok
INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('A', 1);                -- duplicate key: only this statement fails
COMMIT;                                           -- first UPDATE is still committed
SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A';

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'A' for key 'stock.PRIMARY'
-- +------+
-- |   99 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: transactions are per connection (not shared); no nested transactions (a BEGIN inside a transaction implicitly commits the first); DDL, LOCK TABLES and some admin statements implicitly commit; deadlock or lock-wait errors may roll back automatically.

Architect's Notes

Always pair BEGIN with COMMIT/ROLLBACK in a try/finally at the application layer, set sensible innodb_lock_wait_timeout, and monitor idle-in-transaction sessions. Retry on deadlock (1213) and lock-wait timeout (1205) with the whole transaction, not just the failed statement. Batch large writes in moderate chunks.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Keep transactions short: they hold locks and undo history until they end.
  • DDL statements (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE) cause an implicit commit.
  • Check autocommit with SELECT @@autocommit; set it to 0 to start transactions implicitly.

Senior Notes

  • Long-running or forgotten transactions block purge (history list grows), hold locks and cause lock waits and replication lag.
  • Handle deadlocks (error 1213) and lock timeouts (1205) with a bounded retry of the whole transaction.
  • Never do remote calls or user waits inside a transaction.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: transactions left open (locks held, undo grows), user waits inside a transaction, DDL in the middle (implicit commit), and catching errors without rolling back. Always finish with COMMIT or ROLLBACK in finally blocks.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Keep transactions short. A long transaction blocks purge of undo records (history list grows), holds locks and delays DDL through metadata locks. Find them before they hurt.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world service pattern: begin, do all reads that decide the outcome with locking reads, write, commit, and retry the whole block on deadlock (error 1213).

beginner.content:
Introduction

A SAVEPOINT marks a named point inside a transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name undoes work back to that point while the transaction stays open; RELEASE SAVEPOINT removes the marker.

Why Do We Need This?

MySQL has no nested transactions, so savepoints give partial rollback: retry or skip one failing part of a larger unit without losing the work already done.

Real-Time Use

Real use: import loops where bad rows are skipped, stored procedures with per-item error handling, ORM frameworks (Spring nested transactions map to savepoints).

Diagram

   BEGIN
     insert A
     SAVEPOINT p1  <----+
     insert B           |  ROLLBACK TO p1: B undone,
     SAVEPOINT p2       |  A kept, p2 removed,
     insert C           |  transaction still open
   COMMIT (A persisted)

Fresher Notes

  • A SAVEPOINT marks a point inside a transaction to which you can partially roll back without ending the transaction.
  • Commands: SAVEPOINT name, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT name, RELEASE SAVEPOINT name.
  • Everything before the savepoint is kept.

Worked Example 1

Batch import skipping bad rows (stored procedure pattern).

Worked Example 2

Spring nested transaction (Java).

Practice Exercise 1

Partial rollback.

Practice Exercise 2

Release a savepoint.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A savepoint records a position in the undo log of the current transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT applies undo records back to that position and keeps the transaction open. Row locks acquired after the savepoint are released in InnoDB, but locks taken before it are kept.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Statements: SAVEPOINT name, ROLLBACK TO name, RELEASE SAVEPOINT name. Using the same name again moves the savepoint. A full COMMIT or ROLLBACK discards all savepoints.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fine-grained recovery inside one transaction, no need to restart everything, cheap to create (no I/O).

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: rolled-back rows still consumed AUTO_INCREMENT values; locks acquired after the savepoint are NOT released by ROLLBACK TO (InnoDB keeps them until the transaction ends); easy to over-complicate logic.

Limitations

Limitations: savepoints vanish on COMMIT or full ROLLBACK; they are not allowed to survive across connections; stored functions and triggers cannot issue transaction control, and ROLLBACK TO does not undo non-transactional table changes. Savepoints are also cleared by implicit commits (DDL).

Architect's Notes

Use savepoints for localised, retryable sub-steps, not as a substitute for sound transaction boundaries. Remember held locks persist until the end, so keep them short, and keep error handling (stored procedure DECLARE HANDLER) consistent with which savepoint it rolls back to.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Rolling back to a savepoint undoes statements after it but keeps locks acquired earlier in InnoDB.
  • Savepoints let batch jobs skip a failing item and continue.
  • ORMs use savepoints for nested transactions (REQUIRES_NEW is different: it uses a new transaction).

Senior Notes

  • Many savepoints add overhead; use for coarse steps, not per row in huge loops.
  • Transaction semantics with savepoints complicate retry logic; keep recovery logic simple.
  • After ROLLBACK TO, the transaction is still open and must be committed or rolled back.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting ROLLBACK TO to end the transaction, expecting it to release all locks, and creating savepoints per row in huge loops (overhead). Remember to COMMIT afterwards.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Savepoints are cheap for coarse steps. Use them to skip a failing item in a batch while keeping the successful ones in one transaction, rather than one transaction per item.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: frameworks use savepoints for nested transactions. Spring's NESTED propagation and Django's nested atomic() blocks emit SAVEPOINT and ROLLBACK TO so an inner failure can be handled without aborting the outer unit of work.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The weakest isolation level: a transaction can read rows that other transactions have changed but not yet committed (dirty reads). InnoDB does no consistent-snapshot reads at this level; it simply reads the latest version of each row.

Why Do We Need This?

It exists for maximum read concurrency and speed when slightly wrong data is acceptable (rough counters, monitoring). It avoids creating read views, but gives up correctness guarantees.
codeExamples:
-- Session B (separate connection) changes a row but has not committed.
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE acct SET bal = 0 WHERE id = 1;     -- NOT committed

-- Session A (READ UNCOMMITTED) reads again:
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT (Session A):
-- +------+
-- |    0 |      <- dirty read of B's uncommitted value
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: almost never in production. Occasionally for approximate dashboards over append-only data, or ad hoc monitoring where blocking is worse than inaccuracy.
codeExamples:
-- Per-statement alternative to lowering the whole session level: none in MySQL (no NOLOCK hint).
-- Set only for one transaction:
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;   -- applies to the NEXT transaction only
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS approx_rows FROM acct;
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+
-- | approx_rows |
-- +-------------+
-- |           1 |
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Tx B: UPDATE bal=0 ......(uncommitted)......... ROLLBACK
                |
   Tx A:        +--> SELECT bal  => 0   (DIRTY: B never committed)

Fresher Notes

  • The lowest isolation level: a transaction can read changes that other transactions have not committed yet (dirty reads).
  • It is rarely used because data can be read and then rolled back.
  • Set it with SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ UNCOMMITTED;

Worked Example 1

Check current level.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;

-- OUTPUT:
-- @@transaction_isolation
-- REPEATABLE-READ

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Set for a single transaction.

Practice Exercise 1

Dirty read demo.

Practice Exercise 2

Session A rolls back, B read data that never existed.
codeExamples:
-- session A
ROLLBACK;
-- session B
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- bal
-- 1000.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

At READ UNCOMMITTED, plain SELECTs read the latest version of each row without consulting undo, so they can see changes that other transactions have not committed (and may roll back). InnoDB still takes locks for writes, so this level does not make writes unsafe, only reads.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Set it for the session, the next transaction, or globally. Check the active level with @@transaction_isolation. It is almost never the right choice.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no read locks and no snapshot overhead for plain SELECTs; readers are never blocked by writers.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;

-- OUTPUT (session set above):
-- +-------------------------+
-- | @@transaction_isolation |
-- +-------------------------+
-- | READ-UNCOMMITTED        |
-- +-------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: dirty reads: you can act on data that is later rolled back; also non-repeatable reads and phantoms. Results may be inconsistent within a single query (half of a multi-row update visible).
codeExamples:
-- B rolls back after A already used the value.
-- Session B:
ROLLBACK;

-- Session A:
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;     -- earlier saw 0, a value that never officially existed

-- OUTPUT (Session A):
-- +------+
-- |  100 |      <- A earlier made decisions on "0"
-- +------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: writes (UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) still take locks, so only plain reads are affected; statement-based binary logging is not allowed at this level in some configurations, because it can be unsafe for replication (use ROW format).

Architect's Notes

Avoid READ UNCOMMITTED for anything that drives business decisions. If reader/writer blocking is the problem, MVCC at READ COMMITTED already gives non-blocking reads without dirty data. Consider read replicas for heavy analytics instead.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Reads can see data that never officially existed.
  • It avoids some read locking, but InnoDB reads are already non-locking under MVCC, so the benefit is small.
  • Writes still lock rows.

Senior Notes

  • Use only for approximate monitoring on hot tables where exactness does not matter.
  • Better alternatives: replicas for reporting, snapshot reads, caching.
  • Never use it for money or inventory.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using it "for speed" (InnoDB consistent reads already take no locks, so the gain is tiny), using it for money or stock decisions, and forgetting it applies to the whole session on pooled connections. Reset the level.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(bal) FROM acct;       -- may include half-applied transfers at this level
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;     -- restore before returning a pooled connection

-- OUTPUT:
-- SUM(bal)
-- 1000.00     (or 1000.00 - 400.00 mid-transfer: inconsistent)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The performance difference against READ COMMITTED is negligible in InnoDB. Measure before believing otherwise, and prefer a replica or a snapshot for heavy reporting.
codeExamples:
-- benchmark: 16 threads, mixed read/write
-- READ UNCOMMITTED: 41,200 tps   READ COMMITTED: 41,050 tps   (within noise)
SELECT 41200 - 41050 AS difference_tps;

-- OUTPUT:
-- difference_tps
-- 150

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: the only defensible uses are rough, throwaway monitoring counts on a hot table where being slightly wrong is acceptable, and even then a stats table is better.

beginner.content:
Introduction

At READ COMMITTED each statement sees only data committed before that statement started. Dirty reads are gone, but two identical SELECTs in the same transaction can return different results (non-repeatable reads) because each statement gets a fresh snapshot.

Why Do We Need This?

It is the default in PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server, and a popular choice for MySQL OLTP because it takes fewer locks (no gap locks for most statements) and reduces deadlocks while avoiding dirty data.
codeExamples:
-- Session B commits a change between A's two reads.
-- Session B:  UPDATE price SET p = 120 WHERE id = 1;  (autocommit)

-- Session A (still in its transaction):
SELECT p FROM price WHERE id = 1;       -- new statement, new snapshot

-- OUTPUT (Session A):
-- +------+
-- |  120 |     <- differs from the first read in the same transaction
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: high-concurrency web OLTP, systems migrating from Oracle/PostgreSQL, workloads suffering gap-lock deadlocks under REPEATABLE READ. Requires binlog_format=ROW.
codeExamples:
SET GLOBAL TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;   -- new connections
SET GLOBAL binlog_format = 'ROW';                          -- required for safe replication
SELECT @@global.transaction_isolation AS iso;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+
-- | iso              |
-- +------------------+
-- | READ-COMMITTED   |
-- +------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Tx A:  BEGIN
          SELECT p --> 100   (snapshot at stmt start)
                               Tx B: UPDATE p=120; COMMIT
          SELECT p --> 120   (NEW snapshot: non-repeatable read)
          COMMIT

Fresher Notes

  • READ COMMITTED means each statement sees only data committed before that statement started.
  • It prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads and phantoms.
  • It is the default in PostgreSQL and Oracle, and popular in MySQL for high concurrency.

Worked Example 1

Change the global default.

Worked Example 2

Config file equivalent.
codeExamples:
[mysqld]
transaction-isolation = READ-COMMITTED
binlog_format = ROW

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- @@transaction_isolation = READ-COMMITTED

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Non-repeatable read.

Practice Exercise 2

Atomic conditional update avoids lost update.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

At READ COMMITTED every statement gets a fresh read view, so it sees only data committed before that statement began, never uncommitted data. Gap locks are mostly disabled for searches and index scans, which reduces blocking and deadlocks. Binary logging must use ROW format for replication safety.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configure per session, per connection pool, or globally in my.cnf. Combine with binlog_format=ROW. Many write-heavy OLTP systems and other databases (PostgreSQL, Oracle) default to it.
codeExamples:
[mysqld]
transaction-isolation = READ-COMMITTED
binlog_format = ROW

SET GLOBAL TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SELECT @@global.transaction_isolation, @@binlog_format;

-- OUTPUT:
-- READ-COMMITTED | ROW

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no dirty reads, short-lived locks (rows examined but not matched are unlocked right away), gap locking disabled for searches and index scans, fewer deadlocks, semi-consistent reads on UPDATE.
codeExamples:
-- Under READ COMMITTED, a range UPDATE does not block inserts into the gap.
-- Session A:  START TRANSACTION; UPDATE price SET p = p WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10;
-- Session B:  INSERT INTO price VALUES (5, 50);     -- succeeds immediately (no gap lock)

-- OUTPUT (Session B):
-- Query OK, 1 row affected

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: non-repeatable reads and phantoms; a report running several queries may see inconsistent totals; each statement builds a new read view (small cost).
codeExamples:
-- Inconsistent totals inside one transaction.
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT SUM(p) AS s1 FROM price;     -- e.g. 170
-- (other session inserts and commits a row of 30)
SELECT SUM(p) AS s2 FROM price;     -- e.g. 200
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- s1 = 170, s2 = 200     <- phantom row appeared between statements

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: binary logging must be ROW format; statement-based replication is unsafe here. It does not stop lost updates by itself: read-modify-write needs FOR UPDATE or atomic UPDATE.

Architect's Notes

READ COMMITTED is a pragmatic OLTP default when you want fewer locks and deadlocks and your code tolerates non-repeatable reads. Use explicit FOR UPDATE or optimistic version columns for read-modify-write, and run consistent reports on a replica or inside REPEATABLE READ snapshots.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Every SELECT gets a fresh snapshot, so repeating a query in the same transaction can return different rows.
  • It takes fewer gap locks, reducing deadlocks and lock waits for write-heavy workloads.
  • With binlog_format=ROW it is safe for replication; statement format is limited.

Senior Notes

  • Many large systems choose READ COMMITTED to lower locking, accepting that logic must tolerate non-repeatable reads.
  • Use explicit locking (FOR UPDATE) or optimistic version checks for invariants.
  • Requires binlog_format=ROW or MIXED for correct replication.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on repeatable reads (a report reads the same table twice and totals do not match), using statement-based binlog, and assuming gap protection against phantom inserts. Use explicit locks or constraints for invariants.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'NEW';        -- 10
-- another session inserts and commits one NEW order
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'NEW';        -- 11 (phantom)
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- 10
-- 11

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Fewer gap locks means fewer lock waits and deadlocks on range updates and deletes. Compare lock waits and deadlock counters after switching.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Innodb_row_lock_waits','Innodb_row_lock_time_avg','Innodb_deadlocks');

-- OUTPUT: (before -> after switching)
-- Innodb_row_lock_waits    | 12400 -> 3100
-- Innodb_row_lock_time_avg |   420 ->  95
-- Innodb_deadlocks         |    38 ->   4

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a multi-user inventory system uses READ COMMITTED with atomic conditional updates for correctness, so concurrent orders do not block each other on gap locks.

beginner.content:
Introduction

REPEATABLE READ is InnoDB's default. The first consistent read in a transaction creates a snapshot (read view); all later plain SELECTs in that transaction see the same data even if others commit changes. InnoDB also uses next-key locks to prevent most phantoms for locking reads.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE price (id INT PRIMARY KEY, p INT) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO price VALUES (1,100);

SELECT @@transaction_isolation;           -- default level

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------------------+
-- | @@transaction_isolation |
-- +-------------------------+
-- | REPEATABLE-READ         |
-- +-------------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Many business operations (reports, multi-step calculations) need to see a stable view of the data. Repeatable read gives that without blocking writers, thanks to MVCC and undo-log version chains.
codeExamples:
-- Session A:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT p FROM price WHERE id = 1;       -- snapshot taken here: 100

-- Session B:  UPDATE price SET p = 150 WHERE id = 1;  (autocommit, committed)

-- Session A:
SELECT p FROM price WHERE id = 1;       -- still the snapshot

-- OUTPUT (Session A, second read):
-- +------+
-- |  100 |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: default for most MySQL OLTP, consistent backups (mysqldump --single-transaction relies on it), reports. Caution: the snapshot is only for plain reads; UPDATE and locking reads see the latest committed data.
codeExamples:
-- Locking reads / writes ignore the snapshot and use "current read".
-- Session A (same transaction as above):
SELECT p FROM price WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;     -- current read: sees 150

UPDATE price SET p = p + 1 WHERE id = 1;          -- operates on 150, not 100

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- |  150 |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Tx A:  BEGIN
          SELECT -> snapshot S0 -----------------------------+
          ...                          Tx B: UPDATE; COMMIT   |
          SELECT -> still reads S0 (via undo version chain) <-+
          UPDATE / FOR UPDATE -> current read (latest committed)

Fresher Notes

  • REPEATABLE READ is the default isolation level in InnoDB. A transaction sees a consistent snapshot taken at its first read.
  • Repeating the same SELECT gives the same rows, even if others commit changes.
  • It prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads.

Worked Example 1

Monitor undo history.
codeExamples:
SELECT count FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- count
-- 245

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Switch level for one session.

Practice Exercise 1

Repeatable read demo.

Practice Exercise 2

Current read versus snapshot read.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;                      -- snapshot: 1000
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;           -- current: 900
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1000.00
-- 900.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

REPEATABLE READ (the InnoDB default) creates one read view at the first consistent read of the transaction. Plain SELECTs read old row versions through undo, so repeated reads agree. Locking reads and writes use the latest committed data and take next-key locks to protect ranges.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Control the snapshot start with WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT. Use FOR SHARE / FOR UPDATE when a decision depends on the latest data. innodb_locks_unsafe_for_binlog is removed; use READ COMMITTED to avoid gap locks.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: consistent snapshot for the whole transaction, no dirty or non-repeatable reads, next-key locking protects range queries from phantoms, readers do not block writers.
codeExamples:
-- Phantoms are hidden from plain reads in the same snapshot.
-- Session A:  START TRANSACTION; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM price;   -- 1
-- Session B:  INSERT INTO price VALUES (2, 10);  COMMIT;
-- Session A:  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM price;                       -- still 1

-- OUTPUT (Session A, second read):
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |        1 |
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: gap and next-key locks block inserts into ranges and raise deadlock risk; long transactions keep old undo versions alive; mixing snapshot reads and current reads gives surprising results.
codeExamples:
-- Gap lock on a range blocks another session's insert.
-- Session A:  START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM price WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE;
-- Session B:  INSERT INTO price VALUES (15, 1);      -- waits...

-- OUTPUT (Session B, after innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 50s):
-- ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the snapshot is established at the first consistent read, not at BEGIN (use WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT for explicit start); phantoms can still appear when you mix a current read after a snapshot read; it does not prevent lost updates for read-modify-write done in application code.
codeExamples:
-- Snapshot started by the first read, or explicitly:
START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT;
-- Phantom via current read: UPDATE touches a row the snapshot cannot see, then it becomes visible.
-- Session B: INSERT INTO price VALUES (3, 5); COMMIT;
UPDATE price SET p = p WHERE id = 3;     -- modifies the row (current read)
SELECT p FROM price WHERE id = 3;        -- now visible to this transaction

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- |    5 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Stay on REPEATABLE READ unless gap-lock deadlocks or contention hurt you. Keep transactions short so undo history (see history list length) stays small, always add retry logic for deadlocks, and use FOR UPDATE or SERIALIZABLE-like patterns where the invariant spans several rows.

Mid-Level Notes

  • InnoDB also prevents most phantom reads using next-key locks for locking reads and a snapshot for plain reads.
  • Writes see the latest committed data, not the snapshot, which can surprise people (UPDATE affects rows newer than the snapshot).
  • Long transactions at this level keep old row versions alive, growing undo.

Senior Notes

  • Gap and next-key locks under REPEATABLE READ can cause unexpected lock waits and deadlocks on range queries.
  • Mixed snapshot reads and current reads in one transaction produce subtle anomalies; use FOR UPDATE for decisions.
  • Monitor history list length; keep transactions short.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mixing snapshot reads and writes in one transaction (the write acts on newer rows than the read saw), long-lived transactions that bloat undo, and being surprised by gap locks blocking inserts. Use locking reads for decisions.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT SUM(qty) FROM stock;                            -- snapshot total
-- another session commits +5 on A1
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty + 1 WHERE sku = 'A1';       -- acts on the latest value
SELECT SUM(qty) FROM stock;                            -- now includes the other commit as well
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- 10
-- 16

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Long snapshots keep old versions alive. Watch the history list length and the age of the oldest transaction, and keep reporting transactions short or run them on replicas.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: consistent backups and exports rely on the snapshot. mysqldump --single-transaction starts a REPEATABLE READ transaction with a consistent snapshot so the dump is a coherent point-in-time copy without blocking writers.
codeExamples:
mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 --routines shop > shop.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (shop.sql: all tables as of one instant; writers kept running)

beginner.content:
Introduction

SERIALIZABLE is the strictest level. In InnoDB it behaves like REPEATABLE READ but converts every plain SELECT into SELECT ... FOR SHARE (when autocommit is off), so readers take shared next-key locks and writers cannot sneak in.

Why Do We Need This?

Some invariants span many rows (no overlapping bookings, sum constraints). Serializable makes transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, so such logic is correct without extra locking code.
codeExamples:
-- Another session trying to modify the row we read must wait.
-- Session B:
UPDATE seat SET taken = 1 WHERE id = 1;     -- blocks until A commits/rolls back

-- OUTPUT (Session B, if A is still open):
-- ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: financial invariants, small critical sections, audits. Rarely the global setting; usually set per transaction for a specific operation.
codeExamples:
-- Use it surgically for one transaction.
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;   -- affects only the next transaction
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS free FROM seat WHERE taken = 0;    -- range read: shared next-key locks
UPDATE seat SET taken = 1 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | free |
-- +------+
-- |    2 |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   isolation   dirty  non-rep  phantom(plain/locking)  locking
   ----------- -----  -------  ----------------------  --------------
   READ UNCOMM  yes     yes      yes                    none for reads
   READ COMM    no      yes      yes                    record only
   REPEAT READ  no      no       mostly no (next-key)   next-key
   SERIALIZABLE no      no       no                     S next-key on reads

Fresher Notes

  • SERIALIZABLE is the strictest level: transactions behave as if they ran one after another.
  • InnoDB turns plain SELECTs into LOCK IN SHARE MODE reads when autocommit is off.
  • It prevents dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads but greatly reduces concurrency.

Worked Example 1

Cheaper invariant with conditional update.

Worked Example 2

Retry loop concept.
codeExamples:
-- pseudo-code
-- for attempt in 1..3: try { run tx } catch (1213 or 1205) { sleep(backoff); }

-- OUTPUT:
-- succeeded on attempt 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Readers block writers.

Practice Exercise 2

Phantom prevented.
codeExamples:
-- session A (SERIALIZABLE)
START TRANSACTION; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct WHERE bal > 500;
-- session B tries INSERT INTO acct VALUES (99, 800) and waits until A commits

-- OUTPUT: (A)
-- COUNT(*)
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

At SERIALIZABLE InnoDB converts plain SELECTs inside a transaction into SELECT ... FOR SHARE (when autocommit is off), so readers take shared next-key locks and block writers to the same ranges. This prevents phantoms and write skew at the cost of concurrency.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use it for short critical sections that must be fully serializable, or prefer narrower tools: unique constraints, conditional updates, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the checked rows, or optimistic versioning.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: no dirty reads, non-repeatable reads or phantoms; simplest correctness reasoning; protects against write skew-style anomalies by blocking.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;

-- OUTPUT (inside the session set above):
-- +-------------------------+
-- | SERIALIZABLE            |
-- +-------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: heavy locking: readers block writers and vice versa, throughput drops, and deadlocks become frequent (two sessions each holding a shared lock then trying to update the same row).
codeExamples:
-- Classic deadlock: both take shared locks, then both try to upgrade.
-- A: SELECT * FROM seat WHERE id = 1;        B: SELECT * FROM seat WHERE id = 1;
-- A: UPDATE seat SET taken=1 WHERE id=1;     (waits for B's S lock)
-- B: UPDATE seat SET taken=1 WHERE id=1;     (waits for A's S lock) -> deadlock

-- OUTPUT (victim session):
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: with autocommit=1 a plain SELECT is not locked (it is a consistent non-locking read in its own transaction); InnoDB's version is lock-based, not SSI like PostgreSQL, so there is no serialisation-failure retry model, only lock waits and deadlocks.
codeExamples:
SET autocommit = 1;
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
SELECT * FROM seat;          -- single statement: plain consistent read, no shared lock

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | taken |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 |     0 |
-- |  2 |     0 |
-- +----+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use SERIALIZABLE only for small, well-understood critical sections; for most invariants a unique constraint, a single atomic UPDATE, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a guard row is cheaper. If you adopt it, budget for retries on deadlock and measure throughput under load.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Readers block writers and vice versa, so lock waits and deadlocks rise.
  • Use only for short critical sections that truly need full isolation.
  • Often a targeted SELECT ... FOR UPDATE at a lower level is enough.

Senior Notes

  • Serializable throughput drops sharply under contention; design with retries.
  • Prefer constraints and conditional updates over blanket serializable isolation.
  • Test under concurrency to see the cost before adopting.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: global SERIALIZABLE (throughput collapses and deadlocks rise), not retrying after deadlock, and expecting it to fix application logic bugs. Design for retries.
codeExamples:
-- session A and B both read then update overlapping ranges:
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
-- handle in code: catch 1213, roll back, retry with backoff (bounded)

SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_deadlocks';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Innodb_deadlocks | 120

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Measure the cost: shared locks on every read multiply lock waits. Compare lock wait counters and latency between isolation levels with a realistic concurrent test.
codeExamples:
-- 64 clients, 90% reads
-- READ COMMITTED : 38,000 tps, p99 18 ms
-- SERIALIZABLE   :  9,200 tps, p99 420 ms
SELECT ROUND(38000 / 9200, 1) AS throughput_ratio;

-- OUTPUT:
-- throughput_ratio
-- 4.1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: use a narrow serializable-like guard instead of global SERIALIZABLE. "At least one doctor on call" is protected by locking the relevant rows.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Three classic anomalies. Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted change. Non-repeatable read: re-reading the same row gives a different value because someone committed an UPDATE. Phantom read: re-running a range query returns extra (or fewer) rows because someone committed an INSERT/DELETE.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, bal INT, owner VARCHAR(5)) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1,100,'amy'),(2,200,'baji');

-- Summary of what each level prevents in MySQL/InnoDB:
SELECT 'READ UNCOMMITTED' AS lvl, 'dirty yes' AS dirty, 'non-rep yes' AS nonrep, 'phantom yes' AS phantom
UNION ALL SELECT 'READ COMMITTED', 'dirty no', 'non-rep yes', 'phantom yes'
UNION ALL SELECT 'REPEATABLE READ', 'dirty no', 'non-rep no', 'phantom mostly no'
UNION ALL SELECT 'SERIALIZABLE', 'dirty no', 'non-rep no', 'phantom no';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+-----------+-------------+-------------------+
-- | lvl              | dirty     | nonrep      | phantom           |
-- +------------------+-----------+-------------+-------------------+
-- | READ UNCOMMITTED | dirty yes | non-rep yes | phantom yes       |
-- | READ COMMITTED   | dirty no  | non-rep yes | phantom yes       |
-- | REPEATABLE READ  | dirty no  | non-rep no  | phantom mostly no |
-- | SERIALIZABLE     | dirty no  | non-rep no  | phantom no        |
-- +------------------+-----------+-------------+-------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Knowing the anomaly vocabulary lets you choose the cheapest isolation level that is still correct, and diagnose "impossible" bugs such as totals that do not add up or balances that jump during a report.
codeExamples:
-- Non-repeatable read (READ COMMITTED):
-- A: BEGIN; SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;            -> 100
-- B: UPDATE acct SET bal=90 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
-- A: SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;                   -> 90   (same row, new value)

-- OUTPUT:
-- first read : 100
-- second read:  90

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real bugs: reports whose parts disagree (phantoms), "check then act" logic that sees stale rows, and dirty reads of rolled-back orders in fulfilment systems.
codeExamples:
-- Phantom (READ COMMITTED): the range count changes inside one transaction.
-- A: BEGIN; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct WHERE bal > 50;   -> 2
-- B: INSERT INTO acct VALUES (3, 300, 'cy'); COMMIT;
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct WHERE bal > 50;          -> 3  (phantom row)

-- OUTPUT:
-- first count : 2
-- second count: 3

beginner.content:
Diagram

   DIRTY          A reads B's UNCOMMITTED write   (B later rolls back)
   NON-REPEATABLE A reads row, B UPDATE+COMMIT, A reads row again -> value changed
   PHANTOM        A reads range, B INSERT+COMMIT, A reads range again -> extra row

   level:  RU   RC   RR   SER
   dirty    Y    N    N    N
   nonrep   Y    Y    N    N
   phantom  Y    Y    ~N   N

Fresher Notes

  • Dirty read: reading uncommitted data. Non-repeatable read: the same row changes between two reads. Phantom read: the same range query returns new rows.
  • Isolation levels decide which of these can happen.
  • READ UNCOMMITTED allows all three; SERIALIZABLE allows none.

Worked Example 1

Locking read blocks the phantom (REPEATABLE READ).
codeExamples:
-- A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM acct WHERE bal > 500 FOR UPDATE;
-- B: INSERT INTO acct VALUES (31, 800);   -- waits (gap lock)

-- OUTPUT: (B)
-- (blocked until A commits or lock wait timeout)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Matrix of anomalies.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'READ UNCOMMITTED' AS level, 'yes' AS dirty, 'yes' AS non_repeatable, 'yes' AS phantom
UNION ALL SELECT 'READ COMMITTED','no','yes','yes'
UNION ALL SELECT 'REPEATABLE READ','no','no','mostly no (InnoDB)'
UNION ALL SELECT 'SERIALIZABLE','no','no','no';

-- OUTPUT:
-- level            | dirty | non_repeatable | phantom
-- READ UNCOMMITTED | yes   | yes            | yes
-- READ COMMITTED   | no    | yes            | yes
-- REPEATABLE READ  | no    | no             | mostly no (InnoDB)
-- SERIALIZABLE     | no    | no             | no

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Non-repeatable read at READ COMMITTED.
codeExamples:
-- A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;   -- 1000
-- B: UPDATE acct SET bal = 900 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
-- A: SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;                      -- 900

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1000.00 then 900.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Phantom at READ COMMITTED.
codeExamples:
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct WHERE bal > 500;   -- 1
-- B: INSERT INTO acct VALUES (30, 700); COMMIT;
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct WHERE bal > 500;   -- 2

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1 then 2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Three read anomalies: a dirty read sees uncommitted data; a non-repeatable read sees a row change between two reads; a phantom read sees a different set of rows for the same predicate. Which are possible depends on the isolation level and on whether the read is a snapshot or a locking read.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'READ UNCOMMITTED' AS level, 'yes' AS dirty, 'yes' AS non_repeatable, 'yes' AS phantom
UNION ALL SELECT 'READ COMMITTED', 'no', 'yes', 'yes'
UNION ALL SELECT 'REPEATABLE READ (InnoDB)', 'no', 'no', 'no for snapshot reads, blocked for locking reads'
UNION ALL SELECT 'SERIALIZABLE', 'no', 'no', 'no';

-- OUTPUT:
-- level                    | dirty | non_repeatable | phantom
-- READ UNCOMMITTED         | yes   | yes            | yes
-- READ COMMITTED           | no    | yes            | yes
-- REPEATABLE READ (InnoDB) | no    | no             | no for snapshot reads, blocked for locking reads
-- SERIALIZABLE             | no    | no             | no

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Reproduce each with two sessions. For phantoms use a range predicate; for non-repeatable reads read the same row twice; for dirty reads set READ UNCOMMITTED in the reader.
codeExamples:
-- phantom at READ COMMITTED
-- A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 500;      -- 3
-- B: INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (1, 900); COMMIT;
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 500;                         -- 4

-- OUTPUT:
-- 3
-- 4

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of knowing them: you can map each anomaly to a prevention tool: dirty reads -> use READ COMMITTED+, non-repeatable -> REPEATABLE READ snapshot, phantoms -> next-key locks or SERIALIZABLE.
codeExamples:
-- REPEATABLE READ hides the phantom from plain SELECTs but a current read reveals it.
-- A: BEGIN; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct;                  -> 3  (snapshot)
-- B: INSERT INTO acct VALUES (4, 10, 'di'); COMMIT;
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct;                         -> 3  (hidden)
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct FOR UPDATE;              -> 4  (locking read sees it)

-- OUTPUT:
-- 3, 3, 4

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the strictest fixes cost concurrency, and some anomalies (lost update, write skew) are not in the classic three, so a correct level does not guarantee a correct application.
codeExamples:
-- Write skew under REPEATABLE READ: two doctors both go off-call.
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oncall WHERE on_duty=1;  -> 2    B: same -> 2
-- A: UPDATE oncall SET on_duty=0 WHERE doc='x';    B: UPDATE oncall SET on_duty=0 WHERE doc='y';
-- both commit -> zero doctors on call, rule broken

-- OUTPUT:
-- on_duty count after both commit: 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the SQL standard defines levels by these three anomalies only, but InnoDB's actual behaviour differs (REPEATABLE READ prevents most phantoms; READ UNCOMMITTED still locks writes). Always test on the engine you run.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@transaction_isolation AS current_level, @@global.transaction_isolation AS global_level;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+-----------------+
-- | current_level   | global_level    |
-- +-----------------+-----------------+
-- | REPEATABLE-READ | REPEATABLE-READ |
-- +-----------------+-----------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick isolation per invariant: the guarantee you need is about business rules (no overbooking, no negative balance), not anomaly names. Encode rules in constraints and atomic statements first, then add FOR UPDATE or stricter isolation only where a multi-row invariant remains.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Table: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty only; REPEATABLE READ prevents dirty and non-repeatable (and mostly phantoms in InnoDB); SERIALIZABLE prevents all.
  • Phantoms involve rows appearing or disappearing from a range or count.
  • Choose a level based on which anomalies your logic can tolerate.

Senior Notes

  • Anomalies appear as rare production bugs (double booking, negative stock); reproduce with two sessions and sleeps.
  • Fix by the narrowest tool: constraint, conditional update, FOR UPDATE, or a higher isolation level.
  • Write tests that run two transactions concurrently for critical flows.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: assuming REPEATABLE READ stops all phantoms (a later UPDATE acts on newer rows), testing concurrency with one session, and fixing anomalies by raising isolation globally. Fix with targeted locks or constraints.
codeExamples:
-- A at REPEATABLE READ
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 500;                   -- 3 (snapshot)
-- B inserts a 900 order and commits
UPDATE orders SET flag = 1 WHERE total > 500;                    -- updates 4 rows including the "phantom"
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE total > 500;                   -- 4: the row appeared

-- OUTPUT:
-- 3
-- 4

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Locking reads protect ranges with next-key locks at REPEATABLE READ, so inserts into the scanned gap wait. This costs concurrency; use only where the invariant needs it.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: ticket booking must not oversell seats. Instead of a high isolation level, lock the seat rows or enforce uniqueness, so two buyers cannot take the same seat even under READ COMMITTED.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value in the application, and both write: the second write overwrites the first, so one update vanishes. It is a read-modify-write race, not covered by the classic three anomalies.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE counter (id INT PRIMARY KEY, n INT, ver INT DEFAULT 0) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO counter VALUES (1, 10, 0);

-- A: SELECT n FROM counter WHERE id=1;            -> 10
-- B: SELECT n FROM counter WHERE id=1;            -> 10
-- A: UPDATE counter SET n = 10 + 1 WHERE id=1;    -- app computed 11
-- B: UPDATE counter SET n = 10 + 5 WHERE id=1;    -- app computed 15, overwrites A
SELECT n FROM counter WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- |   15 |      <- A's +1 was lost (correct total: 16)
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Counters, stock levels, balances and edited documents are all read-modify-write. If correctness matters you must stop the race; neither READ COMMITTED nor REPEATABLE READ snapshots alone prevent it when the arithmetic is done in the app.

Real-Time Use

Real use: pessimistic locking with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE for short critical sections, optimistic locking with a version column for user-edited records (HTTP forms, ORMs like JPA @Version).
codeExamples:
-- Fix 2: pessimistic lock - the second session waits for the first to finish.
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT n FROM counter WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;     -- takes an exclusive row lock
UPDATE counter SET n = 21 + 1 WHERE id = 1;        -- app-computed value is now safe
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- |   21 |
-- +------+
-- Query OK, 1 row affected

beginner.content:
Diagram

   n=10
   A: read 10 -----------------> write 11 --+
   B: read 10 -----> write 15 --------------+--> final = 11 or 15, expected 16
                                  (one update lost)

   Fixes:  UPDATE n = n + 1   |   SELECT .. FOR UPDATE   |   WHERE ver = :ver

Fresher Notes

  • A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, both change it, and the second write overwrites the first.
  • Example: two users read stock = 10, both subtract 1 and write 9, but it should be 8.
  • Avoid it with atomic updates like SET qty = qty - 1.

Worked Example 1

Optimistic locking.

Worked Example 2

Pessimistic locking.

Practice Exercise 1

Racy read-modify-write.
codeExamples:
-- A: SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku='A';          -- 10
-- B: SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku='A';          -- 10
-- A: UPDATE stock SET qty = 9 WHERE sku='A';
-- B: UPDATE stock SET qty = 9 WHERE sku='A';       -- should be 8

-- OUTPUT:
-- qty = 9  (one decrement lost)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Atomic fix.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, compute a new value in the application and write it back: the second write overwrites the first without seeing it. It is a read-modify-write race and is not prevented by READ COMMITTED or by plain snapshot reads.
codeExamples:
-- A: SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku='A1';                 -- 10
-- B: SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku='A1';                 -- 10
-- A: UPDATE stock SET qty = 9 WHERE sku='A1'; COMMIT;
-- B: UPDATE stock SET qty = 9 WHERE sku='A1'; COMMIT;      -- should have been 8

SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1';

-- OUTPUT:
-- qty
-- 9            (one decrement was lost)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Three fixes: do the arithmetic in SQL (atomic UPDATE), lock the row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or use optimistic locking with a version column and check the affected-row count.
codeExamples:
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1' AND qty > 0;                                    -- atomic

START TRANSACTION; SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR UPDATE; UPDATE stock SET qty = 8 WHERE sku = 'A1'; COMMIT;   -- pessimistic

UPDATE documents SET body = 'new', version = version + 1 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 3;             -- optimistic
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS saved;

-- OUTPUT:
-- saved
-- 1

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of the fixes: atomic updates are simplest and fastest; FOR UPDATE gives full control; optimistic versioning scales well with rare conflicts and holds no locks while a user thinks.
codeExamples:
-- Fix 3: optimistic locking with a version column.
UPDATE counter SET n = 30, ver = ver + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND ver = 0;   -- ver we read earlier
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS rows_changed;                                    -- 0 means someone else won

-- OUTPUT (success path):
-- +--------------+
-- | rows_changed |
-- +--------------+
-- |            1 |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: pessimistic locks reduce concurrency and can deadlock; optimistic updates require the application to detect zero affected rows and retry or report a conflict.
codeExamples:
-- Optimistic conflict: stale version, nothing updated.
UPDATE counter SET n = 99, ver = ver + 1 WHERE id = 1 AND ver = 0;   -- ver is already 1
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS rows_changed;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | rows_changed |
-- +--------------+
-- |            0 |      <- app must re-read and retry
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL does not raise "could not serialize" errors at REPEATABLE READ like PostgreSQL: InnoDB lets the second UPDATE proceed on the latest committed row, so detection is your job. Multi-row invariants may need locks on a guard row or SERIALIZABLE.
codeExamples:
-- Under REPEATABLE READ, the snapshot read is stale but the UPDATE applies to the latest row.
-- A: BEGIN; SELECT n FROM counter WHERE id=1;   -> 21 (snapshot)
-- B: UPDATE counter SET n = 100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
-- A: UPDATE counter SET n = 21 + 1 WHERE id=1;  -- silently overwrites B's 100: lost update!
-- A: COMMIT;   -> n = 22

-- OUTPUT:
-- n = 22   (B's change lost; no error is raised)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer the cheapest correct tool: atomic expression updates first, then optimistic versioning for human-speed edits, then FOR UPDATE for critical sections. Add a retry loop with backoff for deadlocks, and keep read-modify-write transactions as short as possible.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Fixes: atomic expression update, SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (pessimistic), version column check (optimistic).
  • Isolation level alone does not prevent it under READ COMMITTED; REPEATABLE READ in InnoDB still allows read-modify-write races with plain SELECT.
  • Use affected-row counts to detect failed optimistic updates.

Senior Notes

  • Optimistic locking scales well for low conflict; pessimistic locking suits high conflict hot rows.
  • For counters under heavy contention use sharded counters or queues.
  • Always read-modify-write inside the database (single statement) when possible.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: read in one request and write in another with no version check, overwriting the whole row with stale values from a form, and assuming transactions alone prevent it. Include a version or use column-level atomic updates.
codeExamples:
UPDATE profiles SET name = 'Abaji', phone = '999', city = 'Pune' WHERE id = 1;      -- stale form overwrites a concurrent phone change
UPDATE profiles SET name = 'Abaji' WHERE id = 1;                                      -- only update the changed columns

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Pessimistic locks hold rows during user think time and reduce concurrency; optimistic checks are free until a conflict happens. Choose by conflict rate: optimistic for low conflict, FOR UPDATE for hot short operations.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROW_COUNT();                      -- 0 means conflict: reload, merge, retry
SELECT trx_state, trx_rows_locked FROM information_schema.innodb_trx;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ROW_COUNT()
-- 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a counter incremented by many requests. Use an atomic UPDATE for exactness, and for extremely hot counters spread across slots and sum on read.

beginner.content:
Introduction

InnoDB has two basic row lock modes. A shared (S) lock lets a transaction read a row and allows other readers to share it; an exclusive (X) lock lets a transaction change or delete a row and blocks every other S or X request on that row. Plain SELECT takes no lock at all (it reads a snapshot).

Why Do We Need This?

Without locks two transactions could change the same row at once and one update would be lost, or a transaction could act on data that is about to vanish. The S/X matrix is the minimum rule set that keeps concurrent writers safe while still letting many readers run together.
codeExamples:
-- Lost update prevented: both sessions do read-modify-write on balance.
-- Session A                                   -- Session B
START TRANSACTION;                             START TRANSACTION;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE;   -- B: same SELECT ... FOR UPDATE blocks here
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE id=1;
COMMIT;                                        -- B is released, now reads 70, not 100
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;

-- OUTPUT (session B after A commits):
-- +------+
-- | bal  |
-- +------+
-- |   70 |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Use S locks when you must make sure a parent row is not deleted or changed while you insert a child (InnoDB does this automatically for foreign keys). Use X locks (FOR UPDATE, UPDATE, DELETE) for read-then-write flows such as inventory and balances. Inspect current locks in performance_schema.data_locks.
codeExamples:
-- See which locks are currently held (MySQL 8).
SELECT object_name, index_name, lock_type, lock_mode, lock_data
FROM performance_schema.data_locks
WHERE object_name = 'acct';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+------------+-----------+---------------+-----------+
-- | object_name | index_name | lock_type | lock_mode     | lock_data |
-- +-------------+------------+-----------+---------------+-----------+
-- | acct        | NULL       | TABLE     | IX            | NULL      |
-- | acct        | PRIMARY    | RECORD    | X,REC_NOT_GAP | 1         |
-- +-------------+------------+-----------+---------------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

Lock compatibility (Y = both can hold it)

              held: S      held: X
  request S :   Y            N
  request X :   N            N

  plain SELECT ----> snapshot (MVCC), no lock
  FOR SHARE    ----> S lock on index records
  UPDATE/FOR UPDATE -> X lock on index records
  table level: IS / IX intention locks announce row locks below

Fresher Notes

  • A shared (S) lock allows reading and lets others also read. An exclusive (X) lock is needed to write and blocks others from reading with locks or writing.
  • Multiple S locks can coexist; an X lock is exclusive.
  • In SQL: FOR SHARE takes S locks; FOR UPDATE takes X locks.

Worked Example 1

Who blocks whom.
codeExamples:
SELECT waiting_pid, waiting_query, blocking_pid, blocking_query FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- waiting_pid | waiting_query            | blocking_pid | blocking_query
-- 22          | UPDATE acct SET bal = ...|           19 | NULL (idle in transaction)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Kill the blocker.

Practice Exercise 1

Shared vs exclusive.
codeExamples:
-- A
START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE;
-- B
SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE;      -- works
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 1 WHERE id = 1;      -- waits

-- OUTPUT: (B update)
-- (blocked until A commits)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

See current locks.
codeExamples:
SELECT object_name, index_name, lock_type, lock_mode, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_name | index_name | lock_type | lock_mode | lock_data
-- acct        | NULL       | TABLE     | IS        | NULL
-- acct        | PRIMARY    | RECORD    | S,REC_NOT_GAP | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

InnoDB uses shared (S) and exclusive (X) locks on records, plus intention locks (IS, IX) on tables. S locks are compatible with S; X is incompatible with everything. Plain consistent SELECTs take no locks; locking reads, UPDATE, DELETE and INSERT do.
codeExamples:
-- A
START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR SHARE;
-- B
SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR SHARE;          -- works
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty + 1 WHERE sku = 'A1';          -- waits for A

SELECT object_name, lock_type, lock_mode, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_name | lock_type | lock_mode     | lock_data
-- stock       | TABLE     | IS            | NULL
-- stock       | RECORD    | S,REC_NOT_GAP | 'A1'

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Syntax: FOR SHARE (S lock), FOR UPDATE (X lock), with NOWAIT or SKIP LOCKED. LOCK IN SHARE MODE is the older spelling.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: correctness under concurrency; many readers can share; consistent reads (MVCC) need no locks so reads never block writes in normal SELECTs.
codeExamples:
-- Compatibility: two S locks coexist, so both FOR SHARE succeed.
-- Session A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id=1 FOR SHARE;
-- Session B: START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id=1 FOR SHARE;   -- no wait
-- Plain SELECT in session C is never blocked either:
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | bal  |
-- +------+
-- |  100 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: locks are held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK, so long transactions block others; S-then-upgrade-to-X patterns cause deadlocks (two sessions each hold S and both want X).
codeExamples:
-- Classic upgrade deadlock.
-- A: SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id=1 FOR SHARE;
-- B: SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id=1 FOR SHARE;
-- A: UPDATE acct SET bal=1 WHERE id=1;     -- waits for B's S lock
-- B: UPDATE acct SET bal=2 WHERE id=1;     -- would wait for A -> cycle
