SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS;                   -- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK section

-- OUTPUT (session B):
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: locks live only inside a transaction (with autocommit=1 they release immediately); MyISAM has no row locks; lock waiting is bounded by innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s); locks are on index records, so a missing index widens them.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_lock_wait_timeout';
SET SESSION innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 5;    -- fail fast in this session
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_lock_wait_timeout';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name            | Value |
-- +--------------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_lock_wait_timeout | 50    |   <- first SHOW
-- | innodb_lock_wait_timeout | 5     |   <- second SHOW
-- +--------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer MVCC reads and keep X-lock windows tiny: do the lock, change, commit in one short transaction. Avoid S-then-X upgrades; take FOR UPDATE up front. Always retry on error 1213 and 1205 in the application layer.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Plain consistent SELECTs take no locks in InnoDB (MVCC).
  • UPDATE and DELETE take X locks on rows they touch.
  • Compatibility: S with S is fine; S with X or X with X must wait.

Senior Notes

  • Inspect locks with performance_schema.data_locks and data_lock_waits (8.0).
  • Keep lock hold time short and access rows in a consistent order.
  • Locking reads inside long transactions are a main source of contention.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: locking reads on unindexed predicates (every scanned row gets locked), long transactions holding locks, and inconsistent lock order across code paths (deadlocks). Index the predicate and always lock in the same order.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE payload = 'x' FOR UPDATE;       -- type=ALL: locks all scanned rows
ALTER TABLE jobs ADD INDEX idx_status (status);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE status = 'NEW' FOR UPDATE;       -- type=ref: locks only matching rows

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- ALL / ref

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Lock waits cost latency. Find who waits for whom, how long, and which statement is the blocker, then shorten or reorder transactions.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world job queue: workers claim distinct rows with SKIP LOCKED so they never wait on each other.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Row-level locks (InnoDB) lock only the index records a statement touches, so different rows can be changed in parallel. Table locks (LOCK TABLES, MyISAM, DDL metadata locks) lock the whole table and serialize access.
codeExamples:
-- Row lock: two sessions update different rows at the same time.
-- Session A: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=1;
-- Session B: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=2;   -- no wait
-- Table lock: blocks everyone else
LOCK TABLES acct WRITE;     -- whole table, this session only may use it
UNLOCK TABLES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (A)
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (B, runs concurrently)
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected  (LOCK TABLES)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Row locks give high write concurrency for OLTP workloads; table locks are simple and cheap, and are needed for backups, maintenance or bulk loads where you want exclusivity. Knowing which one you are getting explains most "why is my query stuck" cases.
codeExamples:
-- A DDL statement waits for a metadata lock held by an open transaction.
-- A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM acct;          -- holds shared MDL, never committed
-- B: ALTER TABLE acct ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(20);   -- waits for MDL
SELECT object_name, lock_type, lock_status
FROM performance_schema.metadata_locks WHERE object_name = 'acct';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+---------------------+-------------+
-- | object_name | lock_type           | lock_status |
-- +-------------+---------------------+-------------+
-- | acct        | SHARED_READ         | GRANTED     |
-- | acct        | EXCLUSIVE           | PENDING     |
-- +-------------+---------------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: web checkout updates thousands of different orders concurrently (row locks); nightly mysqldump of MyISAM tables uses table locks; online schema change tools watch metadata locks. Intention locks (IS, IX) sit on the table to let InnoDB check table-level conflicts cheaply.

Diagram

  OLTP (InnoDB)                      Maintenance / MyISAM
  +-----+  row 1  X (session A)          +----------------------+
  |tbl  |  row 2  X (session B)  ok      | table  WRITE lock    |
  |     |  row 3  free                   | everyone else waits  |
  +-----+                                +----------------------+
  IX on table + X on records             MDL: DDL vs open transactions

  concurrency:  row lock  >>>  table lock
  overhead   :  row lock  >>>  table lock

Fresher Notes

  • Row-level locks lock only the rows touched (InnoDB). Table locks lock the whole table (MyISAM, or LOCK TABLES).
  • Row locks allow many sessions to work on different rows of the same table at once.
  • InnoDB uses row locks by default, plus intention locks on the table.

Worked Example 1

Metadata lock pile-up.
codeExamples:
SELECT object_name, lock_type, lock_status, owner_thread_id FROM performance_schema.metadata_locks WHERE object_name = 'acct';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_name | lock_type    | lock_status | owner_thread_id
-- acct        | SHARED_READ  | GRANTED     | 31
-- acct        | EXCLUSIVE    | PENDING     | 40

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Fail fast on DDL.

Practice Exercise 1

Index limits locked rows.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN UPDATE orders2 SET status = 'X' WHERE customer_id = 7;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key     | rows
-- range | idx_cov | 12      (locks about 12 rows, not the whole table)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Explicit table lock.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

InnoDB locks individual index records (row-level), so sessions can modify different rows of one table at the same time. Table locks (LOCK TABLES, MyISAM) block the whole table. Metadata locks protect table structure and queue behind long transactions.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Explicit table locks: LOCK TABLES t READ/WRITE and FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK (backups), rarely needed with InnoDB. Online DDL uses metadata locks briefly at start and end.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of row locks: parallel writers, small blast radius, rollback of single rows. Table locks: almost no memory, no deadlocks, fast for bulk or read-mostly work.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: row locks use more memory and CPU and can deadlock; table locks block all writers (and readers for WRITE) so concurrency collapses; a stray open transaction blocks DDL.
codeExamples:
-- Without a usable index the UPDATE locks every scanned row (looks like a table lock).
CREATE TABLE tl (id INT PRIMARY KEY, grp INT) ENGINE=InnoDB;   -- no index on grp
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE tl SET id = id WHERE grp = 3;      -- full scan: X lock on each row scanned
SELECT COUNT(*) AS locked FROM performance_schema.data_locks WHERE object_name='tl' AND lock_type='RECORD';

-- OUTPUT (example, 4 rows in table):
-- +--------+
-- | locked |
-- +--------+
-- |      5 |    <- every row plus supremum record
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: LOCK TABLES is released implicitly by START TRANSACTION and cannot be used inside stored programs the same way; InnoDB table locks via LOCK TABLES do not replace row locks; MyISAM has only table locks and no transactions.

Architect's Notes

Default to InnoDB row locks and design indexes so statements touch few rows. Treat metadata locks as an operational hazard: set lock_wait_timeout for DDL, kill idle transactions, and use online DDL or gh-ost/pt-osc for big tables.

Mid-Level Notes

  • InnoDB row locks are placed on index entries; a query without a useful index may lock many rows (or effectively all).
  • Intention locks (IS, IX) at table level signal that row locks exist; they conflict only with table-level locks.
  • LOCK TABLES is rarely needed in InnoDB and blocks concurrency.

Senior Notes

  • A missing index on the WHERE column of an UPDATE can lock far more rows than needed, causing contention; always index update/delete predicates.
  • Metadata locks (MDL) also exist: DDL waits for open transactions on a table and blocks new ones behind it.
  • Long transactions plus ALTER TABLE cause "Waiting for table metadata lock" pile-ups.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: an UPDATE without a usable index (locks every scanned row, effectively the table), DDL queued behind a long transaction (all later queries stack up behind it), and LOCK TABLES in applications. Fail DDL fast with a short lock timeout.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Row locks scale concurrency but have per-lock memory and CPU cost; locking millions of rows in one transaction is slow. Batch large updates and index predicates.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: schema changes at peak hours. Check for open transactions on the table first, use ALGORITHM/LOCK clauses, and a short lock_wait_timeout so the ALTER aborts instead of blocking the application.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Under REPEATABLE READ, InnoDB locks more than the rows it finds. A record lock locks one index record. A gap lock locks the open interval between two index records (stopping inserts there). A next-key lock is a record lock plus the gap before it, and is the default range lock.

Why Do We Need This?

Gap locks exist to prevent phantom rows: if a range scan could be re-run and see a newly inserted row, repeatable read would be broken. Locking the gap makes the range stable for the transaction.
codeExamples:
-- Session A locked the range v in (10,30]. Session B tries to insert inside it.
INSERT INTO gl VALUES (4, 25);            -- Session B

-- OUTPUT (after timeout):
-- ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction
-- But inserting outside the gap works:
-- INSERT INTO gl VALUES (5, 50);   -> Query OK, 1 row affected

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real impact: a "check then insert" job locking a range can freeze unrelated inserts on a busy table, and gap locks are a classic source of surprising deadlocks between two inserters. Unique-index equality lookups on an existing row use only a record lock, avoiding gaps.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM gl WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE;     -- unique index, row exists -> record lock only
SELECT lock_mode, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks WHERE object_name='gl' AND lock_type='RECORD';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+-----------+
-- | lock_mode     | lock_data |
-- +---------------+-----------+
-- | X,REC_NOT_GAP | 2         |
-- +---------------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

index v:   10      20      30
             |  gap  |  gap  |  gap   |
       ------o-------o-------o--------o------>

  record lock : [20]            only that entry
  gap lock    : (10,20)         no inserts in the open interval
  next-key    : (10,20]         gap + record  (default, REPEATABLE READ)
  supremum    : (30, +inf)      last gap

Fresher Notes

  • InnoDB has record locks (on an index entry), gap locks (the gap between entries) and next-key locks (record plus the gap before it).
  • They are used mainly at REPEATABLE READ to prevent phantoms.
  • A gap lock stops other transactions from inserting into the locked range.

Worked Example 1

Same query at READ COMMITTED.

Worked Example 2

Unique equality takes a record lock only.

Practice Exercise 1

Gap lock blocks insert.
codeExamples:
-- table has ids 10 and 20
-- A
START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM t WHERE id BETWEEN 11 AND 19 FOR UPDATE;   -- locks the gap
-- B
INSERT INTO t VALUES (15);

-- OUTPUT: (B)
-- (waits; then ERROR 1205 Lock wait timeout exceeded)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

See gap locks.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, lock_mode, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks WHERE object_name = 't';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name | lock_mode | lock_data
-- PRIMARY    | X,GAP     | 20

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A record lock locks one index entry. A gap lock locks the open interval between entries (preventing inserts there). A next-key lock is a record lock plus the gap before it. At REPEATABLE READ, locking reads and writes over ranges take next-key locks to stop phantoms.
codeExamples:
-- table t(id PK) has ids 10, 20, 30
-- A
START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM t WHERE id BETWEEN 11 AND 25 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT index_name, lock_mode, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks WHERE object_name = 't';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name | lock_mode | lock_data
-- PRIMARY    | X         | 30           (next-key: record 30 and the gap (20,30])
-- PRIMARY    | X,GAP     | 20           (gap before 20)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

An equality search on a unique index that finds the row takes only a record lock; searches for missing keys, non-unique indexes and ranges take gap or next-key locks. READ COMMITTED disables most gap locking.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: real phantom protection at REPEATABLE READ, and replication-safe statement-based logging; no application code needed.
codeExamples:
-- Reads inside the transaction stay identical because the gap cannot gain rows.
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gl WHERE v > 10 FOR UPDATE;   -- 2
-- other session cannot insert v=15 here
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM gl WHERE v > 10 FOR UPDATE;   -- still 2
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |        2 |
-- +----------+   (both times)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: wide locks reduce insert concurrency, raise deadlock probability, and are hard to reason about. Gap locks do not conflict with each other (two sessions can hold the same gap), but both then block inserts.
codeExamples:
-- Two sessions hold the same gap, then both insert into it -> deadlock.
-- A: SELECT * FROM gl WHERE id = 15 FOR UPDATE;   -- id 15 missing -> gap lock (10..)
-- B: SELECT * FROM gl WHERE id = 15 FOR UPDATE;   -- also gets the gap, no wait
-- A: INSERT INTO gl VALUES (15, 1);               -- waits on B's gap
-- B: INSERT INTO gl VALUES (15, 2);               -- cycle

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: gap locking applies to REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE; at READ COMMITTED gap locks are mostly disabled (only for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks). Gap locks need an index; a scan without one locks everything.
codeExamples:
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;   -- no gap locks for ordinary range scans
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM gl WHERE v BETWEEN 15 AND 25 FOR UPDATE;
SELECT lock_mode, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks WHERE object_name='gl' AND lock_type='RECORD';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+-----------+
-- | lock_mode     | lock_data |
-- +---------------+-----------+
-- | X,REC_NOT_GAP | 20, 2     |
-- | X,REC_NOT_GAP | 2         |
-- +---------------+-----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

If gap locks hurt, move hot paths to READ COMMITTED with row-based binary logging, or use unique-key equality access. Always examine data_locks when tuning write contention; the right fix is usually a better index, not a bigger timeout.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Range queries with locking reads (FOR UPDATE) lock the scanned range and the gap after it.
  • Unique index equality on an existing row takes only a record lock; non-unique or missing keys take gap/next-key locks.
  • At READ COMMITTED gap locks are mostly disabled.

Senior Notes

  • Gap locks are a frequent hidden cause of deadlocks and insert stalls; inspect data_locks with lock_mode like X,GAP.
  • Two sessions can both hold the same gap lock (they do not conflict) and then deadlock on inserts.
  • Design queries to use unique equality when possible, narrow ranges and proper indexes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: not realising SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a missing key blocks inserts nearby, deadlocks between sessions holding the same gap lock then inserting, and range deletes locking huge gaps. Use unique-key existence checks and READ COMMITTED where phantoms are acceptable.
codeExamples:
-- A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 15 FOR UPDATE;    -- gap lock
-- B: START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = 16 FOR UPDATE;    -- gap locks are shared: both succeed
-- A: INSERT INTO t VALUES (15);   waits for B's gap lock
-- B: INSERT INTO t VALUES (16);   deadlock

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Diagnose lock footprints with data_locks and the deadlock report. Narrow the lock range with precise, indexed predicates.
codeExamples:
SELECT engine_transaction_id, index_name, lock_type, lock_mode, lock_status, lock_data FROM performance_schema.data_locks ORDER BY engine_transaction_id;
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK ... HOLDS THE LOCK(S): RECORD LOCKS space id 41 index PRIMARY ... lock_mode X locks gap before rec

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a "reserve first free slot" routine locked a large gap and caused insert stalls. Switching to READ COMMITTED and claiming by unique key removed the stalls.

beginner.content:
Introduction

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads rows and places exclusive locks on them for the rest of the transaction. Others can neither update them nor lock them until you commit, so you can safely read, decide, then write.

Why Do We Need This?

A plain read-then-write has a race: two buyers read qty = 1, both decide to buy, stock goes negative. Locking at read time serialises them without changing isolation level for the whole app.
codeExamples:
-- Session B arrives while A holds the lock; B waits, then sees the updated value.
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR UPDATE;   -- blocks until A commits
-- A committed: qty is now 4
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku='A1' AND qty > 0;
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT (B's SELECT, after waiting):
-- +-----+
-- | qty |
-- +-----+
-- |   4 |
-- +-----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used for seat booking, inventory reservation, job queues (pick one pending job), balance transfers. MySQL 8 adds NOWAIT (fail instantly) and SKIP LOCKED (ignore locked rows), ideal for work queues.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE jobs (id INT PRIMARY KEY, state VARCHAR(8)) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO jobs VALUES (1,'NEW'),(2,'NEW'),(3,'NEW');

START TRANSACTION;
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state='NEW' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;  -- worker 1
-- worker 2 running the same query at the same time gets the next unlocked row

-- OUTPUT:
-- worker 1:            worker 2:
-- +----+               +----+
-- | id |               | id |
-- +----+               +----+
-- |  1 |               |  2 |
-- +----+               +----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   worker A                 stock row 'A1'               worker B
   BEGIN
   SELECT .. FOR UPDATE ----->  [X locked by A]
                                                         SELECT .. FOR UPDATE
                                                         (waits...)
   UPDATE qty = qty-1
   COMMIT  ------------------>  [released] ------------>  gets lock, reads fresh qty

   SKIP LOCKED : B jumps to the next free row instead of waiting
   NOWAIT      : B gets error 3572 immediately

Fresher Notes

  • SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads rows and locks them exclusively until the transaction ends, so nobody else can modify them.
  • Use it when you read a value and then update based on it.
  • It must be inside a transaction to be useful.

Worked Example 1

Work queue with SKIP LOCKED.

Worked Example 2

Unindexed predicate locks too much.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE payload = 'x' FOR UPDATE;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | rows
-- ALL  | NULL | 50000     (locks all scanned rows)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Safe transfer.

Practice Exercise 2

NOWAIT fails fast.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE reads the latest committed version of matching rows and takes exclusive locks on the index records it visits (plus gap locks at REPEATABLE READ). The locks last until the transaction ends. It must run inside a transaction to be useful.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: NOWAIT fails immediately, SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows (queues), OF table locks specific tables in a join, FOR SHARE for shared locks. Always add ORDER BY with consistent order for multi-row locking.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: simple pessimistic concurrency control; correct under any isolation level; NOWAIT and SKIP LOCKED give non-blocking behaviour.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;   -- if locked elsewhere: error at once

-- OUTPUT (when another session holds the row):
-- ERROR 3572 (HY000): Statement aborted because lock(s) could not be acquired immediately
--                     and NOWAIT is set.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: holds locks while the application thinks (user pauses, network calls) and blocks others; wide scans lock many rows and gaps; ordering mistakes cause deadlocks.
codeExamples:
-- Deadlock from opposite lock order.
-- A: SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku='A1' FOR UPDATE;
-- B: SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku='B1' FOR UPDATE;
-- A: SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku='B1' FOR UPDATE;   -- waits for B
-- B: SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku='A1' FOR UPDATE;   -- waits for A

-- OUTPUT (victim):
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: only meaningful inside a transaction (autocommit releases immediately); needs InnoDB; locks index records so filter on an index; OF tbl restricts which table in a join is locked.

Architect's Notes

Use pessimistic locks for hot, high-contention rows and optimistic version columns (UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?) for low contention. Always lock in a consistent key order, keep the transaction short, and use SKIP LOCKED for queue tables.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Add NOWAIT to fail immediately or SKIP LOCKED to skip locked rows (8.0), perfect for job queues.
  • Lock only needed rows with an indexed WHERE; otherwise you lock many rows or gaps.
  • FOR SHARE takes a shared lock instead.

Senior Notes

  • SKIP LOCKED enables scalable work queues in MySQL (multiple workers claim different rows).
  • Keep the locked section short; avoid network calls while holding locks.
  • Acquire locks in a consistent order (by primary key) to prevent deadlocks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no index on the predicate (locks all scanned rows), locking in different orders (deadlocks), holding locks during network calls, and using it outside a transaction (the lock is released immediately with autocommit on).
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM jobs WHERE payload = 'x' FOR UPDATE;       -- type=ALL
SELECT * FROM stock WHERE sku = 'A1' FOR UPDATE;                    -- autocommit=1: lock released at statement end
SET autocommit = 0;                                                  -- or wrap in START TRANSACTION

-- OUTPUT:
-- type=ALL         (locks every row it scans)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Keep the locked section as short as possible and measure lock wait time. Contended hot rows limit throughput; consider splitting the hot row or queueing writes.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: seat reservation with a hold. Lock the seat row, check it, insert the hold, commit, then process payment outside the transaction.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Lock contention is many transactions waiting for the same locks. A deadlock is a cycle of waits (A waits for B, B waits for A). InnoDB detects deadlocks, rolls back the cheaper transaction (the victim) and returns error 1213.
codeExamples:
-- Reproduce a deadlock with two sessions.
-- A: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=1;
-- B: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=2;
-- A: UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=2;     -- waits for B
-- B: UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=1;     -- cycle detected

-- OUTPUT (session B):
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Contention reduces throughput and raises latency; deadlocks are inevitable in busy systems, so you need to know how to see, handle and reduce them rather than hope they never occur.

Real-Time Use

In production: wrap transactions in a retry loop for error 1213, log the last deadlock (innodb_print_all_deadlocks=ON), and kill long blockers found with sys.innodb_lock_waits.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- Look for the section:
-- ------------------------
-- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
-- ------------------------
-- *** (1) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=2
-- *** (2) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+1 WHERE id=1
-- *** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)
SET GLOBAL innodb_print_all_deadlocks = ON;     -- also write every deadlock to the error log

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Diagram

  Session A                    Session B
  lock row 1  (held)           lock row 2  (held)
      |                            |
      v                            v
  wants row 2 -----waits-----> held by B
  held by A  <-----waits------ wants row 1

        A ---> B ---> A     cycle -> InnoDB picks victim, ROLLBACK, error 1213

  Fix: same lock order, short transactions, good indexes, retry

Fresher Notes

  • Lock contention is when transactions wait for each other’s locks. A deadlock is a cycle of waits where nobody can proceed.
  • InnoDB detects deadlocks, rolls back one transaction (the victim) and returns error 1213.
  • You must retry the failed transaction.

Worked Example 1

Consistent lock order avoids it.

Worked Example 2

Log all deadlocks.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a deadlock.

Practice Exercise 2

Read the deadlock report.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
-- *** (1) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE acct ... WAITING FOR THIS LOCK TO BE GRANTED
-- *** (2) TRANSACTION: ... HOLDS THE LOCK(S)
-- *** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A deadlock is a cycle of lock waits: A holds X and waits for Y while B holds Y and waits for X. InnoDB detects the cycle by building a wait-for graph and rolls back the transaction that has done the least work (the victim) with error 1213. Lock wait timeout (1205) happens when no cycle exists but the wait is too long.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS (latest deadlock), innodb_print_all_deadlocks (log all), performance_schema.data_locks, innodb_lock_wait_timeout, and innodb_deadlock_detect.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of InnoDB handling: automatic detection in milliseconds, automatic rollback of one side, the other proceeds; rich diagnostics in performance_schema and sys.
codeExamples:
-- Application retry pattern (pseudo-SQL flow).
-- attempt = 0
-- loop:
--   START TRANSACTION; ...work...; COMMIT;
--   on error 1213 or 1205: ROLLBACK; attempt++; sleep(backoff); retry (max 3)
SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE AS deadlocks FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME='Innodb_deadlocks';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------+
-- | deadlocks |
-- +-----------+
-- | 3         |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: deadlock rollback loses work; detection itself costs CPU under extreme load; contention can cascade into thread pile-up and connection exhaustion.
codeExamples:
-- Under heavy hot-row load deadlock detection can be turned off (use a short timeout instead).
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_deadlock_detect';
SET GLOBAL innodb_deadlock_detect = OFF;      -- only for extreme hot-row workloads
SET GLOBAL innodb_lock_wait_timeout = 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name          | Value |
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_deadlock_detect | ON    |
-- +------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB sees only its own row locks; deadlocks that involve table locks (LOCK TABLES) or metadata locks across engines may not be detected and resolve only by timeout. The whole transaction is rolled back on 1213, but only the statement on 1205 by default.
codeExamples:
-- Lock-wait timeout rolls back just the statement unless this is ON.
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_rollback_on_timeout';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name              | Value |
-- +----------------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_rollback_on_timeout | OFF   |
-- +----------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prevent deadlocks by design: touch rows in one global order, keep transactions short, index every filter, and avoid mixed gap/insert patterns. Accept that some will still happen and make every write path idempotent and retry-safe with backoff.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Reduce them: keep transactions short, lock rows in a consistent order, index predicates, avoid user waits inside transactions.
  • Lock wait timeout (error 1205, default 50 s) is different from a deadlock.
  • See the latest deadlock in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS; log all with innodb_print_all_deadlocks=ON.

Senior Notes

  • Design for retries: idempotent operations and bounded retry with jitter.
  • Hot rows (counters, sequences) cause contention; shard them or use queues.
  • Monitor: lock waits, deadlock counts (Innodb_deadlocks), long transactions and p99 latency.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: not retrying, inconsistent lock order, big multi-row updates without indexes, and raising the wait timeout instead of fixing contention. Always lock in a canonical order (for example ascending id) and keep transactions small.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hot rows (counters, sequences, "latest" pointers) serialize all writers. Shard the counter, queue updates, or switch to append-only inserts aggregated later.
codeExamples:
SELECT object_name, COUNT(*) AS waiting FROM performance_schema.data_lock_waits w JOIN performance_schema.data_locks l ON l.engine_lock_id = w.requesting_engine_lock_id GROUP BY object_name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_name | waiting
-- counters    | 48           (a hot row)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world retry wrapper: catch 1213 and 1205, roll back, wait with exponential backoff and jitter, and retry the entire transaction a few times before failing.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A view is a named, stored SELECT. It holds no data of its own; every time you query it, MySQL runs the underlying query. CREATE VIEW defines it, ALTER VIEW (or CREATE OR REPLACE) changes it, DROP VIEW removes it.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji','IT',900),(2,'Ben','HR',700),(3,'Cy','IT',800);

CREATE VIEW v_it AS
SELECT id, name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';   -- stored query only

SELECT * FROM v_it;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+--------+
-- | id | name  | salary |
-- +----+-------+--------+
-- |  1 | Abaji |    900 |
-- |  3 | Cy    |    800 |
-- +----+-------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Complex joins and filters get repeated across reports and services. A view gives them one name, one place to fix, and one stable interface even when the base tables are reorganised.

Real-Time Use

Used for reporting layers, API read models, hiding column renames during migrations, and giving analysts a safe, simple surface. Inspect definitions with SHOW CREATE VIEW or information_schema.
codeExamples:
ALTER VIEW v_it AS
SELECT id, name, salary, dept FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';   -- add a column

SELECT table_name, is_updatable FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS v_emp_boss;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+--------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | IS_UPDATABLE |
-- +------------+--------------+
-- | v_emp_boss | YES          |
-- | v_it       | YES          |
-- +------------+--------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

  app query                       MySQL
  SELECT ... FROM v_it  ----->  view definition (stored text in data dictionary)
                                    |  merge (or temp table)
                                    v
                       SELECT ... FROM emp WHERE dept='IT'
                                    |
                               base table rows

  CREATE VIEW / ALTER VIEW / DROP VIEW change only the definition, never data

Fresher Notes

  • A view is a saved SELECT that behaves like a virtual table. Create it with CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT ....
  • Change it with ALTER VIEW or CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW; remove with DROP VIEW.
  • Query it like a table: SELECT * FROM v.

Worked Example 1

See the definition.
codeExamples:
SHOW CREATE VIEW emp_dept\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- View: emp_dept
-- Create View: CREATE ... VIEW emp_dept AS select e.id AS id, e.name AS name ...

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Find invalid views.

Practice Exercise 1

Create and use a view.
codeExamples:
CREATE VIEW emp_dept AS
SELECT e.id, e.name, d.name AS dept FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept;
SELECT * FROM emp_dept WHERE dept = 'HR';

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | dept
--  1 | Abaji | HR
--  2 | Raoji | HR

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Replace and drop.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A view stores only its SELECT definition in the data dictionary. When you query a view MySQL either merges the definition into your statement (ALGORITHM=MERGE, the default when possible) so indexes of the base tables are used, or materializes it into a temporary table (TEMPTABLE) when it contains GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION, aggregates or LIMIT.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: CREATE OR REPLACE, ALTER VIEW, column lists, ALGORITHM, DEFINER, SQL SECURITY, WITH CHECK OPTION. Drop with DROP VIEW IF EXISTS.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: reuse, simpler queries, one definition to maintain, abstraction over schema changes, and column-level access control.
codeExamples:
-- Rename a base column, keep the old name for consumers via the view.
ALTER TABLE emp RENAME COLUMN salary TO pay;
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_it AS
SELECT id, name, pay AS salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';
SELECT name, salary FROM v_it WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | salary |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Abaji |    900 |
-- +-------+--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: hides cost (a simple-looking view may join five tables); nested views get slow and hard to debug; a view is not materialised, so nothing is cached.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM v_it WHERE id = 3;     -- the optimizer merges the view into the base query

-- OUTPUT (key columns):
-- +-------------+-------+-------+------+
-- | select_type | table | type  | key  |
-- +-------------+-------+-------+------+
-- | SIMPLE      | emp   | const | PRIMARY |
-- +-------------+-------+-------+------+   <- v_it does not appear; it was merged

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: no indexes on a view itself; MySQL has no materialised views; the SELECT cannot contain a user variable or a temporary table; a view that depends on a dropped table becomes invalid and errors when used.

Architect's Notes

Use views as a stable read contract, not as a performance tool. Keep them shallow (one or two levels), pick ALGORITHM = MERGE where possible, and for real precomputation use a summary table refreshed by an event or job.

Mid-Level Notes

  • A view stores no data (unless you build a summary table); each query runs the underlying SELECT.
  • Views simplify complex joins and give a stable interface when tables change.
  • SHOW CREATE VIEW v shows its definition.

Senior Notes

  • Layered views (views on views) hide cost; the optimizer merges simple views but materializes complex ones (GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION) into temp tables.
  • Use ALGORITHM=MERGE or TEMPTABLE deliberately; check with EXPLAIN.
  • Version view changes with migrations; dropping a column in a base table can break views silently until queried.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: views on views several levels deep (hidden cost and hard debugging), SELECT * in the definition (columns fixed at creation time), and base table changes that silently break the view. Name columns and check dependent views after migrations.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A TEMPTABLE view cannot push filters into its aggregate, so it computes everything first. Compare the plans, and consider a summary table when a view is queried often.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a stable reporting layer. Applications and BI tools read views; the physical tables can change underneath, with the views adapted in the same migration.

beginner.content:
Introduction

An updatable view lets you run INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE against it and MySQL forwards the change to the single base table. It must have a clear one-to-one mapping to rows.

Why Do We Need This?

Apps can keep using the old table name via a view during a migration, or give a department a window onto just its own rows while still letting it edit them. WITH CHECK OPTION stops edits that would push a row out of the view.
codeExamples:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_it AS
SELECT id, name, dept, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'
WITH CHECK OPTION;                              -- rows must keep satisfying dept='IT'

UPDATE v_it SET dept = 'HR' WHERE id = 1;       -- would leave the view

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1369 (HY000): CHECK OPTION failed 'db.v_it'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: multi-tenant tables where each tenant view filters tenant_id with CHECK OPTION, so a tenant can never write another tenant's rows.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE doc (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, tenant INT NOT NULL, title VARCHAR(30));
CREATE VIEW doc_t7 AS SELECT id, tenant, title FROM doc WHERE tenant = 7 WITH CHECK OPTION;

INSERT INTO doc_t7 (tenant, title) VALUES (7, 'ok');       -- accepted
INSERT INTO doc_t7 (tenant, title) VALUES (8, 'leak');     -- rejected

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- ERROR 1369 (HY000): CHECK OPTION failed 'db.doc_t7'

beginner.content:
Diagram

  UPDATE v_it SET salary=950 WHERE id=1
          |
          v   (MERGE algorithm: rewrite against base table)
  UPDATE emp SET salary=950 WHERE id=1 AND dept='IT'
          |
          v
     emp row  (triggers, FKs, constraints all still apply)

  Updatable : single table, 1 view row = 1 base row
  Not       : GROUP BY, DISTINCT, UNION, aggregate, window, some subqueries

Fresher Notes

  • A simple view on one table can be updated: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the view change the underlying table.
  • Views with GROUP BY, DISTINCT, aggregates, UNION or some joins are not updatable.
  • Use WITH CHECK OPTION to stop changes that make a row disappear from the view.

Worked Example 1

Check updatability.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, is_updatable FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name | is_updatable
-- hr_emp     | YES
-- dept_stats | NO

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Compatibility view after rename.

Practice Exercise 1

Updating through a view.

Practice Exercise 2

CHECK OPTION blocks escaping rows.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO hr_emp (id, name, salary) VALUES (9, 'Zed', 1);   -- dept not in view columns => dept NULL
UPDATE hr_emp SET salary = 5 WHERE id = 1;                       -- allowed
-- Changing dept would violate:
-- ERROR 1369 (HY000): CHECK OPTION failed 'shop.hr_emp'

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1369 (HY000): CHECK OPTION failed 'shop.hr_emp'

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A view is updatable when each view row maps to exactly one base table row: no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, window functions or subqueries in the select list. MySQL rewrites INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the view into the same statement on the base table.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

WITH CHECK OPTION rejects changes that would make a row disappear from the view (LOCAL checks this view, CASCADED also checks underlying views). Multi-table join views can update columns of one base table per statement.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: transparent writes through an abstraction; CHECK OPTION enforces row-level rules; LOCAL and CASCADED options control nested views.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, is_updatable, check_option
FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_name IN ('v_it','doc_t7');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+--------------+--------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | IS_UPDATABLE | CHECK_OPTION |
-- +------------+--------------+--------------+
-- | doc_t7     | YES          | CASCADED     |
-- | v_it       | YES          | CASCADED     |
-- +------------+--------------+--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: easy to forget that a write lands in a table with defaults, triggers and constraints; rows can vanish from the view after an update unless CHECK OPTION is used.

Limitations

Limitations: a view is NOT updatable if it uses aggregates, GROUP BY, HAVING, DISTINCT, UNION, window functions or certain subqueries; multi-table join views allow only changes touching one base table; INSERT needs every NOT NULL column without default to be exposed.

Architect's Notes

Make views writable only deliberately, always with WITH CHECK OPTION, and test constraints through them. For complex writes prefer stored procedures or explicit table DML so the behaviour is visible in code review.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Join views can sometimes be updated, but only one base table per statement.
  • Columns derived from expressions cannot be updated.
  • Check updatability in information_schema.views.is_updatable.

Senior Notes

  • Updatable views are useful for backward-compatible table rename/split migrations (a view with the old name).
  • Keep write paths simple; routing writes through views complicates debugging.
  • WITH CHECK OPTION enforces row-level policies (like tenant filters) at the view layer.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting an INSERT through a view that omits NOT NULL columns without defaults, updating derived columns, and assuming a join view can change both tables in one statement. Check IS_UPDATABLE and test writes.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO hr_emp (id, name) VALUES (99, 'Zed');                  -- salary NOT NULL, no default
UPDATE emp_with_dept SET dept_name = 'X' WHERE id = 1;               -- column of the other table plus ... not allowed together

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1423 (HY000): Field of view 'shop.hr_emp' underlying table doesn't have a default value

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Updates through a view cost the same as on the base table, plus the check evaluation. Make sure the view's WHERE is indexable, since the rewritten statement uses it.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN UPDATE hr_emp SET salary = salary + 100 WHERE dept = 10;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key      | rows
-- range | idx_dept | 1200

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: keep an old table name working after a rename or split by exposing an updatable compatibility view, giving old applications time to migrate.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A view can expose only chosen columns and rows of a table. If users get SELECT on the view but no privilege on the table, they see just the allowed slice. SQL SECURITY DEFINER runs the view with the creator's rights.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE staff (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), email VARCHAR(30), salary INT, ssn CHAR(9));
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (1,'Abaji','a@x.com',900,'111223333'),(2,'Ben','b@x.com',700,'222334444');

CREATE VIEW v_staff_public AS SELECT id, name, email FROM staff;   -- no salary, no ssn

SELECT * FROM v_staff_public;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+---------+
-- | id | name  | email   |
-- +----+-------+---------+
-- |  1 | Abaji | a@x.com |
-- |  2 | Ben   | b@x.com |
-- +----+------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

MySQL privileges are granted per table or per column, but not per row. Views add row-level filtering and computed masking so you can follow least privilege without duplicating data.

Real-Time Use

Real use: support staff see masked emails and last four digits; each region sees only its rows via CURRENT_USER()-based views; auditors get read-only views.
codeExamples:
CREATE VIEW v_staff_masked AS
SELECT id, name,
       CONCAT('***-**-', RIGHT(ssn, 4)) AS ssn,       -- mask all but last 4
       CONCAT(LEFT(email, 1), '***@', SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1)) AS email
FROM staff;
SELECT * FROM v_staff_masked WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+-------------+------------+
-- | id | name  | ssn         | email      |
-- +----+-------+-------------+------------+
-- |  1 | Abaji | ***-**-3333 | a***@x.com |
-- +----+------+-------------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   user 'report'                                  table staff
      |                                       +-----------------------------+
      | SELECT * FROM v_staff_public          | id | name | email | salary  |
      v                                       +-----------------------------+
   +---------------------+   only these --->   id   name   email   (columns)
   | view v_staff_public |   filter rows ->    WHERE region = ...
   +---------------------+   salary, ssn never reach the user
      |
      X  direct SELECT on staff -> ERROR 1142 (no privilege)

Fresher Notes

  • A view can expose only some columns or rows of a table, hiding sensitive data like salary or password hashes.
  • Grant users access to the view, not the base table.
  • Example: HR sees names and departments but not salaries.

Worked Example 1

Security INVOKER view.

Worked Example 2

Check who defines each view.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, definer, security_type FROM information_schema.views WHERE table_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | definer        | security_type
-- emp_public | admin@localhost| DEFINER

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Hide salary from HR readers.

Practice Exercise 2

Mask a card number.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Security via views works through privileges: a user is granted SELECT on the view, not on the base table. With SQL SECURITY DEFINER the view runs with the creator's rights, so the user can read the exposed columns and rows without any grant on the underlying table.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Techniques: column hiding, row filtering, data masking with functions, and tenant filters. INVOKER security applies the caller's rights and enables per-user filters using USER().

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: least privilege, row and column filtering, masking, a single audited entry point, and no change to the underlying schema.
codeExamples:
-- DEFINER view: callers need rights only on the view.
CREATE DEFINER = 'admin'@'localhost' SQL SECURITY DEFINER VIEW v_my_rows AS
SELECT id, name FROM staff WHERE name = SUBSTRING_INDEX(CURRENT_USER(), '@', 1);
SHOW CREATE VIEW v_my_rows\G

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- View: v_my_rows
-- Create View: CREATE ALGORITHM=UNDEFINED DEFINER=admin@localhost SQL SECURITY DEFINER VIEW ...

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: not a complete defence: DEFINER views run with elevated rights, so a poorly written one leaks data; users can still infer data through side channels such as error messages or timing, and functions with side effects can leak rows.
codeExamples:
-- A user with access to the view calls a function that sees rows before the view filter.
-- Mitigate with SQL SECURITY INVOKER or by revoking CREATE FUNCTION/PROCEDURE rights.
CREATE OR REPLACE SQL SECURITY INVOKER VIEW v_staff_public AS SELECT id, name, email FROM staff;
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'report'@'%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | Grants for report@%                                        |
-- +------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO report@%                             |
-- | GRANT SELECT ON mydb.v_staff_public TO report@%            |
-- +------------------------------------------------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a view cannot hide the existence of rows from someone who has the table; row filters based on CURRENT_USER are only as strong as your user naming; INVOKER views need rights on the base tables too. Roles in MySQL 8 simplify granting.

Architect's Notes

Combine views with roles, least-privilege accounts and DEFINER set to a locked-down no-login account. Do not rely on views alone for compliance; add encryption, auditing (audit plugin) and column masking at the app tier where needed.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use SQL SECURITY DEFINER (runs with the creator’s rights) or INVOKER (caller’s rights) intentionally.
  • Combine views with column-level or table grants for least privilege.
  • Views can mask data: show last 4 digits of a card number.

Senior Notes

  • DEFINER views are an escalation vector if the definer is powerful; use dedicated low-privilege definer accounts.
  • Masking in views is not a substitute for encryption or access auditing.
  • Prefer MySQL roles plus views, and test with the actual restricted account.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: a powerful DEFINER (a view owned by root exposes whatever it reads), forgetting that views are not row-level security by themselves, and masking in views while the base table is still readable elsewhere. Use a minimal-privilege definer and verify with the real restricted account.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Row filters in views must stay indexable. A tenant filter on an indexed column keeps queries fast; a function on the column does not.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: support staff can see customers and orders but never card data or password hashes; analysts get masked and aggregated views; the base tables are accessible only to the application and DBAs.

topics.name: Views vs Tables vs Stored Procedures

beginner.content:
Introduction

A table stores data. A view stores a query and gives a virtual table. A stored procedure stores a program (statements, logic, parameters) that you CALL. Choosing correctly decides performance, security and maintainability.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, cust INT, amt INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,7,50),(2,7,70),(3,8,20);

CREATE VIEW v_cust_total AS SELECT cust, SUM(amt) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY cust;   -- virtual table

DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE p_cust_total(IN c INT) BEGIN SELECT SUM(amt) AS total FROM orders WHERE cust = c; END //
DELIMITER ;

SELECT * FROM v_cust_total;  CALL p_cust_total(7);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+     +-------+
-- | cust | total |     | total |
-- +------+-------+     +-------+
-- |    7 |   120 |     |   120 |
-- |    8 |    20 |     +-------+
-- +------+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Each tool solves a different problem. Tables persist facts. Views simplify and secure reads and can be joined or filtered further. Procedures run multi-step logic with transactions, loops and side effects, and can take parameters and write data.
codeExamples:
-- A view can be filtered and joined like a table; a procedure result cannot.
SELECT * FROM v_cust_total WHERE total > 50;                      -- composable
SELECT o.id, v.total FROM orders o JOIN v_cust_total v ON v.cust = o.cust;

-- CALL p_cust_total(7) cannot appear in FROM or a JOIN.

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+
-- | cust | total |
-- +------+-------+
-- |    7 |   120 |
-- +------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rule of thumb: store it in a table if it is a fact you must keep; use a view for a reusable read shape; use a procedure for a unit of work (transfer money, close a month) that needs validation, several writes and one atomic commit. Use a summary table when a view is too slow.
codeExamples:
-- Summary table = view result physically stored and refreshed.
CREATE TABLE cust_total_cache AS SELECT cust, SUM(amt) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY cust;
ALTER TABLE cust_total_cache ADD PRIMARY KEY (cust);
SELECT total FROM cust_total_cache WHERE cust = 7;       -- index lookup, no aggregation

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | total |
-- +-------+
-- |   120 |
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

             data?     parameters?   logic?    usable in FROM?   writes?
  TABLE       yes        no            no        yes               yes
  VIEW        no         no            no        yes               limited
  PROCEDURE   no         yes           yes       no (CALL only)    yes

  table  = what we KNOW        view = how we LOOK at it
  procedure = what we DO       summary table = a view we cached

Fresher Notes

  • A table stores data. A view is a saved query that looks like a table. A stored procedure is saved code you CALL, which can do many statements.
  • Views are for reading data in a simplified way; procedures are for actions and logic.
  • Only tables hold data on disk.

Worked Example 1

Materialized view emulation.

Worked Example 2

List objects by type.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_type, COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = DATABASE() GROUP BY table_type;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_type | COUNT(*)
-- BASE TABLE |        8
-- VIEW       |        3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Compare the three.
codeExamples:
CREATE VIEW v_hr AS SELECT * FROM emp WHERE dept = 10;                        -- query
CREATE PROCEDURE raise_salary(IN pct INT) UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * (1 + pct/100);  -- action
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM v_hr;
CALL raise_salary(10);

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 2
-- Query OK, 3 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Procedure not allowed in FROM.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A table stores rows. A view stores a query and is expanded at execution time. A stored procedure stores a program and runs when called; its results are returned as result sets or OUT parameters, and it cannot be used in a FROM clause. Only tables occupy data space.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use views to name and reuse queries, procedures for multi-step actions with control flow and transactions, and generated columns or summary tables to store computed results. MySQL has no native materialized views; emulate with a table refreshed by an event.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: tables give speed and indexes; views give abstraction and security with no data duplication; procedures give logic close to data, fewer round trips and one permission surface (GRANT EXECUTE).
codeExamples:
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE mydb.p_cust_total TO 'report'@'%';     -- app can run it, nothing else
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'report'@'%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- | GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE mydb.p_cust_total TO report@% |

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: tables cost storage and need maintenance; views can hide expensive queries; procedures are hard to version, test and debug, tie logic to MySQL and can overload the database CPU.
codeExamples:
-- Cost hidden behind a view: aggregation runs on every call.
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM v_cust_total WHERE cust = 7;

-- OUTPUT (key columns):
-- +-------------+------------+------+---------------------------+
-- | select_type | table      | type | Extra                     |
-- +-------------+------------+------+---------------------------+
-- | PRIMARY     | <derived2> | ref  | NULL                      |
-- | DERIVED     | orders     | ALL  | Using temporary           |
-- +-------------+------------+------+---------------------------+   (example)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: views cannot take parameters or hold variables or multiple statements; procedures cannot be used inside a SELECT (functions can); tables have no logic of their own. MySQL has no materialised views or table-valued functions.
codeExamples:
-- A view cannot take an argument.
CREATE VIEW v_for(c INT) AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE cust = c;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual ... near '(c INT) AS'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep business rules in one place: in a modern stack that is usually the application, with views for read contracts and procedures for a few hot, set-based or security-critical operations. Whatever you choose, keep DDL in version control and migrate it with a tool like Flyway or Liquibase.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Views return a result set you can filter and join; procedures cannot be used in a FROM clause.
  • Procedures can modify data, use variables, loops and transactions; views cannot.
  • Use a view when you need reusable query logic and a procedure when you need a workflow.

Senior Notes

  • Business logic in procedures reduces round trips but couples logic to the database, complicates testing and deployments.
  • Many teams keep logic in application code and use views only for reporting and compatibility.
  • Materialized-view needs (precomputed aggregates) must be built manually with tables and refresh jobs in MySQL.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using a procedure where a view fits (cannot join it), putting business logic in views with side effects expectations, and treating a view as a cache (it is not). Choose by the job: read shape, action, or stored result.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM p_high;                         -- procedures are not tables
SELECT * FROM v_high v JOIN departments d ON d.id = v.id;     -- views join like tables

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'shop.p_high' doesn't exist

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A view costs the query it contains each time; a materialized table costs refresh work but reads instantly. Compare the timing and choose the refresh interval from freshness needs.
codeExamples:
-- view: 2.1 s (aggregates 50M rows on every read)
-- summary table refreshed hourly: 3 ms reads, 40 s refresh once per hour
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, refreshed_at, NOW()) AS data_age_minutes FROM mv_dept_totals LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- data_age_minutes
-- 23

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world layering: tables for data, views for stable reads and security, procedures for controlled multi-step writes with strict EXECUTE privileges and no direct table access for applications.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL kept inside the server. You create it once with CREATE PROCEDURE and run it with CALL. Because the body contains semicolons, client tools need DELIMITER to change the statement terminator while defining it.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE hello()
BEGIN
  SELECT 'Hello from MySQL' AS msg;      -- body can hold many statements
END //
DELIMITER ;

CALL hello();

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+
-- | msg              |
-- +------------------+
-- | Hello from MySQL |
-- +------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without procedures every client re-sends the same multi-statement logic over the network and each application re-implements it. A procedure centralises the logic, saves round trips and lets you grant EXECUTE without table access.

Real-Time Use

Used for month-end closing, batch cleanup, audit-logged operations and as a stable API for legacy apps. Manage them with SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE, information_schema.routines, ALTER (characteristics only) and DROP PROCEDURE.
codeExamples:
SELECT routine_name, routine_type, security_type
FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_schema = DATABASE();

DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS hello;
-- To change the body: DROP and CREATE again (ALTER cannot edit the body).

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------------+--------------+---------------+
-- | ROUTINE_NAME      | ROUTINE_TYPE | SECURITY_TYPE |
-- +-------------------+--------------+---------------+
-- | hello             | PROCEDURE    | DEFINER       |
-- | transfer_1_to_2   | PROCEDURE    | DEFINER       |
-- +-------------------+--------------+---------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

  client                                MySQL server
  CALL transfer_1_to_2();  --------->   +-----------------------------+
        (one round trip)                | procedure body (stored)     |
                                        |  START TRANSACTION          |
                                        |  UPDATE acct ...            |
                                        |  UPDATE acct ...            |
                                        |  COMMIT                     |
  <---------- OK / result sets -------  +-----------------------------+

  vs. app sending 4 statements = 4 round trips

Fresher Notes

  • A stored procedure is a named block of SQL saved in the database and run with CALL name(args).
  • In the mysql client change the delimiter while defining: DELIMITER // ... END // DELIMITER ;.
  • Drop with DROP PROCEDURE name.

Worked Example 1

Inspect and drop.
codeExamples:
SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE emp_by_dept\G
DROP PROCEDURE IF EXISTS emp_by_dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Procedure: emp_by_dept ... (definition shown), then Query OK

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Restrict execution.

Practice Exercise 1

Simple procedure.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE emp_by_dept(IN d INT)
BEGIN
  SELECT id, name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = d ORDER BY id;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL emp_by_dept(10);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | salary
--  1 | Abaji | 60000
--  2 | Raoji | 45000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Transactional procedure.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A stored procedure is compiled to an internal instruction set and cached per connection the first time it is called. CALL executes it inside the calling session, so it sees session variables, current database and the open transaction. Result sets produced inside are returned to the client.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE emp_by_dept(IN p_dept INT)
BEGIN
  SELECT id, name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = p_dept ORDER BY id;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL emp_by_dept(10);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | salary
--  1 | Abaji | 60000
--  2 | Raoji | 45000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: characteristics (DETERMINISTIC, READS SQL DATA, MODIFIES SQL DATA), SQL SECURITY, COMMENT, and multiple result sets. Inspect with SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE and the information_schema.routines table.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fewer round trips, reuse across applications, one place for rules, precompiled per session, and fine-grained GRANT EXECUTE with SQL SECURITY DEFINER.
codeExamples:
-- Give an app user the right to run only this procedure.
CREATE USER 'app'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'S3cret!pass';
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE mydb.transfer_1_to_2 TO 'app'@'%';

-- as app: CALL mydb.transfer_1_to_2();   works
-- as app: SELECT * FROM mydb.acct;       denied

-- OUTPUT (second statement):
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'app'@'localhost' for table 'acct'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: logic lives outside normal source control and CI; debugging is primitive (no breakpoints); business logic on the DB server consumes scarce DB CPU; hard to unit-test.
codeExamples:
-- No built-in debugger: you debug with SELECT statements and a log table.
CREATE TABLE dbg (ts DATETIME DEFAULT NOW(), msg VARCHAR(100));
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE traced()
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO dbg(msg) VALUES ('start');
  INSERT INTO dbg(msg) VALUES ('end');
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL traced();  SELECT msg FROM dbg;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | msg   |
-- +-------+
-- | start |
-- | end   |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a procedure cannot be used in a SELECT; it cannot return a value (use OUT parameters or result sets); recursion is disabled by default (max_sp_recursion_depth = 0); no COMMIT-free DDL inside some contexts; no stored procedure overloading by parameters.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_sp_recursion_depth';
SELECT hello() ;          -- procedure used like a function

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name          | Value |
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- | max_sp_recursion_depth | 0     |
-- +------------------------+-------+
-- ERROR 1305 (42000): FUNCTION mydb.hello does not exist

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use procedures for a small number of atomic, chatty or privileged operations. Keep them thin, version them as migration scripts, and cover them with integration tests; large business logic is usually cheaper to scale in the application tier.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Procedures can run several statements, control flow, transactions and return result sets.
  • They reduce network round trips for multi-step operations.
  • View definitions with SHOW CREATE PROCEDURE.

Senior Notes

  • Version stored routines like code (migrations), keep them small and idempotent.
  • Debugging and profiling are weaker than in application code; log through tables or signals.
  • Execution plans are cached per connection; behaviour can vary with parameters (parameter sniffing is milder in MySQL but exists).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting DELIMITER in the client, parameter names clashing with column names, no error handling around transactions, and deploying procedures by hand. Prefix parameters (p_), add handlers, and version procedures in migrations.
codeExamples:
CREATE PROCEDURE bad(IN dept INT) SELECT * FROM emp WHERE dept = dept;     -- always true: compares the column to itself
CALL bad(10);

-- OUTPUT:
-- (returns all rows; rename the parameter to p_dept)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Procedures save network round trips for multi-statement operations, but their plans and execution are per statement, so index tuning still applies inside them. Profile with the statement digest tables, which break routines down by statement.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, count_star, ROUND(sum_timer_wait/1e9) AS total_ms FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_program WHERE object_name = 'transfer';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name              | count_star | total_ms
-- statement/sp/stmt       |    9120000 |   412000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: batch operations close to the data, such as closing a billing period, with one call from a scheduler and a single privilege to execute it.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Procedure parameters have a direction. IN (default) passes a value in. OUT sends a value back; its starting value inside is NULL. INOUT goes in, can be changed, and comes back. Callers receive OUT and INOUT values through user variables such as @total.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE emp_count(IN dept_name VARCHAR(20), OUT n INT)
BEGIN
  SELECT COUNT(*) INTO n FROM emp WHERE dept = dept_name;    -- fill the OUT parameter
END //
DELIMITER ;

CALL emp_count('IT', @n);
SELECT @n AS it_staff;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | it_staff |
-- +----------+
-- |        2 |
-- +----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Procedures cannot return values like functions. OUT and INOUT parameters are how a procedure hands scalar results, status codes or running totals back without a result set.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE add_tax(INOUT price DECIMAL(10,2), IN rate DECIMAL(4,2))
BEGIN
  SET price = price * (1 + rate);            -- modify the caller's variable
END //
DELIMITER ;

SET @p = 200.00;
CALL add_tax(@p, 0.18);
SELECT @p AS with_tax;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | with_tax |
-- +----------+
-- |   236.00 |
-- +----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: return a generated order id, a success flag, or a message together with a result set. Application drivers register OUT parameters (JDBC CallableStatement.registerOutParameter).

Diagram

   caller                         procedure emp_count(IN dept, OUT n)
  'IT'  ---- IN  --------------->  dept_name = 'IT'
  @n    <--- OUT ----------------  n = COUNT(*)   (n starts as NULL)
  @p    <--> INOUT --------------  price   (read, change, return)

  IN    value copied in
  OUT   value copied out at the end of the call
  INOUT both

Fresher Notes

  • IN passes a value into the procedure. OUT returns a value to the caller. INOUT passes a value in and returns the modified value.
  • Receive OUT values in a session variable: CALL p(@result) then SELECT @result.
  • IN is the default.

Worked Example 1

Name clash pitfall.

Worked Example 2

Status code via OUT.

Practice Exercise 1

OUT parameter.

Practice Exercise 2

INOUT parameter.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Parameters are passed by value for IN, and OUT/INOUT copy the value back into a user variable (@var) when the procedure ends. An OUT parameter starts as NULL inside the procedure. INOUT passes the caller's current value in and returns the modified value.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE dept_count(IN p_dept INT, OUT p_count INT)
BEGIN SELECT COUNT(*) INTO p_count FROM emp WHERE dept = p_dept; END //
CREATE PROCEDURE add_tax(INOUT p_amount DECIMAL(10,2), IN p_rate DECIMAL(4,2))
BEGIN SET p_amount = ROUND(p_amount * (1 + p_rate / 100), 2); END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL dept_count(10, @c); SELECT @c;
SET @a = 1000; CALL add_tax(@a, 18); SELECT @a;

-- OUTPUT:
-- @c      @a
--  2    1180.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use OUT for scalars (status, count, new id), result sets for rows, and INOUT sparingly. Return identifiers with LAST_INSERT_ID(). Signal errors with SIGNAL instead of magic OUT codes where possible.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: typed, self-documenting interface; several return values at once; INOUT supports accumulators.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE min_max(IN dept_name VARCHAR(20), OUT lo INT, OUT hi INT)
BEGIN
  SELECT MIN(salary), MAX(salary) INTO lo, hi FROM emp WHERE dept = dept_name;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL min_max('IT', @lo, @hi);
SELECT @lo AS lo, @hi AS hi;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+
-- | lo   | hi   |
-- +------+------+
-- |  800 |  900 |
-- +------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: OUT values are carried in session variables, which are easy to forget or clash; an OUT parameter is NULL on entry, a common source of bugs; no default values for parameters.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE bad_out(OUT n INT)
BEGIN
  SET n = n + 1;                 -- n is NULL on entry, so result stays NULL
END //
DELIMITER ;
SET @x = 5;
CALL bad_out(@x);
SELECT @x AS x;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | x    |
-- +------+
-- | NULL |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: parameters cannot have defaults or be optional; you cannot pass a literal or an expression for OUT or INOUT (must be a variable); no array or table parameters (use a temporary table or JSON); the call must supply exactly the declared number of arguments.
codeExamples:
CALL emp_count('IT');           -- missing argument
CALL emp_count('IT', 5);         -- literal for an OUT parameter

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1318 (42000): Incorrect number of arguments for PROCEDURE mydb.emp_count; expected 2, got 1
-- ERROR 1414 (42000): OUT or INOUT argument 2 for routine mydb.emp_count is not a variable or NEW pseudo-variable in BEFORE trigger

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer a result set for tabular output and OUT parameters for small status values. Never rely on session variables across pooled connections without resetting them, and keep parameter lists short and stable because they form the procedure's public contract.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Parameters are typed; names should not clash with column names (prefix with p_).
  • OUT parameters are NULL inside the procedure until assigned.
  • For many rows, return a result set instead of OUT parameters.

Senior Notes

  • Prefer returning result sets for data and OUT only for scalars like counts or status codes.
  • Version procedure signatures carefully: changing parameters breaks callers.
  • Use a consistent status/error convention (OUT p_status, SIGNAL for errors).

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting OUT parameters to be readable before assignment, user variables leaking between calls, many OUT parameters instead of a result set, and changing a parameter list (breaking callers). Add new procedures or optional behaviour carefully.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE bad_out(OUT p_val INT) BEGIN SET p_val = p_val + 1; END //
DELIMITER ;
SET @x = 5; CALL bad_out(@x); SELECT @x;

-- OUTPUT:
-- @x
-- NULL        (OUT starts as NULL inside: NULL + 1 = NULL)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Parameters have fixed types; passing a wider value is converted or truncated. Declare precise types so implicit conversions do not defeat indexes inside the procedure.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE find_user(IN p_phone VARCHAR(20)) SELECT id FROM users WHERE phone = p_phone; //     -- same type as the column: index used
DELIMITER ;
CALL find_user('9876543210');

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 12

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world API style: procedures return a status code OUT parameter and the data as a result set, and applications map status codes to messages.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Inside a procedure you declare local variables with DECLARE name TYPE [DEFAULT v] (at the start of a BEGIN block), assign with SET or SELECT ... INTO, and branch with IF ... ELSEIF ... ELSE ... END IF and CASE ... END CASE.

Why Do We Need This?

Real logic needs state and decisions: compute a discount, validate input, pick a path. Plain SQL has CASE expressions, but only procedures can run different statements depending on a condition.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE day_type(IN d INT)         -- 1=Mon ... 7=Sun
BEGIN
  CASE
    WHEN d IN (6,7) THEN SELECT 'Weekend' AS kind;
    WHEN d BETWEEN 1 AND 5 THEN SELECT 'Weekday' AS kind;
    ELSE SELECT 'Invalid' AS kind;
  END CASE;                                  -- no match and no ELSE -> error 1339
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL day_type(7);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+
-- | kind    |
-- +---------+
-- | Weekend |
-- +---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: tiered pricing, status transitions (only PAID orders can ship), and defensive input checks that SIGNAL a clear error. Simple CASE compares one expression to values; searched CASE evaluates conditions.

Diagram

  BEGIN
    DECLARE g CHAR(1) DEFAULT 'F';        variables first
    IF score >= 90   -----> SET g='A'
    ELSEIF score >= 75 ---> SET g='B'
    ELSE             -----> keep default
    END IF;
    CASE x WHEN 1 THEN .. WHEN 2 THEN .. ELSE .. END CASE;
  END

  condition --> true branch only runs; others skipped

Fresher Notes

  • Declare local variables with DECLARE v INT DEFAULT 0; and set them with SET or SELECT ... INTO.
  • IF ... THEN ... ELSEIF ... ELSE ... END IF; and CASE add decisions.
  • DECLARE must be at the start of a BEGIN block.

Worked Example 1

SELECT INTO a variable.

Worked Example 2

NULL in IF is not true.
codeExamples:
SELECT IF(NULL > 5, 'yes', 'no') AS result;

-- OUTPUT:
-- result
-- no

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Branching with variables.

Practice Exercise 2

CASE and SIGNAL.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Local variables (DECLARE) exist only inside their BEGIN...END block and must be declared first; user variables (@x) belong to the session. Control flow statements (IF, CASE) are interpreted by the procedure engine, evaluating each condition in order. A NULL condition is treated as false.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: IF ... ELSEIF ... END IF, simple and searched CASE statements, SELECT ... INTO to fill variables, SET var = (subquery), and SIGNAL for errors.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: real procedural control next to the data; typed locals; SELECT ... INTO loads values; SIGNAL gives meaningful errors.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: DECLARE order rules are strict (variables, then conditions, cursors, handlers); a variable named like a column silently wins over the column, a notorious bug; no block-scoped variables other than nested BEGIN blocks.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE shadow(IN name VARCHAR(20))     -- parameter named like column emp.name
BEGIN
  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM emp WHERE name = name;   -- compares the parameter to itself!
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL shadow('Abaji');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 3 |      <- counts every row, expected 1. Rename the parameter: p_name.
-- +---+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: locals exist only during the call (use @user variables for session state); DECLARE must be first in its block; CASE without a matching WHEN and no ELSE raises error 1339 (Case not found); no GOTO-free structured exceptions beyond handlers.

Architect's Notes

Name parameters and variables with a prefix (p_, v_) to avoid column shadowing. Keep branching logic shallow; if a procedure becomes a decision tree, move rules into a table or into application code where they can be tested.

Mid-Level Notes

  • User variables (@x) live for the session; local variables live in the block.
  • CASE can be a statement (in procedures) or an expression (in SQL).
  • SELECT ... INTO must return exactly one row or you get an error.

Senior Notes

  • Use SIGNAL to raise errors with SQLSTATE and messages for invalid input.
  • Beware of variable name collisions with columns and of NULL handling in IF conditions (NULL is not true).
  • Keep logic simple; complex branching belongs in application code.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: SELECT INTO returning zero or several rows (warning or error), DECLARE after statements, and long IF chains better expressed as data in a table. Handle NOT FOUND and keep logic simple.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Logic inside procedures runs in a single thread per call. For rule-heavy decisions, move the rules into a table and join to it, which scales with indexes and is editable without redeploying code.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: discount calculation with tiers, written as a searched CASE so the rules read top to bottom and the first match wins.
codeExamples:
SELECT order_id, total, CASE WHEN total >= 10000 THEN 0.15 WHEN total >= 5000 THEN 0.10 WHEN total >= 1000 THEN 0.05 ELSE 0 END AS discount_rate FROM orders LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- order_id | total   | discount_rate
--        1 | 12000.00|          0.15

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL has three loop forms. WHILE cond DO ... END WHILE tests before each pass. REPEAT ... UNTIL cond END REPEAT tests after (runs at least once). LOOP ... END LOOP runs forever until you LEAVE its label; ITERATE skips to the next pass.

Why Do We Need This?
