SQL is set-based, but sometimes you must repeat work: seed test data, process a queue in batches, walk a hierarchy, or run an operation on a list. Loops make that possible inside the server.

Real-Time Use

Real use: delete old rows in small batches so locks and undo stay small (a very common production pattern).
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE purge_old()
BEGIN
  DECLARE n INT DEFAULT 1;
  REPEAT
    DELETE FROM logs WHERE created < NOW() - INTERVAL 90 DAY LIMIT 1000;   -- small batch
    SET n = ROW_COUNT();                                                  -- rows deleted
    DO SLEEP(0.1);                                                       -- let replicas catch up
  UNTIL n = 0 END REPEAT;
END //
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT (CALL purge_old()):
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Diagram

  WHILE i<=n DO        test  -->  body  -->  test  -->  ...        (0..n times)
  REPEAT .. UNTIL c    body  -->  test  -->  body  -->  ...        (1..n times)
  lp: LOOP             body  -->  IF .. LEAVE lp  --> body ...
                                  |        |
                              ITERATE lp   exit
  One set-based statement  >>>  loop doing one row per pass

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL has WHILE, REPEAT ... UNTIL and LOOP with LEAVE and ITERATE.
  • Use them to repeat steps, for example generating test data or batching deletes.
  • Each loop needs a counter or a condition that eventually ends it.

Worked Example 1

Batched purge loop.

Worked Example 2

Set-based alternative to a loop.

Practice Exercise 1

Fill test data with WHILE.

Practice Exercise 2

LEAVE and ITERATE.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL has three loop forms. WHILE checks the condition before each pass, REPEAT ... UNTIL checks after (runs at least once), and LOOP runs until an explicit LEAVE label. ITERATE label jumps to the next pass. Each pass executes statements one at a time in the procedure engine.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use loops for control (batching, retries, generating data) and set-based SQL for data work. REPEAT and WHILE equivalents: WHILE i < n DO ... END WHILE and REPEAT ... UNTIL i >= n END REPEAT.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: procedural iteration at the data; labelled LEAVE and ITERATE give precise control; batching reduces lock time.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE factorial(IN n INT, OUT f BIGINT)
BEGIN
  SET f = 1;
  WHILE n > 1 DO SET f = f * n; SET n = n - 1; END WHILE;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL factorial(5, @f);  SELECT @f AS result;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | result |
-- +--------+
-- |    120 |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: row-by-row loops are far slower than one set-based statement; easy to write an infinite loop that hogs a connection; long loops inside one transaction hold locks.
codeExamples:
-- Slow way: loop with 100000 single-row inserts.
-- Fast way: one set-based statement (MySQL 8 recursive CTE).
SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 100000;
INSERT INTO seq
WITH RECURSIVE g(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n+1 FROM g WHERE n < 100000)
SELECT n FROM g;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 100000 rows affected   (about 20x faster than the loop, example)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: no FOR loop and no foreach over a result set (use a cursor); LEAVE and ITERATE work only on labelled blocks or loops; no BREAK or CONTINUE keywords; no timeout other than max_execution_time for SELECT or killing the connection.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE bad_leave()
BEGIN
  WHILE 1 = 1 DO
    LEAVE nolabel;            -- label does not exist
  END WHILE;
END //
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1308 (42000): LEAVE with no matching label: nolabel

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Reach for a loop only when set-based SQL, window functions or recursive CTEs cannot express the job. Batch loops with LIMIT, commit between batches, add a sleep for replication lag, and always include a guaranteed exit condition.

Mid-Level Notes

  • WHILE cond DO ... END WHILE checks before running; REPEAT ... UNTIL cond END REPEAT checks after.
  • LEAVE label exits a loop; ITERATE label jumps to the next pass.
  • Prefer set-based SQL to row-by-row loops where possible.

Senior Notes

  • Loops with per-row statements are slow; batch (LIMIT 1000) and commit between batches for large maintenance jobs.
  • Always add a safety counter to avoid infinite loops.
  • Long loops hold locks; commit regularly in batch jobs and handle replication lag.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: row-by-row loops over large tables, forgetting to change the loop variable (infinite loop), and no batch commit. Always bound loops and prefer set operations.
codeExamples:
-- slow: 1,000,000 single-row inserts ~ 240 s
-- fast: one INSERT ... SELECT ~ 3 s
INSERT INTO archive SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at < '2025-01-01';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1000000 rows affected (3.1 sec)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For maintenance jobs, loop in batches with LIMIT, stop when no rows are affected, sleep briefly between batches, and watch replica lag.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: retry with backoff inside a procedure for a lock-sensitive update, bounded to a fixed number of attempts.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Errors are handled with handlers: DECLARE CONTINUE|EXIT HANDLER FOR condition statement. A condition can be an SQLSTATE, a MySQL error number, SQLEXCEPTION, SQLWARNING or NOT FOUND. SIGNAL raises your own error and RESIGNAL rethrows.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE safe_insert(IN i INT)
BEGIN
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR 1062               -- duplicate key
    SELECT 'Duplicate id, skipped' AS msg;
  INSERT INTO acct(id, bal) VALUES (i, 0);
  SELECT 'Inserted' AS msg;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL safe_insert(1);       -- id 1 already exists

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------------+
-- | msg                   |
-- +-----------------------+
-- | Duplicate id, skipped |
-- +-----------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without handlers an error aborts the call with a raw message and may leave a half-done transaction. Handlers let you roll back cleanly, log, return a friendly status, and continue after expected conditions such as end of cursor.

Real-Time Use

Real use: transactional procedures with ROLLBACK on failure, validation using SIGNAL with a custom SQLSTATE 45000, and cursor loops that exit on NOT FOUND. Use GET DIAGNOSTICS to read the error number and text.

Diagram

  BEGIN
    DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION  ----+
    START TRANSACTION;                          |
    stmt 1                                      |
    stmt 2  --- error 1062/1213/... ------------+--> handler body
    COMMIT;                                          ROLLBACK; RESIGNAL;
  END                                                  |
                                                       v
                                         caller receives the original error

  CONTINUE handler : resume after the failing statement
  EXIT handler     : leave the enclosing BEGIN..END

Fresher Notes

  • Use DECLARE ... HANDLER to catch errors in a procedure, and SIGNAL to raise your own errors.
  • Common handler: DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION BEGIN ROLLBACK; END;.
  • EXIT handlers leave the block; CONTINUE handlers resume after the failing statement.

Worked Example 1

NOT FOUND handler.
codeExamples:
DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET done = 1;

-- OUTPUT: (used with cursors; sets done when FETCH has no more rows)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

RESIGNAL after cleanup.

Practice Exercise 1

Rollback on error.

Practice Exercise 2

Diagnostics.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Handlers react to conditions raised while a procedure runs. An EXIT handler ends the enclosing BEGIN...END block after running; a CONTINUE handler resumes after the failing statement. Conditions can be SQLEXCEPTION, SQLWARNING, NOT FOUND, a SQLSTATE or a MySQL error number.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: SIGNAL raises your own error, RESIGNAL rethrows or changes it, GET DIAGNOSTICS reads the error details (message, error number, SQLSTATE), and named conditions make handlers readable.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: atomic units of work, clear custom errors via SIGNAL, structured diagnostics, and clean cursor termination.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: handler scope and DECLARE ordering are tricky; a CONTINUE handler can hide a real failure; swallowing errors makes bugs invisible; no TRY and CATCH nesting like other languages.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE swallow()
BEGIN
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION BEGIN END;   -- silently ignores EVERYTHING
  INSERT INTO acct(id, bal) VALUES (1, 0);                -- duplicate, ignored
  SELECT 'done, but nothing was inserted' AS msg;
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL swallow();

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------------+
-- | msg                            |
-- +--------------------------------+
-- | done, but nothing was inserted |
-- +--------------------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: handlers cannot catch errors raised in their own body for the same condition; RESIGNAL and GET DIAGNOSTICS only work inside a handler; the diagnostics area is limited; DDL implicitly commits and cannot be rolled back; a handler for a duplicate (1062) must be declared after variables and cursors.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE ddl_demo()
BEGIN
  START TRANSACTION;
  INSERT INTO acct VALUES (9, 0);
  CREATE TABLE tmp_audit (x INT);     -- implicit COMMIT happens here
  ROLLBACK;                           -- too late, the insert is already committed
END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL ddl_demo();  SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM acct WHERE id = 9;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 1 |
-- +---+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Standardise one error contract: EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION with ROLLBACK then RESIGNAL, and SIGNAL SQLSTATE 45000 with distinct MYSQL_ERRNO values for business errors. Make the application retry only on deadlock (1213) and lock wait (1205) errors.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Handlers can target SQLEXCEPTION, SQLWARNING, NOT FOUND or specific error numbers/SQLSTATE.
  • GET DIAGNOSTICS reads the error message and number.
  • RESIGNAL rethrows after cleanup.

Senior Notes

  • Pair transaction control with an EXIT handler so failures always roll back.
  • Log errors to a table in an autonomous way (separate connection) because the main transaction rolls back its logs.
  • Return stable error codes to applications; do not leak internal messages.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: handlers that swallow errors silently, EXIT handlers without ROLLBACK, logging errors inside the transaction that then rolls them back, and exposing internal messages to users. Log outside the transaction and return stable codes.
codeExamples:
DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION BEGIN END;      -- swallows everything: the caller thinks it succeeded
-- better:
DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION BEGIN ROLLBACK; RESIGNAL; END;

-- OUTPUT:
-- (the original error reaches the caller after the rollback)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Handlers add little overhead. The real cost is retries and rolled-back work, so make operations idempotent and short; use error codes to distinguish retryable errors (1213, 1205) from permanent ones (1062, 1452).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a payment procedure maps technical errors to business error codes, so API layers return proper responses without parsing messages.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A stored function is a named routine that takes parameters, RETURNS exactly one scalar value, and can be used inside any expression, such as SELECT, WHERE or ORDER BY. Unlike procedures, you do not CALL it.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION add_tax(price DECIMAL(10,2), rate DECIMAL(4,2))
RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)
DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
  RETURN ROUND(price * (1 + rate), 2);
END //
DELIMITER ;

SELECT add_tax(200, 0.18) AS gross;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | gross  |
-- +--------+
-- | 236.00 |
-- +--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Built-in functions cannot cover every business rule. A stored function encapsulates a calculation once (tax, age band, formatted name) and lets any query reuse it, keeping logic consistent across applications.

Real-Time Use

Real use: currency conversion, slug generation, custom validators, age or fiscal-year helpers and lookups used in reports. Manage with SHOW CREATE FUNCTION, DROP FUNCTION and GRANT EXECUTE.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION age_on(d DATE, ref DATE) RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
  RETURN TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, d, ref);
END //
DELIMITER ;

SELECT first, age_on(dob, '2024-06-01') AS age FROM person;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-----+
-- | first | age |
-- +-------+-----+
-- | Abaji |  24 |
-- | Ben   |  44 |
-- +-------+-----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

  SELECT id, add_tax(price, 0.18) FROM items;
                  |
      for each row |  (called N times)
                  v
        +------------------------+
        | FUNCTION add_tax(...)  |
        |   RETURNS DECIMAL      |
        |   BEGIN ... RETURN x   |   exactly ONE scalar value
        +------------------------+
                  |
                  v
          value placed into the result column / WHERE / ORDER BY

Fresher Notes

  • A stored function takes parameters and returns one value, and can be used inside SQL: SELECT tax(price).
  • Syntax: CREATE FUNCTION f(a INT) RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC BEGIN ... RETURN x; END.
  • Drop with DROP FUNCTION.

Worked Example 1

Binary log requirement error.

Worked Example 2

Fix with a characteristic.

Practice Exercise 1

Simple tax function.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION tax(p_price DECIMAL(10,2)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN
  RETURN ROUND(p_price * 0.18, 2);
END //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT name, price, tax(price) AS gst FROM products;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | price  | gst
-- Pen  |  10.00 |  1.80
-- Book | 150.50 | 27.09

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Use it in a query.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(tax(total)) AS total_tax FROM orders;

-- OUTPUT:
-- total_tax
-- 4210.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A stored function takes parameters, returns exactly one scalar value and can be used inside expressions. It runs once per row where it is called, inside the calling statement, and it cannot return a result set or control transactions. With binary logging on, you must declare its determinism or data access.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION gst(p_price DECIMAL(10,2)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) DETERMINISTIC
BEGIN RETURN ROUND(p_price * 0.18, 2); END //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT name, price, gst(price) AS tax, price + gst(price) AS total FROM products LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | price  | tax   | total
-- Pen  |  10.00 |  1.80 |  11.80
-- Book | 150.50 | 27.09 | 177.59

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Characteristics: DETERMINISTIC, NOT DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL, READS SQL DATA, MODIFIES SQL DATA, SQL SECURITY. Functions can read tables but should not modify them when used in queries.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: usable anywhere an expression is allowed; one definition for a rule; typed result; can read tables (with READS SQL DATA).
codeExamples:
-- Function inside WHERE and ORDER BY.
SELECT first FROM person
WHERE age_on(dob, '2024-06-01') > 30
ORDER BY full_name(first, last);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | first |
-- +-------+
-- | Ben   |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: called once per row, so cost multiplies; wrapping an indexed column in a function disables the index (not sargable); hard to optimise and debug.
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_dob ON person(dob);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM person WHERE age_on(dob, '2024-06-01') > 30;   -- scans every row
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM person WHERE dob < '1994-06-01';               -- can use idx_dob

-- OUTPUT (type column):
-- ALL     <- function on the column
-- range   <- plain comparison

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a function must RETURN one scalar; it cannot return a result set, and cannot use statements that return result sets, COMMIT/ROLLBACK, or most DDL. With binary logging on, you must declare DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL or READS SQL DATA, or you get error 1418 (unless log_bin_trust_function_creators=1 or you have SUPER).
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION bad_fn() RETURNS INT
BEGIN
  RETURN 1;                     -- no DETERMINISTIC / NO SQL / READS SQL DATA characteristic
END //
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT (binary logging enabled):
-- ERROR 1418 (HY000): This function has none of DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL, or READS SQL DATA in its
--                     declaration and binary logging is enabled (you *might* want to use the less
--                     safe log_bin_trust_function_creators variable)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use stored functions for small, pure, reusable calculations. Avoid table lookups inside them on large scans (hidden N+1 inside the engine), keep them sargable-friendly by never wrapping indexed columns, and prefer generated columns when the result must be indexed.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Functions must declare DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL or READS SQL DATA when binary logging is on.
  • They cannot return result sets and cannot use transactions control statements.
  • Use them for reusable calculations and formatting.

Senior Notes

  • A function called in WHERE on an indexed column prevents index use and runs per row; avoid in hot queries.
  • Not allowed to modify data when called from a query in some contexts; side effects are risky for replication.
  • Consider generated columns or application logic for performance-sensitive calculations.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: omitting a characteristic (error 1418 with binary logging), calling a lookup function per row on a big table (hidden N+1), and using functions in WHERE on indexed columns. Replace per-row lookups with joins.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name, dept_name(e.dept) FROM emp e;                                 -- one lookup per row
SELECT e.name, d.name FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept;          -- one join

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | name
-- Abaji | HR

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A function call in WHERE or ORDER BY prevents index use on the argument column and runs for every candidate row. Use generated columns or compute outside the predicate.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a function that formats a business identifier consistently across reports and procedures, so the rule lives in one place.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION invoice_no(p_year INT, p_seq INT) RETURNS VARCHAR(20) DETERMINISTIC
RETURN CONCAT('INV-', p_year, '-', LPAD(p_seq, 6, '0')) //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT invoice_no(2026, 42);

-- OUTPUT:
-- invoice_no(2026, 42)
-- INV-2026-000042

beginner.content:
Introduction

A function is DETERMINISTIC if the same inputs always give the same output. You declare it with the keyword; MySQL trusts the declaration and does not verify it. Alternatives are NOT DETERMINISTIC (default), plus data-access hints NO SQL, READS SQL DATA, MODIFIES SQL DATA.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION area(r DOUBLE) RETURNS DOUBLE
DETERMINISTIC NO SQL
BEGIN
  RETURN ROUND(PI() * r * r, 2);       -- depends only on r
END //
DELIMITER ;

SELECT area(2) AS a;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | a     |
-- +-------+
-- | 12.57 |
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The declaration matters for safe replication and binary logging: statement-based replication replays the function on replicas, so a non-deterministic function (using NOW, RAND, UUID) can give different results on the source and replica. MySQL therefore demands you state your intent.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION today_label() RETURNS VARCHAR(20)
NOT DETERMINISTIC READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
  RETURN CONCAT('Date: ', CURDATE());      -- changes every day
END //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT today_label();

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------------+
-- | today_label()     |
-- +-------------------+
-- | Date: 2026-10-06  |
-- +-------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: label pure calculations DETERMINISTIC so they can be used in generated columns and functional indexes (MySQL 8 requires deterministic expressions there); mark clock or random based ones NOT DETERMINISTIC.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE price (id INT PRIMARY KEY, net DECIMAL(10,2),
  gross DECIMAL(10,2) AS (net * 1.18) STORED);          -- built-in expression is deterministic
INSERT INTO price(id, net) VALUES (1, 100);
CREATE INDEX idx_gross ON price(gross);
SELECT id, gross FROM price;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+
-- | id | gross  |
-- +----+--------+
-- |  1 | 118.00 |
-- +----+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

  same input ---> function ---> same output ?

  DETERMINISTIC       area(r), tax(price)        replica-safe, index-friendly
  NOT DETERMINISTIC   NOW(), RAND(), UUID()      differs per run

  data access hint:  NO SQL | READS SQL DATA | MODIFIES SQL DATA | CONTAINS SQL
  MySQL TRUSTS the keywords -- it never checks them

Fresher Notes

  • A deterministic function always returns the same result for the same inputs. DETERMINISTIC tells MySQL so.
  • Example: a tax calculation is deterministic; a function using RAND() or NOW() is not.
  • Not deterministic is the default if you declare nothing.

Worked Example 1

Reads data: declare READS SQL DATA.

Worked Example 2

Check routine characteristics.
codeExamples:
SELECT routine_name, is_deterministic, sql_data_access FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- routine_name | is_deterministic | sql_data_access
-- circle_area  | YES              | CONTAINS SQL
-- dept_name    | NO               | READS SQL DATA

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Deterministic vs not.

Practice Exercise 2

Used in a generated column (must be deterministic expression).

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

DETERMINISTIC tells MySQL that the function always returns the same result for the same arguments (and no hidden state). The server does not verify it. The flag matters for replication safety (statement-based logging), for generated columns and functional indexes (which require deterministic expressions) and for optimizer assumptions.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION circle_area(r DOUBLE) RETURNS DOUBLE DETERMINISTIC RETURN PI() * r * r //
CREATE FUNCTION now_label() RETURNS VARCHAR(20) NOT DETERMINISTIC NO SQL RETURN DATE_FORMAT(NOW(), '%Y-%m-%d') //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT routine_name, is_deterministic FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_name IN ('circle_area','now_label');

-- OUTPUT:
-- routine_name | is_deterministic
-- circle_area  | YES
-- now_label    | NO

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use the data-access characteristic that matches reality: NO SQL (pure computation), READS SQL DATA (queries tables), MODIFIES SQL DATA (writes). A function that reads tables is not mathematically deterministic and should not be declared so.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: safe replication, correct caching assumptions by the optimizer and eligibility for generated columns and indexes; the declaration documents intent.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: MySQL does not check your claim; a function wrongly declared DETERMINISTIC can return stale or inconsistent data and corrupt replicas silently; declaring NOT DETERMINISTIC may disable optimisations.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION lying() RETURNS DOUBLE DETERMINISTIC NO SQL
BEGIN
  RETURN RAND();                          -- not deterministic, but declared so (BUG)
END //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT lying() = lying() AS same;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------+
-- | same |
-- +------+
-- |    0 |
-- +------+     <- a truly deterministic function would give 1

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: there is no automatic verification; deterministic functions still run per row (MySQL does not memoise results across rows); with binlog_format=ROW the risk is much smaller than with STATEMENT.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_format';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'log_bin_trust_function_creators';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name | Value |
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | binlog_format | ROW   |
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | log_bin_trust_function_creators | OFF |

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Be honest in the declaration; it is a contract with replication and the optimizer. Use ROW-based binary logging, keep functions free of side effects, and never mark a function using time, randomness or mutable tables as DETERMINISTIC.

Mid-Level Notes

  • The optimizer may use the DETERMINISTIC hint, and it matters for safe replication of statement-based logs.
  • Wrongly marking a function DETERMINISTIC can cause inconsistent replicas or wrong cached results.
  • MySQL does not verify your claim.

Senior Notes

  • Mark functions accurately: nondeterminism leaks into replication and generated columns (generated columns require deterministic expressions).
  • Functions that read tables are not deterministic in the mathematical sense; declare READS SQL DATA, not DETERMINISTIC.
  • Prefer pure functions; isolate time and randomness at the call site.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: marking a function that reads tables or uses RAND()/NOW() as DETERMINISTIC (replicas can diverge, indexes on generated columns become wrong), and using a user-defined function in a generated column (not allowed).
codeExamples:
CREATE FUNCTION wrong() RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC RETURN FLOOR(RAND() * 10);     -- lying about determinism
ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN c INT AS (wrong()) STORED;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3763 (HY000): Expression of generated column 'c' contains a disallowed function: wrong.

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Deterministic expressions can be materialized and indexed through generated columns and functional indexes, trading storage for fast predicates.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a deterministic normalization function used by both the application and database, so imports, lookups and uniqueness all treat values the same way.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION norm_phone(p VARCHAR(30)) RETURNS VARCHAR(20) DETERMINISTIC NO SQL
RETURN REGEXP_REPLACE(p, '[^0-9+]', '') //
DELIMITER ;
ALTER TABLE customers ADD COLUMN phone_norm VARCHAR(20) AS (norm_phone(phone)) STORED;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3763 (HY000): Expression of generated column 'phone_norm' contains a disallowed function: norm_phone.
-- (use the built-in REGEXP_REPLACE directly in the generated column instead)

beginner.content:
Introduction

A function returns one value and is used inside expressions. A procedure is invoked with CALL, can return many result sets and OUT parameters, and can freely change data and manage transactions.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION sq(n INT) RETURNS INT DETERMINISTIC NO SQL RETURN n * n //
CREATE PROCEDURE sq_p(IN n INT, OUT r INT) BEGIN SET r = n * n; END //
DELIMITER ;

SELECT sq(7) AS by_function;        -- inside an expression
CALL sq_p(7, @r);  SELECT @r AS by_procedure;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+     +--------------+
-- | by_function |     | by_procedure |
-- +-------------+     +--------------+
-- |          49 |     |           49 |
-- +-------------+     +--------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Choosing wrongly forces awkward workarounds: you cannot filter by a procedure result, and you cannot COMMIT inside a function. Knowing the split tells you which one to write for each job.
codeExamples:
-- Function composes with SQL clauses; a procedure cannot.
SELECT n FROM (SELECT 3 AS n UNION SELECT 8) t WHERE sq(n) > 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | n |
-- +---+
-- | 8 |
-- +---+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rule of thumb: function for a pure calculation or lookup used in queries; procedure for a business action (create order, transfer funds, purge data) with transactions, multiple statements and result sets.

Diagram

                    FUNCTION                    PROCEDURE
  invoked by     expression (SELECT f(x))          CALL p(x)
  returns        1 scalar (RETURN)                 OUT params / result sets
  transactions   no COMMIT / ROLLBACK              yes
  in WHERE/JOIN  yes                               no
  runs           once per row                      once per call

   calculation  ---> FUNCTION          action / workflow ---> PROCEDURE

Fresher Notes

  • A function returns one value and is used inside SQL expressions. A procedure is run with CALL and can return result sets or OUT parameters.
  • Functions are for calculations; procedures are for actions.
  • Procedures can use transactions; functions cannot.

Worked Example 1

Privileges differ per routine.

Worked Example 2

List routines by type.
codeExamples:
SELECT routine_type, COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.routines WHERE routine_schema = DATABASE() GROUP BY routine_type;

-- OUTPUT:
-- routine_type | COUNT(*)
-- FUNCTION     | 3
-- PROCEDURE    | 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Both side by side.

Practice Exercise 2

Function cannot control transactions.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A function is an expression: it is called inside SQL, returns one value and is limited (no result sets, no COMMIT or ROLLBACK, restricted DDL). A procedure is a statement: you CALL it, it can return result sets and OUT parameters and may control transactions. They differ in where and how they can be invoked.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Quick rules: need a value in a query → function; need to perform actions, return several rows or manage a transaction → procedure. Privileges differ: EXECUTE is granted per routine type and name.

expert.content:
Advantages

Function pros: composable in SELECT, WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY; typed return. Procedure pros: transactions, multiple result sets, OUT and INOUT parameters, any DML and most DDL-like control flow.
codeExamples:
-- Procedure may return result sets; function may not.
DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE two_sets() BEGIN SELECT 1 AS a; SELECT 2 AS b; END //
DELIMITER ;
CALL two_sets();

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+     +---+
-- | a |     | b |
-- +---+     +---+
-- | 1 |     | 2 |
-- +---+     +---+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Cons: a function runs per row and can hide big costs; a procedure cannot be composed into a query, and returns values only via OUT or result sets.
codeExamples:
-- Function reading another table = hidden query per row.
DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION cust_total(c INT) RETURNS INT READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
  DECLARE t INT;
  SELECT IFNULL(SUM(amt),0) INTO t FROM orders WHERE cust = c;
  RETURN t;
END //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT cust, cust_total(cust) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT cust FROM orders) c;   -- N hidden queries

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-----------------+
-- | cust | cust_total(cust)|
-- +------+-----------------+
-- |    7 |             120 |
-- |    8 |              20 |
-- +------+-----------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations of functions: no result sets, no explicit COMMIT, ROLLBACK or START TRANSACTION, no dynamic SQL (PREPARE), no DDL; they cannot modify the table being read by the calling statement (error 1442). Procedures cannot appear in expressions.

Architect's Notes

Default to built-ins and plain SQL, add a function only for a reused pure calculation, and a procedure only for a transactional unit of work. Watch per-row function cost in execution plans and slow-log reviews, and keep both under version control with tests.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Functions: single RETURN value, can be used in SELECT/WHERE; restricted statements (no COMMIT, no result sets).
  • Procedures: IN/OUT/INOUT, multiple result sets, transaction control, dynamic SQL via prepared statements.
  • Privileges: EXECUTE is granted separately for each.

Senior Notes

  • Functions in queries can silently run once per row; check complexity before using them on large tables.
  • Use procedures for administrative or batch tasks; use application code for complex business rules.
  • Document side effects: functions that modify data are problematic in replication and queries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: trying to COMMIT inside a function, calling a procedure in SELECT, and a modifying function used in queries (replication hazards). Keep functions pure and put side effects in procedures.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost: a function runs per row, so it multiplies with row count; a procedure runs once per call. Measure the effect by comparing the function-based query with an equivalent join or expression.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(bonus(salary)) FROM big_emp;                         -- function called 5M times
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(salary / 10) FROM big_emp;                             -- inlined expression

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- function version 9.4 s, inlined version 0.6 s

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: reusable rounding and formatting functions in reports, and procedures for each business operation (place order, cancel order, close period) with explicit transactions and error codes.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A BEFORE trigger is a stored routine that MySQL fires automatically before a row is inserted, updated or deleted. Inside it you can read NEW (the incoming row) and OLD (the existing row) and, for INSERT/UPDATE, modify NEW so the corrected value is what actually gets stored.
codeExamples:
-- Self-contained demo: normalise an e-mail before it is stored
CREATE TABLE users (
  id    INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- surrogate key
  email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL             -- we want it lower-case and trimmed
);

DELIMITER $$                              -- change delimiter so the body can contain ;
CREATE TRIGGER trg_users_bi
BEFORE INSERT ON users                    -- fires before each inserted row
FOR EACH ROW                              -- MySQL has only row-level triggers
BEGIN
  SET NEW.email = LOWER(TRIM(NEW.email)); -- rewrite the value that will be stored
END$$
DELIMITER ;

INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('  Anaji@Example.COM ');   -- messy input
SELECT id, email FROM users;                                  -- stored value is clean

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------------------+
-- | id | email             |
-- +----+-------------------+
-- |  1 | anaji@example.com |
-- +----+-------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Rules that must always hold - defaults, normalisation, validation - are safest when the database enforces them, because every client (web app, batch job, DBA console) goes through the same door. BEFORE triggers are the only place where you can fix or reject data before it touches the table; CHECK constraints can reject but cannot rewrite.
codeExamples:
-- Reject invalid data with SIGNAL (custom error) before it is written
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  balance DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);

DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_accounts_bi
BEFORE INSERT ON accounts
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NEW.balance < 0 THEN                                 -- business rule
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000'                               -- 45000 = user-defined error
      SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Opening balance cannot be negative';
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

INSERT INTO accounts (balance) VALUES (100.00);           -- accepted
INSERT INTO accounts (balance) VALUES (-5.00);            -- rejected, whole statement fails

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): Opening balance cannot be negative

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical real uses: stamping updated_at/updated_by, generating a slug or code from other columns, defaulting a column from another table's value (something DEFAULT cannot do pre-8.0.13), and guarding state transitions (an order cannot go from SHIPPED back to NEW).
codeExamples:
-- Guard a state machine: orders may only move forward
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  status ENUM('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED') NOT NULL,   -- ENUM index gives the order
  updated_at DATETIME NULL
);

DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_bu
BEFORE UPDATE ON orders
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NEW.status + 0 < OLD.status + 0 THEN          -- +0 gives the ENUM position (not text)
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Status cannot move backwards';
  END IF;
  SET NEW.updated_at = NOW();                      -- always stamp the change
END$$
DELIMITER ;

INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'PAID', NULL);
UPDATE orders SET status = 'SHIPPED' WHERE id = 1; -- allowed
UPDATE orders SET status = 'NEW'     WHERE id = 1; -- blocked

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (SHIPPED, updated_at stamped)
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): Status cannot move backwards

beginner.content:
Diagram

   INSERT / UPDATE statement
            |
            v
   +---------------------+   for each row
   |   BEFORE trigger    |<--------------+
   |  read OLD / NEW     |               |
   |  edit NEW, or       |               |
   |  SIGNAL = abort     |               |
   +----------+----------+               |
              | (NEW possibly modified)  |
              v                          |
   +---------------------+               |
   |  write row to table |---------------+
   +----------+----------+
              v
   +---------------------+
   |    AFTER trigger    |
   +---------------------+

Fresher Notes

  • A trigger is code that runs automatically when a row is inserted, updated or deleted. BEFORE triggers run before the change is written.
  • Use NEW.col for the new value and OLD.col for the old value.
  • BEFORE triggers can modify NEW values or reject the change with SIGNAL.

Worked Example 1

List triggers.
codeExamples:
SELECT trigger_name, event_manipulation, action_timing, event_object_table FROM information_schema.triggers WHERE trigger_schema = DATABASE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- trigger_name | event_manipulation | action_timing | event_object_table
-- trg_users_bi | INSERT             | BEFORE        | users
-- trg_acct_bu  | UPDATE             | BEFORE        | acct

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Order multiple triggers.

Practice Exercise 1

Normalize email on insert.

Practice Exercise 2

Validation with SIGNAL.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A row-level trigger runs once per affected row inside the same statement and transaction. BEFORE triggers run before the row is written, with NEW values that you may modify and OLD values for UPDATE/DELETE. Raising an error aborts the statement.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Events: BEFORE INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Several triggers per event are allowed with FOLLOWS/PRECEDES. List them in information_schema.triggers. Use SIGNAL to reject invalid changes.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: logic runs for every client with no app change; the trigger can modify NEW so no second UPDATE is needed; rejection is atomic with the statement; central, version-able in DDL scripts.
codeExamples:
-- Advantage: a single BEFORE trigger gives every writer the same default
CREATE TABLE tickets (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  title VARCHAR(50),
  code  VARCHAR(20)
);
DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_tickets_bi BEFORE INSERT ON tickets FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NEW.code IS NULL THEN
    SET NEW.code = CONCAT('TCK-', UPPER(LEFT(NEW.title, 3)));  -- derived default
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;
INSERT INTO tickets (title) VALUES ('printer jam');
SELECT * FROM tickets;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------------+---------+
-- | id | title       | code    |
-- +----+-------------+---------+
-- |  1 | printer jam | TCK-PRI |
-- +----+-------------+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: invisible behaviour (a plain INSERT does more than it says), harder debugging and testing, extra cost per row, and AUTO_INCREMENT values in NEW are still 0 at BEFORE time, so you cannot use the new id there.
codeExamples:
-- Disadvantage: NEW.id is not yet assigned in a BEFORE INSERT trigger
CREATE TABLE t (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, note VARCHAR(30));
DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_t_bi BEFORE INSERT ON t FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  SET NEW.note = CONCAT('id was ', NEW.id);   -- id is 0 here, not the final value
END$$
DELIMITER ;
INSERT INTO t (note) VALUES ('x');
SELECT * FROM t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----------+
-- | id | note     |
-- +----+----------+
-- |  1 | id was 0 |
-- +----+----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: row-level only (no FOR EACH STATEMENT); no COMMIT/ROLLBACK/START TRANSACTION inside; cannot modify the table that fired it with DML (error 1442); no triggers on views or TEMPORARY tables; cascaded foreign-key actions do NOT fire triggers.
codeExamples:
-- Limitation: a trigger cannot UPDATE the very table it is attached to
DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_t_bu BEFORE UPDATE ON t FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE t SET note = 'oops' WHERE id = NEW.id;   -- illegal self-modification
END$$
DELIMITER ;
UPDATE t SET note = 'y' WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1442 (HY000): Can't update table 't' in stored function/trigger
--   because it is already used by statement which invoked this stored function/trigger.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use BEFORE triggers only for small, deterministic, row-local rules (normalise, default, guard). Anything that crosses tables, calls services or needs observability belongs in the application or a procedure, where it is testable and visible. Prefer CHECK constraints and generated columns when they suffice - they are declarative and cheaper - and document every trigger in migrations because they are the classic source of "who changed this value?" mysteries.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Typical uses: normalize data (lowercase email), set defaults, validate rules too complex for CHECK.
  • You can have several triggers per event with FOLLOWS / PRECEDES ordering.
  • Triggers run for each affected row.

Senior Notes

  • Triggers are invisible to application developers, which makes behaviour hard to debug; document and test them.
  • They add latency to every write and can hide lock contention.
  • Prefer constraints, generated columns and application logic when they can do the job.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: heavy logic in triggers (runs for every row), triggers that update the same table (not allowed), forgetting they do not fire for cascaded foreign key actions or TRUNCATE, and hidden behaviour that surprises developers. Prefer CHECK, defaults and generated columns when they suffice.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Triggers add per-row cost: a bulk insert of one million rows runs the trigger a million times. Measure the overhead and keep trigger bodies tiny.
codeExamples:
-- 1M rows: without trigger 6 s, with BEFORE INSERT normalizing trigger 11 s, with AFTER INSERT audit trigger 38 s
SELECT ROUND(11 / 6, 1) AS before_trigger_overhead_x;

-- OUTPUT:
-- before_trigger_overhead_x
-- 1.8

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: enforce a rule that must hold for every writer, including ad hoc SQL, such as keeping an updated_by column and rejecting edits to closed periods.

beginner.content:
Introduction

An AFTER trigger fires once the row change has succeeded. NEW and OLD are read-only here, so AFTER triggers are for side effects: writing to another table, keeping a summary current, or recording history. Because the row exists, NEW.id already holds the generated AUTO_INCREMENT value.
codeExamples:
-- Keep a per-customer order counter in sync
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, order_count INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
CREATE TABLE orders    (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT NOT NULL);

DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_ai
AFTER INSERT ON orders                          -- fires after the row is stored
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE customers
     SET order_count = order_count + 1          -- side effect on another table
   WHERE id = NEW.customer_id;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

INSERT INTO customers (id) VALUES (7);
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (7), (7);   -- two rows -> trigger fires twice
SELECT * FROM customers;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------------+
-- | id | order_count |
-- +----+-------------+
-- |  7 |           2 |
-- +----+-------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Denormalised totals, search tables and history tables must change in the same transaction as the source row, or they drift apart. An AFTER trigger guarantees that: if the outer statement rolls back, the trigger's writes roll back with it.
codeExamples:
-- Atomicity: the trigger's write is undone when the transaction rolls back
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (7);          -- trigger bumps order_count to 3
SELECT order_count FROM customers WHERE id = 7;       -- sees 3 inside the transaction
ROLLBACK;                                             -- undo row AND counter
SELECT order_count FROM customers WHERE id = 7;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+
-- | order_count |
-- +-------------+
-- |           3 |
-- +-------------+
-- +-------------+
-- | order_count |
-- +-------------+
-- |           2 |
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real uses: stock decrement after an order line, maintaining a rolled-up balance, writing outbox rows for an event publisher, or copying deleted rows to an archive table (AFTER DELETE with OLD).

Diagram

   client: INSERT INTO orders ...
        |
        v
   [ BEFORE INSERT ] -> row written -> [ AFTER INSERT ]
                                            |
                         +------------------+------------------+
                         v                                     v
              UPDATE customers.order_count          INSERT INTO outbox(...)
                                                              /
                          +---- same transaction: COMMIT / ROLLBACK together

Fresher Notes

  • AFTER triggers run after the row change has been made. They are used for side effects such as writing to another table.
  • In AFTER triggers NEW and OLD are read-only.
  • Typical use: audit logs, maintaining summary tables.

Worked Example 1

Delete trigger to archive.

Worked Example 2

Drop the trigger.

Practice Exercise 1

Maintain a counter.

Practice Exercise 2

Failure rolls back the statement.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (999, 100);   -- no stats row => trigger raises error

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1644 (45000): customer stats missing

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

AFTER triggers run after the row has been written but still inside the same transaction. NEW and OLD are read-only. If the trigger fails, the whole triggering statement rolls back. They are used for side effects in other tables: audit rows, summaries, outbox events.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

AFTER INSERT can read NEW.id (including auto-increment values). AFTER UPDATE can compare OLD and NEW to log only real changes. AFTER DELETE can archive OLD rows.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE TRIGGER trg_emp_au AFTER UPDATE ON emp FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NOT (OLD.salary <=> NEW.salary) THEN INSERT INTO salary_history (emp_id, old_salary, new_salary, changed_at) VALUES (NEW.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, NOW()); END IF;
END //
CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_ad AFTER DELETE ON orders FOR EACH ROW INSERT INTO orders_archive SELECT OLD.*; //
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: sees the final row (including generated keys); side effects are transactional with the change; cannot be bypassed by any client; ideal for outbox and summary maintenance.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every row pays an extra statement, so a bulk INSERT of 1 million rows runs the trigger 1 million times; failures inside the trigger fail the original statement; hot summary rows become lock hot-spots.
codeExamples:
-- Disadvantage: the counter row is locked by each insert until commit
-- Session A:
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (7);   -- trigger X-locks customers row 7
-- Session B (meanwhile):
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id) VALUES (7);   -- waits for A's lock on customers.id = 7

-- OUTPUT:
-- Session B: blocked until A commits, or
-- ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: cannot change NEW (use BEFORE); no transaction control; no output to the client (a SELECT without INTO is forbidden); cannot call a procedure that returns a result set; changes made by cascading FK actions or by replication row events on a replica do not behave like on the source.
codeExamples:
-- Limitation: a result-returning SELECT is not allowed inside a trigger
DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_bad AFTER INSERT ON orders FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  SELECT 'hello';          -- not allowed to return a result set
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1415 (0A000): Not allowed to return a result set from a trigger

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

AFTER triggers are acceptable for cheap, constant-time side effects. Avoid maintaining a single hot counter row on a high-write table (serialises writers) - use periodic aggregation or sharded counters instead. For cross-system events write an outbox row in the trigger and let a separate relay publish it, rather than calling anything external from the database.

Mid-Level Notes

  • AFTER triggers run inside the same transaction as the triggering statement; if they fail, the whole statement rolls back.
  • Do not call external systems from triggers.
  • AFTER INSERT can use NEW.id (including auto-increment value).

Senior Notes

  • Summary maintenance in triggers creates hot rows and contention; consider asynchronous aggregation.
  • Trigger chains (trigger causing updates that fire other triggers) are fragile; MySQL limits recursion but design to avoid it.
  • Bulk imports multiply trigger cost; consider disabling logic for controlled loads or using batch aggregates.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: maintaining counters on hot rows (lock contention), calling slow external systems, cascades of triggers triggering triggers, and relying on triggers for FK cascade or TRUNCATE (they do not fire). Use an outbox and async processing for integration.
codeExamples:
UPDATE customer_stats SET order_count = order_count + 1 WHERE customer_id = 1;      -- hot row: every order for this customer serializes here
INSERT INTO outbox (event, payload) VALUES ('ORDER_CREATED', JSON_OBJECT('id', NEW.id));   -- append-only: no contention

-- OUTPUT:
-- (append-only inserts scale; a single counter row does not)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

AFTER triggers extend the transaction time and lock duration of the triggering statement. Keep them small, index the tables they touch, and monitor lock waits on those tables.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a transactional outbox filled by a trigger lets an external relay publish events reliably, because the event row commits atomically with the data change.
codeExamples:
DELIMITER //
CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_outbox AFTER INSERT ON orders FOR EACH ROW
INSERT INTO outbox (aggregate, event, payload) VALUES ('order', 'ORDER_CREATED', JSON_OBJECT('id', NEW.id, 'total', NEW.total)); //
DELIMITER ;
SELECT id, event FROM outbox WHERE processed_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | event
--  7 | ORDER_CREATED

beginner.content:
Introduction

Audit logging records who changed what, when, and the before/after values. The classic MySQL pattern is an audit table written by AFTER INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers using OLD, NEW, CURRENT_USER() and NOW().

Why Do We Need This?

Regulations (SOX, GDPR, HIPAA) and ordinary incident work both ask "who changed this value and what was it before?". Application-level logging misses changes made by DBAs, scripts and other services; the database sees them all.
codeExamples:
-- A direct DBA fix is still captured, because the trigger lives in the database
-- (connected as dba@localhost, bypassing the application entirely)
UPDATE salaries SET amount = 56000 WHERE emp_id = 1;
SELECT old_amount, new_amount, changed_by FROM salary_audit ORDER BY audit_id;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+------------+------------------+
-- | old_amount | new_amount | changed_by       |
-- +------------+------------+------------------+
-- |   50000.00 |   55000.00 | app_user@%       |
-- |   55000.00 |   56000.00 | dba@localhost    |
-- +------------+------------+------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real designs: one generic audit table storing JSON snapshots (table name, PK, JSON_OBJECT of old/new) so a single pattern covers many tables; or a shadow _history table per entity with the same columns plus metadata.
codeExamples:
-- Generic JSON audit: one table for any source table
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  tbl VARCHAR(64), pk VARCHAR(64), action CHAR(1),
  old_row JSON, new_row JSON, at DATETIME(3) DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3)
);
CREATE TABLE customers2 (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), city VARCHAR(30));

DELIMITER $$
CREATE TRIGGER trg_cust2_au AFTER UPDATE ON customers2 FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO audit_log (tbl, pk, action, old_row, new_row)
  VALUES ('customers2', NEW.id, 'U',
          JSON_OBJECT('name', OLD.name, 'city', OLD.city),   -- before image
          JSON_OBJECT('name', NEW.name, 'city', NEW.city));  -- after image
END$$
DELIMITER ;

INSERT INTO customers2 VALUES (1, 'Abaji', 'Pune');
UPDATE customers2 SET city = 'Mumbai' WHERE id = 1;
SELECT tbl, pk, action, old_row, new_row FROM audit_log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+----+--------+-----------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
-- | tbl        | pk | action | old_row                           | new_row                             |
-- +------------+----+--------+-----------------------------------+-------------------------------------+
-- | customers2 | 1  | U      | {"city": "Pune", "name": "Abaji"} | {"city": "Mumbai", "name": "Abaji"} |
-- +------------+----+--------+--------------------------------------+---------------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   app / DBA / script
          |  UPDATE salaries ...
          v
   +--------------+   AFTER UPDATE trigger    +---------------------+
   |  salaries    |-------------------------->|  salary_audit       |
   | (live data)  |  OLD, NEW, user, time     |  (append-only)      |
   +--------------+                           +----------+----------+
                                                         | archive job
                                                         v
                                              cold storage / SIEM

Fresher Notes

  • Audit logging records who changed what and when. A trigger can copy old and new values into an audit table on every change.
  • Store table name, row id, action, old/new values, user and timestamp.
  • It works even for changes made outside your application.

Worked Example 1

Query the history of one row.
codeExamples:
SELECT at, action, old_data->>'$.salary' AS old_sal, new_data->>'$.salary' AS new_sal FROM audit_log WHERE tbl='emp' AND row_id = 1 ORDER BY at;

-- OUTPUT:
-- at                  | action | old_sal | new_sal
-- 2026-05-01 10:00:00 | UPDATE | 61000   | 62000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Partition the audit table by month.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE audit_log PARTITION BY RANGE (TO_DAYS(at)) (
  PARTITION p202605 VALUES LESS THAN (TO_DAYS('2026-06-01')),
  PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Audit trigger with JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

Append-only privileges.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An audit trigger copies change details into an append-only audit table in the same transaction, so the audit row exists if and only if the change committed. It works for any writer, including manual SQL. Capture table, key, action, old and new values, database user, application user and time.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Application user: set a session variable on connection checkout (SET @app_user = ...). Log only real changes by comparing OLD and NEW with the NULL-safe operator. Protect the audit table with grants (INSERT only for writers).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: captures every writer; same transaction as the change (no audit gap); no application code; before and after images are both available.
codeExamples:
-- Advantage: audit rows roll back together with the change - no phantom history
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE salaries SET amount = 99999 WHERE emp_id = 1;   -- audit row written
ROLLBACK;                                              -- both gone
SELECT COUNT(*) AS audit_rows FROM salary_audit WHERE new_amount = 99999;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | audit_rows |
-- +------------+
-- |          0 |
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: write amplification (every write becomes two), the audit table grows without bound, the user is the connection user (an app pool shows one account, not the end user), and you need three triggers per table.
codeExamples:
-- Disadvantage: with a shared pool account, CURRENT_USER() is useless for "who"
-- Workaround: the app sets a session variable, the trigger reads it
SET @app_user = 'prataprao.sharma';        -- set by the app after taking a connection
-- inside the trigger:   COALESCE(@app_user, CURRENT_USER())
SELECT COALESCE(@app_user, CURRENT_USER()) AS actor;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | actor        |
-- +--------------+
-- | prataprao.sharma |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: triggers do not fire for TRUNCATE, for DROP TABLE, or for cascading FK deletes; they see only row data, not the SQL text; bulk loads with LOAD DATA do fire row triggers but slowly; and a user with TRIGGER or SUPER privilege can drop the trigger and silently stop auditing.
codeExamples:
-- Limitation: TRUNCATE bypasses row triggers entirely
TRUNCATE TABLE salaries;                        -- all rows gone, no audit rows written
SELECT COUNT(*) AS audit_rows FROM salary_audit;   -- history of earlier updates only

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | audit_rows |
-- +------------+
-- |          2 |      <- nothing recorded for the truncate itself
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Trigger-based audit is simple and complete for row changes, but it taxes the write path and the audit table needs partitioning by date plus an archive policy. For compliance-grade auditing consider the MySQL Enterprise Audit plugin, binary-log based CDC (Debezium) or system-versioned design in the app, and restrict who may DROP TRIGGER. Always have the application pass the real end-user identity via a session variable.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use USER() or CURRENT_USER() for the DB user; the application user needs a session variable (SET @app_user = ...).
  • Store changed values as JSON for flexibility.
  • Partition or archive the audit table; it grows quickly.

Senior Notes

  • Triggers audit within the same transaction, so audit rows are atomic with changes; this is a strength.
  • For high-volume systems prefer binlog-based CDC (Debezium) to avoid write amplification.
  • Protect the audit table with privileges: app users can INSERT via trigger but not UPDATE/DELETE.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: auditing every table at full detail (volume explodes), forgetting INSERT and DELETE triggers, no index on (table, row id), and letting application accounts change or delete audit rows. Audit what matters and secure the table.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Triggers write on every change, increasing latency and binlog volume. For very high write rates use binlog-based change data capture (for example Debezium) which adds no write overhead to the primary.
codeExamples:
-- trigger audit: +1 insert per change in the same transaction
-- CDC audit: reads the binlog asynchronously, no extra writes
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('binlog_format','binlog_row_image');

-- OUTPUT:
-- binlog_format  | ROW
-- binlog_row_image | FULL

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world compliance query: who changed this employee's salary last quarter, and from what to what.
codeExamples:
SELECT at, app_user, old_data->>'$.salary' AS from_sal, new_data->>'$.salary' AS to_sal FROM audit_log
WHERE tbl = 'emp' AND row_id = 1 AND at >= '2026-01-01' AND at < '2026-04-01' AND action = 'UPDATE' ORDER BY at;

-- OUTPUT:
-- at                      | app_user | from_sal | to_sal
-- 2026-02-14 09:20:00.000 | hr_anita | 58000    | 61000

beginner.content:
Introduction

Triggers are powerful but hidden: they run implicitly, per row, inside someone else's statement. Avoid them when the logic is complex, crosses systems, is performance-critical, or can be expressed declaratively with constraints, generated columns, foreign keys or application code.
codeExamples:
-- Prefer declarative tools over a trigger when possible
CREATE TABLE items (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  qty   INT NOT NULL,
  total DECIMAL(12,2) AS (price * qty) STORED,       -- generated column, no trigger needed
  CONSTRAINT chk_qty CHECK (qty >= 0)               -- enforced in MySQL 8.0.16+
);
INSERT INTO items (id, price, qty) VALUES (1, 9.50, 4);
SELECT id, total FROM items;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | total |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | 38.00 |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Knowing the alternatives is the real skill: a CHECK for validation, a generated column for derived values, DEFAULT (expr) for defaults, ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP for timestamps, FK actions for cascades, and application services for workflows.
codeExamples:
-- updated_at without any trigger
CREATE TABLE notes (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  body VARCHAR(50),
  updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
             ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP             -- engine maintains it
);
INSERT INTO notes (id, body) VALUES (1, 'a');
UPDATE notes SET body = 'b' WHERE id = 1;            -- updated_at refreshed automatically

-- OUTPUT:
-- Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  (updated_at refreshed by the engine, no trigger)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real red flags: a trigger that INSERTs into a table having its own trigger (cascades of hidden work), a trigger doing a slow lookup, one calling heavy logic during bulk imports, or an ORM test suite that no longer matches production behaviour.
codeExamples:
-- Find every trigger that exists in a schema (an inventory step before any audit)
SELECT TRIGGER_NAME, EVENT_MANIPULATION AS event, ACTION_TIMING AS timing, EVENT_OBJECT_TABLE AS tbl
FROM   information_schema.TRIGGERS
WHERE  TRIGGER_SCHEMA = DATABASE()
ORDER  BY tbl, timing, event;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------+--------+--------+----------+
-- | TRIGGER_NAME   | event  | timing | tbl      |
-- +----------------+--------+--------+----------+
-- | trg_orders_ai  | INSERT | AFTER  | orders   |
-- | trg_salaries_au| UPDATE | AFTER  | salaries |
-- +----------------+--------+--------+----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Need a rule?
      |
      +-- value check ............ CHECK constraint
      +-- derived value .......... generated column
      +-- default / timestamp .... DEFAULT (expr) / ON UPDATE
      +-- cascade ................ FOREIGN KEY ... ON DELETE
      +-- multi-step workflow .... application service / procedure
      +-- audit every writer ..... small AFTER trigger or CDC
      +-- else: trigger (last resort, keep it tiny)

Fresher Notes

  • Avoid triggers when simple constraints, application code or generated columns can do the job.
  • Triggers hide logic: developers read the application code and do not realise a trigger changes data.
  • They slow bulk operations because they fire per row.

Worked Example 1

Measure trigger overhead.
codeExamples:
-- load 100k rows with and without trigger
-- without: 1.9 s, with AFTER INSERT audit trigger: 14.2 s
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM audit_log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 100000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Transactional outbox instead of a trigger calling services.

Practice Exercise 1

Replace a validation trigger with CHECK.

Practice Exercise 2

Replace a timestamp trigger with a default.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Triggers are invisible to the code that fires them: the application sees one statement, but the server runs more work per row. This hidden behaviour makes performance, locking and debugging harder, and triggers behave differently with bulk loads, replication tools and foreign key cascades.
codeExamples:
SELECT trigger_schema, event_object_table, action_timing, event_manipulation, trigger_name FROM information_schema.triggers WHERE trigger_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY event_object_table;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_object_table | action_timing | event_manipulation | trigger_name
-- orders             | AFTER         | INSERT             | trg_orders_ai
-- orders             | AFTER         | UPDATE             | trg_orders_au      (two triggers on the hottest table)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Alternatives: CHECK constraints, DEFAULT/generated columns, application services, scheduled jobs, binlog CDC, and the transactional outbox pattern. Choose triggers only for rules that must apply to every writer.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE acct ADD CONSTRAINT chk_bal CHECK (bal >= 0);                                    -- replaces a validation trigger
ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY updated_at DATETIME DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP;   -- replaces a timestamp trigger
ALTER TABLE order_items ADD COLUMN line_total DECIMAL(12,2) AS (qty * unit_price) STORED;              -- replaces a calculation trigger

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (x3)

expert.content:
Advantages

Why avoiding them helps: predictable write cost, easy unit testing, clean replication and CDC, and logic that lives in version-controlled application code with proper logging.
codeExamples:
-- The same "order counter" without a trigger: compute on read, always correct
SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM   customers c
LEFT   JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP  BY c.id;                                  -- no stored counter to drift

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+-------------+
-- | id | order_count |
-- +----+-------------+
-- |  7 |           2 |
-- +----+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Costs of avoiding them: rules must be re-implemented in every client, a script or DBA can bypass them, and you must handle consistency yourself (transactions, idempotent jobs).
codeExamples:
-- Without a trigger, a bypassing writer skips the rule entirely
-- App enforces "email lower-case"; a raw script does not:
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('BAJI@EXAMPLE.COM');
SELECT email FROM users WHERE id = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+
-- | email           |
-- +-----------------+
-- | BAJI@EXAMPLE.COM |    <- rule silently not applied
-- +-----------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations to remember: triggers are not fired by cascading FK actions, are not allowed on views, and a bulk operation multiplies their cost by the row count - measure before you ship.
codeExamples:
-- Measure the trigger tax: same bulk insert with and without the trigger
-- 1,000,000 rows into a table WITH an AFTER INSERT audit trigger:
--     typically 2x to 5x slower than the table without it (example)
SHOW TRIGGERS LIKE 'orders';        -- confirm what will fire before a data load
DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS trg_orders_ai;  -- temporary removal during a controlled bulk load

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- no trigger : 1,000,000 rows in  9.1 s
-- with trigger: 1,000,000 rows in 31.4 s

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Adopt a "triggers by exception" policy: each one needs a written reason, a test, and an owner. Prefer declarative constraints first, then application code, then CDC from the binary log for downstream consumers. Where triggers stay, keep them O(1), side-effect-free outward, and listed in an inventory query run in CI.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Problems: hidden side effects, hard debugging, ordering issues, cascade interactions, replication/CDC surprises.
  • Bulk loads fire triggers per row; batch imports can become 10-100x slower.
  • Triggers are not fired by FK cascades in InnoDB and not by TRUNCATE.

Senior Notes

  • Use explicit service-layer code or events for business workflows; use outbox tables for integration.
  • Keep triggers only for cross-cutting data integrity (auditing, normalization) and keep them tiny and tested.
  • Add monitoring on trigger count and review them in schema reviews.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: business workflows in triggers, trigger chains, expecting triggers during bulk imports with disabled checks, and no tests for triggers. Document each trigger and test it.
codeExamples:
TRUNCATE TABLE orders;                          -- DELETE triggers do not fire
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1;               -- ON DELETE CASCADE removes orders but does not fire orders' triggers

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected     (audit rows were never written)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Quantify the overhead before deciding: time a bulk operation with and without the triggers.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: replace "send an email when an order is created" triggers with a transactional outbox and a worker; the database stays fast and the integration becomes retryable and observable.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A cursor lets a stored program walk through a query result one row at a time. The life cycle is fixed: DECLARE (with the SELECT) - OPEN (runs the query) - FETCH ... INTO variables (repeat) - CLOSE. Cursors exist only inside stored procedures, functions and triggers.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji',50000),(2,'Raoji',60000),(3,'Moropant',70000);

DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE first_two()
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_id INT;                       -- 1. variables first (order matters:
  DECLARE v_name VARCHAR(20);             --    variables, cursors, then handlers)
  DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR                  -- 2. declare the cursor with its SELECT
    SELECT id, name FROM emp ORDER BY id;

  OPEN cur;                               -- 3. executes the query
  FETCH cur INTO v_id, v_name;            -- 4. read row 1 into the variables
  SELECT v_id AS id, v_name AS name;
  FETCH cur INTO v_id, v_name;            --    read row 2
  SELECT v_id AS id, v_name AS name;
  CLOSE cur;                              -- 5. release the result set
END$$
DELIMITER ;
CALL first_two();

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | Abaji |
-- +----+-------+
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  2 | Raoji |
-- +------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Plain SQL is set-based and cannot say "for each row, run these several statements with branching". A cursor gives a procedural loop when each row needs custom logic, such as calling another procedure per row.

Real-Time Use

Real uses: legacy data migrations that must call a routine per row, sending each pending job row to a queue table, generating dynamic SQL per table name from information_schema, and row-by-row reconciliation.

Diagram

   DECLARE v_id, v_name ...
   DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR SELECT ...
   DECLARE ... HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND ...
          |
          v
      OPEN cur        run SELECT, materialise result
          |
          v
   +--> FETCH cur INTO v_id, v_name   -- next row, forward only
   |      |  row found ----------------+
   |      |                            |
   +------+ process row                |
          | no more rows -> NOT FOUND handler fires
          v
      CLOSE cur

Fresher Notes

  • A cursor lets a stored program process a query result one row at a time.
  • Steps: DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT ..., OPEN c, FETCH c INTO vars, CLOSE c.
  • Cursors exist only inside stored programs.

Worked Example 1

Set-based equivalent is simpler.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- SUM(salary)
-- 175000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Order mistake.
codeExamples:
-- handler declared before the cursor
-- ERROR 1337 (42000): Variable or condition declaration after handler declaration

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1337 (42000): Variable or condition declaration after handler declaration

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Basic cursor.

Practice Exercise 2

Accumulate in a cursor.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A cursor is a server-side handle on a SELECT result used inside stored programs. DECLARE defines it (after variables, before handlers), OPEN executes the query (results are materialized or streamed), FETCH moves forward one row into variables, and CLOSE releases it. Cursors are read-only and forward-only in MySQL.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

The cursor query can use parameters and variables, joins and ORDER BY. Fetch several columns into several variables in order. The NOT FOUND handler signals the end; reset the flag when reusing it for another cursor.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: full procedural control per row; can read from any SELECT (joins, ordering); the result can be consumed while keeping other state in variables; and it is read-only and asensitive so it is simple to reason about.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: row-by-row is slow (one fetch round of interpreter work per row), consumes server memory for the result set (often a temporary table), and the code is longer than the equivalent SELECT.
codeExamples:
-- The cursor above does what one statement does:
SELECT SUM(salary) AS total FROM emp;       -- set-based, optimised, one line

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | total  |
-- +--------+
-- | 180000 |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: read-only (no UPDATE ... WHERE CURRENT OF), non-scrollable (forward only, no FETCH PRIOR), asensitive (do not rely on seeing changes made after OPEN), and declaration order is enforced - declaring a cursor before a variable is a syntax error.
codeExamples:
-- Limitation: the declaration order is enforced
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE bad_order()
BEGIN
  DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR SELECT id FROM emp;
  DECLARE v INT;                           -- variable AFTER cursor: not allowed
  OPEN cur; CLOSE cur;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1337 (42000): Variable or condition declaration after cursor or handler declaration

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat a cursor as a last resort for work that truly needs per-row procedural logic. Remember it materialises the result, so on large tables it costs memory and tmp-disk; limit the SELECT with WHERE and a sensible ORDER, and process in batches (keyset pagination) if you must loop over millions of rows. Keep cursors inside short transactions to avoid long undo history.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Declarations order: variables, cursors, then handlers.
  • A NOT FOUND handler signals the end of data.
  • Cursors are read-only and forward-only in MySQL.

Senior Notes

  • Cursors materialize results and run row by row; use them only when set-based SQL cannot express the logic.
  • Keep the cursor query narrow and indexed.
  • Close cursors promptly to release resources.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: wrong declaration order (error 1337), using the loop variables before checking the done flag (processing the last row twice), not closing cursors, and using a cursor for work SQL can do in one statement.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept = 10;        -- one statement replaces the whole cursor

-- OUTPUT:
-- SUM(salary)
-- 105000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cursors process rows one by one with per-row overhead; a set-based statement is often tens to hundreds of times faster. If a cursor is needed, keep the query narrow, indexed and ordered by the primary key.
codeExamples:
-- 1,000,000 rows: cursor loop ~ 240 s;  UPDATE ... JOIN ~ 2.5 s
SELECT ROUND(240 / 2.5) AS times_slower;

-- OUTPUT:
-- times_slower
-- 96

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a one-off data repair that must call a routine for each row (with side effects that cannot be expressed in SQL) and logs failures to a table, committing in chunks.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL has no "has next" test. When FETCH runs past the last row it raises SQLSTATE 02000 (NOT FOUND). You catch that with a DECLARE ... HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND that sets a flag, and the loop tests the flag right after the FETCH.

Why Do We Need This?

Without the handler the last FETCH aborts the procedure with error 1329 "No data - zero rows fetched". Handlers are also how you turn errors (duplicate key, deadlock) into controlled flow instead of a crash.

Real-Time Use

Real pattern: loop over pending rows, call a procedure for each, and swallow per-row errors while counting failures so one bad row does not abort the batch.

Diagram

          OPEN cur
             |
        +--> FETCH cur INTO vars -------------------+
        |        |                                  |
        |   row returned                       no row: SQLSTATE 02000
        |        |                                  |
        |   IF done THEN LEAVE?  <---- handler sets done = 1
        |        | no
        |   process row
        +--------+
             CLOSE cur  <----- after loop

Fresher Notes

  • A cursor loop fetches until no rows remain. A NOT FOUND handler sets a flag to leave the loop.
  • Pattern: LOOP, FETCH, check done flag, process, repeat.
  • Always reset the flag if you reuse it.

Worked Example 1

Restartable chunk processing.

Worked Example 2

Commit every 1000 rows (concept).

Practice Exercise 1

Per-row processing with error handling.

Practice Exercise 2

Equivalent set-based statement.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The standard cursor loop is LOOP, FETCH, test the NOT FOUND flag, process, repeat. The handler runs when FETCH finds no row and sets the flag; the loop must test it right after FETCH because the variables still hold the previous row's values.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Nested cursors need an inner BEGIN...END block with its own handler and flag, so the inner NOT FOUND does not end the outer loop. Add specific handlers (for example for duplicate keys) inside the loop to skip bad rows.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: handlers separate flow control from business logic; CONTINUE lets the loop survive errors; EXIT handlers clean up and leave the block; handlers can be scoped to an inner BEGIN...END.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the flag approach is easy to get wrong. If any other statement in the loop also hits NOT FOUND (for example a SELECT ... INTO returning no row), the flag flips and the loop ends early without an error.

Limitations

Limitations: you cannot FETCH from a closed cursor (error 1326); a cursor cannot be reused without CLOSE then OPEN; handler declarations must come after cursors; a handler cannot see which statement raised the condition (use GET DIAGNOSTICS to read details).

Architect's Notes

Put the NOT FOUND flag logic as tightly around the FETCH as possible.
