If the loop body needs a lookup that may legitimately return nothing, wrap it in its own BEGIN...END block with a local NOT FOUND handler, or use aggregate/EXISTS patterns that always return a row. Count and log failures in CONTINUE handlers so batch jobs stay observable.

Mid-Level Notes

  • After the handler fires, the FETCH variables keep the last values; test the flag right after FETCH.
  • Nested cursors need separate flags/handlers via inner BEGIN blocks.
  • Handle errors inside the loop with specific handlers if one row can fail.

Senior Notes

  • For batch jobs, commit every N rows to avoid huge transactions.
  • Log progress and failures to a table so the job can resume.
  • Prefer chunked set-based updates (UPDATE ... LIMIT) to cursors when possible.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: sharing one flag between nested cursors, processing before checking the flag, and a handler declared for all errors that hides real problems. Declare precise handlers and keep each scope clean.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large cursor jobs should commit in chunks and be restartable. Track the last processed id and resume from it, so a failure does not lose hours of work.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: migrate rows to a new schema with per-row validation and a rejects table, so bad rows are recorded and the job continues.

beginner.content:
Introduction

SQL is a set-based language: you describe the whole result and the optimiser chooses how to compute it with indexes, joins and parallel-friendly storage code. A cursor forces row-by-row ("RBAR") processing in the stored-program interpreter. Whenever one statement can express the work, it should win.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Abaji',50000),(2,'Raoji',60000),(3,'Moropant',70000);

-- Task: give everyone below 65000 a 10% raise.
-- SET-BASED (one statement, one pass):
UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE salary < 65000;
SELECT id, salary FROM emp ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+
-- | id | salary |
-- +----+--------+
-- |  1 |  55000 |
-- |  2 |  66000 |
-- |  3 |  70000 |
-- +----+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Choosing correctly is a performance and maintainability decision: the cursor version of the same raise needs a procedure, a handler, a loop and one UPDATE per row, which multiplies statements and lock round trips.

Real-Time Use

Where a cursor is still justified: calling a stored procedure for each row, dynamic SQL per row (PREPARE per table name), side effects that cannot be a single statement, and tiny result sets where clarity matters more than speed.
codeExamples:
-- Rewrite common "needs a loop" tasks as set-based SQL
-- 1) running total - window function instead of a cursor accumulator
SELECT id, salary, SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running
FROM emp;
-- 2) per-group top row - ROW_NUMBER instead of nested loops
-- 3) string aggregation - GROUP_CONCAT instead of a CONCAT loop
SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY id) AS names FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+---------+
-- | id | salary | running |
-- +----+--------+---------+
-- |  1 |  55000 |   55000 |
-- |  2 |  66000 |  121000 |
-- |  3 |  70000 |  191000 |
-- +----+--------+---------+
-- +----------------------+
-- | names                |
-- +----------------------+
-- | Abaji,Raoji,Moropant |
-- +-----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Set-based                            Cursor (RBAR)
   ---------                            -------------
   UPDATE ... WHERE ...                 OPEN cur
        |                               loop: FETCH -> UPDATE one row
        v                                      FETCH -> UPDATE one row
   optimiser + index                           FETCH -> UPDATE one row ...
        |                               CLOSE cur
        v
   one pass over data                   N statements, N plans, N lock steps
   cost ~ O(n) tight                    cost ~ O(n) heavy constant

Fresher Notes

  • Set-based SQL works on all rows at once; cursors process one row at a time.
  • Set-based statements are usually much faster and simpler.
  • Rule: think in sets first; use a cursor only when you must.

Worked Example 1

Chunked update by ranges.

Worked Example 2

Compare timings (conceptual).
codeExamples:
-- cursor over 1,000,000 rows: ~ 240 s
-- single UPDATE ... JOIN: ~ 2.5 s

-- OUTPUT:
-- 96x faster with set-based SQL

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Running total: cursor vs window.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running FROM payments;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | amount | running
--  1 |    100 |     100
--  2 |     50 |     150
--  3 |     25 |     175

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Conditional update without a loop.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Set-based SQL gives the optimizer the whole problem: it can choose indexes, join algorithms, batching and read-ahead. A cursor loop issues one statement per row, each paying parse/dispatch overhead and a separate index lookup. The work is the same logically but far larger in practice.
codeExamples:
-- cursor style: one UPDATE per row
-- set style: one statement
UPDATE emp e JOIN dept_bonus b ON b.dept = e.dept SET e.salary = e.salary + b.amount;
SELECT ROW_COUNT();

-- OUTPUT:
-- ROW_COUNT()
-- 120450        (one statement, one plan)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common cursor-to-SQL conversions: running totals → window SUM OVER; row comparisons with previous → LAG/LEAD; conditional updates → CASE; hierarchies → recursive CTE; ranking → ROW_NUMBER/RANK; per-group top N → window or LATERAL.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of set-based: optimiser-chosen plans, index use, one statement and one lock acquisition pass, easy to read and test, and scales roughly linearly.
codeExamples:
-- EXPLAIN shows the optimiser's plan for set-based work; a cursor has no such plan per loop
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM emp WHERE salary < 65000;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+-------------+
-- | id | table  | type | possible_keys | key  | rows    | Extra       |
-- +----+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+-------------+
-- |  1 | emp    | ALL  | NULL          | NULL |       3 | Using where |
-- +----+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages of cursors: slow, memory heavy, long-held locks (rows read inside a transaction stay locked until commit), and hard to parallelise.
codeExamples:
-- Row-by-row inside one transaction keeps locks for the whole loop
START TRANSACTION;
CALL raise_cursor();            -- touches rows one at a time, X-locks each, holds all
-- other sessions updating those rows now wait until COMMIT
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- other session: UPDATE emp SET salary = 1 WHERE id = 2;  -- waits ... until COMMIT

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations of set-based SQL: some tasks genuinely are sequential - state machines, row-dependent recursion (use a recursive CTE first), or calling external routines. Even then, batch it: process in chunks of a few thousand rows rather than one at a time.
codeExamples:
-- Chunked set-based loop: a few thousand rows per statement, not one
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE purge_old()
BEGIN
  DECLARE n INT DEFAULT 1;
  WHILE n > 0 DO
    DELETE FROM emp WHERE salary < 0 LIMIT 5000;   -- bounded chunk
    SET n = ROW_COUNT();                           -- rows removed this round
    DO SLEEP(0.05);                                -- be kind to replicas
  END WHILE;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Procedure created; loop ends when a DELETE removes 0 rows

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to set-based SQL, window functions and recursive CTEs; use cursors only for per-row side effects and keep them small. When looping is unavoidable do it in the application with chunked, keyset-paginated statements - it is easier to monitor, retry and throttle than a long-running stored procedure that pins a connection and a transaction.

Mid-Level Notes

  • The optimizer can parallelize, use indexes and batch I/O for set operations; cursors defeat this.
  • Window functions, joins, CASE and recursive CTEs replace most cursor logic.
  • A row loop of 1M iterations means 1M statement executions.

Senior Notes

  • Cursor-style logic belongs in application code with batching if row logic is complex, with chunked transactions.
  • If you must loop, process in chunks and avoid per-row network round trips.
  • Benchmark both approaches on realistic volumes; the gap is often 10-1000x.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: porting procedural logic row by row from another system, and keeping a cursor because "it works". Rewrite the logic declaratively; verify equal results on a copy.
codeExamples:
-- verify the rewrite against the cursor result on a copy of the data
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp_cursor_result r JOIN emp_set_result s USING (id) WHERE r.salary <> s.salary;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 0           (identical results)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

When a loop is unavoidable, batch it: process ranges of primary keys per statement instead of per row, commit each batch, and pause on replication lag.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nightly job rewritten from a cursor that took 3 hours to a set-based pipeline that takes 4 minutes, with the same results and far fewer locks held per second.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO daily_balances (account_id, day, balance)
SELECT account_id, CURDATE(), SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id) FROM ledger WHERE posted_on = CURDATE()
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE balance = VALUES(balance);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 48211 rows affected (4.2 sec)

beginner.content:
Introduction

A Common Table Expression is a named, temporary result set defined with WITH name AS (SELECT ...) and usable in the single statement that follows. Think of it as a readable alias for a subquery. CTEs need MySQL 8.0+.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer VARCHAR(10), amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'A',100),(2,'A',300),(3,'B',50),(4,'B',70),(5,'C',500);

WITH customer_totals AS (                 -- name the intermediate result
  SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total   -- one row per customer
  FROM   orders
  GROUP  BY customer
)
SELECT customer, total                    -- then query it like a table
FROM   customer_totals
WHERE  total > 100
ORDER  BY total DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------+
-- | customer | total |
-- +----------+-------+
-- | C        |   500 |
-- | A        |   400 |
-- | B        |   120 |
-- +----------+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Deeply nested subqueries are hard to read and debug. A CTE lets you build a query top-down in named steps, and a CTE referenced twice is written once, so the logic cannot diverge.
codeExamples:
-- Compare each customer's total to the average of all totals - uses the CTE twice
WITH t AS (
  SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer
)
SELECT customer, total,
       total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM t) AS above_avg    -- second use of t
FROM   t
ORDER  BY customer;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------+-----------+
-- | customer | total | above_avg |
-- +----------+-------+-----------+
-- | A        |   400 |         1 |
-- | B        |   120 |         0 |
-- | C        |   500 |         1 |
-- +----------+-------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: reporting pipelines - clean the data in CTE 1, aggregate in CTE 2 (which reads CTE 1), join the results in the final SELECT. Multiple CTEs are separated by commas under a single WITH, and a later one can use an earlier one.
codeExamples:
WITH big AS (                                   -- step 1: filter
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount >= 100
),
per_cust AS (                                     -- step 2: reads step 1
  SELECT customer, COUNT(*) AS n, SUM(amount) AS total
  FROM   big GROUP BY customer
)
SELECT p.customer, p.n, p.total,                  -- step 3: final query
       ROUND(100 * p.total / SUM(p.total) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM   per_cust p
ORDER  BY p.customer;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+---+-------+------+
-- | customer | n | total | pct  |
-- +----------+---+-------+------+
-- | A        | 2 |   400 |  44.4|
-- | C        | 1 |   500 |  55.6|
-- +----------+---+-------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   WITH step1 AS ( SELECT ... FROM base ),
        step2 AS ( SELECT ... FROM step1 ),     <- may use earlier CTEs
        step3 AS ( SELECT ... FROM step2 )
   SELECT ... FROM step3 JOIN step1 ...         <- the one main statement
        |
        v
   result set        (CTEs are discarded; nothing is stored)

Fresher Notes

  • A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named temporary result defined with WITH name AS (SELECT ...) and used in the main query.
  • It makes complex queries readable by splitting them into steps.
  • Needs MySQL 8.0+. The CTE exists only for that one statement.

Worked Example 1

Filter step by step.
codeExamples:
WITH step1 AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'),
     step2 AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent FROM step1 GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT customer_id FROM step2 WHERE spent > 1000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Plan check.

Practice Exercise 1

Multiple CTEs.

Practice Exercise 2

Reuse a CTE twice.
codeExamples:
WITH high AS (SELECT * FROM emp WHERE salary > 50000)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM high) AS n, (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM high) AS avg_sal;

-- OUTPUT:
-- n | avg_sal
-- 2 | 65000.0000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A CTE is a named subquery defined with WITH and visible only to the statement that follows. MySQL treats a simple CTE like a derived table: it is merged into the outer query when possible, so indexes and filters are pushed down. A CTE that is referenced more than once, or that cannot be merged, is materialized once into a temporary table.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Define several CTEs separated by commas; later ones may use earlier ones. Name the columns explicitly when helpful. A CTE can feed SELECT, INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE and CREATE TABLE AS.
codeExamples:
WITH dept_totals (dept, total) AS (SELECT dept, SUM(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept),
     company (grand) AS (SELECT SUM(total) FROM dept_totals)
SELECT d.dept, d.total, ROUND(d.total / c.grand * 100, 1) AS pct FROM dept_totals d CROSS JOIN company c;
WITH old AS (SELECT id FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < NOW()) DELETE s FROM sessions s JOIN old ON old.id = s.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | total  | pct
--   10 | 105000 | 60.0
--   20 |  70000 | 40.0

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: readable top-to-bottom flow, reuse inside one statement, can be used with INSERT ... SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE and CREATE TABLE ... AS, and it is the foundation for recursion.
codeExamples:
-- CTE with DELETE: remove the largest order of each customer
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer ORDER BY amount DESC) AS rn
  FROM   orders
)
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1);
SELECT id, customer, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----------+--------+
-- | id | customer | amount |
-- +----+----------+--------+
-- |  1 | A        |    100 |
-- |  3 | B        |     50 |
-- +----+----------+--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a CTE is not a stored object; it vanishes after the statement. Before MySQL 8.0.x the optimiser could materialise a CTE and not push predicates into it; each reference may be recomputed or materialised once, so cost depends on the plan.
codeExamples:
-- Check how the optimiser treated the CTE
EXPLAIN
WITH t AS (SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer)
SELECT * FROM t WHERE customer = 'A';

-- OUTPUT (example): a DERIVED row (materialised) or, if mergeable, no derived row
-- +----+-------------+------------+-------+
-- | id | select_type | table      | type  |
-- +----+-------------+------------+-------+
-- |  1 | PRIMARY     | <derived2> | ALL   |
-- |  2 | DERIVED     | orders     | ALL   |
-- +----+-------------+------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: scope is one statement; a CTE name shadows a real table of the same name; no CTE in the middle of a statement except in subqueries or derived tables (WITH must be at the start of that query block); you cannot index a CTE.
codeExamples:
-- Limitation: the CTE is gone after its statement
WITH t AS (SELECT 1 AS x) SELECT * FROM t;     -- works
SELECT * FROM t;                               -- different statement: t does not exist

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+
-- | x |
-- +---+
-- | 1 |
-- +---+
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'mydb.t' doesn't exist

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use CTEs to make large analytical SQL reviewable - one idea per CTE with a descriptive name. Do not assume CTE means "computed once": check EXPLAIN, and if a heavy CTE is referenced several times and you need an index on it, switch to a temporary table. Keep each query block self-explanatory so DBAs can tune it later.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Define several CTEs separated by commas; later CTEs can use earlier ones.
  • A CTE can be referenced multiple times in the main query.
  • MySQL may merge a CTE into the outer query or materialize it.

Senior Notes

  • CTEs are not an optimization fence by default; they are inlined when simple. Referenced multiple times, they can be materialized once.
  • Use CTEs for readability, not as a performance trick; check EXPLAIN.
  • Avoid very long CTE chains that become hard to test; consider views for reuse.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting a CTE to be a performance fence or a cache (it is not by default), long chains that are hard to debug, and reusing a name that shadows a real table. Verify the plan and keep chains short and named clearly.
codeExamples:
WITH emp AS (SELECT * FROM emp WHERE dept = 10) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp;     -- shadows the base table inside this statement
WITH recent AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01') SELECT COUNT(*) FROM recent r1 JOIN recent r2 ON r1.customer_id = r2.customer_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 2          (the CTE name hides the real table within the statement)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A CTE referenced several times is computed once (materialized), which is good for expensive logic and bad if each use needs a different filter pushed down. Compare plans and consider a temporary table with an index for heavy multi-step work.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE WITH agg AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id)
SELECT a.customer_id FROM agg a JOIN agg b ON b.customer_id = a.customer_id WHERE a.spent > 1000;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Materialize CTE agg  (actual time=380..380 rows=4200 loops=1)   used by both references

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: readable report logic. Each CTE is one business step (filter, aggregate, rank), which makes the query reviewable and testable step by step.
codeExamples:
WITH paid AS (SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'),
     by_customer AS (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(total) AS spent FROM paid GROUP BY customer_id),
     ranked AS (SELECT *, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spent DESC) AS rk FROM by_customer)
SELECT customer_id, orders, spent FROM ranked WHERE rk <= 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | orders | spent
-- 7           |     31 | 48200.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A recursive CTE references itself. It has an anchor member (the starting rows) combined by UNION ALL with a recursive member that joins the previous iteration's rows; evaluation repeats until the recursive part returns no new rows. Syntax: WITH RECURSIVE.
codeExamples:
-- Generate the numbers 1..5 without any table
WITH RECURSIVE nums (n) AS (
  SELECT 1                                -- anchor: start with 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5      -- recursive: previous row + 1, stop at 5
)
SELECT n FROM nums;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | n    |
-- +------+
-- |    1 |
-- |    2 |
-- |    3 |
-- |    4 |
-- |    5 |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Hierarchies (org charts, categories, bill of materials, folder trees) have unknown depth, which fixed self-joins cannot handle. A recursive CTE walks any depth in one query.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT NULL);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'CEO',NULL),(2,'VP Eng',1),(3,'VP Ops',1),(4,'Dev',2),(5,'Intern',4);

WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS depth,
         CAST(name AS CHAR(200)) AS path             -- cast: width fixed by anchor
  FROM   emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL                -- anchor: the root
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, c.depth + 1,
         CONCAT(c.path, ' > ', e.name)               -- extend the path
  FROM   emp e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id   -- children of previous level
)
SELECT depth, path FROM chain ORDER BY path;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------------------------------+
-- | depth | path                         |
-- +-------+------------------------------+
-- |     0 | CEO                          |
-- |     1 | CEO > VP Eng                 |
-- |     2 | CEO > VP Eng > Dev           |
-- |     3 | CEO > VP Eng > Dev > Intern  |
-- |     1 | CEO > VP Ops                 |
-- +-------+------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real uses: expanding a category tree for a product page, finding all reports (direct and indirect) of a manager, date series for gap-filled reports, and graph reachability with cycle control.
codeExamples:
-- Date series: every day of a week, so a report shows zero-sales days too
WITH RECURSIVE days (d) AS (
  SELECT DATE '2025-03-03'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM days WHERE d < DATE '2025-03-09'
)
SELECT d, DAYNAME(d) AS dow FROM days;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | d          | dow       |
-- +------------+-----------+
-- | 2025-03-03 | Monday    |
-- | 2025-03-04 | Tuesday   |
-- | 2025-03-05 | Wednesday |
-- | 2025-03-06 | Thursday  |
-- | 2025-03-07 | Friday    |
-- | 2025-03-08 | Saturday  |
-- | 2025-03-09 | Sunday    |
-- +------------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   anchor:     SELECT root rows          -> working set W0
                                              |
   recursive:  SELECT ... FROM table JOIN W(k)  -> new rows W(k+1)
                                              |
        repeat while W(k+1) not empty  (limit: cte_max_recursion_depth = 1000)
                                              |
   result = W0 UNION ALL W1 UNION ALL W2 ...

   CEO(0) -> VP Eng(1) -> Dev(2) -> Intern(3)
          -> VP Ops(1)

Fresher Notes

  • A recursive CTE refers to itself to walk hierarchies or generate series: WITH RECURSIVE t AS (anchor UNION ALL recursive_part) SELECT ....
  • The anchor part starts the result; the recursive part adds rows until none are produced.
  • Typical: org charts, category trees, number/date sequences.

Worked Example 1

Depth limit protection.

Worked Example 2

Path column for cycle detection.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT id, CAST(id AS CHAR(200)) AS path FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, CONCAT(w.path, ',', n.id) FROM nodes n JOIN edges e ON e.to_id = n.id JOIN walk w ON w.id = e.from_id
  WHERE FIND_IN_SET(n.id, w.path) = 0)
SELECT path FROM walk;

-- OUTPUT:
-- path
-- 1
-- 1,2
-- 1,2,3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Org chart traversal.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS lvl FROM staff WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, c.lvl + 1 FROM staff s JOIN chain c ON s.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT lvl, name FROM chain ORDER BY lvl, id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- lvl | name
--   1 | Annaji
--   2 | Raoji
--   2 | Moropant
--   3 | Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Generate a date series.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE d AS (SELECT DATE('2026-01-01') AS day UNION ALL SELECT day + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM d WHERE day < '2026-01-05')
SELECT day FROM d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day
-- 2026-01-01
-- 2026-01-02
-- 2026-01-03
-- 2026-01-04
-- 2026-01-05

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A recursive CTE has an anchor SELECT and a recursive SELECT joined by UNION [ALL]. MySQL runs the anchor once, then repeatedly runs the recursive part against the rows produced in the previous iteration until it produces no rows. Each iteration's output is appended to the result.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE nums(n) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5)
SELECT n FROM nums;

-- OUTPUT:
-- n
-- 1
-- 2
-- 3
-- 4
-- 5

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical uses: hierarchies (org charts, categories, folders), graph walks, number and date series, and running calculations. Carry level and path columns. cte_max_recursion_depth (default 1000) stops runaway recursion.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS lvl, CAST(name AS CHAR(300)) AS path FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, o.lvl + 1, CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', s.name) FROM staff s JOIN org o ON s.manager_id = o.id)
SELECT CONCAT(REPEAT('  ', lvl), name) AS chart, path FROM org ORDER BY path;

-- OUTPUT:
-- chart  | path
-- Annaji | Annaji
--   Moropant     | Annaji > Moropant
--   Raoji      | Annaji > Raoji
--     Kanhoji   | Annaji > Raoji > Kanhoji

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: standard SQL, arbitrary depth in one statement, easy path/level tracking, and it can generate series without helper tables.
codeExamples:
-- All subordinates of employee 2 (direct and indirect)
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, name FROM emp WHERE id = 2
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name FROM emp e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id
)
SELECT name FROM sub WHERE id <> 2 ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | name   |
-- +--------+
-- | Dev    |
-- | Intern |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: an infinite loop is possible if the data has a cycle; MySQL stops it only at the safety limits (cte_max_recursion_depth default 1000, or max_execution_time). The recursive member also cannot use aggregates, window functions, DISTINCT or LEFT JOIN on the CTE.

Limitations

Limitations: non-recursive SELECT must come first (the anchor); recursive part must reference the CTE exactly once and not in a subquery; column widths come from the anchor row (hence the CAST above, or strings are truncated or error in strict mode); no ORDER BY or LIMIT inside the recursion that changes semantics.
codeExamples:
-- Detect cycles by tracking the visited path, so the walk stops by itself
WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id, CAST(id AS CHAR(100)) AS seen
  FROM   loop_emp WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT l.id, l.manager_id, CONCAT(w.seen, ',', l.id)
  FROM   loop_emp l JOIN walk w ON l.id = w.manager_id
  WHERE  FIND_IN_SET(l.id, w.seen) = 0            -- do not revisit a node
)
SELECT seen FROM walk;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | seen |
-- +------+
-- | 1    |
-- | 1,2  |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Recursive CTEs are the right tool for modest trees (thousands of nodes). For very large or hot hierarchies, store a path (materialised path), nested set, or closure table so reads are index lookups instead of iterative joins. Always index the parent column, cap depth with a WHERE condition and cycle guard, and raise cte_max_recursion_depth per session rather than globally.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use UNION ALL for speed; UNION removes duplicates and can stop cycles.
  • Set cte_max_recursion_depth (default 1000) to protect against runaway recursion.
  • Track the level or path columns to display or detect cycles.

Senior Notes

  • For graphs with cycles, carry a visited path and filter with FIND_IN_SET/LOCATE, or switch to UNION.
  • Deep or huge hierarchies may be faster with closure tables or materialized paths.
  • Index the parent column used in the recursive join.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: cycles in the data (infinite recursion), UNION instead of UNION ALL where unnecessary, missing index on the parent column, and string columns whose type is fixed by the anchor (path truncated). Cast the anchor to a large enough type and guard against cycles.
codeExamples:
SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 50;
WITH RECURSIVE walk(id, path) AS (
  SELECT id, CAST(id AS CHAR(200)) FROM nodes WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n.id, CONCAT(w.path, ',', n.id) FROM nodes n JOIN edges e ON e.to_id = n.id JOIN walk w ON w.id = e.from_id WHERE FIND_IN_SET(n.id, w.path) = 0)
SELECT path FROM walk;

-- OUTPUT:
-- path
-- 1
-- 1,2
-- 1,2,3        (the cycle back to 1 is cut by the path check)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Recursion performance depends on the join in the recursive part, so index the parent column. For very deep or very wide trees, closure tables or materialized paths make subtree queries a single index range.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: all descendants of a category, with product counts rolled up, for a category tree page.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (SELECT id, id AS root FROM categories UNION ALL SELECT c.id, t.root FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id)
SELECT cat.name, COUNT(p.id) AS products FROM tree t JOIN categories cat ON cat.id = t.root LEFT JOIN products p ON p.category_id = t.id GROUP BY cat.id, cat.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name       | products
-- Office     | 412
-- Stationery | 120

topics.name: CTE vs Subquery vs Temporary Table

beginner.content:
Introduction

All three hold an intermediate result. A subquery (derived table) is inline in one place; a CTE is a named block for the whole statement; a temporary table is a real, session-scoped table you can index, reuse across statements and inspect.

Why Do We Need This?

The choice affects readability, reuse and performance. Same logic, different life-time and optimiser freedom: subqueries and CTEs are merged or materialised by the optimiser; a temporary table is always materialised but can be indexed and used by many statements.
codeExamples:
-- Reuse across statements is only possible with a temporary table
SELECT region, s FROM x ORDER BY s DESC;                     -- statement 1
SELECT SUM(s) AS grand_total FROM x;                         -- statement 2, no recompute
-- A CTE would need to be rewritten (and recomputed) in each statement.

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+----+
-- | region | s  |
-- +--------+----+
-- | S      | 120|
-- | N      |  40|
-- +--------+----+
-- +-------------+
-- | grand_total |
-- +-------------+
-- |         160 |
-- +-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rule of thumb in real projects: subquery for a one-off filter; CTE when readability or recursion matters; temporary table when the intermediate set is big, reused, or needs an index to be joined efficiently.
codeExamples:
-- Big intermediate result joined many times: index the temporary table
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE hot_ids (id INT PRIMARY KEY)          -- PK gives fast joins
  AS SELECT id FROM sales WHERE amt >= 30;
SELECT s.id, s.amt
FROM   sales s JOIN hot_ids h ON h.id = s.id                 -- uses the PK
ORDER  BY s.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-----+
-- | id | amt |
-- +----+-----+
-- |  2 |  30 |
-- |  4 |  40 |
-- |  5 |  60 |
-- +----+-----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

                 lifetime            indexable   reusable   optimiser
   Subquery      one place           no          no         merge/materialise
   CTE           one statement       no          in-stmt    merge/materialise
   TEMP TABLE    session/connection  YES         YES        always real table

   small + once        -> subquery
   readable / recursive-> CTE
   big / reused / join -> temporary table (with index)

Fresher Notes

  • A subquery is nested inside a statement, a CTE is a named block before the statement, and a temporary table is a real table that exists for your session.
  • CTE and subquery last for one statement; a temporary table lasts for the session.
  • Pick by readability and reuse.

Worked Example 1

Temp table disappears after the session.
codeExamples:
-- reconnect
SELECT * FROM tmp_totals;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'shop.tmp_totals' doesn't exist

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Materialization shown in plan.

Practice Exercise 1

Same result three ways.

Practice Exercise 2

Temp table with an index for repeated joins.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A subquery or CTE lives for one statement and is re-evaluated or materialized by the optimizer as needed. A temporary table is a real table in your session: it is created, filled once, can be indexed and updated, and reused by many statements, until you drop it or disconnect.
codeExamples:
WITH a AS (SELECT AVG(salary) AS v FROM emp) SELECT name FROM emp, a WHERE salary > a.v;     -- statement lifetime
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE a_tmp AS SELECT AVG(salary) AS v FROM emp;                                -- session lifetime
SELECT name FROM emp, a_tmp WHERE salary > a_tmp.v;
SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);                               -- inline subquery

-- OUTPUT: (all three)
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose by reuse and size: single use and readability → CTE or subquery; several statements or a large intermediate that needs an index → temporary table; durable staging across sessions or failures → a permanent staging table.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages summary: subquery - zero ceremony and often merged into the outer query; CTE - clarity, multi-use within the statement, recursion; temp table - indexes, statistics, multi-statement reuse, debuggable with plain SELECT.
codeExamples:
-- A temp table's contents can be inspected mid-script; a CTE cannot
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_in_x FROM x;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+
-- | rows_in_x |
-- +-----------+
-- |         2 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages summary: subquery - repeated text if used twice; CTE - not reusable beyond one statement, no index, may be materialised per reference; temp table - extra write cost, cleanup, per-connection state that interacts badly with connection pooling and replication.
codeExamples:
-- Temp table pitfall: it belongs to ONE connection
-- Connection 1:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE t1 (a INT);
-- Connection 2:
SELECT * FROM t1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'mydb.t1' doesn't exist

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a temporary table cannot be referenced twice in the same query (error 1137 - classic restriction, relaxed for CTEs and derived tables); CTEs cannot be indexed; and writes to a temp table inside a replicated statement-based transaction need care.
codeExamples:
-- Same TEMPORARY table twice in one statement is rejected
SELECT a.region, b.region FROM x a JOIN x b ON a.region <> b.region;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1137 (HY000): Can't reopen table: 'a'
-- (a CTE or a permanent table can be joined to itself without this error)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to CTEs for clarity, and promote to a temporary table only when EXPLAIN or the slow log shows repeated expensive recomputation or a missing index on the intermediate set. Under connection pooling prefer explicit DROP TEMPORARY TABLE at the end of a unit of work, and avoid temp tables entirely behind proxies that multiplex sessions.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Temporary tables can be indexed and reused in many statements, and hold data you can update.
  • CTEs and subqueries are re-evaluated per statement; CTEs referenced several times may be materialized once.
  • Temporary tables cost writes (they are tables) but can speed up multi-step ETL.

Senior Notes

  • For heavy multi-step transformations, a temporary table with indexes can outperform repeated CTE expansion.
  • Temp tables increase session state and can cause replication issues in statement-based binlog with certain patterns.
  • Measure: sometimes the optimizer handles a CTE/subquery just as well with no materialization.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: a CTE used many times with different filters (materialized once without them), temp tables left behind in pooled connections, and temp table names that shadow real tables. Drop temp tables explicitly.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Temporary tables cost writes (they are tables, in the TempTable engine or on disk) but give indexes and statistics; CTEs cost nothing to store but may be recomputed. Measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the temp-table counters.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a multi-step reporting job. Step 1 builds a filtered, indexed temp table of the 5M relevant rows; steps 2 to 6 reuse it, instead of recomputing the expensive join six times.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Window functions compute a value for each row using a set of related rows (the "window") without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does. The three ranking functions number rows by an ORDER BY inside OVER (...): ROW_NUMBER is always unique, RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK does not.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE scores (student VARCHAR(10), score INT);
INSERT INTO scores VALUES ('Abaji',90),('Raoji',85),('Moropant',85),('Jiva',70);

SELECT student, score,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rn,     -- 1,2,3,4 (ties broken arbitrarily)
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rnk,    -- ties share rank, next rank skips
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS drnk    -- ties share rank, no gap
FROM   scores
ORDER  BY score DESC, student;

-- OUTPUT (rn for the tied rows may swap - example):
-- +----------+-------+----+-----+------+
-- | student  | score | rn | rnk | drnk |
-- +----------+-------+----+-----+------+
-- | Abaji    |    90 |  1 |   1 |    1 |
-- | Moropant |    85 |  2 |   2 |    2 |
-- | Raoji    |    85 |  3 |   2 |    2 |
-- | Jiva     |    70 |  4 |   4 |    3 |
-- +---------+-------+----+-----+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Leaderboards, "second highest salary", de-duplication and pagination all need ranking. Before MySQL 8.0 this required self-joins or user variables; window functions make it declarative and correct.
codeExamples:
-- Second-highest score, tie-safe, using DENSE_RANK
SELECT student, score
FROM  (SELECT student, score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS d FROM scores) x
WHERE d = 2;                        -- window functions cannot be in WHERE, so wrap them

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------+
-- | student  | score |
-- +----------+-------+
-- | Raoji    |    85 |
-- | Moropant |    85 |
-- +---------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: de-duplicate rows by keeping ROW_NUMBER() = 1 per business key, and rank products within each category by sales.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE contacts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(30), created DATE);
INSERT INTO contacts VALUES (1,'a@x.com','2025-01-01'),(2,'a@x.com','2025-02-01'),(3,'b@x.com','2025-01-15');

-- Keep only the newest row per email
SELECT id, email, created
FROM  (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY created DESC) AS rn
       FROM contacts) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+------------+
-- | id | email   | created    |
-- +----+---------+------------+
-- |  2 | a@x.com | 2025-02-01 |
-- |  3 | b@x.com | 2025-01-15 |
-- +----+---------+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   score:   90   85   85   70
   ---------------------------------
   ROW_NUMBER  1    2    3    4      always unique
   RANK        1    2    2    4      gap after ties
   DENSE_RANK  1    2    2    3      no gap

Fresher Notes

  • Ranking window functions number rows within a partition: ROW_NUMBER gives unique numbers, RANK leaves gaps after ties, DENSE_RANK has no gaps.
  • Syntax: RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC).
  • Used for top-N, de-duplication and leaderboards.

Worked Example 1

Delete duplicates keeping the newest.

Worked Example 2

Leaderboard with ties.
codeExamples:
SELECT player, score, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS position FROM scores;

-- OUTPUT:
-- player   | score | position
-- Raoji    |    95 | 1
-- Abaji    |    95 | 1
-- Moropant |    80 | 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Compare ranking functions.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary,
 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn,
 RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
 DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS drnk
FROM (SELECT 'A' AS name, 100 AS salary UNION ALL SELECT 'B',100 UNION ALL SELECT 'C',90) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | salary | rn | rnk | drnk
-- A    |    100 |  1 |   1 |    1
-- B    |    100 |  2 |   1 |    1
-- C    |     90 |  3 |   3 |    2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Top earner per department.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, salary FROM (SELECT dept, name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn FROM emp) t WHERE rn = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary
--   10 | Abaji    | 60000
--   20 | Moropant | 70000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Ranking functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING over a window defined by PARTITION BY and ORDER BY. MySQL sorts each partition (or reads an index in that order) and assigns numbers. ROW_NUMBER gives unique consecutive numbers; RANK gives ties the same number and skips; DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn, RANK() OVER w AS rnk, DENSE_RANK() OVER w AS drnk
FROM (SELECT 'A' AS name, 100 AS salary UNION ALL SELECT 'B', 100 UNION ALL SELECT 'C', 90) t WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary DESC);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | salary | rn | rnk | drnk
-- A    |    100 |  1 |   1 |    1
-- B    |    100 |  2 |   1 |    1
-- C    |     90 |  3 |   3 |    2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use PARTITION BY to restart numbering per group, add tie-breakers to ORDER BY for deterministic ROW_NUMBER, filter by wrapping in a subquery or CTE, and name the window with the WINDOW clause when reused.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, salary FROM (SELECT dept, name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn FROM emp) t WHERE rn <= 2;
SELECT name FROM (SELECT name, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr FROM emp) t WHERE dr = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary
--   10 | Abaji    | 60000
--   10 | Raoji    | 45000
--   20 | Moropant | 70000

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: rows are preserved, several rankings in one pass, PARTITION BY ranks per group, and the optimiser sorts once when the OVER clauses match.
codeExamples:
-- Per-group ranking in a single query
CREATE TABLE emp (name VARCHAR(10), dept VARCHAR(5), sal INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES ('A','IT',90),('B','IT',80),('C','HR',70),('D','HR',70);
SELECT name, dept, sal,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal DESC) AS dept_rank
FROM emp ORDER BY dept, name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+-----+-----------+
-- | name | dept | sal | dept_rank |
-- +------+------+-----+-----------+
-- | C    | HR   |  70 |         1 |
-- | D    | HR   |  70 |         1 |
-- | A    | IT   |  90 |         1 |
-- | B    | IT   |  80 |         2 |
-- +------+------+-----+-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: ROW_NUMBER on ties is nondeterministic unless you add a unique tie-breaker; the sort can be expensive on large sets; the result cannot be filtered in the same SELECT.
codeExamples:
-- Make it deterministic with a tie-breaker column
SELECT student, score,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC, student ASC) AS rn   -- student breaks ties
FROM scores ORDER BY rn;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------+----+
-- | student  | score | rn |
-- +----------+-------+----+
-- | Abaji    |    90 |  1 |
-- | Moropant |    85 |  2 |
-- | Raoji    |    85 |  3 |
-- | Jiva     |    70 |  4 |
-- +---------+-------+----+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: window functions are allowed only in SELECT and ORDER BY (not WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING); they are evaluated after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING; and they require MySQL 8.0+.

Architect's Notes

Choose by intent: ROW_NUMBER for "exactly one per group" (dedupe, pagination), RANK for competition-style ranking, DENSE_RANK for "Nth distinct value". Support the OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) with a composite index (a, b) so the engine can avoid a filesort, and always add a unique tie-breaker so results are reproducible across runs and replicas.

Mid-Level Notes

  • With ties on salary 100,100,90: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3; RANK 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK 1,1,2.
  • ORDER BY inside OVER decides the ranking; add a tie-breaker for deterministic ROW_NUMBER.
  • Window functions run after WHERE/GROUP BY; filter on them with an outer query or CTE.

Senior Notes

  • De-duplicate keeping the newest: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY key ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1.
  • Index (partition columns, order columns) so the sort is avoided.
  • For top-N per group on huge tables, test against a LATERAL-style or index-assisted alternative.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using RANK when you need exactly N rows, no tiebreaker (unstable results), and filtering on the window function in WHERE (not allowed). Pick ROW_NUMBER for exactly N, DENSE_RANK for "Nth distinct value".

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Windows require sorting each partition. An index on (partition columns, order columns) avoids the sort. Check for "Using filesort" and the temporary table in the plan.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world deduplication: keep the newest row per business key and delete the rest.

beginner.content:
Introduction

NTILE(n) splits the ordered rows of a window into n roughly equal buckets and returns the bucket number (1..n). When rows do not divide evenly, the first buckets get one extra row.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE scores (student VARCHAR(10), score INT);
INSERT INTO scores VALUES ('A',95),('B',90),('C',85),('D',80),('E',75),('F',70),('G',65);

SELECT student, score,
       NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS bucket    -- 7 rows / 3 -> sizes 3,2,2
FROM scores ORDER BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+-------+--------+
-- | student | score | bucket |
-- +---------+-------+--------+
-- | A       |    95 |      1 |
-- | B       |    90 |      1 |
-- | C       |    85 |      1 |
-- | D       |    80 |      2 |
-- | E       |    75 |      2 |
-- | F       |    70 |      3 |
-- | G       |    65 |      3 |
-- +---------+-------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Percentile-style groupings (quartiles, deciles, "top 20% customers") and balanced work distribution (split 1 million ids into 8 equal batches for parallel jobs) need equal-sized groups, not equal-width value ranges.
codeExamples:
-- Label each student by quartile
SELECT student,
       CASE NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY score DESC)
            WHEN 1 THEN 'Top 25%' WHEN 2 THEN 'Upper mid'
            WHEN 3 THEN 'Lower mid' ELSE 'Bottom 25%' END AS band
FROM scores ORDER BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+------------+
-- | student | band       |
-- +---------+------------+
-- | A       | Top 25%    |
-- | B       | Top 25%    |
-- | C       | Upper mid  |
-- | D       | Upper mid  |
-- | E       | Lower mid  |
-- | F       | Lower mid  |
-- | G       | Bottom 25% |
-- +---------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: batch splitting. Assign each row to one of N workers, then each worker processes only its bucket.
codeExamples:
-- Split work for 2 parallel workers; each worker runs WHERE bucket = :worker
SELECT student, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY student) AS worker FROM scores ORDER BY student;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+--------+
-- | student | worker |
-- +---------+--------+
-- | A       |      1 |
-- | B       |      1 |
-- | C       |      1 |
-- | D       |      1 |
-- | E       |      2 |
-- | F       |      2 |
-- | G       |      2 |
-- +---------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   7 rows ordered by score DESC, NTILE(3):

   [ A  B  C ] [ D  E ] [ F  G ]
     bucket 1   bucket 2  bucket 3
     (3 rows)   (2 rows)  (2 rows)    extras go to the first buckets

Fresher Notes

  • NTILE(n) splits the ordered rows of a partition into n roughly equal buckets and gives each row its bucket number.
  • Example: NTILE(4) makes quartiles; NTILE(100) makes percentile-like groups.
  • Bucket sizes differ by at most one row.

Worked Example 1

Split a table into 3 worker slices.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS worker FROM jobs;

-- OUTPUT: (example 7 rows)
-- id | worker
--  1 | 1
--  2 | 1
--  3 | 1
--  4 | 2
--  5 | 2
--  6 | 3
--  7 | 3

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Relative position.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary), 2) AS pr, ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY salary), 2) AS cd FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | pr   | cd
-- Raoji    | 0.00 | 0.33
-- Abaji    | 0.50 | 0.67
-- Moropant | 1.00 | 1.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Quartiles of salary.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS half FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary | half
-- Moropant |  70000 | 1
-- Abaji    |  60000 | 1
-- Raoji    |  45000 | 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Top 25% of customers by spend.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer_id, spent FROM (SELECT customer_id, spent, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY spent DESC) AS q FROM customer_spend) t WHERE q = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | spent
-- 7           | 9800.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

NTILE(n) divides the ordered rows of each partition into n buckets of nearly equal size, numbering them 1..n. If the rows do not divide evenly, the first buckets get one extra row. It counts rows, not values, so equal values can land in different buckets.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS bucket FROM (SELECT 'A' AS name, 90 AS salary UNION ALL SELECT 'B', 80 UNION ALL SELECT 'C', 70 UNION ALL SELECT 'D', 60 UNION ALL SELECT 'E', 50 UNION ALL SELECT 'F', 40 UNION ALL SELECT 'G', 30) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | salary | bucket
-- A    |     90 |      1
-- B    |     80 |      1
-- C    |     70 |      1
-- D    |     60 |      2
-- E    |     50 |      2
-- F    |     40 |      3
-- G    |     30 |      3

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common sizes: NTILE(4) quartiles, NTILE(10) deciles, NTILE(100) percentiles. Combine with PARTITION BY to bucket within groups. For value-based relative position use PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST.
codeExamples:
SELECT customer_id, spent, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY spent DESC) AS quartile, ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY spent), 2) AS pr, ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY spent), 2) AS cd FROM customer_spend;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | spent   | quartile | pr   | cd
-- 7           | 9800.00 |        1 | 1.00 | 1.00

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one function gives equal-population groups; combined with PARTITION BY you get per-group quartiles; trivial to read.
codeExamples:
-- Per-group tiles: split each department's staff into 2 halves
CREATE TABLE emp (name VARCHAR(5), dept VARCHAR(5), sal INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES ('a','IT',9),('b','IT',8),('c','IT',7),('d','IT',6),('e','HR',5),('f','HR',4);
SELECT name, dept, NTILE(2) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal DESC) AS half
FROM emp ORDER BY dept, sal DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+------+
-- | name | dept | half |
-- +------+------+------+
-- | e    | HR   |    1 |
-- | f    | HR   |    2 |
-- | a    | IT   |    1 |
-- | b    | IT   |    1 |
-- | c    | IT   |    2 |
-- | d    | IT   |    2 |
-- +------+------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: tied values can land in different buckets (NTILE splits by position, not value), so two people with the same score may get different quartiles.
codeExamples:
-- Equal scores, different buckets
CREATE TABLE s2 (n VARCHAR(2), score INT);
INSERT INTO s2 VALUES ('a',80),('b',80),('c',80),('d',60);
SELECT n, score, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY score DESC, n) AS b FROM s2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+-------+---+
-- | n | score | b |
-- +---+-------+---+
-- | a |    80 | 1 |
-- | b |    80 | 1 |
-- | c |    80 | 2 |   <- same score as a and b, different bucket
-- | d |    60 | 2 |
-- +---+-------+---+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the argument must be a positive integer constant or a user variable/parameter (not a column); bucket sizes differ by at most one; with fewer rows than buckets, the higher buckets stay empty.
codeExamples:
SELECT n, NTILE(10) OVER (ORDER BY n) AS b FROM s2;      -- 4 rows, 10 buckets

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+---+
-- | n | b |
-- +---+---+
-- | a | 1 |
-- | b | 2 |
-- | c | 3 |
-- | d | 4 |
-- +---+---+     (buckets 5..10 are never used)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

NTILE is positional, so use it for load-balancing and approximate percentiles, not for statistically exact bands where ties matter - use PERCENT_RANK or CUME_DIST (also window functions) or explicit value thresholds in that case. For parallel batch splits on huge tables prefer range-splitting on the primary key; NTILE must sort the whole set first.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use it for quartiles, deciles and splitting data into equal-sized work batches.
  • Rows with equal values may fall into different buckets, because NTILE counts rows, not values.
  • For value-based percentiles use PERCENT_RANK or CUME_DIST.

Senior Notes

  • NTILE is handy for parallel batch processing: assign rows to N workers.
  • On skewed data buckets are equal in rows but not in value ranges.
  • Sort cost matters on large data; index the ORDER BY.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting equal-valued rows in one bucket, relying on bucket sizes being equal when counts do not divide, and ordering without a tiebreaker (bucket membership then changes between runs). Add id to the ORDER BY.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, spent, NTILE(2) OVER (ORDER BY spent) AS half FROM (SELECT 1 AS id, 10 AS spent UNION ALL SELECT 2, 10 UNION ALL SELECT 3, 10 UNION ALL SELECT 4, 10) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | spent | half
--  1 |    10 |    1
--  2 |    10 |    1
--  3 |    10 |    2
--  4 |    10 |    2        (equal values split across buckets: add a tiebreaker for stability)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

NTILE needs a sort of the whole partition. For huge tables compute bucket boundaries from a sample or an index, or run it on a replica or an aggregated table.
codeExamples:
SELECT NTILE(100) OVER (ORDER BY response_ms) AS percentile, MAX(response_ms) AS p_value FROM (SELECT response_ms FROM request_log WHERE day = CURDATE()) t GROUP BY percentile LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- percentile | p_value
-- 1          | 3
-- 2          | 5

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: split a large job into equal-sized worker slices by id, so eight workers each process a contiguous, balanced range.
codeExamples:
SELECT worker, MIN(id) AS from_id, MAX(id) AS to_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM (SELECT id, NTILE(8) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS worker FROM jobs WHERE status = 'NEW') t GROUP BY worker ORDER BY worker;

-- OUTPUT:
-- worker | from_id | to_id | n
-- 1      |       1 | 15000 | 15000
-- 2      |   15001 | 30000 | 15000

beginner.content:
Introduction

LAG(col, n, default) reads the value from n rows before the current row and LEAD from n rows after, within the ordered partition. They replace self-joins for "compare with previous/next row".
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE daily (d DATE, sales INT);
INSERT INTO daily VALUES ('2025-01-01',100),('2025-01-02',130),('2025-01-03',90),('2025-01-04',150);

SELECT d, sales,
       LAG(sales)     OVER (ORDER BY d) AS prev_day,     -- previous row, NULL for the first
       LEAD(sales)    OVER (ORDER BY d) AS next_day,     -- next row, NULL for the last
       sales - LAG(sales, 1, sales) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS change  -- default = own value -> 0
FROM daily ORDER BY d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-------+----------+----------+--------+
-- | d          | sales | prev_day | next_day | change |
-- +------------+-------+----------+----------+--------+
-- | 2025-01-01 |   100 |     NULL |      130 |      0 |
-- | 2025-01-02 |   130 |      100 |       90 |     30 |
-- | 2025-01-03 |    90 |      130 |      150 |    -40 |
-- | 2025-01-04 |   150 |       90 |     NULL |     60 |
-- +------------+-------+----------+----------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Time-series analysis is about change: day-over-day growth, gaps between events, session detection. Doing that with self-joins on "previous id" is fragile when ids have gaps.
codeExamples:
-- Gap detection: find missing days
SELECT d AS from_day, next_d AS to_day
FROM  (SELECT d, LEAD(d) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS next_d FROM daily) x
WHERE DATEDIFF(next_d, d) > 1;                -- more than a day to the next row

-- OUTPUT (after deleting 2025-01-03 for the demo):
-- +------------+------------+
-- | from_day   | to_day     |
-- +------------+------------+
-- | 2025-01-02 | 2025-01-04 |
-- +------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: month-over-month revenue growth percent, time between a user's consecutive logins, price change history, and detecting status changes in an event log.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE monthly (m CHAR(7), revenue INT);
INSERT INTO monthly VALUES ('2025-01',200),('2025-02',250),('2025-03',225);

SELECT m, revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY m)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY m), 1) AS growth_pct
FROM monthly;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------+------------+
-- | m       | revenue | growth_pct |
-- +---------+---------+------------+
-- | 2025-01 |     200 |       NULL |
-- | 2025-02 |     250 |       25.0 |
-- | 2025-03 |     225 |      -10.0 |
-- +---------+---------+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ordered rows:   r1    r2    r3    r4
                    ^     ^     ^     ^
   LAG(x)  at r3  -----> value of r2       (look back 1)
   LEAD(x) at r3  -----> value of r4       (look ahead 1)
   LAG(x,2) at r3 -----> value of r1
   first row LAG -> NULL (or the default argument)

Fresher Notes

  • LAG(col) reads a value from a previous row; LEAD(col) reads from the next row, within the ordered window.
  • Use them for changes over time: this month versus last month.
  • Optional arguments: offset and default value, LAG(col, 1, 0).

Worked Example 1

Time spent in each status.
codeExamples:
SELECT order_id, status, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, status_time, LEAD(status_time) OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY status_time)) AS minutes FROM order_status;

-- OUTPUT:
-- order_id | status  | minutes
--        1 | PLACED  |     120
--        1 | SHIPPED | NULL

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Detect gaps in ids.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, next_id FROM (SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM t) x WHERE next_id - id > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | next_id
--  3 |       7

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Month-over-month.
codeExamples:
SELECT month, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change_amt,
 ROUND((revenue / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) - 1) * 100, 1) AS pct
FROM monthly_rev;

-- OUTPUT:
-- month   | revenue | change_amt | pct
-- 2026-01 |    1000 | NULL       | NULL
-- 2026-02 |    1200 | 200        | 20.0
-- 2026-03 |    1100 | -100       | -8.3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Next value with LEAD and default.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, status_time, LEAD(status_time, 1, NOW()) OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY status_time) AS next_time FROM order_status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | status_time         | next_time
--  1 | 2026-05-01 10:00:00 | 2026-05-01 12:00:00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

LAG(expr, n, default) reads the value n rows before the current row in the window order, LEAD reads n rows after. They are evaluated in a single sorted pass over the partition. The first or last row has no neighbour, so they return NULL unless you give a default.
codeExamples:
SELECT month, revenue, LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev, LEAD(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS next FROM monthly_rev;

-- OUTPUT:
-- month   | revenue | prev | next
-- 2026-01 |    1000 | NULL | 1200
-- 2026-02 |    1200 | 1000 | 1100
-- 2026-03 |    1100 | 1200 | NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical calculations: change from the previous row, percent growth, time between events, gap detection and "next event" lookups. Combine with PARTITION BY to stay inside a group, and offsets greater than 1 for longer look-backs.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: single pass over sorted data, offset and default arguments, works per partition (e.g. per customer), far simpler than correlated subqueries.
codeExamples:
-- Per-customer previous order amount
CREATE TABLE ord (cust VARCHAR(2), seq INT, amt INT);
INSERT INTO ord VALUES ('A',1,10),('A',2,15),('B',1,7),('B',2,3);
SELECT cust, seq, amt, LAG(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY cust ORDER BY seq) AS prev_amt
FROM ord ORDER BY cust, seq;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-----+-----+----------+
-- | cust | seq | amt | prev_amt |
-- +------+-----+-----+----------+
-- | A    |   1 |  10 |     NULL |
-- | A    |   2 |  15 |       10 |
-- | B    |   1 |   7 |     NULL |
-- | B    |   2 |   3 |        7 |
-- +------+-----+-----+----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the first/last row yields NULL unless you give a default, NULL arithmetic then propagates, and a missing ORDER BY makes results meaningless.
codeExamples:
-- NULL propagates unless handled
SELECT d, sales - LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS change_raw,
          sales - COALESCE(LAG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY d), 0) AS change_safe
FROM daily ORDER BY d LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+------------+-------------+
-- | d          | change_raw | change_safe |
-- +------------+------------+-------------+
-- | 2025-01-01 |       NULL |         100 |
-- | 2025-01-02 |         30 |          30 |
-- +------------+------------+-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the offset must be a non-negative integer constant (not a column); LAG/LEAD ignore the frame clause (they use the partition order only); only one window ordering per OVER, so comparing "same weekday last year" needs a join or a calendar table.
codeExamples:
-- Offset is a literal; look back 7 rows for "same weekday last week" on daily data
SELECT d, sales, LAG(sales, 7) OVER (ORDER BY d) AS same_day_last_week FROM daily;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-------+--------------------+
-- | d          | sales | same_day_last_week |
-- +------------+-------+--------------------+
-- | 2025-01-01 |   100 |               NULL |
-- | 2025-01-02 |   130 |               NULL |
-- | 2025-01-03 |    90 |               NULL |
-- | 2025-01-04 |   150 |               NULL |
-- +------------+-------+--------------------+   (only 4 rows, so no row 7 back)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

LAG/LEAD are the standard way to do row-to-row deltas. Guarantee a unique, gapless ordering key (or a calendar table joined first) so "previous" really means previous period. Index (partition_key, order_key) to avoid sorting, and test NULL handling explicitly because growth formulas divide by the lagged value.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Without PARTITION BY the whole result is one window.
  • The first row has no previous row, so LAG returns NULL unless you give a default.
  • Compute differences: amount - LAG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY month).

Senior Notes

  • LAG/LEAD replace self joins on adjacent rows and are much faster.
  • Gaps in dates need a calendar table before LAG, otherwise "previous row" is not "previous month".
  • Index the partition/order columns.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: missing periods (LAG returns the previous existing row, not the previous month), no PARTITION BY across groups, and ties in ORDER BY. Join a calendar first so every period exists.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.month, COALESCE(r.revenue, 0) AS revenue, COALESCE(r.revenue, 0) - LAG(COALESCE(r.revenue, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY c.month) AS change_amt
FROM months c LEFT JOIN monthly_rev r ON r.month = c.month;

-- OUTPUT:
-- month   | revenue | change_amt
-- 2026-03 |       0 | -1200        (the empty month is visible)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

LAG/LEAD replace self joins on adjacent rows and scan once instead of per row. Index (partition, order) columns to avoid the sort.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: session detection. Mark a new session whenever the gap to the previous event exceeds 30 minutes, then number the sessions with a running sum.
codeExamples:
SELECT user_id, event_time, SUM(new_session) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) AS session_no FROM (
  SELECT user_id, event_time, IF(TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time), event_time) > 30 OR LAG(event_time) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_time) IS NULL, 1, 0) AS new_session FROM events) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id | event_time          | session_no
-- 7       | 2026-05-01 09:00:00 | 1
-- 7       | 2026-05-01 09:10:00 | 1
-- 7       | 2026-05-01 11:00:00 | 2

beginner.content:
Introduction

FIRST_VALUE(expr) returns the value from the first row of the window frame and LAST_VALUE(expr) from the last row of the frame. Careful: with an ORDER BY, the default frame ends at the current row, so LAST_VALUE returns the current row's value unless you widen the frame.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (name VARCHAR(8), dept VARCHAR(4), sal INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES ('Abaji','IT',90),('Raoji','IT',80),('Moropant','IT',70),('Zoya','HR',60),('Omar','HR',50);

SELECT name, dept, sal,
       FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal DESC) AS top_earner
FROM emp ORDER BY dept, sal DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+-----+------------+
-- | name     | dept | sal | top_earner |
-- +----------+------+-----+------------+
-- | Zoya     | HR   |  60 | Zoya       |
-- | Omar     | HR   |  50 | Zoya       |
-- | Abaji    | IT   |  90 | Abaji      |
-- | Raoji    | IT   |  80 | Abaji      |
-- | Moropant | IT   |  70 | Abaji      |
-- +-------+------+-----+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You often need to compare each row to the group's best, worst, opening or closing value - "how far is each salary below the department maximum?", "price change since the first quote" - without a separate join.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, sal,
       FIRST_VALUE(sal) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal DESC) - sal AS gap_to_top
FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' ORDER BY sal DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-----+------------+
-- | name     | sal | gap_to_top |
-- +----------+-----+------------+
-- | Abaji    |  90 |          0 |
-- | Raoji    |  80 |         10 |
-- | Moropant | 70  |         20 |
-- +-------+-----+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: OHLC style reports (open = first price of the day, close = last price), "latest status per ticket", and baselines for percent-change charts.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE ticks (sym VARCHAR(3), ts TIME, price DECIMAL(6,2));
INSERT INTO ticks VALUES ('XYZ','09:30',10.0),('XYZ','12:00',12.5),('XYZ','15:30',11.0);

SELECT DISTINCT sym,
  FIRST_VALUE(price) OVER w AS open_px,
  LAST_VALUE(price)  OVER w AS close_px            -- needs the full frame (see window w)
FROM ticks
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY sym ORDER BY ts
             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING);  -- whole partition

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+--------+----------+
-- | sym | open_px| close_px |
-- +-----+--------+----------+
-- | XYZ |  10.00 |    11.00 |
-- +-----+--------+----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   partition (dept IT) ordered by sal DESC

   row        sal   default frame (to current row)   full frame
   Abaji        90   [Abaji]                           [Abaji Raoji Moropant]
   Raoji        80   [Abaji Raoji]                      [Abaji Raoji Moropant]
   Moropant       70   [Abaji Raoji Moropant]                [Abaji Raoji Moropant]
   FIRST_VALUE = first of frame      LAST_VALUE = last of frame

Fresher Notes

  • FIRST_VALUE(col) returns the first value in the window; LAST_VALUE(col) the last.
  • Use them to compare each row with the group’s first or last value, for example the highest salary in the department.
  • They need an ORDER BY in OVER to be meaningful.

Worked Example 1

Default frame trap.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS last_name FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | last_name
-- Raoji    | Raoji
-- Abaji    | Abaji
-- Moropant | Moropant      (not the max: frame ends at current row)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

NTH_VALUE.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS second_highest FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- second_highest
-- Abaji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Gap to the department top.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, salary, FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) - salary AS gap_to_top FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary | gap_to_top
--   10 | Abaji    |  60000 | 0
--   10 | Raoji    |  45000 | 15000
--   20 | Moropant |  70000 | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

LAST_VALUE with the right frame.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (ORDER BY salary ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS highest_paid FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary | highest_paid
-- Raoji    |  45000 | Moropant
-- Abaji    |  60000 | Moropant
-- Moropant |  70000 | Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

FIRST_VALUE(expr) returns the expression's value from the first row of the window frame, LAST_VALUE from the last row, NTH_VALUE from the nth. They depend on the frame. The default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, which is why LAST_VALUE appears to return the current row.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER w AS first_name, LAST_VALUE(name) OVER w AS last_default, LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (ORDER BY salary ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_full
FROM emp WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary | first_name | last_default | last_full
-- Raoji    |  45000 | Raoji      | Raoji        | Moropant
-- Abaji    |  60000 | Raoji      | Abaji        | Moropant
-- Moropant |  70000 | Raoji      | Moropant     | Moropant

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use FIRST_VALUE to compare each row with the group's best (or oldest), NTH_VALUE for the second best, and spell the frame out for LAST_VALUE. Partition to work per group.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, salary, FIRST_VALUE(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) - salary AS gap_to_top, NTH_VALUE(name, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS runner_up FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name  | salary | gap_to_top | runner_up
--   10 | Abaji |  60000 |          0 | Raoji
--   10 | Raoji |  45000 |      15000 | Raoji

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: avoids self-joins and correlated MAX subqueries, can pick any column's value (not just the min/max itself), and works per partition. The named WINDOW clause reuses one definition.
codeExamples:
-- Name of the lowest earner per department (value from another column than the order key)
SELECT DISTINCT dept,
  FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal ASC) AS lowest_paid
FROM emp ORDER BY dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------------+
-- | dept | lowest_paid |
-- +------+-------------+
-- | HR   | Omar        |
-- | IT   | Moropant    |
-- +------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the LAST_VALUE default-frame trap silently returns wrong data; people forget it and see the current row repeated.
codeExamples:
-- The trap: default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
SELECT name, sal,
       LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal DESC) AS last_name
FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' ORDER BY sal DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-----+-----------+
-- | name     | sal | last_name |
-- +----------+-----+-----------+
-- | Abaji    |  90 | Abaji     |   <- not Moropant: frame stops at the current row
-- | Raoji    |  80 | Raoji     |
-- | Moropant |  70 | Moropant  |
-- +----------+-----+-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: with RANGE frames, peer rows (equal ORDER BY values) are all inside the frame, so LAST_VALUE may pick any of the tied rows; NULL values are respected unless you use IGNORE NULLS, which MySQL does not support (it supports RESPECT NULLS only).
codeExamples:
-- Fix the trap with an explicit full frame (or use FIRST_VALUE with reversed ORDER BY)
SELECT name, sal,
  LAST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY sal DESC
       ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS lowest
FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT' ORDER BY sal DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-----+----------+
-- | name     | sal | lowest   |
-- +----------+-----+----------+
-- | Abaji    |  90 | Moropant |
-- | Raoji    |  80 | Moropant |
-- | Moropant |  70 | Moropant |
-- +-------+-----+--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer FIRST_VALUE with the order reversed over LAST_VALUE so you never depend on frame subtleties, or declare a named WINDOW with an explicit ROWS frame and reuse it. For "latest row per group" at scale, ROW_NUMBER = 1 with a supporting index is often cheaper than DISTINCT over a windowed value for every row.

Mid-Level Notes

  • LAST_VALUE surprises people: the default frame ends at the current row, so it returns the current row unless you set the frame to ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING.
  • NTH_VALUE(col, n) gets the n-th row of the frame.
  • Use IGNORE NULLS is not supported in MySQL; handle NULLs yourself.

Senior Notes

  • For "latest value per key" prefer ROW_NUMBER filtering (clearer, can use indexes) over LAST_VALUE.
  • Frames control cost: unbounded frames can scan the partition for each row.
  • Test with large partitions; they are computed in memory/temp tables.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on LAST_VALUE with the default frame, expecting IGNORE NULLS (not supported), and using it where ROW_NUMBER filtering is clearer for "latest row per key". Choose the simplest tool.
codeExamples:
-- latest status per order: ROW_NUMBER is clearer and index friendly
SELECT order_id, status FROM (SELECT order_id, status, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY status_time DESC) AS rn FROM order_status) t WHERE rn = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- order_id | status
--        1 | SHIPPED

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Frames with unbounded following force MySQL to buffer the whole partition. For big partitions prefer MAX/MIN with GROUP BY, or ROW_NUMBER filtering, which can stop early.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: show each product's price versus the cheapest in its category and its category's highest-rated product, in one pass over the data.
codeExamples:
SELECT category_id, name, price, price - FIRST_VALUE(price) OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY price) AS above_cheapest, FIRST_VALUE(name) OVER (PARTITION BY category_id ORDER BY rating DESC, id) AS best_rated FROM products;

-- OUTPUT:
-- category_id | name | price | above_cheapest | best_rated
-- 5           | Pen  | 10.00 |           0.00 | Gel Pen

beginner.content:
Introduction

OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame) has three parts. PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups (like GROUP BY without collapsing). ORDER BY orders rows inside each partition. The frame (ROWS or RANGE BETWEEN ... AND ...) picks which rows around the current row feed the function.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sales (region VARCHAR(5), mon INT, amt INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('N',1,10),('N',2,20),('N',3,30),('S',1,5),('S',2,15);

SELECT region, mon, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY region)                    AS region_total,  -- whole partition
       SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY mon)       AS running        -- start .. current row
FROM sales ORDER BY region, mon;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-----+-----+--------------+---------+
-- | region | mon | amt | region_total | running |
-- +--------+-----+-----+--------------+---------+
-- | N      |   1 |  10 |           60 |      10 |
-- | N      |   2 |  20 |           60 |      30 |
-- | N      |   3 |  30 |           60 |      60 |
-- | S      |   1 |   5 |           20 |       5 |
-- | S      |   2 |  15 |           20 |      20 |
-- +--------+-----+-----+--------------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

GROUP BY gives one row per group, losing the detail. Reports usually need both the detail row and the group figure side by side (each sale and its share of the region). Frames add the "sliding" dimension: last 3 rows, next 2 rows, whole partition.
codeExamples:
-- Each row's share of its region total - detail and aggregate together
SELECT region, mon, amt,
       ROUND(100 * amt / SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY region), 1) AS pct_of_region
FROM sales ORDER BY region, mon;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-----+-----+---------------+
-- | region | mon | amt | pct_of_region |
-- +--------+-----+-----+---------------+
-- | N      |   1 |  10 |          16.7 |
-- | N      |   2 |  20 |          33.3 |
-- | N      |   3 |  30 |          50.0 |
-- | S      |   1 |   5 |          25.0 |
-- | S      |   2 |  15 |          75.0 |
-- +--------+-----+-----+---------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW for 3-period moving figures, UNBOUNDED PRECEDING for cumulative totals, and a named WINDOW w AS (...) shared by several columns so the definition is written once.
codeExamples:
SELECT region, mon, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER w AS sum_prev1_cur,       -- previous row + current row
       MAX(amt) OVER w AS max_prev1_cur
FROM sales
WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY mon
             ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)       -- frame defined once
ORDER BY region, mon;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-----+-----+---------------+---------------+
-- | region | mon | amt | sum_prev1_cur | max_prev1_cur |
-- +--------+-----+-----+---------------+---------------+
-- | N      |   1 |  10 |            10 |            10 |
-- | N      |   2 |  20 |            30 |            20 |
-- | N      |   3 |  30 |            50 |            30 |
-- | S      |   1 |   5 |             5 |             5 |
-- | S      |   2 |  15 |            20 |            15 |
-- +--------+-----+-----+---------------+---------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   PARTITION BY region   ->  [ N: r1 r2 r3 ]   [ S: r1 r2 ]   (independent)

   inside one partition, ordered by mon:
        r1    r2    r3    r4    r5
                    ^ current row
   ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW      -> [ r1  r2  r3 ]
   ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING      ->     [ r2  r3  r4 ]
   ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT  -> [ r1 .. r3 ]

Fresher Notes
