  • OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary) restarts the window per department. A frame limits which rows around the current row are included.
  • Unlike GROUP BY, window functions keep every row.
  • Example: average salary per department shown on each employee row.

Worked Example 1

ROWS vs RANGE with ties.
codeExamples:
SELECT v, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_sum, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS range_sum
FROM (SELECT 1 AS v UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- v | rows_sum | range_sum
-- 1 |        1 |         1
-- 2 |        3 |         5
-- 2 |        5 |         5
-- 3 |        8 |         8

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

3-row frame.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND 1 FOLLOWING) AS window_sum FROM payments;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | amount | window_sum
--  1 |    100 |        150
--  2 |     50 |        175
--  3 |     25 |         75

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Per-department average next to each row.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, dept, salary, ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept), 0) AS dept_avg, salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS diff FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | dept | salary | dept_avg | diff
-- Abaji    |   10 |  60000 |    52500 | 7500
-- Raoji    |   10 |  45000 |    52500 | -7500
-- Moropant |   20 |  70000 |    70000 | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Named window.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, dept, salary, SUM(salary) OVER w AS dept_total, COUNT(*) OVER w AS dept_count FROM emp WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | dept | salary | dept_total | dept_count
-- Abaji    |   10 |  60000 |     105000 | 2
-- Raoji    |   10 |  45000 |     105000 | 2
-- Moropant |   20 |  70000 |      70000 | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

PARTITION BY splits rows into independent groups for the window function, without collapsing rows as GROUP BY does. The frame defines which rows around the current row take part: ROWS counts physical rows, RANGE includes all peers with equal ORDER BY values, GROUPS counts peer groups. With ORDER BY and no frame the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, salary, SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_total, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_n, salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS diff_from_avg FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary | dept_total | dept_n | diff_from_avg
--   10 | Abaji    |  60000 |     105000 |      2 | 7500
--   10 | Raoji    |  45000 |     105000 |      2 | -7500
--   20 | Moropant |  70000 |      70000 |      1 | 0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Frame syntax: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 7 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, UNBOUNDED PRECEDING/FOLLOWING, EXCLUDE is not supported. Name windows with WINDOW and inherit from them.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, sales,
  SUM(sales) OVER w7 AS last7,
  AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND 2 FOLLOWING) AS centered_avg5,
  SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running
FROM daily_sales WINDOW w7 AS (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW);

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales | last7 | centered_avg5 | running
-- 2026-01-07 |   120 |   840 |         118.0 |     840

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one query yields detail plus aggregates, partitions are independent (no cross-group leakage), frames give precise control, and any aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) can be windowed.
codeExamples:
-- ROWS counts physical rows; RANGE counts value peers - difference shows with ties
CREATE TABLE t (v INT);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1),(2),(2),(3);
SELECT v,
  SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v ROWS  BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS by_rows,
  SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS by_range
FROM t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+----------+
-- | v    | by_rows | by_range |
-- +------+---------+----------+
-- |    1 |       1 |        1 |
-- |    2 |       3 |        5 |   <- RANGE includes both peer rows with v = 2
-- |    2 |       5 |        5 |
-- |    3 |       8 |        8 |
-- +------+---------+----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the default frame depends on whether ORDER BY is present (no ORDER BY: whole partition; with ORDER BY: RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW), which surprises people; large partitions need sorting and memory.
codeExamples:
-- Same SUM, different meaning depending on ORDER BY
SELECT mon, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER ()               AS no_order,      -- whole set
       SUM(amt) OVER (ORDER BY mon)   AS with_order     -- cumulative (default frame)
FROM sales WHERE region = 'N';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-----+----------+------------+
-- | mon | amt | no_order | with_order |
-- +-----+-----+----------+------------+
-- |   1 |  10 |       60 |         10 |
-- |   2 |  20 |       60 |         30 |
-- |   3 |  30 |       60 |         60 |
-- +-----+-----+----------+------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: RANGE with a numeric or interval offset (RANGE BETWEEN 7 PRECEDING ...) needs a single numeric/temporal ORDER BY expression; GROUPS frames and EXCLUDE are not supported in MySQL; window functions cannot be nested inside each other.
codeExamples:
-- Time-based range frame: sum of the last 7 days (inclusive), by value not by row count
CREATE TABLE ev (d DATE, n INT);
INSERT INTO ev VALUES ('2025-01-01',1),('2025-01-05',2),('2025-01-09',4);
SELECT d, n,
  SUM(n) OVER (ORDER BY d RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 7 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS last_7d
FROM ev;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+---+---------+
-- | d          | n | last_7d |
-- +------------+---+---------+
-- | 2025-01-01 | 1 |       1 |
-- | 2025-01-05 | 2 |       3 |
-- | 2025-01-09 | 4 |       6 |   <- 01-01 fell out of the 7-day range (01-02..01-09)
-- +------------+---+---------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Be explicit about frames in production SQL: write ROWS or RANGE yourself instead of trusting defaults, and use a named WINDOW so related columns cannot drift apart. Prefer ROWS (cheaper, deterministic) unless you truly want value-based peers. Back each partition/order combination with a matching index and watch memory: huge partitions spill to temporary tables on disk.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Frames: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (physical rows) or RANGE (rows with equal ORDER BY values together).
  • With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING TO CURRENT ROW.
  • Named windows: WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY dept) avoid repeating definitions.

Senior Notes

  • ROWS is predictable and cheaper than RANGE; prefer it for running calculations.
  • Large partitions with big frames can be memory heavy; check EXPLAIN and temp table use.
  • Combine multiple windows with the same definition to share one sort.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: confusing ROWS and RANGE with ties (RANGE gives equal running totals to tied rows), forgetting a unique tiebreaker, and different window definitions per column that each need their own sort. Share one named window.
codeExamples:
SELECT v, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rows_sum, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS range_sum FROM (SELECT 1 AS v UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- v | rows_sum | range_sum
-- 1 |        1 |         1
-- 2 |        3 |         5
-- 2 |        5 |         5
-- 3 |        8 |         8

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large frames and partitions are buffered in memory (or a temp table). Use ROWS with small frames where possible, index the partition and order columns, and check the plan for filesort and temporary table use.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: compare each day with the same weekday's average over the last four weeks to flag anomalies.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, sales, ROUND(AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY WEEKDAY(day) ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), 1) AS weekday_avg_prev4,
  IF(sales < 0.7 * AVG(sales) OVER (PARTITION BY WEEKDAY(day) ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 4 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), 'LOW', 'ok') AS flag FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales | weekday_avg_prev4 | flag
-- 2026-05-04 |    70 |             120.0 | LOW

beginner.content:
Introduction

A running total is a cumulative SUM over an ordered window ending at the current row. A moving average is an AVG over a small sliding frame, which smooths noisy data.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE tx (id INT PRIMARY KEY, day DATE, amount INT);
INSERT INTO tx VALUES (1,'2025-01-01',100),(2,'2025-01-02',-30),(3,'2025-01-03',50),(4,'2025-01-04',20);

SELECT id, day, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS balance
FROM tx;                                    -- account balance after each transaction

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------+--------+---------+
-- | id | day        | amount | balance |
-- +----+------------+--------+---------+
-- |  1 | 2025-01-01 |    100 |     100 |
-- |  2 | 2025-01-02 |    -30 |      70 |
-- |  3 | 2025-01-03 |     50 |     120 |
-- |  4 | 2025-01-04 |     20 |     140 |
-- +----+------------+--------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Balances, cumulative revenue, inventory levels and trend lines are everywhere in finance and analytics. Before MySQL 8.0 you used a correlated subquery (O(n squared)) or a fragile @var := @var + x trick; window frames are one clean pass.
codeExamples:
-- The old way (avoid): correlated subquery, recomputed for every row
SELECT t.id,
       (SELECT SUM(x.amount) FROM tx x WHERE x.day <= t.day AND x.id <= t.id) AS balance_old
FROM tx t;
-- Same numbers, but quadratic work. The window version above is linear.

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------------+
-- | id | balance_old |
-- +----+-------------+
-- |  1 |         100 |
-- |  2 |          70 |
-- |  3 |         120 |
-- |  4 |         140 |
-- +----+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: a 3-day moving average on sales, running total per customer (PARTITION BY), percent of year-to-date, and "days until the balance goes negative" checks.

Diagram

   amount:     100    -30     50     20
   frame:      [100]  [100,-30] [100,-30,50] [100,-30,50,20]
   SUM (run):  100     70     120    140

   moving average, 3-row frame:
   units:   10   20   30   40   20
            [10]                         -> 10
            [10 20]                      -> 15
            [10 20 30]                   -> 20
                 [20 30 40]              -> 30
                      [30 40 20]         -> 30

Fresher Notes

  • A running total adds up values so far: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date).
  • A moving average averages the last N rows: AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
  • Used in finance, sales and monitoring dashboards.

Worked Example 1

Date-range window with INTERVAL.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS last7 FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | last7
-- 2026-01-07 | 1450

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Percent of total.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, salary, ROUND(salary / SUM(salary) OVER () * 100, 1) AS pct_of_company FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | salary | pct_of_company
-- Abaji    |  60000 | 34.3
-- Raoji    |  45000 | 25.7
-- Moropant |  70000 | 40.0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Running balance per account.
codeExamples:
SELECT account_id, txn_date, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY txn_date, id) AS balance FROM txns;

-- OUTPUT:
-- account_id | txn_date   | amount | balance
-- 1          | 2026-01-01 |    500 |     500
-- 1          | 2026-01-05 |   -200 |     300
-- 2          | 2026-01-02 |    100 |     100

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

3-day moving average.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, sales, ROUND(AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS ma3 FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales | ma3
-- 2026-01-01 |   100 | 100.0
-- 2026-01-02 |   200 | 150.0
-- 2026-01-03 |   300 | 200.0
-- 2026-01-04 |   100 | 200.0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A running total is a window SUM with an ordered frame from the start to the current row; a moving average averages a fixed-size frame that slides with the row. Each partition is sorted once and the aggregate is updated incrementally as the frame moves.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, sales, SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running_total, ROUND(AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS ma3 FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales | running_total | ma3
-- 2026-01-01 |   100 |           100 | 100.0
-- 2026-01-02 |   200 |           300 | 150.0
-- 2026-01-03 |   300 |           600 | 200.0
-- 2026-01-04 |   100 |           700 | 200.0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: per-group totals (PARTITION BY), date-based windows (RANGE with INTERVAL), cumulative percentages, and exponential-like smoothing with recursive CTEs. Always add a unique tiebreaker in ORDER BY.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: linear-time, readable, composable with PARTITION BY (per-customer or per-account totals), and the frame states the business rule (3 rows, 7 days) in the SQL itself.
codeExamples:
-- Running total that restarts for every customer
CREATE TABLE pay (cust VARCHAR(3), seq INT, amt INT);
INSERT INTO pay VALUES ('A',1,10),('A',2,5),('B',1,7),('B',2,3),('B',3,1);
SELECT cust, seq, amt,
       SUM(amt) OVER (PARTITION BY cust ORDER BY seq) AS cust_running
FROM pay ORDER BY cust, seq;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-----+-----+--------------+
-- | cust | seq | amt | cust_running |
-- +------+-----+-----+--------------+
-- | A    |   1 |  10 |           10 |
-- | A    |   2 |   5 |           15 |
-- | B    |   1 |   7 |            7 |
-- | B    |   2 |   3 |           10 |
-- | B    |   3 |   1 |           11 |
-- +------+-----+-----+--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the first rows have a shorter frame, so early moving averages are based on fewer points (use NULL-ing with COUNT(*) check if you need full windows); a non-unique ORDER BY with the default RANGE frame lumps ties together.
codeExamples:
-- Tie trap: two transactions on the same day with default frame
CREATE TABLE tt (day DATE, amt INT);
INSERT INTO tt VALUES ('2025-03-01',10),('2025-03-01',5),('2025-03-02',1);
SELECT day, amt, SUM(amt) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running FROM tt;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-----+---------+
-- | day        | amt | running |
-- +------------+-----+---------+
-- | 2025-03-01 |  10 |      15 |   <- both same-day rows show 15
-- | 2025-03-01 |   5 |      15 |
-- | 2025-03-02 |   1 |      16 |
-- +------------+-----+---------+   (fix: ORDER BY day, id with ROWS frame)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a cumulative total over a table of tens of millions of rows must sort and buffer each partition; results are not stored, so repeated dashboards recompute them; and a window result cannot be used in WHERE without a wrapper query.
codeExamples:
-- Filter on a running total: wrap it
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT id, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id) AS balance FROM tx
) b
WHERE balance > 100;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+
-- | id | balance |
-- +----+---------+
-- |  3 |     120 |
-- |  4 |     140 |
-- +----+---------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

For dashboards over big history, precompute daily aggregates into a summary table and apply windows on that small table instead of the raw fact table. Always order by a unique key with ROWS frames for reproducibility, store monetary values as DECIMAL or integer minor units, and decide explicitly how to treat the partial window at the start of the series.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Always add a unique tie-breaker in ORDER BY so the running total is deterministic.
  • Partition by account or product to restart totals.
  • Use ROWS frames for exact row counts and RANGE with INTERVAL for date windows.

Senior Notes

  • If dates have gaps, a "last 7 rows" average is not "last 7 days"; use a RANGE with INTERVAL or join to a calendar.
  • For huge tables compute totals incrementally (summary tables) instead of recomputing per query.
  • Index (partition, order) columns to avoid sorting.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: missing days making "7 rows" different from "7 days", ties without a tiebreaker producing unstable intermediate totals, and recomputing totals for the whole history on each page view. Use a calendar and precomputed daily tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.d, COALESCE(s.sales, 0) AS sales, AVG(COALESCE(s.sales, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY c.d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma7 FROM calendar c LEFT JOIN daily_sales s ON s.day = c.d WHERE c.d BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-31';

-- OUTPUT:
-- d          | sales | ma7
-- 2026-01-07 |     0 | 85.7

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Window functions over millions of rows sort everything unless indexed. Aggregate to the grain you report on (day) first, then run the window over the small table.
codeExamples:
WITH daily AS (SELECT DATE(created_at) AS day, SUM(total) AS sales FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY DATE(created_at))
SELECT day, sales, SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS ytd FROM daily;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales   | ytd
-- 2026-01-01 | 8120.00 | 8120.00

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an account statement with running balance, plus a check that the last running balance equals the account balance column.

beginner.content:
Introduction

"Top-N per group" (best 3 products in each category, latest order per customer) is the most common window-function interview and production pattern: rank rows inside each partition with ROW_NUMBER/RANK/DENSE_RANK, then filter on the rank in an outer query or CTE.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, category VARCHAR(10), name VARCHAR(10), sales INT);
INSERT INTO products VALUES
 (1,'Phone','P1',500),(2,'Phone','P2',900),(3,'Phone','P3',700),(4,'Phone','P4',100),
 (5,'Laptop','L1',300),(6,'Laptop','L2',800);

WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT category, name, sales,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rn   -- rank per category
  FROM products
)
SELECT category, name, sales, rn
FROM   ranked
WHERE  rn <= 2                                  -- top 2 in each category
ORDER  BY category, rn;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+-------+----+
-- | category | name | sales | rn |
-- +----------+------+-------+----+
-- | Laptop   | L2   |   800 |  1 |
-- | Laptop   | L1   |   300 |  2 |
-- | Phone    | P2   |   900 |  1 |
-- | Phone    | P3   |   700 |  2 |
-- +----------+------+-------+----+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

LIMIT applies to the whole result, not to each group. Before 8.0 people used self-joins counting greater rows, or variables; both are slow or unreliable. Window functions express the intent directly.
codeExamples:
-- LIMIT 2 gives the top 2 overall - NOT per category
SELECT category, name, sales FROM products ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | category | name | sales |
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | Phone    | P2   |   900 |
-- | Laptop   | L2   |   800 |
-- +----------+------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: the top 3 customers per region, each user's most recent login, the highest-paid employee per department, newest 5 comments per post for a feed.
codeExamples:
-- Latest row per group (N = 1) with ties kept: use RANK or DENSE_RANK instead of ROW_NUMBER
SELECT category, name, sales
FROM  (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC) AS rk FROM products) t
WHERE rk = 1
ORDER BY category;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | category | name | sales |
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | Laptop   | L2   |   800 |
-- | Phone    | P2   |   900 |
-- +----------+------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   products
   +-----------------------------+      PARTITION BY category
   | Phone  P2 900  -> rn 1  keep|      ORDER BY sales DESC
   | Phone  P3 700  -> rn 2  keep|
   | Phone  P1 500  -> rn 3  drop|      WHERE rn <= 2
   | Phone  P4 100  -> rn 4  drop|
   | Laptop L2 800  -> rn 1  keep|
   | Laptop L1 300  -> rn 2  keep|
   +-----------------------------+

Fresher Notes

  • Top-N per group means the best N rows in each category, for example the top 3 earners in each department.
  • Use a window function: rank rows with ROW_NUMBER/RANK inside each group, then keep rank <= N.
  • Plain GROUP BY or LIMIT cannot do this alone.

Worked Example 1

Latest 3 posts per author with a lateral join (8.0.14+).
codeExamples:
SELECT a.name, p.title FROM authors a JOIN LATERAL (SELECT title FROM posts WHERE author_id = a.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) p;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | title
-- Abaji | Post C
-- Abaji | Post B
-- Abaji | Post A

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Supporting index.

Practice Exercise 1

Top 2 earners per department.
codeExamples:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT dept, name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn FROM emp)
SELECT dept, name, salary FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary
--   10 | Abaji    | 60000
--   10 | Raoji    | 45000
--   20 | Moropant | 70000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Include ties with DENSE_RANK.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, dept, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr FROM emp) t WHERE dr <= 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name     | dept | salary | dr
-- Abaji    |   10 |  60000 | 1
-- Raoji    |   10 |  45000 | 2
-- Moropant |   20 |  70000 | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Top-N per group means the best N rows within each category. LIMIT applies to the whole result, so it cannot do this. The standard method ranks rows inside each partition with a window function and keeps rank <= N in an outer query, because window results cannot be used in WHERE directly.
codeExamples:
WITH ranked AS (SELECT dept, name, salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn FROM emp)
SELECT dept, name, salary FROM ranked WHERE rn <= 2 ORDER BY dept, rn;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary
--   10 | Abaji    | 60000
--   10 | Raoji    | 45000
--   20 | Moropant | 70000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Alternatives: DENSE_RANK to include ties, a LATERAL join (8.0.14+) that runs ORDER BY ... LIMIT N per group, and a correlated count. Pick by tie policy and data size.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one table scan, controllable tie behaviour (ROW_NUMBER exactly N rows, RANK/DENSE_RANK keep ties), works with any N, and is easy to modify.
codeExamples:
-- Tie-aware version: DENSE_RANK <= 2 returns every row tied inside the top 2 distinct scores
CREATE TABLE s (g CHAR(1), v INT);
INSERT INTO s VALUES ('x',10),('x',10),('x',9),('x',5);
SELECT g, v FROM (SELECT g, v, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY v DESC) AS d FROM s) t
WHERE d <= 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---+----+
-- | g | v  |
-- +---+----+
-- | x | 10 |
-- | x | 10 |
-- | x |  9 |
-- +---+----+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: ranks every row before filtering, so on a huge table it sorts all partitions even when you want only 3 per group. A lateral join or a loop over the group table can be faster when the groups are few and indexed.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL 8.0.14+ alternative: LATERAL derived table with LIMIT per group (index-friendly)
CREATE TABLE cats (category VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO cats SELECT DISTINCT category FROM products;

SELECT c.category, p.name, p.sales
FROM   cats c
JOIN   LATERAL (SELECT name, sales FROM products x
                WHERE x.category = c.category
                ORDER BY sales DESC LIMIT 2) p       -- LIMIT applies per category
ORDER  BY c.category, p.sales DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | category | name | sales |
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | Laptop   | L2   |   800 |
-- | Laptop   | L1   |   300 |
-- | Phone    | P2   |   900 |
-- | Phone    | P3   |   700 |
-- +----------+------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the rank cannot be filtered in the same query level (wrap with a CTE or derived table); ROW_NUMBER picks arbitrary rows among ties unless you add a tie-breaker; and a missing supporting index forces a filesort of the whole table.
codeExamples:
-- Add a deterministic tie-breaker and a supporting index
CREATE INDEX idx_cat_sales ON products (category, sales DESC, id);   -- 8.0 supports DESC indexes
SELECT category, name, sales
FROM  (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sales DESC, id) AS rn FROM products) t
WHERE rn = 1 ORDER BY category;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | category | name | sales |
-- +----------+------+-------+
-- | Laptop   | L2   |   800 |
-- | Phone    | P2   |   900 |
-- +----------+------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to ROW_NUMBER in a CTE with a unique tie-breaker and a composite index (group, sort_col DESC, id). If the group count is small relative to rows and N is tiny, test the LATERAL ... LIMIT form, which can stop early per group. Decide on tie semantics as a product requirement (exactly N rows vs all ties) and document it, since RANK and ROW_NUMBER return different counts.

Mid-Level Notes

  • ROW_NUMBER gives exactly N rows per group; RANK/DENSE_RANK may return more when there are ties.
  • The ranking must be computed in a subquery or CTE and filtered outside.
  • Add tie-breakers (id) for stable results.

Senior Notes

  • On big tables use an index on (group, order_col) and consider a lateral-style approach: for each group, SELECT ... ORDER BY ... LIMIT N from a small list of groups.
  • For pagination-like feeds (top 3 posts per category on a homepage), precompute and cache.
  • Check plans: window sorts the whole table unless indexed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no tiebreaker (nondeterministic rows), ROW_NUMBER when ties must all be included, and scanning the whole table for a small N. Choose RANK/DENSE_RANK for ties and index the sort.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

With an index on (group, sort) the LATERAL form touches only N rows per group, while the window form sorts the whole table. Compare with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on large data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: show the latest three posts per author on a profile list, or the top five products per category on a landing page, cached and paginated.
codeExamples:
SELECT a.name, p.title, p.created_at FROM authors a JOIN LATERAL (SELECT title, created_at FROM posts WHERE author_id = a.id ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 3) p WHERE a.id IN (1, 2, 3);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | title  | created_at
-- Abaji | Post C | 2026-05-01 10:00:00

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL 5.7+ has a native JSON column type. The server validates the text on write, stores it in a compact binary format (not as text) and normalises it: keys are sorted by length then bytewise, and whitespace is dropped. JSON_OBJECT() and JSON_ARRAY() build JSON values from SQL values.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE profile (
  id  INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  doc JSON NOT NULL                              -- validated on every write
);

INSERT INTO profile (doc)
VALUES (JSON_OBJECT('name', 'Abaji',              -- key/value pairs
                    'age',  30,
                    'skills', JSON_ARRAY('sql', 'java')));   -- a JSON array

SELECT doc FROM profile;                         -- note the normalised key order

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------------------------------------------------+
-- | doc                                                     |
-- +---------------------------------------------------------+
-- | {"age": 30, "name": "Abaji", "skills": ["sql", "java"]} |
-- +------------------------------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Not every attribute deserves its own column. Product specs, user preferences, webhook payloads and API responses have a shape that varies per row or changes often. JSON lets you store them without a schema migration for each new field, while still being validated and queryable.
codeExamples:
-- Validate and inspect JSON values with built-in functions
SELECT JSON_VALID('{"a": 1}')            AS ok_obj,     -- 1 = valid
       JSON_VALID('{a: 1}')              AS bad_obj,    -- 0 = keys must be quoted
       JSON_TYPE(JSON_OBJECT('k', 1))    AS t_obj,
       JSON_TYPE('[1, 2]')               AS t_arr,
       JSON_TYPE('1')                    AS t_int;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+---------+--------+-------+---------+
-- | ok_obj | bad_obj | t_obj  | t_arr | t_int   |
-- +--------+---------+--------+-------+---------+
-- |      1 |       0 | OBJECT | ARRAY | INTEGER |
-- +--------+---------+--------+-------+---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: an API layer builds its response directly in SQL. JSON_ARRAYAGG and JSON_OBJECTAGG turn grouped rows into nested documents, so the application receives one ready-made JSON string per order.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE line_item (order_id INT, sku VARCHAR(10), qty INT);
INSERT INTO line_item VALUES (1,'P1',2),(1,'P2',1),(2,'P3',5);

SELECT JSON_OBJECT('order', order_id,
                   'items', JSON_ARRAYAGG(JSON_OBJECT('sku', sku, 'qty', qty))) AS payload
FROM   line_item
GROUP  BY order_id
ORDER  BY order_id;

-- OUTPUT (example; array element order is not guaranteed):
-- +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | payload                                                                |
-- +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | {"items": [{"qty": 2, "sku": "P1"}, {"qty": 1, "sku": "P2"}], "order": 1} |
-- | {"items": [{"qty": 5, "sku": "P3"}], "order": 2}                       |
-- +------------------------------------------------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SQL values                           JSON column (binary, validated)
   'Abaji', 30, JSON_ARRAY(...)  ---->   +----------------------------------+
        |                               | header | key table | value table |
   JSON_OBJECT / JSON_ARRAY             +----------------------------------+
                                        keys sorted: len, then bytes
                                             |
                  +--------------------------+-------------------------+
                  v                          v                         v
          doc->'$.k' read            JSON_SET partial update    generated column
          (lookup, no re-parse)      (in-place when it fits)    + index for search

Fresher Notes

  • The JSON type stores JSON documents with validation. JSON_OBJECT() and JSON_ARRAY() build JSON values.
  • Insert JSON as a string: INSERT INTO t(data) VALUES ('{"a":1}').
  • Invalid JSON is rejected.

Worked Example 1

Schema validation constraint.

Worked Example 2

Append to an array.

Practice Exercise 1

Build and store JSON.

Practice Exercise 2

Modify a document.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The JSON type validates documents and stores them in a binary format with a lookup table of keys and values, so reading one path does not re-parse the whole document. Values are normalized: object keys are sorted and duplicates removed. Documents are stored with the row (or off-page when large).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Build with JSON_OBJECT, JSON_ARRAY, JSON_MERGE_PATCH; modify with JSON_SET, JSON_INSERT, JSON_REPLACE, JSON_REMOVE, JSON_ARRAY_APPEND; aggregate with JSON_ARRAYAGG and JSON_OBJECTAGG.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: flexible schema, automatic validation, a rich function set, and efficient partial updates: JSON_SET, JSON_INSERT, JSON_REPLACE, JSON_REMOVE and JSON_ARRAY_APPEND change one path without you rewriting the whole document in application code.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the structure is not enforced (a typo in a key silently creates a new key), there are no foreign keys into a JSON value, and large documents are costly to read and update. Invalid JSON text is rejected at write time, which is good but must be handled by the application.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO profile (doc) VALUES ('{name: "x"}');   -- keys must be double-quoted

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3140 (22032): Invalid JSON text: "Missing a name for object member."
--   at position 1 in value for column 'profile.doc'.

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a JSON column cannot be indexed directly (only through generated columns or functional/multi-valued indexes), the document size is bounded by max_allowed_packet, and numbers beyond DOUBLE/BIGINT precision lose accuracy. JSON columns also cannot have a plain literal DEFAULT (an expression default is allowed from 8.0.13).
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_doc ON profile (doc);               -- direct index on JSON

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3152 (42000): JSON column 'doc' supports indexing only via generated
--   columns on a specified JSON path.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use JSON for genuinely variable or opaque data (payloads, settings, long-tail attributes), never as a way to avoid modelling the core entity. Keep anything you filter, join or constrain on in real columns. Plan for document growth, because every update to a large document is a read-modify-write of that row, and prefer storing small documents (a few KB) rather than a whole object graph.

Mid-Level Notes

  • JSON is stored in an efficient binary format that allows fast access to keys.
  • Update parts with JSON_SET, JSON_INSERT, JSON_REPLACE, JSON_REMOVE.
  • Max size is governed by max_allowed_packet.

Senior Notes

  • Use JSON for sparse or evolving attributes; keep filtered, joined or constrained fields as real columns.
  • Partial updates on large documents are optimized in 8.0 but still cost more than column updates.
  • Schema validation: JSON_SCHEMA_VALID in a CHECK constraint.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: invalid JSON strings (error 3140), expecting key order to be kept, storing numbers as strings, and updating large documents in place often (rewrites). Validate with a CHECK and JSON_SCHEMA_VALID.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

MySQL 8 can do partial updates of JSON in place (logging only the diff) when you use JSON_SET, JSON_REPLACE or JSON_REMOVE on the same column. Large documents still cost I/O, so keep them modest.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, JSON_STORAGE_SIZE(data) AS stored_bytes, JSON_STORAGE_FREE(data) AS free_after_partial_update FROM profiles;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | stored_bytes | free_after_partial_update
--  1 |           78 |                         0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: product attributes that differ by category. Fixed fields stay as columns; variable ones live in a JSON column and are queried through generated columns when needed.

beginner.content:
Introduction

JSON_EXTRACT(doc, path) returns the value at a JSON path as a JSON value (so strings keep their quotes). doc->'$.k' is shorthand for it, and doc->>'$.k' additionally unquotes the result to a plain SQL string. JSON_VALUE (8.0.21+) extracts a scalar and converts it to a SQL type with RETURNING.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE person (id INT PRIMARY KEY, doc JSON);
INSERT INTO person VALUES
 (1, '{"name":"Abaji", "score":9,   "address":{"city":"Pune"},  "tags":["sql","java"]}'),
 (2, '{"name":"Raoji", "score":10,  "address":{"city":"Delhi"}, "tags":[]}'),
 (3, '{"name":"Moropant","score":100, "address":{"city":"Pune"},  "tags":["java"]}');

SELECT doc->'$.name'                    AS as_json,       -- JSON string, quoted
       doc->>'$.name'                   AS as_text,       -- unquoted SQL string
       JSON_EXTRACT(doc, '$.address.city') AS city_json   -- nested path
FROM   person WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------+-----------+
-- | as_json | as_text | city_json |
-- +---------+---------+-----------+
-- | "Abaji" | Abaji   | "Pune"    |
-- +---------+---------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Application queries need typed values, not JSON fragments. JSON_VALUE ... RETURNING gives a correctly typed column, and ON EMPTY / ON ERROR clauses let you supply defaults instead of NULLs or surprises.
codeExamples:
SELECT id,
       JSON_VALUE(doc, '$.score' RETURNING UNSIGNED) + 1            AS next_score,  -- numeric
       JSON_VALUE(doc, '$.nickname' DEFAULT 'none' ON EMPTY)        AS nickname     -- missing key
FROM   person
ORDER  BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------+----------+
-- | id | next_score | nickname |
-- +----+------------+----------+
-- |  1 |         10 | none     |
-- |  2 |         11 | none     |
-- |  3 |        101 | none     |
-- +----+------------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: filter on one attribute, read an array element, count array members, and expand an array into rows with JSON_TABLE (8.0.4+) so it can be joined and grouped like a normal table.
codeExamples:
-- Filter on a nested value, show the first tag and the tag count
SELECT id, doc->>'$.tags[0]' AS first_tag, JSON_LENGTH(doc, '$.tags') AS n_tags
FROM   person
WHERE  doc->>'$.address.city' = 'Pune';

-- Expand arrays into rows
SELECT p.id, jt.tag
FROM   person p,
       JSON_TABLE(p.doc, '$.tags[*]' COLUMNS (tag VARCHAR(20) PATH '$')) AS jt
ORDER  BY p.id, jt.tag;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-----------+--------+
-- | id | first_tag | n_tags |
-- +----+-----------+--------+
-- |  1 | sql       |      2 |
-- |  3 | java      |      1 |
-- +----+-----------+--------+
-- +----+------+
-- | id | tag  |
-- +----+------+
-- |  1 | java |
-- |  1 | sql  |
-- |  3 | java |
-- +----+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   doc = {"name":"Abaji","address":{"city":"Pune"},"tags":["sql","java"]}

   $                     whole document
   $.name                ----------------------->  "Abaji"       (-> keeps quotes)
   $.address.city        ----------------------->  "Pune"
   $.tags[0]             ----------------------->  "sql"
   $.tags[*]             ----------------------->  ["sql","java"]
   $**.city              any depth wildcard

   ->   JSON_EXTRACT                 returns JSON
   ->>  JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT)   returns SQL text
   JSON_VALUE(... RETURNING type)    returns typed scalar

Fresher Notes

  • JSON_EXTRACT(doc, path) (or doc->path) reads a value; ->> also removes quotes. JSON_VALUE(doc, path RETURNING type) returns a typed scalar (8.0.21+).
  • Paths start with $: $.name, $.skills[0].
  • Use them in SELECT, WHERE and ORDER BY.

Worked Example 1

JSON_TABLE.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.id, jt.skill FROM profiles p, JSON_TABLE(p.data, '$.skills[*]' COLUMNS (skill VARCHAR(20) PATH '$')) jt;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | skill
--  1 | SQL
--  1 | Java

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Type pitfall.
codeExamples:
SELECT JSON_EXTRACT('{"n": "5"}', '$.n') = 5 AS cmp_json, JSON_VALUE('{"n": "5"}', '$.n' RETURNING UNSIGNED) = 5 AS cmp_typed;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cmp_json | cmp_typed
--        0 |         1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Extract and filter.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, data->>'$.name' AS name, JSON_VALUE(data, '$.age' RETURNING UNSIGNED) AS age FROM people_json WHERE JSON_VALUE(data, '$.age' RETURNING UNSIGNED) > 25;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | age
--  1 | Abaji | 30

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Array membership.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM profiles WHERE 'SQL' MEMBER OF (data->'$.skills');

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Paths start at $ and use dots for keys and brackets for array positions. JSON_EXTRACT(doc, path) (alias ->) returns a JSON value; ->> additionally unquotes strings. JSON_VALUE(doc, path RETURNING type) returns a typed SQL scalar, which makes comparisons and indexes reliable.
codeExamples:
SELECT data->'$.name' AS json_value, data->>'$.name' AS plain_text, JSON_EXTRACT(data, '$.skills[0]') AS first_skill, JSON_VALUE(data, '$.age' RETURNING UNSIGNED) AS age FROM people_json WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- json_value | plain_text | first_skill | age
-- "Abaji"    | Abaji      | "SQL"       | 30

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Search inside arrays with MEMBER OF, JSON_CONTAINS, JSON_OVERLAPS and JSON_SEARCH; expand arrays to rows with JSON_TABLE; wildcard paths $[*] and $**.key collect many values.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: path expressions reach any depth, wildcards ($.tags[*], $**.city) match many values at once, and JSON_TABLE bridges JSON and relational worlds.
codeExamples:
SELECT JSON_EXTRACT(doc, '$.tags[*]')  AS all_tags,     -- wildcard returns an array
       JSON_EXTRACT(doc, '$**.city')    AS all_cities    -- any key named city, any depth
FROM   person WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+--------------+
-- | all_tags       | all_cities   |
-- +----------------+--------------+
-- | ["sql", "java"]| ["Pune"]     |
-- +----------------+--------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a missing path does not raise an error, it returns NULL, so a typo in a key name looks like "no data". Also, ->> returns text, so sorting or comparing numbers extracted that way is textual unless you cast.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, doc->>'$.score' AS score
FROM   person
ORDER  BY doc->>'$.score';                       -- text sort: '10' < '100' < '9'

SELECT doc->>'$.nme' AS typo_key FROM person WHERE id = 1;   -- silently NULL

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | score |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  2 | 10    |
-- |  3 | 100   |
-- |  1 | 9     |
-- +----+-------+
-- +----------+
-- | typo_key |
-- +----------+
-- | NULL     |
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the -> and ->> operators accept only a column and a literal path (no expressions as path); keys with spaces or special characters need double quotes inside the path; JSON_VALUE needs 8.0.21 or later.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO person VALUES (4, '{"first name": "Zed", "score": 7}');

SELECT doc->>'$."first name"' AS fname FROM person WHERE id = 4;   -- quote the key
SELECT doc->>'$.first name'   AS broken FROM person WHERE id = 4;  -- invalid path

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | fname |
-- +-------+
-- | Zed   |
-- +-------+
-- ERROR 3143 (42000): Invalid JSON path expression. The error is around character position 8.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Standardise on one extraction style per codebase and always cast to the type you compare or sort on. For attributes used in WHERE, JOIN or ORDER BY on large tables, promote them to a generated column with an index instead of extracting on every row. Treat NULL-for-missing-key as a data quality risk and guard it with CHECK or JSON_SCHEMA_VALID.

Mid-Level Notes

  • -> returns a JSON value (strings keep quotes); ->> returns plain text.
  • JSON_VALUE with RETURNING makes comparisons type-safe: RETURNING UNSIGNED.
  • JSON_CONTAINS, JSON_SEARCH and JSON_TABLE query inside arrays.

Senior Notes

  • Without an index, JSON path filters scan every row; add generated columns or functional indexes.
  • JSON_TABLE turns a JSON array into rows for joins and aggregation.
  • Type mix-ups (string "5" vs number 5) are a frequent source of wrong results; extract with explicit types.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: comparing JSON values to SQL values without a cast (-> returns quoted JSON), type confusion between "5" and 5, and filtering on JSON paths with no index. Use ->> or JSON_VALUE with RETURNING.
codeExamples:
SELECT JSON_EXTRACT('{"n": "5"}', '$.n') = 5 AS wrong_cmp, JSON_VALUE('{"n": "5"}', '$.n' RETURNING UNSIGNED) = 5 AS right_cmp, '{"n": 5}'->'$.n' = '5' AS quoted_json;

-- OUTPUT:
-- wrong_cmp | right_cmp | quoted_json
--         0 |         1 |           0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Without an index every JSON filter scans the table. Create generated columns or functional indexes on the exact expression the query uses, with matching cast and collation.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: read webhook payloads stored as JSON, extracting typed fields into reporting columns during a nightly job.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO payment_facts (payment_id, amount, currency, paid_at)
SELECT id, JSON_VALUE(payload, '$.amount' RETURNING DECIMAL(12,2)), JSON_VALUE(payload, '$.currency' RETURNING CHAR(3)), JSON_VALUE(payload, '$.paid_at' RETURNING DATETIME)
FROM webhook_events WHERE type = 'payment.succeeded' AND id > 1000000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 48120 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

A JSON column cannot be indexed directly. You index a generated column (a column computed from an expression such as doc->>'$.email'), or use a functional index on an expression, or a multi-valued index (8.0.17+) that indexes every element of a JSON array. A VIRTUAL generated column is computed on read; a STORED one is written to disk.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE cust (
  id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  doc   JSON,
  email VARCHAR(100) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (doc->>'$.email') VIRTUAL,  -- computed, not stored
  KEY idx_email (email)                                              -- secondary index on it
);
INSERT INTO cust (id, doc) VALUES
 (1, '{"email":"abaji@x.com","score":9, "tags":["sql","java"]}'),
 (2, '{"email":"raoji@x.com","score":10,"tags":["go"]}'),
 (3, '{"email":"moropant@x.com","score":100,"tags":["java"]}');

EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM cust WHERE email = 'abaji@x.com';

-- OUTPUT (example, partial columns):
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+-----------+------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type | key       | rows |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+-----------+------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | cust  | ref  | idx_email |    1 |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+-----------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without an index, every JSON filter is a full table scan that parses each document. With an index the same filter becomes a B-tree lookup, which is the difference between milliseconds and minutes on millions of rows.
codeExamples:
-- Functional index: index the expression itself (no visible extra column)
CREATE INDEX idx_score ON cust ((CAST(doc->>'$.score' AS UNSIGNED)));

-- The query must use the SAME expression to qualify
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM cust WHERE CAST(doc->>'$.score' AS UNSIGNED) = 10;

-- OUTPUT (example, partial columns):
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+-----------+------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type | key       | rows |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+-----------+------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | cust  | ref  | idx_score |    1 |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+-----------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: searching "which customers have the tag java" over an array. A multi-valued index stores one index entry per array element and is used by MEMBER OF, JSON_CONTAINS and JSON_OVERLAPS.
codeExamples:
CREATE INDEX idx_tags ON cust ((CAST(doc->'$.tags' AS CHAR(20) ARRAY)));

SELECT id FROM cust WHERE 'java' MEMBER OF (doc->'$.tags') ORDER BY id;
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM cust WHERE 'java' MEMBER OF (doc->'$.tags');

-- OUTPUT (example for the EXPLAIN, partial columns):
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  1 |
-- |  3 |
-- +----+
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+----------+------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type | key      | rows |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+----------+------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | cust  | ref  | idx_tags |    2 |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+----------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   JSON doc column (not indexable)
        |
        +--> generated col  email = doc->>'$.email'   --> B-tree  idx_email
        |        (VIRTUAL: computed on read, STORED: kept on disk)
        |
        +--> functional index  ((CAST(doc->>'$.score' AS UNSIGNED)))
        |        query must repeat the identical expression
        |
        +--> multi-valued index ((CAST(doc->'$.tags' AS CHAR(20) ARRAY)))
                 one index entry per array element
                 used by MEMBER OF / JSON_CONTAINS / JSON_OVERLAPS

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL cannot index a JSON document directly, but you can index values inside it through a generated column or a functional index.
  • Generated column: ALTER TABLE t ADD city VARCHAR(30) AS (data->>"$.city") STORED, ADD INDEX (city).
  • Queries on that column then use the index.

Worked Example 1

Functional index with a cast.

Worked Example 2

Mismatch ignores the index.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM people_json WHERE data->>'$.age' > '25';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key  | Extra
-- ALL  | NULL | Using where

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Generated column plus index.

Practice Exercise 2

Multi-valued index for tags.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A JSON column cannot be indexed as a whole. Instead you index values derived from it: a generated column (VIRTUAL computes on read, STORED persists) with an ordinary B-tree index, a functional index (8.0.13+), or a multi-valued index (8.0.17+) over array elements. The optimizer uses the index only when the query expression matches the indexed expression exactly.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Multi-valued index for tags: CAST(data->'$.skills' AS CHAR(20) ARRAY), queried with MEMBER OF, JSON_CONTAINS or JSON_OVERLAPS. Use STORED when computing is expensive or when the column must be part of a unique key.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a generated column documents which JSON attribute is "promoted", can be a normal column in SELECT lists, and can carry NOT NULL or UNIQUE rules. Virtual columns cost no disk for the value itself; only the index is stored.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each index adds write cost and storage; a STORED column also duplicates the data on disk; and adding a STORED column rebuilds the table. The extracted text from ->> uses a binary-style (case-sensitive) collation, which can surprise you when you expect case-insensitive email matching.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM cust WHERE email = 'ABAJI@X.COM';     -- case-sensitive compare

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the optimiser uses a functional index only when the query expression matches the indexed one exactly (same cast, same path). A multi-valued index allows only one array part per index, cannot be used for covering reads or ORDER BY, and is 8.0.17+ only.
codeExamples:
-- Different cast than the index definition: the index is NOT used
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM cust WHERE CAST(doc->>'$.score' AS SIGNED) = 10;

-- OUTPUT (example, partial columns):
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+------+------+
-- | id | select_type | table | type | key  | rows |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+------+------+
-- |  1 | SIMPLE      | cust  | ALL  | NULL |    3 |
-- +----+-------------+-------+------+------+------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Index only the 2 to 4 attributes your queries really use; if you find yourself indexing many JSON paths, those attributes belong in real columns. Prefer VIRTUAL generated columns with an index (cheap to add online in many cases) unless you need the value stored for other reasons. Verify with EXPLAIN after every change, because expression mismatch silently falls back to a full scan.

Mid-Level Notes

  • VIRTUAL generated columns compute on read and cost no storage; STORED persist the value. Indexes on virtual columns are stored in the index.
  • Functional indexes (8.0.13+): CREATE INDEX idx ON t ((CAST(data->>"$.age" AS UNSIGNED))).
  • Multi-valued indexes (8.0.17+) index JSON arrays for MEMBER OF/JSON_CONTAINS.

Senior Notes

  • The optimizer uses the index only if the query expression matches exactly (same cast/path).
  • Multi-valued indexes allow efficient "tag" searches without a junction table, but enforce limits (one per index).
  • If you query a field constantly, promote it to a real column.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: mismatched expressions or casts (index ignored), string comparison on numbers, and a multi-valued index with too many elements per row (size explodes). Check EXPLAIN after creating the index and keep arrays small.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Generated columns cost space (STORED) or CPU (VIRTUAL) and slow writes slightly. Index only the fields queried often; promote them to real columns when they become core to the model.
codeExamples:
SELECT index_name, ROUND(SUM(stat_value) * @@innodb_page_size / 1048576, 1) AS mb FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats WHERE table_name = 'people_json' AND stat_name = 'size' GROUP BY index_name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- index_name | mb
-- PRIMARY    | 410.0
-- idx_city   |  42.0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: catalog search by brand and color stored in JSON attributes. Two generated columns and a composite index turn a scan into a lookup.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Both can hold the same facts. Relational columns give you types, constraints, foreign keys, statistics and simple indexes. JSON gives you a flexible shape and one column for many optional attributes. The best design is usually hybrid: core attributes as columns, the long tail as JSON.

Why Do We Need This?

The relational way needs a column (and a migration) for every attribute of every product type, so a catalogue with thousands of different attributes becomes a table of mostly NULLs. The classic alternative, EAV (entity-attribute-value), is slow and untyped. JSON solves the "sparse, evolving attributes" problem.
codeExamples:
-- Adding a new attribute: relational needs DDL, JSON needs none
ALTER TABLE product_rel ADD COLUMN material VARCHAR(20);      -- DDL, schema change

UPDATE product_hyb
SET    attrs = JSON_SET(attrs, '$.material', 'cotton')         -- plain DML
WHERE  id = 1;
SELECT attrs FROM product_hyb WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------------------------------------------+
-- | attrs                                                |
-- +------------------------------------------------------+
-- | {"size": "M", "color": "blue", "material": "cotton"} |
-- +------------------------------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: an e-commerce catalogue keeps price, stock and category as columns (filtered, joined, aggregated constantly) and technical specs as JSON (displayed and occasionally filtered). Money and counts stay relational so SUM, constraints and foreign keys work natively.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, price
FROM   product_hyb
WHERE  price < 1000                                    -- fast, typed, indexable column
  AND  attrs->>'$.color' = 'blue';                     -- long-tail attribute from JSON

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+--------+
-- | name  | price  |
-- +-------+--------+
-- | Shirt | 499.00 |
-- +-------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Entity: product
   +------------------------+--------------------------------------+
   |  RELATIONAL COLUMNS    |  JSON column (attrs)                 |
   |  id, name, price,      |  {"color":"blue","size":"M"}         |
   |  stock, category_id    |  {"ram_gb":16,"cpu":"i7"}            |
   |                        |                                      |
   |  typed, constrained,   |  flexible, optional, sparse          |
   |  indexed, joined       |  index via generated column if hot   |
   +------------------------+--------------------------------------+
        everything you filter / join / sum  -->  column
        everything you only display / rarely filter  -->  JSON

Fresher Notes

  • Relational columns have fixed types and constraints; JSON stores flexible documents in one column.
  • Use columns for core fields (id, email, status) and JSON for optional, varied attributes.
  • You can mix both in one table.

Worked Example 1

Version the JSON shape.

Worked Example 2

Compare storage.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND(data_length/1024/1024,2) AS mb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('events_cols','events_json');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name  | mb
-- events_cols | 120.00
-- events_json | 310.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Hybrid design.

Practice Exercise 2

Constraint comparison.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Relational columns have fixed types, constraints, foreign keys, statistics and efficient indexes. JSON trades those for flexibility: no per-key constraints by default, weaker statistics and joins, bigger rows and more CPU to read paths. The optimizer knows far more about columns than about JSON content.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

A hybrid model is common: core, queried, constrained fields as columns; variable, rarely filtered ones in JSON; and generated columns bridging the two for the few JSON fields you filter on.

expert.content:
Advantages

JSON advantages: no migrations for new optional attributes, natural fit for documents from APIs, fewer joins. Relational advantages: type safety, NOT NULL/UNIQUE/FOREIGN KEY/CHECK, accurate optimiser statistics, narrow rows and cheap updates. You can still add rules to JSON with JSON_SCHEMA_VALID in a CHECK constraint (8.0.17+).
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE product_hyb ADD CONSTRAINT chk_attrs CHECK (
  attrs IS NULL OR JSON_SCHEMA_VALID(
    '{"type":"object","properties":{"ram_gb":{"type":"number"}}}', attrs)
);

INSERT INTO product_hyb VALUES (3,'Phone',20000.00,'{"ram_gb":"eight"}');  -- wrong type

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_attrs' is violated.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages of JSON: no foreign keys into it, weaker optimiser statistics (selectivity of JSON paths is guessed), every access pays an extraction cost, large documents slow row reads, and aggregating requires casts. Disadvantages of relational: rigid shape, sparse NULL-heavy tables, frequent DDL.
codeExamples:
-- Aggregating a JSON number needs an explicit conversion every time
SELECT SUM(JSON_VALUE(attrs, '$.ram_gb' RETURNING UNSIGNED)) AS total_ram
FROM   product_hyb;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+
-- | total_ram |
-- +-----------+
-- |        16 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a JSON column is read as a whole when selected, a covering index cannot cover a JSON path unless it is a generated column, and replication or binlog (row format) records the full document for many updates unless binlog_row_value_options=PARTIAL_JSON is set.
codeExamples:
-- Reduce binlog volume for partial JSON updates (row-based replication)
SET GLOBAL binlog_row_value_options = 'PARTIAL_JSON';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_row_value_options';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------+--------------+
-- | Variable_name            | Value        |
-- +--------------------------+--------------+
-- | binlog_row_value_options | PARTIAL_JSON |
-- +--------------------------+--------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Model the stable core relationally and let JSON carry only genuinely variable attributes; promote a JSON key to a real column the moment it becomes a join key, a frequent filter or a constraint. Document the allowed JSON shape with JSON_SCHEMA_VALID, and keep documents small. If most of your data ends up in JSON and you need cross-document queries, evaluate a document store instead of fighting the relational engine.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Columns win on indexing, constraints, joins and storage efficiency; JSON wins on schema flexibility and nested structures.
  • Updating one JSON key rewrites more data than updating one column (partial update optimizations help).
  • Reporting on JSON fields is slower and more complex.

Senior Notes

  • A common pattern: stable columns plus a JSON "attributes" column for extension, with generated columns for the few fields that get queried.
  • Avoid JSON as a dumping ground; unmanaged shapes become impossible to migrate.
  • Version the JSON shape (schema_version) and validate on write.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: JSON as a dumping ground for everything, using JSON for fields used in joins or foreign keys, and no versioning of the document shape. Add a schema version and validate on write.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Compare query speed for the same filter: a plain indexed column, an indexed generated column over JSON, and a JSON path with no index. The differences are orders of magnitude on large tables.
codeExamples:
-- 10M rows
-- WHERE kind = 'click'                (indexed column)    : 4 ms
-- WHERE kind_gen = 'click'            (indexed generated) : 6 ms
-- WHERE data->>'$.kind' = 'click'     (no index)          : 18 s
SELECT ROUND(18000 / 6) AS slower_without_index;

-- OUTPUT:
-- slower_without_index
-- 3000

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world rule: promote any JSON field that is filtered often, joined, sorted or must be unique into a real column. A migration can do it online with a generated column first, then a real column and backfill.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A FULLTEXT index is an inverted index: it splits text into words (tokens), and for each word stores the list of rows that contain it. It makes word search fast, where LIKE '%word%' would read every row. InnoDB (and MyISAM) support it on CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT columns.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE articles (
  id    INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  title VARCHAR(200),
  body  TEXT,
  FULLTEXT KEY ft_title_body (title, body)        -- one index over two columns
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

INSERT INTO articles (title, body) VALUES
 ('MySQL Tutorial',   'How to install and run MySQL server'),
 ('Optimizing MySQL', 'Indexes make MySQL queries fast'),
 ('Java Streams',     'Functional pipelines in Java'),
 ('Backup Basics',    'Use mysqldump to back up a MySQL database'),
 ('Python Basics',    'Variables loops and functions in Python'),
 ('Cooking Pasta',    'Boil water add salt and pasta'),
 ('Gardening Tips',   'Water plants in the morning');

SHOW INDEX FROM articles WHERE Index_type = 'FULLTEXT';

-- OUTPUT (example, partial columns):
-- +----------+---------------+--------------+-------------+------------+
-- | Table    | Key_name      | Seq_in_index | Column_name | Index_type |
-- +----------+---------------+--------------+-------------+------------+
-- | articles | ft_title_body |            1 | title       | FULLTEXT   |
-- | articles | ft_title_body |            2 | body        | FULLTEXT   |
-- +----------+---------------+--------------+-------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

LIKE '%mysql%' cannot use a B-tree index (leading wildcard), so it scans the whole table, and it knows nothing about words or relevance. A FULLTEXT index turns the same search into an index lookup and can rank the results.

Real-Time Use

Real use: blog, help-centre, product and ticket search. You combine the text match with ordinary filters (category, status, date) in the same WHERE, and tune the index settings (minimum word length, stopwords, ngram parser for Chinese/Japanese/Korean) for your content.
codeExamples:
-- Text match plus a normal filter
SELECT id, title FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql')
  AND  id > 1
ORDER  BY id;

-- Tuning knob (set in my.cnf, then rebuild the index)
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_ft_min_token_size';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------------+
-- | id | title            |
-- +----+------------------+
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL |
-- |  4 | Backup Basics    |
-- +----+------------------+
-- +--------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name            | Value |
-- +--------------------------+-------+
-- | innodb_ft_min_token_size | 3     |
-- +--------------------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   row 1: "MySQL Tutorial ... install and run MySQL server"
   row 2: "Optimizing MySQL ... Indexes make MySQL queries fast"
   row 4: "Backup Basics ... Use mysqldump to back up a MySQL database"
                |
        tokenise (drop stopwords, words shorter than 3 chars)
                v
   inverted index                  word        -> rows (+ positions)
   +--------------------------+    mysql       -> 1, 2, 4
   | ft_title_body            |    tutorial    -> 1
   +--------------------------+    optimizing  -> 2
                                   backup     -> 4
   MATCH(...) AGAINST('mysql') = lookup 'mysql' -> rows 1,2,4 (ranked)

Fresher Notes

  • A FULLTEXT index lets MySQL search words inside text columns quickly, instead of slow LIKE "%word%".
  • Create: CREATE FULLTEXT INDEX ft ON articles (title, body);.
  • Works on CHAR, VARCHAR and TEXT columns in InnoDB.

Worked Example 1

ngram parser.

Worked Example 2

Inspect index words.

Practice Exercise 1

Create and search.

Practice Exercise 2

Check token size.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_ft%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- innodb_ft_min_token_size | 3
-- innodb_ft_enable_stopword| ON

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

InnoDB FULLTEXT builds an inverted index in auxiliary tables: for each token it keeps the document ids (rowids) and positions, plus statistics for ranking. New data goes first to an in-memory cache and is merged into the index in the background; deletes are recorded and purged later. Queries read tokens from the index instead of scanning rows.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: innodb_ft_min_token_size (default 3), innodb_ft_enable_stopword, custom stopword tables, ft_boolean_syntax, and the ngram parser for CJK text. Changing token size requires rebuilding the index.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: built in (no extra servers), transactional storage, automatic maintenance when rows change, relevance ranking, and it combines with SQL joins and filters.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title,
       MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql') AS score      -- relevance as a float
FROM   articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql')
ORDER  BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT (example; the exact scores differ):
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+
-- | id | title            | score              |
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial   | 0.3646776080131531 |
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL | 0.3646776080131531 |
-- |  4 | Backup Basics    | 0.1823388040065765 |
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it matches whole tokens only: no stemming (optimizing and optimize are different words), no typo tolerance, no synonyms and no partial-word match in natural language mode.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysq');       -- partial word
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('optimize');    -- stem differs

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: words shorter than innodb_ft_min_token_size (3) and stopwords (a, the, and, ...) are not indexed; the MATCH column list must equal a FULLTEXT index; and a changed token size or stopword list needs the index rebuilt.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.INNODB_FT_DEFAULT_STOPWORD LIMIT 3;   -- never indexed

SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title) AGAINST('mysql');            -- no index on title alone

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | value |
-- +-------+
-- | a     |
-- | about |
-- | an    |
-- +-------+
-- ERROR 1191 (HY000): Can't find FULLTEXT index matching the column list

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Full-text is excellent for "search box over one database" at millions of rows. Decide analysers up front (minimum token size, stopword table, ngram for CJK) because changing them means a rebuild. Remember that heavy bulk loads are faster with the index added afterwards, and that the index maintains an in-memory cache that is merged lazily (OPTIMIZE TABLE with innodb_optimize_fulltext_only can compact it).

Mid-Level Notes

  • The index stores words (tokens) and where they occur.
  • Short words (under innodb_ft_min_token_size, default 3) and stop words are not indexed.
  • Changes are visible after commit; very large loads should create the index afterwards.

Senior Notes

  • Tune tokenization with stopword tables and token sizes; use the ngram parser for Chinese/Japanese/Korean.
  • InnoDB FULLTEXT adds write overhead and uses an auxiliary cache; bulk load then index for speed.
  • For ranking, typo tolerance and faceting use a dedicated search engine.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting 2-letter words or stop words to match, building the index row by row during a huge load (create it after), searching columns that do not match the index definition, and LIKE '%word%' instead of MATCH. Match exactly the indexed column set.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title) AGAINST ('indexes');       -- index is on (title, body): not usable for title alone
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('indexes');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1191 (HY000): Can't find FULLTEXT index matching the column list

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

FULLTEXT adds write overhead and index size. For bulk loads create the index afterwards, and run OPTIMIZE TABLE to merge pending changes and purge deleted entries when needed.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a help centre search over thousands of articles, ranked by relevance and restricted to published pages, returned with a short snippet.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title, LEFT(body, 120) AS snippet, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('refund policy') AS score FROM articles WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED' AND MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('refund policy') ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title          | snippet                    | score
-- 12 | Refund policy  | How and when refunds are...| 3.4

beginner.content:
Introduction

MATCH(col1, col2) AGAINST('words' [mode]) is the query side of a FULLTEXT index. In a WHERE clause it filters; in a SELECT list it returns a floating-point relevance score (0 means no match). The default mode is natural language.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE docs (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, title VARCHAR(100), body TEXT,
  FULLTEXT KEY ft (title, body)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO docs (title, body) VALUES
 ('MySQL Tutorial',   'How to install and run MySQL server'),
 ('Optimizing MySQL', 'Indexes make MySQL queries fast'),
 ('Backup Basics',    'Use mysqldump to back up a MySQL database'),
 ('Java Streams',     'Functional pipelines in Java'),
 ('Cooking Pasta',    'Boil water add salt and pasta'),
 ('Gardening Tips',   'Water plants in the morning');

SELECT id, title FROM docs
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('install')
ORDER  BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+----------------+
-- | id | title          |
-- +----+----------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial |
-- +----+----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Search results must be ordered by how well they match, not by id. MATCH returns that score, so "best first" needs no extra code. Several words in the query are treated as alternatives: a row matching more of them (or matching rarer ones) ranks higher.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title,
       MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql backup') AS score
FROM   docs
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql backup')       -- same expression: computed once
ORDER  BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT (example; scores vary with the data):
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+
-- | id | title            | score              |
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+
-- |  3 | Backup Basics    | 0.7133517265319824 |
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial   | 0.3646776080131531 |
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL | 0.3646776080131531 |
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: the user types a search string into the application; you bind it as a parameter (never concatenate it) and return the top N with a score cut-off. Always keep the user's text in the AGAINST argument, which is a constant at execution time.
codeExamples:
SET @q = 'mysql server';                              -- value comes from the application

SELECT id, title
FROM   docs
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST(@q)
ORDER  BY MATCH(title, body) AGAINST(@q) DESC
LIMIT  2;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+------------------+
-- | id | title            |
-- +----+------------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial   |
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL |
-- +----+------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   user text ---> AGAINST('mysql backup')
                       |
                       v
   tokenise -> look each word up in the inverted index
                       |
              rows containing ANY word  (natural language mode)
                       |
              score = f(term frequency, rarity, field length)
                       v
   WHERE keeps score > 0       ORDER BY score DESC     LIMIT n

Fresher Notes

  • MATCH(col1, col2) AGAINST ("words") searches a FULLTEXT index and returns a relevance score.
  • The columns in MATCH must match a FULLTEXT index definition.
  • Use it in WHERE to filter and in SELECT or ORDER BY to rank.

Worked Example 1

Plan check.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type     | key         | Extra
-- fulltext | ft_articles | Using where; Ft_hints: sorted

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Filter plus rank.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE status = 'PUBLISHED' AND MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('backup') ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Ranked results.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql indexes') AS score FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql indexes') ORDER BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title        | score
--  1 | Index tuning | 0.62

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Prepared parameter.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MATCH(columns) AGAINST('search') queries a FULLTEXT index. In natural language mode the search string is split into tokens, rows are scored by token frequency (TF-IDF style, rare words weigh more) and only rows with a positive score match. The same expression used in SELECT or ORDER BY returns the relevance score without a second index lookup.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql indexes') AS score FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql indexes') ORDER BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title        | score
--  1 | Index tuning | 0.62

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Modes: IN NATURAL LANGUAGE MODE (default), IN BOOLEAN MODE, WITH QUERY EXPANSION. Combine with ordinary conditions, joins and LIMIT. Pass the search text as a bound parameter.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a SQL-native ranked search that can be mixed with joins, filters and LIMIT; when the same MATCH expression appears in WHERE and ORDER BY, the engine evaluates it once.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.id, d.title
FROM   docs d
JOIN   (SELECT 3 AS id) pick ON pick.id = d.id          -- join with ordinary data
WHERE  MATCH(d.title, d.body) AGAINST('mysqldump');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------------+
-- | id | title         |
-- +----+---------------+
-- |  3 | Backup Basics |
-- +----+---------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: scores are relative to the whole corpus, so they cannot be compared across different queries or stored as absolute values. Also, InnoDB indexes only committed data: a row inserted in an open transaction is not found by full-text search until the commit.

Limitations

Limitations: the MATCH column list must match a FULLTEXT index exactly; the AGAINST argument must be a constant or a variable, not a column of another table (so no row-by-row "find similar" join); and the 'mysql' style words must be at least the minimum token length.
codeExamples:
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM   docs a JOIN docs b
  ON   MATCH(b.title) AGAINST(a.title);                  -- column as search text

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1210 (HY000): Incorrect arguments to AGAINST

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Wrap search in a thin repository method that validates and bounds user input (length, count), binds it as a parameter, and always applies LIMIT. Do not expose raw scores to users and do not build features that depend on a score being stable between releases. If you need joins by similarity or per-row matching, full-text in MySQL is the wrong tool.

Mid-Level Notes

  • The default mode is natural language; add IN BOOLEAN MODE for operators and WITH QUERY EXPANSION for related terms.
  • Relevance is a float; higher means a better match.
  • In natural mode, words appearing in more than 50% of rows are ignored (not in boolean mode).

Senior Notes

  • Always parameterize the search string; never concatenate user input into the query.
  • Combine relevance with other filters (status, date) and paginate with keyset where possible.
  • Check EXPLAIN: the fulltext access type should be used.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: the 50% rule (in natural mode words occurring in more than half the rows are ignored, which surprises tests on tiny tables), concatenating user input into AGAINST, and ordering by something other than the score. Use boolean mode for tiny datasets or tests.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql');                           -- 'mysql' appears in most of 2 rows: ignored
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql' IN BOOLEAN MODE);              -- works

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set
-- id
-- 1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

MATCH is evaluated through the index (look for access type fulltext). Filtering by other columns happens after the fulltext lookup, so keep result sets selective, and paginate with LIMIT.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('refund') AND status = 'PUBLISHED' ORDER BY id LIMIT 10;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type     | key         | Extra
-- fulltext | ft_articles | Using where; Ft_hints: sorted

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: combine relevance with recency, so fresh articles rank higher among similar scores.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('release notes') * (1 + 1 / (1 + DATEDIFF(NOW(), published_at))) AS ranked FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('release notes') ORDER BY ranked DESC LIMIT 10;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title            | ranked
-- 31 | Release notes 5.2| 2.71

beginner.content:
Introduction

Natural language mode (the default) treats the query as free text: any word may match and rows are ranked by relevance. Boolean mode (IN BOOLEAN MODE) lets you write rules with operators: + must contain, - must not contain, * prefix wildcard, "..." exact phrase, > and < raise or lower a word's weight, and ( ) grouping.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE articles (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, title VARCHAR(100), body TEXT,
  FULLTEXT KEY ft (title, body)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO articles (title, body) VALUES
 ('MySQL Tutorial',   'How to install and run MySQL server'),
 ('Optimizing MySQL', 'Indexes make MySQL queries fast'),
 ('Java Streams',     'Functional pipelines in Java'),
 ('Backup Basics',    'Use mysqldump to back up a MySQL database'),
 ('Python Basics',    'Variables loops and functions in Python'),
