 ('Cooking Pasta',    'Boil water add salt and pasta'),
 ('Gardening Tips',   'Water plants in the morning');

-- must contain mysql, must NOT contain backup
SELECT id, title FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('+mysql -backup' IN BOOLEAN MODE)
ORDER  BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------------+
-- | id | title            |
-- +----+------------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial   |
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL |
-- +----+------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Users want precise searches ("both words", "exclude this", "exact phrase", "starts with"). Natural language mode cannot express them, and without operators every extra word widens the result instead of narrowing it.
codeExamples:
-- Natural language: OR semantics, widens the result
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('java python') ORDER BY id;

-- Boolean: AND semantics, narrows the result
SELECT id FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('+java +python' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  3 |
-- |  5 |
-- +----+
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: an advanced-search box. A prefix wildcard gives type-ahead style matching, a quoted phrase finds "mysql server" as adjacent words, and plain words without operators remain optional (OR).
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('optim*' IN BOOLEAN MODE);         -- prefix: Optimizing

SELECT id, title FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('"mysql server"' IN BOOLEAN MODE); -- exact phrase

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------------+
-- | id | title            |
-- +----+------------------+
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL |
-- +----+------------------+
-- +----+----------------+
-- | id | title          |
-- +----+----------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial |
-- +----+----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

                      NATURAL LANGUAGE            BOOLEAN
   input              'mysql backup'              '+mysql -oracle "full text" opt*'
   default logic      OR                          words optional, operators decide
   operators          none                        + - * "" ( ) > < ~
   result order       by relevance                not guaranteed (use ORDER BY score)
   typical use        search box                  advanced search / filters

Fresher Notes

  • Natural language mode ranks documents by similarity to the words. Boolean mode lets you use operators such as + (must), - (must not), * (wildcard) and "phrase".
  • Example: AGAINST ("+mysql -oracle" IN BOOLEAN MODE).
  • Natural mode is the default.

Worked Example 1

Phrase search.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('"binary logs"' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Bad syntax from raw user input.

Practice Exercise 1

Boolean operators.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('+mysql -backup' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title
--  1 | Index tuning

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Prefix wildcard.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('index*' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Natural language mode ranks documents by similarity and ignores operators; the 50% threshold removes very common words. Boolean mode evaluates operators in the search string: + must contain, - must not, * prefix wildcard, "..." exact phrase, > < ( ) weighting and grouping. It has no 50% rule, and does not sort by relevance automatically.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Combine terms with weights and grouping: +mysql +(index replication) means mysql and either index or replication; >word raises and <word lowers relevance. Use ORDER BY MATCH(...) to sort by score in boolean mode.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('+mysql >index <replication' IN BOOLEAN MODE) AS score FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('+mysql >index <replication' IN BOOLEAN MODE) ORDER BY score DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title        | score
--  1 | Index tuning | 0.55

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of boolean mode: explicit control, prefix search, phrases, exclusion, and weight tweaks. Advantages of natural language: zero syntax to learn and relevance-ranked output for casual queries.
codeExamples:
-- Boost one word over another with > and <
SELECT id, title,
       MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('>mysql <backup' IN BOOLEAN MODE) AS score
FROM   articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql backup' IN BOOLEAN MODE)
ORDER  BY score DESC, id;

-- OUTPUT (example; scores vary):
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+
-- | id | title            | score              |
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+
-- |  1 | MySQL Tutorial   | 0.7293552160263062 |
-- |  2 | Optimizing MySQL | 0.7293552160263062 |
-- |  4 | Backup Basics    | 0.3646776080131531 |
-- +----+------------------+--------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the operator syntax is strict, so raw user input containing stray symbols such as a trailing plus can raise a syntax error; without ORDER BY the boolean results are not guaranteed to be sorted by relevance; and you must sanitise or escape operator characters if you want plain-text behaviour.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('mysql +' IN BOOLEAN MODE);       -- dangling operator

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): syntax error, unexpected $end

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: stopwords and short words still are not indexed, and a required stopword makes the whole query return nothing. A leading wildcard (*sql) is not supported, so suffix search needs a different technique (for example an extra reversed-text column).
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('+the +mysql' IN BOOLEAN MODE);  -- 'the' is a stopword

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Offer natural language by default and boolean as an explicit "advanced" option. Never pass user input unchanged into boolean mode: strip or escape the operator characters, or build the boolean string yourself from validated tokens. Test the empty-result and stopword behaviours explicitly, since they are the most common support complaints.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Boolean mode does not sort by relevance automatically and has no 50% threshold.
  • Wildcard * only works at the end of a word: data*.
  • Phrases in double quotes need all words adjacent.

Senior Notes

  • Parse user queries into safe boolean expressions (escape or strip operators) to avoid syntax errors and abuse.
  • Offer natural mode for simple search boxes and boolean for advanced search.
  • Add application-side ranking if relevance alone is not enough.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: passing raw user input into boolean mode (syntax errors from stray operators), expecting stop words to match inside phrases, and using wildcards at the start of a word (not supported). Sanitize or build the boolean expression from validated tokens.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('mysql +' IN BOOLEAN MODE);
-- safer: strip operators from user text and add your own
-- tokens = ['mysql', 'index']  ->  '+mysql* +index*'

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1064 (42000): syntax error, unexpected $end

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Boolean mode can run without a FULLTEXT index (slowly, scanning). Keep the index for real workloads. Prefix searches (word*) are efficient because the token list is sorted.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('repl*' IN BOOLEAN MODE);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type     | key         | Extra
-- fulltext | ft_articles | Using where; Ft_hints: no_ranking

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: advanced search form. Required terms, excluded terms and an exact phrase map to boolean operators built safely in the application.
codeExamples:
-- user entered: must have "replication", exclude "oracle", phrase "binary log"
SELECT id, title FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('+replication* -oracle +"binary log"' IN BOOLEAN MODE) LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title
--  2 | Backup guide

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL full-text is a feature inside your database; Elasticsearch / OpenSearch is a separate distributed search engine built on Lucene. Both use inverted indexes, but a search engine adds analysers (stemming, synonyms, language rules), fuzzy matching, faceting and horizontal scaling.
codeExamples:
-- Assumes the articles table (id, title, body, FULLTEXT ft_title_body) with 7 rows
-- MySQL: word search with ranking
SELECT id, title FROM articles
WHERE  MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('database backup')
ORDER  BY MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('database backup') DESC LIMIT 3;

-- Elasticsearch / OpenSearch: the same intent as a JSON request
-- GET /articles/_search
-- { "query": { "multi_match": { "query": "database backup",
--                               "fields": ["title^2", "body"],
--                               "fuzziness": "AUTO" } },
--   "size": 3 }

-- OUTPUT (MySQL, example):
-- +----+---------------+
-- | id | title         |
-- +----+---------------+
-- |  4 | Backup Basics |
-- +----+---------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Choose by requirements. MySQL full-text suffices when search is one feature of an app with moderate data. A search engine is needed for typo tolerance, language-aware stemming, synonyms, autocomplete, faceted counts, geo search, or search over hundreds of millions of documents.
codeExamples:
-- A typo: MySQL has no fuzziness
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST('backpu');

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

-- Elasticsearch with "fuzziness": "AUTO" would still return "Backup Basics"
-- (it measures edit distance between 'backpu' and 'backup').

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: the database stays the single source of truth, and a search engine is a derived index. Changes are published through a transactional outbox table written in the same transaction as the data; a worker reads it and updates the search index.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE search_outbox (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  article_id INT NOT NULL,
  op ENUM('upsert','delete') NOT NULL,
  sent TINYINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE articles SET title = 'Backup Basics v2' WHERE id = 4;          -- the data change
INSERT INTO search_outbox (article_id, op) VALUES (4, 'upsert');      -- same transaction
COMMIT;

-- Worker: claim a batch without blocking other workers
SELECT id, article_id, op FROM search_outbox
WHERE  sent = 0 ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------+--------+
-- | id | article_id | op     |
-- +----+------------+--------+
-- |  1 |          4 | upsert |
-- +----+------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   WRITE PATH                                       READ PATH
   app --> MySQL (source of truth)                  app --> search box
            |  one transaction                          |
            +--> data row                      small/medium:  MySQL MATCH ... AGAINST
            +--> search_outbox row             large/fuzzy:   Elasticsearch / OpenSearch
                      |
                 worker (poll / CDC)  ---->  search index (derived, rebuildable)
                                              lag = seconds (eventual consistency)

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL FULLTEXT gives basic keyword search inside your database. Elasticsearch/OpenSearch are dedicated search engines with advanced relevance and scale.
  • Use MySQL FULLTEXT for small to medium, simple search needs.
  • Use a search engine when search is a core feature.

Worked Example 1

OpenSearch query equivalent of a typo-tolerant search (REST).
codeExamples:
GET /articles/_search
{ "query": { "multi_match": { "query": "indxes", "fields": ["title^2","body"], "fuzziness": "AUTO" } } }

-- OUTPUT:
-- hits: [{ "_id": "1", "_score": 1.4, "_source": { "title": "Index tuning v2" } }]

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Mark processed after indexing.

Practice Exercise 1

MySQL side: outbox row written in the same transaction.

Practice Exercise 2

Relay reads pending rows.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, entity_id FROM search_outbox WHERE processed_at IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | entity_id
--  7 | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL FULLTEXT is a feature of the database engine: transactional, in the same data store, no extra infrastructure. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch are distributed search engines built around Lucene: analyzers per language, fuzzy matching, synonyms, faceting, highlighting and horizontal scaling, at the cost of running and syncing a second system.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL
SELECT id FROM articles WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('refnd' IN BOOLEAN MODE);              -- typo: no result
-- OpenSearch
-- GET /articles/_search {"query": {"match": {"body": {"query": "refnd", "fuzziness": "AUTO"}}}}

-- OUTPUT:
-- MySQL: Empty set          OpenSearch: hit "Refund policy" (fuzzy match)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Typical architecture: MySQL is the source of truth; changes are copied to the search index through a transactional outbox or change data capture; the application queries the search engine for ids and ranks, then loads full rows from MySQL by primary key.

expert.content:
Advantages

MySQL advantages: no extra system to run, same transaction and security model, joins with relational data, instantly consistent after commit. Engine advantages: rich analysis, fuzzy and phrase scoring (BM25), facets, scalable shards and replicas, and no load on the OLTP database.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL: search and relational data in one statement
SELECT a.id, a.title, c.name AS category
FROM   articles a
JOIN   (SELECT 4 AS id, 'Operations' AS name) c ON c.id = a.id
WHERE  MATCH(a.title, a.body) AGAINST('mysqldump');

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------------+------------+
-- | id | title            | category   |
-- +----+------------------+------------+
-- |  4 | Backup Basics v2 | Operations |
-- +----+------------------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

MySQL disadvantages: no stemming, typo tolerance or synonyms, basic relevance, and search load shares CPU and buffer pool with transactions. Engine disadvantages: a second cluster to operate and secure, eventual consistency (search lags the database), and a pipeline that can fail or drift.
codeExamples:
-- Monitoring the lag of the search pipeline: unsent changes and the oldest one
SELECT COUNT(*) AS backlog, MIN(created_at) AS oldest
FROM   search_outbox WHERE sent = 0;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------+---------------------+
-- | backlog | oldest              |
-- +---------+---------------------+
-- |       1 | 2026-10-06 09:14:02 |
-- +---------+---------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL full-text lives on one server (no sharding of the index; replicas copy everything), supports few languages out of the box (ngram and MeCab parsers for CJK), and has no built-in facets or aggregations over matches. A search engine is not a database: no multi-row transactions, and you must be able to rebuild the index from MySQL at any time.
codeExamples:
-- Rebuild path: the index must be reproducible from the source of truth
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_to_reindex FROM articles;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+
-- | rows_to_reindex |
-- +-----------------+
-- |               7 |
-- +-----------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Start with MySQL full-text and move to a dedicated engine only when a measured requirement (typo tolerance, language analysis, facets, scale, or protecting OLTP latency) justifies the operational cost. If you do split, keep MySQL authoritative, publish changes through an outbox or binlog-based CDC (not dual writes from the app), make indexing idempotent, and build a full-reindex job from day one.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Search engines add typo tolerance, synonyms, stemming per language, facets, highlighting, autocomplete, custom scoring and horizontal scaling.
  • MySQL FULLTEXT is transactional and needs no extra infrastructure.
  • A search engine is a second system you must keep in sync.

Senior Notes

  • Sync via the transactional outbox or CDC (Debezium) from the binlog; treat MySQL as the source of truth and the search index as a rebuildable projection.
  • Plan reindexing, versioned indexes with aliases, and monitoring of lag.
  • Keep security consistent: filter results by permissions at query time.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: dual-writing from the application without a reliable queue (the two stores diverge), no reindex plan, treating the search index as a source of truth, and ignoring permission filtering in search results. Keep the index rebuildable and filter results by access rules.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Choose by need: small corpus and simple keyword search → MySQL FULLTEXT; large corpus, relevance tuning, typo tolerance, autocomplete and facets → a search engine. Measure query latency and operational cost for both.
codeExamples:
-- 100k articles, simple keyword: MySQL FULLTEXT 8 ms p95
-- 50M documents with facets, fuzzy, highlighting: OpenSearch cluster 40 ms p95, MySQL FULLTEXT not suitable
SELECT TABLE_ROWS FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = 'articles';

-- OUTPUT:
-- TABLE_ROWS
-- 98412

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: product search uses OpenSearch for text and facets (brand, price range, color), then MySQL for the authoritative price and stock of the returned ids.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.id, p.name, p.price, i.qty FROM products p JOIN inventory i ON i.product_id = p.id WHERE p.id IN (101, 204, 317, 412) ORDER BY FIELD(p.id, 101, 204, 317, 412);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id  | name | price  | qty
-- 101 | Pen  |  10.00 | 120

beginner.content:
Introduction

CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE makes a real table that exists only for your connection. It is invisible to other sessions, is not listed by SHOW TABLES, and is dropped automatically when the session ends. You can create it empty or fill it from a query.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer VARCHAR(10), amount INT);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'A',100),(2,'A',300),(3,'B',50),(4,'B',70),(5,'C',500);

CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_top AS                  -- structure + data from a query
SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM   orders GROUP BY customer HAVING SUM(amount) > 100;

SELECT * FROM tmp_top ORDER BY customer;
SHOW TABLES;                                       -- the temporary table is not listed

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------+
-- | customer | total |
-- +----------+-------+
-- | A        |   400 |
-- | B        |   120 |
-- | C        |   500 |
-- +----------+-------+
-- +----------------+
-- | Tables_in_mydb |
-- +----------------+
-- | orders         |
-- +----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Complex work often needs an intermediate result that is reused, indexed or updated step by step: ETL stages, report building, de-duplication, batch processing. A temporary table is private scratch space, so concurrent sessions never collide and no clean-up job is needed.

Real-Time Use

Real use: a multi-step report. Step 1 materialises the heavy aggregation once, step 2 enriches it, step 3 returns the final rows, and the intermediate set can be queried several times without being recomputed.
codeExamples:
-- Step 2: enrich the staged data (a window function avoids reading tmp_top twice)
SELECT customer, total, ROUND(100 * total / SUM(total) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM   tmp_top
ORDER  BY total DESC;

-- Step 3: clean up explicitly when the work unit is done
DROP TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_top;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+-------+------+
-- | customer | total | pct  |
-- +----------+-------+------+
-- | C        |   500 | 49.0 |
-- | A        |   400 | 39.2 |
-- | B        |   120 | 11.8 |
-- +----------+-------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Session A                 Session B
   +-----------------+       +-----------------+
   | tmp_top (own)   |       | tmp_top (own)   |    same name, different tables
   | tmp_ids         |       |                 |
   +--------+--------+       +--------+--------+
            |                         |
            |   permanent tables are shared:   orders, customers ...
            v                         v
   disconnect  --> temp tables dropped automatically

   lookup order:  TEMPORARY table  first,  then permanent table

Fresher Notes

  • A temporary table exists only for your session and is dropped automatically when you disconnect.
  • Create with CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE t (...) or from a query with AS SELECT.
  • Other sessions cannot see it; the same name can exist in many sessions.

Worked Example 1

Clean up.

Worked Example 2

Name shadowing.
codeExamples:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE emp (id INT);   -- hides the real emp for this session
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Create and use.

Practice Exercise 2

Not visible elsewhere.
codeExamples:
-- another session
SELECT * FROM high_earners;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'shop.high_earners' doesn't exist

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A temporary table is visible only to the session that created it and disappears automatically when the session ends. It lives in the temporary tablespace (InnoDB session temp tablespace) or in memory depending on engine settings, is not logged for crash recovery, and its name can shadow a permanent table in that session.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Forms: explicit column list, LIKE an existing table, AS SELECT, with engine and indexes. Reopening the same temporary table twice in one query is not allowed (use a copy). DROP TEMPORARY TABLE removes only temporary tables.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: per-session isolation (two sessions can each have a temp table with the same name), automatic cleanup, only the CREATE TEMPORARY TABLES privilege is needed, and temp tables are not written to the redo log like permanent tables, so they are cheap to fill. A temp table can even shadow a permanent table of the same name.
codeExamples:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE orders (x INT);           -- hides the real orders in THIS session
SELECT * FROM orders;
DROP TEMPORARY TABLE orders;                      -- the TEMPORARY keyword is the safety net
SELECT COUNT(*) AS real_rows FROM orders;         -- the permanent table is back

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)
-- +-----------+
-- | real_rows |
-- +-----------+
-- |         5 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the table belongs to one connection. After a reconnect, or when a connection pool or proxy hands you a different physical connection, it is gone, which causes intermittent "table doesn't exist" errors. Writing replicated statements that use temp tables also needs care with statement-based binary logging.
codeExamples:
-- Session 1:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE t1 (a INT);
-- (connection drops and the pool gives you a new one)
-- Session 2:
SELECT * FROM t1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1146 (42S02): Table 'mydb.t1' doesn't exist

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a temporary table cannot be referenced twice in one query (a self-join fails), cannot be renamed with RENAME TABLE (use ALTER TABLE ... RENAME), cannot be used in a view, and cannot have foreign keys.

Architect's Notes

Use temporary tables for bounded, single-connection pipelines: ETL steps, large intermediate sets that need indexes, or work you want to inspect between steps. Always DROP TEMPORARY TABLE at the end of a unit of work, name them with a clear prefix (tmp_), and avoid them behind transaction-mode connection poolers or proxies that multiplex sessions. In replicated setups prefer ROW binlog format, where temporary tables are not replicated at all.

Mid-Level Notes

  • A temporary table can hide a permanent table of the same name for your session.
  • You can index it, insert, update and join like a normal table.
  • Drop it early with DROP TEMPORARY TABLE to release resources.

Senior Notes

  • With connection pools, session state persists across requests; leftover temp tables or name clashes cause bugs. Always drop them explicitly.
  • Temp tables use memory (TempTable engine) then spill to disk; large ones affect resources.
  • Replication: with statement-based binlog, temp tables are replicated via session; prefer ROW format and avoid temp tables across statements in sensitive setups.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: leaving temp tables in pooled connections (the next request inherits them), name collisions with real tables, and using them across sessions (invisible). Always drop explicitly and use unique names.
codeExamples:
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE emp (id INT);          -- shadows the real table in this session
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp;
DROP TEMPORARY TABLE emp;                       -- restore access to the real table

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Temporary tables of any real size consume the session tablespace and I/O. Monitor temp usage and size them to fit; with replication in statement format, avoid relying on temporary tables across transactions.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an ETL step that loads a CSV into a temporary table, validates and transforms it with SQL, then merges into the permanent table in one transaction.

topics.name: Temporary Table vs CTE vs Permanent Table

beginner.content:
Introduction

Three ways to hold an intermediate result. A CTE lives for one statement. A temporary table lives for one session. A permanent (staging) table lives until someone drops it and is visible to everyone with privileges.

Why Do We Need This?

The choice decides who can see the data, how long it lives, whether it can be indexed, and what it does to your transaction. Picking wrongly means stale staging tables, lost data after reconnects, or silent commits in the middle of a transaction.
codeExamples:
-- Reuse across statements: only the table forms keep the data
SELECT SUM(s) AS grand_total FROM tmp_x;           -- statement 1 uses tmp_x
SELECT COUNT(*) AS regions    FROM tmp_x;          -- statement 2 reuses it, no recompute

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+
-- | grand_total |
-- +-------------+
-- |         160 |
-- +-------------+
-- +---------+
-- | regions |
-- +---------+
-- |       2 |
-- +---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: a nightly load. Data is first loaded into a permanent staging table (so it survives crashes and can be inspected by DBAs), validated, then swapped into the live table. A reporting page uses a CTE for readability. A long one-connection batch job uses a temporary table.
codeExamples:
-- Staging pattern: load, validate, then publish
CREATE TABLE stg_sales_load LIKE sales;
INSERT INTO stg_sales_load SELECT * FROM sales WHERE amt >= 20;       -- stand-in for a bulk load

SELECT COUNT(*) AS bad_rows FROM stg_sales_load WHERE amt IS NULL;    -- validation

RENAME TABLE sales TO sales_old, stg_sales_load TO sales;             -- atomic swap
SELECT COUNT(*) AS live_rows FROM sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | bad_rows |
-- +----------+
-- |        0 |
-- +----------+
-- +-----------+
-- | live_rows |
-- +-----------+
-- |         4 |
-- +-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

                  lifetime           visible to      indexable   transaction effect
   CTE            1 statement        that statement  no          none
   TEMP TABLE     1 session          this session    yes         CREATE does not commit
   PERMANENT      until DROP         everyone        yes         CREATE = implicit COMMIT

   readability, one query ------------------------>  CTE
   big / reused / index needed, one connection ---->  TEMPORARY TABLE
   must survive crash, inspect, share, audit ------>  permanent staging table

Fresher Notes

  • A permanent table is stored until dropped and visible to all sessions. A temporary table lasts for one session. A CTE lasts for one statement and stores nothing.
  • Use permanent tables for real data, temporary tables for session work and CTEs for readable queries.
  • They differ in lifetime, visibility and storage.

Worked Example 1

Idempotent merge from staging.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total) SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM stage_orders s
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE total = s.total;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 120 rows affected

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Temp table disk spill counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Created_tmp_disk_tables';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name           | Value
-- Created_tmp_disk_tables | 18

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Three lifetimes.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE stage_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE 1 = 0;               -- permanent
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE scratch AS SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10;               -- session
WITH cte AS (SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 10) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cte;          -- statement

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 10

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Permanent staging cleanup.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Three lifetimes: a CTE exists for one statement and is not stored; a temporary table exists for one session; a permanent table exists until dropped and is shared, logged and recoverable. They differ in visibility, durability, indexability and overhead.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE stage_orders (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, total DECIMAL(12,2));              -- permanent, shared, crash safe
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE scratch_orders LIKE stage_orders;                              -- session only
WITH c AS (SELECT id, total FROM orders LIMIT 10) SELECT COUNT(*) FROM c;             -- statement only

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 10

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Use a permanent staging table for pipelines that must survive crashes, be inspected, be shared by several workers or be resumable. Use a temporary table for fast private scratch work and a CTE for readable single-statement logic.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: CTE - best readability, may be merged into the outer query, supports recursion. Temporary table - indexable, reusable, private, no cleanup job. Permanent table - durable, visible to other sessions and tools, can be partitioned, backed up and audited.
codeExamples:
-- A CTE used twice in one statement: written once, so the logic cannot diverge
WITH t AS (SELECT region, SUM(amt) AS s FROM stg_x GROUP BY region)
SELECT 'max' AS kind, region FROM t WHERE s = (SELECT MAX(s) FROM t)
UNION ALL
SELECT 'min', region FROM t WHERE s = (SELECT MIN(s) FROM t);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+--------+
-- | kind | region |
-- +------+--------+
-- | max  | S      |
-- | min  | N      |
-- +------+--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: CTE - cannot be indexed or reused in the next statement. Temporary table - tied to a connection, extra write cost, awkward with pooling. Permanent staging table - must be cleaned up, collides if two jobs use the same name, and old ones accumulate.
codeExamples:
-- Forgotten staging tables pile up; list them for a clean-up review
SELECT table_name, table_rows
FROM   information_schema.tables
WHERE  table_schema = DATABASE() AND table_name LIKE 'stg%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME    | TABLE_ROWS |
-- +---------------+------------+
-- | stg_x         |          2 |
-- +---------------+------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: creating a permanent table is DDL, and DDL causes an implicit commit that ends your open transaction; a temporary table does not. This is the most important practical difference.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE audit (n INT) ENGINE=InnoDB;

START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO audit VALUES (1);
CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_a (a INT);              -- no implicit commit
ROLLBACK;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS after_temp FROM audit;          -- insert was undone

START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO audit VALUES (2);
CREATE TABLE perm_b (b INT);                       -- DDL: implicit COMMIT
ROLLBACK;                                          -- nothing left to roll back
SELECT COUNT(*) AS after_perm FROM audit;          -- insert survived

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | after_temp |
-- +------------+
-- |          0 |
-- +------------+
-- +------------+
-- | after_perm |
-- +------------+
-- |          1 |
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Default to CTEs, move to a temporary table when EXPLAIN or the slow log shows a repeated expensive intermediate or a missing index, and use permanent staging tables for durable multi-step pipelines with explicit batch ids and a clean-up policy. Never create permanent tables inside a transaction you expect to roll back, and in pooled or proxied environments avoid session-bound state altogether.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Permanent staging tables are good for ETL steps that must survive restarts and be inspected.
  • Temporary tables are lighter for scratch work but vanish on disconnect.
  • CTEs cost nothing to store and cannot be indexed.

Senior Notes

  • Choose by durability and reuse: crash-safe pipeline stages = permanent; fast scratch space = temporary; single query clarity = CTE.
  • Permanent staging tables need cleanup jobs and naming per run to avoid collisions.
  • Monitor temp table spill (Created_tmp_disk_tables) for heavy temp work.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: permanent staging tables never cleaned (they accumulate), temp tables for work that must survive a disconnect, and CTEs reused many times without checking materialization. Name staging tables by run and clean up in a finally step.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, create_time FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' AND table_name LIKE 'stage\_%' AND create_time < NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name               | create_time
-- stage_orders_20260401    | 2026-04-01 02:00:11       (stale: drop it)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost model: permanent tables write to the redo log and binlog (replicated, durable); temporary tables skip most of that and are faster; CTEs write nothing unless materialized. Pick the lightest tool that satisfies durability and reuse needs.
codeExamples:
-- 5M row intermediate result, 6 later steps reuse it
-- CTE recomputed 6x : 6 x 14 s = 84 s
-- temp table        : 14 s build + 6 x 1 s = 20 s
-- permanent table   : 22 s build (redo + binlog) + 6 x 1 s = 28 s, but survives a crash
SELECT 84 - 20 AS seconds_saved_by_temp_table;

-- OUTPUT:
-- seconds_saved_by_temp_table
-- 64

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nightly aggregation pipeline stages raw data in a permanent table (so a failed run can resume), transforms with CTEs, and uses temporary tables for expensive joins reused within the job.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO daily_summary (day, channel, orders, revenue)
WITH base AS (SELECT DATE(created_at) AS day, channel, total FROM stage_orders WHERE created_at >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 1 DAY)
SELECT day, channel, COUNT(*), SUM(total) FROM base GROUP BY day, channel
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE orders = VALUES(orders), revenue = VALUES(revenue);

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 12 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

In MySQL an account is the pair 'user'@'host': the same name from a different host is a different account. CREATE USER makes it (with an authentication plugin, default caching_sha2_password in 8.0), ALTER USER changes password, lock state, limits and TLS rules, and DROP USER removes it with all its privileges.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'app'@'10.0.%'                       -- may connect only from 10.0.x.x
  IDENTIFIED BY 'S3cret!passw0rd'
  PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL 90 DAY                 -- force rotation every 90 days
  FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS 5 PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME 1;   -- lock 1 day after 5 bad logins (8.0.19+)

SELECT user, host, plugin, password_expired, account_locked
FROM   mysql.user WHERE user = 'app';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+--------+-----------------------+------------------+----------------+
-- | user | host   | plugin                | password_expired | account_locked |
-- +------+--------+-----------------------+------------------+----------------+
-- | app  | 10.0.% | caching_sha2_password | N                | N              |
-- +------+--------+-----------------------+------------------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Every client must be identifiable so that privileges, audit trails and limits are per person or per application, not shared. Because the host is part of the identity, you can allow an account only from the application subnet and keep it useless from anywhere else.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'baji'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'Baji!Pass12345';
CREATE USER 'baji'@'%'         IDENTIFIED BY 'Other!Pass12345';   -- a different account!

-- Run after connecting as baji:
SELECT USER() AS asked_as, CURRENT_USER() AS matched_account;

-- OUTPUT (example, connecting from another machine):
-- +----------------+-----------------+
-- | asked_as       | matched_account |
-- +----------------+-----------------+
-- | baji@10.0.3.17  | baji@%           |
-- +----------------+-----------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: joiner/leaver processes and service accounts. A new service gets its own account with a connection cap and mandatory TLS. A leaver is locked first (reversible) and dropped later.
codeExamples:
ALTER USER 'app'@'10.0.%'
  REQUIRE SSL                                     -- refuse unencrypted connections
  WITH MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS 20;                   -- cap parallel sessions

SELECT user, host, ssl_type, max_user_connections
FROM   mysql.user WHERE user = 'app';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+--------+----------+----------------------+
-- | user | host   | ssl_type | max_user_connections |
-- +------+--------+----------+----------------------+
-- | app  | 10.0.% | ANY      |                   20 |
-- +------+--------+----------+----------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   client connects as  baji  from 10.0.3.17
        |
        v   mysql.user  (sorted: most specific host first)
   +-----------------+-----------------------------+
   | 'baji'@'10.0.3.%'| plugin, password, TLS, limit|   <- matched first if present
   | 'baji'@'%'       |                             |
   +-----------------+-----------------------------+
        |
        v   authenticate (caching_sha2_password) + lock/expiry checks
        v
   session with CURRENT_USER() = matched account  --> privileges apply

Fresher Notes

  • CREATE USER adds an account, ALTER USER changes password or settings, DROP USER removes it.
  • An account is user@host; the host part limits where the user can connect from.
  • Always use strong passwords and never share root.

Worked Example 1

Find risky accounts.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE host = '%' OR user = '';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- user | host
-- test | %

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Lock and drop.

Practice Exercise 1

Create with policy.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'svc_app'@'10.0.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'Xk9#mQ2v!zL'
  PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL 90 DAY FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS 5 PASSWORD_LOCK_TIME 1
  WITH MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS 50 REQUIRE SSL;
SELECT user, host, password_lifetime FROM mysql.user WHERE user = 'svc_app';

-- OUTPUT:
-- user    | host   | password_lifetime
-- svc_app | 10.0.% | 90

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Zero-downtime password rotation.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Accounts are rows in the mysql.user system table keyed by user and host. At login the server picks the most specific matching host pattern, runs the authentication plugin (default caching_sha2_password, which stores a salted SHA-256 hash and caches successful verifications) and loads the account's privileges into memory.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Options: authentication plugin, TLS requirement, password expiry and reuse policy, failed-login lockout, resource limits, comment and attributes, default roles. ALTER USER changes any of them; DROP USER removes the account and its grants.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: per-account password policy, expiry, lockout, resource limits and TLS requirements are declarative SQL; ACCOUNT LOCK disables an account while keeping its grants, and RENAME USER moves privileges with it.
codeExamples:
ALTER USER 'app'@'10.0.%' ACCOUNT LOCK;         -- offboarding step 1: reversible
-- A login attempt now fails:

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3118 (HY000): Access denied for user 'app'@'10.0.0.5'. Account is locked.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: dropping a user does not end its open sessions (they keep running until they disconnect or are killed), and objects whose DEFINER was that user (views, routines, triggers, events) fail afterwards.

Limitations

Limitations: user names are at most 32 characters, hosts at most 255; account matching uses the most specific host first (so a stray anonymous or wildcard account can shadow what you expect); and password complexity is enforced only if the validate_password component is installed.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'weak'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'abc';       -- with validate_password enabled

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1819 (HY000): Your password does not satisfy the current policy requirements

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Create one account per application and per human administrator, restrict hosts, require TLS, and set expiry and lockout policies. Prefer ACCOUNT LOCK before DROP USER, check for DEFINER dependencies before dropping, and kill remaining sessions. For large organisations delegate authentication to LDAP/SSO plugins or a secrets manager that rotates credentials, instead of long-lived static passwords.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Useful options: PASSWORD EXPIRE INTERVAL 90 DAY, FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS, WITH MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS, REQUIRE SSL.
  • Lock accounts with ACCOUNT LOCK instead of dropping when you need to preserve grants.
  • Check accounts via SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user.

Senior Notes

  • MySQL 8 supports dual passwords for zero-downtime rotation: RETAIN CURRENT PASSWORD.
  • Use password validation component and external authentication (LDAP, PAM, IAM auth for cloud) for centralized control.
  • Automate account lifecycle with IaC and review accounts periodically; remove anonymous and wildcard-host users.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: wildcard hosts for everything, one shared account for several services, leaving anonymous or test accounts, and rotating passwords with downtime. Use dual passwords and per-service accounts.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Authentication has a cost: the caching plugin makes repeated logins cheap, but connection storms still hurt. Pool connections and avoid per-request logins; monitor aborted connects.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world account lifecycle: create accounts through migration scripts, lock instead of drop when someone leaves (to keep audit history), and review accounts quarterly against an expected list.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host, account_locked, password_last_changed FROM mysql.user WHERE password_last_changed < NOW() - INTERVAL 180 DAY AND user NOT LIKE 'mysql.%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- user  | host | account_locked | password_last_changed
-- jdoe  | %    | N              | 2025-09-12 08:11:00

beginner.content:
Introduction

GRANT gives privileges to an account at a chosen scope: global (*.*), a database (db.*), a table (db.tbl), specific columns, or a routine. REVOKE removes them, and SHOW GRANTS FOR displays what an account has. In MySQL 8 the user must already exist (GRANT no longer creates users).

Why Do We Need This?

Authentication says who you are; authorisation says what you may do. Without GRANT a new account can do nothing except log in (USAGE). Narrow grants limit the damage of a bug, a leaked password or an injection attack.

Real-Time Use

Real use: changing duties. When a team gains write access to one table, grant just that; when a project ends, revoke it. Auditors ask "who can do what", answered by SHOW GRANTS and the privilege tables.
codeExamples:
REVOKE UPDATE ON shop.* FROM 'app'@'%';                -- tighten later
GRANT  SELECT ON shop.customers TO 'report'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION;   -- may pass it on

SELECT grantee, table_schema, privilege_type
FROM   information_schema.schema_privileges
WHERE  grantee = '''app''@''%'''
ORDER  BY privilege_type;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+--------------+----------------+
-- | GRANTEE | TABLE_SCHEMA | PRIVILEGE_TYPE |
-- +---------+--------------+----------------+
-- | 'app'@'%' | shop       | INSERT         |
-- | 'app'@'%' | shop       | SELECT         |
-- +---------+--------------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   scope (widest -> narrowest)            example
   global        *.*                      GRANT SUPER ON *.* ...        (admin)
   database      shop.*                   GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON shop.*
   table         shop.customers           GRANT SELECT ON shop.customers
   column        (id, name)               GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON ...
   routine       PROCEDURE shop.p         GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE ...

   access check =  global OR database OR table OR column privilege (union)
   REVOKE removes exactly what was granted at that scope, nothing more

Fresher Notes

  • GRANT gives privileges, REVOKE removes them, SHOW GRANTS FOR user lists them.
  • Example: GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON shop.* TO "app"@"%";.
  • Privileges can be global, per database, per table or per column.

Worked Example 1

Denied operation.
codeExamples:
-- as shop_app
DROP TABLE shop.emp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): DROP command denied to user 'shop_app'@'localhost' for table 'emp'

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Audit all grants.
codeExamples:
SELECT grantee, table_schema, privilege_type FROM information_schema.schema_privileges ORDER BY grantee;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- grantee         | table_schema | privilege_type
-- 'shop_app'@'%'  | shop         | SELECT

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Least privilege app user.

Practice Exercise 2

Column-level grant and revoke.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Privileges are stored at several levels: global (mysql.user), schema (mysql.db), table, column and routine, plus dynamic privileges. When a statement runs, the server checks the most general level that allows it and falls back to more specific ones. Changes by GRANT and REVOKE take effect for new statements without FLUSH PRIVILEGES.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Granularity: global, per schema, per table, per column (GRANT SELECT (name, dept) ON emp), per routine, plus WITH GRANT OPTION (avoid for apps) and partial revokes. Use roles to attach sets of privileges.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fine-grained (column, table, database, routine), changes by GRANT and REVOKE take effect without restarting the server, and SHOW GRANTS gives a precise, copyable audit.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: broad grants are easy to write and hard to undo (GRANT ALL ON *.* makes an account a de facto administrator), and privileges cached by existing sessions may apply only from the next connection or USE.
codeExamples:
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON *.* TO 'app'@'%';          -- dangerous: global, every privilege
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'app'@'%';

-- OUTPUT (shortened):
-- | GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, RELOAD, SHUTDOWN, PROCESS,
--   FILE, GRANT OPTION, SUPER, ... ON *.* TO 'app'@'%' |
REVOKE ALL PRIVILEGES, GRANT OPTION FROM 'app'@'%';   -- undo it

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: you cannot carve an exception out of a broader grant: revoking one table when the grant is on shop.* fails (MySQL 8.0.16+ has partial revokes only for global grants when partial_revokes is ON). GRANT also cannot create users in MySQL 8 and there are no row-level privileges.
codeExamples:
GRANT SELECT ON shop.* TO 'app'@'%';
REVOKE SELECT ON shop.customers FROM 'app'@'%';           -- grant was at database level
GRANT SELECT ON shop.customers TO 'ghost'@'%';            -- user does not exist

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1147 (42000): There is no such grant defined for user 'app' on host '%'
--   on table 'customers'
-- ERROR 1410 (42000): You are not allowed to create a user with GRANT

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Grant at the narrowest scope that works and avoid ON *.* for anything but DBAs. Store grants as versioned migration scripts (or role definitions) rather than ad-hoc commands, and review SHOW GRANTS periodically. When you need row-level or column masking, put a view with SQL SECURITY DEFINER in front and grant access only to the view.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Grant the minimum required (least privilege); avoid ALL PRIVILEGES and WITH GRANT OPTION for apps.
  • Levels: *.* global, db.*, db.table, column lists.
  • Privilege changes apply to new connections (some to existing sessions at next statement).

Senior Notes

  • Use roles to manage privileges for groups and review grants regularly.
  • Separate accounts for app (DML), migration (DDL), read-only reporting and admin.
  • Audit privilege use with the audit log plugin and alert on privilege changes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: GRANT ALL for applications, granting on *.*, forgetting that revoking a table grant does not remove a schema-level grant that still allows it, and not testing with the real account. Verify with the restricted login.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large privilege tables are cached; thousands of accounts and per-table grants increase memory and slow account loading. Prefer roles and schema-level grants.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world privilege review: list who can do what on the sensitive schema, then compare against an expected baseline in version control.
codeExamples:
SELECT grantee, privilege_type, is_grantable FROM information_schema.schema_privileges WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY grantee, privilege_type;

-- OUTPUT:
-- grantee         | privilege_type | is_grantable
-- 'shop_app'@'%'  | DELETE         | NO
-- 'shop_app'@'%'  | SELECT         | NO

beginner.content:
Introduction

A role is a named bundle of privileges. You create roles, grant privileges to the role, then grant the role to many users. Changing the role's privileges changes every member at once. Roles exist from MySQL 8.0.

Why Do We Need This?

Granting privileges user by user does not scale: 50 analysts means 50 identical GRANT lists that drift apart. Roles model job functions (analyst, support, developer), so onboarding is one statement and audits are readable.

Real-Time Use

Real use: roles per team, activated by default for members, with a server-wide mandatory_roles setting for baseline access. A user can also switch roles for the current session.
codeExamples:
SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO 'ann'@'%';       -- activate granted roles at every login

-- After ann logs in:
SELECT CURRENT_ROLE() AS active_roles;
SET ROLE 'r_read';                          -- narrow down for this session
SELECT CURRENT_ROLE() AS active_roles;

-- OUTPUT (identifiers shown without backticks):
-- +-------------------------+
-- | active_roles            |
-- +-------------------------+
-- | r_read@%,r_write@%      |
-- +-------------------------+
-- +--------------+
-- | active_roles |
-- +--------------+
-- | r_read@%     |
-- +--------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   privileges --GRANT--> role  --GRANT--> user
                                 ^
   r_read  (SELECT)       ---+   |
   r_write (INSERT,...)   ---+---+--> ann   default roles active at login
   r_admin (r_read, r_write, DDL) ---> dba1
                     |
   SET ROLE / SET DEFAULT ROLE decides what is ACTIVE in the session

Fresher Notes

  • A role is a named bundle of privileges that you grant to users: CREATE ROLE reader; GRANT SELECT ON shop.* TO reader; GRANT reader TO user;.
  • Roles make permissions easier to manage for many users.
  • Users must activate roles: SET DEFAULT ROLE or SET ROLE.

Worked Example 1

Mandatory role for everyone.

Worked Example 2

Drop a role.

Practice Exercise 1

Create and use a role.

Practice Exercise 2

Check active role in a session.
codeExamples:
SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();

-- OUTPUT:
-- CURRENT_ROLE()
-- report_ro@%

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A role is an account-like object that holds privileges but cannot log in. Granting a role to a user gives that user the privileges only while the role is active in the session. Roles are stored in mysql.user and the role graph is in mysql.role_edges.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Activate with SET DEFAULT ROLE (at login), SET ROLE (in session), or the activate_all_roles_on_login variable. Roles can be nested; mandatory_roles grants roles to everyone.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: central maintenance, least-privilege sessions (activate only what you need), clearer audits, and a role can include other roles to build a hierarchy.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a granted role is not active until it is made a default role or the user runs SET ROLE. Users who forget this see confusing "access denied" errors right after being granted a role.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'bea'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'Bea!Pass1234567';
GRANT 'r_read' TO 'bea'@'%';                          -- granted, but not a default role

-- Connected as bea:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop.customers;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'bea'@'localhost'
--   for table 'customers'

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: roles are stored as locked accounts that cannot log in; role names share the user namespace (each is 'name'@'host', host defaults to %); and privileges of a role granted after a session started appear only after SET ROLE or reconnect.
codeExamples:
-- Trying to log in as a role
-- mysql -u r_read -p

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 3118 (HY000): Access denied for user 'r_read'@'localhost'. Account is locked.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Define roles by job function, grant privileges only to roles, and attach roles to users; never mix direct grants and role grants for the same duty. Set default roles explicitly (or activate_all_roles_on_login) and document the choice, and use mandatory_roles for the baseline. Keep an admin role separate from day-to-day roles so privileged power is activated deliberately.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Roles are accounts that cannot log in by default (locked), stored in mysql.user.
  • SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO user activates all granted roles at login.
  • Check active roles with SELECT CURRENT_ROLE().

Senior Notes

  • Model roles by job function (app_rw, report_ro, migrator, dba_readonly) and keep them in version control.
  • Combine with host and TLS restrictions at the user level.
  • Avoid role explosion; review unused roles.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: granting a role and expecting immediate effect (it must be active), too many overlapping roles, and managing roles by hand per environment. Keep roles in migration scripts and review them like code.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Roles reduce privilege-table size and administrative errors: change a role once and all members change. Measure by comparing grants per user before and after.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world model: functional roles (app_rw, report_ro, migrator, dba_ro) granted to service accounts, with an access review that lists each user's roles.
codeExamples:
SELECT to_user AS account, GROUP_CONCAT(from_user ORDER BY from_user) AS roles FROM mysql.role_edges GROUP BY to_user;

-- OUTPUT:
-- account  | roles
-- bi       | report_ro
-- shop_app | app_rw

beginner.content:
Introduction

Least privilege means every account gets only the rights its job requires and nothing more. For applications that typically means separate accounts for runtime (DML only), reporting (read only), and schema migration (DDL), never the root account.
codeExamples:
CREATE USER 'shop_app'@'10.0.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'App!Runtime12345';   -- runtime
CREATE USER 'shop_ro'@'10.0.%'  IDENTIFIED BY 'Ro!Report1234567';     -- reports
CREATE USER 'shop_mig'@'10.0.1.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'Mig!Deploy123456';   -- migrations only

GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON shop.* TO 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';
GRANT SELECT                         ON shop.* TO 'shop_ro'@'10.0.%';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES                 ON shop.* TO 'shop_mig'@'10.0.1.%';   -- one schema only

SHOW GRANTS FOR 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';

-- OUTPUT (identifiers shown without backticks):
-- +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | Grants for shop_app@10.0.%                                               |
-- +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+
-- | GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO 'shop_app'@'10.0.%'                                |
-- | GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON shop.* TO 'shop_app'@'10.0.%'    |
-- +--------------------------------------------------------------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Applications get compromised (SQL injection, leaked config, a vulnerable library). The database account is the last line of defence: with DML-only rights an attacker cannot DROP tables, read other schemas, load files or create new users.
codeExamples:
-- Connected as shop_app: the damage an injected statement can do is limited
DROP TABLE shop.customers;
SELECT * FROM mysql.user;
SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): DROP command denied to user 'shop_app'@'10.0.0.5' for table 'customers'
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'shop_app'@'10.0.0.5' for table 'user'
-- +-----------------------+
-- | LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd') |
-- +-----------------------+
-- | NULL                  |
-- +-----------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: the connection string for each service uses its own account, and credentials come from a secrets store. Passwords are rotated without downtime using dual passwords (8.0.14+): the old password keeps working until the fleet has the new one.
codeExamples:
# application.properties (credentials injected from a secret store, not committed)
# spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://db.internal:3306/shop?sslMode=VERIFY_IDENTITY
# spring.datasource.username=shop_app
# spring.datasource.password=<injected at runtime>

-- Zero-downtime rotation
ALTER USER 'shop_app'@'10.0.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'New!Runtime98765' RETAIN CURRENT PASSWORD;
-- ... roll out the new secret to all instances ...
ALTER USER 'shop_app'@'10.0.%' DISCARD OLD PASSWORD;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Internet --> App servers --> MySQL
                  |
   runtime  (shop_app)   DML on shop.*          <- used by the running service
   reports  (shop_ro)    SELECT on views        <- BI tools, analysts
   migrate  (shop_mig)   DDL on shop.*          <- CI/CD pipeline only, restricted host
   admin    (named DBAs) roles, SUPER-like      <- humans, MFA/bastion, audited
        |
   each: restricted host + TLS + rotated secret + connection limit

Fresher Notes

  • Least privilege means each account has only the permissions it needs. Applications should never connect as root.
  • Create a dedicated user per application with rights only on its own schema.
  • Limit the host, enforce TLS and use strong passwords.

Worked Example 1

Find over-privileged accounts.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host FROM mysql.user WHERE Super_priv = 'Y' OR Grant_priv = 'Y' OR File_priv = 'Y';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- user | host
-- root | localhost

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Spring Boot datasource using a dedicated user (config).
codeExamples:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://db.internal:3306/orders?sslMode=VERIFY_IDENTITY
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
spring.datasource.password=(injected from the secrets manager at runtime)

-- OUTPUT:
-- Application connects with minimum privileges over TLS

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

App versus migration accounts.

Practice Exercise 2

Verify an app cannot alter schema.
codeExamples:
-- as orders_app
ALTER TABLE orders.orders ADD COLUMN x INT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): ALTER command denied to user 'orders_app'@'10.0.1.7' for table 'orders'

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Least privilege means every account has exactly the permissions its job needs. An application account normally needs DML (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and EXECUTE on its schema, and nothing else: no DDL, no FILE, no PROCESS, no SUPER or dynamic admin privileges, and no access to other schemas.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Separate accounts by duty: runtime (DML), migration (DDL, used only in the pipeline), read-only reporting, and administrators. Restrict host patterns, require TLS, set connection limits, and keep credentials in a secrets manager.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: smaller blast radius, clear accountability per service, safe reporting access for analysts, and views let you expose only selected columns without any row-level feature in the server.
codeExamples:
CREATE VIEW shop.v_customer_public
  SQL SECURITY DEFINER AS SELECT id, name FROM shop.customers;   -- hides card_no
GRANT SELECT ON shop.v_customer_public TO 'shop_ro'@'10.0.%';

-- Connected as shop_ro:
SELECT * FROM shop.v_customer_public LIMIT 1;
SELECT card_no FROM shop.customers;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | Abaji |
-- +----+-------+
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'shop_ro'@'10.0.0.8' for table 'customers'

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more accounts and grants to manage, more places for a wrong host pattern to lock out a service, and migrations that must run under a separate, more powerful account complicate deployment pipelines.
codeExamples:
-- The runtime account cannot run a schema change - by design
-- Connected as shop_app:
ALTER TABLE shop.customers ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1142 (42000): ALTER command denied to user 'shop_app'@'10.0.0.5' for table 'customers'

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL has no row-level security, so tenant isolation must be done with views, separate schemas or application logic; privileges alone cannot limit a user to certain rows. Also, privilege names like FILE, SUPER, PROCESS and RELOAD are global-only and must never be granted to application accounts.
codeExamples:
-- Audit: which accounts hold powerful global privileges?
SELECT grantee, privilege_type
FROM   information_schema.user_privileges
WHERE  privilege_type IN ('SUPER', 'FILE', 'PROCESS', 'GRANT OPTION')
ORDER  BY grantee;

-- OUTPUT (example; only DBA accounts should appear):
-- +-----------------+----------------+
-- | GRANTEE         | PRIVILEGE_TYPE |
-- +-----------------+----------------+
-- | 'root'@'localhost' | FILE        |
-- | 'root'@'localhost' | GRANT OPTION|
-- | 'root'@'localhost' | PROCESS     |
-- | 'root'@'localhost' | SUPER       |
-- +-----------------+----------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Split accounts by function, restrict by host and require TLS, keep secrets in a vault with dual-password rotation, and run migrations from a pipeline identity that is not available to the running application. Review grants regularly with an automated audit of SUPER, FILE, GRANT OPTION and wildcard-host accounts, and layer defences: parameterised queries first, least privilege second, network controls third.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Typical split: app user (DML), migration user (DDL), read-only reporting user, admin/DBA users.
  • Do not grant FILE, SUPER, PROCESS, GRANT OPTION or global privileges to apps.
  • Use separate accounts per environment and per service.

Senior Notes

  • A compromised app account should not be able to drop tables or read other schemas; combine least privilege with network segmentation and secrets management (Vault, KMS).
  • Rotate credentials and use short-lived credentials (IAM auth, Vault dynamic secrets).
  • Log and alert on connections from unexpected hosts.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: using root in applications, sharing credentials across services, wide host patterns, and over-privileged migration tools left in production. Audit regularly for risky global privileges.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Limit damage from leaked credentials: per-user connection limits, resource limits, network restrictions, short-lived credentials from a vault, and alerts for logins from unusual hosts.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world datasource configuration: a dedicated user, TLS with certificate verification, and the password injected from a secrets manager, not stored in the repository.
codeExamples:
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql://db.internal:3306/orders?sslMode=VERIFY_IDENTITY&connectTimeout=3000
spring.datasource.username=orders_app
spring.datasource.password=(injected at runtime from the secrets manager)

-- OUTPUT:
-- HikariPool-1 - Start completed.   (connected with least privileges over TLS)

beginner.content:
Introduction

SQL injection happens when untrusted input is concatenated into SQL text, so the input is parsed as SQL code instead of a value. The attacker changes the structure of the statement, not just its data.
codeExamples:
-- The application builds this string by concatenation:
--   "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "' AND pwd = '" + pwd + "'"
-- Attacker types:  name = admin' --   (the quote closes the string, -- comments out the rest)
-- The server therefore receives this statement:
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name = 'admin' -- ' AND pwd = 'x';
-- Password check is now a comment -> login succeeds as admin.

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | admin |
-- +----+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Databases cannot tell which parts of a statement the developer meant as code and which came from a user. Understanding the attack is the only way to see why parameter binding (not escaping tricks) is the fix.
codeExamples:
-- Tautology: the classic OR 1=1 turns a filter into "match everything".
-- Input for id:  0 OR 1=1
SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = 0 OR 1=1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----+-------------------+
-- | id | email             |
-- +----+-------------------+
-- |  1 | admin@corp.com    |
-- |  2 | ann@corp.com      |
-- |  3 | baji@corp.com      |
-- +----+-------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real breaches (Heartland, TalkTalk, countless CMS plugins) used injection to dump tables. Typical attack styles: UNION-based data theft, error-based, boolean/time-blind, and stacked queries where the driver allows multi-statements.
codeExamples:
-- UNION-based exfiltration: attacker appends a second SELECT with the same column count.
-- Input for q:  zzz' UNION SELECT user, authentication_string FROM mysql.user --
SELECT id, title FROM products WHERE title = 'zzz'
UNION SELECT user, authentication_string FROM mysql.user -- ';

-- Time-based blind probe (no data shown, but response time leaks 1 bit):
SELECT id FROM products WHERE id = 1 AND IF(SUBSTRING(VERSION(),1,1)='8', SLEEP(3), 0);

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+-------------------------------------------+
-- | id     | title                                     |
-- +--------+-------------------------------------------+
-- | root   | $A$005$...hash...                         |
-- | app    | $A$005$...hash...                         |
-- +--------+-------------------------------------------+
-- (second query: returns after ~3 s when the server is 8.x)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   user input ──► string concat ──► "SELECT ... WHERE name='" + x + "'"
                                         │
                      x = admin' --      ▼
                              SELECT ... WHERE name='admin' -- '
                                         │  parser sees extra SQL
                                         ▼
        DATA became CODE ──► auth bypass / UNION dump / blind probes

   Safe path:  SQL text (fixed) ──► PREPARE ──► plan   +   values bound separately

Fresher Notes

  • SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting an attacker change the query.
  • Example: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'" with input ' OR '1'='1.
  • It can expose, change or delete data.

Worked Example 1

Time-based blind probe.

Worked Example 2

Allow-list for ORDER BY.

Practice Exercise 1

Vulnerable query.
codeExamples:
-- application builds:  "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND pwd = '" + pwd + "'"
-- attacker sends name = admin' --
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'admin' -- ' AND pwd = ''

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | role
--  1 | admin | ADMIN      (password check bypassed)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Data extraction with UNION.
codeExamples:
-- id = 0 UNION SELECT user, password_hash FROM users
SELECT name, email FROM products WHERE id = 0 UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM users;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | email
-- admin | $2a$10$abc...

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SQL injection happens when untrusted input becomes part of the SQL text. The parser cannot tell your code from the attacker's text, so quotes and keywords in the input change the structure of the statement. This is a parsing problem, not a data problem: the fix is to keep SQL and data separate.
codeExamples:
-- vulnerable application code:  "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "' AND pwd = '" + pwd + "'"
-- attacker sends name = admin' --   (the rest becomes a comment)
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = 'admin' -- ' AND pwd = '';

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name  | role
--  1 | admin | ADMIN        (password check bypassed)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Attack families: in-band (UNION to read other tables), error-based, boolean/time-based blind (infer data from true/false or delays), second-order (stored input used unsafely later), and injection in ORDER BY, LIMIT or identifiers that cannot be parameterized.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, email FROM products WHERE id = 0 UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM users;      -- UNION extraction
SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = 1 AND IF(SUBSTRING(DATABASE(), 1, 1) = 's', SLEEP(5), 0);           -- time-based blind
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY (SELECT IF(1 = 1, price, name));                                       -- injection in ORDER BY

-- OUTPUT:
-- name  | email
-- admin | $2a$10$abc...

expert.content:
Advantages

Why it is worth knowing: detection is simple in testing (a single quote causes a syntax error), exploitation tools are automated, and the impact ranges from data theft to full takeover. Knowing the shapes helps you review code and write WAF/audit rules.
codeExamples:
-- Detecting probes in the general log / performance_schema: look for tell-tale tokens.
SELECT DIGEST_TEXT, COUNT_STAR
FROM   performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
WHERE  DIGEST_TEXT LIKE '%SLEEP (%'          -- time-based probes
   OR  DIGEST_TEXT LIKE '%UNION SELECT%'     -- union probes
ORDER  BY COUNT_STAR DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------------------------------------+------------+
-- | DIGEST_TEXT                                  | COUNT_STAR |
-- +----------------------------------------------+------------+
-- | SELECT ... WHERE id = ? AND IF ( ... SLEEP ( ?) |      42 |
-- +----------------------------------------------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages of the vulnerable pattern: data theft and tampering, authentication bypass, and (with FILE privilege) reading or writing server files. Every query built by hand is a new attack surface.
codeExamples:
-- Damage depends on privileges. If the app account has FILE, injection can read files:
SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd');             -- needs FILE privilege and secure_file_priv permitting it
-- Check how exposed your server is:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'secure_file_priv';      -- empty = anywhere (bad), NULL = disabled (good)

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name    | Value |
-- +------------------+-------+
-- | secure_file_priv | NULL  |
-- +------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations of attackers (and of defenders): a single connection normally cannot run stacked statements (multi-statement is off by default in most drivers), and identifiers or LIMIT/ORDER BY parts cannot be parameterized, so they need allow-lists.

Architect's Notes

Treat injection as a design rule, not a patch: no string-built SQL anywhere, ORM or driver binding by default, allow-lists for identifiers, and an app account with minimum privileges so a bug cannot become a breach. Add defence in depth (WAF, query auditing, no FILE privilege, separate read-only accounts), but never rely on escaping or WAFs as the primary control.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Attack types: classic (in-band), blind (true/false or time-based), UNION-based data extraction, second-order (stored then used).
  • Even numeric fields and ORDER BY columns can be injectable.
  • Error messages shown to users help attackers; hide them.

Senior Notes

  • Defense in depth: parameterized queries everywhere, least privilege accounts, input validation by allow-list, WAF and monitoring.
  • Dynamic identifiers (table or column names, ORDER BY direction) cannot be parameters; map from an allow-list.
  • ORMs reduce risk but native queries and string-built JPQL/HQL remain vulnerable.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on escaping functions or blacklists, trusting input from "internal" sources, building ORDER BY or table names from input, and showing database errors to users. Use parameters for values and allow-lists for identifiers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Defence in depth limits impact: least-privilege accounts (no FILE or DDL), no stacked queries (multiStatements=false), generic error pages, WAF rules and monitoring for unusual queries.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world detection: unusual SQL shapes show up in the digest table. A query containing UNION SELECT from information_schema or a SLEEP call from the application account is a strong alert.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 80) AS q, count_star, first_seen FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
WHERE digest_text LIKE '%information_schema%' OR digest_text LIKE '%SLEEP(%' OR digest_text LIKE '%UNION SELECT%' ORDER BY first_seen DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- q                                              | count_star | first_seen
-- SELECT ... UNION SELECT username , password... |          3 | 2026-05-01 03:12:44

beginner.content:
Introduction

A prepared statement sends the SQL text with ? placeholders first; the server parses it once. Values are sent later as data, so they can never change the statement structure.
codeExamples:
-- Server-side prepared statement in plain SQL (drivers do the same over the binary protocol)
PREPARE find_user FROM 'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name = ? AND pwd_hash = ?';
SET @n = 'admin'' --';                       -- hostile value, treated purely as a string
SET @p = 'x';
EXECUTE find_user USING @n, @p;              -- binds values, no parsing of the value
DEALLOCATE PREPARE find_user;                -- free server memory

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)      -- no user is literally named  admin' --

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Escaping functions are easy to get wrong (character sets, numeric contexts). Binding removes the problem by separating code and data at the protocol level.
codeExamples:
-- Numeric context: escaping quotes does NOT help here, binding does.
PREPARE p FROM 'SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE id = ?';
SET @id = '0 OR 1=1';                        -- hostile text
EXECUTE p USING @id;                         -- converted to the number 0, not parsed as SQL
DEALLOCATE PREPARE p;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set, 1 warning (0.00 sec)
-- Warning 1292: Truncated incorrect DOUBLE value: '0 OR 1=1'  (the attack became a harmless value)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

In applications: JDBC PreparedStatement, Python cursor.execute(sql, params), Node mysql2 execute(), PHP PDO, and every ORM. Reused statements also skip repeated parsing.

Diagram

   App                                      MySQL server
   ───                                      ────────────
   1. PREPARE "... WHERE name = ?"  ─────►  parse + validate  ──► statement handle #5
   2. EXECUTE #5 with ['admin'' --'] ────►  bind as VALUE (never re-parsed)
   3. rows  ◄──────────────────────────────  run plan
   4. CLOSE #5                      ─────►  free memory

   SQL structure fixed at step 1; data arrives at step 2 -> injection impossible

Fresher Notes

  • A prepared statement sends the SQL with placeholders (?) first and the values separately, so input is always treated as data, never as SQL.
  • Java: PreparedStatement ps = c.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?"); ps.setString(1, email);.
  • It prevents SQL injection and can be faster for repeated queries.

Worked Example 1

Dynamic IN list.

Worked Example 2

Connection string for statement caching.
codeExamples:
jdbc:mysql://db:3306/shop?useServerPrepStmts=true&cachePrepStmts=true&prepStmtCacheSize=250&prepStmtCacheSqlLimit=2048

-- OUTPUT:
-- Prepared statements parsed once per connection and cached

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Server-side prepared statement.

Practice Exercise 2

Java JDBC example.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

With a prepared statement the SQL text with placeholders (?) is sent and parsed first; parameter values are sent afterwards as typed data in a separate protocol message. The values can never change the structure of the statement, which is why this removes SQL injection for values. The parsed statement can also be reused with different parameters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Drivers expose it as PreparedStatement (JDBC), parameter lists in cursor.execute(sql, params) (Python), execute('... ?', [v]) (Node mysql2), PDO::prepare (PHP). Server-side prepares parse once per connection; client-side emulation escapes values in the driver. Placeholders can only replace values, not identifiers or keywords.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: eliminates value-injection, enables plan/parse reuse, avoids manual quoting and type formatting, and gives cleaner, safer code.
codeExamples:
-- The statement digest is identical for any value, so monitoring groups them nicely:
SELECT DIGEST_TEXT, COUNT_STAR
FROM   performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
WHERE  DIGEST_TEXT LIKE 'SELECT id , name FROM users WHERE name = ?%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------------------------------------------+------------+
-- | DIGEST_TEXT                                         | COUNT_STAR |
-- +-----------------------------------------------------+------------+
-- | SELECT id , name FROM users WHERE name = ? AND ...  |      10234 |
-- +-----------------------------------------------------+------------+
