expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: an extra round trip for the first PREPARE (unless the driver pipelines it), server memory per prepared statement (limited by max_prepared_stmt_count), and some drivers only emulate preparation client-side.
codeExamples:
-- Server memory guard rail:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_prepared_stmt_count';
-- Forgetting DEALLOCATE / closing statements in a pool leaks them until the limit is hit:
-- ERROR 1461 (42000): Can't create more than max_prepared_stmt_count statements (current value: 16382)

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name           | Value |
-- +-------------------------+-------+
-- | max_prepared_stmt_count | 16382 |
-- +-------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: placeholders only stand for values. Table names, column names, ORDER BY direction and the IN-list length cannot be a single ?.

Architect's Notes

Make parameter binding the only allowed way to run SQL (lint/ban string concatenation). Watch for drivers that emulate prepares client-side (for example useServerPrepStmts=false in Connector/J): they escape rather than bind, which is still safe with correct charsets but different in behaviour and plan caching. Pair with least-privilege accounts and allow-listed dynamic identifiers; for stored procedures, never build dynamic SQL from raw parameters.

Mid-Level Notes

  • In MySQL: PREPARE s FROM "..."; EXECUTE s USING @v; DEALLOCATE PREPARE s;.
  • Drivers may emulate prepared statements client-side (useServerPrepStmts=false default in Connector/J); both are safe if parameters are bound, but server-side gives parse reuse.
  • Placeholders cannot replace identifiers or keywords.

Senior Notes

  • Server-side prepared statements cache plans per connection; with pools set cachePrepStmts and prepStmtCacheSize carefully.
  • Large IN lists need dynamic placeholder counts; generate "?,?,?" safely.
  • ORMs use parameters by default; audit native queries and string-built fragments.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: building the SQL string with concatenation "just for the table name", dynamic IN lists with the wrong number of placeholders, LIKE patterns with unescaped wildcards, and unclosed statements piling up (max_prepared_stmt_count).

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Prepared statements give small speed gains for repeated statements (no re-parse), and large safety gains. Configure driver caches (cachePrepStmts, prepStmtCacheSize, useServerPrepStmts) sensibly; test for statement leaks under load.
codeExamples:
jdbc:mysql://db:3306/shop?useServerPrepStmts=true&cachePrepStmts=true&prepStmtCacheSize=250&prepStmtCacheSqlLimit=2048&rewriteBatchedStatements=true

-- OUTPUT:
-- Statements parsed once per connection, batches rewritten to multi-row inserts

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world search endpoint with optional filters: fixed SQL fragments chosen by code, every value bound, and sort columns from an allow-list.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A logical backup exports the data as SQL statements (or delimited text) that can be replayed. A physical backup copies the raw data files (tablespaces, redo, binlog position). Logical is portable and readable; physical is much faster for large data sets.
codeExamples:
# Logical: a text file of CREATE/INSERT statements
mysqldump --single-transaction shop > shop.sql
# Physical: copy of the data directory files (MySQL Enterprise Backup / Percona XtraBackup)
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backups/full1

# OUTPUT (example):
# shop.sql                 -> 120 MB text, human readable
# /backups/full1/          -> ibdata1, shop/orders.ibd, xtrabackup_checkpoints ...
# xtrabackup: completed OK!

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Backups are your last defence against hardware failure, bad deploys, ransomware and human error (DROP TABLE on production). Choosing the type decides how long a restore takes, which is your real recovery time.
codeExamples:
# Rough restore-time comparison for a 500 GB database (example numbers):
#   Logical  : replay INSERTs, rebuild every index   ->  10 to 30 hours
#   Physical : copy files back + crash recovery      ->  30 to 90 minutes
# Estimate your own data size first:
mysql -e "SELECT ROUND(SUM(data_length+index_length)/1024/1024/1024,1) AS size_gb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema='shop'"

# OUTPUT (example):
# +---------+
# | size_gb |
# +---------+
# |   500.3 |
# +---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical use: small and mid databases and schema migrations use mysqldump or MySQL Shell dump utilities; multi-hundred-GB production systems use XtraBackup/MEB or filesystem/cloud snapshots, plus the binary log for point-in-time recovery.
codeExamples:
# MySQL Shell parallel logical dump (much faster than mysqldump, still logical):
mysqlsh root@localhost -- util dump-schemas shop --outputUrl=/backups/shop_dump --threads=8
# Cloud / LVM snapshot is physical: flush, lock briefly, snapshot, unlock
mysql -e "FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK; SYSTEM lvcreate -s -n snap -L20G /dev/vg/mysql; UNLOCK TABLES;"

# OUTPUT (example):
# Dump duration: 00:02:41s
# Data bytes written: 18.4 GB

beginner.content:
Diagram

   LOGICAL                                   PHYSICAL
   ┌────────┐  SELECT/read rows  ┌───────┐   ┌────────┐ copy pages/files ┌────────────┐
   │ Server │ ─────────────────► │ .sql  │   │ Server │ ────────────────►│ .ibd,redo  │
   └────────┘   (slow, portable) └───────┘   └────────┘  (fast, same ver)└────────────┘
   restore = parse + INSERT + build indexes  restore = copy back + crash recovery

Fresher Notes

  • A logical backup exports data as SQL statements (mysqldump). A physical backup copies the actual data files (Percona XtraBackup, MySQL Enterprise Backup, snapshots).
  • Logical backups are portable and easy to restore partly; physical backups are faster for big databases.
  • You need at least one tested restore path.

Worked Example 1

Restore comparison (conceptual).
codeExamples:
-- 500 GB database
-- logical restore (mysql < dump.sql): ~ 18 hours
-- physical restore (copy-back):       ~ 40 minutes

-- OUTPUT:
-- Choose physical for large datasets with strict RTO

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Record binlog position with the backup.
codeExamples:
mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 shop > shop.sql
-- shop.sql contains: -- CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_LOG_FILE='binlog.000042', SOURCE_LOG_POS=1543;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Binlog coordinates saved for point-in-time recovery

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Logical backup of a database.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction --routines --triggers shop > shop.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (shop.sql created: CREATE TABLE and INSERT statements, routines and triggers)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Physical backup with XtraBackup.
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --backup --user=backup --password=*** --target-dir=/backups/full-2026-05-01
xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/backups/full-2026-05-01

-- OUTPUT:
-- completed OK!   (data files copied and made consistent)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A logical backup (mysqldump, mysqlpump, MySQL Shell dump) reads the data through SQL and writes statements or delimited text; restore replays them, rebuilding indexes. A physical backup (Percona XtraBackup, MySQL Enterprise Backup, filesystem or cloud snapshot) copies the data files and the redo log, so restore is a file copy plus crash recovery.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u backup -p --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events shop > shop.sql            # logical
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backups/full-2026-05-01 && xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/backups/full-2026-05-01   # physical

-- OUTPUT:
-- shop.sql (readable SQL)        /backups/full-2026-05-01 (copy of data files, ready to restore)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose by size, RTO and portability. Logical: portable between versions and platforms, easy partial restores, slow for big data. Physical: very fast backup and restore, same version and architecture, partial restores need transportable tablespaces. Snapshots need consistency (flush/quiesce or InnoDB crash recovery).
codeExamples:
util.dumpInstance('/backup/logical', {threads: 8, compression: 'zstd'})
xtrabackup --backup --compress --parallel=8 --target-dir=/backups/phys
FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK; -- snapshot the volume; UNLOCK TABLES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dump: Duration 00:03:10 for 100 GB    physical: 00:11:40 for 100 GB

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: logical = portable across versions/platforms/engines, selective (one table), diff-able; physical = fastest backup and restore, preserves everything byte-for-byte, supports incremental backups.
codeExamples:
# Logical advantage: restore a single table out of a full dump with simple tools
sed -n '/^-- Table structure for table .orders./,/^-- Table structure for table .users./p' shop.sql > orders_only.sql
mysql shop_copy < orders_only.sql
# Physical advantage: incremental backup copies only changed pages
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backups/inc1 --incremental-basedir=/backups/full1

# OUTPUT (example):
# xtrabackup: Transaction log of lsn (9812345) to (9899999) was copied.
# completed OK!

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: logical = slow to restore (index rebuild), large on huge tables; physical = tied to the same major version/OS/architecture, not selective without extra steps, needs consistent copy handling.
codeExamples:
# Physical copy of a RUNNING server without a tool is inconsistent (torn pages, missing redo):
cp -r /var/lib/mysql /backups/bad_copy     # DO NOT do this on a live server
# Restoring such a copy often ends with:
# [ERROR] InnoDB: Database page corruption on disk or a failed file read
# Logical dumps can also be inconsistent if you forget --single-transaction on InnoDB.

# OUTPUT:
# [ERROR] [MY-012153] [InnoDB] Database page corruption detected

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: neither type captures changes after the backup finished; you need binary logs for that. Logical dumps do not include users/privileges unless you dump mysql tables or use SHOW CREATE USER. Backup size/time grows with data.
codeExamples:
-- Users are not in a schema dump; export grants separately:
SHOW CREATE USER 'app'@'%';
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'app'@'%';
-- Backup is only a point in time; record the binlog coordinates for later roll-forward:
SHOW MASTER STATUS;       -- 8.0 syntax; 8.4 uses SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------------+----------+
-- | File             | Position |
-- +------------------+----------+
-- | binlog.000042    |   158732 |
-- +------------------+----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use both: a physical full (plus incrementals) for fast disaster restore, and periodic logical or Shell dumps for portability, upgrades and table-level repair. Always add binlog archiving for point-in-time recovery and, above all, test restores regularly: an untested backup is a hope, not a backup.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Logical: slower to take and restore, readable, works across versions and platforms, small restores of single tables are easy.
  • Physical: very fast backup/restore, hot backup possible with XtraBackup, same version and architecture constraints.
  • Filesystem or cloud snapshots need quiescing or InnoDB crash recovery to be consistent.

Senior Notes

  • Choose by RTO/RPO: multi-hundred GB databases need physical or snapshot backups plus binlogs for point-in-time recovery.
  • Keep multiple tiers: frequent snapshots, daily physical backup, binlog archive, periodic logical dump for portability.
  • Encrypt and store backups off-site; monitor backup size and duration.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no restore test, backups stored on the same disk as the database, backups without the binlog position (no point-in-time recovery), and inconsistent snapshots of live files. Always record coordinates and verify restores.
codeExamples:
mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 shop > shop.sql
grep -m1 "CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO" shop.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- -- CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_LOG_FILE='binlog.000042', SOURCE_LOG_POS=1543;

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Restore time dominates RTO. A 500 GB logical restore can take many hours because of index builds; the physical restore of the same data is minutes to an hour. Measure on your data.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(500 * 1024 / (60 * 200), 1) AS physical_restore_minutes_at_200mb_s;
-- logical restore of the same 500 GB: ~ 18 hours

-- OUTPUT:
-- physical_restore_minutes_at_200mb_s
-- 42.7

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world strategy: nightly physical backups for fast recovery, continuous binlog archiving for point-in-time recovery, and a weekly logical dump of critical schemas for portability and migrations.
codeExamples:
-- cron
-- 02:00 xtrabackup full (Sunday) / incremental (other days)
-- continuous: mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never
-- 04:00 Sunday: mysqlsh dumpSchemas ['shop','billing']

-- OUTPUT:
-- three recovery paths: fast physical, point-in-time via binlog, portable logical

beginner.content:
Introduction

mysqldump is the classic client utility that writes a database as SQL (DDL plus INSERT statements). Restore means feeding that file back through the mysql client.
codeExamples:
# Dump one database, then restore it into an empty one
mysqldump -u root -p shop > shop.sql            # write CREATE TABLE + INSERT statements
mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE shop_copy" # target must exist (no --databases flag used)
mysql -u root -p shop_copy < shop.sql           # replay the file

# OUTPUT:
# (no output on success; verify with)
# mysql> SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_copy.orders;
# +----------+
# | COUNT(*) |
# +----------+
# |    15234 |
# +----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

You need a simple, scriptable way to move or save data: seed a test database, migrate servers, archive a schema, or recover one dropped table. Correct flags decide whether the dump is consistent and complete.
codeExamples:
# Flags that make a dump production-grade for InnoDB:
mysqldump --single-transaction \
          --routines --triggers --events \
          --set-gtid-purged=OFF \
          --master-data=2 \
          shop > shop_full.sql
#  --single-transaction : consistent snapshot via REPEATABLE READ, no table locks
#  --routines/...       : include stored procedures, triggers, events
#  --master-data=2      : write binlog file/pos as a comment (8.4 renamed: --source-data=2)

# OUTPUT (example, first lines of shop_full.sql):
# -- CHANGE MASTER TO MASTER_LOG_FILE='binlog.000042', MASTER_LOG_POS=158732;
# -- MySQL dump 10.13  Distrib 8.0.36

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: nightly cron dump of a small SaaS, dumping just a few tables for a developer, piping a dump straight into another server, and compressing on the fly.
codeExamples:
# Stream and compress, no temp file; copy server A -> server B
mysqldump --single-transaction shop | gzip > shop_$(date +%F).sql.gz
mysqldump --single-transaction shop | mysql -h replica2 shop_copy
# Only some tables, schema only, or data only:
mysqldump shop orders customers > two_tables.sql
mysqldump --no-data shop > schema.sql
mysqldump --no-create-info shop > data.sql

# OUTPUT (example):
# -rw-r--r-- 1 ops ops 18M Oct  6 02:00 shop_2026-10-06.sql.gz

beginner.content:
Diagram

   mysqldump ──► BEGIN snapshot ──► for each table: SELECT * ──► .sql text
                      │                                              │
                 (no locks, InnoDB)                          mysql < file.sql
                                                                     │
                                                      CREATE TABLE ► INSERT ► indexes

Fresher Notes

  • mysqldump creates a logical backup: mysqldump -u root -p dbname > backup.sql. Restore with mysql -u root -p dbname < backup.sql.
  • Dump all databases with --all-databases or one table by naming it.
  • It produces SQL you can read and edit.

Worked Example 1

Dump a single table with a filter.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u root -p shop orders --where="created_at >= '2026-01-01'" > orders_2026.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (orders_2026.sql with only matching rows)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Credentials without a password flag.
codeExamples:
# ~/.my.cnf (chmod 600)
[client]
user=backup
password=***

-- OUTPUT:
-- mysqldump shop > shop.sql   (no password on the command line)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Dump and compress.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u backup -p --single-transaction --routines --events shop | gzip > shop_2026-05-01.sql.gz

-- OUTPUT:
-- shop_2026-05-01.sql.gz  (compressed dump file)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Restore into a new database.
codeExamples:
mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE shop_restore"
gunzip < shop_2026-05-01.sql.gz | mysql -u root -p shop_restore
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_restore.orders"

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 120450

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

mysqldump connects as a client and reads each table with SELECT; with --single-transaction it starts a consistent-snapshot transaction so InnoDB tables are dumped at one point in time without blocking writers. Output is SQL: CREATE TABLE statements and multi-row INSERTs. Restore replays the file through the mysql client.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u backup -p --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events --set-gtid-purged=OFF shop > shop.sql
mysql -u root -p -e "CREATE DATABASE shop_restore"
mysql -u root -p shop_restore < shop.sql
mysql -u root -p -e "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_restore.orders"

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 612044

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Useful options: --no-data (schema only), --where (subset), --tables, --ignore-table, --compress, --source-data=2 (record binlog position), --hex-blob, --default-character-set=utf8mb4. Pipe through gzip for size.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u root -p --no-data --routines shop > schema_only.sql
mysqldump -u root -p shop orders --where="created_at >= '2026-01-01'" > orders_2026.sql
mysqldump -u root -p --single-transaction shop | gzip > shop_2026-05-01.sql.gz
mysqldump -u root -p --all-databases --events --routines --triggers > all.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (four dump files)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: ships with MySQL, human-readable, portable across versions and platforms, easy to edit and diff, works for any engine, and restores selectively.
codeExamples:
# Selective restore: only one table from a full dump, or one database from a multi-db dump
mysql --one-database shop_copy < all_databases.sql    # skip statements for other databases
# Quick sanity peek at what the file contains
grep -c "^INSERT INTO" shop.sql

# OUTPUT (example):
# 1823

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: single-threaded, slow on big data, restore must rebuild every index, large file size, and row-at-a-time inserts unless extended inserts are used (default on).
codeExamples:
# Speed up a restore: disable checks and bulk load inside one session
mysql shop_copy -e "
  SET unique_checks=0; SET foreign_key_checks=0; SET sql_log_bin=0;
  SOURCE shop.sql;
  SET foreign_key_checks=1; SET unique_checks=1;"
# Compare: a 200 GB schema can take a day with plain mysqldump | mysql

# OUTPUT (example):
# Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)
# ... (long replay) ...

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: without --single-transaction (or locks) the dump may be inconsistent; MyISAM tables need --lock-all-tables; DDL during the dump can break the snapshot; the dump is as of one moment; mysql system users are not included by default.

Architect's Notes

mysqldump is the right tool up to roughly tens of GB. Beyond that, use MySQL Shell dump/load (parallel, chunked) or physical backups. Always script it with --single-transaction, record the binlog position, store dumps off-host and encrypted, and rehearse a full restore into a scratch server on a schedule.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Important flags: --single-transaction (consistent InnoDB snapshot without locks), --routines --triggers --events, --source-data, --set-gtid-purged.
  • Compress: | gzip > backup.sql.gz.
  • Always test a restore to a scratch server.

Senior Notes

  • For big data prefer mysqlpump/MySQL Shell dump utilities (parallel) or physical backups.
  • Restoring into production needs care: disable foreign key checks during load and use the same SQL mode/collation.
  • Do not store passwords on the command line; use an option file with restricted permissions.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting --single-transaction on InnoDB (locks tables), omitting routines and events, restoring into a server with different sql_mode or charset, and putting the password on the command line. Use an option file or login path.
codeExamples:
# ~/.my.cnf (chmod 600)
[client]
user=backup
password=***
mysqldump --single-transaction --routines shop > shop.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (no password on the command line or in shell history)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Speed up large dumps and restores: dump on a replica, use parallel tools (MySQL Shell, mydumper), relax durability during restore (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2, bigger redo log), disable foreign key and unique checks inside the dump, and avoid extra indexes until load finishes.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world verification: restore the latest dump into a scratch server nightly, compare table counts and checksums with production, and alert when they differ.
codeExamples:
CHECKSUM TABLE shop.orders, shop_restore.orders;
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders) - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop_restore.orders) AS difference;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table                | Checksum
-- shop.orders          | 2918457613
-- shop_restore.orders  | 2918457613
-- difference
-- 0

beginner.content:
Introduction

A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the previous backup; a differential copies changes since the last full. A strategy combines them with retention rules.
codeExamples:
# Weekly full + daily incremental with XtraBackup (physical)
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backups/full_sun
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backups/inc_mon --incremental-basedir=/backups/full_sun
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/backups/inc_tue --incremental-basedir=/backups/inc_mon

# OUTPUT (example):
# full_sun : 480 GB   inc_mon : 6 GB   inc_tue : 7 GB

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Full backups of terabytes every night are too slow and expensive. Incrementals shrink the backup window and storage but lengthen the restore chain, so the plan balances cost against recovery time.
codeExamples:
-- Size of change per day tells you if incrementals are worthwhile
-- (daily binlog volume ~ daily change volume)
SHOW BINARY LOGS;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------+-----------+-----------+
-- | Log_name      | File_size | Encrypted |
-- +---------------+-----------+-----------+
-- | binlog.000040 | 1073741824| No        |
-- | binlog.000041 |  913002113| No        |
-- +---------------+-----------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical production plan: weekly full, daily incremental, continuous binlog shipping, 30 days retention, monthly archived copy to cold storage, and a nightly automated restore test on a spare host.
codeExamples:
# Cron schedule (crontab -e)
# 02:00 Sunday   full
0 2 * * 0   /opt/bk/full.sh
# 02:00 Mon-Sat  incremental against yesterday
0 2 * * 1-6 /opt/bk/incr.sh
# every 5 min    ship closed binlogs off-host (RPO of minutes)
*/5 * * * * rsync -a /var/lib/mysql/binlog.0* backup-host:/binlogs/

# OUTPUT:
# (cron jobs registered; check logs in /var/log/bk.log)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Sun         Mon         Tue         Wed   ...
   [FULL]──►  [INC1]──►   [INC2]──►   [INC3]
   480 GB      6 GB        7 GB        5 GB
   Restore Wed =  FULL + INC1 + INC2 + INC3  (+ binlogs to the exact second)

Fresher Notes

  • A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup (or last full).
  • Typical plan: weekly full, daily incremental, plus binary logs for point-in-time recovery.
  • The schedule must match how much data you can afford to lose (RPO).

Worked Example 1

Weekly schedule (cron).
codeExamples:
0 2 * * 0  /opt/backup/full.sh      # Sunday full
0 2 * * 1-6 /opt/backup/inc.sh      # Mon-Sat incremental

-- OUTPUT:
-- (backups created nightly, retained 30 days)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Backup success monitoring.
codeExamples:
SELECT MAX(finished_at) AS last_backup, TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, MAX(finished_at), NOW()) AS hours_ago FROM backup_log WHERE status = 'OK';

-- OUTPUT:
-- last_backup         | hours_ago
-- 2026-05-01 02:14:00 |         9

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Full then incremental with XtraBackup.
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/b/full
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/b/inc1 --incremental-basedir=/b/full

-- OUTPUT:
-- completed OK!   (inc1 holds only changed pages)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Archive binary logs.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --host=db --raw --stop-never binlog.000042

-- OUTPUT:
-- (binlog files streamed to local disk continuously)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A full backup captures everything at one point in time. An incremental backup captures only changes since a previous backup: XtraBackup incrementals copy changed pages (tracked by LSN), and binary logs record every change as a stream. Restoring needs the full backup plus each incremental (or the binlogs) in order.
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/b/full
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/b/inc1 --incremental-basedir=/b/full
xtrabackup --backup --target-dir=/b/inc2 --incremental-basedir=/b/inc1
cat /b/inc2/xtrabackup_checkpoints

-- OUTPUT:
-- backup_type = incremental
-- from_lsn = 412988871    to_lsn = 413420133

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design from RPO and RTO: frequent fulls shorten restores but cost storage; incrementals save space but lengthen restores; continuous binlog archiving gives near-zero RPO. Retention policy, encryption and off-site copies belong in the plan.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --host=db --user=repl --raw --stop-never --result-file=/backup/binlogs/ binlog.000042
-- retention: 7 daily fulls, 4 weekly fulls, 12 monthly fulls, binlogs for 14 days

-- OUTPUT:
-- (binlog files streamed continuously to the backup host)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: shorter backup windows, less I/O and storage, finer recovery points, and the option to prune old chains while keeping the latest full.
codeExamples:
# Prepare (apply redo) the full, then roll each incremental onto it, then restore
xtrabackup --prepare --apply-log-only --target-dir=/backups/full_sun
xtrabackup --prepare --apply-log-only --target-dir=/backups/full_sun --incremental-dir=/backups/inc_mon
xtrabackup --prepare              --target-dir=/backups/full_sun --incremental-dir=/backups/inc_tue
xtrabackup --copy-back --target-dir=/backups/full_sun

# OUTPUT (example):
# xtrabackup: completed OK!   (after each step)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: restore needs the whole chain (one lost incremental breaks later ones), more moving parts, more testing, and chain corruption is easy to miss until restore day.
codeExamples:
# Integrity: record checksums so a broken link is detected before you need it
cd /backups && sha256sum full_sun/xtrabackup_checkpoints inc_mon/xtrabackup_checkpoints > chain.sha256
sha256sum -c chain.sha256
# Chain continuity rule: each incremental's from_lsn must equal the previous to_lsn
grep -E "from_lsn|to_lsn" inc_mon/xtrabackup_checkpoints

# OUTPUT (example):
# full_sun/xtrabackup_checkpoints: OK
# inc_mon/xtrabackup_checkpoints: OK
# from_lsn = 9812345
# to_lsn = 9899999

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB incrementals track changed pages (LSN), but MyISAM tables are copied whole; logical backups cannot be truly incremental (use binlogs instead). Schema changes and encryption/compression settings must match across the chain.
codeExamples:
# Logical "incremental" = binary logs since the last dump, replayed with mysqlbinlog
mysqlbinlog --start-position=158732 binlog.000042 binlog.000043 | mysql -u root -p
# Convert dump position to a human check:
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -v binlog.000043 | head -n 12

# OUTPUT (example):
# # at 4
# #261006  2:00:01 server id 1  end_log_pos 126  Start: binlog v 4, server v 8.0.36

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick the chain length by your RTO: long chains mean slower, riskier restores. Many teams prefer a frequent full from a replica (so production is untouched) plus binlog archiving, which is simple and gives per-second recovery. Automate verification and keep at least one independent, immutable copy.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Incremental in MySQL: XtraBackup incremental (changed pages) or archived binary logs.
  • Restore needs the full backup plus every incremental or binlog in order.
  • Keep multiple generations and test restore regularly.

Senior Notes

  • Define RPO and RTO first, then design: continuous binlog shipping gives near-zero RPO; frequent snapshots reduce RTO.
  • Protect backups: encrypt, store off-site/immutable, restrict access and monitor success.
  • Automate verification: periodic restore-and-check jobs that alert on failure.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: a broken incremental chain (one missing file makes later ones useless), untested restores, backups readable by everyone, and retention shorter than the time to notice a problem. Verify the chain and protect the files.
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --prepare --apply-log-only --target-dir=/b/full
xtrabackup --prepare --apply-log-only --target-dir=/b/full --incremental-dir=/b/inc1
xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/b/full --incremental-dir=/b/inc2

-- OUTPUT:
-- completed OK!    (full backup now contains the changes of inc1 and inc2)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Backup load affects production I/O. Throttle, run on a replica, and watch lag and latency. Compress and encrypt on the way out with parallel streams.
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --backup --throttle=200 --parallel=4 --compress --encrypt=AES256 --encrypt-key-file=/secure/key --stream=xbstream > /backup/full.xbstream

-- OUTPUT:
-- completed OK!    (I/O limited to 200 operations per second)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world schedule with monitoring: weekly full, daily incremental, continuous binlogs, a nightly automated restore test, and an alert when the last verified backup is older than 26 hours.
codeExamples:
SELECT backup_name, finished_at, verified_at, TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, verified_at, NOW()) AS hours_since_verified FROM ops.backup_catalog ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- backup_name      | finished_at         | verified_at         | hours_since_verified
-- inc-2026-05-01   | 2026-05-01 03:10:00 | 2026-05-01 05:40:00 |                    5

beginner.content:
Introduction

Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) restores a backup and then replays binary logs up to a chosen moment, such as just before an accidental DELETE. It needs a base backup plus all binlogs since.
codeExamples:
# 1) restore last night's full backup, 2) replay binlogs up to 09:59:59
mysql shop < shop_2026-10-06.sql
mysqlbinlog --stop-datetime="2026-10-06 09:59:59" binlog.000042 binlog.000043 | mysql

# OUTPUT:
# (silent success; data now equals the state at 09:59:59)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A nightly backup alone loses up to 24 hours of data. PITR cuts the loss to seconds and is the only way to undo a logical mistake (a bad UPDATE) without losing everything after it.

Real-Time Use

Recovery runbook: stop writes, restore the base backup to a separate server, apply binlogs up to the bad event, validate, then switch or copy the missing rows back.
codeExamples:
# Replay from the backup's recorded position up to just before the bad statement (pos 8110)
mysqlbinlog --start-position=158732 --stop-position=8021 binlog.000042 | mysql
# Or skip the bad transaction and continue after it
mysqlbinlog --start-position=9902 binlog.000043 binlog.000044 | mysql
# GTID setups: exclude a single transaction instead
#   SET GTID_NEXT='uuid:1234'; BEGIN; COMMIT; SET GTID_NEXT=AUTOMATIC;

# OUTPUT:
# (no errors; verify)  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders;  ->  15234

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Mon 02:00      Mon 10:00        Mon 10:00:01
   [FULL BACKUP]──binlog events────► DELETE FROM orders  (mistake)
        │             │  replay ───────────►│ stop before
        ▼             ▼
   restore  +  mysqlbinlog --stop-position  ==> state at 09:59:59

Fresher Notes

  • Point-in-time recovery (PITR) restores the database to a chosen moment, for example just before a bad DELETE.
  • Method: restore the last full backup, then replay binary logs up to the target time or position.
  • It requires binary logging to be enabled before the incident.

Worked Example 1

Recover into a side server and copy back one table.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u root -p recovered orders > orders_recovered.sql
mysql -u root -p shop < orders_recovered.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (orders table restored in production)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Check binlog retention.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_expire_logs_seconds';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name             | Value
-- binlog_expire_logs_seconds | 604800

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Replay until just before the incident.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --start-position=1543 --stop-datetime="2026-05-01 10:14:00" binlog.000042 binlog.000043 | mysql -u root -p

-- OUTPUT:
-- (changes applied up to 10:14:00; the bad DELETE at 10:14:05 is not replayed)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Find the offending statement.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv binlog.000043 | grep -n "DELETE FROM orders"

-- OUTPUT:
-- 8841:### DELETE FROM shop.orders
-- (note the "at 9102" position just before it)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Point-in-time recovery restores a backup and then replays binary log events up to a chosen moment, such as just before an accidental DELETE. It relies on two things: a backup that records the binlog position it corresponds to, and an unbroken sequence of binlog files from that position to the target time.
codeExamples:
# 1. restore the last full backup (recorded position: binlog.000042:1543)
# 2. replay until just before the incident
mysqlbinlog --start-position=1543 --stop-datetime="2026-05-01 10:14:00" binlog.000042 binlog.000043 | mysql -u root -p

-- OUTPUT:
-- (all changes before 10:14:00 applied; the bad statement at 10:14:05 is not)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Choose the stop point by time (--stop-datetime) or exact position (--stop-position); skip a single bad transaction with GTIDs; extract only certain databases (--database); decode row events to read what changed (--base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv).
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv --start-datetime="2026-05-01 10:10:00" --stop-datetime="2026-05-01 10:20:00" binlog.000043 | grep -n "DELETE FROM"
mysqlbinlog --database=shop --stop-position=9102 binlog.000043 | mysql -u root -p shop_recovered

-- OUTPUT:
-- 8841:### DELETE FROM shop.orders
-- (stop-position 9102 is the end of the last good transaction)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: near-zero data loss (RPO of seconds), reverses human errors, works with any consistent backup, and can restore into a clone for investigation.
codeExamples:
-- Restore into a scratch instance, query the lost rows, copy only those back:
INSERT INTO prod.orders SELECT * FROM scratch.orders WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 15234
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE total = VALUES(total);   -- VALUES() deprecated in 8.0.20 but still works

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 15234 rows affected (1.20 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: needs binlogs kept and archived, replay can be slow, mistakes in position or timezone give wrong results, and the process is manual and stressful at 3 AM unless rehearsed.
codeExamples:
# Time zone pitfall: --stop-datetime is interpreted in the client's local zone
mysqlbinlog --stop-datetime="2026-10-06 09:59:59" binlog.000043 | grep -c "Delete_rows"
# Safer: use positions, or run with TZ set explicitly
TZ=UTC mysqlbinlog --stop-datetime="2026-10-06 04:29:59" binlog.000043 | grep -c "DELETE"

# OUTPUT (example):
# 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: requires binlog (log_bin on, row-based preferred, sufficient binlog_expire_logs_seconds), cannot recover past purged logs, and cannot undo DDL that was not logged or happened before the backup.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('log_bin','binlog_format','binlog_expire_logs_seconds','sync_binlog');

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------------------+--------+
-- | Variable_name              | Value  |
-- +----------------------------+--------+
-- | binlog_expire_logs_seconds | 604800 |   -- 7 days: PITR window limit unless archived
-- | binlog_format              | ROW    |
-- | log_bin                    | ON     |
-- | sync_binlog                | 1      |
-- +----------------------------+--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

PITR quality is determined by binlog hygiene: sync_binlog=1, row format, off-host streaming (mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never), retention longer than backup interval, and delayed replicas as a fast alternative. Rehearse the runbook and write the position-finding steps down.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use mysqlbinlog --start-position / --stop-position or --stop-datetime and pipe into mysql.
  • Find the bad statement by scanning binlogs; stop just before it.
  • With GTIDs you can skip a specific transaction.

Senior Notes

  • Practice PITR in drills; incidents are stressful and mistakes are costly.
  • Restore to a separate server first, verify, then extract and re-apply only the damaged tables if production kept running.
  • Keep binlog retention longer than your backup interval and protect binlog files like backups.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: recovering straight into production (do it on a side server first), missing or purged binlogs, non-ROW formats that make decoding hard, and no practice. Rehearse the whole procedure and keep binlog retention longer than the backup interval.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Recovery time is the sum of restoring the backup and replaying the binlog; large binlog volumes replay slowly because they run through one thread. Shorten it with more frequent backups and by recovering only the affected tables.
codeExamples:
mysqldump -u root -p shop_recovered orders > orders_recovered.sql
mysql -u root -p shop < orders_recovered.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (only the damaged table is restored into production; the rest stayed online)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world incident: an UPDATE without WHERE ruined a column at 10:14. The team restored last night's backup to a side server, replayed the binlog until 10:13:59, exported the column and patched production with a join update.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The binary log (binlog) is a sequence of files recording every change made to data and structure (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL) in commit order. It is written by the MySQL server layer, independent of the storage engine.

Why Do We Need This?

Without a change log, a server cannot feed replicas, cannot roll a backup forward to an exact time, and cannot feed CDC tools like Debezium. The binlog is the single source of truth for what changed and when.

Real-Time Use

Real use: replication, PITR, auditing "who changed what" (row format), change-data-capture into Kafka, and cache invalidation.
codeExamples:
# Read the log in human form
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv /var/lib/mysql/binlog.000002 | tail -n 12

# OUTPUT (example):
# ### INSERT INTO demo.t
# ### SET
# ###   @1=1 /* INT meta=0 nullable=0 is_null=0 */
# ###   @2='a' /* VARSTRING(10) meta=10 nullable=1 is_null=0 */
# COMMIT/*!*/;

beginner.content:
Diagram

   client COMMIT
       │
       ▼
   InnoDB prepare ──► write binlog event ──► fsync binlog ──► InnoDB commit
                           │
                           ▼
   binlog.000001 ─► binlog.000002 ─► ...   binlog.index (list of files)
                           │
         replicas (IO thread) / mysqlbinlog / CDC readers

Fresher Notes

  • The binary log (binlog) records every change to data (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDL) in order.
  • It is used for replication and point-in-time recovery.
  • Enable with log_bin (on by default in MySQL 8).

Worked Example 1

Set retention to 7 days.

Worked Example 2

Purge old logs.

Practice Exercise 1

Inspect binary logs.
codeExamples:
SHOW BINARY LOGS;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Log_name      | File_size
-- binlog.000041 | 157286400
-- binlog.000042 |  42115

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Peek at events.
codeExamples:
SHOW BINLOG EVENTS IN 'binlog.000042' LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Pos | Event_type  | Info
-- 4   | Format_desc | Server ver: 8.0.36
-- 126 | Previous_gtids |
-- 157 | Query       | BEGIN

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The binary log is a sequence of numbered files (binlog.000001...) plus an index file. Each committed transaction is written as a group of events in commit order, together with a header describing the server, format and (with GTIDs) the transaction id. It is separate from the InnoDB redo log: redo is for crash recovery, the binlog is for replication and point-in-time recovery.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Key settings: log_bin, server_id, binlog_format, binlog_row_image, max_binlog_size, binlog_expire_logs_seconds, sync_binlog, binlog_cache_size. Rotate with FLUSH BINARY LOGS.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: enables replication and PITR, is sequential (cheap to write), has a defined commit order, can be streamed remotely, can be encrypted and compressed (8.0.20+).
codeExamples:
-- Retention and safety knobs
SET PERSIST binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 604800;   -- keep 7 days (default 30 days)
SET PERSIST sync_binlog = 1;                       -- fsync at every commit: durable
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_%compression%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name         | Value |
-- +-----------------------+-------+
-- | binlog_transaction_compression | OFF |
-- +-----------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: extra disk I/O on every commit (two-phase commit with InnoDB redo), disk space growth, and it can contain sensitive data in clear text unless encrypted.
codeExamples:
-- Cost check: how much binlog does the workload produce, and how much commit waiting happens?
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Binlog_cache_disk_use';   -- transactions that spilled to a temp file
SHOW BINARY LOGS;                                  -- sum the sizes per day

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name         | Value |
-- +-----------------------+-------+
-- | Binlog_cache_disk_use |   412 |
-- +-----------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it records only committed changes (not SELECTs), a file purged is gone for good, it does not contain data from before it was enabled, and statements changing non-transactional tables are logged even on rollback.

Architect's Notes

Keep binlogs on durable storage with sync_binlog=1 and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 when you cannot lose committed data. Size retention to cover your backup interval plus replica downtime, archive off-host for PITR, and treat the logs as sensitive data (encrypt at rest, restrict REPLICATION CLIENT access).

Mid-Level Notes

  • List logs with SHOW BINARY LOGS and the current position with SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS (or SHOW MASTER STATUS in older versions).
  • Files rotate by size (max_binlog_size) and expire by binlog_expire_logs_seconds.
  • Read them with the mysqlbinlog tool.

Senior Notes

  • sync_binlog=1 makes each commit durable in the binlog at a performance cost.
  • Binlog disk space and I/O matter on write-heavy systems; monitor growth and retention.
  • Never delete binlog files manually; use PURGE BINARY LOGS so replicas and indexes stay consistent.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: deleting binlog files from the operating system (index and replicas break), retention too short for the backup cycle or a downed replica, and a full disk from unbounded binlogs. Purge with SQL and monitor space.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(file_size) / 1073741824, 1) AS binlog_gb FROM performance_schema.binary_log_transaction_compression_stats;
-- shell: df -h /var/lib/mysql

-- OUTPUT: (illustrative)
-- binlog_gb
-- 24.8

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Binary logging costs write I/O and durability fsyncs. sync_binlog=1 and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 give full durability; group commit amortizes the fsyncs across concurrent commits. Large transactions fill the binlog cache and spill to disk.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world sizing: binlog retention must cover your longest backup interval plus recovery time and the longest tolerated replica outage, with disk headroom for write bursts.
codeExamples:
SELECT 7 AS retention_days, ROUND(24.8 / 1, 1) AS gb_per_day, ROUND(7 * 24.8, 1) AS disk_needed_gb;

-- OUTPUT:
-- retention_days | gb_per_day | disk_needed_gb
--              7 |       24.8 |          173.6

beginner.content:
Introduction

binlog_format chooses what is logged. STATEMENT logs the SQL text, ROW logs the before/after image of each changed row, MIXED uses statement unless it is unsafe, then switches to row. ROW is the default since MySQL 5.7.7.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_format';
SET SESSION binlog_format = 'ROW';      -- changeable per session (needs privilege)
SET PERSIST binlog_format = 'ROW';      -- global (deprecated setting in 8.0 but still supported)

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name | Value |
-- +---------------+-------+
-- | binlog_format | ROW   |
-- +---------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some statements give different results when replayed on a replica (NOW(), UUID(), RAND(), LIMIT without ORDER BY, UDFs). Statement logging can make a replica silently drift; row logging replays the exact result.
codeExamples:
-- Non-deterministic: unsafe in STATEMENT format
UPDATE users SET token = UUID() WHERE active = 1;
-- STATEMENT: replica runs UUID() itself -> different values -> data divergence
--            (server warns: Statement is unsafe because it uses a system function that may return a different value on the slave)
-- ROW:       replica receives the actual token values -> identical

-- OUTPUT (example, STATEMENT mode):
-- Query OK, 3 rows affected, 1 warning (0.01 sec)
-- Warning 1592: Unsafe statement written to the binary log using statement format

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

ROW is standard for replication, CDC (Debezium needs ROW with full row image) and auditing. STATEMENT can still help for huge bulk updates where row logging would be gigantic.
codeExamples:
-- A bulk update touching 1,000,000 rows:
UPDATE events SET status = 'archived' WHERE created_at < '2020-01-01';
-- STATEMENT: one small event (~100 bytes)
-- ROW      : 1,000,000 before+after images (hundreds of MB)
-- Control the size of row images:
SET PERSIST binlog_row_image = 'MINIMAL';     -- FULL (default) | MINIMAL | NOBLOB

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Query OK, 1000000 rows affected (12.40 sec)
-- binlog growth: STATEMENT ~0 MB, ROW FULL ~410 MB, ROW MINIMAL ~180 MB

beginner.content:
Diagram

   UPDATE t SET v = UUID();
      │
      ├─ STATEMENT : log "UPDATE t SET v = UUID()"        small, replica re-executes (can differ)
      ├─ ROW       : log  row1 old/new, row2 old/new ...  big, exact
      └─ MIXED     : safe statement -> STATEMENT ; unsafe -> ROW

Fresher Notes

  • The binlog format decides what is logged: STATEMENT logs the SQL text, ROW logs the changed rows, MIXED picks automatically.
  • ROW is the default and safest in MySQL 8.
  • Set with binlog_format.

Worked Example 1

Minimal row image.

Worked Example 2

Read row events.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv binlog.000042 | head -20

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- ### UPDATE shop.orders
-- ### WHERE @1=1 @2=7 @3=100.00
-- ### SET   @1=1 @2=7 @3=120.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Check and set format.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@binlog_format, @@binlog_row_image;

-- OUTPUT:
-- @@binlog_format | @@binlog_row_image
-- ROW             | FULL

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Statement format hazard.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In STATEMENT format the binlog stores the SQL text, so replicas re-execute it: compact, but unsafe when results depend on time, random values, user variables or storage details. In ROW format it stores the before and after images of each changed row, so replicas apply exact changes. MIXED chooses statement logging and falls back to row for unsafe statements.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

ROW is the default and required for READ COMMITTED safety, change data capture and some features. binlog_row_image can be FULL, MINIMAL or NOBLOB to reduce size; MINIMAL logs only changed columns plus the key.
codeExamples:
SET PERSIST binlog_format = 'ROW';
SET PERSIST binlog_row_image = 'MINIMAL';
mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv binlog.000042 | head -12

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- ### UPDATE shop.orders
-- ### WHERE @1=1
-- ### SET   @3=120.00         (only the changed column and the key)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: ROW = safe and deterministic, audit-ready, required for most tools, and lets replicas apply by primary key. STATEMENT = compact. MIXED = compromise.
codeExamples:
-- Reading ROW events shows exactly what changed:
-- mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS -vv binlog.000002
-- ### UPDATE demo.t
-- ### WHERE
-- ###   @1=1
-- ###   @2='a'
-- ### SET
-- ###   @1=1
-- ###   @2='b'

-- OUTPUT:
-- Before image (WHERE) and after image (SET) are both visible.

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: ROW produces larger logs and cannot be read as plain SQL without decoding; STATEMENT risks drift and needs more locks (gap locks in REPEATABLE READ); MIXED hides which format ran and is harder to reason about.
codeExamples:
-- Tables without a primary key are slow to apply in ROW format (replica scans the table per row)
CREATE TABLE logs_nopk (msg VARCHAR(100));
-- Fix: add a PK (or a hidden generated invisible PK in 8.0.30+)
ALTER TABLE logs_nopk ADD COLUMN id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY FIRST;
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'sql_require_primary_key';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name            | Value |
-- +--------------------------+-------+
-- | sql_require_primary_key  | OFF   |
-- +--------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: you cannot change binlog_format inside a transaction or while temporary tables are open in a session; statement format cannot be used safely with READ COMMITTED for InnoDB; and mixing formats across sources in a topology complicates tools.

Architect's Notes

Default to ROW with binlog_row_image=FULL (or MINIMAL if you control every consumer). Use ROW for CDC and multi-source topologies. Require primary keys on every table, and make large batch jobs chunked so row events stay manageable.

Mid-Level Notes

  • STATEMENT is small but unsafe for non-deterministic functions (NOW(), UUID(), RAND()) and some statements.
  • ROW is exact and deterministic but produces larger logs for bulk changes.
  • MIXED logs statements normally and rows for unsafe ones.

Senior Notes

  • ROW format is required for READ COMMITTED isolation safety, CDC tools (Debezium) and reliable replication.
  • binlog_row_image=MINIMAL reduces size by logging only changed columns plus keys.
  • Large updates/deletes inflate row logs; batch and monitor.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: statement format with non-deterministic functions, tables without primary keys under ROW format (replicas scan for each row), and huge multi-row updates creating enormous binlog events. Give every table a primary key and batch large changes.
codeExamples:
SELECT t.table_name FROM information_schema.tables t LEFT JOIN information_schema.statistics s ON s.table_schema=t.table_schema AND s.table_name=t.table_name AND s.index_name='PRIMARY' WHERE t.table_schema='shop' AND t.table_type='BASE TABLE' AND s.index_name IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name
-- legacy_import       (row-based replication of this table will be very slow)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Row format log size grows with rows changed, not statement length: one UPDATE of 10 million rows writes 10 million row images. Compare sizes and batch big maintenance jobs.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: change data capture. Tools such as Debezium read ROW events to produce an ordered stream of inserts, updates and deletes for search indexes, caches and warehouses, with no triggers and no extra writes on the primary.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('binlog_format','binlog_row_image','binlog_row_metadata','log_bin');

-- OUTPUT:
-- binlog_format       | ROW
-- binlog_row_image    | FULL
-- binlog_row_metadata | FULL      (column names included for CDC consumers)

beginner.content:
Introduction

The binlog is the transport and the history. A replica's I/O thread copies events from the source's binlog into a relay log, and a SQL thread applies them. For recovery, mysqlbinlog replays the same events onto a restored backup.
codeExamples:
-- On the replica: which source file/position has it read and applied?
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example, abridged):
-- *************************** 1. row ***************************
--          Replica_IO_State: Waiting for source to send event
--              Source_Log_File: binlog.000042
--          Read_Source_Log_Pos: 158732
--          Replica_IO_Running: Yes
--         Replica_SQL_Running: Yes

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Replication and recovery both need an ordered, complete list of changes plus a way to say "start here". Coordinates (file + position) or GTIDs give that starting point.
codeExamples:
-- Coordinates of "now" on the source (use these when seeding a replica from a backup)
SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS;          -- 8.2+ ; older: SHOW MASTER STATUS

-- Point a new replica at the source from those coordinates
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO
    SOURCE_HOST = 'db1', SOURCE_USER = 'repl', SOURCE_PASSWORD = 'secret',
    SOURCE_LOG_FILE = 'binlog.000042', SOURCE_LOG_POS = 158732;
START REPLICA;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.05 sec)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real flows: seed a replica from a backup then stream binlogs; CDC pipelines read the binlog as a client; and ops teams run mysqlbinlog to extract a transaction for a hot-fix or audit.
codeExamples:
# Stream binlogs continuously to a backup host (acts as a replica client, no SQL thread)
mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --host=db1 --user=repl --password \
            --raw --stop-never --result-file=/binlog_archive/ binlog.000042
# Extract just one database's changes from a file
mysqlbinlog --database=shop binlog.000042 > shop_changes.sql

# OUTPUT (example):
# (running; files binlog.000042 ... appear in /binlog_archive/)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SOURCE                                REPLICA                     RECOVERY HOST
   commit ► binlog.00042 ──(I/O thread)► relay log ─(SQL threads)► data
                  │
                  └── mysqlbinlog ──► .sql ──► mysql  (roll a restored backup forward)

Fresher Notes

  • Replicas copy the primary’s binary log events and apply them. For recovery, you replay binlog events after restoring a backup.
  • So the binlog powers both high availability and PITR.
  • The primary writes events; replicas read them through a network connection.

Worked Example 1

Relay log files on the replica.
codeExamples:
SHOW RELAY LOGS;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Log_name           | File_size
-- relay-bin.000007   | 1048576

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Stream binlogs off-host.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --host=primary --user=repl --raw --stop-never --result-file=/backup/binlogs/ binlog.000042

-- OUTPUT:
-- (new events appended to local files continuously)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Replica status.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Replica_IO_Running: Yes
-- Replica_SQL_Running: Yes
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Primary status.
codeExamples:
SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS;

-- OUTPUT:
-- File          | Position | Executed_Gtid_Set
-- binlog.000042 |     1543 | 3e11fa47-...:1-1850

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A replica runs an I/O thread that connects to the source, reads binlog events and appends them to its own relay log, and an SQL (applier) thread that executes the relay log events. The position is tracked by file and offset or by GTID set, so the replica can resume after a restart.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Replica_IO_Running: Yes
-- Replica_SQL_Running: Yes
-- Source_Log_File: binlog.000042   Read_Source_Log_Pos: 1543
-- Retrieved_Gtid_Set: 3e11...:1-1850   Executed_Gtid_Set: 3e11...:1-1850
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

The same stream serves recovery: restore a backup then apply binlog events from the recorded position. Tools: mysqlbinlog, SHOW BINLOG EVENTS, CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO, relay log settings and compression of the binlog (binlog_transaction_compression).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: one mechanism serves replication, backup roll-forward and CDC; changes are replayable and filterable; the same log is the audit trail.
codeExamples:
-- Filter a replica to a subset of databases (set on the replica, per channel)
CHANGE REPLICATION FILTER REPLICATE_DO_DB = (shop, billing);
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Replicate_Do_DB: shop,billing

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: replicas depend on the source retaining logs; if logs are purged before a replica reads them the replica breaks (error 1236); replay is single-stream unless multi-threaded replication is configured.
codeExamples:
-- Typical failure when the source purged logs the replica still needs:
-- Last_IO_Error: Got fatal error 1236 from source when reading data from binary log:
--   'Could not find first log file name in binary log index file'
-- Prevent it: retention longer than the worst replica outage
SET PERSIST binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 1209600;    -- 14 days

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: replaying a binlog onto a server in a different state (wrong starting point, missing tables) fails or corrupts; GTID gaps and non-deterministic statements need care; DDL replays are not transactional.
codeExamples:
-- Safer replay: GTID auto-positioning removes manual file/position math
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_HOST='db1', SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1;
-- Check which transactions the replica already has:
SELECT @@GLOBAL.gtid_executed;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------------------------------------+
-- | @@GLOBAL.gtid_executed                       |
-- +----------------------------------------------+
-- | 3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-1523  |
-- +----------------------------------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer GTIDs plus row format for both replication and recovery: positions become portable and failover safe. Stream binlogs to an archive host so loss of the primary does not lose the log. Monitor retention against the slowest replica and test that a restore plus replay lands on the expected GTID set.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Replication threads: the replica I/O (receiver) thread copies events to a relay log; the SQL (applier) thread executes them.
  • Binlog position or GTID tells the replica where to continue.
  • Keep binlogs long enough for a lagging or temporarily down replica to catch up.

Senior Notes

  • If a replica needs events that were purged, you must rebuild it from a backup.
  • GTIDs make failover and recovery simpler by identifying transactions globally.
  • For recovery, store binlogs off-host in near real time (mysqlbinlog --stop-never) so a lost primary does not lose its log.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: purging binlogs a replica still needs (it cannot catch up and must be rebuilt), keeping binlogs only on the primary (lost with the server), and running replicas with different formats or versions without testing. Archive binlogs off-host and monitor the oldest required file.
codeExamples:
SHOW BINARY LOGS;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Last_IO_Error: Got fatal error 1236 from source when reading data from binary log: 'Could not find first log file name in binary log index file'

-- OUTPUT:
-- (the replica needs a fresh clone: restore a backup and start replication from its GTID set)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Apply speed decides lag. Multi-threaded replication (replica_parallel_workers, replica_parallel_type=LOGICAL_CLOCK) applies independent transactions in parallel. Large transactions and missing primary keys slow the applier.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: continuous off-host binlog archiving gives point-in-time recovery even if the primary and its disks are lost.
codeExamples:
mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --host=primary --user=repl --raw --stop-never --result-file=/backup/binlogs/ binlog.000042
aws s3 sync /backup/binlogs/ s3://dr-backups/binlogs/ --storage-class STANDARD_IA

-- OUTPUT:
-- upload: binlogs/binlog.000043 to s3://dr-backups/binlogs/binlog.000043

beginner.content:
Introduction

In MySQL replication a source (formerly master) accepts writes and records them in its binary log; one or more replicas copy that log into a relay log and apply it, keeping their data in step. Two replica threads do the work: the I/O thread fetches, the SQL (applier) thread executes.
codeExamples:
# my.cnf on the SOURCE
# [mysqld]
# server-id = 1
# log_bin   = binlog
# gtid_mode = ON
# enforce_gtid_consistency = ON
# my.cnf on the REPLICA
# [mysqld]
# server-id = 2          # must be unique in the topology
# relay_log = relay
# read_only = ON
# super_read_only = ON   # block even privileged users from writing

-- On the source, create the replication account:
CREATE USER 'repl'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'S3cret!pw';
GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'repl'@'%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

One server cannot scale reads forever and is a single point of failure. A replica gives read capacity, a safe place to run backups and reports, and a standby copy for failover.
codeExamples:
-- On the replica: connect and start (GTID auto-positioning)
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO
    SOURCE_HOST = 'db1', SOURCE_PORT = 3306,
    SOURCE_USER = 'repl', SOURCE_PASSWORD = 'S3cret!pw',
    SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION = 1, SOURCE_SSL = 1;
START REPLICA;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example, abridged):
--      Replica_IO_Running: Yes
--     Replica_SQL_Running: Yes
--  Seconds_Behind_Source: 0

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical topologies: one source with N read replicas behind a load balancer, a chain (replica of a replica) for cross-region, a delayed replica as an undo button, and multi-source replicas that merge shards for analytics.

Diagram

   Clients (writes)                       Clients (reads)
        │                                   │       │
        ▼                                   ▼       ▼
   ┌─────────┐   binlog     ┌─ I/O thread ─► relay log ─► SQL threads ─┐
   │ SOURCE  │ ───────────► │             REPLICA 1                    │ data
   │ (R/W)   │   binlog     ├─ I/O thread ─► relay log ─► SQL threads ─┤
   └─────────┘ ───────────► │             REPLICA 2   (read_only)      │ data
                            └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

Fresher Notes

  • In replication one server (source/primary) accepts writes and one or more replicas copy its changes.
  • Replicas are read-only copies used for reads, reports and backups.
  • Application writes go to the source; reads can go to replicas.

Worked Example 1

Verify.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Replica_IO_Running: Yes
-- Replica_SQL_Running: Yes
-- Last_Error:

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Read-only replica.

Practice Exercise 1

Configure the source.
codeExamples:
-- my.cnf (source)
[mysqld]
server_id = 1
log_bin = binlog
gtid_mode = ON
enforce_gtid_consistency = ON

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- SELECT @@server_id, @@gtid_mode;  =>  1 | ON

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Connect the replica.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In asynchronous replication the source commits and returns to the client without waiting for replicas. Replicas pull the binlog, copy it to a relay log and replay it. Replicas are therefore always slightly behind. Writes go to the source; reads that tolerate staleness can go to replicas.
codeExamples:
-- source my.cnf
[mysqld]
server_id = 1
log_bin = binlog
gtid_mode = ON
enforce_gtid_consistency = ON
binlog_format = ROW

CREATE USER 'repl'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'R3pl#Pass1';
GRANT REPLICATION SLAVE ON *.* TO 'repl'@'%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Topologies: one replica, several replicas, chained replicas, delayed replicas (protect against mistakes), multi-source replication, and group-based clusters. Replicas should be read-only (super_read_only). Provision a replica from a backup that records its GTID set.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: read scaling, built in, low overhead, geographic distribution, backup offloading, and a warm standby.
codeExamples:
-- Backups from a replica leave the source untouched
STOP REPLICA SQL_THREAD;                 -- freeze applying, keep fetching
-- ... take mysqldump / snapshot here ...
START REPLICA SQL_THREAD;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: replicas lag, writes do not scale (every replica applies every write), schema changes and large transactions delay replicas, and applications must handle read-after-write staleness.

Limitations

Limitations: a single source for writes (no built-in write scaling or conflict resolution), replicas must be same or newer version than the source, and writing directly to a replica causes divergence unless super_read_only is set.
codeExamples:
-- Accidental write on a replica with super_read_only=ON:
INSERT INTO orders (id, total) VALUES (999, 1);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1290 (HY000): The MySQL server is running with the --super-read-only option so it cannot execute this statement

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Replication is for read scale and availability, not write scale; if writes are the limit, shard. Use GTID, row format, super_read_only on replicas, SSL for the channel, and a unique server_id plan. Keep replicas at least the source's hardware class: a weaker replica becomes permanently lagged.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Setup: enable binlog and server_id on source, create a replication user, point the replica at the source (CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO ...) and start it.
  • Replication is asynchronous by default: replicas may lag.
  • Topologies: single replica, multiple replicas, chain (replica of replica), multi-source.

Senior Notes

  • Reading from replicas means handling stale reads: route read-your-writes traffic to the primary or use session tokens/GTID wait.
  • Replicas can be a bottleneck if single-threaded apply; use multi-threaded replication (replica_parallel_workers).
  • Consider semi-sync or Group Replication for stronger durability.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: writing to a replica (diverging data), reading your own writes from a replica (stale reads), different server_id values missing, and ignoring errors (a stopped SQL thread). Route read-your-writes to the primary, or wait for the GTID.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Replicas offload reads and backups. Scale reads by adding replicas behind a router or proxy that keeps lagging nodes out of the pool. The primary still limits write throughput.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: reporting runs on a replica, nightly backups run on another replica, and a delayed replica one hour behind gives a safety net against accidental deletes.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt, delayed replica)
-- SQL_Delay: 3600   Seconds_Behind_Source: 3600   (use it to recover from a mistaken DELETE made within the last hour)

beginner.content:
Introduction

In asynchronous replication the source commits and answers the client without waiting for any replica. In semi-synchronous replication the source waits until at least one replica acknowledges that it has received (written to its relay log) the transaction, before returning success.

Why Do We Need This?

With plain async, if the source dies right after a commit, the replica may never have received it, so promoting that replica loses data. Semi-sync narrows that window: an acknowledged commit exists on at least two machines.
codeExamples:
-- Async data-loss window:
--  t0 client: COMMIT -> source says OK
--  t1 source crashes before sending the event
--  t2 replica promoted: the transaction is gone (RPO > 0)
-- Semi-sync (AFTER_SYNC): the source does not tell the client OK until a replica has the event
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------------------+------------+
-- | Variable_name                        | Value      |
-- +--------------------------------------+------------+
-- | rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point      | AFTER_SYNC |
-- +--------------------------------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real use: payment and order systems use semi-sync (or Group Replication) so that failover loses nothing; read-heavy content sites stay on async for lowest write latency.
codeExamples:
-- Is semi-sync actually active right now?
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status';
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_yes_tx';     -- commits acknowledged by a replica
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx';      -- commits that timed out to async

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_status   ON
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_yes_tx   1829934
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx    0

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ASYNC                              SEMI-SYNC (AFTER_SYNC)
   client ─COMMIT─► SOURCE            client ─COMMIT─► SOURCE ─binlog─► REPLICA
   client ◄──OK──── SOURCE                              SOURCE ◄──ACK─── (relay log written)
          (replica gets it later)     client ◄──OK─────

Fresher Notes

  • Asynchronous replication: the source commits without waiting for replicas. Semi-synchronous: the source waits until at least one replica has received the event.
  • Async is fastest but a crash can lose recent commits that never reached a replica.
  • Semi-sync reduces that loss at a small latency cost.

Worked Example 1

Check ack counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_yes_tx';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name                | Value
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_yes_tx  | 482113

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Fallback to async detected.

Practice Exercise 1

Enable semi-sync on the source.

Practice Exercise 2

Enable on the replica.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

In asynchronous replication a transaction is committed on the source without waiting for any replica. If the source fails right after, recent commits that never reached a replica are lost. In semi-synchronous replication the source waits, before returning COMMIT to the client, until at least one replica acknowledges that it has received and logged the event (the acknowledgement point is configurable).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point (AFTER_SYNC is lossless), wait_for_replica_count, timeout. On the replica enable rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled and restart the I/O thread. For stronger guarantees use Group Replication.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: async = fastest commits and no dependency on replicas; semi-sync = much lower data-loss risk, simple to adopt, uses existing replication.
codeExamples:
-- Choose how many replica acks are required (8.0.26+)
SET PERSIST rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_for_replica_count = 2;   -- ack from 2 replicas
-- AFTER_SYNC (lossless): waits before the commit is visible to other sessions

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: async can lose acknowledged commits; semi-sync adds a network round trip to each commit, and after a timeout silently degrades to async, giving a false sense of safety.
codeExamples:
-- If the replica is down longer than rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout, source falls back:
-- Error log: Timeout waiting for reply of binlog (file: binlog.000042, pos: 158732),
--            semi-sync up to file binlog.000042, position 158700.
-- Alert on the status flag:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_status   OFF      <- running in async mode now

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: semi-sync only guarantees the event was received (relay log), not applied, so replicas can still lag; it does not give automatic failover or consensus; it is not a substitute for Group Replication when zero data loss is mandatory.
codeExamples:
-- Received vs applied are different counters:
SELECT CHANNEL_NAME, SERVICE_STATE FROM performance_schema.replication_connection_status;
SELECT CHANNEL_NAME, SERVICE_STATE FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------+---------------+
-- | CHANNEL_NAME | SERVICE_STATE |
-- +--------------+---------------+
-- |              | ON            |
-- +--------------+---------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use semi-sync when RPO must be near zero but you want familiar source/replica operations; set the timeout and monitor the fallback flag as a first-class alert. If you need guaranteed consistency and automatic membership, move to Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Semi-sync setting: rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled and rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_for_replica_count (via plugins/components).
  • If no replica acknowledges within a timeout, the source falls back to async.
  • Received is not the same as applied: a replica can still lag in applying.

Senior Notes

  • For no data loss use Group Replication or InnoDB Cluster (consensus-based) or cloud-managed multi-AZ storage replication.
  • Semi-sync with AFTER_SYNC (lossless) ensures committed data reached a replica before the client sees success.
  • Measure latency impact between data centers; semi-sync across regions can be costly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: assuming semi-sync guarantees the replica has applied the data (only received), forgetting the timeout fallback to asynchronous mode, and placing the acknowledging replica far away. Monitor the status and the fallback counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Rpl_semi_sync_source_status','Rpl_semi_sync_source_yes_tx','Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx','Rpl_semi_sync_source_clients');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_status | ON
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_yes_tx | 482113
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_no_tx  |    120       (commits that fell back to async)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Semi-sync adds the replica round trip to every commit, so use a nearby replica for the acknowledgement. Measure commit latency with and without it.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(AVG_TIMER_WAIT / 1e9, 2) AS avg_commit_ms FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest WHERE digest_text LIKE 'COMMIT%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- async: 0.9 ms   semi-sync same AZ: 1.8 ms   semi-sync cross-region: 62 ms
-- avg_commit_ms
-- 1.84

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: payment systems use semi-sync (or Group Replication) with a replica in another availability zone, accepting extra commit latency to avoid losing acknowledged payments on a primary crash.
codeExamples:
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_status';
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT:
-- Rpl_semi_sync_source_status | ON

beginner.content:
Introduction

Replication lag is the delay between a change committing on the source and being applied on a replica. It appears as Seconds_Behind_Source and is caused by slow network, a slow applier, or large transactions.
codeExamples:
-- Quick lag reading on the replica
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- OUTPUT (example, abridged):
--    Seconds_Behind_Source: 37
--   Replica_SQL_Running_State: Waiting for dependent transaction to commit

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Lag makes read replicas return stale data and extends failover time (the replica must finish applying before promotion). Knowing the cause tells you whether to fix network, schema, queries or hardware.
codeExamples:
-- Precise lag in 8.0: compare original commit time with apply time per worker
SELECT WORKER_ID, LAST_APPLIED_TRANSACTION,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, LAST_APPLIED_TRANSACTION_ORIGINAL_COMMIT_TIMESTAMP,
                             LAST_APPLIED_TRANSACTION_END_APPLY_TIMESTAMP) AS lag_s
FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status_by_worker;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------+---------------------------------------------+-------+
-- | WORKER_ID | LAST_APPLIED_TRANSACTION                    | lag_s |
-- +-----------+---------------------------------------------+-------+
-- |         1 | 3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:15234  |     2 |
-- +-----------+---------------------------------------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Common real causes: one huge UPDATE/DELETE, DDL like ALTER TABLE, tables without primary keys, a weaker replica, a long-running read on the replica blocking the applier, and single-threaded applying.

Diagram

   SOURCE commit ─► binlog ─► network ─► relay log ─► apply ─► visible
        t0                      +d1        +d2         +d3
   Lag = t(visible on replica) - t0 = d1 + d2 + d3
   d1 network | d2 I/O + disk | d3 applier (single thread? big txn? no PK?)

Fresher Notes

  • Replication lag is the delay between a change on the source and its application on a replica.
  • See it with Seconds_Behind_Source in SHOW REPLICA STATUS.
  • Reads from a lagging replica show old data.

Worked Example 1

Heartbeat lag measurement.
codeExamples:
-- source: every second
REPLACE INTO ops.heartbeat (id, ts) VALUES (1, NOW(6));
-- replica:
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, ts, NOW(6)) / 1000000 AS lag_seconds FROM ops.heartbeat WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- lag_seconds
-- 0.84

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Per-worker apply status.
codeExamples:
SELECT worker_id, last_applied_transaction, applying_transaction FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status_by_worker;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
