-- worker_id | last_applied_transaction | applying_transaction
-- 1         | 3e11...:1850             | 3e11...:1852

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Check lag.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 37
-- Replica_SQL_Running_State: Waiting for dependent transaction to commit

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Enable parallel apply.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Lag is the delay between a commit on the source and its application on the replica. It has three parts: transfer time to the relay log, queueing in the relay log, and apply time. Seconds_Behind_Source is computed from event timestamps, so it can mislead (zero while stalled, jumps after idle periods).
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 37
-- Replica_SQL_Running_State: Waiting for dependent transaction to commit
-- Relay_Log_Space: 804212736

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common causes: large transactions, single-threaded apply, replica hardware or I/O weaker than the source, missing primary keys under row format, heavy reads on the replica, and DDL. Mitigations: parallel workers, smaller transactions, indexes and key columns, better I/O.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of measuring and managing it: you can route reads by freshness, alert before users notice, and pick the correct fix (parallelism, batching, schema) instead of guessing.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages / traps: Seconds_Behind_Source is only approximate (it is 0 when idle or NULL when stopped, and can jump), and big transactions make lag appear in sudden spikes.
codeExamples:
-- A 5-million-row delete runs for minutes on the source and again on the replica:
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01';
-- Fix: batch it so each transaction is small
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < '2024-01-01' LIMIT 10000;   -- repeat in a loop with a short sleep

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Query OK, 10000 rows affected (0.15 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: zero lag cannot be guaranteed with asynchronous replication; parallel workers help only if transactions are independent; heartbeat (pt-heartbeat) is needed for accurate measurement across chains.
codeExamples:
-- Heartbeat table pattern (what pt-heartbeat does): source writes now() every second
CREATE TABLE ops.heartbeat (id INT PRIMARY KEY, ts TIMESTAMP(6) NOT NULL);
REPLACE INTO ops.heartbeat VALUES (1, NOW(6));      -- run on source every second
-- On replica, true lag is:
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, ts, NOW(6))/1000 AS lag_ms FROM ops.heartbeat WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+
-- | lag_ms |
-- +--------+
-- | 1043.7 |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Design applications to tolerate staleness: read-your-writes through the source or GTID wait, and route only freshness-insensitive queries to replicas. Fix lag at the root with small transactions, primary keys, parallel replication, and capacity parity; alert on lag with a heartbeat, not on Seconds_Behind_Source alone.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Causes: big transactions, single-threaded apply, heavy replica load, slow disks, missing indexes for row-based updates, network issues.
  • Mitigate with multi-threaded replication, smaller batches, indexes on replicas and better hardware.
  • Seconds_Behind_Source can be misleading; use heartbeat tables for accurate lag.

Senior Notes

  • Design apps to tolerate lag: read-your-writes on primary, lag-aware routing (ProxySQL), circuit-break to the primary when lag is high.
  • Alert on lag thresholds and trends, not only absolute values.
  • Large DDL or bulk updates are classic lag sources; throttle them and use online schema tools that observe lag.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: trusting Seconds_Behind_Source alone, reading from a lagging replica for critical data, and running huge batch jobs in one transaction. Use a heartbeat table for accurate lag and batch maintenance with throttling.
codeExamples:
-- on the source, every second
REPLACE INTO ops.heartbeat (id, ts) VALUES (1, NOW(6));
-- on the replica
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, ts, NOW(6)) / 1000000 AS lag_seconds FROM ops.heartbeat WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- lag_seconds
-- 0.84

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Application strategy: route read-your-writes to the primary, route others only to replicas below a lag threshold, and fall back to the primary when lag is high. Proxies (ProxySQL, MySQL Router) can enforce lag limits.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nightly purge once caused 40 minutes of lag. The fix was batching deletes by 2,000 rows with a pause that waits for lag to drop under a threshold before the next batch.
codeExamples:
DELETE FROM events WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 90 DAY LIMIT 2000;
-- loop: sleep until (SELECT lag_seconds FROM replica_lag) < 3 before the next batch

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2000 rows affected   (replication lag stays below 3 seconds)

beginner.content:
Introduction

A read replica serves SELECT traffic so the source can focus on writes. Failover is promoting a replica to become the new source when the old one fails and re-pointing the other replicas and applications.
codeExamples:
-- Application-level read/write split (pseudocode against two hostnames)
--   writes  -> db-primary.example.com:3306
--   reads   -> db-replica.example.com:3306   (DNS or proxy balances many replicas)
-- Verify which role a connection landed on:
SELECT @@hostname AS host, @@read_only AS ro, @@super_read_only AS sro;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+----+-----+
-- | host   | ro | sro |
-- +--------+----+-----+
-- | db2    |  1 |   1 |
-- +--------+----+-----+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Read traffic is often 80-95% of load, and a failed source must be replaced quickly. Replicas solve both if there is a rehearsed promotion procedure.

Real-Time Use

Real systems: ProxySQL or MySQL Router splits reads and writes, Orchestrator or cloud managers detect failure and promote, and cloud read replicas (RDS, Cloud SQL) are provisioned with a click.
codeExamples:
-- ProxySQL rules (admin interface): send SELECTs to hostgroup 20 (replicas), the rest to 10 (source)
INSERT INTO mysql_query_rules (rule_id, active, match_digest, destination_hostgroup, apply)
VALUES (1, 1, '^SELECT .* FOR UPDATE', 10, 1),
       (2, 1, '^SELECT',               20, 1);
LOAD MYSQL QUERY RULES TO RUNTIME;  SAVE MYSQL QUERY RULES TO DISK;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected (0.00 sec)

beginner.content:
Diagram

                 ┌── writes ──► SOURCE (db1) ──binlog──┐
   App ─► Proxy ─┤                                     ├─► REPLICA db2  ◄─ reads
                 └── reads  ──────────────────────────► REPLICA db3  ◄─ reads
   db1 fails ─► fence db1 ─► promote most-advanced replica ─► repoint db3 + proxy

Fresher Notes

  • A read replica serves read-only queries to reduce load on the primary. Failover promotes a replica to primary when the primary fails.
  • Reads can scale by adding replicas; writes still go to one primary.
  • Failover can be manual or automatic.

Worked Example 1

ProxySQL read/write rules.

Worked Example 2

Fence a failed primary.

Practice Exercise 1

Promote a replica.

Practice Exercise 2

Wait for GTIDs before reading (read-your-writes).
codeExamples:
SELECT WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET('3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-1850', 1) AS ok;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ok
-- 0     (0 = replica caught up within 1 second)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A read replica serves read-only queries. Failover promotes a replica to primary when the primary fails: stop replication on the candidate, make sure it applied everything it received, make it writable, point other replicas and clients at it, and fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes (avoiding split-brain).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Routing options: application-level read/write split, ProxySQL query rules, MySQL Router ports (6446 read/write, 6447 read-only), or cloud endpoints. Automated failover tools: InnoDB Cluster, Orchestrator, MHA, managed services.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: horizontal read scale, isolation of reporting load, and a ready standby so recovery takes seconds to minutes instead of hours.
codeExamples:
-- Pick the most up-to-date replica to promote: compare executed GTID sets
SELECT @@GLOBAL.gtid_executed;      -- run on each replica; choose the superset
SELECT GTID_SUBSET('uuid:1-1500', 'uuid:1-1523') AS is_behind;   -- 1 = first set contained in second

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------+
-- | is_behind |
-- +-----------+
-- |         1 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: failover is risky (split brain if the old source comes back writable), applications see stale reads, connection routing must be updated, and unreplicated transactions may be lost on async.
codeExamples:
-- Split-brain guard: fence the old primary before promoting
-- (OS level)   systemctl stop mysqld   or remove its VIP / security-group access
-- If it ever comes back, force it read-only immediately:
SET GLOBAL super_read_only = ON;
SET GLOBAL read_only = ON;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: plain replication gives no automatic promotion or quorum; reads from replicas are eventually consistent; and multi-primary writes across replicas need Group Replication or application sharding.
codeExamples:
-- Detect a broken replica before sending it traffic:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Only route when ALL of these are true:
--   Replica_IO_Running = Yes, Replica_SQL_Running = Yes, Seconds_Behind_Source below your threshold

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Replica_IO_Running: Yes   Replica_SQL_Running: Yes   Seconds_Behind_Source: 0

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Automate failover with a tested tool (Orchestrator, MySQL InnoDB Cluster, or your cloud's managed failover) and always fence the old primary. Design reads with explicit staleness tolerance, avoid sending read-after-write paths to replicas, and rehearse failover quarterly with real traffic in staging.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Routing: application-level read/write split, or a proxy such as ProxySQL / MySQL Router that sends writes to the primary and reads to replicas.
  • Promotion steps: stop writes to the old primary, ensure the chosen replica has applied everything (GTID), make it writable, point others to it.
  • Fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes.

Senior Notes

  • Split-brain (two writable primaries) is the worst failure; use fencing (STONITH), consensus (Group Replication/Orchestrator with Raft) and clear leader election.
  • Test failover regularly; automatic failover without drills is risky.
  • Account for data loss in async replication: transactions not yet replicated may be lost or need reconciliation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: split-brain from an old primary that comes back writable, promoting a lagging replica (lost transactions), clients that cache the old address, and untested failover. Fence, check GTIDs and drill regularly.
codeExamples:
SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT('3e11...:1-1900', @@gtid_executed) AS missing_on_candidate;
SET PERSIST super_read_only = ON;       -- fence the old primary when it returns

-- OUTPUT:
-- missing_on_candidate
-- 3e11...:1851-1900         (50 transactions would be lost: choose a more advanced replica or recover them)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Read replicas scale reads linearly until replication lag or the primary's write rate becomes the limit. Measure per-replica query load and lag, and add replicas before saturation.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world failover drill: kill the primary in a staging copy of production, measure detection and promotion time, verify no lost or duplicated writes, and record the result against the RTO target.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_after, MAX(id) AS max_id FROM orders;
-- compare with the counts captured before the failure

-- OUTPUT:
-- rows_after | max_id
-- 612044     | 612044          (no lost writes; recovery completed in 27 seconds)

beginner.content:
Introduction

A GTID (Global Transaction Identifier) is a unique id source_uuid:sequence assigned to every committed transaction. Replicas track which GTIDs they have executed, so they can pick up exactly where they left off without file names or positions.
codeExamples:
-- Enable GTID (my.cnf or SET PERSIST on a quiesced server, in this order for online change)
-- gtid_mode = ON ; enforce_gtid_consistency = ON
SELECT @@GLOBAL.gtid_mode, @@GLOBAL.enforce_gtid_consistency;
SELECT @@GLOBAL.gtid_executed;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------------+-----------------------------------+
-- | @@GLOBAL.gtid_mode | @@GLOBAL.enforce_gtid_consistency |
-- +--------------------+-----------------------------------+
-- | ON                 | ON                                |
-- +--------------------+-----------------------------------+
-- 3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-1523

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

File and position coordinates differ on every server, which makes failover and re-pointing error-prone. GTIDs are the same everywhere: a replica simply says "I have these, send the rest".

Real-Time Use

Real use: automated failover tools rely on GTIDs, backups store the gtid_executed set so a restored node can join, and operators skip a poison transaction by committing an empty one with that GTID.

Diagram

   SOURCE uuid=3e11...                        REPLICA
   tx1 = 3e11:1   ─┐                          gtid_executed = 3e11:1-3
   tx2 = 3e11:2    ├─ binlog ─────────────►   "send me everything not in 3e11:1-3"
   tx3 = 3e11:3   ─┤                          source sends 3e11:4, 3e11:5 ...
   tx4 = 3e11:4   ─┘

Fresher Notes

  • A GTID (Global Transaction ID) uniquely identifies every transaction, written as source_uuid:sequence.
  • With GTIDs a replica asks "give me everything I have not executed" instead of tracking file and position.
  • Enable with gtid_mode=ON and enforce_gtid_consistency=ON.

Worked Example 1

Detect errant transactions.
codeExamples:
SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT(@@gtid_executed, '3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-1850') AS errant;

-- OUTPUT:
-- errant
-- 9a1b...:1-3     (executed here, not on the source)

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Replica using auto position.

Practice Exercise 1

See executed GTIDs.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@gtid_executed;

-- OUTPUT:
-- @@gtid_executed
-- 3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-1850

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Skip a transaction.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A GTID is source_uuid:transaction_number, assigned at commit and written to the binlog with the transaction. Each server tracks the set of GTIDs it has executed (gtid_executed). A replica using auto-positioning tells the source its executed set, and the source sends exactly the missing transactions, so file names and offsets are not needed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Operations: compare sets with GTID_SUBTRACT, wait for a transaction with WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET, skip a failing transaction by committing an empty one with its GTID, and enable GTIDs online through the permissive modes.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: trivial re-pointing, safe failover, easy to prove that a replica has (or lacks) a transaction, auto-skip of already executed transactions, and required by Group Replication and InnoDB Cluster.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: enabling requires planning, some statements are forbidden (CREATE TABLE ... SELECT in older versions, mixing transactional and non-transactional tables in one transaction), and errant GTIDs on a replica are hard to explain at first.
codeExamples:
-- Errant transaction: a write made directly on a replica gets its own UUID
-- On replica:  gtid_executed = srcUUID:1-1523, replicaUUID:1
-- If this replica is promoted, the extra replicaUUID:1 spreads confusion. Detect it:
SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT(@@GLOBAL.gtid_executed, '3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-1523') AS errant;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------------------------------+
-- | errant                               |
-- +--------------------------------------+
-- | 9b2c1a10-0000-11ee-aaaa-0242ac110003:1 |
-- +--------------------------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: gtid_purged must cover logs that no longer exist; a replica can only auto-position if the source still has the binlogs it needs; and you cannot turn GTID mode off while GTID transactions are still being applied.

Architect's Notes

Standardize on GTID with enforce_gtid_consistency for any topology you intend to fail over. Store gtid_executed with each backup, never write on replicas (super_read_only), and monitor for errant GTIDs because they block clean promotion.

Mid-Level Notes

  • SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 lets replicas find their place automatically.
  • Failover is simpler: a new primary and any replica agree on which transactions are applied.
  • Skip a bad transaction by injecting an empty transaction with its GTID.

Senior Notes

  • Constraints: no CREATE TABLE ... SELECT in older versions, no mixing non-transactional engines in one transaction; enforce_gtid_consistency checks these.
  • Compare gtid_executed sets to detect divergence or errant transactions on replicas.
  • Backups should record the GTID set to rebuild replicas precisely.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: errant transactions (writes made directly on a replica) that block promotion, statements not allowed under GTID consistency (non-transactional engines mixed in a transaction), and enabling GTID in one step on a busy system. Detect errant GTIDs and step through the modes.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

GTIDs make replica creation and failover faster and less error-prone, and let proxies check freshness. Their cost is small: the gtid tables and binlog headers. Keep gtid_executed compact by letting the server compress it periodically.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: read-your-writes. After a write on the primary, capture its GTID and ask the replica to wait for it before reading, so the user always sees their own change.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (1, 500);
SELECT @@global.gtid_executed;                    -- on the primary
SELECT WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET('3e11...:1-1851', 1);   -- on the replica

-- OUTPUT:
-- 0       (the replica has applied the write; safe to read)

beginner.content:
Introduction

Monitoring replication means regularly checking that threads run, lag is low, data matches, and errors are caught. The main sources are SHOW REPLICA STATUS and the performance_schema replication tables.
codeExamples:
-- Thread health, in a query-friendly form
SELECT c.CHANNEL_NAME, c.SERVICE_STATE AS io_state, a.SERVICE_STATE AS sql_state,
       c.LAST_ERROR_MESSAGE AS io_err
FROM   performance_schema.replication_connection_status c
JOIN   performance_schema.replication_applier_status    a USING (CHANNEL_NAME);

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------+----------+-----------+--------+
-- | CHANNEL_NAME | io_state | sql_state | io_err |
-- +--------------+----------+-----------+--------+
-- |              | ON       | ON        |        |
-- +--------------+----------+-----------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Replication fails silently: a stopped thread or a drifted row may be noticed only when a failover goes wrong. Monitoring turns hidden risk into alerts.
codeExamples:
-- The fields that matter in SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
--   Replica_IO_Running / Replica_SQL_Running   (both must be Yes)
--   Seconds_Behind_Source                      (lag)
--   Last_IO_Error / Last_SQL_Error             (cause of a stop)
--   Retrieved_Gtid_Set vs Executed_Gtid_Set    (fetched vs applied)
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example, a broken replica):
--   Replica_SQL_Running: No
--   Last_SQL_Errno: 1062
--   Last_SQL_Error: Could not execute Write_rows event on table shop.orders; Duplicate entry '501' for key 'PRIMARY'

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real setups: Prometheus mysqld_exporter plus Grafana, PMM, cloud metrics; an alert if lag above 30 s for 5 minutes, any thread down, or a replica missing from SHOW REPLICAS.
codeExamples:
-- Source-side view: which replicas are connected and how far they have read?
SELECT * FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;   -- group replication only
SHOW REPLICAS;
SHOW PROCESSLIST;     -- look for "Binlog Dump GTID" threads, one per replica

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- | 12 | repl | db2:51822 | NULL | Binlog Dump GTID | 80233 | Source has sent all binlog to replica; waiting for more updates | NULL |

beginner.content:
Diagram

   REPLICA ──► SHOW REPLICA STATUS / performance_schema
                    │ (scrape every 15 s)
                    ▼
              exporter ─► Prometheus ─► Grafana dashboards
                                   └──► Alertmanager ─► page: IO/SQL down, lag, errant GTID
   Periodic:  pt-table-checksum  ► detect silent data drift

Fresher Notes

  • Monitor replication to know if replicas are running and how far behind they are.
  • Check SHOW REPLICA STATUS: Replica_IO_Running, Replica_SQL_Running, Seconds_Behind_Source and Last_Error.
  • Set alerts for stopped threads and growing lag.

Worked Example 1

Detect divergence.
codeExamples:
pt-table-checksum --host=primary --user=chk --password=*** --databases=shop

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- TS ERRORS DIFFS ROWS CHUNKS SKIPPED TIME TABLE
-- 05-01 0 0 120450 12 0 4.2 shop.orders

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Prometheus alert rule.
codeExamples:
- alert: MySQLReplicaLagHigh
  expr: mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_master > 30
  for: 5m

-- OUTPUT:
-- Alert fires when lag stays above 30 s for 5 minutes

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Quick health query.
codeExamples:
SELECT channel_name, service_state, last_error_message FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status_by_coordinator;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- channel_name | service_state | last_error_message
--              | ON            |

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Connection details.
codeExamples:
SELECT source_uuid, service_state, last_heartbeat_timestamp FROM performance_schema.replication_connection_status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- source_uuid | service_state | last_heartbeat_timestamp
-- 3e11fa47... | ON            | 2026-05-01 10:00:00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Replication health has three layers: are the I/O and SQL threads running, how far behind is the replica, and is the data identical. MySQL exposes them through SHOW REPLICA STATUS and Performance Schema replication tables; consistency needs checksum tools.
codeExamples:
SELECT channel_name, service_state, last_error_message FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status_by_coordinator;
SELECT channel_name, source_uuid, service_state, last_heartbeat_timestamp FROM performance_schema.replication_connection_status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- channel_name | service_state | last_error_message
--              | ON            |
-- source_uuid  | service_state | last_heartbeat_timestamp
-- 3e11fa47...  | ON            | 2026-05-01 10:00:00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Collect metrics with exporters (mysqld_exporter, PMM, cloud monitoring): Seconds_Behind_Source, thread states, retrieved vs executed GTID gaps, relay log space, apply worker states, semi-sync status. Heartbeat tables (pt-heartbeat) give accurate lag.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: early detection, data for capacity planning, evidence for post-mortems, and safe automation of failover decisions.
codeExamples:
-- Detect data drift between source and replica: checksum a table on both and compare
-- (pt-table-checksum does this safely in chunks). Manual spot check:
CHECKSUM TABLE shop.orders;

-- OUTPUT (example, run on source then replica; values must be equal):
-- +-------------+------------+
-- | Table       | Checksum   |
-- +-------------+------------+
-- | shop.orders | 2381732011 |
-- +-------------+------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: monitoring adds queries and tooling to maintain; naive checks (lag only) miss stopped threads; checksums load the server on big tables.
codeExamples:
-- Naive trap: Seconds_Behind_Source is NULL when the SQL thread is stopped, not "0".
-- Alert logic must treat NULL as critical:
SELECT IF(Seconds_Behind_Source IS NULL, 'CRITICAL', 'ok') AS state;   -- conceptual; read from status output

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- state: CRITICAL

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: status values are point-in-time and approximate; performance_schema must be enabled (default) and has little history; row-level drift needs extra tools; cross-region links add measurement noise.
codeExamples:
-- Keep history yourself: persist a sample every minute
CREATE TABLE ops.repl_samples (ts DATETIME PRIMARY KEY, lag_s INT, io VARCHAR(3), sql_thr VARCHAR(3));
-- cron job (shell) inserts a row from SHOW REPLICA STATUS output.
SELECT MAX(lag_s) AS worst_lag_last_hour FROM ops.repl_samples WHERE ts > NOW() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------------+
-- | worst_lag_last_hour |
-- +---------------------+
-- |                  12 |
-- +---------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Alert on symptoms (threads down, lag above SLO, errors) and on risk (errant GTIDs, binlog retention shorter than worst outage, semi-sync fallback). Schedule checksum jobs for drift, and review the monitoring itself after every incident.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Performance Schema tables: replication_connection_status, replication_applier_status, replication_applier_status_by_worker.
  • Track binlog and relay log disk usage and GTID gaps.
  • Use dashboards (Prometheus mysqld_exporter, Percona PMM, CloudWatch).

Senior Notes

  • Alert on errors, lag, thread state, GTID divergence, and replica read-only flag changes.
  • Automate safe responses: remove lagging replicas from the read pool and page for stopped replication.
  • Test the monitoring by simulating failures regularly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: alerting only on thread state (silent lag), no checksum for silent divergence, no alert on read_only changes, and ignoring the error log. Combine liveness, lag and consistency checks.
codeExamples:
pt-table-checksum --host=primary --user=chk --password=*** --databases=shop

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- TS ERRORS DIFFS ROWS CHUNKS SKIPPED TIME TABLE
-- 05-01 0 0 612044 12 0 6.1 shop.orders        (DIFFS 0 means identical)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Alert on symptoms and capacity: stopped threads, lag above a threshold for several minutes, relay log space growth, and GTID gaps. Keep dashboards for trends and let alerts page only when action is needed.
codeExamples:
- alert: MySQLReplicaLagHigh
  expr: mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_master > 30
  for: 5m
- alert: MySQLReplicationStopped
  expr: mysql_slave_status_slave_sql_running == 0 or mysql_slave_status_slave_io_running == 0
  for: 1m

-- OUTPUT:
-- alerts fire only when the condition persists

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world remediation runbook: if the SQL thread stops on an error, read Last_SQL_Error, decide whether to skip (with GTID), fix data, or rebuild the replica from a backup; record the cause.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Last_SQL_Error: Could not execute Update_rows event on table shop.orders; Can't find record in 'orders'
-- decision: the row was changed directly on the replica -> rebuild the replica from a fresh backup

-- OUTPUT:
-- (replica rebuilt and replication resumed with no data loss)

beginner.content:
Introduction

Failover is moving the write role from a failed primary to a healthy replica so the application keeps working. Manual failover is a human promoting a replica; automatic failover means a controller (InnoDB Cluster, Orchestrator, a cloud service) detects the failure and promotes for you.
codeExamples:
-- On the replica, check that it has caught up before promoting it
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Key fields to read:
--   Replica_IO_Running / Replica_SQL_Running : both must be Yes
--   Seconds_Behind_Source                    : lag in seconds
--   Retrieved_Gtid_Set vs Executed_Gtid_Set  : what is received vs applied

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- Replica_IO_Running: Yes
-- Replica_SQL_Running: Yes
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 0
-- Retrieved_Gtid_Set: 3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:1-5002
-- Executed_Gtid_Set:  3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:1-5002

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A single primary is a single point of failure. Without failover, a crashed server means downtime until someone restores a backup. Automatic failover shrinks that outage from hours to seconds.
codeExamples:
-- Manual promotion of a replica after the primary is lost
STOP REPLICA;                                  -- stop applying from the dead source
RESET REPLICA ALL;                             -- forget the old source configuration
SET GLOBAL super_read_only = OFF;              -- allow writes on the new primary
SET GLOBAL read_only = OFF;
SELECT @@global.read_only AS ro, @@global.super_read_only AS sro;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-----+
-- | ro | sro |
-- +----+-----+
-- |  0 |   0 |
-- +----+-----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

In production an orchestrator watches heartbeats, picks the replica with the most complete GTID set, promotes it, and repoints the other replicas and the application endpoint (proxy, VIP or DNS).
codeExamples:
-- Repoint a surviving replica to the new primary using GTID auto-positioning
STOP REPLICA;
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO
    SOURCE_HOST = 'db2.internal',
    SOURCE_USER = 'repl',
    SOURCE_PASSWORD = 'secret',
    SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION = 1;                  -- GTIDs: no binlog file/offset needed
START REPLICA;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- Source_Host: db2.internal
-- Auto_Position: 1
-- Replica_IO_Running: Yes
-- Replica_SQL_Running: Yes

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Before                              After failover
   ┌─────────┐  async   ┌─────────┐      ┌─────────┐ X        ┌─────────┐
   │ PRIMARY │ ───────► │ REPLICA │      │ old PRI │          │ NEW PRI │ (promoted)
   └────▲────┘          └─────────┘      └─────────┘          └────▲────┘
        │ writes                                                   │ writes
     [ App ]                                                    [ App ] via proxy / DNS
   Orchestrator: detect (heartbeat) -> elect (most GTIDs) -> promote -> repoint -> fence old

Fresher Notes

  • Failover means switching to a standby server when the primary fails so the application keeps working.
  • Manual failover is done by an operator; automatic failover is done by software that detects failure and promotes a replica.
  • The goal is to reduce downtime.

Worked Example 1

Check cluster status (MySQL Shell).

Worked Example 2

Planned switchover.

Practice Exercise 1

Manual promotion steps (conceptual).
codeExamples:
-- 1. make the old primary unwritable (if reachable)
SET GLOBAL super_read_only = ON;
-- 2. on the chosen replica: ensure it applied everything
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- 3. promote
STOP REPLICA; RESET REPLICA ALL; SET GLOBAL super_read_only = OFF;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected   (replica is now the writable primary)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Client-side reconnect settings.
codeExamples:
jdbc:mysql://router:6446/shop?connectTimeout=3000&socketTimeout=30000&autoReconnect=false&failOverReadOnly=false

-- OUTPUT:
-- (driver fails fast; the application retries the transaction on the new primary)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Automatic failover has four jobs: detect that the primary is gone (heartbeats, quorum), choose the best replica (most up-to-date GTID set, healthy, in the right zone), promote it and re-point other replicas, and redirect clients. Group Replication does this with consensus; external tools such as Orchestrator use observation plus a decision rule.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: planned switchover (graceful, no data loss), unplanned failover (crash), manual failover with scripts, and managed-service failover (RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora). Tune detection timeouts, fencing and the preferred candidate order.
codeExamples:
cluster.setPrimaryInstance('db2:3306');                    -- planned switchover
cluster.forceQuorumUsingPartitionOf('db2:3306');           -- emergency: regain quorum in a partition
cluster.rejoinInstance('db1:3306');                        -- bring the old primary back as secondary
SELECT member_host, member_role FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;

-- OUTPUT:
-- member_host | member_role
-- db2         | PRIMARY
-- db1         | SECONDARY

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: short outage, no human at 3 a.m., consistent runbook. With GTIDs, any replica can follow any new primary without hunting for binlog coordinates.
codeExamples:
-- GTID mode is what makes repointing painless; verify it is on
SELECT @@gtid_mode AS gtid_mode, @@enforce_gtid_consistency AS enforce;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+---------+
-- | gtid_mode | enforce |
-- +-----------+---------+
-- | ON        | ON      |
-- +-----------+---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: with asynchronous replication the new primary may be missing the last committed transactions (data loss), and a false positive (network blip) can cause a needless failover or split brain, where two servers accept writes.
codeExamples:
-- Transactions committed on the old primary but never shipped are lost on promotion.
-- Compare GTID sets to see what the new primary is missing:
SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT('3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:1-5010',
                     '3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:1-5002') AS lost_gtids;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------------------------------------+
-- | lost_gtids                                   |
-- +----------------------------------------------+
-- | 3E11FA47-71CA-11E1-9E33-C80AA9429562:5003-5010 |
-- +----------------------------------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: failover does not fix applications that cache connections or DNS; clients must reconnect, and in-flight transactions are rolled back. Plain MySQL never fails over by itself; you need tooling.
codeExamples:
-- An application talking to a dead primary sees errors until it reconnects
SELECT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 2013 (HY000): Lost connection to MySQL server during query
-- (client must reconnect to the new primary endpoint and retry the transaction)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Automatic failover is a trade between availability and the risk of split brain, so always fence the old primary (read_only, STONITH, remove from the proxy). Pair it with semi-synchronous replication or Group Replication if losing the last few transactions is unacceptable, and rehearse failover regularly.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Automatic failover needs reliable failure detection, leader election, fencing of the old primary and client redirection.
  • Tools: InnoDB Cluster (Group Replication + MySQL Router), Orchestrator, MHA, cloud-managed failover (RDS Multi-AZ, Aurora).
  • Clients must reconnect: use retry logic, DNS/VIP updates or a proxy.

Senior Notes

  • False positives (a network blip triggers failover) cause outages; tune timeouts and require quorum.
  • Fencing prevents split-brain: the old primary must be unable to accept writes.
  • Rehearse failovers, measure RTO and verify data consistency afterwards; document runbooks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: aggressive timeouts causing failovers on network blips (flapping), no fencing of the old primary (split-brain), two-node clusters without a tiebreaker, and applications that cache the old address. Use three or more voters, fencing and connection retry.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Measure the real recovery time: detection time plus election plus client reconnect. The slowest part is often clients that wait on dead TCP connections; set connect and socket timeouts and use a router.
codeExamples:
jdbc:mysql://router:6446/shop?connectTimeout=3000&socketTimeout=30000&tcpKeepAlive=true

-- OUTPUT:
-- total unavailability in the last drill: detection 5 s + election 3 s + client recovery 8 s = 16 s

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world drill checklist: kill the primary, record timestamps, verify no lost or duplicated writes, check application error rates and retries, and re-add the old node. Repeat each quarter.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_after, MAX(id) AS max_id FROM orders;
SELECT GTID_SUBTRACT('3e11...:1-1900', @@gtid_executed) AS lost_transactions;

-- OUTPUT:
-- rows_after | max_id
-- 612044     | 612044
-- lost_transactions
-- (empty)

beginner.content:
Introduction

RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long you can afford to be down. They are business targets that drive technical design.
codeExamples:
-- RPO in practice: how far behind is the replica right now?
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Seconds_Behind_Source is an approximate lower bound of the data you could lose on async failover

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 3
-- => with async replication, RPO right now is roughly 3 seconds of writes

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without agreed numbers, teams over-spend (zero loss for a blog) or under-protect (daily backup for payments). RPO and RTO turn vague wishes into a cost-justified architecture.
codeExamples:
-- Backup-only strategy: RPO = time since last backup + binlog gap, RTO = restore time.
-- Compute how stale the last nightly backup is, from a backup log table
CREATE TABLE backup_log (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, finished_at DATETIME);
INSERT INTO backup_log (finished_at) VALUES ('2026-10-05 02:10:00');
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, MAX(finished_at), '2026-10-05 14:10:00') AS hours_of_data_at_risk
FROM backup_log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------------+
-- | hours_of_data_at_risk |
-- +-----------------------+
-- |                    12 |
-- +-----------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

A typical tier table: payments RPO 0 / RTO under 1 min (Group Replication), orders RPO under 5 s / RTO 5 min (async + orchestrator), reporting RPO 24 h / RTO 4 h (nightly backup).
codeExamples:
-- Enable semi-synchronous replication to push RPO toward zero (MySQL 8.0.26+ names)
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source  SONAME 'semisync_source.so';
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = 1;
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 1000;   -- ms to wait for a replica ack, then fall back to async
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name                | Value |
-- +------------------------------+-------+
-- | rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled | ON    |
-- +------------------------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   time ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────►
        last good data      DISASTER        service restored
   ───────────●────────────────X────────────────●──────────
              │◄──── RPO ─────►│◄──── RTO ─────►│
              data lost         downtime
   Smaller RPO  -> more frequent backup / sync replication
   Smaller RTO  -> warm standby, automatic failover

Fresher Notes

  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is how long you can afford to be down.
  • Example: RPO 5 minutes, RTO 30 minutes.
  • They guide backup, replication and failover design.

Worked Example 1

Targets table.
codeExamples:
SELECT service, rpo_minutes, rto_minutes FROM dr_targets ORDER BY rto_minutes;

-- OUTPUT:
-- service  | rpo_minutes | rto_minutes
-- payments |           0 |          5
-- reports  |          60 |        240

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Drill result tracking.

Practice Exercise 1

Estimate current RPO from replica lag.
codeExamples:
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, ts, NOW()) AS replication_lag_seconds FROM ops.heartbeat WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- replication_lag_seconds
-- 2          (worst-case RPO on failover is about this value for async replication)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Backup-based RTO estimate.
codeExamples:
-- restore throughput 200 MB/s, database 600 GB
SELECT ROUND(600 * 1024 / 200 / 60, 1) AS restore_minutes;

-- OUTPUT:
-- restore_minutes
-- 51.2

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum tolerated data loss measured in time; RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum tolerated outage time. They are business requirements that decide architecture: asynchronous replication gives an RPO of the replication lag, backups give an RPO of the backup interval unless binlogs are archived, and each recovery step adds to the RTO.
codeExamples:
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, ts, NOW()) AS replication_lag_seconds FROM ops.heartbeat WHERE id = 1;
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, MAX(finished_at), NOW()) AS minutes_since_last_binlog_archive FROM ops.binlog_archive_log;

-- OUTPUT:
-- replication_lag_seconds
-- 2
-- minutes_since_last_binlog_archive
-- 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Map targets to techniques: RPO 0 → synchronous commit (Group Replication, semi-sync AFTER_SYNC); RPO seconds → async replica plus binlog shipping; RPO hours → backups. RTO seconds → automatic failover; minutes → manual promotion; hours → restore from backup.
codeExamples:
SELECT 'payments' AS service, 0 AS rpo_seconds, 60 AS rto_seconds, 'Group Replication + Router' AS design
UNION ALL SELECT 'orders', 30, 300, 'async replica + binlog archive + managed failover'
UNION ALL SELECT 'reports', 3600, 14400, 'nightly physical backup + restore';

-- OUTPUT:
-- service  | rpo_seconds | rto_seconds | design
-- payments |           0 |          60 | Group Replication + Router

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a shared vocabulary for engineers and business, a basis for budgeting, and measurable acceptance tests for HA and backup designs.
codeExamples:
-- Make RPO measurable: a heartbeat row written every second on the primary
CREATE TABLE heartbeat (id INT PRIMARY KEY, ts TIMESTAMP(3) NOT NULL);
REPLACE INTO heartbeat VALUES (1, NOW(3));
-- on the replica: true lag in ms, not the coarse Seconds_Behind_Source
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, ts, NOW(3)) / 1000 AS lag_ms FROM heartbeat WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+
-- | lag_ms |
-- +--------+
-- | 41.000 |
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: tighter targets cost exponentially more (extra replicas, cross-zone latency, tooling, on-call). RPO 0 means every commit waits for a remote acknowledgement, which adds write latency.
codeExamples:
-- Latency price of RPO 0: commit waits for a replica ack (example numbers)
-- async      commit ~ 0.4 ms
-- semi-sync  commit ~ 0.4 ms + network RTT to replica (same zone 0.5 ms, cross region 40+ ms)
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Rpl_semi_sync_source_avg_net_wait_time';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------------------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name                           | Value |
-- +-----------------------------------------+-------+
-- | Rpl_semi_sync_source_avg_net_wait_time  | 480   |   (microseconds)
-- +-----------------------------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: RTO is only real if you have tested it; an untested restore of a 2 TB backup may take many hours. RPO figures from replication lag are estimates, not guarantees.
codeExamples:
-- RTO check: time a restore drill and record it, never assume
-- shell:
--   time mysql -u root < full_backup.sql
-- OUTPUT (example):
-- real    94m12.3s     => RTO for a full logical restore is ~1.6 hours, not the 15 minutes in the SLA

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Set RPO and RTO per service tier with the business, then choose the cheapest design that meets them: backups (hours), async replica (seconds), semi-sync or Group Replication (near zero). Validate with game days, because the number that matters is the one you measured.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Lower RPO needs more frequent or continuous copying (binlog shipping, synchronous replication).
  • Lower RTO needs ready standbys, automation and rehearsed runbooks.
  • Cost rises sharply as targets approach zero.

Senior Notes

  • Set RPO/RTO per service with the business; not everything needs five nines.
  • Validate with drills, measuring real recovery time, not estimates.
  • Document dependencies (DNS, secrets, config) that stretch RTO.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: targets nobody agreed on, estimated instead of measured RTO, forgetting dependencies (DNS, secrets, config, application warm-up), and testing only the happy path. Time each recovery step.
codeExamples:
-- restore 600 GB at 200 MB/s plus 10 minutes of binlog replay plus 5 minutes of checks
SELECT ROUND(600 * 1024 / 200 / 60) + 10 + 5 AS estimated_rto_minutes;

-- OUTPUT:
-- estimated_rto_minutes
-- 67

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cost grows steeply as targets approach zero. Present options to the business with their cost and residual risk, and review targets as the data grows (restore time grows with size).
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(data_length + index_length) / 1073741824) AS db_gb, ROUND(SUM(data_length + index_length) / 1073741824 * 1024 / 200 / 60) AS restore_minutes_at_200mbs FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT:
-- db_gb | restore_minutes_at_200mbs
--   612 |                        52

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world SLO record: keep a table of drills with measured RPO and RTO per service and compare with the targets, so evidence exists for audits.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Disaster Recovery (DR) is the plan and infrastructure to resume service after losing a whole site or region (fire, power, cloud region outage, ransomware). HA protects against a server failing; DR protects against the datacenter failing.
codeExamples:
-- A DR replica in another region is just a replica with a long link
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO
    SOURCE_HOST = 'primary.eu-west.example.com',
    SOURCE_USER = 'repl', SOURCE_PASSWORD = 'secret',
    SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION = 1, SOURCE_SSL = 1;   -- encrypt traffic over the WAN
START REPLICA;
SELECT SERVICE_STATE FROM performance_schema.replication_connection_status;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+
-- | SERVICE_STATE |
-- +---------------+
-- | ON            |
-- +---------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Replicas in the same rack share the same fate. Corruption, an accidental DROP or ransomware replicate instantly to every copy, so DR also needs point-in-time recovery from backups and binary logs.
codeExamples:
-- Accidental DELETE replicates to all replicas. Use a delayed replica as a safety net:
STOP REPLICA;
CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_DELAY = 3600;   -- apply changes 1 hour late
START REPLICA;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- SQL_Delay: 3600
-- SQL_Remaining_Delay: 3421

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real setups: a primary region with HA, an asynchronous DR replica in a second region, nightly full backups copied off-site, and binlogs streamed to object storage for point-in-time recovery.
codeExamples:
-- Point-in-time recovery: restore backup, then replay binlogs up to just before the mistake
-- shell:
--   mysql -u root < full_backup.sql
--   mysqlbinlog --start-position=157 --stop-datetime="2026-10-05 13:59:59" binlog.000042 | mysql -u root

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- tables restored, replay applied 18,204 events, stopped before the bad DELETE

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Region A (primary)                         Region B (DR)
   ┌──────────────────────┐  async/WAN       ┌──────────────────────┐
   │ Primary + local HA   │ ───────────────► │ DR replica (warm)    │
   └──────────┬───────────┘                  └──────────┬───────────┘
              │ backups + binlogs                       │ promote on disaster
              ▼                                         ▼
        [ Off-site object storage ]  ◄── PITR source ──[ App in Region B ]

Fresher Notes

  • Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan and setup to restore service after a major failure such as a data centre or region outage.
  • It combines off-site backups, replicas in another region and documented procedures.
  • It is different from high availability within one site.

Worked Example 1

DR runbook checklist (tracked).
codeExamples:
SELECT step_no, action FROM dr_runbook WHERE plan = 'region-loss' ORDER BY step_no LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- step_no | action
-- 1       | Declare disaster, freeze deploys
-- 2       | Promote DR replica, enable writes
-- 3       | Switch DNS/Router to DR region

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Verify the DR copy is current.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 4

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Cross-region replica as a DR copy.

Practice Exercise 2

Immutable backup upload (shell).
codeExamples:
aws s3 cp /backups/full-2026-05-01.xbstream s3://dr-backups-us/ --storage-class STANDARD_IA
aws s3api put-object-retention --bucket dr-backups-us --key full-2026-05-01.xbstream --retention Mode=COMPLIANCE,RetainUntilDate=2026-08-01T00:00:00Z

-- OUTPUT:
-- upload: ... to s3://dr-backups-us/full-2026-05-01.xbstream

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Disaster recovery restores service after loss of a whole site or region. It is different from high availability inside one site. It rests on copies of data and configuration in another failure domain (asynchronous cross-region replica, off-site backups and binlogs), plus a tested procedure and the supporting systems (DNS, secrets, certificates, deployment).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns from cheapest to fastest: backup and restore, pilot light (small standby that can scale up), warm standby (scaled-down running copy), and active-active across regions. Choose by RPO/RTO and budget. Keep backups immutable and in a separate account.
codeExamples:
aws s3 cp /backups/full-2026-05-01.xbstream s3://dr-backups-us/ --storage-class STANDARD_IA
aws s3api put-object-retention --bucket dr-backups-us --key full-2026-05-01.xbstream --retention Mode=COMPLIANCE,RetainUntilDate=2026-08-01T00:00:00Z

-- OUTPUT:
-- upload: ... to s3://dr-backups-us/full-2026-05-01.xbstream    (object locked until 2026-08-01)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: survives region loss, protects against logical errors (with delay or PITR), and satisfies compliance requirements.
codeExamples:
-- Binary logging must be on and retained long enough for PITR
SELECT @@log_bin AS log_bin, @@binlog_expire_logs_seconds / 86400 AS retention_days;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+----------------+
-- | log_bin | retention_days |
-- +---------+----------------+
-- |       1 |         7.0000 |
-- +---------+----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: duplicated infrastructure that sits mostly idle, cross-region bandwidth cost, and operational complexity. A DR site that was never exercised often fails when needed.
codeExamples:
-- Cross-region replicas lag; check regularly
SELECT CHANNEL_NAME, SERVICE_STATE, LAST_ERROR_MESSAGE
FROM performance_schema.replication_applier_status_by_worker LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------+---------------+--------------------+
-- | CHANNEL_NAME | SERVICE_STATE | LAST_ERROR_MESSAGE |
-- +--------------+---------------+--------------------+
-- |              | ON            |                    |
-- +--------------+---------------+--------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: asynchronous DR means non-zero RPO; promoting the DR site is a deliberate decision with data-loss implications. Failing back to the original region is often harder than failing over.
codeExamples:
-- After promoting the DR site, the old primary may hold transactions the DR never saw.
-- Detect divergence by comparing GTID sets before re-attaching it:
SELECT GTID_SUBSET('uuid-A:1-120', 'uuid-A:1-100') AS old_primary_is_subset;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------------+
-- | old_primary_is_subset |
-- +-----------------------+
-- |                     0 |    (0 = old primary has extra GTIDs; rebuild it from a fresh copy)
-- +-----------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Follow the 3-2-1 rule (3 copies, 2 media, 1 off-site) and keep at least one copy that an attacker with production credentials cannot delete (immutable storage). Document the failover and failback runbooks, and schedule restore drills; DR you have not tested is a hope, not a plan.

Mid-Level Notes

  • DR patterns: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active across regions.
  • Keep backups and binlogs in a different region/account; make them immutable.
  • Include non-database parts: secrets, configuration, DNS, certificates and application deployment.

Senior Notes

  • Test DR end to end at least yearly; untested DR is a hope, not a plan.
  • Cross-region replication is asynchronous; accept an RPO equal to lag or use Group Replication/ Aurora Global with known limits.
  • Plan failback: returning to the original region safely after recovery.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: backups in the same region and account as production, never practised, forgetting non-database dependencies, and no failback plan. Write the full runbook including secrets, DNS and application configuration.
codeExamples:
SELECT step_no, action, owner, est_minutes FROM ops.dr_runbook WHERE plan = 'region-loss' ORDER BY step_no;

-- OUTPUT:
-- step_no | action                               | owner | est_minutes
-- 1       | Declare disaster, freeze deploys      | IC    | 5
-- 2       | Promote DR replica, enable writes     | DBA   | 10
-- 3       | Switch DNS / Router to DR region      | SRE   | 10

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Cross-region replication is asynchronous, so RPO equals the lag across regions. Monitor it and size the link. Compress binlog transactions to save bandwidth.
codeExamples:
SET PERSIST binlog_transaction_compression = ON;
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 4

-- OUTPUT:
-- (compressed binlog events reduce cross-region traffic by about 70%)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world annual DR test: restore production backups into the DR region, run the application against it, measure time, and fix every gap found, then publish the report.
codeExamples:
SELECT scenario, started_at, finished_at, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, started_at, finished_at) AS minutes, gaps_found FROM ops.dr_tests ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- scenario    | started_at          | finished_at         | minutes | gaps_found
-- region-loss | 2026-04-20 09:00:00 | 2026-04-20 10:12:00 |      72 |          6

beginner.content:
Introduction

Group Replication is a MySQL plugin that forms a group of servers which agree on every transaction using a Paxos-based protocol. InnoDB Cluster bundles Group Replication + MySQL Shell (AdminAPI) + MySQL Router into a managed HA solution with automatic failover.
codeExamples:
-- Typical cluster creation with MySQL Shell (JavaScript mode)
-- shell:  mysqlsh root@db1:3306
--   dba.configureInstance('root@db1:3306')
--   var cluster = dba.createCluster('prodCluster')
--   cluster.addInstance('root@db2:3306')
--   cluster.addInstance('root@db3:3306')
--   cluster.status()

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- "clusterName": "prodCluster",
-- "status": "OK",
-- "statusText": "Cluster is ONLINE and can tolerate up to ONE failure.",
-- primary: db1:3306 (R/W), db2:3306 (R/O), db3:3306 (R/O)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Asynchronous replication can lose transactions and needs external failover logic. Group Replication provides built-in membership, quorum, automatic primary election and no split brain.
codeExamples:
-- Inspect group members from any node
SELECT MEMBER_HOST, MEMBER_STATE, MEMBER_ROLE
FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+--------------+-------------+
-- | MEMBER_HOST | MEMBER_STATE | MEMBER_ROLE |
-- +-------------+--------------+-------------+
-- | db1         | ONLINE       | PRIMARY     |
-- | db2         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY   |
-- | db3         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY   |
-- +-------------+--------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used for payment and order systems that need near-zero data loss and failover in seconds. Three nodes is the common minimum (tolerates one failure); five tolerates two. Single-primary mode is the default and safest.
codeExamples:
-- Which node is the current primary? Applications and Router use this concept
SELECT MEMBER_HOST AS primary_node
FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members
WHERE MEMBER_ROLE = 'PRIMARY';

-- Required settings on every member (my.cnf):
--   binlog_format = ROW, gtid_mode = ON, enforce_gtid_consistency = ON
--   all tables must be InnoDB with a primary key

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | primary_node |
-- +--------------+
-- | db1          |
-- +--------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

        ┌──────────┐   Paxos / certification   ┌──────────┐
        │  db1 PRI │ ◄───────────────────────► │ db2 SEC  │
        └────┬─────┘                           └────┬─────┘
             │            ┌──────────┐              │
             └──────────► │ db3 SEC  │ ◄────────────┘
                          └──────────┘
        write on PRI -> broadcast -> majority certifies -> commit everywhere
        quorum = majority (2 of 3). Lose quorum -> group blocks writes (no split brain)
        [ MySQL Router ] sends R/W to PRI and R/O to SECs

Fresher Notes

  • Group Replication keeps several MySQL servers in sync with consensus. InnoDB Cluster combines Group Replication, MySQL Shell (AdminAPI) and MySQL Router.
  • A cluster typically has 3 or more nodes; one primary accepts writes and others are secondaries.
  • It provides automatic failover.

Worked Example 1

Router bootstrap.
codeExamples:
mysqlrouter --bootstrap root@db1:3306 --directory /opt/router --user=mysqlrouter

-- OUTPUT:
-- MySQL Classic protocol: Read/Write 6446, Read/Only 6447

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Tables without a PK block Group Replication writes.

Practice Exercise 1

Create a cluster with the shell.

Practice Exercise 2

Group membership from SQL.
codeExamples:
SELECT member_host, member_state, member_role FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;

-- OUTPUT:
-- member_host | member_state | member_role
-- db1         | ONLINE       | PRIMARY
-- db2         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY
-- db3         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Group Replication is a multi-node protocol based on Paxos: a transaction is certified by the group (checked for conflicts with concurrently committing transactions) and commits when a majority accepts it. InnoDB Cluster = Group Replication + MySQL Shell AdminAPI to manage it + MySQL Router to route clients. A group of 3 tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Modes: single-primary (default, recommended) and multi-primary. Requirements: InnoDB tables with primary keys, GTIDs, row binlog. Recovery of a joining member uses the clone plugin or incremental recovery. ClusterSet links clusters across regions.
codeExamples:
SELECT member_host, member_state, member_role FROM performance_schema.replication_group_members;
SELECT * FROM performance_schema.replication_group_member_stats\G
cluster.addInstance('root@db4:3306', {recoveryMethod: 'clone'});

-- OUTPUT:
-- member_host | member_state | member_role
-- db1         | ONLINE       | PRIMARY
-- db2         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: automatic failover with no data loss for committed transactions, automatic membership and rejoin, conflict detection, built-in tooling via AdminAPI.
codeExamples:
-- Group Replication certifies each transaction; conflicts are rolled back, not lost silently
SELECT COUNT_TRANSACTIONS_CHECKED, COUNT_CONFLICTS_DETECTED
FROM performance_schema.replication_group_member_stats LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------------------+--------------------------+
-- | COUNT_TRANSACTIONS_CHECKED | COUNT_CONFLICTS_DETECTED |
-- +----------------------------+--------------------------+
-- |                     182340 |                        0 |
-- +----------------------------+--------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: commit latency includes a group round trip, so nodes should be in low-latency networks; one slow member can trigger flow control and slow the whole group; more moving parts to operate.
codeExamples:
-- Flow control throttles writers when a member's apply queue grows
SELECT MEMBER_ID, COUNT_TRANSACTIONS_IN_QUEUE AS apply_queue
FROM performance_schema.replication_group_member_stats;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------+-------------+
-- | MEMBER_ID | apply_queue |
-- +-----------+-------------+
-- | 8a1c...   |           0 |
-- | 9b2d...   |        1840 |   <- slow node; group may throttle
-- +-----------+-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB only, every table needs a primary key, no SERIALIZABLE isolation in multi-primary mode, limited to 9 members, and large transactions are capped by group_replication_transaction_size_limit. Losing quorum (majority) blocks writes.

Architect's Notes

Prefer single-primary mode: it avoids write conflicts and gives simpler semantics. Place members in separate failure domains (zones) but with low latency, and for cross-region DR attach an asynchronous replica (InnoDB ClusterSet) rather than stretching the group. Budget for the commit-latency tax and monitor flow control.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Group Replication uses a Paxos-like protocol: a transaction commits when a majority certify it.
  • Modes: single-primary (default, recommended) and multi-primary.
  • MySQL Router routes read/write traffic to the right nodes and adapts after failover.

Senior Notes

  • Requires InnoDB, primary keys on all tables, GTIDs and row-based binlog.
  • Majority needed: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Place nodes in separate failure domains.
  • Network latency affects commit latency; keep nodes close. Use ClusterSet for cross-region DR.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: tables without primary keys (writes rejected), large transactions (certification limits), stretching one group across high-latency links, and expecting a two-node group to survive one failure (no majority). Use three nodes and keep them in low-latency zones.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Commit latency includes a network round trip to a majority; keep members close (same region), and use flow control settings to stop slow members from lagging. Watch the certification queue and apply queue sizes.
codeExamples:
SELECT member_id, count_transactions_in_queue AS cert_queue, count_transactions_remote_in_applier_queue AS apply_queue FROM performance_schema.replication_group_member_stats;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- member_id | cert_queue | apply_queue
-- 3e11...   |          0 |           2

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a three-node cluster across three availability zones with two routers, giving automatic failover and read scaling. Applications connect to the router only.
codeExamples:
mysqlrouter --bootstrap root@db1:3306 --directory /opt/router --user=mysqlrouter
-- apps: jdbc:mysql://router:6446/shop (read/write)   jdbc:mysql://router:6447/shop (read-only)

-- OUTPUT:
-- MySQL Classic protocol: Read/Write 6446, Read/Only 6447

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL Router is a lightweight proxy that sits between applications and a MySQL cluster. It knows the cluster topology from its metadata and routes connections: read/write traffic to the primary and read-only traffic to secondaries, so apps never hard-code which node is primary.
codeExamples:
-- Bootstrap the router against an InnoDB Cluster (shell)
--   mysqlrouter --bootstrap root@db1:3306 --directory /opt/router --user=mysqlrouter
--   /opt/router/start.sh

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- Classic MySQL protocol connections to cluster 'prodCluster':
-- - Read/Write Connections: localhost:6446
-- - Read/Only  Connections: localhost:6447

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

When failover happens the primary changes address. Without a router every app config must change; with a router the app keeps connecting to the same port and the router redirects after the topology change.
codeExamples:
-- App connects to the router's R/W port, not to a specific server
--   mysql -h router1 -P 6446 -u app -p -e "SELECT @@hostname"
-- After failover from db1 to db2 the same command returns the new primary

-- OUTPUT (example, before failover):
-- +------------+
-- | @@hostname |
-- +------------+
-- | db1        |
-- +------------+
-- OUTPUT (example, after failover, same connection string):
-- | db2        |

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Run one router per application host (co-located, no extra hop and no single router to fail) or a pair behind a load balancer. Use the read-only port for reporting queries to offload the primary.
codeExamples:
# mysqlrouter.conf (generated by bootstrap, simplified)
[routing:prod_rw]
bind_address = 0.0.0.0
bind_port = 6446
destinations = metadata-cache://prodCluster/?role=PRIMARY
routing_strategy = first-available

[routing:prod_ro]
bind_port = 6447
destinations = metadata-cache://prodCluster/?role=SECONDARY
routing_strategy = round-robin

# OUTPUT:
# router listens on 6446 (writes -> primary) and 6447 (reads -> secondaries, round-robin)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   ┌──────────┐        ┌──────────────────┐   :6446 RW   ┌──────────────┐
   │  App 1   │ ─────► │                  │ ───────────► │ db1 PRIMARY  │
   └──────────┘        │   MySQL Router   │              └──────────────┘
   ┌──────────┐        │ (metadata cache) │   :6447 RO   ┌──────────────┐
   │  App 2   │ ─────► │                  │ ───────────► │ db2 / db3    │
   └──────────┘        └─────────┬────────┘  round-robin └──────────────┘
                                 │ polls cluster metadata, reroutes after failover

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL Router is a lightweight proxy that routes application connections to the right MySQL servers.
  • Apps connect to the Router (for example ports 6446 for read/write and 6447 for read-only), not directly to a database node.
  • It follows cluster topology changes automatically.

Worked Example 1

Router status via REST.

Worked Example 2

See where connections land.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@hostname, @@read_only;

-- OUTPUT: (through port 6446)
-- @@hostname | @@read_only
-- db1        | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Application connection strings.
codeExamples:
# writes
jdbc:mysql://router1:6446/shop
# reporting reads
jdbc:mysql://router1:6447/shop

-- OUTPUT:
-- 6446 -> current PRIMARY, 6447 -> SECONDARY nodes (round-robin)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Router config excerpt.
codeExamples:
[routing:prod_rw]
bind_port=6446
destinations=metadata-cache://prod/?role=PRIMARY
routing_strategy=first-available

-- OUTPUT:
-- (Router listens on 6446 and always sends to the current primary)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL Router is a transport-layer proxy. It reads cluster metadata (which node is primary, which are secondaries), listens on ports for read/write and read-only traffic, and forwards each client connection to a chosen backend. It does not parse SQL; routing decisions are per connection, and it reacts to topology changes.
codeExamples:
mysqlrouter --bootstrap root@db1:3306 --directory /opt/router --user=mysqlrouter
cat /opt/router/mysqlrouter.conf | grep -A4 "routing:"

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- [routing:prod_rw]
-- bind_port=6446
-- destinations=metadata-cache://prod/?role=PRIMARY
-- routing_strategy=first-available

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Strategies: first-available (primary), round-robin (secondaries), round-robin-with-fallback, and connection limits. The REST API exposes status and metrics. Run several routers, usually one per application host, so the proxy is not a single point of failure.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: transparent failover for clients, read/write splitting by port, connection routing without app changes, small footprint, and it is part of the MySQL ecosystem and supported with InnoDB Cluster.
codeExamples:
-- Verify where reads and writes land
--   mysql -h router1 -P 6447 -e "SELECT @@hostname, @@read_only"

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------+-------------+
-- | @@hostname | @@read_only |
-- +------------+-------------+
-- | db2        |           1 |
-- +------------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it routes at connection level, not per statement, so read/write splitting is by port and the app must choose. An extra network hop adds slight latency, and a stale metadata cache can briefly misroute.
codeExamples:
-- Read-your-writes can break if a read goes to a lagging secondary via the RO port
-- App writes via 6446, then immediately reads via 6447:
INSERT INTO orders(id) VALUES (900);        -- on primary
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 900;        -- on secondary, may not be applied yet

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)      <- replica lag, not data loss

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: no query rewriting, no connection multiplexing or pooling (unlike ProxySQL), and it is designed for InnoDB Cluster, ClusterSet or ReplicaSet metadata rather than arbitrary topologies.
codeExamples:
-- Router does not pool: 500 app connections become 500 server connections
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------------+-------+
-- | Variable_name     | Value |
-- +-------------------+-------+
-- | Threads_connected | 503   |
-- +-------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Deploy Router next to each app instance so it is never a shared single point of failure, and use application-level connection pooling since Router does not pool. If you need statement-level read/write splitting, query caching or multiplexing, evaluate ProxySQL, accepting the extra component to operate.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Bootstrapped against an InnoDB Cluster, it reads metadata to learn which node is primary and which are secondaries.
  • Reads can be load-balanced (round-robin) across secondaries.
  • Router instances are stateless; run one per app host or a pool behind a load balancer.

Senior Notes

  • The Router keeps connections to the primary short-lived during failover; apps must retry.
  • It does not parse SQL (Layer 4 routing); for query-based routing use ProxySQL.
  • Secure traffic with TLS, restrict Router metadata accounts, and monitor with its REST API.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: clients not retrying after failover (connections drop during the switch), connection pooling that keeps stale connections, and expecting SQL-level read/write splitting (Router routes by port). Retry on connection errors and use separate pools for read and write ports.
codeExamples:
-- application: two datasources
-- write pool -> router:6446    read pool -> router:6447
-- retry connection errors 2003, 2006, 2013 with backoff

SELECT @@hostname, @@read_only;

-- OUTPUT: (through 6447)
-- @@hostname | @@read_only
-- db2        |           1

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Router adds a hop with small latency and reuses connection routing efficiently; its throughput is rarely the limit. Monitor active connections and blocked hosts, and size file descriptors.
codeExamples:
ulimit -n
curl -s -u admin:*** http://router1:8443/api/20190715/metadata/prod/status

-- OUTPUT:
-- 65535
-- {"refreshFailed":0,"refreshSucceeded":4120,"timeLastRefreshSucceeded":"2026-05-01T10:00:00"}

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: ProxySQL vs Router. Router for simple, topology-aware routing of an InnoDB Cluster; ProxySQL when you need query rules, caching, multiplexing or lag-aware read routing across arbitrary topologies.
codeExamples:
SELECT rule_id, match_digest, destination_hostgroup FROM mysql_query_rules ORDER BY rule_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- rule_id | match_digest | destination_hostgroup
-- 1       | ^SELECT      | 20

beginner.content:
Introduction

Partitioning splits one logical table into several physical pieces (partitions) by a rule on a column. Applications still query one table name; MySQL decides which pieces hold the rows. In MySQL each partition is its own InnoDB tablespace file.
codeExamples:
-- One logical table, physically split by year
CREATE TABLE sales (
    id        BIGINT NOT NULL,
    sold_on   DATE   NOT NULL,
    amount    DECIMAL(10,2),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, sold_on)                -- partition column must be in every unique key
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(sold_on)) (
    PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN (2025),
    PARTITION p2025 VALUES LESS THAN (2026),
    PARTITION pmax  VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);
SELECT PARTITION_NAME, TABLE_ROWS FROM information_schema.PARTITIONS
WHERE TABLE_NAME = 'sales';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | PARTITION_NAME | TABLE_ROWS |
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | p2024          |          0 |
-- | p2025          |          0 |
-- | pmax           |          0 |
-- +----------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Very large tables make maintenance painful: purging old rows with DELETE is slow and bloats undo, index trees grow deep, and backups or ALTERs take hours. Partitioning lets you drop old data instantly and touch only relevant slices.
codeExamples:
-- Retention: dropping a whole partition is a metadata operation, DELETE is millions of row changes
ALTER TABLE sales DROP PARTITION p2024;      -- instant, no undo per row, frees the file

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.02 sec)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical homes: logs, audit trails, IoT readings, time-series and order history, where data has a natural time key and old data expires on a schedule.
codeExamples:
-- Queries that filter on the partition key touch fewer partitions
EXPLAIN SELECT SUM(amount) FROM sales WHERE sold_on >= '2025-03-01' AND sold_on < '2025-04-01';

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+--------+------------+------+
-- | id | table  | partitions | rows |
-- +----+--------+------------+------+
-- |  1 | sales  | p2025      | 9421 |   <- only 1 of 3 partitions read
-- +----+--------+------------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   logical table  sales
   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ p2024.ibd      │ p2025.ibd      │ pmax.ibd              │
   │ rows 2024      │ rows 2025      │ rows 2026+            │
   └────────────────┴────────────────┴───────────────────────┘
   WHERE sold_on in 2025  -> only p2025 opened   (pruning)
   DROP PARTITION p2024   -> one file removed    (instant purge)

Fresher Notes

  • Partitioning splits one big table into smaller physical pieces (partitions) while it still looks like one table.
  • Reasons: faster queries that touch one partition, easier deletion of old data, easier maintenance.
  • MySQL partitions by RANGE, LIST, HASH or KEY.

Worked Example 1

Instant purge of old data.

Worked Example 2

PK must include the partition column.

Practice Exercise 1

Range partition by year.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE events (id BIGINT NOT NULL, created_at DATE NOT NULL, payload VARCHAR(100), PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at))
PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at)) (
  PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN (2025), PARTITION p2025 VALUES LESS THAN (2026), PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE);
SELECT partition_name, table_rows FROM information_schema.partitions WHERE table_name = 'events';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- partition_name | table_rows
-- p2024          | 120000
-- p2025          | 340000
-- pmax           |  15000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Pruning in the plan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-04-01';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- partitions | type
-- p2025      | range

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A partitioned table is one logical table made of several physical tablespaces. A partitioning function maps each row to a partition. The optimizer prunes partitions that cannot match the WHERE clause, so a query on one month reads one partition. Each partition has its own B-tree for the clustered index and for each secondary index.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Good reasons: instant data retention (drop old partitions), prune-friendly queries on time or tenant ranges, manageable maintenance (rebuild one partition), and spreading I/O. Bad reasons: "make everything faster" (queries without the partition key scan all partitions).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fast bulk purge via DROP/TRUNCATE PARTITION, partition pruning for time-bounded queries, smaller per-partition indexes, and the option to place partitions on different disks.
codeExamples:
-- Truncate just one slice, others untouched
ALTER TABLE sales TRUNCATE PARTITION p2025;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a query that does not filter on the partition key must open every partition; many partitions add overhead; schema rules become stricter; and it does not speed up a well-indexed point lookup.
codeExamples:
-- No pruning: filter on a non-partition column scans all partitions
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sales WHERE amount = 500.00;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+-------+-----------------------+------+
-- | id | table | partitions            | type |
-- +----+-------+-----------------------+------+
-- |  1 | sales | p2024,p2025,pmax      | ALL  |
-- +----+-------+-----------------------+------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB partitioning has no foreign keys (neither from nor to a partitioned table), every unique key must include the partitioning columns, at most 8192 partitions, and the partition expression must be integer-valued (or DATE/DATETIME via functions like YEAR or TO_DAYS) for RANGE.
codeExamples:
-- Unique key that omits the partition column is rejected
CREATE TABLE bad (id INT, d DATE, UNIQUE KEY (id))
PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(d)) (PARTITION p0 VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1503 (HY000): A UNIQUE INDEX must include all columns in the table's partitioning function

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Partition for data lifecycle (purge and archive) first, performance second; a good index usually beats partitioning for query speed. Pick a key that appears in nearly every query and in all unique keys, keep partitions in the tens or low hundreds, and consider sharding or archival tables if you need cross-server scale instead.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Partition pruning lets MySQL read only the partitions that match the WHERE.
  • Dropping an old partition is instant compared with a huge DELETE.
  • Every unique key (including the primary key) must include the partitioning column.

Senior Notes

  • Partitioning is not a general performance fix; queries without the partition key scan all partitions and can be slower.
