  • Too many partitions waste memory and metadata; keep tens to a few hundred.
  • Often a better first step is a good index; partition mainly for data lifecycle management.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: partitioning without including the partition column in every unique key (error), too many partitions (memory and metadata cost, keep tens to a few hundred), and partition keys that queries do not use. Check pruning with EXPLAIN.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Partitioning does not reduce the index depth per query as much as people expect, but it reduces per-partition index size and allows partition-level operations. Compare a single-table delete with a partition drop.
codeExamples:
DELETE FROM events_unpartitioned WHERE created_at < '2025-01-01';           -- hours, huge undo and binlog
ALTER TABLE events DROP PARTITION p2024;                                     -- milliseconds

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 48000000 rows affected (3 hours 12 min)
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.12 sec)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: log and event tables partitioned by month with automated creation of future partitions and dropping of expired ones.

beginner.content:
Introduction

RANGE partitioning assigns rows to partitions by which interval the expression falls in (dates, ids). LIST assigns by explicit value sets (region codes, status ids). RANGE COLUMNS and LIST COLUMNS allow non-integer columns directly such as DATE or strings.
codeExamples:
-- RANGE COLUMNS on a DATE directly, no YEAR() needed
CREATE TABLE logs (
    id BIGINT NOT NULL, logged_on DATE NOT NULL, msg VARCHAR(100),
    PRIMARY KEY (id, logged_on)
)
PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (logged_on) (
    PARTITION p_q1 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-04-01'),
    PARTITION p_q2 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-07-01'),
    PARTITION p_max VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
);
INSERT INTO logs VALUES (1,'2026-02-10','a'),(2,'2026-05-05','b');
SELECT PARTITION_NAME, TABLE_ROWS FROM information_schema.PARTITIONS WHERE TABLE_NAME='logs';

-- OUTPUT (example; TABLE_ROWS is an estimate):
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | PARTITION_NAME | TABLE_ROWS |
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | p_q1           |          1 |
-- | p_q2           |          1 |
-- | p_max          |          0 |
-- +----------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Time data needs range slices that can be rotated; categorical data (countries, tenants) needs list slices that group related values together so one group can be moved or dropped.

Real-Time Use

Monthly log tables rotated by a scheduled job: add next month's partition, drop partitions older than the retention window.
codeExamples:
-- Monthly rotation: split the catch-all partition to create the next range
ALTER TABLE logs REORGANIZE PARTITION p_max INTO (
    PARTITION p_q3  VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-10-01'),
    PARTITION p_max VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
);
ALTER TABLE logs DROP PARTITION p_q1;        -- expire the oldest quarter

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.05 sec)
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   RANGE (by date)                         LIST (by region)
   ┌────────┬────────┬────────┐            ┌──────────┬──────────┬─────────┐
   │ < Apr  │ < Jul  │ MAXVAL │            │ 1,2,3    │ 4,5      │ 6,7,8   │
   │  p_q1  │  p_q2  │ p_max  │            │ p_asia   │ p_europe │ p_other │
   └────────┴────────┴────────┘            └──────────┴──────────┴─────────┘
   boundary grows with time                values enumerated explicitly
   REORGANIZE splits p_max for the next period

Fresher Notes

  • RANGE partitioning puts rows in partitions by ranges of a column (dates, ids). LIST partitioning assigns rows by specific values (country codes, region ids).
  • Range is perfect for time-based data; list for categorical groups.
  • Use a MAXVALUE catch-all partition for range.

Worked Example 1

Add the next month.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE logs REORGANIZE PARTITION pmax INTO (
  PARTITION p202603 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-04-01'),
  PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE));

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Archive with EXCHANGE PARTITION.

Practice Exercise 1

RANGE COLUMNS by date.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE logs (id BIGINT NOT NULL, logged_on DATE NOT NULL, msg VARCHAR(100), PRIMARY KEY (id, logged_on))
PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (logged_on) (
  PARTITION p202601 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-02-01'),
  PARTITION p202602 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-03-01'),
  PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE));
INSERT INTO logs VALUES (1,'2026-01-15','a'),(2,'2026-02-20','b');
SELECT partition_name, table_rows FROM information_schema.partitions WHERE table_name = 'logs';

-- OUTPUT:
-- partition_name | table_rows
-- p202601        | 1
-- p202602        | 1
-- pmax           | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

LIST partition by region.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

RANGE partitions rows by which interval of a column (or expression) they fall into; LIST by membership in explicit value lists. RANGE COLUMNS and LIST COLUMNS partition directly on one or more columns of many types (dates, strings) without wrapping them in functions, which keeps pruning reliable.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE logs (id BIGINT NOT NULL, logged_on DATE NOT NULL, msg VARCHAR(200), PRIMARY KEY (id, logged_on))
PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (logged_on) (
  PARTITION p202601 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-02-01'),
  PARTITION p202602 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-03-01'),
  PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE));
CREATE TABLE sales_r (id INT NOT NULL, region_id INT NOT NULL, amt DECIMAL(10,2), PRIMARY KEY (id, region_id))
PARTITION BY LIST (region_id) (PARTITION north VALUES IN (1,2), PARTITION south VALUES IN (3,4));

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (x2)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Maintenance operations: ADD PARTITION, DROP PARTITION, REORGANIZE PARTITION (split or merge), EXCHANGE PARTITION (swap with a standalone table for archiving), TRUNCATE PARTITION. Keep a MAXVALUE catch-all or monitor missing partitions.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: intuitive, supports pruning for range and equality predicates, makes rotation and archival trivial, and keeps related rows together (LIST).
codeExamples:
-- Pruning on a range predicate
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE logged_on BETWEEN '2026-05-01' AND '2026-05-31';

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+-------+------------+------+
-- | id | table | partitions | type |
-- +----+-------+------------+------+
-- |  1 | logs  | p_q2       | ALL  |
-- +----+-------+------------+------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: hot spots (all new writes hit the newest RANGE partition), manual maintenance to add future ranges, and a catch-all MAXVALUE partition that grows unbounded if you forget to split it.
codeExamples:
-- LIST has no catch-all: an unlisted value is an error, not a default bucket
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (2, 99, 'Nobody');

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1526 (HY000): Table has no partition for value 99

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: RANGE needs ascending boundaries, LIST values must be unique across partitions, and with the older single-expression form the expression must return an integer. NULL goes to the lowest RANGE partition and to a LIST partition only if NULL is explicitly listed.

Architect's Notes

Use RANGE for time-based data with a scheduled job that pre-creates future partitions so inserts never hit an unbounded catch-all; use LIST sparingly because every new category needs DDL. Avoid hot-spotting the newest partition on very high write rates by combining RANGE with HASH subpartitions or using a different scaling strategy.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Add new partitions ahead of time with REORGANIZE PARTITION on the catch-all; or use ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION when there is no MAXVALUE.
  • Use RANGE COLUMNS/LIST COLUMNS to partition on dates, strings or multiple columns without function wrapping.
  • Archive by dropping or exchanging partitions (EXCHANGE PARTITION).

Senior Notes

  • Automate monthly partition creation and retention with events or external jobs and alert if the future partition is missing.
  • Choose granularity by volume: daily for very high volume, monthly otherwise.
  • A row that matches no partition (no MAXVALUE) causes an insert error; monitor for it.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no partition for a value (insert fails with error 1526), partition keys unused by queries, and monthly partition creation forgotten. Automate creation and alert when the next period is missing.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Choose granularity by volume: daily for very large streams, monthly for moderate. Partition count affects open-table and metadata memory. Verify pruning for typical queries and avoid cross-partition joins on large ranges.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: scheduled partition management with an event that creates next month's partition and drops partitions older than the retention period.
codeExamples:
CREATE EVENT ev_rotate_logs ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 DAY DO
  ALTER TABLE logs REORGANIZE PARTITION pmax INTO (PARTITION p_next VALUES LESS THAN (DATE_FORMAT(CURDATE() + INTERVAL 2 MONTH, '%Y-%m-01')), PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE));

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

HASH partitioning distributes rows by MOD(expression, N) over N partitions; KEY partitioning does the same using MySQL's internal hash function over one or more columns (defaulting to the primary key), so it works with non-integer columns too. LINEAR variants use a power-of-two algorithm that makes adding partitions cheaper but less even.
codeExamples:
-- HASH on an integer, 4 partitions
CREATE TABLE sessions (
    id BIGINT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT, data VARCHAR(50)
)
PARTITION BY HASH (id) PARTITIONS 4;
INSERT INTO sessions VALUES (1,10,'a'),(2,11,'b'),(3,12,'c'),(4,13,'d'),(5,14,'e');
SELECT PARTITION_NAME, TABLE_ROWS FROM information_schema.PARTITIONS WHERE TABLE_NAME='sessions';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | PARTITION_NAME | TABLE_ROWS |
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | p0             |          1 |   (id 4)
-- | p1             |          2 |   (ids 1,5)
-- | p2             |          1 |   (id 2)
-- | p3             |          1 |   (id 3)
-- +----------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Some data has no natural range, so range partitions would pile into one slice. Hash spreads rows evenly, which reduces contention on a single big file and spreads I/O across disks.
codeExamples:
-- KEY partitioning on a string column (hash function chosen by MySQL)
CREATE TABLE users (
    email VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(40)
)
PARTITION BY KEY () PARTITIONS 8;            -- empty column list = use the primary key
INSERT INTO users VALUES ('a@x.com','A'),('b@x.com','B');
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM information_schema.PARTITIONS WHERE TABLE_NAME='users';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |        8 |
-- +----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Used for session stores, user tables and other uniformly accessed data where the goal is balanced size and parallel I/O, not lifecycle management.
codeExamples:
-- Point lookup by the hash column prunes to a single partition
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE id = 3;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+----------+------------+-------+
-- | id | table    | partitions | type  |
-- +----+----------+------------+-------+
-- |  1 | sessions | p3         | const |
-- +----+----------+------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   id -> MOD(id, 4)
   ┌──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
   │ p0       │ p1       │ p2       │ p3       │
   │ id 4,8.. │ id 1,5.. │ id 2,6.. │ id 3,7.. │
   └──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘
   WHERE id = 3        -> only p3
   WHERE id > 100    -> all four (no pruning)

Fresher Notes

  • HASH partitioning spreads rows evenly across N partitions using a hash of an integer expression. KEY partitioning is similar but MySQL computes the hash from the column(s).
  • They balance data without defining ranges.
  • Example: PARTITION BY HASH(user_id) PARTITIONS 8.

Worked Example 1

Pruning with equality.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE user_id = 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- partitions | type
-- p3         | ref

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Changing the count rebuilds the table.

Practice Exercise 1

HASH partitioning.

Practice Exercise 2

KEY partitioning on the primary key.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

HASH partitioning computes expression MOD n to pick one of n partitions, spreading rows evenly. KEY partitioning is the same idea but MySQL hashes the specified columns (any type) itself, by default the primary key. Neither gives time-based retention; they balance data and contention.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: LINEAR HASH and LINEAR KEY (powers-of-two algorithm that makes adding partitions cheaper but distribution slightly uneven), and subpartitioning (hash inside range). Pruning works for equality on the partition expression.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: even distribution with no maintenance of boundaries, pruning for equality lookups, and KEY works on any column type.
codeExamples:
-- Changing the partition count redistributes rows evenly
ALTER TABLE sessions COALESCE PARTITION 2;   -- shrink from 4 to 2 partitions, data re-hashed
SELECT COUNT(*) AS parts FROM information_schema.PARTITIONS WHERE TABLE_NAME='sessions';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | parts |
-- +-------+
-- |     2 |
-- +-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: no pruning for range predicates, no cheap way to drop old data, and changing N rebuilds (re-hashes) the whole table.
codeExamples:
-- A range predicate on a HASH column cannot prune
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE id BETWEEN 100 AND 200;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | partitions | p0,p1 |   <- every partition is searched

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the HASH expression must be an integer, KEY cannot partition by BLOB/TEXT columns, unique keys must contain the partitioning columns, and HASH or KEY gives no data-lifecycle benefit.
codeExamples:
-- HASH expression must yield an integer
CREATE TABLE t2 (name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL) PARTITION BY HASH (name) PARTITIONS 4;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1697 (HY000): VALUES value for partition 'p0' must have type INT
-- (use PARTITION BY KEY (name) for strings)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose a power-of-two partition count up front, since changing it re-hashes everything. Use HASH or KEY to remove a single-file bottleneck, not as a performance cure-all; if you want horizontal scale across machines, partitioning inside one server is not a substitute for sharding.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Good for even distribution and reducing contention, not for data lifecycle (you cannot drop by time).
  • LINEAR HASH makes adding/removing partitions faster but distribution less even.
  • KEY can use the primary key columns by default and accepts non-integer types.

Senior Notes

  • Hash partitioning supports pruning only for equality conditions on the partition expression.
  • Changing the number of partitions rewrites data; choose a count with growth in mind (power of two, few).
  • If your goal is horizontal scale, sharding across servers is the real tool; hash partitions stay on one server.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting range queries to prune (they do not), changing the partition count casually (rebuilds and redistributes all rows), and using hash partitioning when the real need is sharding across servers. Pick the count with growth in mind.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sessions WHERE user_id BETWEEN 1 AND 3;       -- scans all four partitions
ALTER TABLE sessions COALESCE PARTITION 2;                          -- rebuilds the table to 2 partitions

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 5 rows affected  (data redistributed)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hash partitions reduce contention on index structures and spread I/O across files; each partition has smaller trees. The gain is workload-dependent; measure insert and lookup throughput before and after.
codeExamples:
-- 32 threads inserting random user_ids: unpartitioned 22k/s, 16 hash partitions 31k/s
SELECT ROUND(31 / 22, 2) AS speedup;

-- OUTPUT:
-- speedup
-- 1.41

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a very hot session or counter table partitioned by hash on user id to relieve contention on a single index tree, while old data is removed by TTL deletes in batches.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Partition pruning is the optimizer skipping partitions that cannot contain matching rows, based on the WHERE clause. Management means adding, dropping, splitting, exchanging and rebuilding partitions with ALTER TABLE.
codeExamples:
-- See which partitions the optimizer will read (MySQL 8 shows them in plain EXPLAIN)
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sales WHERE sold_on = '2025-06-15';

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- +----+-------+------------+------+
-- | id | table | partitions | type |
-- +----+-------+------------+------+
-- |  1 | sales | p2025      | ref  |
-- +----+-------+------------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Pruning is where the read benefit comes from, and management is where the operational benefit comes from. Without both, partitioning only adds complexity.
codeExamples:
-- Wrapping the partition column in a function can defeat pruning
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sales WHERE YEAR(sold_on) = 2025;           -- may prune for RANGE(YEAR()) tables
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM sales WHERE DATE_ADD(sold_on, INTERVAL 1 DAY) = '2025-06-16';  -- cannot prune

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- query 1 partitions: p2025
-- query 2 partitions: p2024,p2025,pmax

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Operations teams automate: add next partition, archive old ones by swapping them into a plain table with EXCHANGE PARTITION, and rebuild fragmented partitions.

Diagram

   SELECT ... WHERE sold_on = '2025-06-15'
                        │
                  optimizer evaluates partition expression
                        ▼
   ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐
   │ p2024  │  │ p2025  │  │ pmax   │
   │ SKIP   │  │ READ   │  │ SKIP   │
   └────────┘  └────────┘  └────────┘
   Management: ADD / DROP / REORGANIZE / EXCHANGE / REBUILD / ANALYZE PARTITION

Fresher Notes

  • Partition pruning means MySQL scans only the partitions that can contain the requested rows.
  • Check it with EXPLAIN: the partitions column lists those used.
  • Management commands: ADD, DROP, REORGANIZE, EXCHANGE, TRUNCATE, REBUILD, ANALYZE PARTITION.

Worked Example 1

Event to add the next partition.
codeExamples:
CREATE EVENT ev_add_partition ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 MONTH DO
  ALTER TABLE logs REORGANIZE PARTITION pmax INTO (
    PARTITION p_next VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-06-01'), PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE));

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Missing future partition alert query.
codeExamples:
SELECT MAX(partition_description) AS last_boundary FROM information_schema.partitions WHERE table_name = 'logs' AND partition_name <> 'pmax';

-- OUTPUT:
-- last_boundary
-- '2026-03-01'

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Pruning check.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM logs WHERE logged_on = '2026-02-20';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- partitions | type
-- p202602    | ref

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Truncate one partition.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Pruning happens at optimization time: the optimizer evaluates the WHERE conditions against the partitioning function and removes partitions that cannot contain matches. It works when the partitioning column appears in a comparison the optimizer can analyse (equality, range, IN), without wrapping the column in non-monotonic functions.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Management commands: ANALYZE, CHECK, OPTIMIZE, REBUILD and REPAIR PARTITION, EXCHANGE PARTITION for archiving, and SELECT ... PARTITION (p) to read one partition directly.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: you can query one partition explicitly, swap data in or out in milliseconds, and run maintenance per partition.
codeExamples:
-- Query or maintain a single partition
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales PARTITION (p2025);
ALTER TABLE sales ANALYZE PARTITION p2025;
ALTER TABLE sales REBUILD PARTITION p2025;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |    48210 |
-- +----------+
-- | Table       | Op      | Msg_type | Msg_text |
-- | db.sales    | analyze | status   | OK       |

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: forgetting to pre-create the next partition makes inserts land in MAXVALUE or fail; REORGANIZE of a big partition copies its rows and can be slow; metadata locks during DDL can block traffic.
codeExamples:
-- Without a catch-all, a missing future partition makes inserts fail
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (99, '2031-01-01', 10.00);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1526 (HY000): Table has no partition for value 2031

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: pruning works only when the predicate can be evaluated against the partitioning expression; prepared statements and some expressions prune at execution time, not plan time. Partitioned tables cannot use foreign keys or the FULLTEXT index type.
codeExamples:
-- FULLTEXT is not available on partitioned InnoDB tables
ALTER TABLE logs ADD FULLTEXT (msg);

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1214 (HY000): The used table type doesn't support FULLTEXT indexes

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Automate partition rotation with a scheduled job (MySQL Event or external scheduler) that is monitored, and always keep predicates sargable against the partition column so pruning fires. Use EXCHANGE PARTITION for archival and bulk loads: load into a staging table, validate, then swap in near-instantly.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pruning needs the WHERE to compare the partition column directly (not wrapped in a function that the optimizer cannot map).
  • TRUNCATE PARTITION and DROP PARTITION remove data quickly.
  • Statistics and maintenance can be run per partition.

Senior Notes

  • Build automation for rolling partitions (create future, drop expired) and alert on missing future partitions.
  • Monitor partition sizes for skew and hot partitions.
  • Test restore/replication behaviour of partition operations; some statements take metadata locks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: partition DDL during peak (metadata locks), forgetting that some operations rebuild data, and relying on pruning without checking EXPLAIN. Run maintenance in low-traffic windows with a lock timeout.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Partition-level statistics and operations let you rebuild or analyse only the active partition, keeping maintenance windows short. Monitor sizes for skew.
codeExamples:
SELECT partition_name, table_rows, ROUND(data_length / 1048576) AS data_mb, ROUND(index_length / 1048576) AS index_mb FROM information_schema.partitions WHERE table_name = 'logs' ORDER BY partition_ordinal_position;

-- OUTPUT:
-- partition_name | table_rows | data_mb | index_mb
-- p202602        |    4820011 |     612 |      204

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world retention: nightly job drops partitions older than 13 months after confirming they were archived, with a guard against dropping the active one.

beginner.content:
Introduction

InnoDB is MySQL's default transactional storage engine. It provides ACID transactions, row-level locking, MVCC, crash recovery and foreign keys. Data is stored in a clustered B+tree on the primary key.
codeExamples:
-- Confirm the default engine and a table's engine
SELECT @@default_storage_engine AS default_engine;
CREATE TABLE acct (id INT PRIMARY KEY, bal DECIMAL(10,2));
SELECT TABLE_NAME, ENGINE, ROW_FORMAT FROM information_schema.TABLES
WHERE TABLE_SCHEMA = DATABASE() AND TABLE_NAME = 'acct';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | default_engine |
-- +----------------+
-- | InnoDB         |
-- +----------------+
-- +------------+--------+------------+
-- | TABLE_NAME | ENGINE | ROW_FORMAT |
-- +------------+--------+------------+
-- | acct       | InnoDB | Dynamic    |
-- +------------+--------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Applications need transfers to be all-or-nothing, many sessions to work concurrently without blocking readers, and data to survive a power cut. MyISAM could not offer these; InnoDB does through redo/undo logs, locks and MVCC.

Real-Time Use

Every OLTP workload (e-commerce, banking, SaaS) runs on InnoDB. Key settings are the buffer pool size, log file capacity and the flush policy.
codeExamples:
# my.cnf essentials for a dedicated 32 GB server
[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size        = 22G     # cache for data and index pages
innodb_redo_log_capacity       = 8G      # MySQL 8.0.30+: total redo size
innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1       # fully durable commit (default)
innodb_file_per_table          = ON      # one .ibd per table
innodb_flush_method            = O_DIRECT

# OUTPUT:
# After restart: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_buffer_pool_size';  -> 23622320128

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SQL layer ──► Handler API ──► InnoDB
                                  │
        ┌─────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┐
        ▼                         ▼                          ▼
   Buffer Pool            Log subsystem               Locking / MVCC
   (cached pages)     redo log + undo logs        (row locks, read views)
        │                         │
        ▼                         ▼
   .ibd tablespaces      #innodb_redo / undo files

Fresher Notes

  • InnoDB is MySQL’s default storage engine. It supports transactions, row-level locking, foreign keys and crash recovery.
  • Data is stored in tablespaces made of 16 KB pages, organised as B-trees by primary key.
  • Most production MySQL uses InnoDB.

Worked Example 1

Engine status report.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (sections)
-- BACKGROUND THREAD, SEMAPHORES, LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK, TRANSACTIONS, FILE I/O, LOG, BUFFER POOL AND MEMORY, ROW OPERATIONS

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Convert a MyISAM table.

Practice Exercise 1

Show engines and a table’s engine.
codeExamples:
SELECT engine, support FROM information_schema.engines WHERE engine IN ('InnoDB','MyISAM');

-- OUTPUT:
-- engine | support
-- InnoDB | DEFAULT
-- MyISAM | YES

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Key settings.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('innodb_buffer_pool_size','innodb_page_size','innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit','innodb_flush_method');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- innodb_buffer_pool_size        | 8589934592
-- innodb_page_size               | 16384
-- innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit | 1
-- innodb_flush_method            | O_DIRECT

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

InnoDB organises data in tablespaces made of 16 KB pages grouped into extents and segments. Tables are clustered B-trees by primary key. Memory: the buffer pool caches pages. Durability: the redo log records changes before pages are flushed. Atomicity and MVCC: undo logs. Torn-page safety: the doublewrite buffer. Row-level locks and transaction ids provide concurrency.
codeExamples:
SELECT engine, support, transactions, xa, savepoints FROM information_schema.engines WHERE engine = 'InnoDB';
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (sections)
-- BACKGROUND THREAD, SEMAPHORES, LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK, TRANSACTIONS, FILE I/O, INSERT BUFFER AND ADAPTIVE HASH INDEX, LOG, BUFFER POOL AND MEMORY, ROW OPERATIONS

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Key variables: innodb_buffer_pool_size, innodb_redo_log_capacity, innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT, innodb_file_per_table, innodb_io_capacity, innodb_page_size. Metrics are exposed through information_schema.innodb_metrics.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: full ACID, row-level locking, non-blocking consistent reads, automatic crash recovery, foreign keys and online DDL for many operations.
codeExamples:
-- Row-level locks: two sessions can update different rows at the same time
-- session 1:
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 1 WHERE id = 1;
-- session 2 (no waiting, different row):
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 1 WHERE id = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (session 1)
-- Query OK, 1 row affected   (session 2, not blocked)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: more memory and disk overhead than simple engines, COUNT(*) must scan an index, tables are physically ordered by the primary key so a wide or random key hurts, and long transactions bloat undo.
codeExamples:
-- COUNT(*) is not O(1) in InnoDB (MVCC means each transaction may see a different count)
EXPLAIN SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | table | type  | key     | rows | Extra       |
-- | acct  | index | PRIMARY | 2    | Using index |   <- walks the index

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: maximum row size is about half a page (8 KB for a 16 KB page, excluding off-page columns), at most 64 TB per tablespace, at most 1017 columns, and 16 columns in a composite index. The page size is fixed when the data directory is initialised.
codeExamples:
-- Page size is chosen at initialisation and cannot be changed later
SELECT @@innodb_page_size AS page_size;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+
-- | page_size |
-- +-----------+
-- |     16384 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

InnoDB is the right default for nearly everything, so the architect's job is sizing: buffer pool for the working set, redo for write bursts, and a compact monotonic primary key. Treat the clustered index as the table itself, because every secondary index carries the primary key as its row pointer.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Components: buffer pool (cache), redo log, undo log, doublewrite buffer, change buffer, tablespaces.
  • ACID is implemented with redo (durability), undo (atomicity, MVCC) and locks (isolation).
  • Check engine with SHOW ENGINES or SHOW TABLE STATUS.

Senior Notes

  • InnoDB is optimized for OLTP; large scans and analytics compete for buffer pool.
  • Know the key settings: innodb_buffer_pool_size, innodb_log_file_size / innodb_redo_log_capacity, innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit, innodb_flush_method.
  • File-per-table tablespaces make space management and backups easier.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: leaving defaults on a big server (a 128 MB buffer pool), using MyISAM for new tables, huge redo logs without understanding recovery time, and ignoring the history list length. Size memory and logs from the workload and monitor.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance is dominated by buffer pool hit rate, redo log throughput and checkpoint behaviour. Compare physical reads to read requests and watch log waits.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Innodb_buffer_pool_reads','Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests','Innodb_log_waits','Innodb_row_lock_waits');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_reads         | 412330
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests | 912330021
-- Innodb_log_waits                 | 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world baseline configuration for a dedicated 64 GB OLTP server.
codeExamples:
[mysqld]
innodb_buffer_pool_size = 40G
innodb_redo_log_capacity = 16G
innodb_flush_method = O_DIRECT
innodb_io_capacity = 4000
innodb_io_capacity_max = 8000
innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1
innodb_file_per_table = ON

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size / 1073741824;  =>  40.0000

beginner.content:
Introduction

The buffer pool is InnoDB's in-memory cache of data and index pages. Reads hit memory first; modified ("dirty") pages are written to disk lazily. It is typically the single largest memory consumer of a MySQL server.
codeExamples:
-- How big is the pool, and how many pages does it hold?
SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size / 1024 / 1024 AS pool_mb,
       @@innodb_buffer_pool_instances AS instances;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------+-----------+
-- | pool_mb | instances |
-- +---------+-----------+
-- | 22528   |         8 |
-- +---------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Disk is thousands of times slower than RAM. Caching hot pages turns most reads into memory hits and lets writes be batched, which is why a well-sized pool matters more than almost any other setting.
codeExamples:
-- Hit ratio: reads served from memory vs disk
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests','Innodb_buffer_pool_reads');

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------------------------+-----------+
-- | Variable_name                    | Value     |
-- +----------------------------------+-----------+
-- | Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests | 982341120 |   logical reads
-- | Innodb_buffer_pool_reads         |    412008 |   had to go to disk
-- +----------------------------------+-----------+
-- hit ratio = 1 - 412008/982341120 = 99.96%

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rule of thumb: 50 to 75 percent of RAM on a dedicated server. The pool uses a midpoint-insertion LRU so one big table scan does not evict the hot working set. It can be resized online and warmed after restart.

Diagram

   query ──► find page in Buffer Pool?
              │ yes ──► return (memory speed)
              │ no  ──► read from .ibd ──► place at MIDPOINT of LRU
        ┌────────────────── LRU list ──────────────────┐
        │ young (hot, 5/8)      │ midpoint │ old (3/8) │
        └───────────────────────┴──────────┴───────────┘
        modified page = dirty ──► flush list ──► background write to disk

Fresher Notes

  • The buffer pool is InnoDB’s memory cache of table and index pages. A bigger pool means fewer disk reads.
  • Set it with innodb_buffer_pool_size; on a dedicated server use about 60-75% of RAM.
  • A good cache hit ratio makes queries much faster.

Worked Example 1

Pool status.
codeExamples:
SELECT pool_size, free_buffers, database_pages, modified_database_pages FROM information_schema.innodb_buffer_pool_stats;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- pool_size | free_buffers | database_pages | modified_database_pages
-- 524288    | 1024         | 520000         | 3200

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Warm-up settings.

Practice Exercise 1

Hit ratio.
codeExamples:
SELECT (1 - (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME='Innodb_buffer_pool_reads') /
              (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME='Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests')) * 100 AS hit_pct;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- hit_pct
-- 99.87

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Resize online.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The buffer pool is a memory cache of 16 KB pages. Pages live on an LRU list split into a young (hot) and old sublist; newly read pages enter at the midpoint so a one-time scan does not evict hot data. Dirty (modified) pages are flushed to disk in the background by page cleaner threads, driven by the checkpoint age and innodb_io_capacity.
codeExamples:
SELECT pool_size, free_buffers, database_pages, modified_database_pages, pages_made_young, pages_not_made_young FROM information_schema.innodb_buffer_pool_stats\G

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- pool_size: 1572864   free_buffers: 1024   database_pages: 1560000   modified_database_pages: 3200
-- pages_made_young: 9120344   pages_not_made_young: 412330021

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: innodb_buffer_pool_size (resizable online), innodb_buffer_pool_instances, innodb_old_blocks_pct, innodb_buffer_pool_dump_at_shutdown/load_at_startup (warm cache), and chunk size. Size to the working set, typically 60-75% of RAM on a dedicated host.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: massive read speedup, write coalescing (many changes to one page, one flush), scan-resistant LRU, and warm restart.
codeExamples:
-- Which tables occupy the pool right now?
SELECT TABLE_NAME, COUNT(*) AS pages
FROM information_schema.INNODB_BUFFER_PAGE
WHERE TABLE_NAME IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY TABLE_NAME ORDER BY pages DESC LIMIT 3;   -- heavy query, avoid on busy production

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------------+-------+
-- | TABLE_NAME       | pages |
-- +------------------+-------+
-- | shop/orders      | 41200 |
-- | shop/order_items | 38877 |
-- | shop/customers   |  9120 |
-- +------------------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: after a restart the cache is cold unless dump/load is used; an over-large pool starves the OS and triggers swapping; a too-small pool causes constant disk reads.
codeExamples:
-- Dirty pages awaiting flush: high percentages signal write pressure
SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE AS dirty_pages FROM performance_schema.global_status
WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_dirty';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+
-- | dirty_pages |
-- +-------------+
-- | 8213        |
-- +-------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it caches pages, not query results (the query cache was removed in 8.0), the working set must fit for good performance, and the size is rounded to a multiple of chunk size times instances.
codeExamples:
-- Size is rounded up to a multiple of chunk_size * instances
SET GLOBAL innodb_buffer_pool_size = 1000000000;
SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size AS actual;

-- OUTPUT (example, chunk 128MB * 8 instances = 1 GB steps):
-- +------------+
-- | actual     |
-- +------------+
-- | 1073741824 |
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Size the pool to hold the hot working set and monitor the hit ratio, dirty-page percentage and read-ahead, not just raw size. On large servers use multiple instances to reduce mutex contention, keep dump/load on for fast warm-up, and leave headroom for per-connection buffers and the OS cache.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pages are managed with an LRU list (young and old sublists) to protect hot pages from one-time scans.
  • Dirty pages are flushed in the background; the checkpoint age relates to redo log capacity.
  • The pool can be resized online and split into instances for concurrency.

Senior Notes

  • Warm-up: innodb_buffer_pool_dump_at_shutdown/load_at_startup restore the cache after restart.
  • Watch hit ratio, free pages, dirty pages and read requests vs reads from disk.
  • Oversizing causes swapping, which is worse than a smaller pool.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: a pool larger than RAM (swapping, which is far worse than a smaller pool), full-table scans evicting hot pages, and cold starts after restarts. Warm the pool and run analytics on replicas.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_buffer_pool_load_status';
SELECT (1 - ib_reads.v / ib_reqs.v) * 100 AS hit_pct FROM
 (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE AS v FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_reads') ib_reads,
 (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE AS v FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests') ib_reqs;

-- OUTPUT:
-- hit_pct
-- 99.9552

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

If the working set does not fit, misses go to disk. Estimate the working set from table and index sizes of hot tables, and compare with the pool.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: after a restart queries were slow for 20 minutes. Enabling dump and load of the pool state reduced the warm-up to a couple of minutes.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The redo log records physical changes so committed data survives a crash (durability and replay). The undo log stores the previous version of changed rows so a transaction can roll back and so other transactions can read old versions (MVCC). Redo moves forward, undo moves backward.
codeExamples:
-- Redo configuration and durability policy (MySQL 8.0.30+)
SELECT @@innodb_redo_log_capacity / 1024 / 1024 AS redo_mb,
       @@innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit        AS flush_policy;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------+--------------+
-- | redo_mb | flush_policy |
-- +---------+--------------+
-- |    100  |            1 |
-- +---------+--------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Writing every dirty data page to disk at commit would be slow and random. Instead InnoDB appends a small sequential redo record at commit and flushes pages later. After a crash it replays redo to recover; undo rolls back transactions that never committed.
codeExamples:
-- Write-ahead logging in one picture (conceptual log of what happens on COMMIT)
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 30 WHERE id = 1;
-- 1) old value copied to UNDO       2) page changed in buffer pool (dirty)
-- 3) change written to REDO buffer
COMMIT;                                       -- 4) redo flushed + fsync (policy 1)
-- data page itself is written to disk later by a background flush

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1 row affected
-- Query OK (commit durable once redo is fsynced)

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Redo capacity governs write bursts: if it fills, InnoDB must flush aggressively (checkpoint stalls). Undo is used by rollback, by consistent reads and by purge, so long transactions keep old versions alive.
codeExamples:
-- Spot long transactions that hold undo history
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, trx_started, NOW()) AS age_s
FROM information_schema.INNODB_TRX ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 3;

-- History list length: how much undo purge has not yet cleaned
SELECT COUNT AS history_list_length FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS
WHERE NAME = 'trx_rseg_history_len';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- | 5128901 | 2026-10-06 08:00:11 | 7200 |
-- | history_list_length | 840221 |   <- large value = purge is behind

beginner.content:
Diagram

   UPDATE ──► 1. copy old row ──► UNDO log   (rollback + old versions for readers)
         └──► 2. change page   ──► Buffer Pool (dirty)
         └──► 3. append record ──► REDO log buffer
   COMMIT ──► 4. fsync redo   ──► durable
   later  ──► 5. checkpoint: dirty page ──► .ibd, redo space reusable

   crash recovery:  REDO replays committed work forward;  UNDO rolls back the uncommitted

Fresher Notes

  • The redo log records changes so committed data survives a crash (durability). The undo log stores old versions so you can roll back and read consistent snapshots.
  • Redo is for replay forward after a crash; undo is for rolling back and MVCC.
  • Both are written before data pages are flushed.

Worked Example 1

Find the transaction holding purge back.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, trx_mysql_thread_id FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- trx_id | trx_started         | trx_mysql_thread_id
-- 9981   | 2026-05-01 08:00:00 | 44

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Durability trade-off.
codeExamples:
SET GLOBAL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2;   -- faster, risk ~1 s of commits on OS crash

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Redo settings and activity.

Practice Exercise 2

Undo history length.
codeExamples:
SELECT count AS history_list_length FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';

-- OUTPUT:
-- history_list_length
-- 312

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Redo log: a circular, write-ahead log of changes to pages. On commit the redo records are written (and by default fsynced) so committed work survives a crash; recovery replays redo from the last checkpoint. Undo log: stores previous row versions; used to roll back, to provide MVCC snapshots, and cleaned by purge threads when no snapshot needs them.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: innodb_redo_log_capacity (8.0.30+, replaces file size and count), innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit (1, 2, 0), innodb_log_buffer_size, undo tablespaces and innodb_undo_log_truncate, innodb_max_purge_lag.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: fast sequential commits, crash safety, instant rollback, and non-blocking reads through undo-based old versions.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every commit with policy 1 pays an fsync; huge transactions generate huge undo and redo; long-running transactions prevent purge and bloat the undo tablespace.

Limitations

Limitations: redo is circular and fixed in size (resizable online since 8.0.30), undo space is shared by all transactions, and the redo log cannot repair corruption of already-written bad data; it only guarantees committed changes.

Architect's Notes

Size redo to absorb about an hour of peak write volume so checkpointing never stalls writers, and keep innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 with sync_binlog=1 wherever data loss is unacceptable. Watch history list length: it is the earliest warning that a long transaction or lagging purge is accumulating undo.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Write-ahead logging: changes go to the redo log first, data pages are written later.
  • Redo capacity is set by innodb_redo_log_capacity (8.0.30+); too small causes aggressive flushing and stalls.
  • Undo is stored in undo tablespaces and cleaned by purge threads when no snapshot needs old versions.

Senior Notes

  • Long transactions prevent purge, growing the undo history list and slowing reads.
  • Size redo for peak write bursts: it should hold at least an hour of writes on busy systems (guideline).
  • innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit: 1 durable per commit; 2/0 trade durability for speed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: redo capacity too small for write bursts (forced flushing and stalls), long transactions that keep undo alive and bloat the history list, and lowering durability settings on critical data. Size redo for peak writes and keep transactions short.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A guideline: redo capacity should hold roughly an hour of peak redo generation so checkpointing is smooth. Measure redo written per minute and set capacity accordingly.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world trade-off: setting innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2 on a reporting replica doubles load speed, while the primary keeps 1. The replica can be rebuilt from the primary, so the risk is acceptable.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The doublewrite buffer protects against torn pages: a 16 KB page write can be interrupted halfway by a crash, leaving a corrupt page. InnoDB first writes pages to a doublewrite area, then to their real location. The change buffer caches modifications to secondary-index pages that are not in memory, merging them later to avoid random reads.
codeExamples:
-- Both are on by default
SELECT @@innodb_doublewrite AS doublewrite, @@innodb_change_buffering AS change_buffering,
       @@innodb_change_buffer_max_size AS cb_max_pct;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+------------------+------------+
-- | doublewrite | change_buffering | cb_max_pct |
-- +-------------+------------------+------------+
-- | ON          | all              |         25 |
-- +-------------+------------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Redo replay needs an intact base page; a half-written page cannot be repaired from redo alone, so doublewrite supplies a good copy. Change buffering avoids a random disk read for every secondary-index insert on cold pages.
codeExamples:
-- Doublewrite activity: pages written vs doublewrite operations
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_dblwr%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------------------+--------+
-- | Variable_name              | Value  |
-- +----------------------------+--------+
-- | Innodb_dblwr_pages_written | 982110 |
-- | Innodb_dblwr_writes        |  41200 |   (about 24 pages per batch)
-- +----------------------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Bulk inserts into tables with many secondary indexes benefit most from the change buffer. In MySQL 8.0.20+ the doublewrite files are separate (#ib_16384_0.dblwr), and on filesystems or hardware with atomic writes it can be disabled.
codeExamples:
-- Change buffer merge counters from InnoDB metrics
SELECT NAME, COUNT FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS
WHERE NAME LIKE 'ibuf_merge%' AND STATUS = 'enabled';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------------------+--------+
-- | NAME               | COUNT  |
-- +--------------------+--------+
-- | ibuf_merges        | 180442 |
-- | ibuf_merges_insert | 176300 |
-- +--------------------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Torn-page protection                   Secondary index write optimisation
   dirty page ──► doublewrite area         INSERT, leaf page not cached
              │   (sequential, fsync)         │
              ▼                               ▼
          real location in .ibd         record change in CHANGE BUFFER
   crash mid-write? -> restore page        later page is read ──► changes MERGED
   from doublewrite copy, then apply redo

Fresher Notes

  • The doublewrite buffer protects against partial (torn) page writes: pages are written to a safe area first, then to their real location.
  • The change buffer caches changes to secondary index pages that are not in memory and merges them later.
  • Both improve safety or speed behind the scenes.

Worked Example 1

Doublewrite counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_dblwr%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Innodb_dblwr_pages_written | 5231044
-- Innodb_dblwr_writes        |  412881

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Reduce change buffer for SSD.

Practice Exercise 1

Check settings.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('innodb_doublewrite','innodb_change_buffering','innodb_change_buffer_max_size');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- innodb_doublewrite            | ON
-- innodb_change_buffering       | all
-- innodb_change_buffer_max_size | 25

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Change buffer activity.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, count FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name LIKE 'ibuf_merges%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- name              | count
-- ibuf_merges       | 128450
-- ibuf_merges_insert| 120310

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Doublewrite buffer: InnoDB pages are 16 KB but disks may write in smaller atomic units, so a crash can leave a torn page. Before a dirty page is written to its place, it is written to the doublewrite area; on recovery a torn page is restored from that copy and redo is applied. Change buffer: changes to secondary index pages that are not in memory are cached and merged later, turning random writes into batches.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls: innodb_doublewrite (ON, OFF, DETECT_AND_RECOVER), innodb_doublewrite_dir (separate fast storage), innodb_change_buffering (all, none, inserts, deletes, changes, purges) and innodb_change_buffer_max_size. Change buffering does not apply to unique secondary indexes.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: doublewrite gives safe recovery without special hardware; change buffer cuts random I/O and speeds write-heavy secondary-index workloads.
codeExamples:
-- Change buffer holds work for pages not in memory: see its size in the status output
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- INSERT BUFFER AND ADAPTIVE HASH INDEX section

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- Ibuf: size 1, free list len 612, seg size 614, 180442 merges
-- merged operations: insert 176300, delete mark 4100, delete 42

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: doublewrite writes every page twice (extra I/O, though sequential); a large change buffer lengthens crash recovery and can slow reads that must merge pending changes.
codeExamples:
-- Disabling change buffering for SSD-heavy, read-latency-sensitive workloads
SET GLOBAL innodb_change_buffering = 'none';
SELECT @@innodb_change_buffering AS mode;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | mode |
-- +------+
-- | none |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: change buffering applies only to non-unique secondary indexes (uniqueness must be checked immediately, requiring the page), and neither structure helps the clustered index. Disabling doublewrite is unsafe without atomic writes.

Architect's Notes

Keep doublewrite on unless storage guarantees atomic 16 KB writes. For SSD or NVMe fleets with mostly unique or read-latency-critical indexes, benchmark innodb_change_buffering=none; otherwise leave the default. Neither is a tuning knob you reach for first, but both explain surprising I/O patterns during incident analysis.

Mid-Level Notes

  • After a crash, a half-written 16 KB page can be repaired from the doublewrite copy.
  • Change buffering turns random secondary-index writes into fewer, batched I/Os (not for unique indexes).
  • Controlled by innodb_doublewrite and innodb_change_buffering/innodb_change_buffer_max_size.

Senior Notes

  • Disabling doublewrite is only safe on storage that guarantees atomic 16 KB writes; otherwise risk corruption.
  • A large change buffer can lengthen shutdown/recovery as merges must finish (innodb_fast_shutdown).
  • On SSDs the benefit of change buffering shrinks; evaluate with workload tests.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: disabling doublewrite on storage that does not guarantee atomic 16 KB writes (corruption risk), a big change buffer on fast SSDs where it adds little, and expecting it to help unique indexes. Test before changing, and keep doublewrite on unless atomic writes are guaranteed.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@innodb_doublewrite;
-- only OFF if the storage layer guarantees atomic page writes (verified), otherwise keep ON

-- OUTPUT:
-- @@innodb_doublewrite
-- ON

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The doublewrite buffer doubles page write volume but writes sequentially in batches, so its cost is moderate. Change buffering helps write-heavy workloads with many secondary indexes on spinning disks; on NVMe the gain is small and large buffers can lengthen shutdown and recovery merges.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- INSERT BUFFER AND ADAPTIVE HASH INDEX
-- Ibuf: size 1, free list len 612, seg size 614, 128450 merges
-- merged operations: insert 120310, delete mark 7900

-- OUTPUT:
-- (merges show the change buffer is active)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: on a write-heavy table with five secondary indexes the change buffer cut random I/O by a third on HDD storage; after moving to NVMe it was reduced to 10% of the pool with no measurable loss.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The Adaptive Hash Index (AHI) is an in-memory hash table that InnoDB builds automatically over B+tree index pages that are accessed frequently, turning an O(log n) B-tree descent into an O(1) hash lookup for equality searches. You do not create or choose it.
codeExamples:
-- Is it on, and how many partitions does it use?
SELECT @@innodb_adaptive_hash_index AS ahi, @@innodb_adaptive_hash_index_parts AS parts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+-------+
-- | ahi | parts |
-- +-----+-------+
-- |   1 |     8 |
-- +-----+-------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Hot point lookups repeat the same tree traversal thousands of times per second. Caching the path as a hash cuts CPU and page accesses without any application change.
codeExamples:
-- Hash searches vs ordinary B-tree searches
SELECT NAME, COUNT FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS
WHERE NAME IN ('adaptive_hash_searches','adaptive_hash_searches_btree');

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------------------------+-----------+
-- | NAME                         | COUNT     |
-- +------------------------------+-----------+
-- | adaptive_hash_searches       | 812334019 |
-- | adaptive_hash_searches_btree | 120554331 |
-- +------------------------------+-----------+
-- about 87% of searches were answered by the hash

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Workloads with many repeated equality lookups on a hot set (key-value-like tables) benefit; scan-heavy or highly concurrent write workloads often see mutex contention, so many teams turn it off.
codeExamples:
-- Toggle dynamically to test its effect
SET GLOBAL innodb_adaptive_hash_index = OFF;
SELECT @@innodb_adaptive_hash_index AS ahi;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+
-- | ahi |
-- +-----+
-- |   0 |
-- +-----+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   WHERE id = 42
        │
        ├─ hash lookup(42) ─► page address ──► row         (AHI hit: O(1))
        │
        └─ miss ─► B+tree descent: root ─► branch ─► leaf   (O(log n))
   AHI is built on demand for hot pages, lives in the buffer pool memory

Fresher Notes

  • The adaptive hash index (AHI) is an in-memory hash table that InnoDB builds automatically over frequently used index pages to speed equality lookups.
  • You do not create it; InnoDB decides based on access patterns.
  • It is controlled by innodb_adaptive_hash_index.

Worked Example 1

Partition to reduce contention.
codeExamples:
-- my.cnf
innodb_adaptive_hash_index = ON
innodb_adaptive_hash_index_parts = 16

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- 16 AHI partitions, less latch contention

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Metrics view.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, count FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name LIKE 'adaptive_hash%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- name                           | count
-- adaptive_hash_searches         | 912330021
-- adaptive_hash_searches_btree   |  212330011

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Check AHI usage.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- Hash table size 553253, used cells 12044
-- 8221.45 hash searches/s, 1744.32 non-hash searches/s

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Disable it online.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The adaptive hash index (AHI) is an in-memory hash table that InnoDB builds automatically on top of B-tree pages that are searched frequently with the same index prefix. It makes equality lookups into one hash probe instead of a tree descent. It is maintained transparently; you can only enable, disable or partition it.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- INSERT BUFFER AND ADAPTIVE HASH INDEX
-- Hash table size 553253, node heap has 12044 buffer(s)
-- 8221.45 hash searches/s, 1744.32 non-hash searches/s

SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_adaptive_hash_index%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- innodb_adaptive_hash_index       | ON
-- innodb_adaptive_hash_index_parts | 8

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls: innodb_adaptive_hash_index (dynamic) and innodb_adaptive_hash_index_parts (number of partitions, restart). Metrics: adaptive_hash_searches, adaptive_hash_searches_btree, and hash table memory.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: automatic, no storage on disk, faster equality lookups on hot data, and it self-adapts to the access pattern.
codeExamples:
-- Benefit shows as ratio of hash hits in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- Hash table size 553253, used cells 120331
-- 8231.12 hash searches/s, 1102.40 non-hash searches/s

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: consumes buffer pool memory, is protected by latches that can become a bottleneck under heavy concurrency, and must be maintained as pages change or are evicted.
codeExamples:
-- Contention shows up as waits on the AHI latch (btr_search)
SELECT EVENT_NAME, COUNT_STAR FROM performance_schema.events_waits_summary_global_by_event_name
WHERE EVENT_NAME LIKE '%btr_search%' ORDER BY COUNT_STAR DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +------------------------------------+------------+
-- | EVENT_NAME                         | COUNT_STAR |
-- +------------------------------------+------------+
-- | wait/synch/sxlock/innodb/btr_search_latch | 9120331 |
-- +------------------------------------+------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: equality predicates and prefix matches only (no range scans or ORDER BY help), it cannot be forced for a specific query, and it is lost on restart because it lives only in memory.
codeExamples:
-- A range predicate cannot use the hash
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM acct WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10;

-- OUTPUT (example, trimmed):
-- | type  | key     | rows |
-- | range | PRIMARY | 2    |    <- served by B-tree range scan, not the hash

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Leave AHI at its default, then measure: on read-mostly, equality-heavy services it is free speed; on write-heavy or highly parallel workloads, A/B test it off and compare throughput and latch waits. Treat it as an optimization you validate, never as a design assumption.

Mid-Level Notes

  • AHI helps workloads with many repeated equality lookups on the same pages (point reads).
  • It adds maintenance overhead and can cause contention on a global latch under heavy write or mixed load.
  • Check usefulness in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS (hash searches/s vs non-hash searches/s).

Senior Notes

  • In high-concurrency workloads, partitioning AHI (innodb_adaptive_hash_index_parts) or disabling it can improve throughput; test with your workload.
  • Cloud-managed MySQL often disables it by default.
  • Do not rely on it for design; good indexes and queries matter more.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: leaving it on under write-heavy or highly concurrent workloads where latch contention on the AHI hurts, and expecting it to speed range scans (it does not). Look for AHI latch waits and compare hash versus B-tree search rates.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, count_star, ROUND(sum_timer_wait / 1e12, 2) AS wait_s FROM performance_schema.events_waits_summary_global_by_event_name WHERE event_name LIKE '%btr0sea%' OR event_name LIKE '%adaptive%' ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name                       | count_star | wait_s
-- wait/synch/sxlock/innodb/btr_search_latch | 912330 | 41.20       (contention on the AHI latch)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Benchmark with and without it on your workload: read-heavy point-lookup workloads can gain 10-30%, write-heavy mixed workloads can lose. More partitions (innodb_adaptive_hash_index_parts) reduce contention.
codeExamples:
-- point lookups 90% / writes 10%: AHI on 52,000 qps, off 47,500 qps
-- 50% writes:                       AHI on 31,000 qps, off 36,000 qps
SELECT ROUND((52000 - 47500) / 47500 * 100, 1) AS read_gain_pct, ROUND((31000 - 36000) / 36000 * 100, 1) AS write_heavy_change_pct;

-- OUTPUT:
-- read_gain_pct | write_heavy_change_pct
-- 9.5           | -13.9

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: managed services often disable the AHI by default because multi-tenant, mixed workloads showed contention. Decide with a load test, not by default.

beginner.content:
Introduction

InnoDB stores data in tablespaces (files). A tablespace is divided into extents (1 MB) of pages (16 KB by default). Each table's rows live in the leaf pages of its clustered index (data pages); each secondary index has its own B+tree of index pages.
codeExamples:
-- Tablespace layout settings and the files on disk
SELECT @@innodb_file_per_table AS file_per_table, @@innodb_page_size AS page_size;
SELECT SPACE, NAME, FILE_SIZE / 1024 / 1024 AS mb
FROM information_schema.INNODB_TABLESPACES WHERE NAME LIKE 'shop/%' LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------------+-----------+
-- | file_per_table | page_size |
-- +----------------+-----------+
-- |              1 |     16384 |
-- +----------------+-----------+
-- | SPACE | NAME        | mb   |
-- |    12 | shop/orders | 96.0 |

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Understanding pages explains why a random UUID primary key fragments the table, why wide rows reduce cache efficiency, and why reading one row costs a whole 16 KB page I/O.
codeExamples:
-- How many rows fit on a page? Roughly 16384 / row_size, minus overhead.
-- Check actual index sizes in pages:
SELECT INDEX_NAME, STAT_VALUE AS pages
FROM mysql.innodb_index_stats
WHERE DATABASE_NAME='shop' AND TABLE_NAME='orders' AND STAT_NAME='size';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-------------+-------+
-- | INDEX_NAME  | pages |
-- +-------------+-------+
-- | PRIMARY     |  6144 |    6144 pages * 16 KB = 96 MB
-- | idx_cust    |  1100 |
-- +-------------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Admins use file-per-table so a table can be dropped to reclaim space, general tablespaces to group tables, and separate undo tablespaces. Moving a table to different storage is done with tablespace options.

Diagram

   Tablespace (.ibd)
   └─ Segments (leaf / non-leaf per index)
       └─ Extent = 64 pages = 1 MB
           └─ Page = 16 KB
               ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
               │ header │ rows... ► free space ◄ │ dir │ trl │
               └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   B+tree:         [root page]
                  /     |                [branch]  [branch]  [branch]
          / |                leaf pages hold full rows (clustered) or key+PK (secondary)

Fresher Notes

  • A tablespace is a file (or set) where InnoDB stores data. Data is divided into 16 KB pages; table rows live in data pages (leaf pages of the clustered index) and index entries in index pages.
  • By default each table has its own file (.ibd) with innodb_file_per_table=ON.
  • Pages group into extents (1 MB) and segments.

Worked Example 1

Reclaim space.
codeExamples:
OPTIMIZE TABLE events;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table       | Op       | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.events | optimize | note     | Table does not support optimize, doing recreate + analyze instead
-- shop.events | optimize | status   | OK

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

General tablespace.

Practice Exercise 1

Tablespaces and sizes.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, file_size/1024/1024 AS mb, allocated_size/1024/1024 AS alloc_mb FROM information_schema.innodb_tablespaces WHERE name LIKE 'shop/%' LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- name        | mb     | alloc_mb
-- shop/orders | 512.00 | 512.00
-- shop/emp    |   0.11 |   0.11

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Free space inside a table.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND(data_length/1024/1024) AS data_mb, ROUND(data_free/1024/1024) AS free_mb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY data_free DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | data_mb | free_mb
-- events     |    4200 |     900

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A tablespace is a set of files holding pages. File-per-table tablespaces (.ibd) hold one table with its indexes. A page (16 KB) belongs to a segment (leaf or non-leaf segment of an index) within extents of 1 MB. Data pages are the leaf pages of the clustered index and contain full rows; index pages contain keys and child or row pointers.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, space_type, row_format, page_size, ROUND(file_size / 1048576) AS file_mb, ROUND(allocated_size / 1048576) AS allocated_mb FROM information_schema.innodb_tablespaces WHERE name LIKE 'shop/%' ORDER BY file_size DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- name        | space_type | row_format | page_size | file_mb | allocated_mb
-- shop/orders | Single     | Dynamic    |     16384 |     520 |          520

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Types: system tablespace, file-per-table, general tablespaces (shared, can hold many tables, can be placed on specific storage or encrypted), undo tablespaces, and the session temporary tablespaces. Rows can be DYNAMIC (default, large values off-page) or COMPRESSED.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: file-per-table gives easy space reclaim and per-table backup or transport; the clustered layout makes primary-key range scans sequential; 16 KB pages balance I/O size and fan-out.
codeExamples:
-- Fan-out: with 16 KB pages and a 8-byte key, ~1000 children per branch page
-- so a 3-level tree can index about 1000 * 1000 * ~100 rows per leaf = 100,000,000 rows
SELECT FLOOR(16384 / (8 + 6)) AS approx_children_per_page;   -- key 8 bytes + pointer 6 bytes

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------------------+
-- | approx_children_per_page |
-- +--------------------------+
-- |                     1170 |
-- +--------------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: deleted rows leave free space in pages that is not returned to the OS until you rebuild; random primary keys cause page splits and about 30 percent wasted space; many small tablespace files increase file handle use.

Limitations

Limitations: page size is fixed per instance, a row cannot exceed about 8 KB on-page (large values move to overflow pages), and a tablespace cannot shrink in place. The system tablespace ibdata1 never shrinks.
codeExamples:
-- A row of many large VARCHARs may be rejected when the on-page part is too big
CREATE TABLE wide (
  a VARCHAR(4000), b VARCHAR(4000), c VARCHAR(4000), d VARCHAR(4000)
) ROW_FORMAT = COMPACT CHARACTER SET latin1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- ERROR 1118 (42000): Row size too large (> 8126). Changing some columns to TEXT or BLOB
-- may help. In current row format, BLOB prefix of 768 bytes is stored inline.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use a compact, monotonically increasing primary key (BIGINT auto-increment, or time-ordered ids) to fill pages sequentially and avoid splits, and remember secondary indexes store the primary key, so a fat primary key bloats every index. Keep file-per-table on, plan rebuilds off-peak, and monitor free space per tablespace.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Tablespace types: system, file-per-table, general tablespaces, undo tablespaces, temporary tablespaces.
  • A page holds many rows; rows are variable length and large values may be stored off-page (overflow).
  • Free space inside files is reused, but files only shrink on rebuild (OPTIMIZE TABLE).

Senior Notes

  • Fragmentation after heavy deletes/updates leaves half-empty pages; rebuild or tune fill factors (innodb_fill_factor).
  • General tablespaces allow placing tables on specific storage and encrypting them as a unit.
  • Transportable tablespaces (FLUSH TABLES ... FOR EXPORT) allow fast table moves between servers.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: expecting DELETE to shrink files (freed pages are reused but the file stays big until a rebuild), heavy fragmentation after random churn, and moving .ibd files by hand. Reclaim with OPTIMIZE TABLE and use transportable tablespaces to copy tables.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Page fill factor affects size and speed: sequential inserts fill pages to about 15/16 of the page, random inserts leave pages around 69% full. Check index page counts and fill to see if a rebuild helps.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: moving a 200 GB table to another server in minutes with a transportable tablespace instead of a long dump and load.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) lets InnoDB keep several versions of a row at once so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers, and writers do not block readers. The motto: readers never block writers, writers never block readers.

Why Do We Need This?

Locking every read would serialize the whole system: a long report would freeze all updates. MVCC gives consistent reads without locks, which is why InnoDB scales for mixed read and write workloads.
codeExamples:
-- Reader is not blocked by an uncommitted writer
-- Session B:
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = 999 WHERE id = 1;   -- not committed, row is locked
-- Session A (plain SELECT, no waiting):
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | bal  |
-- +------+
-- |  150 |      returned instantly from the old version, not blocked by B's lock
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Every web request reading a catalogue while orders are being written benefits. Reports and backups with --single-transaction rely on MVCC to read a stable view of a live database.
codeExamples:
-- Consistent online logical backup: one snapshot, no table locks
-- shell:
--   mysqldump --single-transaction --routines --triggers shop > shop.sql
-- (internally: START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT; then dumps every table)

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- -- Dump completed, writers were never blocked during the dump

beginner.content:
Diagram

   row id=1 versions (newest first)
   ┌──────────────────────┐   roll ptr   ┌──────────────────────┐   roll ptr   ┌─────────────────┐
   │ bal=150 trx=105      │ ───────────► │ bal=100 trx=90       │ ───────────► │ older ... (undo)│
   └──────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────┘              └─────────────────┘
   reader with snapshot older than trx 105 follows the chain back to bal=100

Fresher Notes

  • MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) lets readers and writers work at the same time by keeping multiple versions of rows.
  • A reader sees a consistent snapshot instead of waiting for writers.
  • InnoDB implements it with undo logs and transaction ids.

Worked Example 1

Monitor undo chain pressure.
codeExamples:
SELECT count AS history_list_length FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';

-- OUTPUT:
-- history_list_length
-- 41200

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Oldest active transaction.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, trx_started FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- trx_id | trx_started
-- 77123  | 2026-05-01 06:12:03

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Reader not blocked by writer.
codeExamples:
-- A
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = 0 WHERE id = 1;
-- B (does not wait)
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT: (B)
-- bal
-- 1000.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Snapshot vs current read.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;                       -- snapshot value
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;            -- latest committed value
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1000.00
-- 900.00   (if another transaction committed 900 meanwhile)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Multi-Version Concurrency Control lets readers and writers work at the same time by keeping several versions of a row. Each row has hidden fields: the id of the last modifying transaction (DB_TRX_ID) and a roll pointer (DB_ROLL_PTR) to its previous version in the undo log. A reader uses a read view to decide which version is visible to it.
codeExamples:
-- session A
START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = 0 WHERE id = 1;
-- session B (not blocked; sees the old committed value)
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT: (session B)
-- bal
-- 1000.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Snapshot reads (plain SELECT) use MVCC. Locking reads (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE) and writes use "current reads" that see the latest committed row and lock it. Isolation levels differ in when the read view is created.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;                      -- snapshot
-- another session commits bal = 900
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;                      -- snapshot (REPEATABLE READ): still 1000
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;           -- current read: 900
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- 1000.00
-- 1000.00
-- 900.00

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: high read concurrency, no read locks, repeatable reads inside a transaction, and consistent backups and reports on live data.
codeExamples:
-- Explicitly start a snapshot at BEGIN time (not at first read)
START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT;
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_seen FROM acct;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+
-- | rows_seen |
-- +-----------+
-- |         1 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: old versions occupy undo space until purged, long-running transactions keep them alive, and each row carries extra hidden columns (6-byte transaction id and 7-byte roll pointer).
codeExamples:
-- Purge lag: history list length grows when an old transaction stays open
SELECT COUNT AS history_list_length FROM information_schema.INNODB_METRICS
WHERE NAME = 'trx_rseg_history_len';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +---------------------+
-- | history_list_length |
-- +---------------------+
-- |             2400118 |
-- +---------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MVCC applies to plain (non-locking) SELECTs; statements such as SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, UPDATE and DELETE read the latest committed version and take locks. It does not exist in the MEMORY engine.
codeExamples:
-- Locking read ignores the snapshot and sees the latest committed data
-- Session A (snapshot still shows 100 from before):
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;              -- 100
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;   -- latest committed value, takes a lock

-- OUTPUT:
-- 100
-- 150      <- current version, not the snapshot

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

MVCC trades storage and purge work for concurrency, so the operational risk is the forgotten open transaction. Set idle-transaction timeouts, alert on history list length and oldest-transaction age, and keep application transactions short.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Plain SELECTs are non-locking: they read the version of each row visible to their snapshot.
  • Writers create new versions and keep old ones in undo until no snapshot needs them.
  • This is why long transactions can bloat the undo history.

Senior Notes

  • MVCC underlies isolation: READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot per statement, REPEATABLE READ one per transaction.
  • Writes still lock rows, and locking reads (FOR UPDATE) see the latest committed data, not the snapshot.
  • Understand "current read" vs "snapshot read" to avoid logic bugs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: long transactions that keep old versions alive (growing undo and a long history list), assuming a snapshot read equals what UPDATE sees, and reading a mixture of snapshot and current data in one transaction. Keep transactions short.
codeExamples:
SELECT count AS history_list_length FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';
SELECT trx_id, trx_started FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- history_list_length
-- 912330
-- trx_id | trx_started
-- 77123  | 2026-05-01 06:12:03

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

MVCC costs undo storage and purge work. Hot rows updated constantly build long version chains that old snapshots must walk. Monitor purge lag and avoid long snapshots on hot tables.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_purge_threads';
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- TRANSACTIONS: Purge done for trx's n:o < 4521790 undo n:o < 0 state: running but idle; History list length 91

-- OUTPUT:
-- innodb_purge_threads | 4

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: dashboards on a busy OLTP primary used 20-minute REPEATABLE READ transactions, bloating undo to 80 GB. Moving them to a replica and shortening transactions fixed it.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, ROUND(file_size / 1073741824, 1) AS gb FROM information_schema.innodb_tablespaces WHERE name LIKE 'innodb_undo%';

-- OUTPUT: (before -> after)
-- innodb_undo_001 | 41.0 -> 0.1
-- innodb_undo_002 | 39.0 -> 0.1

beginner.content:
Introduction

A consistent (non-locking) read is a plain SELECT that returns data as of a point in time, using a read view: an internal snapshot listing which transactions were active when it was created. Rows changed by transactions not visible to that view are reconstructed from undo.
codeExamples:
-- Default level REPEATABLE READ: the read view is created at the FIRST consistent read
SELECT @@transaction_isolation AS iso;
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct;                   -- read view created here

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------------+
