-- | iso             |
-- +-----------------+
-- | REPEATABLE-READ |
-- +-----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Within one transaction you want one stable picture of the data: totals that add up, no rows that appear and vanish between two SELECTs. The read view provides that without locking.

Real-Time Use

Reporting transactions use REPEATABLE READ for stable results; high-throughput OLTP often picks READ COMMITTED to hold fewer gap locks and shorter-lived versions. Consistent snapshot is explicit with WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT.
codeExamples:
-- REPEATABLE READ: second read in the same transaction is the same snapshot
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;           -- 100, read view created
-- other session commits bal = 150
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;           -- still 100
COMMIT;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;           -- new transaction, new snapshot

-- OUTPUT:
-- 100
-- 100
-- 150

beginner.content:
Diagram

   REPEATABLE READ                         READ COMMITTED
   BEGIN ──► 1st SELECT ─┐                 BEGIN ──► SELECT ─► [view 1]
                         ▼                          SELECT ─► [view 2]
                    [ one read view ]               SELECT ─► [view 3]
   all later SELECTs reuse it               each statement sees newest commits

Fresher Notes

  • A consistent read shows data as of a snapshot. InnoDB builds a read view that lists which transactions’ changes are visible.
  • At REPEATABLE READ the read view is created at the first consistent read; at READ COMMITTED it is created for each statement.
  • START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT creates it immediately.

Worked Example 1

READ COMMITTED sees new commits each statement.

Worked Example 2

Find long read views.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, trx_started, NOW()) AS minutes_open FROM information_schema.innodb_trx WHERE trx_started < NOW() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE;

-- OUTPUT:
-- trx_id | minutes_open
-- 77123  | 55

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Consistent snapshot.
codeExamples:
START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;      -- counts as of snapshot
-- other sessions insert more rows
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;      -- same count
COMMIT;

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 1000
-- COUNT(*)
-- 1000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Backup with a snapshot.
codeExamples:
mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 shop > shop.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- (consistent dump taken without blocking writers)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A read view records which transactions were active when it was created: a low-water mark (all transaction ids below it are committed and visible), a high-water mark (ids at or above it started later and are invisible) and the list of active ids in between. A row version is visible if its transaction id is below the low mark, not in the active list, or is your own transaction.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

At REPEATABLE READ the read view is created at the first consistent read (or immediately with WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT) and reused; at READ COMMITTED a new one is created for every statement. mysqldump --single-transaction relies on a consistent snapshot.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: stable results, no locks taken, and cheap: no copying of data, only version lookups through undo.
codeExamples:
-- A plain SELECT sets no row locks: confirm no lock entries for this transaction
SELECT COUNT(*) AS my_locks FROM performance_schema.data_locks
WHERE ENGINE_TRANSACTION_ID = (SELECT trx_id FROM information_schema.INNODB_TRX
                               WHERE trx_mysql_thread_id = CONNECTION_ID());

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------+
-- | my_locks |
-- +----------+
-- |        0 |
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: a stale snapshot can mislead logic (read then write based on old data), and the surprise "lost update" or write-skew appears when you compute in the app from snapshot values.
codeExamples:
-- Snapshot says 100, but UPDATE operates on the latest committed value
-- Session A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT bal ... -> 100
-- Session B: UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 50 WHERE id = 1; COMMIT;   (now 150)
-- Session A:
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 10 WHERE id = 1;     -- applies to 150, not 100
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | bal  |
-- +------+
-- |  160 |      A now sees its own write on top of the latest value
-- +------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a read view only affects consistent reads; the read view of REPEATABLE READ starts at the first read, not at BEGIN; and DDL such as ALTER TABLE is not versioned, so a snapshot cannot read through it.

Architect's Notes

Pick the isolation level per workload: REPEATABLE READ (default) for consistent multi-statement reads, READ COMMITTED for lower lock footprint and fresher data in OLTP. Never assume a read-then-write is safe: use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or an atomic UPDATE for read-modify-write logic.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Rows changed by transactions that were active (uncommitted) or started after the read view are invisible; InnoDB follows the undo chain to older versions.
  • Your own changes are always visible to you.
  • A consistent read does not take locks, so it does not block anyone.

Senior Notes

  • Consistent snapshot plus mysqldump --single-transaction yields a point-in-time backup without blocking writes.
  • Mixing snapshot reads and locking reads in one transaction can show surprising differences.
  • Long-lived read views are the main source of undo growth.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: long-lived read views (undo growth), forgetting that the snapshot does not cover DDL, and expecting read views to protect against writes in the same transaction. Close report transactions promptly.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, trx_started, NOW()) AS minutes_open, trx_state FROM information_schema.innodb_trx WHERE trx_started < NOW() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE;

-- OUTPUT:
-- trx_id | minutes_open | trx_state
-- 77123  |           55 | RUNNING

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Snapshots are cheap to create but expensive to hold. For big exports use short transactions in chunks by primary key range, or a replica with a dedicated snapshot.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: consistent backup. A logical dump takes one snapshot for all tables, recording the binlog position at the same instant, so the dump plus binlog replay gives exact point-in-time recovery.
codeExamples:
mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 --routines shop > shop.sql
grep -m1 "CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO" shop.sql

-- OUTPUT:
-- -- CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_LOG_FILE='binlog.000042', SOURCE_LOG_POS=1543;

beginner.content:
Introduction

Every InnoDB row has hidden columns: DB_TRX_ID (id of the transaction that last changed it) and DB_ROLL_PTR (pointer to the undo record holding the previous version). Undo logs chain these versions together. Each read-write transaction gets an increasing transaction id.
codeExamples:
-- See your own transaction id (assigned when a transaction first writes)
START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (5, 500);
SELECT trx_id, trx_state, trx_rows_modified
FROM information_schema.INNODB_TRX WHERE trx_mysql_thread_id = CONNECTION_ID();

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+-----------+-------------------+
-- | trx_id | trx_state | trx_rows_modified |
-- +--------+-----------+-------------------+
-- | 105233 | RUNNING   |                 1 |
-- +--------+-----------+-------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

To give readers old versions and to roll back, InnoDB must remember what each row looked like before. Undo records are that memory, and transaction ids tell the engine which version belongs to whom.
codeExamples:
-- Undo tablespaces hold the undo logs (MySQL 8: separate undo_001, undo_002 files)
SELECT NAME, FILE_SIZE / 1024 / 1024 AS mb, STATE
FROM information_schema.INNODB_TABLESPACES WHERE NAME LIKE 'innodb_undo%';

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +-----------------+------+--------+
-- | NAME            | mb   | STATE  |
-- +-----------------+------+--------+
-- | innodb_undo_001 | 16.0 | active |
-- | innodb_undo_002 | 16.0 | active |
-- +-----------------+------+--------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Background purge threads delete undo records and physically remove delete-marked rows once no active read view can need them. Undo space can shrink automatically when truncation is enabled.
codeExamples:
# my.cnf settings controlling undo
[mysqld]
innodb_undo_log_truncate = ON      # shrink undo tablespaces after purge
innodb_max_undo_log_size = 1G      # threshold that triggers truncation
innodb_purge_threads     = 4       # parallel purge workers

# OUTPUT:
# SELECT @@innodb_undo_log_truncate;  -> 1

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Clustered index record for id=1:
   ┌────────┬──────────────┬───────────────────┬───────┐
   │ id = 1 │ DB_TRX_ID=105│ DB_ROLL_PTR ──┐   │ bal   │
   └────────┴──────────────┴───────────────┼───┴───────┘
                                           ▼
        UNDO: (trx 98, bal=120) ──► (trx 90, bal=100) ──► (insert marker)
   purge thread removes undo older than the oldest live read view

Fresher Notes

  • Each InnoDB row has hidden fields: a transaction id (DB_TRX_ID) of the last change and a roll pointer to its previous version in the undo log.
  • Undo records let InnoDB reconstruct older versions for consistent reads and roll back.
  • Transaction ids increase with each write transaction.

Worked Example 1

Purge lag.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- TRANSACTIONS
-- Trx id counter 4521881
-- Purge done for trx's n:o < 4521790 undo n:o < 0
-- History list length 91

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rollback uses undo.

Practice Exercise 1

Undo tablespaces.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, state, file_size/1024/1024 AS mb FROM information_schema.innodb_tablespaces WHERE name LIKE 'innodb_undo%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- name           | state  | mb
-- innodb_undo_001| active | 16.00
-- innodb_undo_002| active | 16.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Truncation setting.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Every modification writes an undo record holding the old values and a pointer to the previous undo record, forming a version chain: current row → undo record → older undo record. The hidden columns DB_TRX_ID and DB_ROLL_PTR in the row point into this chain. Rollback applies undo records; consistent reads follow the chain until they find a visible version.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Undo lives in undo tablespaces (innodb_undo_*.ibu). Purge threads delete undo records when no read view needs them. Tuning: innodb_undo_tablespaces, innodb_undo_log_truncate, innodb_purge_threads, innodb_max_purge_lag.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: cheap rollback, version chain gives readers old data with no copying at read time, and undo doubles as input for crash recovery of uncommitted transactions.
codeExamples:
-- Rollback relies on undo: 1 million row change reverted by walking undo records
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 1;               -- writes undo for every row
ROLLBACK;
SELECT SUM(bal) FROM acct;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +----------+
-- | SUM(bal) |
-- +----------+
-- |      650 |
-- +----------+   unchanged

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: huge updates create huge undo and take long to roll back (rolling back is often slower than the original change); long read views block purge; secondary-index lookups of old versions are costlier.
codeExamples:
-- Find the oldest transaction that is pinning undo
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, trx_mysql_thread_id
FROM information_schema.INNODB_TRX ORDER BY trx_started LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT (example):
-- +--------+---------------------+---------------------+
-- | trx_id | trx_started         | trx_mysql_thread_id |
-- +--------+---------------------+---------------------+
-- | 99871  | 2026-10-05 22:14:03 |                 311 |   <- open for 10+ hours
-- +--------+---------------------+---------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: transaction ids are 48-bit and shared across the instance, read-only transactions (autocommit SELECTs) get no id until they write, and the number of concurrent write transactions is bounded by rollback segments (128 per undo tablespace).
codeExamples:
-- Kill the offender after confirming it is idle
KILL 311;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected
-- (purge can now reclaim undo up to the newest read view)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat undo as a shared resource: keep transactions short, batch big updates in chunks (for example 5,000 rows per transaction), and enable undo truncation. Alert on history list length and the age of the oldest transaction, since a single idle connection can quietly degrade the whole instance.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Versions form a chain: current row to undo record to older undo record, and so on.
  • Purge threads remove undo records no snapshot needs.
  • Rolling back replays undo to restore the previous values.

Senior Notes

  • Heavy updates to the same row create long version chains; readers on old snapshots must walk them, slowing queries.
  • Undo tablespaces can be truncated automatically (innodb_undo_log_truncate).
  • Monitor history length, purge lag and undo tablespace size.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: giant transactions (undo for every changed row), hot rows with long snapshots, and ignoring purge lag until queries slow down. A huge rollback can take as long as the original work.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, trx_rows_modified, trx_state FROM information_schema.innodb_trx ORDER BY trx_rows_modified DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- trx_id | trx_rows_modified | trx_state
-- 77123  |          48000000 | ROLLING BACK        (a mass update being undone)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Undo growth slows reads (long chains) and uses disk. Keep transactions short, batch large updates, and spread hot-row updates. Watch history length with an alert.
codeExamples:
UPDATE orders SET archived = 1 WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND archived = 0;     -- batch of 10,000
SELECT count FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len';

-- OUTPUT:
-- count
-- 120

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a nightly archive job once held one transaction for 40 minutes and grew undo to 60 GB. Batching by primary key range with a commit per batch kept undo small and reads fast.
codeExamples:
UPDATE orders SET archived = 1 WHERE id BETWEEN 10001 AND 20000 AND archived = 0;
-- commit, sleep 100 ms, next range

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 10000 rows affected

beginner.content:
Introduction

When a read view is created InnoDB records up_limit_id (lowest active trx id), low_limit_id (next id to be assigned) and the list of active ids. A row version with DB_TRX_ID below the low limit and not in the active list was committed before the snapshot and is visible; otherwise follow the undo chain to an older version. This gives snapshot-style isolation for reads.
codeExamples:
-- Rules for row version with trx id T and a read view (creator C):
--   T == C                          -> visible (my own change)
--   T <  up_limit_id                -> visible (committed before every active trx)
--   T >= low_limit_id               -> NOT visible (started after the snapshot)
--   up_limit_id <= T < low_limit_id -> visible only if T is NOT in the active list

-- OUTPUT (example for read view: up=101, low=106, active={101,103}):
--   T=99  visible   | T=102 visible (committed) | T=103 not visible (active) | T=107 not visible

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without clear visibility rules two readers could disagree about which rows exist. Deterministic rules make every transaction see a coherent state that matches some point in time.
codeExamples:
-- Phantom prevention demo at REPEATABLE READ: consistent read does not see new rows
-- Session A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct;      -- 1
-- Session B: INSERT INTO acct VALUES (9, 90); COMMIT;
-- Session A:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM acct;                                -- still snapshot

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----+
-- | cnt |
-- +-----+
-- |   1 |
-- +-----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The isolation levels map to read view timing: READ COMMITTED builds a view per statement; REPEATABLE READ builds one per transaction; SERIALIZABLE turns plain SELECTs into shared-lock reads; READ UNCOMMITTED reads latest versions without visibility checks.

Diagram

   read view: up_limit=101  low_limit=106  active={101,103}
   trx id:   ...99 ─ 100 ─ 101 ─ 102 ─ 103 ─ 104 ─ 105 │ 106 ─ 107 ...
   status:   visible ───────────┤ per active list ├────│ not visible (future)
                                 101 hidden, 102 visible, 103 hidden, 104 visible
   not visible? ─► follow DB_ROLL_PTR into undo ─► test the older version again

Fresher Notes

  • Visibility rules decide whether a row version is visible to a read view: versions from committed transactions before the snapshot are visible, others are not.
  • Snapshot isolation means a transaction sees the database as of its start time.
  • InnoDB’s REPEATABLE READ is similar to snapshot isolation for reads.

Worked Example 1

Own changes are visible.

Worked Example 2

Constraint-based guard.

Practice Exercise 1

Write skew example.
codeExamples:
-- rule: at least one doctor must be on call
-- A: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oncall WHERE on_call = 1;   -- 2
-- B: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM oncall WHERE on_call = 1;   -- 2
-- A: UPDATE oncall SET on_call = 0 WHERE doctor = 'Abaji';
-- B: UPDATE oncall SET on_call = 0 WHERE doctor = 'Raoji';
-- both commit

-- OUTPUT:
-- no doctor on call (invariant broken)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Fix with locking read.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Visibility rules decide which row version a read view may see: a version is visible if the transaction that created it committed before the read view was created (its id is below the low-water mark and not in the active list), or if it was created by the reading transaction itself. Otherwise InnoDB follows the roll pointer to an older version and applies the same test.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Snapshot isolation means a transaction sees the database as it was at its start. InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ gives this for plain reads. It is not full serializability: write skew is possible, where two transactions read the same data and update different rows, breaking an invariant that spans them. Guard the invariant with locking reads, constraints or SERIALIZABLE.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: consistent, lock-free reads that match a point in time; no dirty reads; repeatable reads without range locks for plain SELECTs.
codeExamples:
-- Dirty read is impossible at the default level
-- Session B: START TRANSACTION; UPDATE acct SET bal = 777 WHERE id = 1;   (uncommitted)
-- Session A (REPEATABLE READ or READ COMMITTED):
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | bal  |
-- +------+
-- |  100 |       B's uncommitted 777 is invisible
-- +------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: InnoDB REPEATABLE READ is not full snapshot isolation for writes: a transaction can modify rows committed after its snapshot (it sees them when it writes), producing write skew and surprising phantoms through locking reads.
codeExamples:
-- Phantom through a mix of snapshot read and locking read at REPEATABLE READ
-- Session A: START TRANSACTION; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct;               -- 1 (snapshot)
-- Session B: INSERT INTO acct VALUES (9, 90); COMMIT;
-- Session A:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM acct FOR UPDATE;                                     -- locking read: latest data

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | COUNT(*) |
-- +----------+
-- |        2 |    <- the row appeared, snapshot and locking reads disagree
-- +----------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: visibility is per row version, so it cannot protect invariants spanning rows (for example "at least one doctor on call"); that requires locking reads, SERIALIZABLE, or constraints. Secondary-index entries carry only max trx id per page, so some old-version checks need a clustered-index lookup.

Architect's Notes

Know which guarantees you actually have: InnoDB gives snapshot reads plus gap and next-key locking for locking reads, which is not the same as serializable. For invariants across rows, use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, unique constraints or SERIALIZABLE, and keep isolation level and retry-on-deadlock logic part of the application design.

Mid-Level Notes

  • A version is visible if its transaction id is below the read view’s low-water mark, not in the active list, and not the creator’s future changes.
  • The transaction sees its own changes.
  • Otherwise InnoDB follows the roll pointer to an older version.

Senior Notes

  • Snapshot isolation allows write skew: two transactions read overlapping data and update different rows, breaking an invariant.
  • Prevent it with locking reads (FOR UPDATE on the checked rows), constraints or SERIALIZABLE.
  • Understand that InnoDB REPEATABLE READ is not full serializability.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: assuming snapshot isolation prevents all anomalies, deciding from a snapshot read and writing, and testing concurrency with one session. Use a locking read on the rows that define the rule.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Locking reads reduce concurrency but are cheap for small rule sets. A unique constraint is cheaper still for rules it can express (one booking per seat), because the index enforces it with no extra reads.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world rule of thumb: keep snapshot reads for reporting and display, use conditional updates or unique constraints for counters and bookings, and lock explicit rows only for rules that span several rows.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The slow query log records every statement that runs longer than long_query_time seconds (default 10). It is the first tool for finding which queries hurt, because it records real workload, not guesses.
codeExamples:
-- Turn the slow log on at runtime (no restart); persists only if also in my.cnf
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log      = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL long_query_time     = 0.5;      -- seconds; applies to NEW connections
SET GLOBAL log_output          = 'FILE';   -- or TABLE (mysql.slow_log)
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'slow_query_log_file';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name        | Value
-- slow_query_log_file  | /var/lib/mysql/db01-slow.log (example)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without the log you tune blindly. A page that is "slow" may come from one query in a thousand; the log ranks them by total time so you fix the biggest offender first.
codeExamples:
-- Typical entry in the file (what you read with mysqldumpslow / pt-query-digest)
-- # Time: 2026-10-06T10:12:44.100000Z
-- # Query_time: 2.314  Lock_time: 0.000  Rows_sent: 20  Rows_examined: 1840233
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_email = 'a@b.com' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Rows_examined 1.8M vs Rows_sent 20  => missing index on customer_email.

SHOW GLOBAL VARIABLES LIKE 'long_query_time';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name   | Value
-- long_query_time | 0.500000

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

In production teams run with long_query_time around 0.5-1 s, enable log_queries_not_using_indexes only temporarily, and rotate the file; pt-query-digest then groups by fingerprint.
codeExamples:
SET GLOBAL log_queries_not_using_indexes = 'ON';      -- noisy: use for a short window
SET GLOBAL min_examined_row_limit = 1000;               -- skip tiny scans
SET GLOBAL log_slow_extra = 'ON';                       -- 8.0.14+: more fields per entry
-- shell: mysqldumpslow -s t -t 5 /var/lib/mysql/db01-slow.log   (top 5 by total time)
SELECT @@log_queries_not_using_indexes AS no_idx, @@min_examined_row_limit AS min_rows;

-- OUTPUT:
-- no_idx | min_rows
--      1 |     1000

beginner.content:
Diagram

   client ──► MySQL server ──► execute statement
                                   │ finished, time > long_query_time ?
                              ┌────┴─────┐
                              ▼ yes      ▼ no
                      slow log (FILE/TABLE)   (nothing)
                              │
                              ▼
                  mysqldumpslow / pt-query-digest ──► ranked list ──► EXPLAIN ──► fix

Fresher Notes

  • The slow query log records statements that run longer than long_query_time, so you can find and fix them.
  • Enable: SET GLOBAL slow_query_log = ON; SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 1;.
  • Summarise it with mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest.

Worked Example 1

Summarize top offenders.
codeExamples:
mysqldumpslow -s t -t 5 /var/lib/mysql/db-slow.log

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Count: 412  Time=2.31s (951s)  Lock=0.00s  Rows=20.0 (8240)
--   SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_note LIKE 'S' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT N

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Rotate the log.

Practice Exercise 1

Turn it on.

Practice Exercise 2

Example log entry.
codeExamples:
-- # Time: 2026-05-01T10:15:22
-- # Query_time: 2.314  Lock_time: 0.000  Rows_sent: 20  Rows_examined: 1204331
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_note LIKE '%refund%' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- (2.3 s, 1.2M rows examined to return 20 rows: needs an index or fulltext)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

When a statement finishes and its execution time exceeds long_query_time, the server writes an entry to the slow log (file or table) with the time, user, query time, lock time, rows sent and rows examined, and the statement text. Optional extras (log_slow_extra) add temporary table, sort and I/O counters.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls: log_queries_not_using_indexes, min_examined_row_limit, log_slow_admin_statements, log_output (FILE or TABLE), per-session thresholds, and rotation with FLUSH SLOW LOGS. Summarize with mysqldumpslow or pt-query-digest.
codeExamples:
mysqldumpslow -s t -t 5 /var/lib/mysql/db-slow.log
pt-query-digest /var/lib/mysql/db-slow.log --limit 10 > slow_report.txt
FLUSH SLOW LOGS;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Count: 412  Time=2.31s (951s)  Lock=0.00s  Rows=20.0 (8240)
--   SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_note LIKE 'S' ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT N

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: real workload evidence, tiny overhead when threshold is sane, works on any version, can be written to a table for SQL analysis.
codeExamples:
-- Log to a table and query it with SQL itself
SET GLOBAL log_output = 'TABLE';
SELECT start_time, query_time, rows_examined, LEFT(sql_text, 40) AS q
FROM   mysql.slow_log
ORDER  BY query_time DESC
LIMIT  2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- start_time          | query_time | rows_examined | q
-- 2026-10-06 10:12:44 | 00:00:02   |       1840233 | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_ema
-- 2026-10-06 10:13:01 | 00:00:01   |        950000 | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE type=

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it logs only after completion, so a query that never finishes is invisible; with threshold 0 the file grows fast and the disk I/O itself slows the server.
codeExamples:
-- Capturing everything for 60 seconds, then restoring: a sampling pattern
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 0;      -- log ALL statements (heavy!)
DO SLEEP(60);
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 1;      -- back to normal
SELECT @@global.long_query_time AS t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- t
-- 1.000000

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it shows duration, not why; it cannot tell waits (locks, I/O) apart without extra fields; fast but extremely frequent queries (0.2 ms x millions) never reach the threshold.
codeExamples:
-- A 0.3 ms query run 5 million times/hour costs 25 minutes of server time,
-- yet never appears with long_query_time = 1. Use Performance Schema digests for that.
SELECT DIGEST_TEXT, COUNT_STAR, ROUND(SUM_TIMER_WAIT/1e12,1) AS total_s
FROM   performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
ORDER  BY SUM_TIMER_WAIT DESC LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- DIGEST_TEXT                          | COUNT_STAR | total_s
-- SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?     |    5000000 |  1500.0

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use the slow log for outliers and Performance Schema digests for aggregate cost; together they cover both "rare and slow" and "fast but constant". Ship logs to a central store, keep sampling thresholds in config management, and watch disk usage on the log volume.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Useful extras: log_queries_not_using_indexes, log_slow_extra (8.0.14+), min_examined_row_limit.
  • Each entry shows Query_time, Lock_time, Rows_sent and Rows_examined.
  • Rotate the file to avoid large logs; log to FILE rather than TABLE for performance.

Senior Notes

  • Lower long_query_time temporarily (0.1 s or 0) on a sample to capture the real workload, then raise it.
  • Use digests (Performance Schema) for continuous aggregated view and the slow log for samples with actual parameters.
  • Correlate with deployments: new slow queries often follow a release.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: logging at 10 seconds (misses the damage done by frequent 200 ms queries), leaving it at zero threshold on a busy server (huge file and overhead), and reading single entries instead of aggregating. Sample with a low threshold for a short window, then raise it.
codeExamples:
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 0;          -- capture everything for 5 minutes
-- ... wait, then
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- (a representative sample of the whole workload for pt-query-digest)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Rank by total time, not by single slowest. Look at rows examined versus rows sent: a large ratio means wasted work (missing index or non-sargable predicate). The digest tables give the same view continuously.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 60) AS q, count_star, ROUND(sum_timer_wait/1e12, 1) AS total_s, ROUND(sum_rows_examined / NULLIF(sum_rows_sent, 0)) AS examined_per_sent FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- q                                       | count_star | total_s | examined_per_sent
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id  |     912000 |   410.5 |                12

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world loop: weekly review of the top ten digests, fix the worst with an index or rewrite, deploy, and compare the same digest next week.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Performance Schema is an in-memory instrumentation engine that records statements, waits, stages, locks and memory use. The sys schema is a set of readable views on top of it, so you rarely query the raw tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@performance_schema AS enabled;
SELECT query, exec_count, total_latency
FROM   sys.statement_analysis
LIMIT  2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- enabled
-- 1
-- query                              | exec_count | total_latency
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ...     |      15200 | 4.12 m
-- INSERT INTO events (...) VALUES... |     980000 | 2.51 m

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The slow log answers "which query"; Performance Schema answers "where did the time go" - lock waits, file I/O, temp tables, full scans - without external tools.
codeExamples:
-- Which tables are read the most, and how slowly?
SELECT object_schema, object_name, count_read, ROUND(sum_timer_read/1e12,2) AS read_s
FROM   performance_schema.table_io_waits_summary_by_table
WHERE  object_schema = 'shop'
ORDER  BY sum_timer_read DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_schema | object_name | count_read | read_s
-- shop          | orders      |   12400000 |  93.40
-- shop          | order_items |    8100000 |  41.07

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

DBAs use sys views daily: statements doing full scans, unused indexes, who holds locks, which host consumes the most connections.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM sys.schema_unused_indexes WHERE object_schema = 'shop' LIMIT 2;
SELECT * FROM sys.statements_with_full_table_scans LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_schema | object_name | index_name
-- shop          | orders      | idx_orders_legacy_flag
-- shop          | customers   | idx_cust_fax
-- query                         | exec_count | no_index_used_count
-- SELECT * FROM audit WHERE ... |        310 |                 310

beginner.content:
Diagram

   server code ──► instruments (setup_instruments)
                        │ events
                        ▼
            performance_schema.* tables  (in memory, raw)
                        │ views
                        ▼
                   sys schema  (readable: latency, rows, MB)
                        │
                        ▼
          DBA queries / exporters (mysqld_exporter, PMM)

Fresher Notes

  • Performance Schema is MySQL’s built-in instrumentation that records what the server is doing. The sys schema provides readable views on top of it.
  • Ask questions like "which queries are slowest?" or "which indexes are unused?" with simple SELECTs on sys.
  • Examples: sys.statement_analysis, sys.schema_unused_indexes, sys.innodb_lock_waits.

Worked Example 1

Statements with full table scans.
codeExamples:
SELECT query, exec_count, no_index_used_count FROM sys.statements_with_full_table_scans LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- query                                 | exec_count | no_index_used_count
-- SELECT * FROM events WHERE note LIKE? |       5200 |                5200

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Memory usage by area.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, current_alloc FROM sys.memory_global_by_current_bytes LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name                    | current_alloc
-- memory/innodb/buf_buf_pool    | 8.00 GiB
-- memory/sql/thd::main_mem_root | 112.00 MiB

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Top statements.
codeExamples:
SELECT query, exec_count, total_latency, avg_latency, rows_examined_avg FROM sys.statement_analysis ORDER BY total_latency DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- query                           | exec_count | total_latency | avg_latency | rows_examined_avg
-- SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ...  |     412000 | 15.2 min      | 2.21 ms     | 1840
-- UPDATE inventory SET qty = ...  |     980000 | 9.8 min       | 0.60 ms     |    1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Unused and redundant indexes.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM sys.schema_unused_indexes WHERE object_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_schema | object_name | index_name
-- shop          | orders      | idx_old_status

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The Performance Schema instruments the server in memory: statements, stages, waits, locks, memory, file I/O, connections, replication. Data lives in tables with the PERFORMANCE_SCHEMA engine and is aggregated into summary tables (by digest, thread, account, event). The sys schema is a set of views and procedures that read those tables in a friendly form.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Configure what is collected through setup_instruments, setup_consumers, setup_actors and setup_objects. Useful views: sys.statements_with_full_table_scans, sys.statements_with_temp_tables, sys.host_summary, sys.memory_global_by_current_bytes, sys.io_global_by_wait_by_latency.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: built in, low overhead (about 5-10%), SQL-queryable, covers far more than the slow log, and sys gives human units (ms, MB).
codeExamples:
-- Who is blocking whom right now?  (sys view over data_locks / data_lock_waits)
SELECT waiting_pid, waiting_query, blocking_pid, blocking_query
FROM   sys.innodb_lock_waits;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- waiting_pid | waiting_query                    | blocking_pid | blocking_query
--          42 | UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-5 WHERE..|           37 | NULL (idle in transaction)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: consumers use memory, data resets on restart, some instruments are off by default, and the raw table names are hard to remember.
codeExamples:
-- Some consumers/instruments are disabled by default: enable only what you need
UPDATE performance_schema.setup_consumers
SET    enabled = 'YES'
WHERE  name = 'events_statements_history_long';

SELECT name, enabled FROM performance_schema.setup_consumers
WHERE  name LIKE 'events_statements_history%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- name                            | enabled
-- events_statements_history       | YES
-- events_statements_history_long  | YES

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it is not persistent (restart clears it), the digest table keeps a bounded number of distinct statements (performance_schema_digests_size), and it cannot be changed from a read-only account.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Performance_schema_digest_lost';
SELECT @@performance_schema_digests_size AS digest_slots;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name                 | Value
-- Performance_schema_digest_lost| 0
-- digest_slots
-- 10000

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep Performance Schema on in production; the cost is far lower than blind debugging. Export digests to a time-series store so you see regressions after deploys, and never grant broad access to it because query text can contain sensitive literals.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Performance Schema tables hold statement digests, waits, stages, memory and lock data with small overhead.
  • Instruments and consumers can be enabled or disabled to balance detail and cost.
  • Counters reset on restart; export metrics regularly.

Senior Notes

  • Build dashboards from digests (calls, total time, rows examined, no-index-used) and alert on regressions.
  • Use events_statements_history_long or the slow log for concrete examples of a digest.
  • Watch memory instrumentation to find leaks or large allocations.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: enabling every instrument and consumer on a busy server (overhead), forgetting counters reset at restart, and reading numbers without context. Enable what you need, snapshot metrics regularly into your monitoring system.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, enabled FROM performance_schema.setup_consumers WHERE name LIKE 'events_waits%';
TRUNCATE TABLE performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest;       -- reset the digest counters for a fresh measurement window

-- OUTPUT:
-- name                       | enabled
-- events_waits_current       | NO
-- events_waits_history_long  | NO

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Overhead is typically a few percent with the defaults. Measure memory use of the schema itself and sizes of history tables; use the digest summaries (always on) instead of heavy history tables for routine monitoring.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a regression detector. Snapshot the digest table every hour into your own table, then alert when a digest's average latency or rows examined jumps against its own history.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Index and query tuning means making the optimizer read fewer rows: add the right indexes, write predicates that can use them, and verify the plan with EXPLAIN.

Why Do We Need This?

A full scan is fine for 100 rows and a disaster for 100 million. Indexes turn O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups, and tuning stops one query from starving every other.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_cust_created (customer_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE  customer_id = 7 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER  BY created_at;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type  | key              | rows | Extra
-- range | idx_cust_created |   40 | Using where; Using index
-- no filesort: index order already matches ORDER BY

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical wins in real projects: composite index matching WHERE+ORDER BY, covering index for hot reads, removing functions on indexed columns, replacing OFFSET paging with keyset.
codeExamples:
-- BAD: function on the column defeats the index
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-01';
-- GOOD: sargable range
EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-02';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- BAD : type=index  key=idx_cust_created rows=2400000  (scans whole index)
-- GOOD: type=range  key=idx_created      rows=1800

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Query ──► Optimizer ──► candidate plans ──► pick lowest cost
                 │ uses
                 ▼
        index stats (cardinality)   <──  ANALYZE TABLE
                 │
   rows read:  full scan 1,000,000  vs  index range 40
                 │
              EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to verify

Fresher Notes

  • Tuning means making slow queries faster, mostly with better indexes and better SQL. Start from the slowest or most frequent queries.
  • Workflow: find the query, run EXPLAIN, change the index or SQL, measure again.
  • Typical wins: add a composite index, avoid functions on indexed columns, select fewer columns.

Worked Example 1

Update statistics.
codeExamples:
ANALYZE TABLE orders;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table       | Op      | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.orders | analyze | status   | OK

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Find duplicate indexes.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name FROM sys.schema_redundant_indexes WHERE table_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | redundant_index_name | dominant_index_name
-- orders     | idx_customer         | idx_cust_status_created

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Before and after.

Practice Exercise 2

Remove a function on the column.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Tuning is an experiment loop: pick the query with the largest total cost, read its plan with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, form a hypothesis (missing index, non-sargable predicate, wrong join order, too many columns), change one thing, and measure again. The plan shows which rows are read and why.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Checklist: make predicates sargable (no function on the column, matching types), order composite index columns (equality, range, order), use covering indexes for hot reads, select only needed columns, paginate with keyset, replace correlated subqueries, and keep statistics fresh.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' AND created_at < '2026-05-02';        -- not DATE(created_at)
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7;                                              -- not SELECT *
ANALYZE TABLE orders;
SELECT id FROM orders WHERE (created_at, id) < ('2026-05-01 10:00:00', 9120) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table       | Op      | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.orders | analyze | status   | OK

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: orders-of-magnitude speedups with no hardware cost; EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) shows actual rows and time per step.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) FROM orders
WHERE  created_at >= '2026-10-01' GROUP BY customer_id;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Group aggregate: count(0)  (cost=420 rows=300) (actual time=0.21..3.4 rows=250 loops=1)
--     -> Index range scan on orders using idx_created ... (actual time=0.1..2.9 rows=1800 loops=1)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: every extra index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and uses disk and buffer pool; too many indexes confuse the optimizer and make maintenance heavy.
codeExamples:
-- Find indexes that cost writes but are never read
SELECT object_name, index_name
FROM   sys.schema_unused_indexes
WHERE  object_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- object_name | index_name
-- orders      | idx_status_legacy

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: low-selectivity columns (status with 3 values) rarely benefit alone, statistics can be stale, and the optimizer may ignore an index when it expects to read more than about 20-30% of the table.
codeExamples:
ANALYZE TABLE orders;                       -- refresh statistics
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID';   -- 90% rows are PAID
SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM orders GROUP BY status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- EXPLAIN: type=ALL key=NULL      (full scan is cheaper than 90% random lookups)
-- status | COUNT(*)
-- PAID   | 900000
-- NEW    |  80000
-- VOID   |  20000

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Tune from evidence: slow log or digest -> EXPLAIN ANALYZE -> smallest index change -> re-measure. Prefer fewer wide composite indexes designed around real query shapes, use invisible indexes (8.0) to test drops safely, and review index set after each feature release.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Checklist: sargable WHERE, correct composite order, covering index for hot reads, avoid SELECT *, limit result size, paginate with keyset.
  • Rewrite correlated subqueries, avoid OR across columns, avoid implicit type conversions.
  • Check cardinality and update statistics (ANALYZE TABLE).

Senior Notes

  • Validate with production-sized data; plans differ at scale.
  • Balance read gains with write cost: every index slows inserts/updates.
  • Prevent regressions with query review, plan snapshots, load tests and dashboards for top queries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: adding an index per slow query without checking overlaps (index sprawl), tuning on tiny test data, changing several things at once, and ignoring write cost. Remove unused or redundant indexes and test on production-sized data.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Quantify gains: record latency percentiles and rows examined before and after under the same load, and keep the evidence. A 100x gain on a rare query matters less than a 2x gain on a query that runs millions of times.
codeExamples:
SELECT 912000 * (3.2 - 0.4) / 1000 / 60 AS minutes_saved_per_day;

-- OUTPUT:
-- minutes_saved_per_day
-- 42.56

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: slow admin search. The fix was a mandatory date filter, a covering composite index and keyset pagination, taking the query from 6 seconds to 8 ms.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The InnoDB buffer pool caches table and index pages in RAM. Reading a cached page costs microseconds; reading from disk costs milliseconds, so buffer pool size is the biggest memory lever.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_size/1024/1024/1024 AS pool_gb,
       @@innodb_buffer_pool_instances       AS instances;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- pool_gb | instances
-- 12.0000 | 8

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

If the working set does not fit in memory, every query becomes a disk read. Right-sizing the pool (and per-connection buffers) avoids both I/O storms and swapping.
codeExamples:
-- Hit ratio: reads that had to go to disk vs total read requests
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN
 ('Innodb_buffer_pool_reads','Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name                     | Value
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_reads          | 1200000      (disk reads)
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests  | 480000000    (logical reads)
-- hit ratio = 1 - 1.2M/480M = 99.75%

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Rule of thumb on a dedicated server: 60-75% of RAM for the pool; resize online in chunks since 5.7; warm it after restart with the dump/load feature.
codeExamples:
SET GLOBAL innodb_buffer_pool_size = 16 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024;   -- online resize
SELECT @@innodb_buffer_pool_dump_at_shutdown AS dump,
       @@innodb_buffer_pool_load_at_startup  AS load_;
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Innodb_buffer_pool_resize_status';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- dump | load_
--    1 |     1
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_resize_status | Completed resizing buffer pool at 261006 10:20:11.

beginner.content:
Diagram

   RAM
   ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
   │ OS + file cache │ per-conn buffers │ BUFFER POOL (60-75%) │
   └───────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                │
              read hit ◄────────┤────────► miss ──► disk (ms)
              (microseconds)    │
                         young list | midpoint | old list  (LRU)

Fresher Notes

  • Memory tuning decides how much RAM goes to the InnoDB buffer pool, connection buffers and temp tables.
  • The biggest lever is innodb_buffer_pool_size.
  • Do not set global buffers so large that the server swaps.

Worked Example 1

Largest memory consumers.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, current_alloc FROM sys.memory_global_by_current_bytes LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name                 | current_alloc
-- memory/innodb/buf_buf_pool | 10.00 GiB

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Swap check (Linux shell).
codeExamples:
vmstat 1 3

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- si so columns should stay 0 (no swapping)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Worst-case memory estimate.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND((@@innodb_buffer_pool_size + @@max_connections * (@@sort_buffer_size + @@join_buffer_size + @@read_buffer_size + @@read_rnd_buffer_size)) / 1024 / 1024 / 1024, 1) AS worst_case_gb;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- worst_case_gb
-- 14.3

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Per-session boost for one report.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL memory has global areas (InnoDB buffer pool, log buffer, caches) and per-connection areas (sort, join, read buffers, temp tables, thread stack) that multiply with connections. The buffer pool is the largest and most important: it should hold the working set so reads rarely touch disk.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND((@@innodb_buffer_pool_size + @@max_connections * (@@sort_buffer_size + @@join_buffer_size + @@read_buffer_size + @@read_rnd_buffer_size + @@thread_stack)) / 1073741824, 1) AS worst_case_gb;
SELECT event_name, current_alloc FROM sys.memory_global_by_current_bytes LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- worst_case_gb
-- 28.3
-- event_name                 | current_alloc
-- memory/innodb/buf_buf_pool | 24.00 GiB

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Sizing rules: buffer pool 60-75% of RAM on a dedicated host; keep per-session buffers modest and raise them per session only for specific reports; set tmp_table_size/max_heap_table_size consciously; leave memory for the OS cache and connections; avoid swap (vm.swappiness low).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: huge read speedup, absorbs write bursts (dirty pages flushed later), online resize, LRU with midpoint insertion resists scan pollution.
codeExamples:
SELECT pool_id, pages_made_young, pages_not_made_young
FROM   information_schema.INNODB_BUFFER_POOL_STATS LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- pool_id | pages_made_young | pages_not_made_young
--       0 |            90210 |              4510222

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: memory is shared with the OS and per-connection buffers, so oversizing causes swapping; cold start after restart is slow without warm-up.
codeExamples:
-- Worst-case memory = pool + connections x per-thread buffers
SELECT ROUND(@@innodb_buffer_pool_size/1073741824,1) AS pool_gb,
       @@max_connections AS conns,
       ROUND((@@sort_buffer_size + @@join_buffer_size + @@read_buffer_size)/1048576,1) AS per_conn_mb;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- pool_gb | conns | per_conn_mb
--    12.0 |   500 |         3.5     (500 x 3.5 MB = 1.7 GB extra at worst)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: it only helps reads/writes of data that fit; a huge scan can evict useful pages; flushing speed depends on disk capacity (innodb_io_capacity), not pool size.

Architect's Notes

Size to the working set, not to total data. Monitor hit ratio and page-read rate rather than a fixed percentage, keep swap off for the database host, and set io_capacity to the real IOPS of the storage so flushing keeps up with writes.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Per-connection buffers (sort_buffer_size, join_buffer_size, read_buffer_size) multiply by connections; keep them modest and raise per session only for heavy reports.
  • Temp tables: tmp_table_size, max_heap_table_size.
  • Estimate worst-case memory: buffer pool + max_connections x per-connection memory + OS.

Senior Notes

  • Use Performance Schema memory instrumentation (sys.memory_global_by_current_bytes) to see actual usage.
  • On containers, set limits and make mysqld aware (cgroups) to avoid OOM kills.
  • Disable swap or set vm.swappiness low on database hosts; use huge pages cautiously.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: very large global sort and join buffers (allocated per operation and connection, causing out-of-memory), buffer pool bigger than free RAM (swapping), and container limits lower than the configured memory (the process is killed). Compare the configured total with the real limit.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@max_connections * (@@sort_buffer_size + @@join_buffer_size) / 1073741824 AS potential_gb_from_buffers;
-- shell: free -m ; cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max

-- OUTPUT:
-- potential_gb_from_buffers
-- 14.6          (if all connections ran a big sort and join at once)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Watch the effects: buffer pool hit rate, pages read from disk, free pages, and swap activity. If the working set is larger than RAM, add memory, reduce the working set (archive, better indexes) or move analytics off the primary.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Innodb_buffer_pool_reads','Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests','Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_free');
-- shell: vmstat 1 3   (si and so columns must stay 0)

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_reads         | 412330
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests | 912330021
-- Innodb_buffer_pool_pages_free    | 1024

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a container with a 32 GB limit ran MySQL with a 28 GB buffer pool and was OOM-killed under load. Setting the pool to 20 GB and bounding connections stabilised it.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Each client connection uses a server thread and memory; the disk subsystem handles page flushes and redo/binlog writes. Tuning these three limits how much concurrency the server sustains.
codeExamples:
SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('max_connections','thread_cache_size','innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Variable_name                  | Value
-- max_connections                | 500
-- thread_cache_size              | 64
-- innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit | 1

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Too many connections cause memory exhaustion and context-switch thrash; too few cause "Too many connections" errors. Disk settings decide the trade-off between durability and commit speed.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN
 ('Threads_connected','Threads_running','Max_used_connections','Connection_errors_max_connections');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Threads_connected | 180
-- Threads_running   | 12
-- Max_used_connections | 410
-- Connection_errors_max_connections | 0

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real servers keep Threads_running small (about 2x CPU cores), use app-side pooling instead of thousands of raw connections, and use NVMe plus innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT.

Diagram

   App pool (20 conns) ─┐
   App pool (20 conns) ─┼─► MySQL: thread per conn ─► InnoDB
   App pool (20 conns) ─┘          │ thread cache          │
                                   ▼                       ▼
                         Threads_running ~ 2 x cores   redo log ─ fsync
                                                        data pages ─ background flush

Fresher Notes

  • MySQL uses one thread per connection. Too many connections waste memory and CPU; slow disks make every query slow.
  • Check connections with SHOW STATUS LIKE "Threads_connected" and limit with max_connections.
  • Use connection pooling in the application.

Worked Example 1

I/O waits.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, count_star, total_latency FROM sys.io_global_by_wait_by_latency LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name              | count_star | total_latency
-- wait/io/file/innodb/redo|   9120344  | 3.1 min

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Set I/O capacity for NVMe.

Practice Exercise 1

Connection health.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Threads_connected','Threads_running','Max_used_connections','Aborted_connects');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Threads_connected    | 118
-- Threads_running      |   6
-- Max_used_connections | 143
-- Aborted_connects     |  12

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Who uses connections.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host, COUNT(*) AS conns FROM information_schema.processlist GROUP BY user, host ORDER BY conns DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- user    | host       | conns
-- shop_app| 10.0.1.12  |    60

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

MySQL (community) uses one operating system thread per client connection. Threads cost memory (stack, buffers) and context switches, so connection count and concurrency are separate: Threads_connected is how many are open, Threads_running how many execute at this instant. Past a point more concurrency reduces throughput because of contention.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Threads_connected','Threads_running','Max_used_connections','Aborted_connects','Connection_errors_max_connections');
SELECT @@max_connections, @@thread_cache_size;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Threads_connected    | 118
-- Threads_running      |   6
-- Max_used_connections | 143
-- @@max_connections | @@thread_cache_size
--               300 |                  64

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: max_connections, thread_cache_size, wait_timeout, innodb_thread_concurrency, innodb_io_capacity, innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT, innodb_read_io_threads/write_io_threads. Use application pools and, when needed, a proxy that multiplexes connections.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: thread cache avoids thread creation cost; configurable durability lets analytics nodes trade safety for speed; read/write I/O threads parallelise disk work.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: relaxed fsync loses committed data on crash; a high max_connections hides pooling problems and lets a traffic spike overload the CPU.
codeExamples:
-- Reserved admin slot: SUPER/CONNECTION_ADMIN users can connect at max_connections + 1
SELECT @@max_connections AS max_c, @@admin_address AS admin_addr;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- max_c | admin_addr
--   500 | NULL

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: storage IOPS is a hard ceiling; doublewrite buffer and binlog add write amplification; each connection still costs roughly several MB.

Architect's Notes

Cap connections with pooling (HikariCP, ProxySQL), keep max_connections modest, and benchmark fsync latency of the storage. Decide durability per tier: strict (1/1) for ledgers, relaxed only for rebuildable data.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Watch Threads_running (active) versus Threads_connected (open).
  • Disk tuning: innodb_io_capacity, innodb_flush_method=O_DIRECT, fast SSD/NVMe, separate redo/binlog volumes if needed.
  • Thread pool is available in enterprise/Percona; community relies on pooling and limits.

Senior Notes

  • Hundreds of running threads at once usually means contention, not capacity; reduce concurrency (pool size) rather than increasing max_connections.
  • Monitor I/O: latency, IOPS, queue depth, fsync times; check sys.io_global_by_wait_by_latency.
  • Right-size pools: connections ≈ cores x 2 + effective spindle count is a common starting heuristic.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: raising max_connections to fix "too many connections" (hides pool leaks and increases contention), pools that are far larger than the database can run in parallel, and idle connections held for hours. Size pools from cores, not user count.
codeExamples:
SELECT 12 AS app_instances, 20 AS pool_size_each, 12 * 20 AS total_possible_connections, @@max_connections AS max_connections;

-- OUTPUT:
-- app_instances | pool_size_each | total_possible_connections | max_connections
--            12 |             20 |                        240 |             300      (little headroom for admin and replicas)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Disk performance sets the ceiling for write-heavy work: fsync latency decides commit latency, random read IOPS decide cache-miss cost. Measure I/O waits and give redo and binlog fast storage.
codeExamples:
SELECT event_name, count_star, total_latency, avg_latency FROM sys.io_global_by_wait_by_latency LIMIT 3;
-- shell: iostat -x 1 3   (watch await and %util)

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- event_name                | count_star | total_latency | avg_latency
-- wait/io/file/innodb/redo  |    9120344 | 3.10 min      | 20.4 us

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a service with 400 concurrent database threads slowed down. Cutting the pool to 40 connections (and queueing the rest in the application) raised throughput by 30% and cut p99 latency in half.

topics.name: SHOW PROCESSLIST & SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS

beginner.content:
Introduction

SHOW PROCESSLIST lists every connection and what it is doing now. SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS prints an InnoDB snapshot: latest deadlock, transactions, semaphores, buffer pool and log state.
codeExamples:
SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Id | User | Host            | db   | Command | Time | State     | Info
-- 37 | app  | 10.0.0.5:51022  | shop | Sleep   |   45 |           | NULL
-- 42 | app  | 10.0.0.6:40110  | shop | Query   |   31 | updating  | UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-5 WHERE id=1
-- 51 | root | localhost       | NULL | Query   |    0 | executing | SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

When the site hangs you need to see right now who is running, who waits, and who holds locks, before you can fix anything.
codeExamples:
-- Same data, but filterable with SQL
SELECT id, user, time, state, LEFT(info,50) AS q
FROM   information_schema.PROCESSLIST
WHERE  command <> 'Sleep' AND time > 5
ORDER  BY time DESC;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | user | time | state    | q
-- 42 | app  |   31 | updating | UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-5 WHERE id=1

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

On-call engineers use it to kill runaway queries and to spot a long idle-in-transaction connection blocking others.
codeExamples:
SELECT trx_id, trx_started, trx_mysql_thread_id AS thread, trx_state
FROM   information_schema.INNODB_TRX
ORDER  BY trx_started LIMIT 2;
KILL QUERY 42;       -- stops the statement, keeps the connection
-- KILL 37;          -- closes the whole connection and rolls back its transaction

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- trx_id | trx_started         | thread | trx_state
-- 90113  | 2026-10-06 09:58:01 |     37 | RUNNING   (idle, holds locks)
-- Query OK

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SHOW PROCESSLIST ──► who / what / how long ──► KILL QUERY id
   INNODB_TRX       ──► open transactions
   data_lock_waits  ──► waiter ──blocked by──► holder
   INNODB STATUS    ──► LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK ──► fix lock order

Fresher Notes

  • SHOW PROCESSLIST lists current connections and what they are running. SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS prints InnoDB internals including locks, deadlocks and buffer pool info.
  • They are first-aid tools when the server feels slow or stuck.
  • Kill a runaway query with KILL QUERY id (or KILL id to drop the connection).

Worked Example 1

Lock waits.
codeExamples:
SELECT waiting_pid, blocking_pid, wait_age FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- waiting_pid | blocking_pid | wait_age
-- 22          | 19           | 00:00:42

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Engine status excerpt.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt)
-- ---TRANSACTION 4521880, ACTIVE 380 sec
-- 2 lock struct(s), heap size 1128, 1 row lock(s)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Spot long-running queries.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, user, db, time, state, LEFT(info, 60) AS query FROM information_schema.processlist WHERE command <> 'Sleep' ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- id | user     | db   | time | state                          | query
-- 31 | shop_app | shop | 412  | Waiting for table metadata lock | ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN x INT
-- 27 | report   | shop | 380  | executing                      | SELECT ... FROM orders ...

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Kill the blocker.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

SHOW PROCESSLIST lists current connections with state, time, and statement. SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS prints InnoDB internals: the latest deadlock, transactions and locks, semaphore waits, buffer pool, log and I/O statistics. They are the first tools when the server feels slow or stuck.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Better alternatives for investigation: sys.processlist, performance_schema.threads, sys.innodb_lock_waits, performance_schema.metadata_locks. End a statement with KILL QUERY id or the connection with KILL id.
codeExamples:
SELECT * FROM sys.innodb_lock_waits\G
SELECT object_name, lock_type, lock_status, owner_thread_id FROM performance_schema.metadata_locks WHERE object_name = 'orders';
KILL QUERY 27;

-- OUTPUT:
-- object_name | lock_type    | lock_status | owner_thread_id
-- orders      | EXCLUSIVE    | PENDING     | 31
-- orders      | SHARED_READ  | GRANTED     | 27

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: instant, no setup, shows live state; INNODB STATUS exposes the exact statements of the last deadlock.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- Look for sections:  LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK, TRANSACTIONS, BUFFER POOL AND MEMORY

-- OUTPUT: (excerpt, example)
-- LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK
-- *** (1) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE acct SET bal=bal-5 WHERE id=1
-- *** (2) TRANSACTION: ... UPDATE acct SET bal=bal+5 WHERE id=2
-- *** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: it is a point-in-time snapshot with no history; the INNODB STATUS output is truncated to about 1 MB and is hard to parse.
codeExamples:
-- Poor man's history: sample it yourself every second
-- shell: while true; do mysql -e "SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST" >> pl.log; sleep 1; done
SELECT COUNT(*) AS active
FROM   information_schema.PROCESSLIST WHERE command <> 'Sleep';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- active
-- 12

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: you need the PROCESS privilege to see other users; Info is truncated to 100 chars without FULL; the deadlock section shows only the latest deadlock.
codeExamples:
-- Log every deadlock, not only the latest
SET GLOBAL innodb_print_all_deadlocks = ON;
-- Prefer Performance Schema (no mutex) for live thread data:
SELECT thread_id, processlist_id, processlist_command
FROM   performance_schema.threads WHERE type = 'FOREIGN' LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- thread_id | processlist_id | processlist_command
--        62 |             37 | Sleep
--        67 |             42 | Query

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Treat these as triage tools, not monitoring. Automate sampling into your metrics system, alert on transactions older than a threshold, and set innodb_lock_wait_timeout plus app-side timeouts so one stuck session cannot take the system down.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST to see the full SQL text; or query performance_schema.threads / sys.processlist for richer data.
  • In INNODB STATUS read sections: LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK, TRANSACTIONS, SEMAPHORES, LOG, BUFFER POOL AND MEMORY.
  • State values like "Waiting for table metadata lock" point to DDL blockers.

Senior Notes

  • Investigate in this order: long-running transactions, lock waits (sys.innodb_lock_waits), metadata locks, then I/O and CPU.
  • Avoid heavy diagnostic queries on an already overloaded server; use Performance Schema views which are lighter.
  • After the incident, capture evidence (processlist snapshot, status) for the postmortem.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: killing the blocked session instead of the blocker, running heavy diagnostic queries on an overloaded server, and reading INNODB STATUS without knowing its sections. Find the blocker first and kill carefully; capture evidence before acting.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

A sequence for a stall: processlist (what states?), long transactions (innodb_trx), lock waits, metadata locks, then resources (CPU, I/O, memory, swap). Most "database is slow" incidents are a long transaction, a metadata lock pile-up or a bad plan after a deploy.
codeExamples:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G
-- TRANSACTIONS
-- ---TRANSACTION 4521880, ACTIVE 380 sec
-- 2 lock struct(s), heap size 1128, 1 row lock(s)
-- SEMAPHORES: OS WAIT ARRAY INFO: reservation count 412330

-- OUTPUT:
-- (read LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK, TRANSACTIONS and SEMAPHORES first)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world incident: all application queries piled up in "Waiting for table metadata lock". The cause was a forgotten open transaction from a reporting tool that blocked an ALTER TABLE, which blocked everything behind it. Killing the idle transaction released the queue.

beginner.content:
Introduction

The connection layer accepts client connections, authenticates them (plugins such as caching_sha2_password), checks privileges, and assigns each connection a thread that lives until disconnect.

Why Do We Need This?

Every query needs an identity and a session context (database, character set, transaction state, SQL mode). The layer isolates users from each other and enforces limits.
codeExamples:
-- Per-account limits enforced at connect/execute time
CREATE USER 'report'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'S3cret!pw'
  WITH MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS 5 MAX_QUERIES_PER_HOUR 20000;
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'report'@'%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Grants for report@%
-- GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO report@% WITH MAX_QUERIES_PER_HOUR 20000 MAX_USER_CONNECTIONS 5

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Production: TLS between app and server, connection pooling in the app, a proxy (ProxySQL/MySQL Router) to multiplex, and wait_timeout to drop abandoned sessions.

Diagram

   Client ──TCP/socket──► [ handshake ► TLS ► authenticate ► privilege check ]
                                        │
                                  assign thread (thread cache)
                                        │
                           session: db, charset, sql_mode, txn state
                                        ▼
                         Parser ─► Optimizer ─► Executor ─► Engine

Fresher Notes

  • The connection layer is the first part of MySQL a client meets: it accepts connections, handles authentication, TLS and manages threads.
  • Each connection gets a thread and a session with its own variables.
  • Clients connect over TCP, Unix socket or named pipe.

Worked Example 1

Check TLS on the current connection.
codeExamples:
SHOW SESSION STATUS LIKE 'Ssl_version';

-- OUTPUT:
-- Variable_name | Value
-- Ssl_version   | TLSv1.3

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Aborted connections.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS LIKE 'Aborted%';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Aborted_clients  | 24
-- Aborted_connects | 12

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Session and timeouts.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@wait_timeout, @@interactive_timeout, @@max_connections, @@require_secure_transport;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- @@wait_timeout | @@interactive_timeout | @@max_connections | @@require_secure_transport
-- 28800          | 28800                 | 151                | 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

See the authentication plugin of users.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host, plugin FROM mysql.user WHERE user IN ('root','shop_app');

-- OUTPUT:
-- user     | host | plugin
-- root     | localhost | caching_sha2_password
-- shop_app | %         | caching_sha2_password

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The connection layer handles everything before SQL is parsed: accepting the TCP, socket or pipe connection, the handshake (protocol version, capabilities, TLS), authentication through the account's plugin, checking host and account limits, then creating (or reusing from the thread cache) a thread and a session. Afterwards it runs a command loop: read a packet, dispatch, send results.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Settings: max_connections, max_connect_errors, wait_timeout, interactive_timeout, net_read_timeout, require_secure_transport, bind_address, skip_name_resolve (avoid DNS lookups), admin_address and admin_port (an extra connection for emergencies).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: thread-per-connection is simple and gives full session isolation; thread cache makes reconnects cheap; pluggable auth (LDAP, PAM, Kerberos in Enterprise).
codeExamples:
-- Session state stays private to the connection
SET @cart_id = 99;                  -- user variable, visible only here
SET SESSION sql_mode = 'STRICT_ALL_TABLES';
SELECT @cart_id AS cart, @@session.sql_mode AS mode;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cart | mode
--   99 | STRICT_ALL_TABLES

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: each connection costs memory and a thread; thousands of connections cause scheduler thrash; the TCP+TLS+auth handshake is expensive per connection.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Connections','Aborted_connects','Threads_connected');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Connections       | 9100233
-- Aborted_connects  | 41
-- Threads_connected | 320

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: max_connections is a hard cap; password-less or old auth plugins limit client driver compatibility; the Thread Pool plugin is only in Enterprise/Percona.
codeExamples:
-- A legacy driver may fail with caching_sha2_password; per-user workaround:
ALTER USER 'legacy'@'%' IDENTIFIED WITH mysql_native_password BY 'S3cret!pw';
SELECT user, plugin FROM mysql.user WHERE user IN ('legacy','report');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- user   | plugin
-- legacy | mysql_native_password
-- report | caching_sha2_password

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep connection counts low and pooled, terminate TLS on the server for compliance, and give every application its own account with limits. Use a proxy when you need failover, read/write split or connection multiplexing.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Steps: network handshake, authentication plugin (caching_sha2_password), authorization checks, session setup, then the command loop.
  • Settings: max_connections, wait_timeout, interactive_timeout, max_allowed_packet, require_secure_transport.
  • Idle connections still consume memory.

Senior Notes

  • The server trusts the connection layer for security: enforce TLS, strong auth, host-based access and rate limiting (max_connect_errors).
  • Connection storms after a restart can overwhelm the server; use pools with backoff.
  • Proxies (ProxySQL, Router) can multiplex connections to reduce server threads.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: DNS resolution slowing every login, connection storms after restarts, host blocking after too many failed attempts (max_connect_errors) that locks out a load balancer, and plain-text connections inside a "trusted" network. Disable name resolution, retry with backoff, require TLS.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Each connection consumes memory and a thread. Use pooling and a thread cache so connection setup is not repeated for each request, and cap total connections across all application instances.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Threads_created','Connections','Threads_cached');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Connections     | 9120344
-- Threads_created |     412        (a good thread cache: only 412 new threads for 9M connections)
-- Threads_cached  |      54

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world hardening: bind to a private interface, enforce TLS with certificate verification, allow only application subnets in firewalls and account hosts, and alert on login failures.
codeExamples:
# my.cnf
[mysqld]
bind_address = 10.0.1.5
require_secure_transport = ON
tls_version = TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3

-- OUTPUT: (after restart)
-- SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'tls_version';  =>  TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3

beginner.content:
Introduction

The parser turns SQL text into a parse tree and checks syntax; the optimizer rewrites it and chooses a cost-based execution plan (index choice, join order, join algorithm).
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'IN' GROUP BY c.name;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Table scan on <temporary>
--     -> Aggregate using temporary table
--         -> Nested loop inner join
--             -> Index lookup on c using idx_country (country='IN')
--             -> Index lookup on o using idx_cust (customer_id=c.id)

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Many plans return the same rows with a thousand-fold difference in cost. SQL says what, not how; the optimizer decides how, using table statistics.

Real-Time Use

When a query regresses after data growth, you look at EXPLAIN, refresh statistics, add hints or histograms, and check the optimizer trace.
codeExamples:
ANALYZE TABLE orders UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON status WITH 16 BUCKETS;
SELECT column_name, JSON_EXTRACT(histogram,'$."number-of-buckets-specified"') AS buckets
FROM   information_schema.COLUMN_STATISTICS WHERE table_name='orders';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Table      | Op        | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.orders| histogram | status   | Histogram statistics created for column 'status'.
-- column_name | buckets
-- status      | 16

beginner.content:
Diagram

   SQL text
     │ lexer/parser           ──► syntax error?  (ERROR 1064)
     ▼
   Parse tree ─► resolve names/privileges ─► rewrite (views, subquery → semijoin)
     ▼
   Cost-based optimizer ◄── statistics, histograms, cost model
     │ chooses: indexes, join order, algorithm (nested loop / hash join)
     ▼
   Execution plan ──► Executor

Fresher Notes

  • The SQL parser checks syntax and turns text into an internal tree. The optimizer then chooses the cheapest way to run the query (indexes, join order).
  • Parsing errors give messages like "You have an error in your SQL syntax".
  • The optimizer is cost-based: it uses statistics to estimate costs.

Worked Example 1

Optimizer trace.

Worked Example 2

Plan hint with index hint.

Practice Exercise 1

Syntax error from the parser.

Practice Exercise 2

Optimizer hint.
codeExamples:
SELECT /*+ JOIN_ORDER(d, e) */ e.name FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept WHERE d.name = 'HR';

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Abaji
-- Raoji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The parser tokenizes and parses SQL into a parse tree, resolves names and checks privileges. The optimizer then transforms the tree (constant folding, subquery to semijoin, merging derived tables, outer-to-inner join conversion), estimates the cost of access paths and join orders using statistics, and produces an execution plan that the executor runs.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

You influence the optimizer with statistics (ANALYZE TABLE, histograms), indexes, optimizer_switch flags, optimizer hints (/*+ JOIN_ORDER() INDEX() NO_INDEX() SET_VAR() */), and old-style index hints (USE/FORCE/IGNORE INDEX). Prefer fixing statistics and indexes over hints.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: declarative SQL, automatic plan choice adapts to data growth, optimizer hints and invisible indexes allow controlled experiments.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: estimates can be wrong (skew, correlated columns), plans can flip after statistics update, and cost constants are generic.
codeExamples:
-- Plan instability: same query, different plan after sampling changes
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_stats_persistent%';
