Online schema change with gh-ost.
codeExamples:
gh-ost --host=db --user=ghost --password=*** --database=shop --table=orders --alter="ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(100)" --max-lag-millis=1500 --execute

-- OUTPUT: (progress)
-- Copy: 8200000/8200000 100.0%; ... Done

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Backfill in batches.
codeExamples:
UPDATE orders SET new_status = status WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND new_status IS NULL;
-- loop by id ranges, sleep between batches

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 10000 rows affected

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Flyway migration files.

Practice Exercise 2

History table.
codeExamples:
SELECT version, description, success FROM flyway_schema_history ORDER BY installed_rank;

-- OUTPUT:
-- version | description    | success
-- 1       | create orders  | 1
-- 2       | add status     | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A migration tool keeps a history table (flyway_schema_history, databasechangelog, django_migrations) listing applied migrations with version and checksum. At startup or in the pipeline it applies pending migrations in order, once, and refuses to proceed if an applied script was modified.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Practices: one logical change per migration (MySQL DDL is not transactional), repeatable migrations for views and routines, separate data migrations from schema changes, run migrations from a dedicated account in the pipeline, and test them on a copy of production-sized data.
codeExamples:
-- R__views.sql (repeatable: re-applied when its checksum changes)
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW report_orders AS SELECT id, customer_id, total FROM orders;
-- run in CI against a real MySQL container
flyway -url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shop -user=migrate -password=*** migrate

-- OUTPUT:
-- Successfully applied 2 migrations to schema shop (execution time 00:00.081s)

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: reproducible environments, code-review of schema, audit trail, rollbacks via down scripts, automated in pipelines.
codeExamples:
-- Checksums detect tampering with already-applied scripts
SELECT version, checksum FROM flyway_schema_history WHERE version = '1';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- version | checksum
-- 1       | 1872340091
-- (editing V1 later => "Validate failed: checksum mismatch")

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: large ALTERs can lock or slow production, DDL in MySQL is not transactional (a failed script can leave half-applied changes), and down scripts are rarely tested.
codeExamples:
-- MySQL DDL auto-commits: if statement 2 fails, statement 1 stays applied
CREATE TABLE a (id INT);          -- committed immediately
CREATE TABLE a (id INT);          -- ERROR 1050: Table 'a' already exists
-- Keep each migration to ONE logical DDL statement, so failure is easy to repair.

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1050 (42S01): Table 'a' already exists

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: some changes (column type change, adding a primary key) rebuild the table with a copy algorithm and block writes; online tools like gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change are needed for very large tables.

Architect's Notes

Make every migration backward compatible with the previous app version so rollbacks and rolling deploys work. Gate big-table changes with ALGORITHM/LOCK clauses so they fail fast instead of blocking, and rehearse on a production-sized copy.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Never edit a migration that has already been applied elsewhere; add a new one.
  • MySQL DDL is not transactional: a failed multi-statement migration can leave partial changes; keep one logical change per migration.
  • Run migrations in CI against a real MySQL (Testcontainers).

Senior Notes

  • Use expand/contract for zero-downtime: add new column (nullable), deploy code writing both, backfill in batches, switch reads, drop old later.
  • For big tables use online DDL (ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE) or gh-ost/pt-online-schema-change; throttle on replica lag.
  • Make each release compatible with the previous schema to allow rollbacks.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: editing an applied migration (checksum failure), a blocking ALTER on a big table at peak, dropping a column that the previous application version still reads, and no rollback plan. Use backward-compatible steps and online DDL.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large tables need online schema change. Use gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change with throttling on replica lag, and track progress; backfill data in batches outside the DDL.
codeExamples:
gh-ost --host=db --user=ghost --password=*** --database=shop --table=orders --alter="ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(100)" --max-lag-millis=1500 --chunk-size=1000 --execute

-- OUTPUT: (progress)
-- Copy: 8200000/8200000 100.0%; Applied: 0; Backlog: 0/1000; Time: 12m3s; ETA: due

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world expand/contract rename: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, then drop the old column in a later release, keeping every release compatible with the previous schema so rollbacks are safe.

beginner.content:
Introduction

JPA is the Java specification for object-relational mapping, Hibernate is its main implementation, and Spring Data JPA generates repositories from interfaces so you rarely write boilerplate.

Why Do We Need This?

Mapping rows to objects by hand is repetitive and error-prone. JPA gives dirty checking (changes saved automatically), caching, relations and portability.

Real-Time Use

Typical: CRUD services, paging with Pageable, optimistic locking with @Version, and custom JPQL or native queries for reports.

Diagram

   Service ─► Repository (Spring Data) ─► EntityManager / Hibernate
                                              │ persistence context (L1 cache, dirty check)
                                              ▼
                              SQL generation ─► HikariCP ─► JDBC ─► MySQL

Fresher Notes

  • JPA is the Java standard for ORM, Hibernate is the most common implementation and Spring Data JPA adds repository interfaces on top.
  • Entities map classes to tables with annotations like @Entity, @Id, @ManyToOne.
  • You work with objects; the framework generates SQL.

Worked Example 1

Show SQL and parameters.
codeExamples:
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE

-- OUTPUT:
-- select p1_0.id,p1_0.name from products p1_0 where p1_0.id=?
-- binding parameter (1:BIGINT) <- [7]

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Bulk update bypassing the persistence context.

Practice Exercise 1

Entity and generated SQL.

Practice Exercise 2

Dirty checking.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

JPA is a specification; Hibernate implements it; Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations on top. Hibernate keeps a persistence context per transaction: entities loaded or saved are tracked (managed), changes are detected by comparing snapshots (dirty checking) and flushed as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements at flush or commit.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls: entity states (transient, managed, detached, removed), flush modes, @Version for optimistic locking, @DynamicUpdate (only changed columns), cascade types, @Modifying bulk updates, native queries, second-level cache, ID generators (IDENTITY disables insert batching).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: productivity, schema generation, caching levels (L1 session, L2 optional), vendor-neutral JPQL, rich relationship mapping.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: learning curve, hidden SQL, N+1 and lazy exceptions, memory overhead of the persistence context on big batches, GenerationType.IDENTITY disables JDBC insert batching.

Limitations

Limitations: complex reports and window functions are awkward in JPQL, hbm2ddl auto is unsafe for production, and entity state is tied to a session lifetime.
codeExamples:
# application.properties - production-safe defaults
# spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate        (never update/create in prod; use Flyway)
# spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
# spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
# spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
SELECT @@version AS mysql_ver;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- mysql_ver
-- 8.0.36

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Use JPA for transactional CRUD and jOOQ/JdbcTemplate/native SQL for reporting and bulk operations. Keep associations lazy, use DTO projections for reads, validate (not generate) schema, and log SQL in lower environments to catch N+1 early.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Understand the persistence context (first-level cache), dirty checking (changes auto-flushed at commit), flush modes and entity states (new, managed, detached).
  • Show SQL with spring.jpa.show-sql=true or org.hibernate.SQL logging and bind parameters trace.
  • IDENTITY ids disable JDBC insert batching; use sequences/table generators or tune accordingly.

Senior Notes

  • Check the generated SQL for every query path; add indexes to match it.
  • Tune: hibernate.jdbc.batch_size, order_inserts/updates, default_batch_fetch_size, second-level cache only with care.
  • Use native queries or jOOQ/JdbcTemplate for complex reporting.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: relying on lazy loading in the web layer, N+1 queries, merging detached entities blindly, IDENTITY ids with large batches, huge persistence contexts in batch jobs (memory), and bulk updates that bypass the persistence context leaving stale entities. Flush and clear in batches, and refresh after bulk updates.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Always read the generated SQL and check indexes. Enable statistics to see statement counts, and use EXPLAIN on slow ones. Batch settings and fetch strategies decide most of the performance.
codeExamples:
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=500
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true

-- OUTPUT: (statistics)
-- 10000 entities inserted in 20 JDBC batches

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: use JPA for transactional writes and simple reads, and drop to SQL (jOOQ, JdbcTemplate, native queries) for reports and bulk operations, keeping each tool where it is strongest.

beginner.content:
Introduction

SQLAlchemy (Core + ORM, explicit sessions, Alembic migrations) and the Django ORM (active-record style, built-in migrations) both map Python classes to MySQL tables and build SQL from Python expressions.
codeExamples:
# SQLAlchemy 2.0
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, String, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id:   Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50))

engine = create_engine("mysql+pymysql://app:secret@127.0.0.1/shop")
with Session(engine) as s:
    print(s.scalars(select(User).where(User.name == "Abaji")).all())

# OUTPUT: (example)
# [<User id=1 name='Abaji'>]

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Hand-built SQL strings are unsafe and untestable. The ORM composes queries, parameterises them and returns objects.
codeExamples:
# Django ORM equivalent
class User(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=50)

User.objects.filter(name__startswith="A").order_by("-id")[:5]
print(User.objects.filter(name="Abaji").query)

# OUTPUT:
# SELECT shop_user.id, shop_user.name FROM shop_user WHERE shop_user.name = Abaji

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Real code uses sessions or transactions per request, joined loading to avoid N+1, and raw SQL for complex reports.
codeExamples:
# SQLAlchemy: eager load with a JOIN
from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload
stmt = select(Order).options(selectinload(Order.items)).where(Order.status == "NEW")
# Django:
# Order.objects.filter(status="NEW").prefetch_related("items")

# OUTPUT:
# SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE status = 'NEW'
# SELECT ... FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (1, 2, 3)      (2 queries, no N+1)

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Python objects ─► ORM (Session / QuerySet) ─► SQL builder ─► DBAPI driver ─► MySQL
        ▲                      │ identity map / lazy queryset
        └──── rows ◄───────────┘
   Alembic / Django migrations manage schema

Fresher Notes

  • SQLAlchemy (Core and ORM) and Django ORM are the main Python ORMs. Both map tables to Python classes and build SQL from Python code.
  • Django ORM comes with Django and migrations; SQLAlchemy is a flexible toolkit used with Alembic migrations.
  • Both can show the SQL they generate.

Worked Example 1

Atomic update with F.
codeExamples:
Account.objects.filter(id=1).update(balance=F("balance") - 100)

-- OUTPUT:
-- UPDATE accounts SET balance = (balance - 100) WHERE id = 1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Stream large result.
codeExamples:
for row in Event.objects.filter(kind="click").iterator(chunk_size=2000):
    process(row)

-- OUTPUT:
-- constant memory; rows fetched in chunks of 2000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Django queryset to SQL.
codeExamples:
qs = Order.objects.select_related("customer").filter(status="NEW").order_by("-created_at")[:20]
print(qs.query)

-- OUTPUT:
-- SELECT ... FROM orders INNER JOIN customers ON ... WHERE status = 'NEW' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

SQLAlchemy select.
codeExamples:
stmt = select(Order).options(selectinload(Order.items)).where(Order.status == "NEW").limit(20)
orders = session.scalars(stmt).all()

-- OUTPUT: (SQL, 2 statements)
-- SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE status = %s LIMIT %s
-- SELECT ... FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (%s, %s, ...)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Django ORM is built in and opinionated: models define tables, QuerySets are lazy and chainable, and the compiler produces SQL when evaluated. SQLAlchemy has two layers: Core (SQL expression language) and ORM (unit of work with a Session identity map). Both generate parameterized SQL and manage connections through pools.
codeExamples:
qs = Order.objects.select_related("customer").filter(status="NEW").order_by("-created_at")[:20]
print(qs.query)

stmt = select(Order).options(selectinload(Order.items)).where(Order.status == "NEW").limit(20)
orders = session.scalars(stmt).all()

-- OUTPUT: (SQL)
-- SELECT ... FROM orders INNER JOIN customers ON ... WHERE status = 'NEW' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20
-- SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE status = %s LIMIT %s ;  SELECT ... FROM order_items WHERE order_id IN (%s, %s, ...)

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Toolbox: Django F(), Q(), annotate/aggregate, Subquery/Exists, bulk_*, transaction.atomic, select_for_update; SQLAlchemy loader options (selectinload, joinedload), session.execute(text(...)), yield_per, Alembic migrations.
codeExamples:
from django.db.models import F, Q, Sum
Account.objects.filter(id=1).update(balance=F("balance") - 100)
Order.objects.filter(Q(status="NEW") | Q(total__gt=1000)).aggregate(total=Sum("total"))
for row in session.execute(select(Event).where(Event.kind == "click").execution_options(yield_per=2000)):
    process(row)

-- OUTPUT: (SQL)
-- UPDATE accounts SET balance = (balance - 100) WHERE id = 1

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: safe parameter binding, migrations, composable queries, database portability, SQLAlchemy Core gives near-raw control.
codeExamples:
from sqlalchemy import func
stmt = select(Order.customer_id, func.sum(Order.total)).group_by(Order.customer_id).having(func.sum(Order.total) > 100)
print(stmt)

# OUTPUT:
# SELECT orders.customer_id, sum(orders.total) AS sum_1 FROM orders GROUP BY orders.customer_id HAVING sum(orders.total) > :sum_2

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: generated SQL can be suboptimal, Django ORM is limited for complex joins/window functions, SQLAlchemy sessions require understanding of flush and expire.
codeExamples:
# Updating many rows one by one is slow
for u in User.objects.all():
    u.active = False; u.save()           # N UPDATE statements
# Better: set-based
User.objects.update(active=False)        # 1 statement

# OUTPUT:
# UPDATE shop_user SET active = 0

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL-specific features (index hints, generated columns, partitions, JSON functions) need raw SQL or dialect extras; async support depends on aiomysql/asyncmy and is newer.
codeExamples:
from sqlalchemy import text
with engine.begin() as c:
    rows = c.execute(text("SELECT id, name FROM users USE INDEX (PRIMARY) WHERE id > :i"), {"i": 0}).all()
    print(rows)

# OUTPUT: (example)
# [(1, 'Abaji'), (2, 'Raoji')]

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Choose SQLAlchemy for complex domain models and explicit unit of work; Django ORM for rapid CRUD inside Django. In both, count queries in tests, prefer bulk operations, and keep a documented escape hatch to raw SQL.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Django: Model.objects.filter(...), select_related, prefetch_related, F() and Q() expressions, bulk_create.
  • SQLAlchemy: sessions and units of work, select() constructs, selectinload/joinedload.
  • Use transactions explicitly (atomic() / session commit).

Senior Notes

  • Inspect SQL with queryset.query or echo=True; compare with EXPLAIN.
  • Avoid loading entire tables into memory; use iterator/yield_per and chunking.
  • Use raw SQL or SQLAlchemy Core for complex analytics and bulk operations.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: loading whole tables into memory, read-modify-write in Python (lost updates), N+1 in templates or serializers, and relying on lazy relations after the session closes (DetachedInstanceError). Use atomic expressions, prefetching and chunked iteration.
codeExamples:
for e in Event.objects.filter(kind="click").iterator(chunk_size=2000):
    process(e)
with self.assertNumQueries(2):
    list(Order.objects.prefetch_related("items"))

-- OUTPUT:
-- (flat memory; the test fails with the executed SQL when the query count changes)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Check the SQL with queryset.explain() or SQLAlchemy echo, then EXPLAIN it. Remember connection pooling: Django uses CONN_MAX_AGE; SQLAlchemy has a built-in pool (pool_size, max_overflow, pool_recycle).
codeExamples:
print(Order.objects.filter(customer_id=7).explain())
engine = create_engine("mysql+pymysql://shop_app:***@db/shop?charset=utf8mb4", pool_size=10, max_overflow=5, pool_recycle=1500, pool_pre_ping=True)

-- OUTPUT:
-- -> Index lookup on orders using idx_customer (customer_id=7)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a service uses the ORM for CRUD and a few raw, reviewed SQL statements for analytics, wrapped in repository functions with tests that check query counts.
codeExamples:
rows = session.execute(text("SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent FROM orders WHERE created_at >= :since GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY spent DESC LIMIT 10"), {"since": since}).all()

-- OUTPUT:
-- [(7, Decimal('48200.00')), (3, Decimal('39000.00'))]

beginner.content:
Introduction

Prisma, Sequelize and TypeORM are Node.js ORMs for MySQL. Prisma uses a schema file and generates a typed client; Sequelize and TypeORM use JS/TS model classes.

Why Do We Need This?

In a Node codebase raw query strings are loosely typed. These tools give typed results, relations and migrations so refactors are checked at compile time.

Real-Time Use

Used in NestJS APIs and serverless backends. Transactions and migrations are part of normal workflow.

Diagram

   schema / models ─► codegen ─► typed client ─► query engine ─► mysql2 pool ─► MySQL
        │
        └──► migrate dev / deploy ──► SQL migration files

Fresher Notes

  • Prisma, Sequelize and TypeORM are popular Node.js ORMs. They map tables to JavaScript/TypeScript models and generate SQL.
  • Prisma uses a schema file and generates a typed client; Sequelize and TypeORM use model classes/decorators.
  • All support migrations.

Worked Example 1

Enable query logs.

Worked Example 2

Raw query for a report.

Practice Exercise 1

Prisma schema and query.

Practice Exercise 2

Sequelize.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Node ORMs map models to tables and build SQL through a query API. Prisma has a schema file and generates a typed client with its own query engine; Sequelize and TypeORM use JavaScript/TypeScript classes (decorators in TypeORM). All of them use a connection pool and send parameterized statements.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Features: relations and includes (joins or batched queries), transactions (prisma.$transaction, Sequelize sequelize.transaction, TypeORM QueryRunner), raw SQL escape hatches, migrations (prisma migrate, sequelize-cli, TypeORM migrations), and logging.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: TypeScript types, auto-generated clients, readable relations, built-in migrations, safe parameter binding.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: large generated client (Prisma), lazy-relation pitfalls (TypeORM), Sequelize typing is weaker; deep includes can generate heavy queries or multiple round trips.

Limitations

Limitations: no full MySQL feature coverage (generated columns, fulltext, window functions often need raw queries); Prisma migrations are forward-only SQL files; connection pool is per process, which matters in serverless.

Architect's Notes

Prefer Prisma or TypeORM when type-safety matters, and keep raw SQL for reporting. In serverless, place a connection proxy in front of MySQL, limit per-instance pool size to 1-2, and review the generated SQL for heavy includes.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Prisma: prisma.order.findMany({ include: { items: true } }) and prisma migrate.
  • Sequelize: Order.findAll({ include: Item }); TypeORM: repositories and QueryBuilder.
  • Enable query logging to see SQL.

Senior Notes

  • Check for N+1 and over-fetching: use select/include carefully, and raw queries for hot paths.
  • Connection pooling: configure pool size per instance and use a proxy in serverless setups.
  • Run migrations in CI/CD with locking so two instances do not migrate at once.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: over-fetching with nested includes, N+1 through per-item queries in loops, forgetting indexes behind relation filters, running migrations automatically in every instance at startup, and unsafe raw queries built from strings. Select needed fields, batch, and run migrations as a separate job.
codeExamples:
const names = await prisma.user.findMany({ select: { id: true, name: true } });                 // not the whole row
const ids = orders.map(o => o.customerId);
const customers = await prisma.customer.findMany({ where: { id: { in: ids } } });                  // one batched query

-- OUTPUT: (SQL)
-- SELECT id, name FROM users
-- SELECT ... FROM customers WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3, ...)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Pool and engine settings matter in serverless runtimes: many short-lived instances can exhaust max_connections. Use a connection proxy, cap the pool (connection_limit in the URL) and reuse the client across invocations.
codeExamples:
DATABASE_URL="mysql://shop_app:***@proxy:3306/shop?connection_limit=5&pool_timeout=10"

-- OUTPUT:
-- each instance holds at most 5 connections; the proxy multiplexes them to the database

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a Prisma service logs queries in staging, a CI test counts queries per endpoint, and slow ones are explained against a production-sized copy.

topics.name: Inspecting the SQL an ORM Generates

beginner.content:
Introduction

ORMs hide SQL, so you must see it: turn on the ORM's SQL logging, use the MySQL general or slow log, or read Performance Schema digests, then EXPLAIN the statements.
codeExamples:
# Application side: print every SQL (Spring Boot)
# spring.jpa.show-sql=true
# logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG
# logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE      (shows bound values)
# SQLAlchemy:  create_engine(url, echo=True)

# OUTPUT: (example)
# select u1_0.id, u1_0.name from users u1_0 where u1_0.id=?

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

What the ORM runs, not what you meant, decides performance. Only the SQL reveals N+1, missing indexes, SELECT * and unexpected full scans.

Real-Time Use

During development use query counters; in production use digests (no per-statement overhead) and trace IDs in comments to tie SQL back to code.
codeExamples:
SELECT DIGEST_TEXT, COUNT_STAR, ROUND(AVG_TIMER_WAIT/1e9,2) AS avg_ms
FROM   performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
WHERE  SCHEMA_NAME = 'shop'
ORDER  BY SUM_TIMER_WAIT DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- DIGEST_TEXT                              | COUNT_STAR | avg_ms
-- SELECT ... FROM order_items WHERE ...    |    2400000 | 0.41
-- SELECT ... FROM orders WHERE ...         |      15000 | 7.90

beginner.content:
Diagram

   code ─► ORM ─► SQL text ─► driver ─► MySQL ─► plan ─► rows
                     │ log (show-sql / echo)        │ slow log, digests
                     ▼                              ▼
              count + read it                  EXPLAIN ANALYZE ─► add index / fix mapping

Fresher Notes

  • ORMs hide SQL, but you must still read it. Turn on SQL logging, then run EXPLAIN on the statements to see index use.
  • Look for N+1 patterns, SELECT * of wide tables, unexpected joins and missing WHERE limits.
  • The database does not care which ORM wrote the SQL; the plan matters.

Worked Example 1

Tag queries by route (comment).

Worked Example 2

General log for a few seconds in dev.

Practice Exercise 1

Log SQL in Spring Boot.
codeExamples:
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE

-- OUTPUT:
-- select o1_0.id, o1_0.total from orders o1_0 where o1_0.customer_id=?

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

EXPLAIN the logged statement.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Every ORM call becomes SQL text plus bound parameters. The way to understand cost is to capture that SQL (ORM logging, the MySQL general log in development, Performance Schema digests in production) and run EXPLAIN on it. The database does not care which framework produced a statement; only the plan matters.
codeExamples:
spring.jpa.show-sql=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.format_sql=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE

-- OUTPUT:
-- select o1_0.id, o1_0.total from orders o1_0 where o1_0.customer_id=?
-- binding parameter (1:BIGINT) <- [7]

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Capture points: framework logs (Hibernate, Django django.db.backends, SQLAlchemy echo, Prisma log), the driver (logger=Slf4JLogger in Connector/J), MySQL slow log and digests, APM traces. Add SQL comments with request or route names to link statements to code.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: reveals real behaviour, works for any ORM, and lets you EXPLAIN the exact statement.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT u1_0.id, u1_0.name FROM users u1_0 WHERE u1_0.email = 'a@b.com';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Filter: (u1_0.email = 'a@b.com')  (actual time=21..21 rows=1)
--     -> Table scan on u1_0  (actual time=0.1..19 rows=100000)     <- missing index on email

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the general log is very heavy and logs sensitive data; show-sql output lacks bound values and timing; prepared statements show ? placeholders.
codeExamples:
-- Statements with ? placeholders: find real values via Performance Schema history
SELECT SQL_TEXT FROM performance_schema.events_statements_history
WHERE  SQL_TEXT LIKE 'select u1_0%' LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- SQL_TEXT
-- select u1_0.id,u1_0.name from users u1_0 where u1_0.email=?

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: EXPLAIN on a placeholder query needs literal values, plans depend on data volume (dev with 10 rows hides problems), and not every ORM exposes timings.
codeExamples:
# Query-count test helper (Django) and slow-query alert (SQLAlchemy)
from sqlalchemy import event
@event.listens_for(engine, "before_cursor_execute")
def log_sql(conn, cursor, statement, params, context, executemany):
    print("SQL:", statement[:60], params)

# OUTPUT: (example)
# SQL: SELECT users.id, users.name FROM users WHERE users.email = %s ('a@b.com',)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Make SQL visibility a standard: SQL logging in dev, query-count assertions in tests, digest dashboards in production, and request IDs injected as SQL comments. Test with production-like data volume or plans will mislead you.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Where to look: ORM logs, MySQL general log (briefly, dev only), slow query log, Performance Schema digests, APM traces.
  • Compare the number of queries per request and rows examined.
  • Parameter binding shows values; digests normalise them.

Senior Notes

  • Build a habit: any new endpoint gets its SQL reviewed with production-like data.
  • Add query-count and latency assertions to integration tests.
  • Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the exact statement with realistic parameters, not a handwritten approximation.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: logging SQL only in development, reviewing statements without parameters, the general log on production (heavy), and fixing symptoms in the ORM layer when an index is missing. Review generated SQL as part of code review for new endpoints.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT o.id, o.total FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = 7 AND o.status = 'NEW' ORDER BY o.created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Sort: o.created_at DESC (actual time=92..92 rows=20)  -> Index lookup on o using idx_customer (rows=14000)
-- => needs idx (customer_id, status, created_at)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Quantify per endpoint: statements per request, rows examined, total database time. A test harness can assert budgets so regressions fail the build.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(digest_text, 60) AS q, count_star, ROUND(sum_rows_examined / count_star) AS rows_examined_avg FROM performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest WHERE schema_name = 'shop' ORDER BY sum_timer_wait DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- q                                          | count_star | rows_examined_avg
-- select o1_0 . id , o1_0 . total from orders| 912000     |             18400

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: tracing a slow API call from the APM span to the SQL statement, to its EXPLAIN, to the missing index, to the migration that fixed it.

beginner.content:
Introduction

An e-commerce schema separates who buys (customers), what is sold (products), and what happened (orders and order_items). Orders are one-to-many with order_items; order_items is the bridge between orders and products.
codeExamples:
-- Core e-commerce tables (MySQL 8, InnoDB, utf8mb4)
CREATE TABLE customers (
    id         BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    email      VARCHAR(190)    NOT NULL,
    name       VARCHAR(100)    NOT NULL,
    created_at DATETIME        NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    UNIQUE KEY uq_customers_email (email)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE products (
    id    BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name  VARCHAR(150)  NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),   -- money is DECIMAL, never FLOAT
    stock INT           NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE orders (
    id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    status      ENUM('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW',
    created_at  DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    KEY ix_orders_customer (customer_id, created_at),
    CONSTRAINT fk_orders_customer FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE order_items (
    order_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    product_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    qty        INT NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
    unit_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,                 -- price snapshot at purchase time
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_oi_order   FOREIGN KEY (order_id)   REFERENCES orders(id),
    CONSTRAINT fk_oi_product FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

SHOW TABLES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | Tables_in_shop |
-- +----------------+
-- | customers      |
-- | order_items    |
-- | orders         |
-- | products       |
-- +----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Why not store the product price only in products? Prices change. An order must remember what the customer actually paid, so order_items copies the price at purchase time. Reading the live price would rewrite history.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE products    (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50), price DECIMAL(10,2));
CREATE TABLE order_items (order_id INT, product_id INT, qty INT, unit_price DECIMAL(10,2));
INSERT INTO products    VALUES (1, 'Keyboard', 50.00);
INSERT INTO order_items VALUES (1, 1, 2, 50.00);        -- bought 2 at 50.00

UPDATE products SET price = 60.00 WHERE id = 1;         -- price rise next week

SELECT oi.qty * oi.unit_price AS paid_snapshot,
       oi.qty * p.price       AS wrong_live_price
FROM   order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+------------------+
-- | paid_snapshot | wrong_live_price |
-- +---------------+------------------+
-- |        100.00 |           120.00 |
-- +---------------+------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical business questions: revenue per customer, best sellers, orders to ship. Cancelled orders must not count as revenue.

Diagram

   customers 1 ───< orders 1 ───< order_items >─── 1 products
   +--------+      +----------+   +-------------+    +----------+
   | id  PK |      | id    PK |   | order_id PK |    | id    PK |
   | email  |      | cust  FK |   | product_id  |    | name     |
   +--------+      | status   |   |   (PK, FK)  |    | price    |
                   +----------+   | qty         |    | stock    |
                                  | unit_price  | <- price snapshot
                                  +-------------+

Fresher Notes

  • An e-commerce database stores users, products, categories, carts, orders, order items, payments and addresses.
  • Core relationships: user has many orders; order has many order_items; product belongs to a category.
  • Order items snapshot the price at purchase time.

Worked Example 1

Order history query served by the index.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | status | total
--  9 | NEW    | 20.00

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Best sellers last 30 days.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS sold FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 30 DAY GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY sold DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | sold
-- Pen  | 420

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Core schema.

Practice Exercise 2

Place an order safely.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An e-commerce database has customers, a catalog (categories, products, variants), inventory, carts, orders with order items, payments, shipments and addresses. The central rule: an order records what happened at the time (prices, addresses, tax) and must not change when the catalog changes, so order items snapshot values.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Design options: variants as a separate table with its own SKU and stock, categories as an adjacency list or closure table, prices in a price-history table, addresses as snapshots on the order, payments as an append-only ledger with idempotency keys, inventory with reservations that expire.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: foreign keys, CHECK constraints and the composite primary key make bad data impossible at the database level, not just in application code.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: normalised data needs joins to rebuild an order, and concurrent buyers can oversell stock if the check and the update are separate steps.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, stock INT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO products VALUES (1, 3);

-- WRONG: SELECT stock, check in app, then UPDATE  => two buyers both see 3
-- RIGHT: one atomic conditional update
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 5 WHERE id = 1 AND stock >= 5;
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS rows_changed;                     -- 0 means: not enough stock

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | rows_changed |
-- +--------------+
-- |            0 |
-- +--------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a fixed-column products table cannot hold attributes that differ per product (color, RAM, size). Use a JSON column for the flexible part and keep the searchable core in real columns.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE products (
    id    INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name  VARCHAR(50),
    attrs JSON                                          -- flexible per-category attributes
);
INSERT INTO products VALUES
  (1, 'Laptop', '{"ram_gb": 16, "color": "grey"}'),
  (2, 'Shirt',  '{"size": "M",  "color": "red"}');

SELECT name, attrs->>'$.color' AS color
FROM   products
WHERE  attrs->>'$.color' = 'red';

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+-------+
-- | name  | color |
-- +-------+-------+
-- | Shirt | red   |
-- +-------+-------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep money as DECIMAL, snapshot prices, and make stock changes atomic with conditional UPDATEs. Expect the catalogue to need search (Elasticsearch) and the orders table to need archiving or partitioning by date at scale; model addresses and payments as separate tables so PII can be isolated and encrypted.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Tables: users, addresses, categories, products, product_variants, carts/cart_items, orders, order_items, payments, shipments, inventory.
  • Indexes: orders (user_id, created_at), order_items (order_id), products (category_id, status), inventory (sku).
  • Money as DECIMAL, status columns with CHECK or lookup tables, created/updated timestamps.

Senior Notes

  • Inventory needs concurrency control: conditional UPDATE (qty = qty - ? WHERE qty >= ?) or reservations with expiry.
  • Payments: idempotency keys and immutable ledger-style rows; never update amounts in place.
  • Scale reads with caching/search for the catalog; keep orders in OLTP with partitioning/archival for history.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: reading the current product price for old orders, decrementing stock with read-then-write (overselling), storing money in floats, no idempotency on payments (double charges on retry), and one wide orders table that mixes unrelated concerns. Use snapshots, conditional updates and unique keys.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hot paths: product listing (category plus active plus price), order history (user plus time), inventory updates (single row), best-sellers (aggregation). Index for each, cache the catalog, and keep the orders path lean. Partition or archive old orders by date.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world reports: best sellers last 30 days and revenue by day, from the order items snapshot (not the current prices).
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS sold, SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) AS revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
WHERE o.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 30 DAY AND o.status = 'PAID' GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY sold DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | sold | revenue
-- Pen  |  420 | 4200.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A banking schema is built on correctness: accounts hold the balance, and an append-only ledger records every movement. A transfer is two ledger rows (debit and credit) inside one transaction.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    id      BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    owner   VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL,
    balance DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0)         -- no overdraft
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE ledger (
    id         BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2)   NOT NULL,                -- signed: debit negative, credit positive
    ref        VARCHAR(40)     NOT NULL,                -- transfer id shared by both rows
    created_at DATETIME(3)     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(3),
    KEY ix_ledger_account (account_id, created_at),
    CONSTRAINT fk_ledger_acc FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES accounts(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

DESCRIBE accounts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
-- | Field   | Type          | Null | Key | Default | Extra          |
-- +---------+---------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+
-- | id      | bigint unsigned | NO | PRI | NULL    | auto_increment |
-- | owner   | varchar(100)  | NO   |     | NULL    |                |
-- | balance | decimal(15,2) | NO   |     | 0.00    |                |
-- +---------+---------------+------+-----+---------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A single balance column tells you what but not why. Auditors need history: the ledger can always reproduce the balance, and a mismatch reveals bugs or fraud.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE ledger (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, account_id INT, amount DECIMAL(15,2), ref VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, amount, ref) VALUES
  (1,  1000.00, 'deposit'),
  (1,  -250.00, 'T-1'),     -- transfer out
  (2,   250.00, 'T-1');     -- transfer in

SELECT account_id, SUM(amount) AS balance_from_ledger
FROM   ledger
GROUP  BY account_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+---------------------+
-- | account_id | balance_from_ledger |
-- +------------+---------------------+
-- |          1 |              750.00 |
-- |          2 |              250.00 |
-- +------------+---------------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The transfer procedure: lock both accounts, move money, write both ledger rows, commit. Any failure rolls everything back.

Diagram

   Transfer T-1 (one transaction)
   +----------+  -250   +--------------------+  +250   +----------+
   | acct 1   | ------> | ledger  (append)   | <------ | acct 2   |
   | balance  |         | T-1 debit  -250    |         | balance  |
   +----------+         | T-1 credit +250    |         +----------+
        ^               +--------------------+              ^
        +------- SUM(ledger) must equal balance -------------+

Fresher Notes

  • A banking database stores customers, accounts, transactions and beneficiaries. Accuracy and auditability matter most.
  • Money uses DECIMAL, never floating point.
  • A transfer is one transaction touching two accounts.

Worked Example 1

Books balance.

Worked Example 2

Statement query.
codeExamples:
SELECT created_at, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, id) AS running_balance FROM ledger WHERE account_id = 1 ORDER BY created_at, id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- created_at          | amount | running_balance
-- 2026-05-01 10:00:00 |  1000  | 1000
-- 2026-05-01 11:30:00 |  -500  |  500

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Accounts and ledger.

Practice Exercise 2

Transfer.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A banking schema is built for correctness and audit: customers, accounts, an immutable ledger of postings, transfers, and beneficiaries. Money uses DECIMAL; a balance is either derived from the ledger or stored and updated in the same transaction as the ledger entries, and the two are reconciled. Records are never deleted, only closed or reversed.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Patterns: double-entry bookkeeping (every transaction has balanced debit and credit entries), reversal entries instead of updates, idempotency references per transaction, optimistic version or pessimistic row locks on accounts, holds (authorisations) separate from postings, and strict isolation for balance changes.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the CHECK constraint is the last line of defence: even buggy code cannot create a negative balance. MySQL 8.0.16+ enforces CHECK.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: row locks create contention on hot accounts, and two transfers in opposite directions can deadlock if they lock rows in different orders.
codeExamples:
-- Session A: transfer 1 -> 2            Session B: transfer 2 -> 1
-- A: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;   (A holds row 1)
-- B: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 2;   (B holds row 2)
-- A: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;   (A waits for B)
-- B: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 1;   (B waits for A)  => cycle
-- FIX: always lock the lower id first
SELECT id FROM accounts WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
-- (one victim is rolled back; with ordered locking this no longer occurs)

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL has no append-only table type, so immutability of the ledger is enforced with a trigger. Run a reconciliation query regularly to compare balances with the ledger.

Architect's Notes

Use InnoDB with REPEATABLE READ or READ COMMITTED, short transactions, and a fixed lock order. Add an idempotency key (unique ref) so a retried transfer cannot post twice. At scale, shard by account and treat the ledger as the source of truth, with balances as a derived cache that a nightly job reconciles.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Model transactions as an immutable ledger of entries (debit/credit) and compute balances from them or keep a balance column updated in the same transaction.
  • Use constraints (CHECK balance >= 0 where allowed), unique transaction references and strict isolation for balance updates.
  • Audit tables record who did what and when.

Senior Notes

  • Double-entry bookkeeping: every transaction creates balanced entries; totals per transaction must be zero.
  • Lock accounts in a consistent order (by id) to avoid deadlocks during transfers.
  • Idempotency keys prevent duplicate postings from retries; reconciliation jobs compare ledgers with external systems.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: updating or deleting ledger rows, floating point money, balance changes outside the transaction that writes the ledger, missing idempotency (retries double post), and locking accounts in different orders (deadlocks). Make the ledger append-only and enforce it with privileges or triggers.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Hot accounts (a merchant receiving thousands of payments) serialize on one row. Reduce contention with batched postings, per-currency or sub-accounts, and by deriving some balances from the ledger. Index ledger by (account, time) for statements.
codeExamples:
SELECT account_id, COUNT(*) AS postings FROM ledger WHERE posted_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR GROUP BY account_id ORDER BY postings DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- account_id | postings
-- 9001       |    41200       (a hot account: consider sub-accounts)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world controls: every transaction nets to zero, the stored balance equals the ledger sum, and the checks run continuously.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A social schema is mostly many-to-many relationships: users follow users, like posts, and comment on posts. Composite primary keys make each relationship unique by construction.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (
    id       BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    handle   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    bio      VARCHAR(255)
);
CREATE TABLE posts (
    id         BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id    BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    body       VARCHAR(500)    NOT NULL,
    like_count INT UNSIGNED    NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,       -- denormalised counter
    created_at DATETIME        NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    KEY ix_posts_user_time (user_id, created_at),
    FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);
CREATE TABLE follows (
    follower_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    followee_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id),
    KEY ix_followee (followee_id),                       -- who follows me?
    FOREIGN KEY (follower_id) REFERENCES users(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (followee_id) REFERENCES users(id)
);
CREATE TABLE likes (
    user_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    post_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, post_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id),
    FOREIGN KEY (post_id) REFERENCES posts(id)
);
SHOW TABLES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------------+
-- | Tables_in_social  |
-- +-------------------+
-- | follows           |
-- | likes             |
-- | posts             |
-- | users             |
-- +-------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Without a unique pair, a user could follow the same person twice and inflate counts. The composite primary key rejects the duplicate and INSERT IGNORE makes a double-click harmless.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE follows (follower_id INT, followee_id INT, PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id));
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1, 2);
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1, 2);                       -- duplicate => error
INSERT IGNORE INTO follows VALUES (1, 2);                -- silently skipped
SELECT ROW_COUNT() AS inserted;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1-2' for key 'follows.PRIMARY'
-- +----------+
-- | inserted |
-- +----------+
-- |        0 |
-- +----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The home feed: latest posts from the people I follow. The follows primary key and the (user_id, created_at) index make this a join plus a sort.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE follows (follower_id INT, followee_id INT);
CREATE TABLE posts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, user_id INT, body VARCHAR(40), created_at DATETIME);
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1, 2), (1, 3);
INSERT INTO posts VALUES
  (10, 2, 'hello world',  '2024-05-01 10:00:00'),
  (11, 3, 'lunch time',   '2024-05-01 12:30:00'),
  (12, 4, 'not followed', '2024-05-01 13:00:00'),
  (13, 2, 'good night',   '2024-05-01 22:00:00');

SELECT p.id, p.user_id, p.body
FROM   follows f
JOIN   posts   p ON p.user_id = f.followee_id
WHERE  f.follower_id = 1
ORDER  BY p.created_at DESC
LIMIT  3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+-------------+
-- | id | user_id | body        |
-- +----+---------+-------------+
-- | 13 |       2 | good night  |
-- | 11 |       3 | lunch time  |
-- | 10 |       2 | hello world |
-- +----+---------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   users ---< posts ---< likes >--- users
     |                             ^
     |   +---< follows >------------+   follows(follower, followee)
     |                                  PK(follower, followee) = no duplicates
   Feed = follows JOIN posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT n

Fresher Notes

  • A social app stores users, posts, comments, likes, followers and messages.
  • Followers form a many-to-many self relationship on users.
  • Likes and comments reference posts and users.

Worked Example 1

Like once only.

Worked Example 2

Mutual followers.
codeExamples:
SELECT a.followee_id AS user_id FROM follows a JOIN follows b ON b.follower_id = a.followee_id AND b.followee_id = a.follower_id WHERE a.follower_id = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id
-- 5

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Schema.

Practice Exercise 2

Simple feed (fan-out on read).
codeExamples:
SELECT p.id, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN follows f ON f.followee_id = p.user_id WHERE f.follower_id = 1 AND p.created_at < '2026-05-01 12:00:00' ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | body  | created_at
-- 88 | hello | 2026-05-01 11:59:12

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A social schema has users, posts, comments, likes, follows (a self-referencing many-to-many on users) and messages. The hard part is the feed: reading the latest posts of everyone you follow. Reads dominate, so the model, indexes and often a derived feed or cache are designed around that query.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Feed strategies: fan-out on read (query followees' posts at request time, simple, expensive for many followees), fan-out on write (push each post into followers' feed tables, fast reads, heavy writes), and a hybrid for accounts with very many followers. Time-ordered ids (snowflake, UUIDv7) allow sorting by id.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.id, p.user_id, p.body, p.created_at FROM posts p JOIN follows f ON f.followee_id = p.user_id
WHERE f.follower_id = 1 AND (p.created_at, p.id) < ('2026-05-01 12:00:00', 9000) ORDER BY p.created_at DESC, p.id DESC LIMIT 20;
INSERT INTO feed (user_id, post_id, created_at) SELECT f.follower_id, 9001, NOW() FROM follows f WHERE f.followee_id = 7;      -- fan-out on write

-- OUTPUT:
-- id   | user_id | body | created_at
-- 8999 |       5 | ...  | 2026-05-01 11:59:12

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: likes are cheap to write and to count thanks to the (user_id, post_id) key, and one user can never like the same post twice.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: counting likes on every page view is expensive for viral posts, so a counter column is kept. Update it in the same transaction as the like row.

Limitations

Limitations: relational joins are poor at deep graph questions. Friends-of-friends needs a self join, and arbitrary depth needs a recursive CTE; huge graphs belong in a graph store.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE follows (follower_id INT, followee_id INT, PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id));
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1,2),(2,3),(2,4),(1,3);

-- People followed by the people I follow, that I do not already follow
SELECT DISTINCT f2.followee_id AS suggestion
FROM   follows f1
JOIN   follows f2 ON f2.follower_id = f1.followee_id
WHERE  f1.follower_id = 1
  AND  f2.followee_id <> 1
  AND  f2.followee_id NOT IN (SELECT followee_id FROM follows WHERE follower_id = 1);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+
-- | suggestion |
-- +------------+
-- |          4 |
-- +------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Feeds are the scaling problem: fan-out on read (the join above) is simple but slows for users who follow thousands; fan-out on write (a per-user feed table or Redis list) trades storage and write cost for fast reads. Use keyset pagination (created_at, id) rather than OFFSET, and move counters and timelines to a cache once like traffic is hot.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Tables: users, posts, comments, likes (unique user_id+post_id), follows (follower_id, followee_id), messages, media.
  • Indexes: posts (user_id, created_at), follows (followee_id, follower_id), likes (post_id).
  • Counters (like_count) denormalized for speed and updated asynchronously or via batched jobs.

Senior Notes

  • Feed generation is the hard part: fan-out on write (precompute feeds) versus fan-out on read (query followees’ posts); hybrid for celebrities.
  • Use keyset pagination and cache hot feeds; MySQL is the source of truth.
  • Shard by user_id when a single node cannot hold the data; design ids (snowflake) for sharding.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: counting likes with COUNT(*) on every view, a single hot counter row for popular posts, deleting users with millions of rows via cascade, and OFFSET pagination in feeds. Use counters with slots or async aggregation, soft deletes with batch purge, and keyset pagination.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Scale by caching feeds, sharding by user id, moving search and recommendations to specialised systems, and keeping MySQL as the system of record. Generate ids that sort by time and are unique across shards.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND((data_length + index_length) / 1073741824, 1) AS gb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name IN ('posts','follows','likes') ORDER BY gb DESC;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name | gb
-- likes      | 84.0
-- posts      | 62.0
-- follows    | 31.0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world features: mutual followers, suggestions (friends of friends), and unread counts, each expressed with self-joins on the follows table and supported by both directions of index.
codeExamples:
SELECT b.followee_id AS suggestion, COUNT(*) AS mutuals FROM follows a JOIN follows b ON b.follower_id = a.followee_id
WHERE a.follower_id = 1 AND b.followee_id <> 1 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM follows x WHERE x.follower_id = 1 AND x.followee_id = b.followee_id)
GROUP BY b.followee_id ORDER BY mutuals DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- suggestion | mutuals
-- 12         |       9

beginner.content:
Introduction

A job portal links companies that post jobs, candidates who apply, and skills that connect both. Applications are a many-to-many between jobs and candidates with a status; skills are many-to-many with both jobs and candidates.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE companies  (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE jobs (
    id         INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    company_id INT NOT NULL,
    title      VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL,
    salary_min DECIMAL(10,2), salary_max DECIMAL(10,2),
    posted_at  DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    FOREIGN KEY (company_id) REFERENCES companies(id),
    FULLTEXT KEY ft_title (title)
);
CREATE TABLE candidates  (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, email VARCHAR(190) UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE skills      (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE job_skills       (job_id INT, skill_id INT, PRIMARY KEY (job_id, skill_id));
CREATE TABLE candidate_skills (candidate_id INT, skill_id INT, PRIMARY KEY (candidate_id, skill_id));
CREATE TABLE applications (
    job_id       INT NOT NULL,
    candidate_id INT NOT NULL,
    status       ENUM('APPLIED','SHORTLISTED','REJECTED','HIRED') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'APPLIED',
    applied_at   DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (job_id, candidate_id)                   -- one application per candidate per job
);
SHOW TABLES;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------------+
-- | Tables_in_portal |
-- +------------------+
-- | applications     |
-- | candidate_skills |
-- | candidates       |
-- | companies        |
-- | job_skills       |
-- | jobs             |
-- | skills           |
-- +------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Recruiters need ranked matches, not a flat list. Skill tables let SQL count how many required skills each candidate has.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE job_skills       (job_id INT, skill_id INT);
CREATE TABLE candidate_skills (candidate_id INT, skill_id INT);
CREATE TABLE candidates       (id INT, name VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO candidates       VALUES (1,'Abaji'),(2,'Raoji');
INSERT INTO job_skills       VALUES (1,1),(1,2);          -- job 1 needs Java(1), SQL(2)
INSERT INTO candidate_skills VALUES (1,1),(1,2),(2,1);    -- Abaji: both, Raoji: Java only

SELECT c.name,
       COUNT(*)                                             AS matched,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM job_skills WHERE job_id = 1)   AS required
FROM   candidates c
JOIN   candidate_skills cs ON cs.candidate_id = c.id
JOIN   job_skills js       ON js.skill_id = cs.skill_id AND js.job_id = 1
GROUP  BY c.id, c.name
ORDER  BY matched DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+---------+----------+
-- | name  | matched | required |
-- +-------+---------+----------+
-- | Abaji |       2 |        2 |
-- | Raoji |       1 |        2 |
-- +------+---------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Candidates search by title, and recruiters track the funnel: how many applications are at each status for a job.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE applications (job_id INT, candidate_id INT, status VARCHAR(12));
INSERT INTO applications VALUES
  (1,1,'APPLIED'),(1,2,'SHORTLISTED'),(1,3,'APPLIED'),(1,4,'HIRED'),(2,1,'APPLIED');

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM   applications
WHERE  job_id = 1
GROUP  BY status
ORDER  BY n DESC, status;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+---+
-- | status      | n |
-- +-------------+---+
-- | APPLIED     | 2 |
-- | HIRED       | 1 |
-- | SHORTLISTED | 1 |
-- +-------------+---+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   companies --< jobs --< applications >-- candidates
                  |                            |
                  +--< job_skills >-- skills --< candidate_skills
   Match score = COUNT(candidate skills that are in job_skills) / COUNT(job_skills)

Fresher Notes

  • A job portal stores users, companies, jobs, applications and skills. Candidates and employers use different features.
  • Applications link a user to a job; skills link many-to-many to candidates and jobs.
  • Indexes support search by location, skill and date.

Worked Example 1

Applications per job.
codeExamples:
SELECT j.title, COUNT(a.id) AS applicants FROM jobs j LEFT JOIN applications a ON a.job_id = j.id WHERE j.company_id = 3 GROUP BY j.id, j.title;

-- OUTPUT:
-- title           | applicants
-- Java Developer  | 41
-- QA Engineer     |  9

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Search with filters.
codeExamples:
SELECT id, title FROM jobs WHERE status = 'OPEN' AND city = 'Pune' ORDER BY posted_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | title
-- 10 | Java Developer

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Core tables.

Practice Exercise 2

Rank candidates for a job.
codeExamples:
SELECT cs.user_id, COUNT(*) AS matched FROM job_skills js JOIN candidate_skills cs ON cs.skill_id = js.skill_id WHERE js.job_id = 10 GROUP BY cs.user_id ORDER BY matched DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id | matched
-- 12      | 4
-- 31      | 3

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A job portal has users (candidates and recruiters), companies, jobs, applications, skills, and links between them: candidate skills and job skills (junction tables), saved jobs and application history. Applications are unique per candidate and job, and stage changes are kept as history.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Search and matching: structured filters (status, city, salary band) use composite indexes; keyword search uses FULLTEXT or a search engine; candidate-job matching counts overlapping skills through the junction tables. Stage transitions are validated and logged in a history table.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the application primary key stops duplicate applications, and ENUM status keeps values valid and compact.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE applications (
    job_id INT, candidate_id INT,
    status ENUM('APPLIED','SHORTLISTED','REJECTED','HIRED') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'APPLIED',
    PRIMARY KEY (job_id, candidate_id)
);
INSERT INTO applications (job_id, candidate_id) VALUES (1, 1);
INSERT INTO applications (job_id, candidate_id) VALUES (1, 1);     -- applied twice
UPDATE applications SET status = 'PENDING' WHERE job_id = 1;      -- not an allowed value

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '1-1' for key 'applications.PRIMARY'
-- ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' at row 1   (strict mode: error)

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: LIKE '%java%' cannot use an index. Use a FULLTEXT index and MATCH ... AGAINST for keyword search.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE jobs (id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(100), FULLTEXT KEY ft_title (title));
INSERT INTO jobs VALUES (1,'Senior Java Developer'),(2,'Python Developer'),(3,'Data Analyst');

SELECT id, title
FROM   jobs
WHERE  MATCH(title) AGAINST ('java' IN NATURAL LANGUAGE MODE);

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-----------------------+
-- | id | title                 |
-- +----+-----------------------+
-- |  1 | Senior Java Developer |
-- +----+-----------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: InnoDB FULLTEXT ignores short words (innodb_ft_min_token_size is 3) and a list of stopwords, so searching "C" or "it" finds nothing. Salary ranges need two columns and an overlap test.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@innodb_ft_min_token_size AS min_token;

CREATE TABLE jobs (id INT PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(50), salary_min INT, salary_max INT);
INSERT INTO jobs VALUES (1,'A',40000,60000),(2,'B',70000,90000),(3,'C',55000,75000);

-- Jobs whose range overlaps the wanted 50000..65000
SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE salary_min <= 65000 AND salary_max >= 50000;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+
-- | min_token |
-- +-----------+
-- |         3 |
-- +-----------+
-- +----+
-- | id |
-- +----+
-- |  1 |
-- |  3 |
-- +----+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Keep the relational core for applications and state changes, but plan a search engine (Elasticsearch or OpenSearch) once you need typo tolerance, relevance ranking and facets; FULLTEXT is a good first step. Add a status history table to audit the hiring funnel, and treat candidate data as PII with retention and deletion rules.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Tables: users, companies, jobs, applications (unique user_id+job_id), skills, candidate_skills, job_skills, saved_jobs.
  • Status columns for application stages (APPLIED, SHORTLISTED, REJECTED, HIRED) with history table for audit.
  • Full-text or external search for job search; filters by structured columns.

Senior Notes

  • Matching candidates to jobs by skills is a many-to-many overlap query; precompute scores for scale.
  • Soft delete jobs; keep closed jobs for analytics. Partition or archive old applications.
  • Privacy: candidate data needs access control, retention policies and audit.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: allowing duplicate applications (no unique key), free-text skills (typos split the data), no stage history, and loading all applicants of a job into memory. Use a unique key, a skills dictionary and keyset pagination.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Performance: the open-jobs listing (status, city, newest first) uses the composite index with keyset pagination; applicant lists per job use (job, stage, time); skill matching uses the junction indexes in both directions. Precompute match scores for large candidate pools.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT id, title FROM jobs WHERE status = 'OPEN' AND city = 'Pune' ORDER BY posted_at DESC LIMIT 20;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- type | key                     | Extra
-- ref  | idx_status_city_posted  | Backward index scan

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world analytics: funnel counts from application to hire per job, and time spent in each stage from the history table.
codeExamples:
SELECT j.title, SUM(a.stage = 'APPLIED') AS applied, SUM(a.stage = 'SHORTLISTED') AS shortlisted, SUM(a.stage = 'HIRED') AS hired FROM jobs j LEFT JOIN applications a ON a.job_id = j.id WHERE j.company_id = 3 GROUP BY j.id, j.title;

-- OUTPUT:
-- title          | applied | shortlisted | hired
-- Java Developer |      41 |          12 |     2

beginner.content:
Introduction

Classic question: return the Nth highest distinct salary. The cleanest MySQL 8 answer ranks salaries with DENSE_RANK(), which gives tied salaries the same rank and no gaps.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'A',5000),(2,'B',7000),(3,'C',7000),(4,'D',6000),(5,'E',4000);

-- 2nd highest salary (change 2 to N for any rank)
SELECT DISTINCT salary AS second_highest
FROM  (SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM emp) t
WHERE  rnk = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | second_highest |
-- +----------------+
-- |           6000 |
-- +----------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Why not ROW_NUMBER or a plain LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1? With ties (two people at 7000) they return the second row, which is still 7000, not the second distinct salary.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,5000),(2,7000),(3,7000),(4,6000),(5,4000);

SELECT salary AS wrong_second FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;          -- second row
SELECT DISTINCT salary AS right_second FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1; -- second value

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+
-- | wrong_second |
-- +--------------+
-- |         7000 |
-- +--------------+
-- +--------------+
-- | right_second |
-- +--------------+
-- |         6000 |
-- +--------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Interviews often ask for a reusable function getNthHighestSalary(N) that returns NULL when N is too large.

Diagram

   salary : 7000 7000 6000 5000 4000
   ROW_NUMBER: 1    2    3    4    5     (arbitrary on ties)
   RANK      : 1    1    3    4    5     (gap after ties)
   DENSE_RANK: 1    1    2    3    4     <- use this for "Nth highest"

Fresher Notes

  • Find the second (or Nth) highest salary. Common methods: subquery with MAX, LIMIT/OFFSET, or window functions with DENSE_RANK.
  • Use DISTINCT so duplicate salaries count once.
  • Return NULL when there is no second salary.

Worked Example 1

Nth per department.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, salary FROM (SELECT dept, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr FROM emp GROUP BY dept, salary) t WHERE dr = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | salary
--   10 | 45000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Stored function for Nth.

Practice Exercise 1

Second highest, three ways.

Practice Exercise 2

NULL when missing.
codeExamples:
SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 5) AS sixth;

-- OUTPUT:
-- sixth
-- NULL

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The question is about the Nth distinct value in descending order. Think of it as ranking the distinct salaries and picking rank N. Three standard ways: a subquery with MAX (only for second), LIMIT/OFFSET over DISTINCT values, and a window function with DENSE_RANK. Each handles ties and missing values differently.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: Nth highest overall, per department, with ties included (return all employees with that salary), and returning NULL when the Nth value does not exist. Wrap LIMIT/OFFSET in a scalar subquery to get NULL instead of an empty result.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages of the subquery form: it works on any MySQL version, including 5.7 without window functions. The 2nd highest is the maximum of everything below the maximum.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,5000),(2,7000),(3,7000),(4,6000);

SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM   emp
WHERE  salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp);       -- NULL automatically if there is no second value

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | second_highest |
-- +----------------+
-- |           6000 |
-- +----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the generic correlated form (count how many distinct salaries are higher) is O(n squared): every row runs a subquery.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,5000),(2,7000),(3,7000),(4,6000),(5,4000);

SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary AS third_highest
FROM   emp e1
WHERE  (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary) = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+
-- | third_highest |
-- +---------------+
-- |          5000 |
-- +---------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: NULL salaries must be excluded, otherwise they can take a rank. Per-department Nth highest needs PARTITION BY (see the next topics).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,5000),(2,7000),(3,NULL),(4,6000);

SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
FROM   emp
WHERE  salary IS NOT NULL;                    -- remove NULLs before ranking

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+-----+
-- | salary | rnk |
-- +--------+-----+
-- |   7000 |   1 |
-- |   6000 |   2 |
-- |   5000 |   3 |
-- +--------+-----+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

State the tie semantics first (distinct value or Nth row) because it decides the function. DENSE_RANK scans and sorts the table once, which is fine; an index on salary lets LIMIT/OFFSET stop early. For Nth highest per group on big tables, index (dept, salary) and rank per partition.

Mid-Level Notes

  • DENSE_RANK handles ties correctly: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) = N.
  • LIMIT/OFFSET: SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1.
  • Wrap in a scalar subquery so an empty result becomes NULL.

Senior Notes

  • Per-department version needs PARTITION BY dept.
  • On large tables an index on salary lets LIMIT/OFFSET stop early; window functions sort everything unless indexed.
  • Clarify tie semantics with the interviewer: "second highest value" vs "second row".

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: forgetting DISTINCT (duplicates make the "second row" equal the highest), using ROW_NUMBER or RANK where DENSE_RANK is needed, and returning an empty set instead of NULL when the rank does not exist. Test with ties and with fewer than N distinct values.
codeExamples:
SELECT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;          -- returns 100 again (duplicate)
SELECT salary FROM (SELECT salary, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM emp) t WHERE rk = 2;   -- empty: ranks are 1,1,3

-- OUTPUT:
-- salary
-- 100
-- Empty set

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

With an index on salary, LIMIT/OFFSET over DISTINCT stops early and is cheap; a window function sorts all rows. For huge tables prefer the index-friendly form and check the plan.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world interview answer: a reusable function that returns the Nth highest salary, with N validated and NULL for out-of-range values.

beginner.content:
Introduction

Find duplicates by grouping on the columns that must be unique and keeping groups with more than one row.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,'b@x.com'),(3,'a@x.com'),(4,'a@x.com'),(5,'c@x.com');

SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM   users
GROUP  BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+--------+
-- | email   | copies |
-- +---------+--------+
-- | a@x.com |      3 |
-- +---------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

To delete safely you first need to decide which copy to keep. ROW_NUMBER numbers the copies per email; every number above 1 is a surplus row.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,'b@x.com'),(3,'a@x.com'),(4,'a@x.com'),(5,'c@x.com');

SELECT id, email
FROM  (SELECT id, email,
              ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn   -- keep the lowest id
       FROM users) t
WHERE  rn > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+---------+
-- | id | email   |
-- +----+---------+
-- |  3 | a@x.com |
-- |  4 | a@x.com |
-- +----+---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The delete itself: a multi-table DELETE with a self join removes every row that has a lower-id twin.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,'b@x.com'),(3,'a@x.com'),(4,'a@x.com'),(5,'c@x.com');

DELETE u1
FROM   users u1
JOIN   users u2 ON u2.email = u1.email AND u2.id < u1.id;

SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected
-- +----+---------+
-- | id | email   |
-- +----+---------+
-- |  1 | a@x.com |
-- |  2 | b@x.com |
-- |  5 | c@x.com |
-- +----+---------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   id  email            ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id)
   1   a@x.com     ->   1   keep
   3   a@x.com     ->   2   delete
   4   a@x.com     ->   3   delete
   2   b@x.com     ->   1   keep

Fresher Notes

  • Find duplicates with GROUP BY and HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 on the columns that define a duplicate.
  • Remove them while keeping one row: keep the smallest or latest id.
  • Always back up or preview before deleting.

Worked Example 1

Prevent them.

Worked Example 2

Swap-in dedupe for huge tables.

Practice Exercise 1

Find and delete duplicates.

Practice Exercise 2

With ROW_NUMBER.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A duplicate is defined by the columns that should be unique (a business key), not by the whole row. Find them by grouping on that key and keeping groups with more than one row. To remove, decide which row survives (lowest id, newest timestamp), then delete the others.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Delete patterns: self join (a.id > b.id), window function (ROW_NUMBER() ... rn > 1), NOT IN with MIN(id), or rebuild into a new table with a unique key using INSERT IGNORE and swap names.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: once cleaned, a UNIQUE key makes duplicates impossible forever, which is the real fix.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: "same" is not always byte-equal. The default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci ignores case but NOT trailing spaces, so a dirty copy hides from GROUP BY until you normalise it.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,'A@X.COM'),(3,'a@x.com ');

SELECT TRIM(LOWER(email)) AS norm, COUNT(*) AS copies   -- TRIM fixes the space case
FROM   users
GROUP  BY TRIM(LOWER(email));

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+--------+
-- | norm    | copies |
-- +---------+--------+
-- | a@x.com |      3 |
-- +---------+--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: adding a UNIQUE key fails while duplicates exist, and one giant DELETE on a big table creates a huge transaction. Delete in batches.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(40));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com'),(2,'a@x.com');

ALTER TABLE users ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_email (email);       -- dupes exist => fails

-- Batch pattern: collect ids to remove, then delete 1000 at a time (single-table form allows LIMIT)
-- DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM dup_ids) LIMIT 1000;   -- repeat until 0 rows

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'a@x.com' for key 'users.uq_email'

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Always SELECT the doomed rows first and back up the table (CREATE TABLE users_bak AS SELECT ...). Prefer preventing duplicates with UNIQUE keys and INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE. On large tables delete in small batches to avoid long locks and replication lag.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Delete with a self join: DELETE a FROM t a JOIN t b ON a.email = b.email AND a.id > b.id.
  • Or ROW_NUMBER: number rows per key and delete those with rn > 1.
  • Prevent future duplicates with a UNIQUE constraint.

Senior Notes

  • On large tables delete in batches and in a transaction per batch; watch replica lag.
  • Adding a UNIQUE key to a table with duplicates fails; clean first.
  • Decide the survivor rule (newest, oldest, most complete) with the business and log removed ids.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: deleting without previewing, choosing the survivor arbitrarily, case or whitespace differences hiding duplicates, and not adding a unique constraint afterwards (duplicates return). Normalize values, preview with SELECT, and add the constraint.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

On very large tables delete in batches or rebuild: create a clean copy with a unique index, copy distinct rows, then rename tables atomically. This avoids huge transactions and long lock times.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: deduplicate contacts imported from two systems, keeping the most complete record and logging removed ids for audit.

topics.name: Employees Earning More Than Their Manager

beginner.content:
Introduction

A self join treats the same table as two roles: employee (e) and manager (m), linked by manager_id. Then compare their salaries.
codeExamples:
