CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Boss',9000,NULL),(2,'Ann',9500,1),(3,'Baji',7000,1),(4,'Cy',7500,3),(5,'Di',6000,3);

SELECT e.name AS employee
FROM   emp e
JOIN   emp m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE  e.salary > m.salary
ORDER  BY e.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | employee |
-- +----------+
-- | Ann      |
-- | Cy       |
-- +----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

The same result with a correlated subquery. Interviewers like seeing both because the join is usually faster and easier to extend.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Boss',9000,NULL),(2,'Ann',9500,1),(3,'Baji',7000,1),(4,'Cy',7500,3),(5,'Di',6000,3);

SELECT e.name
FROM   emp e
WHERE  e.salary > (SELECT m.salary FROM emp m WHERE m.id = e.manager_id)
ORDER  BY e.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+
-- | name |
-- +------+
-- | Ann  |
-- | Cy   |
-- +------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Reports usually also show the manager and the gap, which the join form gives for free.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Boss',9000,NULL),(2,'Ann',9500,1),(3,'Baji',7000,1),(4,'Cy',7500,3),(5,'Di',6000,3);

SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager, e.salary - m.salary AS gap
FROM   emp e JOIN emp m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE  e.salary > m.salary
ORDER  BY gap DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+---------+-----+
-- | employee | manager | gap |
-- +----------+---------+-----+
-- | Ann      | Boss    | 500 |
-- | Cy       | Baji    | 500 |
-- +----------+---------+------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

          Boss 9000
          /            Ann 9500 *    Baji 7000
                   /                  Cy 7500 *   Di 6000        * = earns more than direct manager
   e.manager_id ----> m.id   (same table, two aliases)

Fresher Notes

  • Compare each employee with their manager using a self join on manager_id.
  • Query: join emp e to emp m on e.manager_id = m.id and filter e.salary > m.salary.
  • Employees without a manager are excluded by INNER JOIN.

Worked Example 1

Earning more than any ancestor.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE anc AS (
  SELECT id, manager_id AS anc_id FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL SELECT a.id, s.manager_id FROM anc a JOIN staff s ON s.id = a.anc_id WHERE s.manager_id IS NOT NULL)
SELECT DISTINCT e.name FROM staff e JOIN anc a ON a.id = e.id JOIN staff x ON x.id = a.anc_id WHERE e.salary > x.salary;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Index for the join.

Practice Exercise 1

Self join.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- OUTPUT:
-- employee | salary | manager | manager_salary
-- Kanhoji  |  90000 | Raoji   | 80000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Correlated subquery version.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM staff e WHERE salary > (SELECT salary FROM staff m WHERE m.id = e.manager_id);

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Each employee row stores the manager's id, so the manager's salary lives in another row of the same table. A self join matches each employee to their manager row, and a WHERE compares the two salaries. Employees without a manager (the top of the tree) have no match in an inner join and are excluded.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Alternatives: a correlated subquery, a window function with a join to the manager, and a recursive CTE when the question is "more than anyone above them". Pick the self join for clarity.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: an index on manager_id (and the primary key on id) makes the join a fast key lookup per employee.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the top boss has manager_id NULL, so an INNER JOIN drops him. That is right here, but wrong if you must list everyone with a flag.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Boss',9000,NULL),(2,'Ann',9500,1),(3,'Baji',7000,1);

SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager, (e.salary > m.salary) AS earns_more   -- NULL when no manager
FROM   emp e LEFT JOIN emp m ON m.id = e.manager_id
ORDER  BY e.id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+------------+
-- | name | manager | earns_more |
-- +------+---------+------------+
-- | Boss | NULL    |       NULL |
-- | Ann  | Boss    |          1 |
-- | Baji | Boss    |          0 |
-- +------+---------+------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a join only sees the direct manager. To compare with any ancestor you need a recursive CTE.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT, manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Boss',9000,NULL),(2,'Ann',9500,1),(3,'Baji',7000,1),(4,'Cy',7500,3),(5,'Di',6000,3);

WITH RECURSIVE anc AS (
    SELECT id, manager_id AS anc_id FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT a.id, e.manager_id FROM anc a JOIN emp e ON e.id = a.anc_id WHERE e.manager_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT e.name, m.name AS ancestor
FROM   anc a JOIN emp e ON e.id = a.id JOIN emp m ON m.id = a.anc_id
WHERE  e.salary > m.salary
ORDER  BY e.name, m.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+----------+
-- | name | ancestor |
-- +------+----------+
-- | Ann  | Boss     |
-- | Cy   | Baji     |
-- +------+----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Model the hierarchy with an indexed manager_id; for deep or frequently queried trees consider a closure table or materialised path so ancestor questions become plain joins. Remember that self-referencing foreign keys allow cycles unless the application prevents them.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Use aliases to tell the two roles apart.
  • A correlated subquery also works but the self join is clearer and usually faster.
  • Index manager_id and id (primary key).

Senior Notes

  • Hierarchies deeper than one level (earning more than any manager above) need a recursive CTE.
  • Handle NULL salaries with explicit conditions.
  • For analytics at scale precompute manager salary into a denormalized column or snapshot table.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no table aliases (ambiguous columns), LEFT JOIN and then forgetting the NULL manager case, comparing with NULL salaries (unknown), and joining on the wrong key. State assumptions: are salaries nullable, can there be several top managers?
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name FROM staff e LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;        -- NULL manager gives unknown: row excluded anyway
SELECT e.name FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > COALESCE(m.salary, 0) AND m.salary IS NOT NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Kanhoji

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The join uses the manager's primary key, so each lookup is a single-row index probe, and an index on manager_id helps hierarchy queries in the other direction. The plan should show eq_ref for the manager lookup.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN SELECT e.name FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table | type   | key
-- e     | ALL    | NULL
-- m     | eq_ref | PRIMARY

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world audit: list pay-compression cases with the size of the gap, sorted by the largest difference.
codeExamples:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager, e.salary - m.salary AS gap FROM staff e JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary ORDER BY gap DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- employee | manager | gap
-- Kanhoji  | Raoji   | 10

topics.name: Department-wise Highest Salary & Top 3 per Department

beginner.content:
Introduction

The highest salary per department: aggregate in a subquery, then join back to find who earns it (ties return every top earner).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Ann','Eng',9000),(2,'Baji','Eng',8000),(3,'Cy','Eng',8000),(4,'Di','Eng',7000),
                       (5,'Ed','Eng',6000),(6,'Fay','Sales',5000),(7,'Gus','Sales',4000);

SELECT e.dept, e.name, e.salary
FROM   emp e
JOIN  (SELECT dept, MAX(salary) AS mx FROM emp GROUP BY dept) m
       ON m.dept = e.dept AND m.mx = e.salary
ORDER  BY e.dept;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+--------+
-- | dept  | name | salary |
-- +-------+------+--------+
-- | Eng   | Ann  |   9000 |
-- | Sales | Fay  |   5000 |
-- +-------+------+--------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Top 3 per department needs ranking inside each group. DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ...) restarts the numbering for every department.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Ann','Eng',9000),(2,'Baji','Eng',8000),(3,'Cy','Eng',8000),(4,'Di','Eng',7000),
                       (5,'Ed','Eng',6000),(6,'Fay','Sales',5000),(7,'Gus','Sales',4000);

SELECT dept, name, salary, rnk
FROM  (SELECT dept, name, salary,
              DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
       FROM emp) t
WHERE  rnk <= 3
ORDER  BY dept, rnk, name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+--------+-----+
-- | dept  | name | salary | rnk |
-- +-------+------+--------+-----+
-- | Eng   | Ann  |   9000 |   1 |
-- | Eng   | Baji |   8000 |   2 |
-- | Eng   | Cy   |   8000 |   2 |
-- | Eng   | Di   |   7000 |   3 |
-- | Sales | Fay  |   5000 |   1 |
-- | Sales | Gus  |   4000 |   2 |
-- +-------+------+--------+-----+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

If the business wants exactly three people per department (not three salary levels), use ROW_NUMBER with a tie-breaker.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Ann','Eng',9000),(2,'Baji','Eng',8000),(3,'Cy','Eng',8000),(4,'Di','Eng',7000),
                       (6,'Fay','Sales',5000),(7,'Gus','Sales',4000);

SELECT dept, name, salary
FROM  (SELECT dept, name, salary,
              ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS rn   -- id breaks ties
       FROM emp) t
WHERE  rn <= 3
ORDER  BY dept, rn;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+------+--------+
-- | dept  | name | salary |
-- +-------+------+--------+
-- | Eng   | Ann  |   9000 |
-- | Eng   | Baji |   8000 |
-- | Eng   | Cy   |   8000 |
-- | Sales | Fay  |   5000 |
-- | Sales | Gus  |   4000 |
-- +-------+------+--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Eng  : Ann 9000 | Baji 8000 | Cy 8000 | Di 7000 | Ed 6000
   PARTITION BY dept  (separate window per department)
          DENSE_RANK:  1        2         2         3         4
          keep rnk<=3 ---------------------------^  (Ed dropped)
   Sales: Fay 5000 | Gus 4000   ->  ranks restart at 1

Fresher Notes

  • Highest salary per department: GROUP BY dept with MAX(salary). To also show who earns it, join back or use a window function.
  • Top 3 per department: rank rows inside each department and keep rank <= 3.
  • DENSE_RANK includes ties; ROW_NUMBER gives exactly three rows.

Worked Example 1

Lateral join version.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name, t.name AS employee, t.salary FROM departments d JOIN LATERAL (SELECT name, salary FROM emp e WHERE e.dept = d.id ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | employee | salary
-- HR   | Abaji    | 60000
-- HR   | Raoji    | 45000
-- IT   | Moropant | 70000

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Supporting index.

Practice Exercise 1

Top earner per department with name.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name AS dept, e.name, e.salary FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept
WHERE (e.dept, e.salary) IN (SELECT dept, MAX(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept);

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary
-- HR   | Abaji    | 60000
-- IT   | Moropant | 70000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Top 3 per department.
codeExamples:
SELECT dept, name, salary FROM (SELECT dept, name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM emp) t WHERE rk <= 3 ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name     | salary
--   10 | Abaji    | 60000
--   10 | Raoji    | 45000
--   20 | Moropant | 70000

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

"Highest per group" is a grouped MAX; to also show who earns it you must join back or rank rows. "Top N per group" needs ranking within each group: a window function numbers rows per department by salary, and an outer query keeps ranks up to N. LIMIT alone cannot do this because it limits the whole result.
codeExamples:
SELECT d.name AS dept, e.name, e.salary FROM emp e JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.dept WHERE (e.dept, e.salary) IN (SELECT dept, MAX(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept);
WITH ranked AS (SELECT dept, name, salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM emp)
SELECT dept, name, salary FROM ranked WHERE rk <= 3 ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- dept | name | salary
--   10 | A    |    100
--   10 | B    |    100
--   10 | C    |     90

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Decide the tie policy: ROW_NUMBER gives exactly N rows (with an explicit tiebreaker), RANK and DENSE_RANK include all tied rows. A LATERAL join (8.0.14+) runs ORDER BY ... LIMIT N per department and can use an index.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: window functions keep the detail rows while adding group facts, e.g. each person next to the department maximum.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Ann','Eng',9000),(2,'Baji','Eng',8000),(6,'Fay','Sales',5000),(7,'Gus','Sales',4000);

SELECT name, dept, salary,
       MAX(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept)          AS dept_max,
       MAX(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) - salary AS below_top
FROM   emp ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+-------+--------+----------+-----------+
-- | name | dept  | salary | dept_max | below_top |
-- +------+-------+--------+----------+-----------+
-- | Ann  | Eng   |   9000 |     9000 |         0 |
-- | Baji | Eng   |   8000 |     9000 |      1000 |
-- | Fay  | Sales |   5000 |     5000 |         0 |
-- | Gus  | Sales |   4000 |     5000 |      1000 |
-- +------+-------+--------+----------+-----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the three ranking functions disagree on ties; picking the wrong one silently returns the wrong number of rows.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Ann',9000),(2,'Baji',8000),(3,'Cy',8000),(4,'Di',7000);

SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn, RANK() OVER w AS rk, DENSE_RANK() OVER w AS drk
FROM   emp
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary DESC);

-- OUTPUT: (example: which tied row gets rn 2 or 3 is not guaranteed)
-- +------+--------+----+----+-----+
-- | name | salary | rn | rk | drk |
-- +------+--------+----+----+-----+
-- | Ann  |   9000 |  1 |  1 |   1 |
-- | Baji |   8000 |  2 |  2 |   2 |
-- | Cy   |   8000 |  3 |  2 |   2 |
-- | Di   |   7000 |  4 |  4 |   3 |
-- +------+--------+----+----+-----+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: window functions cannot be used directly in WHERE. Wrap the ranking in a derived table or CTE and filter outside.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept VARCHAR(10), salary INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Eng',9000),(2,'Eng',8000);

SELECT * FROM emp WHERE RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1;   -- not allowed

-- FIX
WITH r AS (SELECT *, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM emp)
SELECT id, dept, salary FROM r WHERE rk = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3593 (HY000): You cannot use the window function 'rank' in this context.
-- +----+------+--------+
-- | id | dept | salary |
-- +----+------+--------+
-- |  1 | Eng  |   9000 |
-- +----+------+--------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Pick the function from the business rule (levels vs people). An index on (dept, salary DESC) lets MySQL read each partition in order and avoid a big filesort. For huge tables, a LATERAL join per department or a pre-aggregated table can beat a full-table window.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Pattern: WITH r AS (SELECT ..., DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rk FROM emp) SELECT ... WHERE rk <= 3.
  • Join with departments for names.
  • Add id as a tie-breaker for ROW_NUMBER.

Senior Notes

  • Index (dept, salary DESC) to avoid sorting everything.
  • Large tables: lateral join per department with LIMIT 3 can beat a full-table window.
  • Decide tie policy explicitly and test with duplicated salaries.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: filtering the window result in WHERE (not allowed), no tiebreaker (unstable rows), and using GROUP BY with non-aggregated columns. Wrap the ranking in a CTE or derived table and filter outside.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Index (dept, salary) lets the LATERAL form read three entries per department and avoids sorting the table; the window form sorts everything. Compare with EXPLAIN ANALYZE on large data.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a leaderboard page showing the top three sellers per region, cached and refreshed hourly.
codeExamples:
SELECT region, seller, revenue FROM (SELECT region, seller, SUM(total) AS revenue, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY SUM(total) DESC) AS rn FROM sales WHERE created_at >= '2026-05-01' GROUP BY region, seller) t WHERE rn <= 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- region | seller | revenue
-- West   | Abaji  | 48200.00

beginner.content:
Introduction

A running total is a window SUM() over an ordered frame from the first row to the current row.

Why Do We Need This?

Before window functions the same result needed a self join that sums all earlier rows. It still appears in interviews and in MySQL 5.7 systems, but it re-reads rows many times.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sales (day DATE PRIMARY KEY, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('2024-01-01',100),('2024-01-02',200),('2024-01-03',150);

SELECT a.day, SUM(b.amount) AS running_total
FROM   sales a JOIN sales b ON b.day <= a.day
GROUP  BY a.day
ORDER  BY a.day;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+---------------+
-- | day        | running_total |
-- +------------+---------------+
-- | 2024-01-01 |           100 |
-- | 2024-01-02 |           300 |
-- | 2024-01-03 |           450 |
-- +------------+---------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

A 3-day moving average smooths noisy daily numbers (dashboards, trend lines): average the current row and the two before it.

Diagram

   amount :  100   200   150   300   250
   running: 100   300   450   750  1000      frame = [first .. current]
   moving3:                                  frame = [cur-2 .. cur]
   row 4  :        [200   150   300] -> 216.67
   row 5  :              [150   300   250] -> 233.33

Fresher Notes

  • A running total adds values cumulatively; a moving average averages a sliding window.
  • Use SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY d) and AVG(x) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW).
  • Partition by group to restart per customer or product.

Worked Example 1

Calendar join for gaps.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.d, COALESCE(s.sales, 0) AS sales, AVG(COALESCE(s.sales,0)) OVER (ORDER BY c.d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ma7
FROM calendar c LEFT JOIN daily_sales s ON s.day = c.d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- d          | sales | ma7
-- 2026-01-07 |   0   | 85.7

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Validate with a total.
codeExamples:
SELECT MAX(running) = (SELECT SUM(sales) FROM daily_sales) AS ok FROM (SELECT SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running FROM daily_sales) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ok
-- 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Running total and percent.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, sales, SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS running, ROUND(sales / SUM(sales) OVER () * 100, 1) AS pct FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales | running | pct
-- 2026-01-01 |   100 |     100 | 20.0
-- 2026-01-02 |   200 |     300 | 40.0
-- 2026-01-03 |   200 |     500 | 40.0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

3-day moving average.
codeExamples:
SELECT day, ROUND(AVG(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS ma3 FROM daily_sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | ma3
-- 2026-01-01 | 100.0
-- 2026-01-02 | 150.0
-- 2026-01-03 | 166.7

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A running total is a window SUM from the first row to the current row; a moving average is an AVG over a fixed-size frame. Both are single-pass window functions over rows in a defined order. Without window functions you would need a self join or correlated subquery, which is quadratic.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: per-group totals with PARTITION BY, percent of total (x / SUM(x) OVER ()), cumulative percentage, date-range frames (RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING), and the older self-join form for databases without windows.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: PARTITION BY gives a separate running total per group, e.g. per store, in one pass.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the default frame is RANGE, not ROWS. Rows with the same ORDER BY value are treated as peers and share one total, which surprises people.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, day DATE, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'2024-01-01',100),(2,'2024-01-01',100),(3,'2024-01-02',50);

SELECT id, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)                                  AS default_range,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day, id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)     AS rows_frame
FROM   sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+--------+---------------+------------+
-- | id | amount | default_range | rows_frame |
-- +----+--------+---------------+------------+
-- |  1 |    100 |           200 |        100 |
-- |  2 |    100 |           200 |        200 |
-- |  3 |     50 |           250 |        250 |
-- +----+--------+---------------+------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: a ROWS frame counts rows, not days. With missing dates, "3 rows" spans more than 3 days. Use a RANGE frame with an INTERVAL to get a true calendar window.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sales (day DATE PRIMARY KEY, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES ('2024-01-01',100),('2024-01-02',200),('2024-01-05',300);

SELECT day, amount,
       AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS  BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)             AS by_rows,
       AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 2 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS by_days
FROM   sales;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+--------+----------+----------+
-- | day        | amount | by_rows  | by_days  |
-- +------------+--------+----------+----------+
-- | 2024-01-01 |    100 | 100.0000 | 100.0000 |
-- | 2024-01-02 |    200 | 150.0000 | 150.0000 |
-- | 2024-01-05 |    300 | 200.0000 | 300.0000 |
-- +------------+--------+----------+----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Window functions need a sort, so index the ORDER BY (and PARTITION BY) columns. Prefer pre-aggregated daily tables for dashboards instead of windowing raw events. Always specify the frame explicitly (ROWS or RANGE) so behaviour is obvious to the next reader.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Add a tie-breaker to ORDER BY. Use ROWS frames for exact row windows.
  • Date-based windows need RANGE with INTERVAL or a calendar table when days are missing.
  • Percent-of-total: x / SUM(x) OVER ().

Senior Notes

  • For large reporting tables precompute daily aggregates then apply windows over the small table.
  • Index (partition, order) columns to avoid sorts.
  • Mind NULLs and gaps; define whether a missing day counts as zero.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: no unique tiebreaker in ORDER BY (ties give arbitrary intermediate totals), RANGE instead of ROWS with duplicate dates, and missing days that make "last 7 rows" different from "last 7 days". Join a calendar table first.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.d, COALESCE(s.sales, 0) AS sales, ROUND(AVG(COALESCE(s.sales, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY c.d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 1) AS ma7 FROM calendar c LEFT JOIN daily_sales s ON s.day = c.d WHERE c.d BETWEEN '2026-01-01' AND '2026-01-10';

-- OUTPUT:
-- d          | sales | ma7
-- 2026-01-07 |     0 | 85.7

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

On big tables aggregate to the reporting grain (day) first, then apply the window over the small result. Index the order column if you must window the raw table.
codeExamples:
WITH daily AS (SELECT DATE(created_at) AS day, SUM(total) AS sales FROM orders WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' GROUP BY DATE(created_at))
SELECT day, sales, SUM(sales) OVER (ORDER BY day) AS ytd FROM daily;

-- OUTPUT:
-- day        | sales   | ytd
-- 2026-01-01 | 8120.00 | 8120.00

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world account statement: running balance after each transaction, with a check that the final balance equals the account's stored balance.

topics.name: Consecutive Dates, Missing Numbers & Gaps and Islands

beginner.content:
Introduction

Islands are runs of consecutive values; gaps are the holes between them. The trick: subtract a row number from the value. Consecutive values then produce the same constant, which identifies the island.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE logins (day DATE PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO logins VALUES ('2024-01-01'),('2024-01-02'),('2024-01-03'),('2024-01-05'),('2024-01-06'),('2024-01-09');

SELECT MIN(day) AS streak_start, MAX(day) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS days
FROM  (SELECT day,
              DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day) DAY) AS grp
       FROM logins) t
GROUP  BY grp
ORDER  BY streak_start;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+------------+------+
-- | streak_start | streak_end | days |
-- +--------------+------------+------+
-- | 2024-01-01   | 2024-01-03 |    3 |
-- | 2024-01-05   | 2024-01-06 |    2 |
-- | 2024-01-09   | 2024-01-09 |    1 |
-- +--------------+------------+------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Missing numbers: find where the next id is more than 1 larger than the current one. LEAD() looks at the following row without a self join.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE t (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1),(2),(4),(5),(8);

SELECT id + 1 AS gap_start, next_id - 1 AS gap_end
FROM  (SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM t) x
WHERE  next_id - id > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-----------+---------+
-- | gap_start | gap_end |
-- +-----------+---------+
-- |         3 |       3 |
-- |         6 |       7 |
-- +-----------+---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

A product question: the longest login streak per user (engagement, gamification, fraud signals).
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE activity (user_id INT, day DATE, PRIMARY KEY (user_id, day));
INSERT INTO activity VALUES (1,'2024-01-01'),(1,'2024-01-02'),(1,'2024-01-03'),(1,'2024-01-05'),(1,'2024-01-06'),
                            (2,'2024-01-01'),(2,'2024-01-02');

SELECT user_id, MAX(days) AS longest_streak
FROM  (SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS days
       FROM  (SELECT user_id, day,
                     DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) DAY) AS grp
              FROM activity) a
       GROUP  BY user_id, grp) s
GROUP  BY user_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+----------------+
-- | user_id | longest_streak |
-- +---------+----------------+
-- |       1 |              3 |
-- |       2 |              2 |
-- +---------+----------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   day      : 01 02 03 . 05 06 . . 09
   row_num  :  1  2  3   4  5   6   (numbers keep counting)
   day - rn :  0  0  0   1  1   3   <- same constant = same island
   island A = 01..03, island B = 05..06, island C = 09

Fresher Notes

  • Gaps and islands problems find runs of consecutive values (islands) and the missing values between them (gaps), such as login streaks or missing invoice numbers.
  • Classic trick: subtract ROW_NUMBER() from the value; consecutive values give the same difference, which identifies the island.
  • Missing numbers can be found with LEAD/LAG or an anti-join to a number series.

Worked Example 1

All missing numbers via series.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE s AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM s WHERE n < 10)
SELECT s.n FROM s LEFT JOIN invoices i ON i.id = s.n WHERE i.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- n
-- 4
-- 5
-- 6

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Consecutive 3 days using LAG.
codeExamples:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM (SELECT user_id, login_date, LAG(login_date, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS two_back FROM (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins) x) t WHERE DATEDIFF(login_date, two_back) = 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id
-- 1

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Longest streak.
codeExamples:
WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, login_date FROM logins),
g AS (SELECT user_id, login_date, DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) DAY) AS grp FROM d)
SELECT user_id, MIN(login_date) AS start_d, MAX(login_date) AS end_d, COUNT(*) AS days FROM g GROUP BY user_id, grp ORDER BY days DESC LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id | start_d    | end_d      | days
-- 1       | 2026-04-01 | 2026-04-05 | 5

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Missing ids.
codeExamples:
SELECT id + 1 AS gap_start, next_id - 1 AS gap_end FROM (SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id FROM invoices) t WHERE next_id - id > 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- gap_start | gap_end
-- 4         | 6

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Gaps-and-islands problems find runs of consecutive values (islands) and the breaks between them (gaps). Key idea: for a sequence with no duplicates, subtract the row number from the value; consecutive values produce the same difference, so the difference identifies the island. Alternatives use LAG/LEAD to compare neighbours.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: longest streak (take MAX of island lengths), users with at least N consecutive days (HAVING COUNT(*) >= N), missing ids (LEAD gap), all missing values (series LEFT JOIN), and consecutive rows with the same status (compare ROW_NUMBER over two partitionings).

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: a recursive CTE can generate the full expected sequence, and a LEFT JOIN lists every missing number individually.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE t (id INT PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1),(2),(4),(5),(8);

WITH RECURSIVE seq AS (
    SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < 8
)
SELECT seq.n AS missing
FROM   seq LEFT JOIN t ON t.id = seq.n
WHERE  t.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+
-- | missing |
-- +---------+
-- |       3 |
-- |       6 |
-- |       7 |
-- +---------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the row-number trick assumes unique values. Duplicate dates break the arithmetic, so de-duplicate first.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE ev (day DATE);
INSERT INTO ev VALUES ('2024-01-01'),('2024-01-01'),('2024-01-02');     -- duplicate day

SELECT COUNT(*) AS days_in_streak
FROM  (SELECT day, DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day) DAY) AS grp
       FROM  (SELECT DISTINCT day FROM ev) d) t           -- DISTINCT makes the trick valid
GROUP  BY grp;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------------+
-- | days_in_streak |
-- +----------------+
-- |              2 |
-- +----------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: recursive CTEs stop after cte_max_recursion_depth (default 1000) iterations, so generating a long sequence needs a higher limit or a numbers table.
codeExamples:
SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 1000;
WITH RECURSIVE s AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM s WHERE n < 5000)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s;                                  -- needs 5000 iterations

SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 10000;             -- raise the guard, then it works
WITH RECURSIVE s AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM s WHERE n < 5000)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM s;

-- OUTPUT:
-- ERROR 3636 (HY000): Recursive query aborted after 1001 iterations. Try increasing @@cte_max_recursion_depth to a larger value.
-- +------+
-- | cnt  |
-- +------+
-- | 5000 |
-- +------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Gaps-and-islands is a single pass over sorted data, so index the ordering column (user_id, day). Store dates as DATE, not strings. For sequences over a few thousand values prefer a permanent numbers or calendar table instead of recursive CTEs on every query.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Streak of consecutive dates: DATE_SUB(login_date, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY login_date) DAY) as group key.
  • Gaps: LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) - id > 1.
  • Remove duplicates first (DISTINCT date per user).

Senior Notes

  • For large data keep an index on (user, date) and process per partition.
  • Handle time zones and date definitions before streak logic.
  • Generate series with recursive CTEs for full calendars to find all missing values.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: duplicate dates breaking the row-number trick (deduplicate first), time zones changing the date, and using BETWEEN logic that includes boundaries twice. Normalize the date column and use DISTINCT before numbering.
codeExamples:
WITH d AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(login_at) AS login_date FROM login_events)
SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) FROM d GROUP BY user_id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- user_id | COUNT(*)
-- 1       |        5

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Window passes need a sort by (partition, order). An index on (user_id, login_date) removes the sort. For huge event tables, aggregate to one row per user and day first.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: find customers on a purchase streak of at least four consecutive weeks for a loyalty reward.
codeExamples:
WITH w AS (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, YEARWEEK(created_at, 3) AS wk FROM orders),
g AS (SELECT customer_id, wk, wk - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY wk) AS grp FROM w)
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS streak_weeks FROM g GROUP BY customer_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 4;

-- OUTPUT:
-- customer_id | streak_weeks
-- 7           |            6

beginner.content:
Introduction

A recursive CTE walks a tree: an anchor query selects the roots, and a recursive part repeatedly joins children to the rows found so far, until no new rows appear.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'CEO',NULL),(2,'CTO',1),(3,'CFO',1),(4,'Dev1',2),(5,'Dev2',2),(6,'Acct',3);

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
    SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth, CAST(name AS CHAR(200)) AS path
    FROM   emp WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, o.depth + 1, CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', e.name)
    FROM   emp e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT CONCAT(REPEAT('  ', depth), name) AS tree, depth, path
FROM   org ORDER BY path;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------------+-------+------------------+
-- | tree         | depth | path             |
-- +--------------+-------+------------------+
-- | CEO          |     0 | CEO              |
-- |   CFO        |     1 | CEO > CFO        |
-- |     Acct     |     2 | CEO > CFO > Acct |
-- |   CTO        |     1 | CEO > CTO        |
-- |     Dev1     |     2 | CEO > CTO > Dev1 |
-- |     Dev2     |     2 | CEO > CTO > Dev2 |
-- +--------------+-------+------------------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Plain self joins handle a fixed number of levels only. Each extra level needs another JOIN, and the depth of a real organisation is unknown.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'CEO',NULL),(2,'CTO',1),(4,'Dev1',2),(7,'Intern',4);

-- Two joins reach only two levels below the CEO: the Intern is missed
SELECT e0.name AS l0, e1.name AS l1, e2.name AS l2
FROM   emp e0
LEFT JOIN emp e1 ON e1.manager_id = e0.id
LEFT JOIN emp e2 ON e2.manager_id = e1.id
WHERE  e0.manager_id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+------+
-- | l0   | l1   | l2   |
-- +------+------+------+
-- | CEO  | CTO  | Dev1 |
-- +------+------+------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Typical request: everyone who reports (directly or indirectly) to the CTO, for approvals or access reviews.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'CEO',NULL),(2,'CTO',1),(3,'CFO',1),(4,'Dev1',2),(5,'Dev2',2),(7,'Intern',4);

WITH RECURSIVE reports AS (
    SELECT id, name FROM emp WHERE manager_id = 2          -- direct reports of CTO (id 2)
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name FROM emp e JOIN reports r ON e.manager_id = r.id
)
SELECT name FROM reports ORDER BY name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+
-- | name   |
-- +--------+
-- | Dev1   |
-- | Dev2   |
-- | Intern |
-- +--------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   CEO (anchor, depth 0)
    +-- CTO  (iteration 1)
    |    +-- Dev1, Dev2   (iteration 2)
    +-- CFO  (iteration 1)
         +-- Acct         (iteration 2)
   Each iteration joins emp.manager_id = previous level's id; stops when no rows.

Fresher Notes

  • Hierarchies (managers and reports, categories, folders) are stored with a parent id and walked with a recursive CTE.
  • The anchor selects the root; the recursive part joins children to the rows found so far.
  • Add level and path columns to show depth and order.

Worked Example 1

Closure table for fast subtrees.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE staff_closure (ancestor INT, descendant INT, depth INT, PRIMARY KEY (ancestor, descendant), INDEX idx_desc (descendant));
SELECT s.name FROM staff_closure c JOIN staff s ON s.id = c.descendant WHERE c.ancestor = 1 AND c.depth > 0;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Raoji
-- Moropant
-- Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Materialized path.
codeExamples:
SELECT name FROM staff WHERE path LIKE '/1/2/%';

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Raoji
-- Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Indented org chart.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS lvl, CAST(name AS CHAR(200)) AS path FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, o.lvl + 1, CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', s.name) FROM staff s JOIN org o ON s.manager_id = o.id)
SELECT CONCAT(REPEAT('  ', lvl), name) AS chart FROM org ORDER BY path;

-- OUTPUT:
-- chart
-- Annaji
--   Moropant
--   Raoji
--     Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Team size per manager.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (SELECT id AS mgr, id AS member FROM staff UNION ALL SELECT t.mgr, s.id FROM t JOIN staff s ON s.manager_id = t.member)
SELECT s.name, COUNT(*) - 1 AS team_size FROM t JOIN staff s ON s.id = t.mgr GROUP BY t.mgr, s.name HAVING team_size > 0;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name   | team_size
-- Annaji | 3
-- Raoji  | 1

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

An organisation is stored as an adjacency list: each row has a parent (manager) id. A recursive CTE walks it: the anchor selects the root(s), the recursive part joins children to the rows found so far, repeating until no new rows appear. Level and path columns record depth and ordering.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS lvl, CAST(name AS CHAR(300)) AS path FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, o.lvl + 1, CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', s.name) FROM staff s JOIN org o ON s.manager_id = o.id)
SELECT CONCAT(REPEAT('  ', lvl), name) AS chart FROM org ORDER BY path;

-- OUTPUT:
-- chart
-- Annaji
--   Moropant
--   Raoji
--     Kanhoji

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Common questions: all reports under a manager (anchor at that manager), the chain of managers above an employee (walk upward), team size per manager, depth of the tree, and leaf employees. Closure tables and materialized paths trade write cost for fast subtree reads.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE up AS (SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS steps FROM staff WHERE id = 4 UNION ALL SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, u.steps + 1 FROM staff s JOIN up u ON s.id = u.manager_id)
SELECT name, steps FROM up ORDER BY steps;
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (SELECT id AS mgr, id AS member FROM staff UNION ALL SELECT t.mgr, s.id FROM t JOIN staff s ON s.manager_id = t.member)
SELECT s.name, COUNT(*) - 1 AS team_size FROM t JOIN staff s ON s.id = t.mgr GROUP BY t.mgr, s.name HAVING team_size > 0;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name    | steps
-- Kanhoji | 0
-- Raoji   | 1
-- Annaji  | 2

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: aggregate over a subtree, e.g. the number of people under each manager, in one statement.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'CEO',NULL),(2,'CTO',1),(3,'CFO',1),(4,'Dev1',2),(5,'Dev2',2),(6,'Acct',3);

WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
    SELECT id AS root_id, id AS member_id FROM emp
    UNION ALL
    SELECT s.root_id, e.id FROM sub s JOIN emp e ON e.manager_id = s.member_id
)
SELECT e.name, COUNT(*) - 1 AS total_reports
FROM   sub s JOIN emp e ON e.id = s.root_id
GROUP  BY e.id, e.name
ORDER  BY total_reports DESC, e.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------------+
-- | name | total_reports |
-- +------+---------------+
-- | CEO  |             5 |
-- | CTO  |             2 |
-- | CFO  |             1 |
-- | Acct |             0 |
-- | Dev1 |             0 |
-- | Dev2 |             0 |
-- +------+---------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: bad data with a cycle (A manages B, B manages A) loops until the recursion limit. Guard by tracking the visited ids in the path.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE emp (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES (1,'Root',NULL),(7,'X',8),(8,'Y',7);          -- 7 and 8 manage each other

WITH RECURSIVE walk AS (
    SELECT id, name, CAST(id AS CHAR(100)) AS ids FROM emp WHERE id = 7
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.id, e.name, CONCAT(w.ids, ',', e.id)
    FROM   emp e JOIN walk w ON e.manager_id = w.id
    WHERE  FIND_IN_SET(e.id, w.ids) = 0                              -- stop when already visited
)
SELECT name, ids FROM walk;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+------+
-- | name | ids  |
-- +------+------+
-- | X    | 7    |
-- | Y    | 7,8  |
-- +------+------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: iteration is capped by cte_max_recursion_depth (default 1000), and the recursive part cannot use aggregate or window functions on the CTE itself. Very deep or hot trees may need a closure table.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@cte_max_recursion_depth AS default_depth;
SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 5000;
SELECT @@cte_max_recursion_depth AS new_depth;

-- Alternative: closure table, ancestor questions become one indexed join
-- CREATE TABLE emp_closure (ancestor INT, descendant INT, depth INT, PRIMARY KEY (ancestor, descendant));

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------------+
-- | default_depth |
-- +---------------+
-- |          1000 |
-- +---------------+
-- +-----------+
-- | new_depth |
-- +-----------+
-- |      5000 |
-- +-----------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Index manager_id; the recursion is then a series of index lookups. Add a depth limit and cycle guard for untrusted data. For read-heavy hierarchies (permissions, categories) store a materialised path or closure table so reads avoid recursion, and keep recursive CTEs for ad hoc reports.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Show an indented tree with CONCAT(REPEAT(" ", level), name) and order by path.
  • To list all descendants of a node, start the anchor at that node.
  • Protect from cycles with a path check or depth limit.

Senior Notes

  • Alternative models: materialized path (/1/4/9/), nested sets and closure tables trade write cost for fast subtree reads.
  • Index parent_id for the recursion; for huge trees prefer closure or path models.
  • Aggregations over subtrees (headcount, total salary) are natural with recursive CTEs plus GROUP BY on the root.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: cycles in the data (infinite recursion), several roots with NULL parent handled wrongly, path columns too short (truncation) and no index on the parent column. Guard with a path check and a recursion limit.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

For frequent subtree queries on large trees use a closure table (ancestor, descendant, depth) with an index on each side, making a subtree a single index range.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE staff_closure (ancestor INT, descendant INT, depth INT, PRIMARY KEY (ancestor, descendant), KEY idx_desc (descendant));
SELECT s.name FROM staff_closure c JOIN staff s ON s.id = c.descendant WHERE c.ancestor = 1 AND c.depth > 0;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name
-- Raoji
-- Moropant
-- Kanhoji

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: roll up total salary cost per manager, including all indirect reports, for a budgeting report.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE t AS (SELECT id AS mgr, id AS member FROM staff UNION ALL SELECT t.mgr, s.id FROM t JOIN staff s ON s.manager_id = t.member)
SELECT m.name, SUM(e.salary) AS total_cost, COUNT(*) AS headcount FROM t JOIN staff m ON m.id = t.mgr JOIN staff e ON e.id = t.member GROUP BY t.mgr, m.name ORDER BY total_cost DESC;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name   | total_cost | headcount
-- Annaji |        390 | 4

beginner.content:
Introduction

The anti-join: LEFT JOIN customers to orders and keep rows where the order side is NULL, which means no match was found.

Why Do We Need This?

NOT EXISTS expresses the same idea directly and is often the clearest, because it says "there is no order for this customer".

Real-Time Use

Marketing variation: customers with no order in the last 30 days (win-back campaign). Use a fixed reference date to keep it reproducible.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20));
CREATE TABLE orders    (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, created_at DATE);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Abaji'),(2,'Raoji'),(3,'Moropant');
INSERT INTO orders    VALUES (1,1,'2024-01-05'),(2,1,'2024-02-20'),(3,3,'2023-12-01');

SELECT c.name
FROM   customers c
WHERE  NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
                   WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
                     AND o.created_at >= DATE_SUB('2024-03-01', INTERVAL 30 DAY))
ORDER  BY c.name;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | name     |
-- +----------+
-- | Moropant |
-- | Raoji    |
-- +-------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   customers               orders
   +----+----------+       +----+-------------+
   | 1  | Abaji    |-----> | 1  | customer 1  |
   | 2  | Raoji    |   X   |    (no match)    |   -> o.id IS NULL  => Raoji
   | 3  | Moropant |-----> | 3  | customer 3  |
   +----+----------+       +----+-------------+

Fresher Notes

  • Find customers with no orders using an anti-join: LEFT JOIN orders and keep rows where the order id IS NULL, or use NOT EXISTS.
  • It answers "who has not bought anything?".
  • Avoid NOT IN when the subquery can return NULLs.

Worked Example 1

NOT IN trap.
codeExamples:
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);   -- orders has a NULL customer_id

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Index and plan.

Practice Exercise 1

Anti-join.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- OUTPUT:
-- id | name
--  2 | Raoji

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

NOT EXISTS with a date window.
codeExamples:
SELECT c.id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= NOW() - INTERVAL 90 DAY);

-- OUTPUT:
-- id
-- 2
-- 5

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

This is an anti-join: customers with no matching order. MySQL 8 recognises NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL as an antijoin and executes them with an index probe into the orders table for each customer, stopping at the first match. NOT IN is risky because a NULL in the subquery makes the whole predicate unknown.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: no orders ever, no orders in the last 90 days, no PAID orders, orders but never a refund. Put the extra conditions inside the NOT EXISTS subquery (or the ON clause of the LEFT JOIN), not in the outer WHERE.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe and the optimiser turns it into an efficient anti-join using the index on orders.customer_id.

Disadvantages

Disadvantages: NOT IN is a trap. If the subquery returns even one NULL, the comparison becomes unknown and the whole result is empty.

Limitations

Limitations: with LEFT JOIN the filter on the right table must go in ON, not WHERE. A WHERE condition on the right side silently turns the outer join into an inner join.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20));
CREATE TABLE orders    (id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, status VARCHAR(10));
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Abaji'),(2,'Raoji');
INSERT INTO orders    VALUES (1,1,'CANCELLED');

-- Customers with no PAID order
SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'PAID'
WHERE  o.id IS NULL ORDER BY c.name;                                  -- correct: condition in ON

SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE  o.id IS NULL AND o.status = 'PAID';                            -- wrong: always empty

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------+
-- | name  |
-- +-------+
-- | Abaji |
-- | Raoji |
-- +-------+
-- Empty set (0.00 sec)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Prefer NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe, optimiser-friendly) and index orders.customer_id. Define the business meaning first: never ordered, no paid order, or none recently. For big marketing queries run on a replica or a summary table, not on the primary.

Mid-Level Notes

  • NOT EXISTS is clear and NULL-safe; LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL is equivalent in MySQL 8 (antijoin).
  • Index orders(customer_id) so the check is cheap.
  • Add conditions inside the ON or subquery to scope by date or status (customers with no PAID orders).

Senior Notes

  • On large data use anti-join plans; verify with EXPLAIN that it does not scan orders per customer.
  • For marketing lists add exclusion rules and de-duplicate by email.
  • Snapshot results for repeatability: customer sets change as orders arrive.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: NOT IN with NULLs returning an empty set, filtering the right table in WHERE (turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join, losing the unmatched rows), and using COUNT(*) = 0 forms that scan more. Use NOT EXISTS.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (12, NULL);
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);            -- empty because of the NULL
SELECT id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);    -- correct

-- OUTPUT:
-- Empty set
-- id: 2, 3

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

The antijoin needs an index on orders.customer_id; without it each customer scans the orders table. Check for "Nested loop antijoin" and an index lookup in the tree plan.
codeExamples:
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT c.id FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -> Nested loop antijoin
--     -> Table scan on c
--     -> Single-row covering index lookup on o using idx_customer (customer_id=c.id)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a win-back campaign list: customers who signed up more than 30 days ago and still have no paid order, saved with a timestamp so later orders do not change the targeted set.
codeExamples:
INSERT INTO campaign_targets (campaign, customer_id, selected_at) SELECT 'winback-2026-05', c.id, NOW() FROM customers c
WHERE c.created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 30 DAY AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'PAID');

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 1840 rows affected

topics.name: Most Frequently Purchased Product & Monthly Revenue

beginner.content:
Introduction

Most purchased: sum quantity per product and take the top. Here Pen leads with 6 units.

Why Do We Need This?

LIMIT 1 hides ties. If two products share the top quantity, use RANK() = 1 to return all of them.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE sold (product VARCHAR(10), units INT);
INSERT INTO sold VALUES ('Pen',6),('Book',6),('Bag',1);

SELECT product, units
FROM  (SELECT product, units, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY units DESC) AS rk FROM sold) t
WHERE  rk = 1
ORDER  BY product;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+-------+
-- | product | units |
-- +---------+-------+
-- | Book    |     6 |
-- | Pen     |     6 |
-- +---------+-------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Monthly revenue is the staple report: group by year-month and sum quantity times the price snapshot.

Diagram

   orders --< order_items >-- products
      |             |
      |  month      |  qty * price
      +--> GROUP BY month --> SUM = revenue
   SUM(qty) GROUP BY product ORDER BY DESC LIMIT 1 --> best seller

Fresher Notes

  • Most frequently purchased product: group order items by product, sum quantity (or count orders), order descending and take the top row.
  • Monthly revenue: group by year and month of the order date and sum totals.
  • Use DATE_FORMAT or YEAR/MONTH for grouping.

Worked Example 1

Ties with DENSE_RANK.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, units FROM (SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS units, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(oi.qty) DESC) AS rk FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.id, p.name) t WHERE rk = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | units
-- Pen  | 420
-- Bag  | 420

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Zero-filled months.
codeExamples:
WITH RECURSIVE m AS (SELECT DATE('2026-01-01') AS d UNION ALL SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 MONTH FROM m WHERE d < '2026-03-01')
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(m.d,'%Y-%m') AS month, COALESCE(SUM(o.total),0) AS revenue FROM m LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.created_at >= m.d AND o.created_at < m.d + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AND o.status='PAID' GROUP BY m.d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- month   | revenue
-- 2026-01 | 12000.00
-- 2026-02 | 0.00
-- 2026-03 | 9000.00

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Top product.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS units FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY units DESC LIMIT 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | units
-- Pen  | 420

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Monthly revenue.
codeExamples:
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m') AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

-- OUTPUT:
-- month   | revenue
-- 2026-01 | 12000.00
-- 2026-02 | 15400.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

The most purchased product is a grouped aggregate over order items: group by product, sum quantity (or count orders), order descending and take the first row (or rank to include ties). Monthly revenue groups paid orders by month and sums totals. Both read the order tables once.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty) AS units FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY units DESC LIMIT 1;
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m') AS month, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' GROUP BY month ORDER BY month;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | units
-- Pen  |   420
-- month   | revenue
-- 2026-01 | 12000.00
-- 2026-02 | 15400.00

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Variants: ties for top product (DENSE_RANK), top product per category, months with zero revenue (calendar or recursive month series), revenue by product category, and revenue net of refunds.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: combine both: the best seller of every month with ROW_NUMBER over a partition.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE m (month CHAR(7), product VARCHAR(10), units INT);
INSERT INTO m VALUES ('2024-01','Pen',5),('2024-01','Book',1),
                     ('2024-02','Book',2),('2024-02','Bag',1),('2024-02','Pen',1);

SELECT month, product, units
FROM  (SELECT month, product, units,
              ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY month ORDER BY units DESC, product) AS rn
       FROM m) t
WHERE  rn = 1;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------+-------+
-- | month   | product | units |
-- +---------+---------+-------+
-- | 2024-01 | Pen     |     5 |
-- | 2024-02 | Book    |     2 |
-- +---------+---------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: months without sales do not appear at all, which leaves holes in charts. Generate the calendar and LEFT JOIN to fill zeros.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE rev (month DATE, revenue DECIMAL(10,2));
INSERT INTO rev VALUES ('2024-01-01',100),('2024-02-01',190);          -- March has no sales

WITH RECURSIVE cal AS (
    SELECT DATE '2024-01-01' AS month UNION ALL SELECT DATE_ADD(month, INTERVAL 1 MONTH) FROM cal WHERE month < '2024-03-01'
)
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(cal.month, '%Y-%m') AS month, COALESCE(rev.revenue, 0) AS revenue
FROM   cal LEFT JOIN rev ON rev.month = cal.month;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+---------+
-- | month   | revenue |
-- +---------+---------+
-- | 2024-01 |  100.00 |
-- | 2024-02 |  190.00 |
-- | 2024-03 |    0.00 |
-- +---------+---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: wrapping the date column in a function (DATE_FORMAT, YEAR) in WHERE prevents index use. Filter on a half-open date range instead.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE orders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, order_date DATE, KEY ix_date (order_date));
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'2024-01-10'),(2,'2024-01-20'),(3,'2024-02-05');

SELECT COUNT(*) AS jan_slow FROM orders WHERE DATE_FORMAT(order_date,'%Y-%m') = '2024-01';   -- full scan
SELECT COUNT(*) AS jan_fast FROM orders
WHERE  order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2024-02-01';                           -- index range

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----------+
-- | jan_slow |
-- +----------+
-- |        2 |
-- +----------+
-- +----------+
-- | jan_fast |
-- +----------+
-- |        2 |
-- +----------+
-- (same answer; EXPLAIN shows type ALL for the first and range for the second)

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Report from a pre-aggregated daily or monthly fact table once raw order_items grows into the hundreds of millions. Use half-open date ranges and covering indexes, store revenue snapshots in order_items, and run heavy analytics on a replica or in a warehouse to protect the primary.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Ties for top product: use DENSE_RANK or return all products with the max.
  • Include months with no sales via a calendar table and LEFT JOIN.
  • Revenue should come from order_items price x qty (or order totals) consistently, excluding cancelled orders.

Senior Notes

  • Group by an indexed date range per month for performance; avoid wrapping the date column in functions in WHERE.
  • Pre-aggregate daily/monthly summary tables for dashboards.
  • Time zones: group in the business time zone, not the server time zone.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: counting cancelled or unpaid orders, summing order totals after joining items (fan-out), grouping by a formatted month string on a huge table (no index), and ignoring time zones. Aggregate in a derived table, filter statuses and use date ranges.
codeExamples:
SELECT SUM(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id;      -- order total repeated per item
SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID';                              -- correct

-- OUTPUT:
-- first query overstates revenue; second is correct

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Speed up reporting with an index (status, created_at, total) and by pre-aggregating into a daily summary table that dashboards read instead of the raw tables.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world dashboard query: top five products this month with their revenue share of the month's total.
codeExamples:
SELECT p.name, SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) AS revenue, ROUND(100 * SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price) / SUM(SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM order_items oi JOIN orders o ON o.id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE o.status = 'PAID' AND o.created_at >= '2026-05-01' GROUP BY p.id, p.name ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 5;

-- OUTPUT:
-- name | revenue | pct
-- Pen  | 4200.00 | 18.2

beginner.content:
Introduction

Year-over-year growth compares each year with the previous one: (current - previous) / previous. LAG() fetches the previous row.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE yearly (yr INT PRIMARY KEY, revenue DECIMAL(12,2));
INSERT INTO yearly VALUES (2021,1000),(2022,1200),(2023,1500),(2024,1350);

SELECT yr, revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr)) / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr), 2) AS yoy_pct
FROM   yearly;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+---------+
-- | yr   | revenue | yoy_pct |
-- +------+---------+---------+
-- | 2021 | 1000.00 |    NULL |
-- | 2022 | 1200.00 |   20.00 |
-- | 2023 | 1500.00 |   25.00 |
-- | 2024 | 1350.00 |  -10.00 |
-- +------+---------+---------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

A previous value of zero would divide by zero. In MySQL that gives NULL (with a warning in strict DML), so protect with NULLIF and handle it explicitly.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE yearly (yr INT PRIMARY KEY, revenue DECIMAL(12,2));
INSERT INTO yearly VALUES (2020,0),(2021,1000);

SELECT yr, ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr))
                      / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr), 0), 2) AS yoy_pct
FROM   yearly;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------+---------+
-- | yr   | yoy_pct |
-- +------+---------+
-- | 2020 |    NULL |
-- | 2021 |    NULL |      <- previous was 0: growth undefined, not an error
-- +------+---------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Retention: of the users who first appeared in a month, how many came back the next month? Cohort = month of first activity.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE activity (user_id INT, m DATE);                  -- m = first day of the active month
INSERT INTO activity VALUES (1,'2024-01-01'),(1,'2024-02-01'),(1,'2024-03-01'),
                            (2,'2024-01-01'),(2,'2024-02-01'),
                            (3,'2024-01-01'),
                            (4,'2024-02-01'),(4,'2024-03-01');

WITH f AS (SELECT user_id, MIN(m) AS cohort FROM activity GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT f.cohort,
       COUNT(DISTINCT f.user_id)                                         AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)                                         AS retained_m1,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT f.user_id), 2) AS retention_pct
FROM   f LEFT JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = f.user_id AND a.m = DATE_ADD(f.cohort, INTERVAL 1 MONTH)
GROUP  BY f.cohort
ORDER  BY f.cohort;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+-------------+-------------+---------------+
-- | cohort     | cohort_size | retained_m1 | retention_pct |
-- +------------+-------------+-------------+---------------+
-- | 2024-01-01 |           3 |           2 |         66.67 |
-- | 2024-02-01 |           1 |           1 |        100.00 |
-- +------------+-------------+-------------+---------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Cohort Jan: u1 u2 u3   (3)
   month 0 : u1 u2 u3  = 3   100%
   month 1 : u1 u2     = 2    66.7%
   month 2 : u1        = 1    33.3%
   YoY = (this year - last year) / last year  via LAG or self join on yr - 1

Fresher Notes

  • Year-over-year (YoY) growth compares a period with the same period last year: (this_year - last_year) / last_year.
  • Retention measures how many customers return after their first purchase or signup.
  • Both use aggregation plus window functions like LAG.

Worked Example 1

Retention percentage.
codeExamples:
SELECT cohort, month_offset, ROUND(users * 100 / FIRST_VALUE(users) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort ORDER BY month_offset), 1) AS retention_pct FROM cohort_counts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cohort     | month_offset | retention_pct
-- 2026-01-01 | 0            | 100.0
-- 2026-01-01 | 1            |  42.0

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Quarter-over-quarter.
codeExamples:
SELECT q, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY q) AS qoq_change FROM (SELECT CONCAT(YEAR(created_at),'-Q',QUARTER(created_at)) AS q, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY q) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- q       | revenue | qoq_change
-- 2026-Q1 |   40000 | NULL
-- 2026-Q2 |   46000 | 6000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

YoY growth.
codeExamples:
SELECT yr, revenue, ROUND((revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr)) / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr), 0) * 100, 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM (SELECT YEAR(created_at) AS yr, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' GROUP BY YEAR(created_at)) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- yr   | revenue | yoy_pct
-- 2024 |  100000 | NULL
-- 2025 |  130000 | 30.0
-- 2026 |  117000 | -10.0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Cohort retention.
codeExamples:
WITH first_order AS (SELECT user_id, DATE_FORMAT(MIN(created_at),'%Y-%m-01') AS cohort FROM orders GROUP BY user_id),
act AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_FORMAT(created_at,'%Y-%m-01') AS m FROM orders)
SELECT f.cohort, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, f.cohort, a.m) AS month_offset, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS users
FROM first_order f JOIN act a ON a.user_id = f.user_id GROUP BY f.cohort, month_offset ORDER BY f.cohort, month_offset;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cohort     | month_offset | users
-- 2026-01-01 | 0            | 100
-- 2026-01-01 | 1            |  42
-- 2026-01-01 | 2            |  31

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Year-over-year growth compares a period with the same period a year earlier: (current - previous) / previous. Aggregate revenue per year (or month), then bring the previous value alongside with LAG (or a self join). Retention analysis assigns each customer to a cohort (their first month) and counts how many are active in each later month.
codeExamples:
SELECT yr, revenue, ROUND((revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr)) / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY yr), 0) * 100, 1) AS yoy_pct
FROM (SELECT YEAR(created_at) AS yr, SUM(total) AS revenue FROM orders WHERE status = 'PAID' GROUP BY YEAR(created_at)) t;

-- OUTPUT:
-- yr   | revenue | yoy_pct
-- 2024 |  100000 | NULL
-- 2025 |  130000 | 30.0
-- 2026 |  117000 | -10.0

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Cohort retention: cohort = month of first order; activity = distinct months with an order; month offset = months between cohort and activity month; retention percent = active users divided by cohort size. Month-over-month and same-month-last-year comparisons use LAG with offsets 1 and 12.
codeExamples:
WITH first_order AS (SELECT user_id, DATE_FORMAT(MIN(created_at), '%Y-%m-01') AS cohort FROM orders GROUP BY user_id),
act AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE_FORMAT(created_at, '%Y-%m-01') AS m FROM orders)
SELECT f.cohort, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, f.cohort, a.m) AS month_offset, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS users FROM first_order f JOIN act a ON a.user_id = f.user_id GROUP BY f.cohort, month_offset ORDER BY f.cohort, month_offset;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cohort     | month_offset | users
-- 2026-01-01 | 0            | 100
-- 2026-01-01 | 1            |  42
-- 2026-01-01 | 2            |  31

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the same pattern gives the whole retention triangle: count active users at each month offset since the cohort month.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE activity (user_id INT, m DATE);
INSERT INTO activity VALUES (1,'2024-01-01'),(1,'2024-02-01'),(1,'2024-03-01'),
                            (2,'2024-01-01'),(2,'2024-02-01'),(3,'2024-01-01'),
                            (4,'2024-02-01'),(4,'2024-03-01');

WITH f AS (SELECT user_id, MIN(m) AS cohort FROM activity GROUP BY user_id)
SELECT f.cohort, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH, f.cohort, a.m) AS month_offset, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS users
FROM   f JOIN activity a ON a.user_id = f.user_id
GROUP  BY f.cohort, month_offset
ORDER  BY f.cohort, month_offset;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +------------+--------------+-------+
-- | cohort     | month_offset | users |
-- +------------+--------------+-------+
-- | 2024-01-01 |            0 |     3 |
-- | 2024-01-01 |            1 |     2 |
-- | 2024-01-01 |            2 |     1 |
-- | 2024-02-01 |            0 |     1 |
-- | 2024-02-01 |            1 |     1 |
-- +------------+--------------+-------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: LAG looks at the previous row, not the previous year. If a year is missing, it compares against the wrong period.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE yearly (yr INT PRIMARY KEY, revenue DECIMAL(12,2));
INSERT INTO yearly VALUES (2021,1000),(2022,1200),(2024,1500);          -- 2023 missing

-- Wrong: 2024 compared with 2022
SELECT yr, LAG(yr) OVER (ORDER BY yr) AS compared_with FROM yearly;

-- Right: join on the exact previous year
SELECT c.yr, ROUND(100 * (c.revenue - p.revenue) / p.revenue, 2) AS yoy_pct
FROM   yearly c LEFT JOIN yearly p ON p.yr = c.yr - 1
ORDER  BY c.yr;

-- OUTPUT:
-- 2021 NULL | 2022 2021 | 2024 2022     (wrong pairing)
-- +------+---------+
-- | yr   | yoy_pct |
-- +------+---------+
-- | 2021 |    NULL |
-- | 2022 |   20.00 |
-- | 2024 |    NULL |
-- +------+---------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: MySQL division returns a DECIMAL with div_precision_increment extra digits (default 4), and integer division needs DIV. Round explicitly for reports.

Architect's Notes

Compute cohorts once into a summary table (cohort, offset, users) refreshed daily; do not rescan raw events for every dashboard load. Define active, cohort and period precisely with stakeholders because retention numbers are easy to make misleading. Use a self join or calendar join when periods can be missing.

Mid-Level Notes

  • YoY: aggregate revenue by year, then LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY year) to get the previous year.
  • Cohort retention: assign each user a cohort (first month), then count active users per cohort per month offset.
  • Divide by cohort size for percentages; guard against divide by zero with NULLIF.

Senior Notes

  • Use a user activity table (user_id, activity_month) to simplify cohorts.
  • Large datasets: pre-aggregate monthly activity per user into a summary table.
  • Be precise on definitions (active = purchase vs login; rolling vs calendar months) and document them.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: undefined "active" (purchase, login, any event?), comparing partial periods (the current month versus a full previous month), division by zero, and mixing calendar and rolling months. Fix the definitions and document them with the query.
codeExamples:
SELECT cohort, month_offset, ROUND(100 * users / FIRST_VALUE(users) OVER (PARTITION BY cohort ORDER BY month_offset), 1) AS retention_pct FROM cohort_counts;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cohort     | month_offset | retention_pct
-- 2026-01-01 | 0            | 100.0
-- 2026-01-01 | 1            |  42.0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Large event tables should be reduced first to one row per user and month in a summary table, then cohort queries become small joins. Index (user_id, month) and (month).

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a growth dashboard showing revenue, year-over-year change and month-1, month-3 and month-6 retention by signup cohort, refreshed nightly from summary tables.
codeExamples:
SELECT cohort, MAX(CASE WHEN month_offset = 1 THEN retention_pct END) AS m1, MAX(CASE WHEN month_offset = 3 THEN retention_pct END) AS m3, MAX(CASE WHEN month_offset = 6 THEN retention_pct END) AS m6 FROM retention_pivot GROUP BY cohort ORDER BY cohort;

-- OUTPUT:
-- cohort     | m1   | m3   | m6
-- 2026-01-01 | 42.0 | 31.0 | 24.0

beginner.content:
Introduction

Production MySQL is watched through three signals: metrics (status counters), logs (slow query, error) and traces of statements (performance_schema). Start with the handful of counters that predict trouble.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS
WHERE Variable_name IN ('Threads_connected','Threads_running','Slow_queries','Aborted_connects','Questions');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-------------------+----------+
-- | Variable_name     | Value    |
-- +-------------------+----------+
-- | Aborted_connects  | 3        |
-- | Questions         | 18450211 |
-- | Slow_queries      | 41       |
-- | Threads_connected | 87       |
-- | Threads_running   | 4        |
-- +-------------------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Raw numbers are useless without capacity context. Connection usage as a percentage of max_connections is the classic alert: at 100 percent new clients are refused.
codeExamples:
SELECT ts.VARIABLE_VALUE                       AS connected,
       @@max_connections                        AS max_conn,
       ROUND(100 * ts.VARIABLE_VALUE / @@max_connections, 1) AS pct_used
FROM   performance_schema.global_status ts
WHERE  ts.VARIABLE_NAME = 'Threads_connected';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-----------+----------+----------+
-- | connected | max_conn | pct_used |
-- +-----------+----------+----------+
-- | 87        |      500 |     17.4 |
-- +-----------+----------+----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

The slow query log is the first tool for finding bad SQL. Enable it dynamically, then rank statements with the sys schema.
codeExamples:
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log      = 'ON';
SET GLOBAL long_query_time      = 0.5;                  -- seconds
SET GLOBAL log_slow_extra       = 'ON';                 -- more fields per entry (8.0.14+)

SELECT query, exec_count, avg_latency, rows_examined_avg
FROM   sys.statement_analysis
ORDER  BY total_latency DESC
LIMIT  3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +--------------------------------------------+------------+-------------+-------------------+
-- | query                                      | exec_count | avg_latency | rows_examined_avg |
-- +--------------------------------------------+------------+-------------+-------------------+
-- | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = ?      |      12044 | 812.40 ms   |            480211 |
-- | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE ts > ?   |        930 | 1.92 s      |           2210007 |
-- | UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - ? WHERE id = ?|      88201 | 1.10 ms     |                 1 |
-- +--------------------------------------------+------------+-------------+-------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   MySQL --status counters--> exporter --> Prometheus --> Grafana --> alerts
     |---- slow log / error log --> Loki / ELK ---------> search
     +---- performance_schema (digests, waits) --> sys schema --> top queries
   Golden signals: latency, traffic (QPS), errors, saturation (connections, buffer pool, replica lag)

Fresher Notes

  • Monitoring watches the health of MySQL: availability, connections, queries, replication, disk and memory.
  • Logs: error log, slow query log, binary log, general log (rarely).
  • Metrics are numbers over time: QPS, latency, connections, buffer pool hit rate, replication lag.

Worked Example 1

Disk space alert query (OS metric).
codeExamples:
node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/var/lib/mysql"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes < 0.2

-- OUTPUT:
-- fires when less than 20% disk remains on the data volume

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Error log tail.
codeExamples:
SELECT logged, prio, error_code, LEFT(data, 80) AS msg FROM performance_schema.error_log ORDER BY logged DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- logged              | prio  | error_code | msg
-- 2026-05-01 10:00:01 | Note  | MY-010931  | /usr/sbin/mysqld: ready for connections

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Key status counters.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Questions','Threads_connected','Threads_running','Slow_queries','Aborted_connects','Uptime');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Questions         | 98765432
-- Slow_queries      | 412
-- Threads_connected | 118
-- Threads_running   | 6
-- Aborted_connects  | 12
-- Uptime            | 864000

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Prometheus alert examples.
codeExamples:
- alert: MySQLDown
  expr: mysql_up == 0
  for: 1m
- alert: MySQLTooManyConnections
  expr: mysql_global_status_threads_connected / mysql_global_variables_max_connections > 0.8
  for: 5m

-- OUTPUT:
-- alerts fire only when the condition persists

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Monitoring turns server internals into signals you can alert on. Metrics come from status counters (SHOW GLOBAL STATUS), the Performance Schema and sys schema, the OS (CPU, memory, disk, network) and the application. Logs complement metrics: the error log, slow query log, binary log, audit log and general log (rarely). Use the four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
codeExamples:
SHOW GLOBAL STATUS WHERE Variable_name IN ('Questions','Threads_connected','Threads_running','Slow_queries','Aborted_connects','Uptime','Innodb_row_lock_waits');
SELECT logged, prio, error_code, LEFT(data, 70) AS msg FROM performance_schema.error_log ORDER BY logged DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Questions         | 98765432
-- Threads_running   |        6
-- Slow_queries      |      412
-- logged              | prio | error_code | msg
-- 2026-05-01 10:00:01 | Note | MY-010931  | /usr/sbin/mysqld: ready for connections

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Collection stack: mysqld_exporter into Prometheus and Grafana, Percona PMM, or cloud monitoring (CloudWatch, Datadog). Rates come from counter differences over time, not raw values. Keep application-side metrics too: pool wait time, error rate, query latency per endpoint.
codeExamples:
# prometheus rules
- record: mysql:qps
  expr: rate(mysql_global_status_questions[1m])
- alert: MySQLTooManyConnections
  expr: mysql_global_status_threads_connected / mysql_global_variables_max_connections > 0.8
  for: 5m
- alert: MySQLDown
  expr: mysql_up == 0
  for: 1m

-- OUTPUT:
-- alerts fire only when the condition persists for the stated duration

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: performance_schema groups statements by digest (normalised text), so thousands of similar queries become one row with count and total time. It is built in and needs no agent.
codeExamples:
SELECT LEFT(DIGEST_TEXT, 40)                 AS query,
       COUNT_STAR                             AS calls,
       ROUND(SUM_TIMER_WAIT / 1e12, 2)        AS total_s,
       ROUND(AVG_TIMER_WAIT / 1e9, 2)         AS avg_ms
FROM   performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest
ORDER  BY SUM_TIMER_WAIT DESC
LIMIT  2;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +------------------------------------------+-------+---------+--------+
-- | query                                    | calls | total_s | avg_ms |
-- +------------------------------------------+-------+---------+--------+
-- | SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = ?    | 12044 |    9784 | 812.40 |
-- | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE ts > ? |   930 |    1786 |1920.00 |
-- +------------------------------------------+-------+---------+--------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: observability has a cost. The general log records every statement and can fill a disk and slow the server, so it stays off in production; slow logs need rotation.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@general_log AS general_log, @@slow_query_log AS slow_log, @@slow_query_log_file AS slow_file;

FLUSH SLOW LOGS;          -- reopen the slow log file after logrotate renamed it

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-------------+----------+-------------------------------+
-- | general_log | slow_log | slow_file                     |
-- +-------------+----------+-------------------------------+
-- |           0 |        1 | /var/lib/mysql/db1-slow.log   |
-- +-------------+----------+-------------------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations
