Limitations: status counters are cumulative since startup and reset on restart. Rates come from the difference of two samples, which your monitoring system (Prometheus mysqld_exporter, PMM) computes. Only the latest deadlock is kept unless you log all of them.

Architect's Notes

Alert on symptoms users feel (latency, errors, replication lag, disk, connections) and keep causes (digests, locks, buffer pool) for diagnosis. Keep long_query_time low enough to be useful but sample or rotate to bound cost, and ship logs off the box. Dashboards without runbooks do not reduce downtime.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Collect with exporters (mysqld_exporter), Percona PMM, CloudWatch or Datadog, and visualize in Grafana.
  • Use golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.
  • Alert on symptoms (high latency, errors, lag) and on capacity (disk < 20%, connections > 80%).

Senior Notes

  • Alert fatigue kills monitoring: page only on actionable issues; send the rest to dashboards or tickets.
  • Keep long-term metrics for capacity planning and seasonality.
  • Monitor from the application side too (error rates, pool wait times) because DB health alone does not show user impact.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: alerting on every metric (alert fatigue), no baselines (what is normal?), monitoring only the database and not user impact, and no disk-space or replication alerts. Alert on symptoms and capacity, and review noisy alerts regularly.
codeExamples:
- alert: MySQLDiskSpaceLow
  expr: node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/var/lib/mysql"} / node_filesystem_size_bytes < 0.2
  for: 10m
- alert: MySQLReplicaLagHigh
  expr: mysql_slave_status_seconds_behind_master > 30
  for: 5m

-- OUTPUT:
-- the two alerts that most often prevent outages: disk space and replication lag

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Dashboards worth having: QPS and latency percentiles, connections and running threads, buffer pool hit rate and dirty pages, InnoDB row lock waits and deadlocks, history list length, replication lag, temp tables on disk, top digests by total time, disk and I/O latency.
codeExamples:
SELECT (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_row_lock_waits') AS lock_waits,
       (SELECT VARIABLE_VALUE FROM performance_schema.global_status WHERE VARIABLE_NAME = 'Created_tmp_disk_tables') AS disk_tmp,
       (SELECT count FROM information_schema.innodb_metrics WHERE name = 'trx_rseg_history_len') AS history_len;

-- OUTPUT:
-- lock_waits | disk_tmp | history_len
-- 8120       |    18200 |         312

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world on-call runbook entry: an alert fires on high running threads. Steps: check processlist states, long transactions, lock waits, top digests, recent deploys, then decide to kill, roll back or scale.

beginner.content:
Introduction

EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) runs the query and prints the plan with real timings and row counts, so you see where time is actually spent.

Why Do We Need This?

Capacity planning starts with knowing where the bytes are. information_schema.TABLES gives data and index size per table.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name,
       ROUND(data_length  / 1024 / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS data_gb,
       ROUND(index_length / 1024 / 1024 / 1024, 2) AS index_gb,
       table_rows
FROM   information_schema.TABLES
WHERE  table_schema = 'shop'
ORDER  BY data_length + index_length DESC
LIMIT  3;

-- OUTPUT: (example; table_rows is an estimate)
-- +-------------+---------+----------+------------+
-- | table_name  | data_gb | index_gb | table_rows |
-- +-------------+---------+----------+------------+
-- | order_items |   41.20 |    18.75 |  310000000 |
-- | orders      |   12.40 |     6.10 |   95000000 |
-- | customers   |    1.10 |     0.40 |    4200000 |
-- +-------------+---------+----------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Record size snapshots on a schedule and project growth. This turns "the disk is full" surprises into a planned purchase.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE capacity_log (month DATE PRIMARY KEY, gb DECIMAL(8,2));
INSERT INTO capacity_log VALUES ('2024-01-01',100),('2024-02-01',110),('2024-03-01',121);

WITH d AS (SELECT month, gb, gb - LAG(gb) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS delta FROM capacity_log)
SELECT MAX(gb)                              AS now_gb,
       ROUND(AVG(delta), 2)                 AS avg_gb_per_month,
       ROUND(MAX(gb) + 6 * AVG(delta), 2)   AS in_6_months
FROM   d;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +--------+------------------+-------------+
-- | now_gb | avg_gb_per_month | in_6_months |
-- +--------+------------------+-------------+
-- | 121.00 |            10.50 |      184.00 |
-- +--------+------------------+-------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   query --> EXPLAIN ANALYZE --> estimated rows vs actual rows --> index / rewrite
   data growth: size now ---- +10.5 GB/month ----> in 6 months 184 GB
   disk budget = projection x (1 + 30% headroom) + backups + binlogs
   memory: working set vs innodb_buffer_pool_size (hit ratio near 99.9%)

Fresher Notes

  • Query profiling finds where a query spends time. Capacity planning predicts when you will run out of CPU, memory, disk or connections.
  • Tools: EXPLAIN ANALYZE, Performance Schema stages, sys schema, APM traces.
  • Plan by looking at growth trends.

Worked Example 1

Forecast runway.
codeExamples:
SELECT 400 AS disk_gb, 310 AS used_gb, 9 AS growth_gb_per_month, ROUND((400 * 0.8 - 310) / 9, 1) AS months_until_80pct;

-- OUTPUT:
-- disk_gb | used_gb | growth_gb_per_month | months_until_80pct
-- 400     | 310     | 9                   | 1.1

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Working set check.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(SUM(data_length + index_length)/1024/1024/1024,1) AS total_gb, ROUND(@@innodb_buffer_pool_size/1024/1024/1024,1) AS pool_gb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT:
-- total_gb | pool_gb
-- 190.0    | 64.0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Profile stages.

Practice Exercise 2

Table growth.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND((data_length + index_length)/1024/1024/1024, 2) AS gb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY gb DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- table_name  | gb
-- order_items | 84.20
-- orders      | 41.70

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Profiling finds where a query spends time: EXPLAIN ANALYZE (per iterator), Performance Schema stages and waits, sys views, and APM traces. Capacity planning predicts when a resource (CPU, memory, disk, IOPS, connections) will run out, from growth trends and load tests, so you scale before saturation.

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Inputs for planning: data growth per month and retention, index overhead, row and request growth, peak versus average load, working set size against RAM, IOPS and throughput needs, connection counts, and failure headroom (what happens when a node is down). Load tests provide the missing numbers.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, ROUND((data_length + index_length) / 1073741824, 1) AS gb FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_schema = 'shop' ORDER BY gb DESC LIMIT 3;
SELECT ROUND(400 * 0.8 - 310) / 9 AS months_until_80pct_disk;

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name  | gb
-- order_items | 84.2
-- months_until_80pct_disk
-- 1.1111

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the sys schema finds waste: indexes never used still cost write time, memory and disk.
codeExamples:
SELECT object_schema, object_name, index_name
FROM   sys.schema_unused_indexes
WHERE  object_schema = 'shop';

SELECT table_name, redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name
FROM   sys.schema_redundant_indexes
WHERE  table_schema = 'shop';

-- OUTPUT: (example; usage is counted since the last restart, so check after a full business cycle)
-- +---------------+-------------+-----------------+
-- | object_schema | object_name | index_name      |
-- +---------------+-------------+-----------------+
-- | shop          | orders      | ix_orders_notes |
-- +---------------+-------------+-----------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: the memory side of capacity is the buffer pool. If reads constantly miss it, the disk becomes the bottleneck. EXPLAIN ANALYZE also really executes the statement, so use care on heavy queries.
codeExamples:
SELECT ROUND(100 * (1 - r.VARIABLE_VALUE / q.VARIABLE_VALUE), 2) AS buffer_pool_hit_pct
FROM   performance_schema.global_status r, performance_schema.global_status q
WHERE  r.VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_reads'
  AND  q.VARIABLE_NAME = 'Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +----------------------+
-- | buffer_pool_hit_pct  |
-- +----------------------+
-- |                99.97 |
-- +----------------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: the optimiser works from statistics. When estimated rows differ wildly from actual rows, the plan is probably bad; refresh statistics or add a histogram.
codeExamples:
ANALYZE TABLE orders;                                        -- refresh index statistics
ANALYZE TABLE orders UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON status WITH 16 BUCKETS;   -- 8.0: data distribution for non-indexed columns

-- Plan line to inspect in EXPLAIN ANALYZE: (cost=... rows=EST) (actual ... rows=ACT)
--   EST 10 vs ACT 480000 => stale or skewed stats

-- OUTPUT:
-- +-------------+-----------+----------+-----------------------------------------------+
-- | Table       | Op        | Msg_type | Msg_text                                      |
-- +-------------+-----------+----------+-----------------------------------------------+
-- | shop.orders | analyze   | status   | OK                                            |
-- | shop.orders | histogram | status   | Histogram statistics created for column 'status'. |
-- +-------------+-----------+----------+-----------------------------------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Plan capacity on the slowest resource: usually IO and the working set in memory, not CPU. Track growth per table, add headroom of at least 30 percent for online DDL and backups, and review unused indexes regularly. Load-test with production-sized data, since plans change with table size.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Profile with EXPLAIN ANALYZE per node and Performance Schema events_stages_* for waits.
  • Capacity inputs: data growth per month, QPS growth, working set versus RAM, IOPS and throughput limits.
  • Run load tests that mimic production patterns to find limits.

Senior Notes

  • Forecast with headroom (e.g. keep peak below 60-70% of capacity) and plan lead times for scaling or archiving.
  • Identify the first bottleneck: often I/O or a hot row/lock, not CPU.
  • Record baselines per release to spot regressions that change capacity needs.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: planning from averages instead of peaks, ignoring growth of indexes and backups, testing with data too small to show cache effects, and no headroom for failover (when one replica is down the others carry its load). Plan for peak plus a safety margin, typically 30-40% free.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Load test realistically: production-like data volume and skew, replayed or synthetic traffic with the real mix of reads and writes, warm caches, and measurement of latency percentiles and saturation indicators, not just throughput.
codeExamples:
sysbench oltp_read_write --mysql-host=db --mysql-user=bench --mysql-password=*** --mysql-db=bench --tables=16 --table-size=10000000 --threads=64 --time=300 run

-- OUTPUT: (summary)
-- transactions: 41200 per sec   latency 95th percentile: 18.95 ms   errors: 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: a table growing 9 GB per month on a 400 GB volume had one month of runway. Capacity review caught it, and the fix was partitioning with retention plus archiving, not just a bigger disk.

beginner.content:
Introduction

A backup is only real if it restores. Logical backups with mysqldump are portable and readable; --single-transaction takes a consistent InnoDB snapshot without locking writers, and --source-data=2 records the binlog position as a comment.
codeExamples:
-- Run from the shell (shown as comments):
--   mysqldump --single-transaction --routines --triggers --events --source-data=2 shop > shop_full.sql
-- Check the recorded binlog coordinates in the dump header:
--   grep -m1 "CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE" shop_full.sql

SHOW MASTER STATUS;       -- same coordinates on the live server (SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS in newer 8.4)

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- -- CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO SOURCE_LOG_FILE='binlog.000412', SOURCE_LOG_POS=157;
-- +---------------+----------+
-- | File          | Position |
-- +---------------+----------+
-- | binlog.000412 |      157 |
-- +---------------+----------+

beginner.content:
Why Do We Need This?

Untested backups fail when needed (truncated file, missing grants, wrong version). Restore into a scratch server on a schedule and compare row counts and checksums with the source.
codeExamples:
-- On source and on the restored copy, run the same checks and compare:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS order_rows FROM shop.orders;
CHECKSUM TABLE shop.orders, shop.customers;

-- Automate: restore latest dump -> run checks -> alert if any value differs or restore fails.

-- OUTPUT: (example; both servers must print identical values)
-- +------------+
-- | order_rows |
-- +------------+
-- |    9500000 |
-- +------------+
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | Table          | Checksum   |
-- +----------------+------------+
-- | shop.orders    | 2841190325 |
-- | shop.customers | 1209981172 |
-- +----------------+------------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Disaster recovery needs point-in-time recovery (PITR): restore the last full backup, then replay binary logs up to just before the mistake (for example an accidental DROP at 14:05).
codeExamples:
SHOW BINARY LOGS;

-- Shell: replay from the backup position to one second before the bad statement
--   mysqlbinlog --start-position=157 --stop-datetime="2024-05-10 14:04:59" binlog.000412 binlog.000413 | mysql -u root -p

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +---------------+-----------+-----------+
-- | Log_name      | File_size | Encrypted |
-- +---------------+-----------+-----------+
-- | binlog.000412 | 104857712 | No        |
-- | binlog.000413 |  52113640 | No        |
-- +---------------+-----------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   full backup (nightly) ---+
   binlogs (continuous) ----+--> restore full --> replay binlog to T-1s --> verify --> cut over
   scratch server: weekly automated restore + CHECKSUM compare  (proves the backup)
   store copies off-site and in another region; encrypt them

Fresher Notes

  • A backup you have never restored is not a backup. Verification means regularly restoring and checking the data.
  • Disaster recovery uses verified backups and standbys to bring service back in another location.
  • Automate checks and alert on failures.

Worked Example 1

Record results.

Worked Example 2

Alert if the last verified backup is old.
codeExamples:
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, MAX(restored_at), NOW()) AS hours_since_verified FROM ops.backup_checks WHERE status = 'OK';

-- OUTPUT:
-- hours_since_verified
-- 14

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Restore and validate (script outline).
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/restore/latest
# start a temporary mysqld on port 3399 with datadir=/restore/latest
mysql -P3399 -e "CHECK TABLE shop.orders; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders;"

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table       | Op    | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.orders | check | status   | OK
-- COUNT(*)
-- 120450889

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Compare checksums with the source replica.
codeExamples:
CHECKSUM TABLE shop.orders;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table       | Checksum
-- shop.orders | 2918457613

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

A backup is only proven when it has been restored. Verification means restoring into a scratch environment, checking the database starts, running integrity checks (CHECK TABLE, checksums, row counts), and exercising the application against it. It also measures real restore time, which is your actual RTO.
codeExamples:
xtrabackup --prepare --target-dir=/restore/latest
# start a temporary mysqld on port 3399 with datadir=/restore/latest
mysql -P3399 -e "CHECK TABLE shop.orders; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM shop.orders;"

-- OUTPUT:
-- Table       | Op    | Msg_type | Msg_text
-- shop.orders | check | status   | OK
-- COUNT(*)
-- 120450889

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Automate it: a nightly job restores the latest backup, replays binlogs to a target time, runs validation queries, compares checksums or row counts with a replica, records duration, and alerts on failure. Disaster recovery adds a standby in another failure domain and a rehearsed runbook.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: the Clone plugin (8.0.17+) copies a whole physical data directory quickly, handy for seeding replicas and fast restores of big servers.
codeExamples:
INSTALL PLUGIN clone SONAME 'mysql_clone.so';
CLONE LOCAL DATA DIRECTORY = '/backup/clone_2024_05_10';        -- target must not exist
SELECT STATE, ERROR_NO FROM performance_schema.clone_status;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-----------+----------+
-- | STATE     | ERROR_NO |
-- +-----------+----------+
-- | Completed |        0 |
-- +-----------+----------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: logical dumps are slow to restore for terabytes, and --single-transaction is only consistent for InnoDB. Find non-transactional tables before you trust a dump.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_schema, table_name, engine
FROM   information_schema.TABLES
WHERE  engine <> 'InnoDB'
  AND  table_schema NOT IN ('mysql','sys','information_schema','performance_schema');

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +--------------+------------+--------+
-- | table_schema | table_name | engine |
-- +--------------+------------+--------+
-- | legacy       | sessions   | MyISAM |
-- +--------------+------------+--------+      <- not covered by a consistent snapshot

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: recovery points depend on binlog retention. If binlogs expire before the next full backup you cannot do PITR across that gap. RPO is the data you can lose; RTO is the time to be back.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@binlog_expire_logs_seconds / 86400 AS retention_days,
       @@sync_binlog                          AS sync_binlog,
       @@innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit       AS flush_at_commit;

-- RPO ~ 0 needs sync_binlog=1 and innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 (durable) plus replication/off-site binlog copy
-- RTO ~ restore time + binlog replay time (measure it in drills)

-- OUTPUT: (example, defaults)
-- +----------------+-------------+-----------------+
-- | retention_days | sync_binlog | flush_at_commit |
-- +----------------+-------------+-----------------+
-- |        30.0000 |           1 |               1 |
-- +----------------+-------------+-----------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Define RPO and RTO with the business, then choose tools: logical dumps for small data, XtraBackup or Clone for large, binlog shipping for PITR, and replicas or a cluster for fast failover. Backups do not replace replication and replication does not replace backups (a bad DELETE replicates instantly). Run restore drills and time them.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Verify: restore to a scratch server, run integrity checks (CHECK TABLE, row counts, checksums) and sample queries.
  • Record restore time to validate RTO.
  • Keep backups encrypted and off-site with retention rules.

Senior Notes

  • Automate a nightly restore-and-validate pipeline; publish results as metrics.
  • Test point-in-time recovery, not only full restores.
  • Run DR game days: simulate region loss and measure real RTO/RPO and the effort needed.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: never testing restores, backups stored beside the data, missing binlogs (no point-in-time recovery), encrypted backups with lost keys, and a runbook nobody has run. Test restore and decryption with the keys stored separately.
codeExamples:
SELECT backup_name, TIMESTAMPDIFF(HOUR, verified_at, NOW()) AS hours_since_verified FROM ops.backup_catalog ORDER BY finished_at DESC LIMIT 1;
-- alert when hours_since_verified > 26

-- OUTPUT:
-- backup_name    | hours_since_verified
-- full-2026-05-01|                    5

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Measure recovery time and data loss in drills and compare with the targets. Break the time down: fetch backup, decrypt, copy, prepare, replay binlog, validation, DNS and application warm-up.
codeExamples:
SELECT step, minutes FROM ops.restore_timing WHERE drill_id = 7 ORDER BY step_no;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- step              | minutes
-- fetch from S3     |      14
-- prepare           |      11
-- binlog replay     |       6
-- validation        |       4
-- total             |      35

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world: an annual region-loss exercise restores production backups in the DR region, runs the application against it and records every gap found (missing secrets, outdated runbook, wrong DNS TTL), with owners and deadlines.
codeExamples:
SELECT scenario, TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE, started_at, finished_at) AS minutes, gaps_found, gaps_fixed FROM ops.dr_tests ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 2;

-- OUTPUT:
-- scenario    | minutes | gaps_found | gaps_fixed
-- region-loss |      72 |          6 |          6

beginner.content:
Introduction

Hardening starts with least privilege: each application gets its own account, restricted by host and by the exact privileges it needs, never root.

Why Do We Need This?

Granting privileges user by user does not scale. Roles (MySQL 8) bundle privileges so a new analyst gets the right access with one statement.

Real-Time Use

Production accounts must connect over TLS and use strong passwords. Enforce both on the server and per user.
codeExamples:
ALTER USER 'shop_app'@'10.0.%' REQUIRE SSL;                 -- this user may only connect over TLS
SET PERSIST require_secure_transport = ON;                   -- or for everyone (TCP clients)
INSTALL COMPONENT 'file://component_validate_password';
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'validate_password.policy';
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Ssl_cipher';                               -- in a TLS session

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +--------------------------+--------+
-- | Variable_name            | Value  |
-- +--------------------------+--------+
-- | validate_password.policy | MEDIUM |
-- +--------------------------+--------+
-- +---------------+------------------------+
-- | Variable_name | Value                  |
-- +---------------+------------------------+
-- | Ssl_cipher    | TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 |
-- +---------------+------------------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   Internet --> [firewall/VPC] --> app tier --TLS--> MySQL
                                        |            |-- per-app user @ host (least privilege)
                                        |            |-- roles, column grants
   secrets in vault <-------------------+            |-- encryption at rest (keyring)
                                                     +-- audit + backups encrypted

Fresher Notes

  • Security hardening reduces the ways MySQL can be attacked: strong auth, least privilege, encryption, patching and network restrictions.
  • Start with: remove test data and anonymous users, set strong passwords, disable remote root, bind to private addresses.
  • Keep MySQL updated.

Worked Example 1

Disable risky features.

Worked Example 2

Firewall rule (Linux).
codeExamples:
ufw allow from 10.0.1.0/24 to any port 3306 proto tcp
ufw deny 3306

-- OUTPUT:
-- Rule added

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Quick audit.

Practice Exercise 2

Encrypt a table.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Hardening shrinks the attack surface. Layers: network (private subnets, firewall, TLS), authentication (strong unique credentials, no anonymous accounts, secrets in a vault), authorization (least privilege, roles), data protection (encryption in transit and at rest, backup encryption, masking), and operations (patching, auditing, monitoring).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Controls in MySQL: require_secure_transport, TLS versions, account-level REQUIRE SSL, password policy components (validate_password), password expiry and lockout, local_infile=OFF, secure_file_priv, InnoDB tablespace encryption with a keyring, binary log and redo encryption, audit log plugin, and no direct FILE privilege for applications.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: regular audits are cheap SQL. Look for accounts open to any host and for expired or passwordless accounts.
codeExamples:
SELECT user, host, plugin, password_expired
FROM   mysql.user
WHERE  host = '%'
   OR  authentication_string = ''
ORDER  BY user;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-----------+------+-----------------------+------------------+
-- | user      | host | plugin                | password_expired |
-- +-----------+------+-----------------------+------------------+
-- | moropant     | %    | caching_sha2_password | N                |
-- | old_admin | %    | mysql_native_password | N                |   <- review or drop
-- +-----------+------+-----------------------+------------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: broad grants (ALL on *.*) hide risk. Column-level privileges hide sensitive columns such as email or salary from reporting users, at the price of more grants to manage.
codeExamples:
GRANT SELECT (id, name) ON shop.customers TO 'report'@'%';
-- Logged in as report:
SELECT id, name  FROM shop.customers LIMIT 1;           -- allowed
SELECT id, email FROM shop.customers LIMIT 1;           -- email not granted

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+-------+
-- | id | name  |
-- +----+-------+
-- |  1 | Abaji |
-- +----+-------+
-- ERROR 1143 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'report'@'localhost' for column 'email' in table 'customers'

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: encryption at rest needs a keyring (component_keyring_file or a KMS) configured first; without it the ALTER fails. File import/export is limited by secure_file_priv. Neither protects against SQL injection, which only parameterised queries stop.
codeExamples:
SELECT @@secure_file_priv AS file_dir;
ALTER TABLE shop.customers ENCRYPTION = 'Y';              -- needs a keyring component loaded
SELECT table_name, create_options
FROM   information_schema.TABLES
WHERE  table_schema = 'shop' AND table_name = 'customers';

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-----------------------+
-- | file_dir              |
-- +-----------------------+
-- | /var/lib/mysql-files/ |
-- +-----------------------+
-- +------------+-----------------------+
-- | table_name | create_options        |
-- +------------+-----------------------+
-- | customers  | ENCRYPTION='Y'        |
-- +------------+-----------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Layer the defences: network isolation, TLS, least-privilege accounts and roles, secret rotation through a vault, encryption at rest and an audit trail (Enterprise Audit or Percona audit log plugin). Keep MySQL patched, remove anonymous and test accounts, disable LOCAL INFILE unless needed, and test restores of encrypted backups including key recovery.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Enable TLS (require_secure_transport), encrypt data at rest (InnoDB tablespace encryption with a keyring), encrypt backups.
  • Restrict network access with firewalls/security groups; do not expose 3306 publicly.
  • Enable audit logging and password policies; disable local_infile unless needed.

Senior Notes

  • Use a secrets manager and short-lived credentials; rotate regularly.
  • Separate duties: admin, application, read-only and migration accounts; review privileges periodically.
  • Defence in depth: WAF and input validation upstream, parameterized queries, monitoring for anomalies and regular vulnerability scans.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: exposing port 3306 to the internet, shared root credentials, plain-text connections inside "trusted" networks, secrets in source control, unpatched servers, and encryption at rest without key management. Patch regularly and manage keys properly.
codeExamples:
# firewall: only the application subnet
ufw allow from 10.0.1.0/24 to any port 3306 proto tcp
ufw deny 3306
SELECT VERSION();

-- OUTPUT:
-- 8.0.36            (check against the vendor's security advisories monthly)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Security features have costs: TLS adds CPU for handshakes (pools hide this), encryption at rest adds a small overhead, auditing adds I/O. Measure on your workload, and filter audit rules to what you need.

Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world audit routine: list high-risk accounts and privileges, accounts without TLS, recent privilege changes, and failed logins; compare with a baseline stored in version control.

beginner.content:
Introduction

MySQL 8 supports online DDL. ALGORITHM=INSTANT changes only metadata, so adding a column to a billion-row table finishes immediately without blocking reads or writes.

Why Do We Need This?

Always name the algorithm and lock level. Then MySQL refuses an operation that would silently lock or copy the table, instead of surprising you in production.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE orders (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, total DECIMAL(10,2), status VARCHAR(10));

ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX ix_status (status), ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;     -- online, allowed
ALTER TABLE orders MODIFY total DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL, ALGORITHM=INSTANT;          -- not instant-capable

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.04 sec)
-- ERROR 1845 (0A000): ALGORITHM=INSTANT is not supported for this operation. Try ALGORITHM=COPY/INPLACE.

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

For changes that need a rebuild, use expand and contract: add the new column, backfill in small batches, switch the application, then drop the old column in a later release.
codeExamples:
CREATE TABLE users (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(60), email_norm VARCHAR(60) NULL);
INSERT INTO users (id, email) VALUES (1,'A@X.com'),(2,'B@X.com'),(3,'C@X.com');

-- 1) expand: new column added (INSTANT); app starts dual-writing
-- 2) backfill in small id ranges so locks and replication lag stay short
UPDATE users SET email_norm = LOWER(email) WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 1000 AND email_norm IS NULL;
-- repeat for the next range until ROW_COUNT() = 0; 3) switch reads; 4) contract: drop old column later

SELECT id, email_norm FROM users ORDER BY id;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +----+------------+
-- | id | email_norm |
-- +----+------------+
-- |  1 | a@x.com    |
-- |  2 | b@x.com    |
-- |  3 | c@x.com    |
-- +----+------------+

beginner.content:
Diagram

   expand ---------> backfill ----------> switch ----------> contract
   add column        copy in batches      app reads new      drop old column
   (INSTANT)         (small id ranges)    column             (next release)
   old and new code both work at every step => rollback is always possible
   big rebuilds: gh-ost: shadow table + binlog sync + atomic RENAME

Fresher Notes

  • A schema migration changes tables safely. Zero-downtime migrations change the schema without stopping the application.
  • Use versioned migration tools (Flyway, Liquibase) and review every change.
  • The key rule: every step must work with both the old and new application versions.

Worked Example 1

Fail fast instead of blocking.

Worked Example 2

Verify before dropping the old column.
codeExamples:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE new_status <> status_old OR (new_status IS NULL) <> (status_old IS NULL);

-- OUTPUT:
-- COUNT(*)
-- 0

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Online column add.

Practice Exercise 2

Backfill in batches.
codeExamples:
UPDATE orders SET channel = 'WEB' WHERE channel IS NULL AND id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000;
-- repeat per range; pause when Seconds_Behind_Source > 5

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 10000 rows affected

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Zero-downtime migration changes the schema while the application keeps serving requests. The principle is compatibility: at every moment the database schema must work with both the old and the new application version, so you split a change into small steps that are each backward compatible (expand, migrate, contract).

Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Tools: MySQL online DDL (ALGORITHM=INSTANT, INPLACE, LOCK=NONE), gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change for operations that rebuild the table, migration frameworks (Flyway, Liquibase), feature flags to decouple deploy from switch, and shadow writes or dual reads to verify.
codeExamples:
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_channel (channel), ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;
gh-ost --host=db --user=ghost --password=*** --database=shop --table=orders --alter="MODIFY total DECIMAL(14,2) NOT NULL" --max-lag-millis=1500 --chunk-size=1000 --execute

-- OUTPUT:
-- Copy: 41000000/41000000 100.0%; Backlog: 0/1000; Time: 41m12s

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: for operations online DDL cannot do, external tools gh-ost and pt-online-schema-change build a shadow table, copy rows in chunks, keep it in sync, and swap names atomically.
codeExamples:
-- Shell, shown as comments:
--   gh-ost --host=db1 --database=shop --table=orders \
--          --alter="MODIFY total DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL" \
--          --max-lag-millis=1500 --chunk-size=1000 --execute
-- Copy progress is throttled by replica lag, and the cut-over is a quick rename.

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- Copy: 5400000/9500000 56.8%; Applied: 12044; Backlog: 0/1000; Elapsed: 18m; ETA: 14m
-- [info] Done migrating shop.orders

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: even "online" DDL needs a brief metadata lock. A long-running transaction on the table blocks the ALTER, and then every new query queues behind the ALTER. Set a short lock wait and retry.
codeExamples:
SET SESSION lock_wait_timeout = 5;                       -- give up quickly instead of piling up queries
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN flag TINYINT NULL, ALGORITHM=INSTANT;

-- Who is holding or waiting for metadata locks?
SELECT object_name, lock_type, lock_status, owner_thread_id
FROM   performance_schema.metadata_locks
WHERE  object_schema = 'shop' AND object_name = 'orders';

-- OUTPUT: (example when blocked)
-- ERROR 1205 (HY000): Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction
-- +-------------+-------------------+-------------+-----------------+
-- | object_name | lock_type         | lock_status | owner_thread_id |
-- +-------------+-------------------+-------------+-----------------+
-- | orders      | SHARED_READ       | GRANTED     |              88 |   <- the old transaction
-- | orders      | EXCLUSIVE         | PENDING     |              91 |   <- our ALTER waiting
-- +-------------+-------------------+-------------+-----------------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: INSTANT changes are versioned inside the table; MySQL allows a limited number (64 row versions in 8.0.29+) before a rebuild is required. Changing a column type, or the primary key, rebuilds the table.
codeExamples:
SELECT name, total_row_versions
FROM   information_schema.INNODB_TABLES
WHERE  name = 'shop/orders';

-- After the limit is reached, further INSTANT column changes fail until:
ALTER TABLE orders ENGINE = InnoDB, ALGORITHM=INPLACE;       -- rebuild, resets row versions

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-------------+--------------------+
-- | name        | total_row_versions |
-- +-------------+--------------------+
-- | shop/orders |                  3 |
-- +-------------+--------------------+

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Make every migration backward compatible with the previous app version, ship schema and code in separate steps, and put migrations through Flyway or Liquibase in CI against a production-size copy. Check the metadata lock risk (long transactions, replicas lagging) before running, set lock_wait_timeout, and keep a tested rollback.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Expand/contract: add new nullable column or table, deploy code that writes both, backfill in batches, switch reads, then remove old structures later.
  • Use online DDL (ALGORITHM=INPLACE/INSTANT, LOCK=NONE) when possible; otherwise gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change.
  • Avoid long metadata locks: kill or wait for long transactions first; set lock_wait_timeout.

Senior Notes

  • Throttle on replica lag and load; make migrations pausable and resumable.
  • Use feature flags to decouple deploys from data switches, and keep rollback paths until verified.
  • Test on a production-sized clone and rehearse timing and failure modes.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: a plain ALTER that rebuilds a 500 GB table and blocks writes, a long transaction holding a metadata lock that queues all queries behind the ALTER, renaming a column in place while old code still reads the old name, and no tested rollback. Set lock_wait_timeout and check open transactions first.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Control load and lag: throttle backfills and online copies on replica lag and server load, run in off-peak windows, and verify equality (counts, checksums) before switching. Online DDL still needs temporary space and a log of concurrent changes.
codeExamples:
SHOW REPLICA STATUS\G
-- Seconds_Behind_Source: 1   (continue)    ... 12 (pause the backfill)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS mismatches FROM users WHERE name <> full_name OR (name IS NULL) <> (full_name IS NULL);

-- OUTPUT:
-- mismatches
-- 0

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world data type change: widen an INT primary key to BIGINT on a huge table with gh-ost, with foreign keys migrated in lockstep and a rehearsal on a production-sized clone to estimate the duration.
codeExamples:
SELECT table_name, auto_increment, ROUND(auto_increment / 2147483647 * 100, 1) AS pct_of_int_max FROM information_schema.tables WHERE table_name = 'events';
gh-ost --database=shop --table=events --alter="MODIFY id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT" --execute

-- OUTPUT:
-- table_name | auto_increment | pct_of_int_max
-- events     |     1612004113 | 75.1

beginner.content:
Introduction

Scale reads first with replication: a primary takes writes and replicas copy its binary log. GTIDs make attaching a replica simple.

Why Do We Need This?

Replicas must be read-only so an accidental write cannot create divergence. Check the flags and measure lag before sending reads there.
codeExamples:
SET PERSIST read_only = ON;
SET PERSIST super_read_only = ON;                       -- blocks even privileged accounts
SELECT @@read_only AS ro, @@super_read_only AS super_ro, @@hostname AS host;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +----+----------+-----------+
-- | ro | super_ro | host      |
-- +----+----------+-----------+
-- |  1 |        1 | db-rep-01 |
-- +----+----------+-----------+

beginner.content:
Real-Time Use

Applications should not hard-code which server to use. A proxy such as ProxySQL routes writes to the primary and SELECTs to replicas, and also pools connections.
codeExamples:
-- ProxySQL admin interface (it speaks the MySQL protocol)
INSERT INTO mysql_query_rules (rule_id, active, match_digest, destination_hostgroup, apply)
VALUES (10, 1, '^SELECT .* FOR UPDATE', 10, 1),     -- locking reads go to the primary (hostgroup 10)
       (20, 1, '^SELECT',               20, 1);     -- other reads go to the replicas (hostgroup 20)
LOAD MYSQL QUERY RULES TO RUNTIME;
SAVE MYSQL QUERY RULES TO DISK;

-- OUTPUT:
-- Query OK, 2 rows affected (0.00 sec)
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.01 sec)

beginner.content:
Diagram

                  +---------+  writes   +----------+
   App --> Proxy -+ Primary +---------->| binlog   |
            |     +---------+           +----+-----+
            | reads                          | replicate
            +----> Replica 1 <---------------+
            +----> Replica 2 <---------------+
   Failover: Orchestrator / Group Replication promotes a replica; Router/Proxy redirects

Fresher Notes

  • Deployment strategies for MySQL: single primary with replicas, managed cloud services, containers/Kubernetes operators.
  • Scale reads with replicas and caching; scale writes by tuning, bigger hardware (vertical) or sharding (horizontal).
  • Start simple and scale only when measurements show the need.

Worked Example 1

Rolling upgrade sequence.
codeExamples:
-- 1. upgrade replica A, verify replication and queries
-- 2. switchover: promote replica A
CALL mysql.rds_failover_db_instance();   -- or: dba.getCluster().setPrimaryInstance('A')
-- 3. upgrade the old primary and rejoin as a replica

-- OUTPUT:
-- failover completed in 27 seconds

beginner.content:
Worked Example 2

Kubernetes operator (config excerpt).
codeExamples:
apiVersion: mysql.oracle.com/v2
kind: InnoDBCluster
spec: { instances: 3, router: { instances: 2 }, secretName: mysql-root }

-- OUTPUT:
-- innodbcluster/prod created (3 members ONLINE, 2 routers)

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 1

Scaling ladder as a checklist.
codeExamples:
-- 1 queries/indexes  2 cache  3 read replicas  4 partition/archive  5 scale up  6 shard
SELECT step, action FROM scaling_playbook ORDER BY step;

-- OUTPUT:
-- step | action
-- 1    | Fix top 10 queries by total time
-- 2    | Add Redis cache for hot reads
-- 3    | Add 2 read replicas behind Router

beginner.content:
Practice Exercise 2

Shard routing by tenant.

Deep Dive: Internals - How It Works

Scaling follows a ladder from cheap to complex: fix queries and indexes, cache hot reads, add read replicas, partition and archive data, scale the primary up (CPU, RAM, faster storage), and finally shard. Each step buys capacity at a cost in complexity; take the next step only when measurements show the current one is exhausted.
codeExamples:
SELECT step, action FROM ops.scaling_playbook ORDER BY step;

-- OUTPUT:
-- step | action
-- 1    | Fix the top 10 queries by total time (indexes, rewrites)
-- 2    | Add a cache (Redis) for hot reads
-- 3    | Add read replicas behind Router or ProxySQL
-- 4    | Partition and archive old data
-- 5    | Scale up the primary
-- 6    | Shard by tenant or user id

beginner.content:
Deep Dive: Syntax Options & Variants

Deployment options: self-managed on VMs or bare metal with Ansible, containers on Kubernetes with an operator (MySQL Operator for Kubernetes, Percona Operator), and managed services (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL) with automated backups, patching and failover. Pick by team skills, control needs and compliance.

expert.content:
Advantages

Advantages: InnoDB Cluster (Group Replication + MySQL Router) gives automatic failover: if the primary dies, the group elects a new one and the router redirects clients.
codeExamples:
SELECT member_host, member_state, member_role
FROM   performance_schema.replication_group_members
ORDER  BY member_host;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +-------------+--------------+-------------+
-- | member_host | member_state | member_role |
-- +-------------+--------------+-------------+
-- | db1         | ONLINE       | PRIMARY     |
-- | db2         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY   |
-- | db3         | ONLINE       | SECONDARY   |
-- +-------------+--------------+-------------+

expert.content:
Disadvantages

Disadvantages: replication is asynchronous by default, so a replica can be behind and a user may not see their own write. Read-your-writes can be enforced by waiting for the transaction's GTID.
codeExamples:
-- Primary: after the write, remember its GTID (also returned in the OK packet when session tracking is on)
SELECT @@gtid_executed;

-- Replica: wait up to 1 second until that transaction is applied before reading
SELECT WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET('3e11fa47-71ca-11e1-9e33-c80aa9429562:1-100', 1) AS waited;

-- OUTPUT: (example)
-- +--------+
-- | waited |
-- +--------+
-- |      0 |      <- 0 = applied in time, 1 = timeout (fall back to the primary)
-- +--------+

expert.content:
Limitations

Limitations: replicas scale reads only. Write throughput is limited by one primary, so the next step is sharding (splitting data by a key across servers), which complicates joins, transactions and resharding.
codeExamples:
-- Simple range or modulo sharding by user id across 4 servers
SELECT user_id, MOD(user_id, 4) AS shard
FROM  (SELECT 1001 AS user_id UNION ALL SELECT 1002 UNION ALL SELECT 1003 UNION ALL SELECT 1004) u;

-- OUTPUT:
-- +---------+-------+
-- | user_id | shard |
-- +---------+-------+
-- |    1001 |     1 |
-- |    1002 |     2 |
-- |    1003 |     3 |
-- |    1004 |     0 |
-- +---------+-------+
-- Changing 4 to 8 shards moves most rows: use a lookup table or consistent hashing.

expert.content:
Architect's Notes

Scale in order: tune queries and indexes, add caching, add read replicas, partition or archive, then shard only when a single primary cannot take the writes. Prefer managed services or InnoDB Cluster for failover, test failover regularly, and monitor replica lag so the proxy can drop lagging replicas. Choose a shard key that keeps related rows together and avoids hot spots.

Mid-Level Notes

  • Scaling ladder: fix queries and indexes, add caching, add read replicas, partition/archive, scale up the primary, then shard.
  • Connection management with pools and proxies; separate analytics workloads to replicas or a warehouse.
  • Use infrastructure as code and automated failover for repeatable deployments.

Senior Notes

  • Sharding adds complexity: shard key choice, cross-shard queries, transactions and resharding; consider Vitess, TiDB or application-level sharding only when required.
  • Capacity targets and SLOs drive architecture: define RPO/RTO, latency and availability goals first.
  • Blue/green or rolling upgrades with replicas minimize downtime; test failover paths regularly.

Deep Dive: Common Mistakes & Fixes

Mistakes: sharding too early (cross-shard queries and transactions, resharding pain), scaling reads when writes are the bottleneck, ignoring connection limits when adding app instances, stateful pods without proper storage and anti-affinity, and upgrades without rehearsal.

Deep Dive: Performance & Tuning

Sharding needs a shard key with high cardinality that appears in most queries (tenant id, user id), a routing layer (application or Vitess), global id generation, and a plan for cross-shard operations and resharding. Test hot-key skew before committing to a key.
codeExamples:
SELECT CRC32('tenant-42') % 8 AS shard;
SELECT tenant_id, COUNT(*) AS rows_n FROM orders GROUP BY tenant_id ORDER BY rows_n DESC LIMIT 3;

-- OUTPUT:
-- shard
-- 2
-- tenant_id | rows_n
-- 17        | 8120344          (one huge tenant: a poor shard key if it cannot be split)

expert.content:
Deep Dive: Real-World Scenario

Real-world rolling upgrade with minimal downtime: upgrade replicas one at a time, verify, switch the primary to an upgraded replica, upgrade the old primary and rejoin it, with backups and a rollback path at each step.

cheatNotes: CREATE DATABASE dbname - Create a new database
USE dbname - Select database to work with
DROP DATABASE dbname - Permanently delete a database
Client-Server architecture - MySQL server handles requests from client apps/tools
Storage engine - InnoDB (default, supports transactions) vs MyISAM (no transactions)
DDL - CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE - Defines/modifies schema structure
CREATE TABLE - Create a new table with columns and constraints
ALTER TABLE - Add/modify/drop columns or constraints
DROP TABLE - Permanently delete a table and its data
TRUNCATE TABLE - Remove all rows, keep table structure (faster than DELETE)
DML - INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT - Manipulates data inside tables
INSERT INTO - Add new row(s) of data
SELECT * FROM - Query and retrieve data
UPDATE ... SET - Modify existing rows
DELETE FROM - Remove rows (can use WHERE, logged, rollback-able)
DCL - GRANT, REVOKE - Controls user access permissions
TCL - COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT - Controls transactions
COMMIT - Permanently saves transaction changes
ROLLBACK - Undoes changes since last COMMIT
SAVEPOINT - Marks a point within a transaction to rollback to
ACID - Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - transaction guarantees
INT, BIGINT, DECIMAL - Numeric data types
VARCHAR(n), CHAR(n), TEXT - String data types
DATE, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP - Date/time data types
BOOLEAN - Stored as TINYINT(1) internally in MySQL
PRIMARY KEY - Uniquely identifies each row, not null, one per table
FOREIGN KEY - Enforces referential integrity between tables
UNIQUE KEY - Ensures non-NULL values are distinct; MySQL permits multiple NULLs
Composite key - Primary key made of two or more columns
NOT NULL - Column cannot store NULL values
DEFAULT - Sets a default value when none is provided
AUTO_INCREMENT - Automatically generates sequential numeric values
CHECK - Validates values against a condition
WHERE - Filters rows before grouping
GROUP BY - Groups rows sharing a column value
HAVING - Filters groups after aggregation (unlike WHERE)
ORDER BY - Sorts result set (ASC default, or DESC)
LIMIT - Restricts number of rows returned
DISTINCT - Removes duplicate rows from result
INNER JOIN - Returns only matching rows from both tables
LEFT JOIN - All rows from left table + matched rows from right
RIGHT JOIN - All rows from right table + matched rows from left
FULL JOIN - All rows from both tables (emulated in MySQL via UNION)
SELF JOIN - Table joined with itself using aliases
CROSS JOIN - Cartesian product of two tables
COUNT() - Counts number of rows
SUM() - Adds up numeric values
AVG() - Calculates average value
MIN()/MAX() - Finds smallest/largest value
Subquery - Query nested inside another query (WHERE/FROM/SELECT)
Correlated subquery - Inner query depends on outer query per row
INDEX - Speeds up SELECT queries at cost of slower writes
Composite index - Index on multiple columns, order matters
1NF - Atomic column values, no repeating groups
2NF - 1NF + no partial dependency on composite key
3NF - 2NF + no transitive dependency on non-key columns
VIEW - Virtual table based on a stored SELECT query
Stored Procedure - Precompiled, reusable SQL routine
Trigger - Auto-executes on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE events
Nth highest salary - Use LIMIT with OFFSET or subquery with DISTINCT
Find duplicates - GROUP BY column HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
Second highest without LIMIT - Correlated subquery with COUNT(DISTINCT)
